articles.title: Global pension trends for 2027: The new retirement paradigm - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
The pensions industry is shifting to further focus on delivering sustainable, long-term retirement income and managing longevity risks

Investment strategies are evolving towards total portfolio management, while scale is becoming increasingly important

Governance, sustainability and AI are helping drive more resilient and outcome-focused retirement systems

The global pensions industry is entering a new phase of development. Having spent much of the past two decades focused on pension accumulation, deficit recovery and investment returns, attention is shifting towards the delivery of sustainable retirement income and the management of retirement risks.

Several structural trends are converging. Pension liabilities continue to migrate towards insurers and specialist consolidators through buyouts, longevity hedging and other risk-transfer solutions, while collective risk-sharing arrangements are re-emerging to address the limitations of purely individual retirement systems.

Scale is becoming increasingly important as pension providers seek access to private markets, technology and retirement-income capabilities. At the same time investment strategies are evolving towards whole-portfolio management, supported by greater exposure to private assets and renewed interest in fixed income.

Meanwhile, stronger governance, artificial intelligence and financially material sustainability practices1 are enhancing decision-making and risk management. Together, these developments are creating a more integrated, resilient and outcome-focused retirement system. Below, we outline the areas which we believe will dominate the pension landscape in the coming year.

1: Risk transfer and risk pooling

A defining theme of the 2027 pensions market will, in our view, be the simultaneous growth of risk transfer and risk pooling.

Improved funding levels, supported by the higher interest rates that we have seen between 2022 and 2025, have enabled many defined benefit schemes to move beyond deficit repair and focus on endgame strategies.

Buy-ins, buyouts, longevity swaps, superfund2 transfers and run-on approaches are becoming increasingly common, with insurers assuming a larger role as pension liabilities migrate from corporate balance sheets.

The debate, however, is no longer whether risks should be transferred, but which risks should be retained. For some well-funded schemes, selective retention of liabilities through run-on strategies may offer greater value than full insurance transactions.

At the same time, policymakers are revisiting collective approaches to retirement provision. Collective defined contribution schemes, target benefit plans, shared-risk models and longevity pools are attracting renewed interest as mechanisms for sharing investment and longevity risks without recreating traditional defined benefit guarantees.

Together, these developments reflect a more sophisticated approach to retirement risk allocation.

2: Scale, consolidation and the retirement ecosystem

Retirement systems are becoming increasingly concentrated and interconnected.

As pension risk transfers accelerate and retirement income solutions expand, insurers, pension funds and asset managers are operating within a more integrated retirement ecosystem. Scale is emerging as a key competitive advantage, providing access to private markets, technology, internal expertise and lower operating costs.

This is driving consolidation across UK defined contribution schemes, Australian superannuation funds, Canadian pension plans and European pension institutions. By 2027, smaller schemes are likely to face growing pressure to demonstrate superior member outcomes or seek consolidation.

3: The retirement income revolution

After decades of focusing on accumulation, the industry is turning its attention towards retirement income.

Across developed markets, policymakers increasingly recognise that successful saving does not guarantee successful retirement outcomes. Individuals are expected to manage investment risk, inflation, longevity and withdrawal decisions simultaneously, despite limited expertise.

As a result, managed retirement income solutions, deferred annuities, lifetime-income products, longevity pools and blended drawdown structures are gaining momentum. The next major battleground for pension providers will be retirement-income delivery rather than accumulation – especially for the emerging Asian middle class that has benefitted from a very rapid asset accumulation.

4: Asset allocation

Pension investing continues to evolve from asset-class optimisation towards whole-portfolio management.

The Total Portfolio Approach (TPA), where instead of managing individual asset classes the portfolio is managed as a whole, is gaining wider adoption as asset owners focus on long-term outcomes, governance efficiency and portfolio resilience. At the same time, higher interest rates have restored fixed income as a potentially meaningful source of income, diversification and liability matching.

Governments are also encouraging pension funds to direct their capital to support infrastructure, energy transition, housing and digital development. The challenge for trustees is balancing these opportunities with fiduciary obligations and member outcomes.

5: Asset classes

Private markets are now core portfolio holdings rather than specialist allocations.

Infrastructure, private credit and real assets continue to attract capital because of their potential for long-duration cash flows, diversification benefits and inflation protection. Meanwhile, investors are reassessing the role of concentrated equity portfolios as a means of improving stewardship, transparency and customisation, although concerns regarding concentration risk remain.

The return of attractive bond yields has also improved the investment case for fixed income and strengthened retirement income and insurance solutions.

6: Risk management

Risk management is becoming broader and more forward-looking. Investors are focusing less on short-term volatility and more on resilience across liquidity, valuation, climate and demographic risks. As private market allocations expand, governance, liquidity management and valuation discipline are becoming increasingly important.

Sustainability considerations are also being assessed primarily through a financial materiality lens, with climate, nature-related and transition risks integrated into portfolio construction and oversight. At the same time, longevity risk is re-emerging as populations age and retirement periods lengthen.

7: Governance, AI and sustainability

Governance is becoming one of the most important differentiators among pension institutions. Competitive advantage increasingly stems from decision-making quality, oversight and execution rather than investment complexity alone.

AI is beginning to reshape pension administration, member engagement, actuarial modelling, portfolio construction and risk management. Here, its greatest long-term potential could lie in delivering more personalised retirement solutions tailored to individual circumstances and objectives.

Sustainability is also entering a more pragmatic phase. Rather than focusing primarily on disclosure and compliance, pension investors are increasingly evaluating climate, biodiversity, human capital and governance factors for their impact on long-term cash flows, liabilities and portfolio resilience.

The combination of strong governance, AI-enabled decision making and financially material sustainability practices is likely to distinguish the leading pension organisations of the future.

The emergence of a new pensions era

As such, the defining feature of the pension landscape in 2027 is the convergence of multiple structural transformations.

Risk transfer is accelerating, collective risk-sharing is re-emerging, retirement-income solutions are becoming central, and investment strategies are evolving towards more integrated portfolio management. At the same time, scale, governance, technology and sustainability are reshaping how pension institutions operate.

The most successful organisations will recognise these developments not as isolated trends, but as elements of a broader transition.

The industry’s objective is no longer simply to maximise pension wealth. Increasingly, it is to deliver resilient, inflation-aware and lifelong retirement income. That shift is likely to define the global pensions market for the remainder of the decade.

[1] Financially material sustainability refers to the sustainability and environmental, social and governance factors that could have direct consequences for a company’s financial performance. It seeks to identify those issues, such as regulatory risks, climate-related costs, or supply chain disruptions, which could influence a company’s key financial metrics.

[2] Pension superfunds are pension scheme consolidators which aim to make a profit and are a relatively new development in the UK. When a pension scheme transfers to a UK superfund, the employer no longer guarantees the pension payments. Instead, the superfund takes over, using a capital buffer (assets held in reserve) to provide security. If the scheme struggles to pay pensions in the future, the capital buffer can be used. The capital buffer might come from investors looking for profit, payments from the employer who wants to end their guarantee, or existing surplus funds within the pension scheme (Source: Pensions: defined benefit superfunds – House of Commons Library).

}Source: GettyCommentaryStrategic EuropeStarlink Should Make Europe Act StrategicallyToo many national interests, too many EU institutions, and too little political will are preventing Europe from acting in its own best interests.Link CopiedBy Judy DempseyPublished on Nov 17, 2026Surely, now is the time for the EU to grasp how dependence on the Starlink satellite system threatens the bloc’s security.The evidence of this dependence is clear. Over the past six weeks, the billionaire SpaceX founder Elon Musk has twice used his influence at Starlink’s parent company to reduce the speed of the satellite system used by Ukraine to intercept Russian drones.Restricting Starshield, the Starlink service funded by the Pentagon, has left Ukraine vulnerable. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the speed limits were “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine.” According to Ukrainian officials, that restricted range was U.S. President Donald Trump’s way of putting pressure on Zelensky to make concessions in peace talks.The country’s dependence on Starlink has lessons and implications for Europe. They are dependent on the system, just as they are on the United States’ nuclear security umbrella. They also rely on a plethora of American military systems, such as Patriot missiles, which, in turn, Ukraine desperately needs to protect civilians from Russia’s incessant bombing of cities, towns, and critical infrastructure. Despite promises made several months ago to supply them, as well as offers by Europe to buy and deliver them to Kyiv, Trump has refused both.The upshot is that Ukraine no longer has any illusions about Trump’s unequivocal support for Russian President Vladimir Putin. Neither have European governments. Yet, the problem for the EU is that a combination of national interests and a reactive decisionmaking culture is preventing the bloc as a whole from acting strategically toward Musk, Trump, and Putin. Acting strategically means having a critical collective outlook and goal that takes precedence over national interests.European leaders realize that Starlink’s pressure on Ukraine means they need a satellite system of their own. They don’t want their dependence on the United States to be weaponized, which is what is happening in Ukraine. Imagine if Starlink were to be restricted while a NATO ally was under attack. The Europeans also know they face a tough fight with the White House if, when the spectrum coverage arrangements for satellite-to-device internet communication come up for renewal, they choose European companies—U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder warned of a “devastating” retaliation.Ironically, that intervention might be the spur for the bloc to build up its own capabilities in critical technologies.Maybe.Several European companies are either working together or competing with each other to develop their own equivalent of Starlink. They need scale, finance, know-how, speed, collaboration, and strong political will from the EU. All are lacking. If they could harness all six, maybe Europe could reduce its dependence on the United States over time.That’s a big if. The union has a history of national interests getting in the way when Brussels wants to act big and creatively.Remember Galileo, the EU’s satellite navigation system? It was first proposed back in 1981! After years of haggling, endless committees, member states quarrelling over which companies would build what, and spiraling costs, the first part of the system became operable in 2011. The second part followed a few years later. A European Parliament report was blunt in its assessment: “[There were] divisions between companies but also between member states, which intervened in the interest of their national industries and held up decisions.”Security and defense is another example. In June 2025, France and Germany abandoned the €100 billion ($109 billion) Future Combat Air System, a manned fighter jet designed to replace France’s Rafale jets and the Eurofighter Typhoon fleets. The collapse of the venture followed bitter disputes between France’s Dassault Aviation and Airbus over leadership, the distribution of the costs, and the division of labor.Infighting also hampered the Eurofighter. The consortium, which consists of Italy, Germany, Spain, and the UK, has been plagued by export vetoes among many other issues. These projects were supposed to have given Europe its own military and defense capability.These disputes continue even when Europe is caught between two antagonist pressures. On the one hand is the political and economic pressure by the Trump administration, which has disdain for the EU and NATO. On the other, Europe faces Russian hybrid attacks: cybersecurity threats, the explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport, and threats to prominent business executives, not to mention support for anti-Ukraine and anti-immigration political parties throughout Europe.These pressures mean that the continent can no longer rely on the United States for its security or as a defender of democratic values. Trump’s stance plays into Putin’s hands. His agenda is to weaken and divide NATO and the EU. The question is how Europe should respond—strategically. That is why a European alternative to Starlink is a strategic necessity to wean the continent off the negative aspects of American dependence. But any European alternative to Starlink must avoid becoming embroiled in national interests.All of this is a big if. It’s about turning these initiatives into a competitive European industry—and response—instead of a collection of national and protected projects. So much is at stake. So much rides on the ability of member states to see the strategic logic in pulling together. Don’t bank on it.Get more news and analysis fromStrategic EuropeSubscribe to Strategic Europe, delivered every Tuesday and Thursday!About the AuthorJudy DempseyNonresident Senior Fellow, Carnegie EuropeJudy Dempsey is a nonresident senior fellow at Carnegie EuropeRecent WorkCommentaryGermany’s Shattered ConsensusJudy DempseyCommentaryEurope Needs to Hear What America is SayingJudy DempseyEUForeign PolicyDefenseTechnologyEuropeUnited StatesUkraineCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from Strategic EuropeCommentaryStrategic EuropeHow Realistic Is Peace in Ukraine?Russia’s maximalist demands are preventing any serious attempt at ending the war in Ukraine. To make peace a realistic prospect, Putin must recognize that diplomacy is a two-way street.Kadri LiikCommentaryStrategic EuropeTaking the Pulse: Can Europe Fund Ukraine Without Russian Assets?A sizeable funding shortfall looks increasingly likely to hit Ukraine in 2027. Can the Europeans, with their strained budgets and economies, come up with the cash without seizing frozen Russian assets?Rym Momtaz, ed.CommentaryStrategic EuropeNo, A Democratic Congress Won’t Save EuropeA blue wave has swept over the U.S. midterms, with Democrats regaining control of both houses of Congress. But Europeans hoping for a return to business as usual should think again.Rym MomtazCommentaryStrategic EuropeIs Russia Winning the Perception War in Germany?In Germany, competing perceptions of Russia are highlighting a tension between public opinion and government policy. articles.title: Technology investment outlook 2027: AI moves from promise to proof - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
AI shifts from promise to measurable return on investment: 2027 should see AI move further from experimentation toward monetisation, productivity gains, and demonstrable returns, particularly across cloud and enterprise applications

AI infrastructure spending remains strong: Demand for GPUs, custom silicon, optical networking, data center power, and other infrastructure should remain robust, with supply constraints persisting in several areas

A constructive outlook balanced by rising risks: Technology valuations remain broadly supportive, but higher interest rates, debt-financed AI capex, geopolitics, and AI safety concerns could create periods of volatility

After several years of rapid innovation, the year ahead could mark the point at which artificial intelligence’s economic impact becomes increasingly visible.

The conversation is likely to shift from technological possibility to real-world adoption, monetisation, and return on investment.

Personal AI agents, enterprise automation, physical AI, and cloud infrastructure are all moving from experimentation toward broader deployment at scale.

The companies best positioned to monetise new products and distribute this innovation should be the primary beneficiaries of the AI cycle’s next phase.

Personal AI agents go mainstream

2027 could be the year that agentic AI transitions from an emerging technology to a mainstream consumer product.

Rather than simply answering questions, personal AI agents will increasingly perform tasks on a user’s behalf. Common use cases could include prioritising email messages, booking travel, scheduling appointments, managing subscriptions, and coordinating household services.

Improvements in reasoning, memory, and tool use should allow these agents to operate across applications and websites with minimal user input.

Adoption will likely be driven less by model breakthroughs and more by convenience, reliability, and integration into products consumers already use. Over time, personal AI agents could become a new interface layer for the internet.

AI moves into core enterprise workflows

Enterprise AI use cases will expand beyond coding assistants and customer service into agentic capabilities that augment core business workflows.

Organisations will increasingly deploy AI across functions such as finance, sales, human resources, and supply chain management. The next stage of the AI cycle will be defined not only by model capabilities, but also by the ability to deliver useful intelligence at an attractive cost.

Smaller models are likely to handle routine tasks, while larger models are reserved for more complex reasoning. Increasingly sophisticated orchestration software will manage these interactions behind the scenes, making AI more seamless for end users.

As adoption broadens, the focus should shift from experimentation to measurable productivity gains.

AI safety and cybersecurity remain top of mind

The AI safety debate will continue in 2027. Many industry experts fear a major cybersecurity breach or biohazard attack by bad actors using AI models. It is increasingly clear that cybersecurity, governance, and observability software will play a critical role going forward.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and others have advocated for deterministic supervisory software monitoring each AI model to build in policy guardrails for governance, compliance, and security.1

Other suggestions by industry experts include third-party auditing of training workloads and independent testing of models before public release. There is a growing consensus that governments need to regulate the industry, but also significant disagreement over how such regulations should be formulated.

Physical AI and edge computing build momentum

Next year could be a pivotal period for physical AI and edge computing – where data processing and storage is physically closer to the data source – as advances in AI begin translating into real-world automation.

Adoption is likely to accelerate first in structured environments such as factories, warehouses, and logistics networks, where intelligent robots can improve productivity and help address labour shortages.

Likewise, AI-enabled wearables, such as smart glasses, could emerge as an important new computing category by bringing contextual intelligence into everyday activities.

Humanoid robots may also make meaningful technical progress, but large-scale adoption likely remains several years away. Taken together, 2027 may represent the beginning of a new phase in which AI expands beyond software and digital workflows into the physical world.

Sector outlook

Semiconductors and hardware: Demand continues to exceed supply

We expect AI infrastructure demand to continue to outpace supply through 2027. Demand remains strong with hyperscalers and other customers providing suppliers with orders stretching through 2027 and beyond.

Optical components, semiconductors, and power for data centres will continue to be key constraints on the supply side. Leadership will continue to diversify as investors look for the next area of investment to support training and inferencing applications, especially as model innovations open new opportunities.

One key risk to monitor is access to capital at an economic cost, especially in a rising interest rate environment. It is unreasonable to expect the buildout to proceed in a linear fashion, but it is hard to know the timing of any digestion period or interruption in the AI infrastructure race.

Given the magnitude of outperformance of technology infrastructure names particularly during the first half of 2026, it would not be surprising to see continued volatility through 2027 as investors debate the relative merits of software versus semiconductors.

Cloud service providers: Return on investment comes into focus.

2027 could be the year that cloud service providers prove the return on investment for their unprecedented AI infrastructure spending.

Cloud service providers are uniquely positioned to monetise AI given their unmatched data centre footprints, access to graphics processing units, rapidly expanding custom silicon programmes, and highly profitable core businesses which support funding needs.

Investors should become more constructive as cloud revenue growth accelerates, capex growth moderates, and cloud margins remain healthy. Together, these factors could provide compelling evidence that AI infrastructure can generate attractive long-term returns rather than simply support an arms race.

Software: Careful navigation required

The software sector will require increasingly careful navigation as investors distinguish between AI beneficiaries and companies vulnerable to AI disruption.

Broad-based scepticism toward application software should give way to a more nuanced assessment of which companies can leverage AI to expand their total addressable markets and strengthen their competitive positions.

While AI monetisation is likely to accelerate across the industry, it will still represent a relatively small portion of revenue for most software companies in 2027.

We remain constructive on cybersecurity and infrastructure software, where AI is driving both increased demand and new product opportunities, though we are mindful of premium valuations given strong performance in 2026.

The first wave of frontier AI IPOs arrives

The potential public listings of leading frontier AI labs in the year ahead would mark a significant milestone. The initial public offerings would likely represent some of the most notable technology debuts since the emergence of the cloud service providers.

Beyond expanding the investable universe, these listings could provide investors with direct pure play exposure to the development and monetisation of frontier AI models, potentially attracting significant capital flows and reshaping technology indices.

More broadly, due to public market scrutiny, these companies will be under pressure to demonstrate sustainable revenue growth, scalability, margins, and returns on capital.

Valuations bolster environment

Valuations across much of the technology sector remain supportive, providing a constructive backdrop for investors.

While select AI beneficiaries continue to command premium multiples, many software, semiconductor, and hardware names trade at levels that appear reasonable relative to their growth and earnings outlooks.

The average forward price-to-earnings ratio for the semiconductor industry has declined to below 19 times (as of mid-October 2026) compared to the five-year average closer to 25, and the software sector’s enterprise value-to-sales ratio is moderately below its long-term average.2

Semiconductor stock valuations look reasonable given earnings momentum. In the semiconductor industry group, valuations are compelling, but for companies in commodity markets for standardised components like memory chips, investors are hesitant to put high multiples on what could prove to be peak earnings expectations

Valuations remain compelling for select application software companies that can monetise AI and defend their competitive positions against disruption.Outside of application software,widely perceived AI beneficiaries including certain data management and cybersecurity companies now command premium valuation multiples. Meanwhile, the cloud service providers appear undervalued, particularly if further evidence emerges that AI investments are generating attractive returns

Select hardware stocks are undervalued. Optical and other data centre infrastructure stocks have pulled back on concerns about the sustainability of supply shortages and of demand, and perhaps in relation to the prospects of a Democratic sweep in the US (which we believe would not in and of itself have a major impact on data centre approvals); select stocks look compelling

The long-term opportunity created by AI remains significant, but investors should remain mindful of several risks that could slow adoption or pressure valuations.While these risks are worth monitoring, the balance of evidence continues to support a constructive outlook for the sector. Key risks include, but are not limited to:

High interest rates could result in valuation pressure for long duration assets and could raise the cost of capital for financing AI infrastructure

The geopolitical environment is uncertain and makes it more likely that there will be competing AI ecosystems, inefficient supply chains, and physical risks to AI infrastructure

AI safety concerns could slow development, particularly if there is a cyber or biological attack by a bad actor, and/ or if there are more breaches by AI agents going rogue

Financing challenges could slow AI investment, especially as a higher portion of capex is being debt financed

Trends could give rise to the formation of an AI bubble, including circular relationships, increasing use of debt financing and off-balance sheet vehicles, lax regulation, private market valuations moving into the public markets with IPOs, and rising interest rates (which could pop a bubble)

However, mitigating factors include investor scepticism, encouraging AI adoption trends in consumer and enterprise applications which demonstrate paths to positive return on investment, and reasonable valuations that are not yet at dotcom bubble levels.

The next stage

The next phase of the AI cycle is likely to be defined less by technological breakthroughs and more by execution, adoption, and monetisation.

Companies that can translate AI investment into sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on capital should emerge as the long-term winners.

While periodic volatility is inevitable, we remain constructive on the technology sector and the opportunities created by the ongoing AI transformation.

[1] The choices we make about AI now are critical | Bill Gates / Dario Amodei — We Must Pace the Frontier / https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/a-warning-about-model-welfare

[2] Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management, FactSet.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesOutlooksWill the UK Economy Beat Expectations Again in 2027?Nov 17, 2026Share Goldman Sachs Research forecasts that the UK economy will expand 1.4% in 2027 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter), above the consensus of analyst estimates. Growth is expected to slow in the near term before picking up again in the second half of the year amid strong investment, improving productivity, and declining energy prices. Our economists forecast that the Bank of England will hike once more in February 2027; markets are pricing three more hikes. Strong business investment, improving productivity, and AI adoption could provide boosts in the near term.The UK economy faces a series of headwinds in the coming months after outperforming economists’ expectations in 2026. But Goldman Sachs Research expects GDP growth to accelerate again in late 2027, boosted by strong investment, improving productivity, and declining energy prices, producing another year of above-consensus growth.
What is the outlook for UK GDP growth in 2027?

Our economists forecast that UK real GDP will grow 1.4% in 2027 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter). That’s down from an estimated 1.6% this year, but above the 1.2% consensus of economists’ expectations.
“We see compelling reasons to be constructive on the economic outlook for 2027,” write Senior UK Economist James Moberly and Chief European Economist Jari Stehn.

The UK economy proved “surprisingly resilient” in 2026, Moberly and Stehn write. Growth accelerated despite the energy shock keeping inflation elevated and causing the Bank of England to pivot from cutting to hiking. The labor market also showed signs of improvement, with unemployment falling and employment growth indicators ticking up. The new government also navigated a challenging fiscal backdrop to maintain its path of consolidation.
Why the UK economy is predicted to slow over the coming months

“The coming quarters are likely to prove more challenging in several respects,” Moberly and Stehn write. They expect growth to slow in the near term, running slightly below trend in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first half of 2027.
The impact of the energy shock on household finances is likely to build over the winter, with weak real disposable income growth resulting in a slowdown in consumer spending. Our economists anticipate that rising inflation will push the BoE to hike rates by 25 basis points to 4.25%, probably in February.
Tighter financial conditions should also weigh on growth as mortgages are refixed at higher rates. Fiscal policy is likely to have a more negative impact on economic growth in 2027 given that current plans imply a larger consolidation than in 2026.
Our economists also see signs that the labor market could weaken gradually. They project that the unemployment rate will rise from 4.7% to 5% by the middle of 2027.
Why Britain’s economy could keep outperforming estimates

“Despite these cyclical challenges, we see several reasons to be more constructive on the UK’s economic prospects for 2027,” Moberly and Stehn write.
Some of the factors boosting growth in 2026 look like long-term advantages for the UK. Strong business investment has partly reflected rising capex in information and communications and in utilities, both of which look likely to continue. This should in turn support continued growth in technology services output, where demand has increased on the back of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.
The productivity trend also appears to be improving as growth in output per worker has increased significantly.
At the same time, the worst of Brexit’s economic impact has probably passed, and survey data indicates that early gains from AI adoption could have started to modestly boost growth.
“These factors, together with declines in energy prices, should mean that growth reaccelerates through the second half of next year,” Moberly and Stehn write.
They also expect labor cost inflation to be well below the levels seen in recent years as a looser labor market reduces the extent to which higher headline inflation passes through into wage pressures. This should help to “keep a lid” on underlying services inflation despite pressures from higher food and energy prices, they write.
What is the outlook for BoE rate hikes in 2027?

Given their expectations of moderate second-round inflation effects from the energy shock, our economists think that the BoE will hike less than the market is pricing.
“After tightening policy in February, we expect the Monetary Policy Committee to keep Bank Rate at 4.25% for the rest of the year, whereas the market implies two further rate increases,” they write.
The UK government is also likely to make more progress on reducing its deficit in 2027, with a significant reduction planned.
“Further consolidation should mean that the UK continues to compare favorably to other advanced economies in terms of reducing borrowing,” Moberly and Stehn write. This could in turn bring down borrowing costs.
While next year’s Spending Review by the Office for Budget Responsibility poses a challenge for the government, it is possible that changes in the economic forecast could help the chancellor, Moberly and Stehn observe. The OBR’s wage growth forecast looks low, they write, and an upgrade would boost the tax revenues projection, increasing fiscal space.
What’s the long-term outlook for the UK economy?

“We also see scope for sentiment around the UK’s longer-term economic prospects to improve,” Moberly and Stehn write.
The UK’s specialization in high-value-added services makes it well-placed to benefit from AI adoption. Estimates from the International Monetary Fund indicate that a relatively high share of the UK workforce is exposed to AI, with a particularly large number of workers in roles that may see productivity gains but are less likely to be replaced by the technology. Survey data also suggests that firms expect adoption to result in sizable productivity increases in the coming years.
And the UK is well-positioned in several high-growth innovative industries, including a world-leading position in life sciences such as pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medical technology, and genomics, Moberly and Stehn note.
Closer ties with the EU could provide another potential boost. The prime minister has indicated that he will outline options for how the relationship might develop following the upcoming summit. Those options might include a customs union, rejoining the single market, or even a second referendum on membership. Any reset would require negotiation, trade-offs, and time, Stehn and Moberly observe. “But it could bring significant economic upside, so signals towards improved trading links could start to lift optimism on the UK’s growth prospects,” they add.

articles.title: When productivity booms, do interest rates rise?
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 20, 2026
When productivity booms, do interest rates rise?
Antoine Lepetit, and David Miller1
1. Introduction

Long-term interest rates have risen sharply since the COVID period. Concurrently, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have raised the prospect of a sustained increase in productivity growth. As many observers have noted, standard macroeconomic theory predicts that expectations of faster productivity growth should push interest rates higher. Expecting higher future incomes, households may boost current spending and reduce their saving rate. Simultaneously, firms anticipating higher returns on capital may front-load investment. Together, the combination of lower saving supply and higher investment demand should exert upward pressure on interest rates.

In this Note, we estimate a vector autoregressive (VAR) model to empirically examine the link between productivity growth and interest rates. Contrary to standard theory, we find that shocks that lead to a persistent increase in total factor productivity (TFP) growth, and that are foreseen by the public, result in declines in both the 10-year Treasury yield and the expected real short rate 5-to-10 years ahead—a common measure of r*, the long-run equilibrium level of the real federal funds rate (see Figure 1). The decline in the 10-year Treasury yield reflects two offsetting forces: a modest temporary rise in short-run interest rates and a larger fall in the term premium. It follows that, from the model's point of view, the recent rise in interest rates cannot be explained by anticipated higher productivity growth.

Figure 1. Impulse responses of selected variables to a TFP news shock

Accessible version

Previous empirical work generally finds little correlation between productivity (or output) growth and interest rates (Lunsford and West, 2019; Hamilton et al, 2016). Correlational studies cannot isolate the underlying causal mechanisms. To uncover the causal relationship between productivity growth and interest rates, we employ a structural VAR model and identify a shock containing advance information about the future path of TFP—that is, a TFP news shock—using the approach of Barsky and Sims (2011) and Francis et al. (2014). In part, our results are informed by the only episode of a large, sustained change in productivity growth in recent history: the tech boom of the late 1990s. Although our methodological approach differs, our findings align closely with recent studies that achieve causal identification using high-frequency data and show that news surrounding the release of major AI models is associated with declines in r* (Christensen and Rudebusch, 2026; Willens, Cavallo, and Beaudry, 2026).

2. TFP booms and long-term interest rates

We estimate several Bayesian VARs over the 1990-2019 sample period.2 All models include five core quarterly series, each expressed in logarithms: (1) utilization-adjusted TFP (Fernald, 2012); (2) real per capita GDP; (3) real per capital business fixed investment; (4) real per capita consumption; and (5) the S&P 500 deflated by the consumer price index (CPI). To this core specification, we add the following auxiliary variables one at a time: (1) the nominal 10-year Treasury yield; (2) the real 10-year Treasury yield from the term structure model of D'Amico, Kim, and Wei (2018), as updated in Kim, Walsh, and Wei (2019);3 (3) the real federal funds rate, measured as the effective federal funds rate minus CPI inflation; and (4) the expectations and term premium components of the D'Amico, Kim, and Wei (2018) real 10-year yield. We identify a TFP news shock using the max-share approach, which isolates the structural shock that best explains future movements in TFP at a 10-year horizon.4

Figure 2 plots the impulse responses of the core VAR variables to an identified TFP news shock. The largest effects on the level of TFP materialize several years after the initial shock. This trajectory is consistent with the gradual diffusion of productivity-enhancing technologies and suggests that the productivity gains may have been anticipated by economic agents well in advance. Consistent with this view, and the theory laid out at the beginning of this Note, investment and the stock market rise immediately, long before the bulk of the TFP increase occurs.

Figure 2. Impulse responses of core variables to an identified technology shock

Accessible version

Figure 3 shows the impulse responses of the auxiliary variables.5 Our main finding is that the nominal 10-year Treasury yield falls in response to a positive TFP news shock that generates persistently higher TFP growth over the subsequent decade. The second panel demonstrates that this result is not driven by a fall in inflation expectations as the real 10-year Treasury yield exhibits a similar behavior. The final two panels decompose the real 10-year yield into its expectations and term premium components. Following the shock, the expectations component rises briefly—mirroring the path of the real federal funds rate in the third panel—but this temporary increase is more than offset by a large, persistent decline in the real term premium.

Figure 3. Impulse responses of auxiliary variables to an identified technology shock

Accessible version

Several channels could account for this statistically significant decline in the term premium. Most directly, the term premium reflects a countercyclical market price of risk, which falls as the productivity shock boosts output and consumption (Figure 2). When the economy does well, investors demand less extra compensation for tying up their money in long-term Treasuries. In addition, because output expands without a corresponding rise in inflation, uncertainty surrounding the future path of monetary policy diminishes, increasing demand for longer-term bonds. Finally, the positive economic effects extend to the fiscal outlook. By raising real output and the tax base, the productivity shock expands fiscal space, which is associated with lower long-term yields and term premia (Plante et al., 2025).

3. The recent rise in long-term yields through the lens of the model

Next, we evaluate whether news about future TFP can explain the recent path of long-term Treasury yields. Because our focus is on productivity expectations fueled by advances in AI and public awareness of generative AI was limited prior to the release of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022 (Christensen and Rudebusch, 2026), we begin our evaluation period in 2022Q4.

Figure 4 plots an eight-quarter moving average of the model's estimated TFP news shocks over the 2022Q4-2026Q2 period. Reflecting the 2022 equity market downturn, the shock realizations are initially negative. Over the subsequent three years, however, the model estimates that we have repeatedly received good news about future TFP. This shift is consistent with the view that rapid developments in AI technology have brightened prospects for future productivity growth.

Figure 4. Estimated TFP news shocks

Accessible version

Figure 5 shows a historical decomposition of the real 10-year Treasury yield, tracing the contribution of these TFP news shocks since 2022Q4. The black line represents the VAR forecast error. In the absence of shocks, the model projected that long-term rates would revert toward their low pre-pandemic baseline; consequently, the forecast error widens to 200 basis points by early 2026, even though the actual yield increased by only 90 basis points between 2022Q3 and 2026Q2. The blue line depicts the contribution of TFP news shocks to this forecast error. While this contribution is initially positive—as negative news in 2022 pushed yields higher—it steadily declines thereafter as the positive shocks of 2023-2025 exert downward pressure on rates. By 2026Q2, the net contribution is near zero or slightly negative, suggesting that news about future TFP arriving since the launch of ChatGPT has had virtually no cumulative impact on current 10-year Treasury yields.

Figure 5. VAR forecast error for real 10-year Treasury yields

Accessible version

4. TFP booms and r*

We also examine the behavior of the longer-run equilibrium real interest rate, r*, defined here as the real federal funds consistent with the economy operating at potential once the transitory effects of shocks have abated. Because r* is unobserved, researchers often proxy for it using the expected real short rate 5-to-10 years ahead (e.g., Christensen and Rudebusch, 2019; Cho and Williams, 2025). Stripped of the term premium, this measure captures market expectations of where the real policy rate will settle once cyclical fluctuations have dissipated. Although standard macroeconomic theory predicts that r* should rise in response to an anticipated, persistent increase in TFP growth, Figure 6 shows that the expected real short rate 5-to-10 years ahead actually declines following a positive TFP news shocks. As the shock also leads to higher growth (Figure 2), this result calls into question approaches that estimate r* by enforcing a tight relationship between r* and the medium-run growth rate of the economy, such as Laubach and Williams (2003).

Figure 6. Impulse response of the expected real short rate 5-to-10 years ahead

Accessible version

5. Conclusion

In this Note, we show that positive shocks to expectations of future productivity growth lower both long-term Treasury yields and a common measure of r*. These findings present a challenge to textbook macroeconomic theory and suggest that modelling the term premium's reaction to shocks is of first-order importance. Applying our framework to the post-2022 period, we find that AI-related optimism about future productivity cannot explain the recent surge in long-term Treasury yields, pointing instead to other macroeconomic factors.

articles.title: UK Retail Payments Infrastructure: moving from vision to design − speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
UK Retail Payments Infrastructure: moving from vision to design − speech by Victoria Cleland

Given at the FTT Fintech Festival

Published on
11 November 2026

The UK’s next-generation retail payments infrastructure is being designed to meet evolving needs of the whole ecosystem. It must enable different payment journeys and forms of money and provide a platform for innovation. Victoria Cleland explains how industry inputs are shaping the Blueprint for the new core infrastructure. She also explains why collaboration remains essential, throughout the process.

Speech
It is a pleasure to join you this morning at the FTT Fintech Festival, with an exciting update on our journey to create a next generation retail payments infrastructure for the UK. And when I say “our journey”, I do not just mean the Bank of England. I do not just mean the other authorities. I mean everyone in this room, and the whole payments ecosystem. To design and deliver an infrastructure that is well used, trusted and truly valued requires strong collaboration between the public and the private sectors, between incumbents and fintechs, and between providers and users.
Payments are a key part of all our lives, and the lifeblood of the economy and of the financial system. And we need to keep them relevant in an ever-changing landscape. Technology, about which we are hearing so much at today’s Festival, is reshaping how payments are initiated and authorised. And demand is changing, with expectations of speed and functionality increasing as payments respond to our "always on" world.
So, what is our destination?
Last year the Payments Vision Delivery Committee (PVDC) footnote [1] outlined five key outcomes for a next generation infrastructure:

greater choice of innovative and cost-effective payment options;
interoperability across a multi-money ecosystem;
protection from fraud and wider financial crime;
fair and transparent access that supports competition and innovation; and
an operationally and financially resilient payments ecosystem.

Together these will make a real difference for consumers and businesses, enhance resilience and support competition and innovation.
To help realise this ambition, the Retail Payments Infrastructure Board (RPIB) was established. I chair the RPIB, which brings together a range of industry experts, with the FCA/PSR participating as an observer, to translate these PVDC outcomes into a high-level design for the core clearing and messaging infrastructure. Next Spring the Blueprint will be handed over to the industry led Delivery Company to deliver the new infrastructure.
We took an important step towards this in June this year when the RPIB issued a public consultation inviting respondents to help shape the design of the new infrastructure. The consultation asked what payment journeys the infrastructure should support; the principles and characteristics that should guide its design; and the role of the core infrastructure as a platform for innovation across the wider payments ecosystem.
Today, I want to explain what we heard, how that feedback is helping us on our journey from vision to design, and the next steps.
Respondents
First, I would like to say an enormous thank you to everyone who contributed to the consultation. I was really encouraged by the diversity of organisations responding and by the insightful feedback in the 121 responses. We received responses from: financial institutions, payment firms, technology firms, merchants, consumers as well as trade bodies, consultants and individuals. This feedback has been supplemented by a variety of roundtables, forums and discussions, with the high level of engagement underlining how important payments are to so many players.
Feedback demonstrated broad support for the direction of travel, and for moving at pace. Respondents saw the payment journeys, design principles and conceptual architecture as a strong basis for the next stage.
Of course, broad support does not mean that every detail has been agreed and every question has been answered. Important choices remain: where the boundary of the core should sit, how interoperability should work in practice, and how migration should be managed safely. But we have strong buy-in for the overall destination and we know the big questions that need to be addressed.
From feedback to design
I cannot do justice to all of the feedback this morning - there is far more detail in our published consultation response - but I would like to focus on a few of the key points that will be front of my mind as we move into the co-creation phase.
There was strong support for the proposed payment journeys: both the existing journeys and the new and emerging journeys including A2A at point of sale, payments between different forms of money, instant payments using aliases, advanced delegated payments, programmable and deferred payments. This endorsement was very good news, as ultimately payments need to meet users’ needs. And importantly the new infrastructure will enable not just different types of payments but also different types of money, with a core infrastructure that can support many different products. I sometimes refer to this as being able to plug and play products, be they faster payments, stablecoins, programmable payments and much more, into an infrastructure that supports future developments such as those being discussed at the Festival today.
Interoperability between these different forms of money, allowing a payer to initiate a payment in one form of money and a payee to receive it in another form of money frictionlessly and at par, was welcomed. This will be a crucial feature of the new infrastructure and will greatly enhance choice for consumers and scope for Fintechs to develop new solutions.
An ecosystem that prevents fraud and financial crime was a priority for respondents. While some features will be included in layers above the core, it is essential that the new infrastructure can support and enable effective controls across the ecosystem. They need to be designed in from the start.
Respondents were supportive of a ‘layered’ architecture footnote [2] for the wider payments ecosystem where the core infrastructure can act as a platform for innovation. They also welcomed the proposed modular and extensible approach, footnote [3] designed around common capabilities, rather than around each product in isolation. This should support existing payment journeys and provide a foundation to enable new products and forms of money to be included in the future. And extensibility will be key as the new infrastructure will need to be able to scale as payment volumes grow.
As we reflect on these responses, we will be considering that there was a preference for a relatively thin core, footnote [4] that is the element that will be common to all products. However, there was a range of views as to precisely how thin the core should be, and where certain capabilities should sit. Respondents placed varying levels of emphasis on the role shared services and common capabilities should play, and whether these should sit within the core.
There was little disagreement though on the crucial importance of security, resilience and cyber security, in particular, in the context of AI and developments in frontier technologies. Respondents emphasised secure, resilient, and adaptable infrastructure, with sufficient flexibility to support future requirements. We envisage a system that will be designed to exacting levels of operational resilience. And the core infrastructure will connect to the Bank’s RTGS service for settlement in central bank money, supporting confidence and financial stability by providing a safe and final means of settlement.
Respondents highlighted common messaging, interfaces and technical standards as important foundations for the new infrastructure. And these, together with ISO20022 messaging, a consistent implementation of standards, and strong governance would be important to support interoperability in its broadest sense.
There were many comments emphasising the importance of a smooth and safe transition to the next generation infrastructure. Planning the transition will be crucial and will need to draw on the input from many players, but it can only be planned once we have a clearer idea of what is being built and hence what is being transitioned to.
The core infrastructure is only part of the ecosystem
The next-generation infrastructure will be a critical layer of the UK retail payments ecosystem. But it is only one layer. It cannot deliver successful payment journeys on its own. Product and scheme arrangements, payment services providers, consumer protection, liability, merchant acceptance, commercial incentives, financial inclusion and access will all need to develop alongside the core. For the core we need to ensure that it can enable what is needed in the product layers that sit above it. And there is also a strong complementary role for the payments industry and financial institutions to leverage the core infrastructure to develop their product offerings to provide open, transparent and accessible payments. This an exciting opportunity to innovate, for all types of customers including the most vulnerable.
The PVDC set out its thinking on this wider picture in its July 2026 update on Roles and Responsibilities in the future Retail Payments Ecosystem Opens in a new window. It is important now that the industry maintains momentum and stays focused, with Pay.UK continuing its vital role as Payment System Operator of the current systems, and the Delivery Company preparing to take forward the Blueprint for the next generation infrastructure.
What happens next
The valuable consultation responses, combined with insightful feedback from wider engagement, provide a strong foundation from which to develop the Blueprint for the next-generation infrastructure. This will set out the high-level design proposals to enable the Delivery Company to take forward the detailed design and delivery of the core.
We are now entering a period of co-creation, bringing together public and private sector expertise. This will enable the golden thread of public policy objectives to run through a design, with industry helping to shape the requirements in a way that will enable them to operate effectively. RPIB, the Design Authority, representatives from the Delivery Company, and industry experts will work together and incorporate feedback from this and our future outreach activities.
The Blueprint will then be handed over to the Delivery Company in Spring 2027, so that they can take forward detailed design, procurement, build and implementation. Ongoing public and private sector engagement will be important in ensuring that the design supports delivery of RPIB’s vision for the new infrastructure and can adapt to the changing technological and demand landscape.
This work does not mean that other innovation should stop and wait. We want it to continue, and we look forward to working with innovators so that it can align with the overall vision.
This is an exciting journey, and we need to keep up momentum. Our destination is a core infrastructure that enables: greater choice, more innovation, and a payments ecosystem that is operationally and financially resilient. The feedback from the consultation has added more detail to our map. And we have a route from high-level design to industry led delivery. I would encourage everyone to move in the same direction together, to point out safe short cuts, and to encourage other passengers to join along the way. The destination is one where we can all thrive.
I would like to thank Katie Britton and Sofia Edrihen Ruiz for helping with the preparation of these remarks.

On 7 November 2025, the PVDC published its strategic outcomes for the future UK retail payments infrastructure, building on the ambitions set out in the government’s National Payments Vision.

Layered models are commonly used to represent complex payment systems and are not specific to this work.

Modular and extensible approach – designing the core infrastructure as a combination of discrete, self-contained components that can be upgraded independently over time, while allowing new functionality and capabilities to be added without requiring fundamental redesign or replacement of the entire core.

Thin core – a core that operates core messaging, clearing, shared services, and settlement coordination services while leaving sufficient room for private sector innovation and competition.

Footnote [4]
Thin core – a core that operates core messaging, clearing, shared services, and settlement coordination services while leaving sufficient room for private sector innovation and competition.

Footnote [3]
Modular and extensible approach – designing the core infrastructure as a combination of discrete, self-contained components that can be upgraded independently over time, while allowing new functionality and capabilities to be added without requiring fundamental redesign or replacement of the entire core.

Footnote [2]
Layered models are commonly used to represent complex payment systems and are not specific to this work.

Footnote [1]
On 7 November 2025, the PVDC published its strategic outcomes for the future UK retail payments infrastructure, building on the ambitions set out in the government’s National Payments Vision.

Victoria Cleland
Senior Advisor to the Governors

The rise of content as data: How AI is reshaping market insights
[Music]
Edwina Lowe: Hi and welcome to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense. I'm Edwina Lowe from our Data Assets and Alpha group. And today I'm delighted to be joined by Camila Penna, who is co-head of Global Cash Equity Sales. So Camila, thank you so much for joining me on the podcast today.
Camila Penna: Thank you for having me, Edwina.
Edwina Lowe: So Camila, could you start by introducing yourself and your role here?
Camila Penna: Yeah, so I am co-head of Global Cash Equity Sales at J.P. Morgan. I've spent more than two decades in financial markets across New York, Brazil, and London, and I've always been extremely interested just in technology, data, AI, how it's been reshaping the way that investors make decisions.
When I think about when I started back in the financial markets. I remember waiting on faxes. Then when BlackBerry's arrived, it felt completely transformational. Then we started to see changes in electronic trading platforms, data platforms, and just the pace of technology changing accelerated enormously. But the reality is I haven't seen a pace of transformational change like what we are going through today.
Investment managers still want original information, differentiated thinking, market intelligence, good ideas from research people, from salespeople. None of that has ultimately changed. However, AI is changing the consumption model.
Edwina Lowe: Yes, I think it's fair to say that what we're seeing is content, which in and of itself has not changed, becoming a form of data in and of itself.
Camila Penna: Yes. So reality is that written research remains the most prominent product, and the one originating the most market dialogue. But content is much broader than traditional research. It's also a salesperson's morning note. It's themes from a company meeting. It comes from our conferences, from spec sales commentary, from market intelligence, from our traders providing color on flows, volumes, positioning, analyst discussions. So content is actually extremely broad and becoming broader.
So for over 10 years, we've had quant funds that have consumed our written research through machine-readable format. Machine-readable research, in other words, content as data, is not necessarily a new thing. It wasn't until LLMs were introduced that the demand started to trend drastically. So this is no longer exclusively about a quant consuming a data set. PMs, analysts, fundamental firms are now wanting to interrogate content. We are seeing investment teams that build agents around these contents. We have traders that want to consume sales and trading color programmatically, internal platforms that can combine content with proprietary and third-party data. We're seeing so many different usages of content as data now on the street that the reality is that this is what is really transformational around the content space.
Edwina Lowe: That really begs the question, what are we doing about this here at J.P. Morgan? And in your seat, Camila, I know you spend a lot of time talking to clients about what they need and what they're looking for from our markets business. How have you thought about implementing that change into our workflows at J.P. Morgan?
Camila Penna: So Edwina, you're right, this content journey is a perfect example of where clients have made us better. Their expectations of where the content world is going has forced us to rethink our own workflows and our own investments around content. We have an industry-leading research franchise that has around 500 authors publishing over 100,000 pieces of written content annually, and it was already way advanced in the journey of machine-readable distribution. As I mentioned, a lot of the quant funds were already consuming it.
What else could we be applying the same principles of how we were delivering the machine-readable research to other contexts across the market sales organization?
To use an example of the cash equities world, salespeople across our organization, they create content every day, And just to give you an idea of our scale, we have, over 400 people around the world writing over 20,000 emails a year. We have people in 25 different locations. And the reality is, it was just too fragmented.
So we created Content Hub. Essentially, it's a one-stop shop for market commentary. It centralizes the content written across our sales organization.
I'll give you like a practical example. We come in in the morning in London and Asia already is in half their day. There's a lot of salespeople that have already written content throughout the day. And now anyone can just go into Content Hub and see all of the pieces that have been written throughout the morning. You are able to query it through our AI search engine, and prompt it to be able to already deliver all of the key insights that one should know of all of the aggregated content that was written in that morning. That's something new that we've never had in the past. And it wasn't until we were able to aggregate all of the content into a single place, into a single depository, that we're able to find uses like that.
Edwina Lowe: Absolutely. And really my natural question would be to ask how that impacts the day job of a salesperson and, of course, their client relationships.
Camila Penna: So there was a lot of questioning when we created Content Hub around, does this make the salesperson less important? And funny enough, I actually think that it's the exact opposite. Technology ends up automating low value tasks. Copying, forwarding, reformatting, searching, redistributing, and multiple rewriting of the same material. That arguably is what goes away with centralizing the content into a single place. This creates actually more time for original insight to be created, client dialogue, ideas, interpretation, connecting information across the platform, and ultimately just having more time to have proper dialogue discussions and see clients face to face.
Relationships have always been and continue to be at the heart of what we do. It's the most important thing in the salesperson's day to day.
Edwina Lowe: The efficiency gains are loud and clear. So you're making this content coming from the markets business on top of the research machine readable content that we've done for a decade or so, available via API or MCP. What are clients actually doing with these feeds and how is it informing their own investment workflows?
Camila Penna: So the main usage, I would say, really is to be able to put this content as data into LLMs, to be able to search, summarize, retrieve relevant materials and just being able to prompt and surface information faster, quicker.
We've seen a few clients that have been able to take this to the next level and start to find signal generation, you know, research synthesis, more thesis monitoring, idea discovery. Some have been able to insert this into their risk hedging process. And we're starting to see clients creating agents that feed relevant commentary into already their existing workflows.
Does this actually change the relationship between trading and investing? And the reality is that a trading desk equipped with better information can become more consultative to the investment organization, bringing market context, flow, positioning, related ideas, and risk indicators back to PMs. It's moving useful information closer to the point of decision making.
Edwina Lowe: So we've discussed how up until fairly recently, it really was the quant funds who were the primary consumers of systematic data. But arguably, as you've said, the rise of LLMs has really democratized and leveled the playing field when it comes to the consumption of data across the full breadth of client types and strategy types. What's your take on this? How sophisticated are clients today when it comes to evolving their use of these types of tools?
Camila Penna: So in theory, Edwina, that is true. However, the dispersion is still vast. There's still quite a big spectrum here of the differences within the clients and what they want. So on the one end, you have some clients that are quite advanced in this sophisticated data and AI infrastructure build. They're coming into us with new requests of unstructured content and really pushing us to think about what are the arts of the possible. And then you have another end of clients that are just simply still in the journey of consuming machine-readable research through API feeds. And they're really just looking for efficiency gains for their PMs and their analysts and are using LLMs to swift through larger amounts of content as data. You know AI is still very expensive. Building out your new technology or new infrastructure requires a huge lift. And I would say that for many of them, it is still the very beginning of this journey. And so we are here to service all styles of clients and we are here to service our clients throughout where they are in the journey, not necessarily where we are in the journey.
So for example, we have thousands of clients that we service, and I would say it's only 10% of them that are probably consuming these feeds today. So as you can see, there is still a wide journey to go through.
Edwina Lowe: And what does that mean when it comes to content availability, content explosion, a world in which there is infinite content?
Camila Penna: Yeah, look, the amount of available content is exploding at a pace that I think no one imagined possible. Now, more information does mean more noise, which increases the premium on trust and differentiation. So from J.P. Morgan perspective there's so much rigor in everything that we do, be it from creation of content, from making sure that the delivery mechanisms meet all of the right standards. We go through compliance, we look at cross border regulations I would say that there should always be an extra confidence from the client around what it is that we're delivering, how and why. And so this isn't really about commercializing and monetizing an API. We're also recognizing the enterprise rights to a premium intellectual property as data that we consider carries a lot of value.
Edwina Lowe: It's really clear to me, it's imperative that the end consumer needs to have absolute confidence in the credibility of the content that they receive. And can you expand upon that point on commercial value?
Camila Penna: So we invest heavily in differentiated intellectual property and in the people who create it. The value that we see isn't simply in a delivery mechanism. It's in the right to consume the content programmatically, systematically across an enterprise with structured metadata, inside proprietary applications and AI workflow with appropriate governance, appropriate attribution. And the reality is that the arts of the possible of delivering content as data is so drastic that we see a different value today with the possibilities that AI brings than we ever have in the past.
Edwina Lowe: So Camila, it would be remiss of me not to ask about the risks. What could go wrong? This is all very new.
Camila Penna: I mean, Edwina, where do I even begin with what could go wrong and risks? I mean, anything involving innovation and such a rapid pace of change, there are many things that keep me awake at night. And look, if I'm just going to talk about a few things we want clients using our content and using this data, but the usage needs to remain appropriately governed. We want to be able to have some agreement or control around how our proprietary data is getting used.
I think a lot about things like machine readable content, risking disintermediating the creators, where we stress a point a lot with our clients is that when we deliver this content as data, we really care about the attribution back to the creator.
That a machine doesn't just surface a note. It actually surfaces content that can then lead to conversations that can then lead to strengthening relationships that can lead to actual interactions as to why that content mattered, why it was created. And we don't want any of that to go away. On the contrary, we're hoping that it enhances that relationship aspect within the clients and our content creators.
Another risk that we think about is efficiency versus differentiation. If everyone has similar AI tooling, productivity alone isn't really an edge, is it? The edge increasingly moves upstream to proprietary information, to insight, to judgment and differentiated people. And one of the greatest risks we have, honestly, is the need to be agile, the need to be flexible, the need to be quick. I mean, for many years, we were talking about how we could deliver content via an FTP. And from there, we built APIs. And almost immediately, we're getting clients questioning about how can the delivery be via an MCP. And now we do have MCP connectivity. So what's next? What is going to be the new ask? And that is definitely what keeps us on our toes.
Edwina Lowe: You talked about the sort of most sophisticated end of that client spectrum, constantly asking for more. So what is next? Can you give us a sense of what you're working on to continue to innovate in this space?
Camila Penna: So I would say that what's next is starting to come at us quite quickly, which is spoken content being transformed into transcripts. So think of transcripts of expert discussions, conferences, webinars, analyst media. There's an enormous amount of institutional knowledge that is created verbally today that historically disappears so making it more discoverable actually with shelf life is quite a valuable thing.
So when we think about the next steps of Content Hub a big part of it that we will be launching soon is the expansion beyond equities of the content that lays there. We're going to be launching macro, commodities, credit, it's going to go across asset classes.
Then there's like an even bigger question. What if email and chat eventually aren't the primary interface at all? I mean, a client actually recently told us that they're close to having all of their PMs and analysts operating outside of email. They're not going to be using email at all.
Edwina Lowe: Wow!
Camila Penna: That is where they're landing basically here. And if a machine becomes an interface between the investment professional and the information they need, what else needs to become a feed? And that's what we're constantly thinking about.
But most importantly here, Edwina, really is that we want to be flexible throughout this journey. We want to be able to deliver to the clients wherever this world is taking us. And that's the most important part here, is to be able to listen, to be able to be adaptable, and to be able to change with them.
Edwina Lowe: Absolutely. So you've talked about this journey. Where are we today?
Camila Penna: I would say that, to use a very simple analogy we're probably at iPhone 1. And I think the important point here isn't predicting what iPhone 15 is going to look like. It is recognizing that the interface has fundamentally changed. We know content is becoming data. We know AI is changing how people consume it. What none of us knows yet exactly is where that's going to lead us. The firms that do best will be the ones that keep listening to clients, protect what makes their content valuable, and adapt quickly as the technology changes.
Edwina Lowe: Yeah, I love that analogy. And I can't wait to see how this evolves myself. Thank you so much, Camila, for joining me today and for sharing your insights. It's going to be really fascinating to see where this journey continues.
Camila Penna: Definitely. And thank you, Edwina, for your insightful questions. We are very excited to continue with this journey.
Edwina Lowe: Thank you to our listeners for tuning into this episode of Making Sense. And with that, we’ll close.
