You are expressly advised to consult with qualified legal counsel and/or financial advisor(s0 before acting on any of the information contained in this Case Study and you are solely responsible for evaluating the merits and risks associated with using any information contained herein.
Throughout the preparation and drafting of this Case Study Consulting maintained full independence and editorial control and had no obligation to adopt any findings, conclusions, or interpretations inconsistent with its independent analysis. Because this Case Study is intended to be public-facing, Consulting maintains a policy under which Consulting reserves the right to release the Case Study into the public domain first. This policy has been adopted as a safeguard to ensure that the contents of the Case Study are intact and unadulterated at the time of publication. Consulting places paramount importance on the integrity of its work and has a strict prohibition on unauthorized modifications to the content of its work product by clients; however, modifications are permitted, upon mutual consent, to correct factual inaccuracies. This Case Study is based on information provided by the Client, consequently Consulting makes no representations regarding the accuracy, adequacy, completeness, or timeliness of its contents.
Without limiting the foregoing, Delphi Research, and its affiliates may, from time to time, have investments, or hold interest, in digital assets or protocols referenced in this Case Study.
Introduction
Perpetual futures have reached escape velocity and are now the primary way traders express their views on assets. Perps are easy to understand, offer 24/7 exposure without expiry, and allow traders to access a wide range of leverage. But for all their flexibility, the exposure you get from them remains linear. A trader holding one BTC contract only gains or loses the same dollar amount for each dollar move in BTC.
This leaves no room for outsized, non-linear payoffs, like a 0DTE option 10x’ing from a 2% move, or a 5x from a short-dated binary option.
For a trader who expects BTC to go much higher, the default answer is to increase the size of the long. That raises the potential payoff but also the exposure from the moment the trade opens. The position doesn’t become more sensitive as the rally develops unless the trader actively adds to it. And adding leverage inevitably brings liquidation closer if the market moves against them first.
A better way to express this view on the market is upside convexity. With a convex long position, exposure to BTC increases as its price rises, allowing gains to accelerate as the move continues. If BTC falls, the position’s sensitivity decreases, so each additional dollar decline has a smaller effect. More upside, less downside. Anyone who has traded options will recognize the appeal of a payoff that changes as the underlying moves.
The growth of the options markets shows how much demand for convexity exists. In 2017, traders bought and sold roughly 4.2 billion U.S. options contracts. That same year, Robinhood introduced commission-free options trading, simplifying the instrument and opening the door to a much wider group of traders. By 2025, annual volume had more than tripled to over 15 billion contracts.
Retail has played a huge part in that growth. Robinhood customers alone traded 905 million options contracts in Q3 ‘26, generating $399 million in options transaction revenue. Citadel also reported that retail investors traded an average of roughly $6.8 billion in options premium per day through its platform in June 2026, 65% above its 2025 average.

Traders use options for all sorts of reasons, from protecting existing positions to making highly speculative bets. The unwavering growth is a case in point of people wanting more control over their exposure than a linear long or short provides.
You see a similar appetite for outsized payoffs in prediction markets. In a study of resolved Polymarket markets, roughly 18% of purchases were of contracts priced below 10¢, with traders spending about $274 million on them. Buying a contract at 10¢ gives a trader a potential 10x payout if the outcome resolves in their favor, while limiting the upfront cost. People are chasing convexity.
But prediction markets are all built around a specific outcome. A trader betting that BTC will exceed a certain price by a set date receives the same payout at resolution whether BTC barely clears that level or rallies far beyond it. If the condition isn’t met, the contract expires worthless, even if BTC rose substantially along the way.
Traditional options come with their own trade-offs. A BTC call gives a trader convex exposure, but they must choose a strike and expiry, pay a premium, and find liquidity in that particular contract. If the rally takes longer than expected, the call can expire worthless even if BTC moves in the right direction.
Power Perps are Paragon’s new product bringing the convexity of options right into the simplicity of a perpetual future. Instead of tracking the underlying asset’s price directly, Power Perps reference an index based on that price raised to a power, such as squared or cubed.
For the trader expecting a large rally, Power Perps let their position gain exposure as the underlying rises or shed exposure as it falls, without choosing a strike or expiry. Compared with a linear long that starts with the same exposure, that means more upside if the asset rises and a smaller price loss if it falls.
They can hold the position through a familiar perp for as long as they want, and they don’t need to add leverage to introduce convexity. Funding still affects the cost of holding the trade, but traders now have a way to access that exposure alongside the spot and perp markets they already use.

Paragon is a market deployer on Hyperliquid, offering perps tracking assets ranging from individual stocks to rates and crypto. Its Power Perps are launched via HIP-3, Hyperliquid’s framework for third-party teams to launch their own perps.
A deployer chooses what its markets track and is responsible for the contract specifications, price feeds, and settings (such as leverage limits). The markets then use Hyperliquid’s trading infrastructure, including its order books and margin system. In Paragon’s case, that same framework gives the team room to introduce a market based on squared or cubed exposure.
The First Time Around
This idea of trading squared exposure through a perpetual isn’t entirely new. Many natives may remember when Opyn introduced Squeeth in 2022, giving traders ETH-squared exposure through a token called oSQTH. Users could buy the token on Uniswap to go long, while traders looking to take the other side could deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, and sell it.

Squeeth became a building block for other products. Opyn’s “Crab” strategy combined a short Squeeth position with ETH exposure and packaged it into a vault for users who wanted to take the other side of the trade without managing the position themselves. We covered both Squeeth and Crab at the time, as traders experimented with ways to bring options-like exposure and volatility strategies onchain.
Squeeth is a great history lesson. It showed what needed to change to build a sustainable market around this type of exposure. Traders looking to take the short side had to deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, and sell it through a Uniswap pool, then manage their ETH hedge separately. Trading and rebalancing on Ethereum mainnet meant paying high gas costs, while execution depended on pool liquidity.
Those costs and extra steps made taking the other side much more involved, limiting competition among short sellers. Funding rates then suffered, particularly when traders expected large moves in ETH, making Squeeth a much more expensive hold than a linear perp. The product in this iteration was not feasible.
Yet, for a product built around a relatively unfamiliar derivative, Squeeth found a real audience. By the time it shut down in November 2024, more than 18,000 unique users had traded over $1.8 billion in ETH exposure.
Paragon is bringing this idea into a different environment, one where onchain finance is now more mature. Power Perps will trade through HyperCore’s order book infra, alongside the existing spot and perp markets traders already use. A trader opens and manages the position in a familiar format, while market makers can use those surrounding markets to hedge the exposure they take on. Hyperliquid’s unified account and portfolio margin features can make it even easier to put existing capital to work here, while HyperEVM opens the door for developers to build new products and strategies around Power Perps.
For those traders willing to take the short side, that means no minting of an extra token, selling it through an AMM, or managing the trade across separate protocols. They can quote or open a Power Perp position directly and adjust their hedge using the surrounding spot and perp markets. An established base of traders and market makers gives Paragon a much stronger starting point for attracting both sides of the trade, with more participation creating the potential for tighter execution and more competitive funding.
The great thing about Power Perps is that this tool opens up far more possibilities than the simple linear directional view you’re limited to with regular perps. Users who expect a large rally could use a Power Perp alongside a regular perp to shape their exposure, adjusting how much they stand to gain or lose as the underlying price changes. Traders can take the other side of that long, using combinations of Power Perps, linear perps, options, and spot to build strategies around their views on volatility, hedge positions, or shape their exposure to different price moves. A great new tool for the house of all finance.
Paragon is bringing the first of these markets to Hyperliquid with HYPE², where traders can take either side of this exposure through a single order book. Rather than spreading that activity across contracts with different strikes and expiries, users seeking convex HYPE exposure can meet in one market.
Why Convexity Beats Simply Adding Leverage
A regular HYPE perp references the spot price of HYPE directly. HYPE² instead references an index based on the price of HYPE squared. To keep this index price easy to read, Paragon scales it down by HYPE’s price at launch.
If HYPE were $100 at launch, its squared price would be 10,000. Dividing that by the $100 launch price gives us an index that also starts at $100.
For a simple example of your possible returns trading this product, assume the HYPE² index starts at $100. If HYPE rises 20% to $120, the squared index rises 44% to $144. If HYPE instead falls 20% to $80, the index falls 36% to $64.
The result is more upside and less downside than a regular perp on 2x leverage for the same move.
The Power Perp benefits become more obvious when we compare them to a regular leveraged perp trade. Say you want $1 million of exposure to HYPE.
You could open a 2x linear long using $500,000 of margin, or a 1x HYPE² long with the same margin. If HYPE rises 20%, the squared position shows a $220,000 price gain, compared with $200,000 for the linear long.
If HYPE falls 20%, the squared position shows a $180,000 loss, compared with $200,000 for the linear long.
The table below compares both squared and cubed exposure with a linear long starting with the same HYPE exposure. We use 2x leverage for the linear comparison with HYPE² and 3x for the comparison with HYPE³, so each pair starts with the same margin.

Options traders call this sensitivity to the underlying delta. Gamma measures how much that delta changes as the underlying moves. A fixed-size linear perp position has a constant delta. But a long HYPE² position has positive gamma.
So its delta increases as HYPE rises and decreases as HYPE falls. For a fixed number of HYPE² units, gamma stays constant. Meaning delta changes by the same amount for each $1 move in HYPE.
This can be a bit confusing. In practice, it simply means your long position picks up exposure to HYPE as the price rises. If the rally keeps going, each additional dollar of upside matters more to your position.
And the other side of the coin: when HYPE falls, the position sheds exposure, so each additional dollar of decline has a smaller effect than the last.
That’s the true appeal of convexity. With the same starting exposure, the Power Perp gives you more upside as HYPE rises and cushions your losses as it falls, compared to a linear position. The drawback is a higher funding rate.

A 1x HYPE² position begins with the same dollar sensitivity as a 2x linear HYPE position of equal margin.
But if HYPE rallies, the squared position’s exposure grows. The trader captures more of each further gain as the move develops. If HYPE falls, that exposure shrinks.
A fixed-size linear long keeps the same dollar sensitivity throughout, whether the trade is working or not.

The power of the contract is separate from added leverage. A trader can hold HYPE² at 1x and still have a convex position, or use leverage to increase its size relative to their margin. However, adding leverage amplifies both gains and losses and brings liquidation closer, so a trader can lose the position before their view plays out.
It’s Not All Roses. Holding that convexity comes with a cost in the funding rate, similar to the time decay an options trader pays to hold a position. Like a regular perp, Power Perps use funding payments between longs and shorts. Longs generally pay, though the rate and direction can change.
Paragon calculates the base funding rate using HYPE’s recent volatility, funding on the underlying perp, and the power of the contract. The final rate depends on where HYPE² trades relative to its index. Hyperliquid’s existing spot and perp markets give traders a familiar place to hedge, which may help attract more participation to the other side of the trade. Funding can run higher than on a regular perp, so the real question is whether it stays reasonable enough for traders to pay up for convexity.
Where Power Perps Can Fit Between Spot, Perps, and Options
Understanding what benefits Power Perps have over other trading instruments, and how they behave, is one part of the equation. The other is where they best fit in a trader’s toolkit.
A regular perp is a straightforward way to take a directional position. A trader who wants to be long HYPE can choose their position size and leverage, then adjust or close the trade as their view changes.
Options offer more control over how a position pays out, but require precision. A trader expecting an announcement or major price move by a particular date can choose an expiry around that event and select a strike that reflects the size of the move they’re targeting. They can combine contracts to set up spreads, protect a spot position, or express a view on volatility. That flexibility comes with more decisions to manage, including the premium, time remaining, and liquidity available in each contract.
Power Perps fill a gap between those two ways of trading. They give you a position whose exposure changes with the underlying; in a perp, you can hold it without choosing a strike or rolling an expiry. That makes it easier to stay positioned for a larger move when you don’t have a precise date in mind.
You give up some of the precision of an options chain, and the position comes with funding and margin requirements. But you gain a different way to carry convex exposure alongside the spot and linear perps already in your account.

The Power Perp’s appeal becomes obvious as HYPE moves higher. In this illustrative example, its gains grow faster than both the linear perp and the call option, giving the trader more upside as the rally continues. The call option does limit the buyer’s downside to the premium paid, though, and its payoff varies with the strike and expiry.
Playing HYPE’s Next Big Move
Imagine a major announcement around changes in HYPE buybacks takes place this week. It’s not clear whether the new stance will be bearish or bullish. But whatever is announced will likely cause a strong HYPE move either way.
In this case, you don’t want to be long or short HYPE. You want exposure to a large move in HYPE without expressing a strong view on the actual direction. The best way to trade this is by going long volatility.
A great way to do this is to go long HYPE² and short enough of the linear HYPE perp to offset the position’s delta at entry.

For a small move around the starting price, gains on one leg roughly offset losses on the other. But as HYPE moves further away, either up or down, the Power Perp’s delta changes while the linear hedge stays fixed.
The combined position develops a curved, straddle-like payoff that benefits from a large move in either direction. It doesn’t matter whether HYPE nukes or pumps, you make money in both scenarios.
To return to our earlier example, assume HYPE and its squared index both start at $100. A trader goes long one unit of HYPE² and shorts two HYPE through a linear perp, matching the squared position’s starting delta. If HYPE rises to $120, the squared leg gains $44 while the linear short loses $40. If HYPE falls to $80, the squared leg loses $36 while the linear short gains $40. In both cases, the combined PnL is positive.
Getting Paid While HYPE Stays Quiet
The opposite combination takes the other side of that curve, essentially selling volatility.

You short HYPE² and buy enough HYPE spot to offset your starting delta. If HYPE stays close to the entry price and funding remains positive, the funding received can outweigh any losses and fees. This trade has a similar appeal to selling a straddle, but collects funding over time instead of premium upfront.
Hedging Your Convexity Around Earnings
Suppose you’re bullish on NVDA over the coming months and want the increasing upside exposure of an NVDA² long, but you’re concerned about a sell-off around its upcoming earnings release. You could buy an NVDA put alongside the Power Perp to protect against some of the downside below the put’s strike until it expires.

Using the same starting prices as above, assume NVDA and its squared index are both at $100. You go long one unit of NVDA² and buy a put covering one NVDA with a $90 strike, paying a $4 premium. If NVDA falls to $80 at the option’s expiry, the NVDA² position would show a $36 loss, while the put would be worth $10. After the premium, the combined price loss would be $30. If NVDA instead rises to $120, the Power Perp would gain $44 and the put would expire worthless, leaving a $40 gain after the premium.
These products trade differently in practice, but can be powerful once combined. An options chain divides activity across contracts with different strikes and expiries. A Power Perp instead brings traders interested in that convex exposure into one order book, without requiring them to roll between expiries.
This concentration into one instrument gives market makers and traders one place to meet for a particular exposure, making deep liquidity much easier to achieve. Spreads, execution size, and funding costs will always depend on how much participation the market attracts.
Why Hyperliquid Is the Best Home for Power Perps
For Power Perps to work, traders need to be willing to take the other side of that accelerating upside, and those counterparties need a way to manage the exposure they take on. Hyperliquid gives Paragon a head start on both. Directional traders already come to the venue for other perps, and market makers have direct access to spot and perp markets for hedging.

This is one reason the Hyperliquid setting is the linchpin for Power Perp’s success. Traders already use the venue for assets like HYPE spot and perps, giving Power Perp participants access to markets they can use to build and adjust positions. A trader who wants to hedge a HYPE² short doesn’t need to find a separate venue and move capital there first.
Portfolio margin can make these positions far more capital-efficient than earlier attempts. For example, if you’re short HYPE² against a spot HYPE position, you can use eligible assets as collateral while managing the trade in one account. That gives you another way to put existing holdings to work, though the benefit will depend on your account setup and the market’s final margin settings.
It also helps explain the opportunity to revisit an idea like Squeeth. The original product showed that traders were interested in both sides of squared exposure, from buying convexity outright to selling it through strategies like Crab. But trading Squeeth came with a lot of moving parts, especially on the short side, where you had to deposit collateral, mint oSQTH, sell it through a Uniswap pool, and manage your ETH hedge separately.
Paragon is abstracting its complexity and making that exposure simpler to trade on Hyperliquid. You can go long or short a Power Perp directly through an order book, then use the spot and linear perp markets on the same venue to hedge, all through a trading interface you already know.
Where Can Power Perps Go From Here?
HYPE² is where Paragon is starting, but the team has a broader set of markets in mind. The next Power Perp launches include ETH, BTC, SP500, and NVDA, bringing the product to assets at the center of some of the largest derivatives markets.
The equity markets are particularly interesting here. Trading traditional assets onchain has gone from a niche idea to a meaningful part of the perp market in a short time. Across onchain venues, monthly RWA perp volume grew from just $21.6 billion in January to $164 billion in October, accounting for roughly 28% of all onchain perp trading that month. Hyperliquid has become a major venue for this activity, with an estimated $76 billion in RWA perp volume in October alone. Traders are already coming onchain to trade these markets, and Paragon wants to give them another way to express those views.

A massive options market also surrounds the same assets. As we covered, options activity has exploded over the past few years, and a lot of that trading happens in names and indices people follow every day. Cboe’s S&P 500 index options alone traded an average of 5.5 million contracts per day in October 2026, a new monthly record. Not all of those traders will be looking for a Power Perp, but it shows how much activity already exists in these markets.
That existing activity could create room for Power Perps alongside the options traders already use. Traders move between stocks, futures, and different options contracts depending on the exposure they want. A Power Perp gives them another choice in that mix, with a position they can hold without choosing a strike or rolling an expiry.

There’s also the obvious bigger shift happening around Hyperliquid itself. Over the past year, the platform has grown beyond its roots in crypto perps, with HIP-3 deployers bringing stocks, indices, commodities, and currencies onchain. Traditional finance has been paying attention.
In March, S&P Dow Jones Indices licensed the S&P 500 to Trade[XYZ] for a perpetual contract on Hyperliquid. More recently, Intercontinental Exchange, the owner of the NYSE, announced a strategic investment in Trade[XYZ] and plans to build a regulated market and clearing structure on Hyperliquid for U.S. perpetual futures.
All of this creates an interesting backdrop for Paragon. As more traders come to Hyperliquid to trade traditional assets, Power Perps give them another way to express those views alongside the linear perps already available. There’s an opportunity to reach options traders who are used to thinking in terms of nonlinear exposure but may find a use for a position they can trade and manage through a perp.
The ICE partnership is with Trade[XYZ], not Paragon, and there’s no indication that Power Perps are part of its proposed U.S. offering. But the broader trend matters for Paragon all the same.
As Hyperliquid brings more traditional markets onchain, it’s attracting traders and liquidity that deployers can build around. Power Perps are an example of what that makes possible, introducing a new way to trade these assets alongside the spot and perp markets already on the platform. The more entrenched Hyperliquid becomes as a venue for trading assets onchain beyond crypto, the bigger the potential audience for new instruments built on top of it.
When Is Convexity Worth Paying For?
If you’re considering a Power Perp long, it comes down to the size of the move you expect and what you’ll pay to stay in the trade. A trader expecting a substantial rally may be willing to pay funding in exchange for exposure that grows as the asset rises. If you expect a smaller move, the extra price gains over a comparable linear position may not leave much room to cover the difference in costs.
The same percentage change on an asset can also look much different depending on how long it takes to play out. Two traders may enter at the same price and exit at the same target, yet have different results if one holds for a few days and the other holds for several months.
A sideways market can be a tough place to hold a directional long. HYPE might rally along the way, but if it ends up back where it started, the squared index will too. A trader who held through the round trip would see those price gains disappear and may have paid funding while waiting.
For the trader on the other side, a quieter market can give a hedged short more time to collect funding. A sharp move can be much harder to manage, as losses can build quickly and the funding collected along the way might not be enough to cover them.
Power Perps let traders stay positioned for a move as their exposure grows with it, without picking a strike or an expiry. That’s a powerful addition to a market where so much activity already happens through perps. Paragon’s bet is that putting this exposure on Hyperliquid, next to the markets traders use every day, can turn an idea that once sat at the edges of DeFi into a regular part of their toolkit. For that to happen, the market still needs tight enough execution, manageable funding, and traders on both sides of the book. If those pieces come together, the product gives Hyperliquid traders a new way to put conviction to work.

Key takeaways

Higher yields strengthen the case for bonds. With elevated yields, high-quality bonds offer attractive income potential and a meaningful cushion against continued market volatility.
Quality and duration look increasingly compelling. Higher real yields and tight credit spreads favor locking in high-quality income while limiting exposure to lower-quality, economically sensitive credit.
Global diversification can broaden opportunity. Select developed and emerging markets offer attractive real yields and strong fundamentals, helping investors diversify beyond U.S. markets.

Bond yields are near levels not seen in about 25 years, driven by an energy price shock in the Middle East and a sharp rise in real interest rates. PIMCO Group CIO Dan Ivascyn talks with strategist Esteban Burbano about why this isn’t a repeat of 2022, and why now may be the time to lock in high-quality income.
Q: Bond yields have risen globally this year. What’s the case for bonds today?
A: The year started well for both bonds and stocks, until the situation in the Middle East deteriorated. Since then, it’s been a challenging environment for bonds. But most of the rise in global interest rates has come from real yields, which are yields after adjusting for inflation. Inflation expectations have risen far less. Yields today, both before and after inflation, are at levels we haven’t seen in about 25 years. That bodes incredibly well for fixed income over the next several years in our view.
We saw similar negative sentiment in 2023, and it set the stage for a very healthy multi-year run in bond markets. Today, starting yields offer a compelling entry point for a three- to five-year time horizon.
What’s especially exciting is that you don’t need to take on much credit risk or economic sensitivity to capture these yields. A high-quality fixed income portfolio can be constructed to be fairly resilient and could even benefit if the economy or markets weaken further.

Watch Dan discuss the opportunity presented by today’s yields in this short video.

Q: What’s our outlook for the macro environment?
A: We expect more near-term uncertainty, and longer-term forces have key implications for our outlook. Energy shocks caused by supply disruptions usually show up first as higher inflation. The longer they linger, the more they turn into broader economic weakness, which could quickly improve conditions for higher-quality bonds. AI adds another layer to the inflation story. It’s probably adding some upward pressure on prices today.
Our base case is that uncertainty continues until we see some stabilization in the Middle East, which we think is likely sometime in the next several months. Over the next few quarters, we expect higher real interest rates to drive some slowing economic growth, with inflation making gradual progress. Ironically, near-term uncertainty is higher, but long-term uncertainty is lower for fixed income because higher real yields provide a cushion. (For more on our macro views, read PIMCO’s latest Cyclical Outlook, Growth Holds, Risks Widen.)
Q: Many investors are asking whether this is a repeat of 2022. How is this time different?
A: It’s very different. Inflation in 2021 and 2022 came from the recovery after COVID, a once-in-a-generation shock met by a massive response from governments and central banks. Looking back, many central banks were also slow to react to inflationary pressure.
The most important difference comes down to simple bond math. At the start of 2021, bonds effectively had no yield cushion. Rates were low, even zero or negative in many places, and then inflation surged far above today’s levels. This time, bonds benefit from a substantial cushion; a broad U.S. bond market index now yields in the mid-5% range. Headline inflation is elevated, mainly because of energy. But core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is in the mid-2% range in the U.S. In 2022, core inflation briefly reached the mid-to-high single digits.
Whatever happens in the short term, a flexible, high-quality approach held over three to five years has the potential to earn today’s yield. And that yield looks exceptionally attractive next to richly valued equities in our view.
Q: How is the team positioning duration, or interest rate exposure?
A: Stocks are very expensive by historical standards, both in terms of price-to-earnings and compared with real interest rates in the bond market. Earnings could stay very high and justify those prices. But we believe investors are paying a very high price for equity risk, and similar levels in the past have tended to lead to weak returns in equity markets. We find duration, or interest rate exposure, very attractive over the medium term, given the income a diversified portfolio can generate. And because higher real yields affect the economy with a delay, it also looks attractive compared with more credit-sensitive parts of the market.
With elevated yields, income can do more of the work. And with central bank rate hikes already priced into markets, bonds can benefit if fewer hikes are delivered and could also help hedge a potential growth shock should the AI boom waver.
There are multiple possible macro scenarios in the next 12 months that could drive positive bond returns. We believe a lot must go right for equities to deliver, while a lot must go wrong for bonds to disappoint.
Credit spreads, the extra yield investors receive for lending to companies instead of governments, are near historically tight levels around the world, including in the U.S. That’s true even with all the economic uncertainty and recent volatility. High-quality bond yields, by contrast, are near their highest levels in about 25 years.
In 2021, ahead of the 2022 selloff, we favored an underweight to interest rate exposure. Today, we prefer to be roughly in line with the broad U.S. bond market index. That reflects how constructive we are about these yields and our desire to lock them in for longer.
We also changed which maturities we prefer. A few years ago, we favored being concentrated in shorter-term bonds. Over the past couple of years, we prefer longer maturities, where rates are among the highest we’ve seen in many years. The goal is to capture income for years ahead.
Q: Where is the team finding opportunities outside the U.S.?
A: U.S. valuations are very attractive, but U.S. government finances are less stable than those of some other countries. The U.S. still runs deficits of around 6% of GDP despite a strong economy. The economy also has more momentum, since almost all U.S. mortgages have 30-year fixed rates, and many homeowners locked in low rates a few years ago.
Elsewhere, some countries present stronger government finances and higher credit quality alongside more fragile economies. All else equal, that’s what you want in a bond market. We like high-quality opportunities in places such as Australia and the U.K. We also like higher-quality emerging markets that fought inflation aggressively and now offer very high real interest rates.
Diversifying across high-quality bond markets around the world is a pillar of our Income approach. It can reduce volatility while improving prospects for total return. It also lets us earn attractive yields without relying on more vulnerable areas of fixed income markets, such as bank loans and high-yield bonds.
Q: You’ve been cautious on corporate credit for several years. How are you positioned across sectors today?
A: The baseline economic outlook looks reasonably bright, but credit and equity markets have more than priced that in. Private credit is a good example. For years it seemed stable, then the market realized lending standards had been loose and spreads were tight, and concerns about AI disruption followed.
We think a similar false sense of stability exists today in tightly priced, lower-quality credit. So we favor being underweight that risk and maintaining dry powder, which gives us the flexibility to act if markets are disrupted.
Instead of leaning into these lower-quality segments, we prefer earning yield in higher-quality areas. Beyond global government bonds, we like resilient parts of the credit market, such as asset-based securities and other senior structured investments that are first in line for repayment. Mortgage-backed securities issued by U.S. government agencies have lagged recently as rates became more volatile, but they offer a very attractive yield advantage over investment-grade corporate bonds.
Our key theme is moving up in quality, and we take less credit risk while maintaining our yield and return potential.
Q: The AI boom is bringing a lot of new borrowing into bond markets. Where do you see opportunities?
A: AI may well be the most consequential technology of our lifetimes, and we’re optimistic about its potential to boost productivity over the long term. But those gains could also be disruptive, upending old-economy business models and displacing workers. Over time, that could push inflation down and hurt heavily indebted, old-economy companies that are disrupted. But for high-quality bonds, those scenarios are extremely favorable in our view.
History also suggests that transformative technologies almost always lead to overinvestment, from the railroads to the internet bubble. As a share of GDP, AI investment is the largest wave of business investment in hundreds of years, and some of it will likely turn out to be bad investments. That risk can surface suddenly, which is one reason we prefer staying up in quality.
The bottom-up opportunity is where we see something genuinely exciting. Across PIMCO, we have a long history of providing financing to companies that need to raise capital. We see a strong pipeline of opportunities with risk profiles similar to investment grade, where PIMCO can shape the terms. Lenders have more bargaining power than they’ve had in many years. Still, there’s a lot of supply, and we’ve been patient about getting the terms we need and very selective about the opportunities we pursue in this space.
Q: Many investors are concerned about U.S. debt sustainability. What’s your view?
A: Over the long run, U.S. debt isn’t sustainable, and it’s unusual to run a 6% deficit with unemployment this low. Still, we think it’s manageable, though the government will have to pay higher rates than it otherwise would. The dollar remains the world’s reserve currency, and the economy is dynamic. The biggest U.S. advantage is that it taxes its population about 15 percentage points less than many developed-market peers. The U.S. has the capacity to trim the deficit, but right now, there doesn’t appear to be the political will.
The good news is that we can lend to the U.S. government at yields we haven’t seen in well over 25 years. And the U.S. isn’t the only game in town. We’re diversifying into markets with stronger government finances with currency risk hedged back into U.S. dollars.
Q: How are we positioned in emerging markets?
A: Emerging markets, including some modest currency exposure, are an important way to diversify without taking too much concentrated credit risk. Our allocations are lower than at many points in the past, but we still like a diversified mix of higher-quality exposures. As I mentioned earlier, we like emerging markets that effectively tamed inflation and now offer attractive real yields. Interest rate positions in countries such as Brazil, Mexico, and South Africa, along with small holdings in bonds issued by government-linked entities, continue to perform well.
Q: Some investors are worried rate volatility will continue and are sitting in cash. What would you say to them?
A: Cash only locks in a yield for one day, and shocks can be quite unexpected. Think back to 2023. Fitch had downgraded the U.S., and inflation was surprising to the upside, much as it is today. Yet the fourth quarter of 2023 was one of the best periods for bond returns in many years. Investors who started from those higher yields and held for three years were able to earn high-single-digit returns in actively managed income-focused bond portfolios.
The environment today is similar. Cash can feel like the lower-risk choice. But often, especially after a big rise in rates, not locking in higher yields turns out to have been the riskier choice.
Higher real rates will begin to strain consumer lending and commercial real estate, albeit slowly. That’s typically how higher rates slow down the economy. We may be at peak nervousness about interest rate exposure, which argues for higher quality and for locking in compelling yields today.

Clashing Tides In The Tasman Sea

Rohan Daswani

Gavekal Research | 19 Nov 2026

For decades, the Australian and New Zealand dollars have moved broadly in tandem against the US dollar, reflecting their shared exposure to global commodity demand, particularly from China. Australia’s exports are dominated by metals and energy, while New Zealand specializes in agricultural products such as dairy and meat. Recently, however, the two currencies have moved in opposite directions as diverging monetary policy expectations and economic prospects have broken their traditional relationship.Strong demand for key Australian commodity exports, including coal and liquefied natural gas, together with a more hawkish central bank, has supported the Australian dollar. Meanwhile, New Zealand has struggled with weaker domestic growth, high unemployment and households still feeling the effects of a prolonged post-Covid property slump. The country’s sluggish recovery from the pandemic has also encouraged its citizens to seek better job opportunities and health care in Australia, adding to the New Zealand dollar’s relative weakness.

Concrete’s role in meeting housing and infrastructure demand to 2050

By Ryan Lee and Adrian Hart

Our new research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable future.

The world is entering a period of unprecedented demand for infrastructure and housing.

Our latest research forecasts that global construction activity will increase by more than 70% by 2050, reaching US$16.6 trillion annually, up from US$9.7 trillion in 2025. Emerging economies across Asia, Africa and the Middle East will be major engines of growth. Delivering these assets will create substantial opportunities across the construction industry.

However, infrastructure need does not automatically nor quickly translate into funded projects. Capacity constraints and financing pressures can slow delivery, while expanding materials supply requires capital and long lead times. This creates a difficult investment decision: committing too early risks underused capacity, while waiting too long can mean supply is unable to respond when projects proceed.

For investors, infrastructure owners and policymakers alike, this means that understanding when and where this growth will occur, and the barriers to delivering it, is essential to planning ahead and capturing the opportunity.

Five megatrends are reshaping global construction demand

The report identifies five interconnected forces that are driving the next generation of infrastructure investment.

The practical implication is that companies need to understand which sectors will expand, how quickly projects can proceed and whether their capabilities match the work coming through. Policymakers and asset owners need to anticipate where competing demands will stretch delivery capacity.

Cement and concrete have a critical strategic role to play in the built environment

Cement and concrete sit at the centre of this outlook. Concrete’s durability, scalability and local availability make it essential to delivering the infrastructure underpinning modern economies.

Our research estimates that annual concrete demand from key infrastructure sectors will reach around 20 billion tonnes by 2050, demonstrating the scale of future opportunities for construction materials producers and suppliers. Transport sectors (roads, and rail and ports) stand out with faster demand growth than other sectors. Nevertheless, the utilities sector remains a large source of demand in absolute terms.

The report also highlights the important contributions the cement and concrete industry make beyond its physical applications. Importantly, these include its contributions to regional economic development and industrial capacity, as well as its crucial role in supporting the transition to a lower-carbon economy through resilience and whole-life asset performance.

Turning rising demand into sustainable delivery

The outlook presents a substantial opportunity, but meeting infrastructure needs will require more than expanding production. As the report details, growing infrastructure investment will need to meet increasingly demanding expectations for affordability, resilience and sustainability.

Innovation in materials, construction methods and circular economy practices will be essential in improving delivery. Clearer and more credible project pipelines and procurement arrangements can give suppliers greater confidence to invest. The opportunity is to deliver more infrastructure and economic value per tonne of concrete, per unit of carbon and per worker.

Understanding where demand is emerging, what could constrain delivery and how requirements are changing will help organisations make better decisions about the capacity, capabilities and assets needed over the coming decades.

articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayNVIDIA’s shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, helping to pull Nasdaq futures around 1% lower and putting pressure on technology-heavy markets in Taiwan and South Korea. The moves followed reports that NVIDIA’s board had met on Wednesday night to discuss whether CEO Jensen Huang should remain in his role, following news that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort and subsequent developments.These headlines come as investors are becoming more selective on the AI trade. Recent technology volatility reflects a shift from rewarding spending commitments toward assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization, and prospective returns. At the same time, underlying demand remains robust: Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity, and we forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.Without taking any views on individual companies, we see several lessons that investors across the technology sector should consider:Key-person risk warrants greater attention. The episode illustrates how leadership and governance can become material investment considerations when a company’s strategy, culture, and market standing are closely associated with an individual. This matters beyond any single company, particularly after several years in which AI-related equity gains have been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of businesses. As investors become more discerning about valuations and returns, governance and clarity around succession planning may play a larger role alongside earnings growth in determining performance.Chip restrictions look unlikely to ease. AI competition between the US and China already operates within tight restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors. We believe recent developments reduce the likelihood of an easing in current restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, while scrutiny of where processors are ultimately deployed could increase. Greater restrictions could weigh on sales in certain overseas markets, though they would not necessarily alter underlying AI demand, with compute capacity remaining in short supply.AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. As advanced computing becomes more strategically important, governments are paying closer attention to where chips are produced, sold, and deployed. This could result in greater tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny, and friction around global AI supply chains, potentially raising costs and restricting access to some overseas markets. Greater geopolitical competition may also spur investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity, reinforcing the importance of distinguishing between strong underlying demand and the companies best positioned to capture it.So, while we retain our conviction in the structural AI opportunity, we think these events reinforce the case for greater selectivity and diversification as the tech investment cycle evolves. We continue to favor financially strong hyperscalers; tighter future compute capacity could increase the value of existing infrastructure, while lower future capital spending could support free cash flow. Within AI “picks and shovels” (semiconductors and hardware), we would stay selective and favor quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, alongside defensive technology exposures such as payment networks and potential beneficiaries of lower memory costs within consumer electronics. For investors whose technology exposure has become overly concentrated, we would consider broadening exposure within technology and diversifying across sectors, asset classes, and geographies.

articles.title: How Congress might take back its trade powers and limit Trump's tariffs
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

How Congress might take back its trade powers and limit Trump's tariffs

Inu Manak (PIIE)

Date
November 13, 2026 12:00 PM

Photo Credit: Sipa USA/Michael Brochstein

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Americans are unhappy with the direction the country is headed and are ready for change. That was the core message from the stunning defeat of the president's party in the midterm elections in November, where the accumulation of unpopular policies—including immigration enforcement, the war in Iran, and tariffs—was thoroughly rebuked. The contribution of those policies to dissatisfaction with the economy is quite clear, and voters expect the incoming Congress to come prepared to tackle them.
Congress may want to start with trade policy. An NBC News exit poll(link is external) from 45 states showed that 66 percent of voters thought President Donald Trump's tariffs had hurt the national economy. With the tariffs' impact being felt by both businesses and consumers, trade policy is an area ripe for reform.
Ending Trump's second-term trade war is also about a lot more than economic costs because the administration has been indiscriminate in targeting allies and adversaries alike. He has focused substantial attention on Canada, which a majority of Americans(link is external) see as misguided. Congress should be equally concerned that Canadians are more likely to view(link is external) the US with suspicion, or as an enemy or potential threat than as a friend.
Reining in the powers that Congress has delegated to the president in the past will not be an easy task politically. Nor will allies suddenly trust the US again even if tariffs are scaled back. Nonetheless, establishing guardrails and repairing alliances are important, and as set out below, there are several ways to do it.
We've Been Here Before
Since Trump's first-term trade war was launched, Congress has debated what kinds of guardrails are necessary to prevent executive abuse of trade authorities. Importantly, while he has used many tools in his battles, some are more harmful than others. Two measures the president uses to avoid accountability are Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, used to impose the "national security" sectoral tariffs, and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is propping up baseline tariffs of 10-12 percent on nearly all US imports. While addressing other tariff abuses is important, reducing the economic harm at home and repairing our relationships with allies such as Canada require Congress to close the loopholes in these two statutes.
Since 2018, lawmakers have discussed a range of bills to address different trade statutes and varying concerns with how they are used. Most of those efforts fall within three categories of reforms: limiting executive abuse, improving transparency and procedural concerns, and clarifying the purpose and scope of specific statutes.
The surefire way to prevent executive abuse is to require that Congress vote on any tariffs. This can take two forms. The first is through a joint resolution of disapproval, where both houses of Congress would be able to vote to repeal a president's tariffs. Currently, Section 232 includes a disapproval resolution only for petroleum imports. Senator Rob Portman (R-OH) put forward a bill in 2019 (the Trade Security Act(link is external)) that would expand this to all Section 232 actions. The main problem with disapproval resolutions is that they require Congress to seek repeal of a president's action after it has been taken. Politically, this can be difficult because the president's party may want to avoid openly questioning the president's policy agenda. Some members of Congress may also shy away from voting to repeal actions benefiting some interests in their districts. However, voters' overwhelmingly anti-tariff sentiment could insulate those members from such pressures.
The second, and more robust, option is a joint resolution of approval, which requires Congress to vote on a proposed tariff action before it is taken. This prevents arbitrary imposition of tariffs and ensures that such serious actions are thoughtfully deliberated. A 2019 bill(link is external)—the Bicameral Congressional Trade Authority Act—from Senators Pat Toomey (R-PA) and Mark Warner (D-VA) would have required an approval resolution within 60 days of the president submitting a report to Congress on the proposed action. A 2025 bill(link is external)—the Trade Review Act—by Senators Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Chuck Grassley (R-IA) would limit new or increased tariffs to 60 days and require a joint resolution of approval to extend them. The bill also would enable Congress to end tariffs at any time through a disapproval resolution. Both approval and disapproval resolutions would be subject to a presidential veto, requiring a two-thirds majority vote of support in both houses to override. The bar would be very high to clear but not impossible.
Another way to limit executive abuse is to narrow the discretion the president has to act. For example, in past Section 232 reform bills, Congress has suggested that the Department of Defense be designated as the appropriate agency to investigate whether a certain product is "being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair national security." Currently, the statute designates the Secretary of Commerce to fulfill that role. Moving this investigative power to the Department of Defense could help ensure that only legitimate national security concerns are being addressed.
Similarly, with Section 301, some have suggested that the investigation conducted by the US Trade Representative (USTR), who is a political appointee reporting directly to the president, be moved to an independent agency(link is external), such as the US International Trade Commission (USITC). This would not only limit the USTR's broad discretion but also ensure that the investigation is data-driven and nonpartisan. A 2023 bill(link is external)—the Global Trade Accountability Act—from Representative Warren Davidson (R-OH) would require the USITC to analyze the impact of some unilateral trade actions on the US economy.
In addition to building backstops to capricious presidential actions, there are other ways Congress could improve transparency in presidential tariff actions and strengthen procedural guardrails. For example, Section 232 could be made subject to judicial review that involves greater scrutiny(link is external) than currently exists, so that court challenges can be seriously considered instead of avoided due to traditional deference to the president on issues relating to national security. The president could also be required to publish or share with Congress the Section 232 reports received from the Secretary of Commerce that are used to make determinations about tariff actions. The first Trump administration's Section 232 investigation on automobiles was released by the Biden administration, for instance. In the second Trump administration, these reports have not been made public, which makes it difficult to assess the rationale behind the actions.
How and why certain products are excluded from tariffs is also a topic Congress may want to address. In 2023, the Government Accountability Office(link is external) critically assessed problems in the Section 232 exclusions process, including the grant of unneeded exclusions. Section 301 does not include a means to grant exclusions, but under the first Trump administration, hundreds of products were exempted from tariffs in an opaque process(link is external). Congress could clarify that exclusions cannot be granted or specify when exclusions would be acceptable (e.g., consumer products, energy, trade agreement partners).
Finally, Congress will need to weigh in on the purpose and scope of these statutes. For example, Congress could define what specific national security threats could warrant tariff actions. For example, the Toomey-Warner bill(link is external) defined national security as "the protection of the United States from foreign aggression; and does not otherwise include the protection of the general welfare of the United States." Congress could also specify where tariffs cannot be applied for national security reasons, such as products where there are no obvious national security applications (e.g., kitchen cabinets and other consumer products, such as groceries(link is external)), towards specific countries that are part of the US defense-industrial base, or security allies.
Such reforms should entail serious reflection about why Congress delegated certain authorities to the president in the first place, and to what end. For example, the primary purpose of Section 301, when it was drafted, was to support the ability of the president to negotiate agreements to reduce foreign trade barriers, rather than to raise US trade barriers. It was, by and large, an investigation-driven enforcement tool to use as leverage in negotiations with a single country(link is external). Today, its application is far removed from that intent. This is one reason why trade experts, including Alan Wolff, the author of the original 301 statute, have been skeptical about the Trump administration's use of Section 301 to impose tariffs allegedly to combat forced labor.
This Time Is Different
The congressional efforts at tariff reform described above suggest that Congress has already put a lot of thought into the persistent problem of executive overreach on trade but has achieved little in terms of concrete outcomes. Political obstacles to action are a main driver of this impasse, but the 2026 midterm election results may have changed past calculations. For one, tariffs are widely unpopular,(link is external) and Democrats spent billions of dollars on TV ads that portrayed tariffs in a negative light. As Democrats take control of both the House and Senate in January, voters are likely expecting the new Congress to deliver on promises to claw back tariffs as one way to lower consumer costs.
Furthermore, Trump's second-term trade war has targeted the whole world, even close US allies such as Canada, and free trade agreement partners such as South Korea. Congress may want to consider Canada-specific legislation, or reforms that prevent the application of tariffs on certain countries entirely. Senator Christopher Coons (D-DE) introduced the Stopping Tariffs on Allies and Bolstering Legislative Exercise of Trade Policy Act(link is external) in 2025, which would limit the president's ability to apply tariffs to members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and major non-NATO allies as well as US free trade agreement partners. However, allies may need more than targeted tariff exemptions to restore trust in the US, when multilateral trade rules and free trade agreements approved by Congress have been violated. Congress may also struggle to build consensus to remove tariffs on all allies, keeping some leverage in place to extract additional concessions.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries—on track to become House Speaker in January—has stated that rolling back Trump's tariffs will be a top priority for Democrats in the next Congress, but he has not specified which tariffs or trade statutes his party will take on. There may be some "low-hanging fruit," such as the authority under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 used by Trump to impose tariffs allegedly to address a US balance of payments problem (tariffs struck down by the US Court of International Trade, although the case is on appeal). Another is the antidiscrimination authority in Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (used against Canada). But tackling these measures will not go far enough in reclaiming trade authorities that Congress has delegated to the president.
Section 338 is also being challenged in court,(link is external) and Trump's tariffs under that statute could be invalidated. For Canada, those tariffs are also not as economically significant as the Section 232 sectoral tariffs, over which negotiations broke down in August. Therefore, Congress will need to develop a comprehensive reform agenda for the two core statutes that have made the trade wars persist since 2018. Anything less will do little to reduce the uncertainty that has plagued US economic relations since Trump ratcheted up his trade war last year.
Of course, for any legislative action to be successful, a veto-proof majority will be required. That may exist for Canada-specific tariff relief but not for broader efforts. However, Congress may still want to vote on legislation regardless of its probability of passage if only to get members on the record for their views on tariffs. As a matter of internal party politics and positioning for the next election, this may prove useful in identifying those members who are serious about tackling this aspect of affordability from those who are not. The incoming Congress may not be able to achieve comprehensive tariff reform due to internal party pressures and special interest lobbying for continued protectionism. However, the debates that unfold over the next two years can lay important groundwork for the next president and Congress to finally restore checks and balances in trade policy and ensure, as James Madison wrote in Federalist 45, that the powers of the federal government are few and defined.

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.

articles.title: Technology investment outlook 2027: AI moves from promise to proof - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
AI shifts from promise to measurable return on investment: 2027 should see AI move further from experimentation toward monetisation, productivity gains, and demonstrable returns, particularly across cloud and enterprise applications

AI infrastructure spending remains strong: Demand for GPUs, custom silicon, optical networking, data center power, and other infrastructure should remain robust, with supply constraints persisting in several areas

A constructive outlook balanced by rising risks: Technology valuations remain broadly supportive, but higher interest rates, debt-financed AI capex, geopolitics, and AI safety concerns could create periods of volatility

After several years of rapid innovation, the year ahead could mark the point at which artificial intelligence’s economic impact becomes increasingly visible.

The conversation is likely to shift from technological possibility to real-world adoption, monetisation, and return on investment.

Personal AI agents, enterprise automation, physical AI, and cloud infrastructure are all moving from experimentation toward broader deployment at scale.

The companies best positioned to monetise new products and distribute this innovation should be the primary beneficiaries of the AI cycle’s next phase.

Personal AI agents go mainstream

2027 could be the year that agentic AI transitions from an emerging technology to a mainstream consumer product.

Rather than simply answering questions, personal AI agents will increasingly perform tasks on a user’s behalf. Common use cases could include prioritising email messages, booking travel, scheduling appointments, managing subscriptions, and coordinating household services.

Improvements in reasoning, memory, and tool use should allow these agents to operate across applications and websites with minimal user input.

Adoption will likely be driven less by model breakthroughs and more by convenience, reliability, and integration into products consumers already use. Over time, personal AI agents could become a new interface layer for the internet.

AI moves into core enterprise workflows

Enterprise AI use cases will expand beyond coding assistants and customer service into agentic capabilities that augment core business workflows.

Organisations will increasingly deploy AI across functions such as finance, sales, human resources, and supply chain management. The next stage of the AI cycle will be defined not only by model capabilities, but also by the ability to deliver useful intelligence at an attractive cost.

Smaller models are likely to handle routine tasks, while larger models are reserved for more complex reasoning. Increasingly sophisticated orchestration software will manage these interactions behind the scenes, making AI more seamless for end users.

As adoption broadens, the focus should shift from experimentation to measurable productivity gains.

AI safety and cybersecurity remain top of mind

The AI safety debate will continue in 2027. Many industry experts fear a major cybersecurity breach or biohazard attack by bad actors using AI models. It is increasingly clear that cybersecurity, governance, and observability software will play a critical role going forward.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and others have advocated for deterministic supervisory software monitoring each AI model to build in policy guardrails for governance, compliance, and security.1

Other suggestions by industry experts include third-party auditing of training workloads and independent testing of models before public release. There is a growing consensus that governments need to regulate the industry, but also significant disagreement over how such regulations should be formulated.

Physical AI and edge computing build momentum

Next year could be a pivotal period for physical AI and edge computing – where data processing and storage is physically closer to the data source – as advances in AI begin translating into real-world automation.

Adoption is likely to accelerate first in structured environments such as factories, warehouses, and logistics networks, where intelligent robots can improve productivity and help address labour shortages.

Likewise, AI-enabled wearables, such as smart glasses, could emerge as an important new computing category by bringing contextual intelligence into everyday activities.

Humanoid robots may also make meaningful technical progress, but large-scale adoption likely remains several years away. Taken together, 2027 may represent the beginning of a new phase in which AI expands beyond software and digital workflows into the physical world.

Sector outlook

Semiconductors and hardware: Demand continues to exceed supply

We expect AI infrastructure demand to continue to outpace supply through 2027. Demand remains strong with hyperscalers and other customers providing suppliers with orders stretching through 2027 and beyond.

Optical components, semiconductors, and power for data centres will continue to be key constraints on the supply side. Leadership will continue to diversify as investors look for the next area of investment to support training and inferencing applications, especially as model innovations open new opportunities.

One key risk to monitor is access to capital at an economic cost, especially in a rising interest rate environment. It is unreasonable to expect the buildout to proceed in a linear fashion, but it is hard to know the timing of any digestion period or interruption in the AI infrastructure race.

Given the magnitude of outperformance of technology infrastructure names particularly during the first half of 2026, it would not be surprising to see continued volatility through 2027 as investors debate the relative merits of software versus semiconductors.

Cloud service providers: Return on investment comes into focus.

2027 could be the year that cloud service providers prove the return on investment for their unprecedented AI infrastructure spending.

Cloud service providers are uniquely positioned to monetise AI given their unmatched data centre footprints, access to graphics processing units, rapidly expanding custom silicon programmes, and highly profitable core businesses which support funding needs.

Investors should become more constructive as cloud revenue growth accelerates, capex growth moderates, and cloud margins remain healthy. Together, these factors could provide compelling evidence that AI infrastructure can generate attractive long-term returns rather than simply support an arms race.

Software: Careful navigation required

The software sector will require increasingly careful navigation as investors distinguish between AI beneficiaries and companies vulnerable to AI disruption.

Broad-based scepticism toward application software should give way to a more nuanced assessment of which companies can leverage AI to expand their total addressable markets and strengthen their competitive positions.

While AI monetisation is likely to accelerate across the industry, it will still represent a relatively small portion of revenue for most software companies in 2027.

We remain constructive on cybersecurity and infrastructure software, where AI is driving both increased demand and new product opportunities, though we are mindful of premium valuations given strong performance in 2026.

The first wave of frontier AI IPOs arrives

The potential public listings of leading frontier AI labs in the year ahead would mark a significant milestone. The initial public offerings would likely represent some of the most notable technology debuts since the emergence of the cloud service providers.

Beyond expanding the investable universe, these listings could provide investors with direct pure play exposure to the development and monetisation of frontier AI models, potentially attracting significant capital flows and reshaping technology indices.

More broadly, due to public market scrutiny, these companies will be under pressure to demonstrate sustainable revenue growth, scalability, margins, and returns on capital.

Valuations bolster environment

Valuations across much of the technology sector remain supportive, providing a constructive backdrop for investors.

While select AI beneficiaries continue to command premium multiples, many software, semiconductor, and hardware names trade at levels that appear reasonable relative to their growth and earnings outlooks.

The average forward price-to-earnings ratio for the semiconductor industry has declined to below 19 times (as of mid-October 2026) compared to the five-year average closer to 25, and the software sector’s enterprise value-to-sales ratio is moderately below its long-term average.2

Semiconductor stock valuations look reasonable given earnings momentum. In the semiconductor industry group, valuations are compelling, but for companies in commodity markets for standardised components like memory chips, investors are hesitant to put high multiples on what could prove to be peak earnings expectations

Valuations remain compelling for select application software companies that can monetise AI and defend their competitive positions against disruption.Outside of application software,widely perceived AI beneficiaries including certain data management and cybersecurity companies now command premium valuation multiples. Meanwhile, the cloud service providers appear undervalued, particularly if further evidence emerges that AI investments are generating attractive returns

Select hardware stocks are undervalued. Optical and other data centre infrastructure stocks have pulled back on concerns about the sustainability of supply shortages and of demand, and perhaps in relation to the prospects of a Democratic sweep in the US (which we believe would not in and of itself have a major impact on data centre approvals); select stocks look compelling

The long-term opportunity created by AI remains significant, but investors should remain mindful of several risks that could slow adoption or pressure valuations.While these risks are worth monitoring, the balance of evidence continues to support a constructive outlook for the sector. Key risks include, but are not limited to:

High interest rates could result in valuation pressure for long duration assets and could raise the cost of capital for financing AI infrastructure

The geopolitical environment is uncertain and makes it more likely that there will be competing AI ecosystems, inefficient supply chains, and physical risks to AI infrastructure

AI safety concerns could slow development, particularly if there is a cyber or biological attack by a bad actor, and/ or if there are more breaches by AI agents going rogue

Financing challenges could slow AI investment, especially as a higher portion of capex is being debt financed

Trends could give rise to the formation of an AI bubble, including circular relationships, increasing use of debt financing and off-balance sheet vehicles, lax regulation, private market valuations moving into the public markets with IPOs, and rising interest rates (which could pop a bubble)

However, mitigating factors include investor scepticism, encouraging AI adoption trends in consumer and enterprise applications which demonstrate paths to positive return on investment, and reasonable valuations that are not yet at dotcom bubble levels.

The next stage

The next phase of the AI cycle is likely to be defined less by technological breakthroughs and more by execution, adoption, and monetisation.

Companies that can translate AI investment into sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on capital should emerge as the long-term winners.

While periodic volatility is inevitable, we remain constructive on the technology sector and the opportunities created by the ongoing AI transformation.

[1] The choices we make about AI now are critical | Bill Gates / Dario Amodei — We Must Pace the Frontier / https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/a-warning-about-model-welfare

[2] Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management, FactSet.

articles.title: View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Chi Lo, Senior Market Strategist, Asia Pacific, Hong Kong

The forces keeping the US Federal Reserve in monetary tightening mode have not faded. Diesel and petrol prices remain high, artificial intelligence-driven inflation has not eased, and the labour market remains resilient. Housing market weakness and the recent wobble in AI optimism may make the Fed cautious, but core inflation is still skewed to the upside.

Listen to the article

Play00:00…Volume

Asian central banks have typically followed the Fed’s rate increases. However, it may be different this time unless the Fed’s hikes cause significant exchange rate depreciation in the region.

US inflationary pressures remain

The underlying inflation dynamics in the US have not changed much since the Fed’s rate increase in September. Global energy prices have remained high and tight diesel markets have boosted diesel price inflation (see Exhibit 1). Diesel prices are pivotal to the pass-through to broader inflationary pressures due to the fuel’s widespread use in transport, manufacturing and farming.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged recently that tighter financial conditions (due to the rise in bond yields) had helped the Fed to contain inflationary pressures. However, he also stressed that the Fed’s job was to ensure that sector-specific price shocks do not broaden out and that inflation expectations would not be unanchored. So, rising bond yields do not necessarily stand in the way of further rate hikes.

Asia is different

The Fed has already raised rates once in September. October’s stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation has increased the markets’ conviction of another Fed rate hike in December. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% month-on-month versus the consensus forecast of 0.3% and core CPI was 0.3% versus consensus expectations of 0.2%.

The European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada have also hiked their rates since September. In Asia (excluding Japan), the picture is more diverse. While a couple of central banks have hiked rates, most have stood pat.

Recent monetary policy cycle experience shows that Asia has not always followed the Fed’s rate moves in lock-step or has followed them with a lag unless the Fed’s hikes triggered sharp exchange rate depreciation. Why is that?

Firstly, Asian central banks have a wider set of policy targets than the Fed. They do not follow the Fed if its moves are inconsistent with their own domestic policy needs. Both market experience and Bank for International Settlements research1 show that Asia’s regional central banks have ‘unwritten targets’ including the exchange rate, economic growth and bond yields.

These factors, in turn, affect domestic inflation. Furthermore, the regional authorities also target headline inflation alongside core inflation. All these are different from the Fed-style dual mandates that put core inflation and maximum employment on an equal footing.

Exchange rate is paramount in Asia

Among these policy targets, the exchange rate is of primary importance for Asian authorities. Fed rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential between Asia and the US and if exchange rates depreciate markedly, this could amplify the inflationary effects on the region’s economies and financial conditions. To contain that potentially greater impact, the regional central banks will follow the Fed or even react more strongly than the Fed’s original move.

However, other than Indonesia and the Philippines, most of Asia’s economies have large current account surpluses (see Exhibit 2) that provide strong support for the region’s exchange rates, thus lessening the pressure to follow the Fed’s rate hikes. The recent downward pressures on Asia’s exchange rates mostly reflect a risk-off sentiment arising from the speed and breadth of the global rates sell-off rather than poor fundamentals and wider interest-rate differentials.

Secondly, despite nine months of high oil prices, core inflation has remained close to, or even lower than, target in most Asian economies, with the notable exceptions of Vietnam and the Philippines (see Exhibit 3). Subsidies have so far helped Asia to contain oil price-induced inflation and the region’s central banks to stay put at low fiscal costs to their treasuries.

However, if the oil shock lasts longer, fiscal pressure will increase and eventually prompt Asian governments to let fuel prices adjust accordingly, unleashing inflationary pressures. This would, in turn, likely prompt regional rate hikes in the wake of those by the Fed.

The bottom lines

The macroeconomic backdrop suggests that Asia is far from being in a broad-based interest-rate hike cycle. Policy rates are currently being driven by the impact of rising oil prices on domestic inflation.

A hawkish Fed may lead to a potential tightening bias in Asia, but it will not likely prompt widespread rate hikes unless interest-rate differentials between Asia and the US result in large and persistent regional exchange-rate depreciation.

Data sources: CEIC, Trading Economics, as of 10 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

[1] The Expansionary Lower Bound: Contractionary Monetary Easing and the Trilemma, Bank for International Settlements, 2019.
