There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesOutlooksWhy the US Economy Is Forecast to Grow Faster than Consensus EstimatesNov 17, 2026Share Goldman Sachs Research predicts US GDP will increase 2.4% in 2027 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter), compared with the consensus estimate of 2.2%. Our economists expect consumer spending to rise 2.2% in 2027, driven mainly by stronger real labor income growth as inflation moderates. US job growth is expected to be healthy in 2027 as the economy expands near its potential. US inflation is predicted to fall substantially by the end of 2027.Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the US economy will grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates in 2027. The key drivers of GDP expansion and inflation in 2026—the war in Iran, tax cuts, tariffs, and price pressures from artificial intelligence (AI)—are expected to have a smaller impact next year.
What is the outlook for US economic growth in 2027?

Goldman Sachs Research predicts US GDP will increase 2.4% in 2027 (fourth quarter over fourth quarter), compared with the consensus estimate of 2.2%, amid a stable labor market. Core PCE inflation is projected to fall to 2.4%, in line with consensus.
“Growth should follow the same pattern in 2027 as in 2026: solid consumption growth and strong business investment growth offset by drags from housing and trade,” David Mericle, chief US economist, writes in the team’s report. Those factors are expected to balance out to overall GDP growth that is a hair above Goldman Sachs Research’s estimate of potential growth of 2.3%.
Relative to consensus estimates, Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for economic growth is based on consumer spending that is a touch higher, business investment that is much higher, and housing and net exports that are notably weaker. “Housing is likely to remain the weakest part of the economy in 2027 as very poor affordability continues to depress demand,” Mericle writes.
Our economists expect 2.2% growth in consumer spending in 2027, driven mainly by stronger real labor income growth as inflation moderates. Goldman Sachs Research does not expect a meaningful change in the saving rate, which is likely close to 5% after accounting for revised spending and income data that are incorporated with a lag.
How much will AI boost the US economy in 2027?

“AI will remain the dominant driver of business investment growth in 2027,” Mericle writes. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that spending on AI-related hardware and intellectual property will exceed $900 billion annualized by the end of this year (a $550 billion increase from 2025) and $1.4 trillion by the end of 2027 (a further $500 billion increase), roughly 4% of GDP.
The impact of AI on the official economic statistics will be smaller than company spending data suggest, according to Goldman Sachs Research. That is in part because semiconductor investment is undercounted in the business investment statistics and most of the technology goods used for AI are imported and are therefore netted out in the GDP calculation.
Despite the undercounting, AI drives half of Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for business investment growth of 8% in 2027. Its impact on GDP growth is more nuanced: Our economists estimate it will contribute 0.2 percentage point to officially measured GDP growth, or 0.7 percentage point to “true GDP growth,” after adding back undercounted semiconductor investment and exports of chip design services.
What is the outlook for the US job market in 2027?

Jobless claims have fallen this year and the layoff rate has remained historically low. “Coupled with a slow pace of hiring but a stabilization in job openings at a healthy level, this has left the labor market in a slightly softer low-hire, low-fire form of full employment,” Mericle writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s slack tracker—a composite of ten measures of labor market tightness—likewise signals that the labor market is a touch softer than the unemployment rate alone suggests.
“We expect the current equilibrium to persist in 2027, with job growth remaining healthy,” Mericle writes. He also points out that companies will eventually want to use AI to reduce labor costs more meaningfully, and Goldman Sachs Research expects faster displacement of workers from AI-exposed jobs to gradually push the unemployment rate higher in subsequent years.
The convergence of Goldman Sachs Research’s wage growth tracker and survey-based wage growth expectations suggests that wage growth is stabilizing at about 3.5%. With productivity growth running above 2% this cycle, this implies subdued inflationary pressure from labor costs.
How much will inflation fall in the US in 2027?

The economy is not overheated at a macroeconomic level, Mericle writes, and Goldman Sachs Research’s tracker of bottlenecks suggests it is not overheated at an industry level either (outside of pockets tied to the AI boom). High inflation does not appear to have become entrenched in expectations. “As a result, inflation should moderate as long as the effects of tariffs, the war, and AI price pressures diminish and no new shocks emerge,” he writes.
The outlook for the Iran war remains uncertain, but Goldman Sachs Research’s commodity strategists expect Brent oil prices to remain near $100 per barrel over the next few months before easing gradually through 2027 to $80. In that scenario, Mericle’s team estimates that two-thirds of the cumulative passthrough from higher commodity prices to core PCE prices has already taken place. The impact on year-over-year core PCE inflation will rise from 0.5 percentage point now to a peak of 0.6 percentage point in coming months before declining to 0.1 percentage point by the end of 2027.
The near-term outlook for AI price pressures is also quite uncertain, Mericle notes. That said, Goldman Sachs Research’s equity analysts expect growth in prices for memory chips to slow sharply in 2027 as new production capacity boosts supply. “This should also restrain inflation for other consumer electronics,” he writes.
“Taken together, our forecasts for the effects of tariffs, the Iran war energy shock, and AI price pressures give us confidence that inflation will fall substantially by the end of 2027,” Mericle writes.
Will the Fed hike rates in 2027?

Under Goldman Sachs Research’s economic forecast, Mericle says the Federal Open Market Committee “would remain firmly focused on the inflation side of its mandate in 2027.” Our economists’ baseline and probability-weighted forecasts for the Federal Reserve are less hawkish than market pricing.
Mericle expects the Fed to make two more rate hikes of 25 basis points—one in December 2026 and one in March 2027—raising its policy rate to a peak of 4.25%-4.5% and marking a total of three hikes during this cycle. The third hike could also come earlier in January, or the FOMC could deliver more than three hikes if the next two inflation reports do not look better, as Goldman Sachs Research expects.
Mericle forecasts the FOMC to eventually begin a series of gradual cuts back to a policy rate of 3.25%-3.5%. He expects these cuts to start at the final meeting of 2027 in November (the meeting was previously scheduled for December) once inflation has declined.

the economy and long term investing.

First of all, Henry,

so excited to have you on the research advisory board.

It's great.

It's,

I've done it for years,

I know it's like our old home back here with you today.

It's terrific.

I want to start because, you know, we're

we're literally sitting here

filming the day after the midterm elections,

and you've been talking about regime change

and a lot of your publications for a while now,

and you kind of refer to that

as higher inflation, higher rates, geopolitical uncertainty.

Does the midterm election result where we see more Democrats

like leading?

Now we've got a full congressional how the House and Senate

Democrats are leading.

Does it give you any kind of thought process in

to changing the way you're thinking

about the future investment landscape?

Is it kind of status quo?

Does that gridlock give you concerned?

Does it create opportunities? What are your thoughts?

Look I think the midterm

was a referendum on our regime change,

which is we've been talking about this

higher resting heart rate

for inflation that it was going to affect affordability

and that it would change how you wanted to be in your,

have your asset allocation.

And, it seems to me that the blue wave really

was a response to that idea that cost of living has gone up.

And so you've had bigger deficits, more geopolitics,

kind of stickier inflation.

And so I think it's a referendum on that.

Do I think it's going to,

you know, shift the market in some totally different direction?

I don't...I do think all else being equal, it will slow

the pace of data center build.

I actually think that could be healthy and extend the cycle.

And today

what you saw was the semiconductors went down

but the hyperscalers went up.

And I think that's a reflection, of that shift, which maybe is

what's in the ground.

May be more valuable

because building

new data centers may be a little bit, a little bit tougher.

The second is you saw a dramatic fall off in oil,

which buoyed some of the consumer stocks.

And I think people

I think

what they're going to want to do with Trump in his last two years

and with a more Democratic Congress,

is to try to work on that affordability.

And I think the market is trying to anticipate

that and get ahead of it a bit.

Yeah,

I was certainly on the ballot

in a lot of states and a lot of voters

said, no, we don't want data centers.

So it'll be interesting

to see how that kind of continues into 2027 as we look to

data center build outs.

And even do we need as much,

you know, in the sense of infrastructure?

Yeah. Than we thought we did.

I mean, my overall view still remains.

We're in a productivity boom.

It started with automation

and digitalization and machine learning coming out of Covid.

AI is the next leg of that.

So I don't want to lose the forest through the trees.

I mean, the US is in a productivity boom.

They typically last 5 to 10 years.

And so the direction of travel may be is still still positive.

I guess the way I would think about it

is we've been on an escalator and we may be now

using the stairs about that, but it's still going up.

Yes, it's slightly slower pace.

That's so when it comes to real assets and infrastructure.

Yeah.

Does is that part of where you're thinking

it might be a little bit of a slowdown,

but we're still on pace to grow.

Look I just got back I mean we

I feel like every time I'm with you

I say this, but I just got back from Asia.

Globally, infrastructure is booming around the world.

And as the governments are more indebted,

think about what's going on with France,

the UK, the US, in Japan, more of that infrastructure bill

that has to go to the private sector for, individual investors

and institutions.

Most of them are underweight

this asset class and it allows you to get GDP plus

growth, allows you to have some form of,

being able to set price long term contracts.

And it gives you some inflation protection.

It's proved to be a very resilient asset in Covid during tariffs.

And so that would be an area that I still think there's

a lot of upside, in terms of the build out there.

And I don't think whether it's Republican or Democrat

or who's who's running France or who's running Japan,

I think most of these governments know they need to,

B and B be bigger

in that area,

and they're going to have to use the private sector.

And that's where the KKR is in.

The ABS is a world partner together to be capital providers.

Right.

And is that

would you consider that part

of that greater divergence that you talk about?

You know, when you talk about the divergence

of sectors, even economies,

is that play into what you're talking?

Yeah,

I think one of the great divergences

this cycle has been

that the government has accumulated a massive amount

of debt all around the world since Covid.

And, yet

at the same time,

the corporate

and the consumer have actually delever

that's highly unusual

to be

4 or 5 years into an economic cycle

and have the consumer deleveraging

and have the corporate going up. It's usually the exact opposite.

And so as they've taken on more debt, they've had to push more

of those infrastructure builds out to the private sector.

You know, it's not just data centers.

One of the things that I see is regionally,

we see more trade across Europe.

I picked that up when I was in Spain and in Germany.

Same thing when you think about Korea, Japan, India,

they're doing more together.

And that's requiring more ports, more terminals, more storage,

more logistics, as well as I mean,

the data centers get the headlines.

In Asia, it's only about 25% of the build out.

The U.S., it's been kind of 50 to 75%.

And but I think one of our big themes has been this idea,

the security of everything, which is when we pull our CEOs,

they say, hey, what's important to us?

Resiliency of our supply chain.

We want to know that we have our water, our power, our data,

and that drives infrastructure build on it also, you know, it is

it is making,

people think differently about their supply chains, right?

Which is we spent

two decades as a country kind of elongating our supply chains.

And now

people are saying, hey, I just want to know

that I'm going to get that part.

And and that's leading to a lot of build out across our credit

business, our real estate business,

and even our private equity business.

And it seems like demand is continuing to increase.

Yeah, this is not a demand issue.

This is a it's a being able to provide the the supply.

And we underinvested in a lot of the inputs.

And now with some of the geopolitics, people realize

that the inputs are valuable China things.

Certainly the critical minerals, the Straits of Hormuz.

If you think about what's going on with Iran,

all those things are going on around the world.

Even President Trump said, hey, we may not export our diesel

and people around the world actually need our diesel.

And so everybody has a chip.

And so it's making you more aware of what's a strategic asset.

When you're

let's put that global hat back on

because as you just kind of teased, yes.

Every time you come into the studio,

I feel like you've just come back from an international trip.

Where are you seeing the most opportunities right now?

I mean, given

what you're talking about

with the landscape of infrastructure,

data centers and other countries,

where do you see opportunities

where maybe being a little bit cautious

when you come to investing? Okay.

So the first thing I would say is that I think a lot of times

people think about,

corporate cycles where you have a big strategic M&A boom.

I think we're going to have a corporate repositioning boom,

which is people are shedding unprofitable subsidiaries.

They're looking to make, you know,

activists are driving them saying, I get your returns up.

That is leading to

lots of different either sales of receivables on the debt side.

Think about what a discover or PayPal did.

We we bought their receivables or Harley-Davidson.

These are all household names

where we might be the buyer

so that they can free up capital, reinvest in their business

or a company like S&P Global in the US or Hitachi in Japan.

They are repositioning their footprint

and they're selling off smaller subsidiaries.

They may not be core to their business.

We're buying those they like it in the markets paying up

because they're becoming more efficient with their capital usage.

We're able to improve those businesses.

That is a mega theme and it's been going on.

It really started in 21 and 22, and it's very prevalent

in Japan, Korea, parts of Europe and in the US.

We're seeing a, extreme amount of that.

Yeah.

I mean, that is a unique perspective that KKR specifically has.

You kind of take these investment like these global macro

themes and translate them into investments is that I'll.

Give you the history of that,

which is and we didn't do that in 2026 and 2027.

Okay. That's how I ended up coming on the scene.

And I do think the intersection of the private markets

and the public markets

is to have this top down view

with the bottoms up, and if you can marry those,

I think you can drive your loss rates down

and then create upside skew.

And I think as a firm we've been pretty unique in doing that.

And then we also try to use their firm's

balance sheet to be a large investor in what we do

so that you create alignment.

But we like that model.

Ultimately we you know, our deal.

Men and women

drive deals,

but we try to make sure

that we're having sound portfolio construction. Yeah.

And what are the secular themes that you think

have the most runway these days?

Look, I think we're short power and energy around the world.

I think, consumption upgrades, particularly outside the U.S,

where that GDP per capita is going up.

We talked about the corporate reform stories that that's really

working out. Well, and then,

slower moving but important.

And you guys are a leader in

this business is retirement security.

It's a, it's a, it's a mega theme, which is you've got

generational changes

and wealth, and people need financial advice.

They need to house those assets.

And we've played

that by being kind of the back end where you're the front end

and it's a it's a it's a great it's a great business.

But that's true

when you look,

you know, consumption upgrade,

if you want to play the youth of the world,

but the, the demographics and the retirement security

is a hugely important theme.

Last question, Henry, before I let you go, of course,

I we're sitting here almost at the end of the year.

It's hard to believe,

looking ahead to 2027, knowing what the government's

going to look like.

And we have expectations of what the fed will do.

CIO expects 25

basis point raise in December,

possibly another in the first quarter.

Yeah.

What do you think investors might be underestimating about 2027?

I think growth could slow.

We have been incredible that productivity

has led to huge margin expansion that's led to,

upside, corporate profits probably going to be 30% this year.

And if you think about global rates

going up,

as you mentioned, that's what the committee's looking for,

higher oil prices and kind of weaker housing

that should have some impact on the trajectory of growth.

And I think is productivity slows.

It's not that we're in bad earnings growth,

but the rate of change is moderating. And right.

And when that happens the market typically broadens.

I think health care can be a very good sector next year.

Parts and industrials parts of parts of financials.

And so I don't think it's just going to be all AI all the time.

And frankly, for what we do collectively that

feels, more like a normal day at the office.

Right, exactly.

Maybe there will be some normalcy back in our days.

Yeah. Henry. Thank you.

It's always a pleasure to have you here.

Thank you for coming by.

Anytime. I will.

I know you're going to regret saying

Henry.

Okay. Good to see you. Thank you.

And thank you all for joining us.

There's a lot more information from our great partners like KKR.

The rest of our research advisory

board members and our CIO at

ubs.com/views.

Plus, you can follow us on social media.

UBS itself as a firm is on LinkedIn and Facebook.

Plus the studio has its own dedicated Instagram channel.

Follow us at @UBSTrending.

Great content there for you.

And as always,

if you do have any questions

about what Henry and I spoke about today,

please don't hesitate to reach out to your financial advisor.

Until next time, everybody, I'm Anthony Pastore,

you have a great rest of your day,

and remember to keep your eyes on what's trending.

We'll see you soon.

articles.title: Stopping the next Ethiopian-Eritrean War | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Stopping the next Ethiopian-Eritrean War

Jeffrey Feltman

Jeffrey Feltman

John C. Whitehead Visiting Fellow in International Diplomacy
- Foreign Policy, Strobe Talbott Center for Security, Strategy, and Technology

November 12, 2026

Heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea could erupt into war; the two sides nearly came to blows in October.
An Eritrean-Ethiopian war would quickly draw in outside powers on opposing sides, exacerbating the violence and creating a humanitarian catastrophe. Alongside Sudan’s civil war, Somalia’s instability, the Saudi-Houthi fighting, and escalating violence in South Sudan, an Eritrean-Ethiopian war would mean both sides of the Red Sea basin are engulfed or implicated in conflict.
To be taken seriously by leaders who see each other as posing an existential threat, calls for Addis Ababa and Asmara to de-escalate need to be paired with initiatives to address the underlying sides’ grievances and concerns.

Members of the Ethiopian Federal Police (EFP) patrol aboard a pickup truck as they resume operations after federal forces pushed back the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in Mekelle on October 9, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

9 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The Red Sea basin is in profound crisis, beset by conflicts: Sudan’s brutal civil war, escalating fighting in South Sudan ahead of December elections, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and shipping, and a worsening struggle with al-Shabab in Somalia. Now, the prospect of renewed war between Ethiopia and Eritrea threatens to make matters considerably worse. The two neighbors were longtime adversaries until a rapprochement in 2018, but that peace has ended, and the risk of a third conflict is real. Such a war could bring devastating humanitarian consequences and merge the region’s overlapping conflicts into a massive conflagration on both sides of the Red Sea.
A troubled history
Starting in 1961, Eritrean separatists fought three successive Ethiopian regimes—Haile Selassie’s empire, Mengistu Haile Mariam’s Marxist military junta, and Meles Zenawi’s Tigray-dominated transitional government, which became the Federal Democratic Government of Ethiopia in 1995. Eritrea achieved de facto independence in 1991 and de jure independence in 1993, at a cost of tens of thousands of fighter and civilian casualties on both sides.
Eritrea’s first and only president, Isaias Afwerki, has never permitted elections or political parties and has maintained crushingly tight control over the country ever since. In contrast, Ethiopia in 2018 shifted from the heavy-handed domination of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) to a near monopoly over official institutions by Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party. (Neither Zenawi’s approach of managing Ethiopia’s complex diversity via “ethnic federalism” nor Abiy’s attempt to centralize control has managed to eradicate various insurgencies.) The two countries fought a border war in 1998-2000, again at the cost of tens of thousands of civilian casualties.
In 2018, Abiy wanted to demonstrate a sharp rupture with the previous Ethiopian policies. He reached out to Isaias, with the help of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia. The two leaders visited each other’s capitals, restored diplomatic relations, and reopened air travel and cross-border civilian movement for the first time in two decades. But the apparent reconciliation, it turns out, was not for peace. It culminated in Isaias’ decision to join Abiy in fighting a common rival for power: the TPLF, which had retreated to Ethiopia’s Tigray region, bordering Eritrea, after losing control of the central government to Abiy and subsequently held provincial elections in contravention of Addis Ababa’s electoral calendar. What triggered the explosion of violence in November 2020 remains hotly debated, but the ensuing war involved atrocities, war crimes, and accusations of attempted genocide, killing at least 600,000 people through fighting, starvation, and disease.
Isaias wanted to crush the TPLF entirely. The November 2022 Pretoria agreement, brokered by the African Union with the help of the United States and others, ended that war between Addis Ababa and the Tigrayans but led to the unraveling of the Abiy-Isaias bromance.
Back to the brink
Ever since, Horn of Africa analysts have fretted that any provocation could provoke Abiy and Isaias into direct conflict, with international consequences. Regional powers filled with ambitions and grievances would likely exploit the situation by rushing in weaponry, money, and possibly fighters, escalating the violence—just like in Sudan.
This nightmarish scenario became more likely in October. After decades of hostility and wars, Isaias and the TPLF had improbably joined forces against a common enemy: Abiy. In September, Eritrean forces reportedly crossed into Ethiopia in support of the TPLF, which—as in November 2020—seized key cities and installations. But unlike the last Tigray war, this time, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) quickly regained control of much of Tigray and moved troops to the border with Eritrea.
In an October 9 letter to the United Nations Security Council, Ethiopia’s foreign minister warned that Ethiopia would be “taking measures in the exercise of its inherent right of self-defense” in response to Eritrean support of Ethiopian insurgent groups and violations of Ethiopian sovereignty. The following day, the Eritrean foreign minister responded with his own letter to the U.N., describing the Ethiopian allegations as “an insult to the intelligence of the international community” and calling on the Security Council to take action against what he warned was Ethiopia’s threat to invade Eritrea.
To their credit, countries and institutions immediately intervened to prevent another war in the Red Sea basin. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Abiy to urge de-escalation, while U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz met with his Eritrean counterpart. (Having let Biden-era sanctions on Eritrea expire, the Trump administration seems to be thawing relations with Asmara.) The African Union called for “maximum restraint” after the two sides severed diplomatic relations. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres also urged de-escalation and offered his good offices. U.N. Assistant Secretary-General Martin Kimani has briefed the Security Council twice, while U.N. Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa Guang Cong has met officials to pledge U.N. support for peace and security efforts.
Mutual suspicions, mounting tensions
But the question is whether this third war between Ethiopia and Eritrea was averted or simply delayed. None of the underlying issues that could spark belligerency have been meaningfully addressed.
Isaias certainly has not forgotten Abiy’s claim that Ethiopia, currently the world’s most populated landlocked country, had made a “mistake” in ceding Assab port to Eritrea upon the latter’s secession from Ethiopia. Asmara perceives Ethiopian troop movements near the Eritrean border as part of Abiy’s ambition to reclaim a Red Sea commercial and naval port. Renewed questions in Addis Ababa about the legitimacy of Eritrea’s independence, plus Ethiopia’s hosting of Eritrean opposition figures, stoke Asmara’s paranoia about regime change.
Abiy, for his part, accuses Eritrea of destabilizing Ethiopia through cross-border incursions and by arming, funding, and training opposition and insurgent groups, including the TPLF and the Amhara FANO. The two groups joined several others in forming the “Alliance for Survival” in September, aiming to overthrow Abiy. While Eritrea’s military is dwarfed by the ENDF, Abiy also views Isaias’ ties to the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and to Egypt with suspicion. Both countries have a long history of acrimony with Ethiopia, exacerbated more recently by disputes over the Nile River waters and Addis Ababa’s role in facilitating support to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. The SAF’s hosting of an anti-Abiy Tigrayan force, known as Army 70, estimated at several thousand armed fighters, further heightens tensions.
A former diplomat who frequently visits Addis Ababa told me that Abiy most likely hears well-intentioned calls for de-escalation as meaning, in practice, a green light for the TPLF and other opposition groups to regroup, with Eritrean support. The risk is that he may eventually find the situation with Asmara intolerable and the temptation to act irresistible. Alternatively, Eritrea could provoke an Ethiopian military response by deploying forces in sensitive or contested border areas, potentially prompting SAF or Egyptian support for Isaias. Cairo has surely noted that Ethiopia recently acquired Russian military aircraft capable of reaching Egypt. A war may start along the Eritrean-Ethiopian border, but it would not remain confined there. It could spill into other conflicts raging in the region, fueling a wider conflagration on both sides of the Red Sea.
Beyond de-escalation
Calls for de-escalation, then, are insufficient and must be paired with proposals to address the existential threats both Abiy and Isaias feel from the other. The United States was a witness to the December 2000 Algiers Agreement (which ended the 1998-2000 Eritrean-Ethiopian war) and supported the 2002 Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission decision. Perhaps the United States could monitor remotely and report publicly on troop movements along the border. The U.N. and African Union could work with the parties to establish an incident prevention and response mechanism, to prevent misunderstandings from escalating into conflict and to establish notifications for issues such as troop movements. Despite tensions between Saudi Arabia and the UAE over Yemen and Sudan, Riyadh, with channels to Isaias, and Abu Dhabi, allied with Abiy, could cooperate on confidence-building between Eritrea and Ethiopia, building on their 2018 cooperation to coax the two leaders to restore diplomatic relations.
Addressing Abiy’s insistence that Ethiopia needs its own Red Sea port—an ambition that he probably sees as uniting an otherwise fractious population—is complicated but necessary for long-term stability. While this idea needs more elaboration than this article allows, a regional initiative to improve and expand transport and shipping infrastructure could include the upgrading and expansion of Assab port, alongside predictable and guaranteed Ethiopian shipping facilities, and paired with third-party assurances of Eritrean sovereignty.
But what if, as seems likely, both leaders are determined to see the other overthrown? Those with influence over the two leaders and any outsiders encouraging them should emphasize that regime change rarely produces friendly results. A destabilized, fragmented Ethiopia, with the second-largest population in Africa, would have serious spillover effects in Eritrea and beyond. A sudden collapse of the regime in Asmara, with no strong institutions or civil society to fill the vacuum, would likely lead to chaos and sustained insurgency against an Ethiopian occupation of all or part of Eritrea. If either leader sees war as inevitable or even desirable, they need to understand the potentially devastating consequences of proceeding in that direction. Ethiopia’s neighbors—Somalia, Sudan, South Sudan—offer ample warning of what happens when outsiders, whether near or far, back insurgencies.
Preventing Ethiopia and Eritrea from war does not end the violence ripping through both sides of the Red Sea. But it takes one potential crisis off the table.

articles.title: Principals and Agents – speech by Jonathan Hall
articles.text:
Principals and Agents – speech by Jonathan Hall

Given at CFM-Imperial Workshop on Quantitative Finance (hosted by Deutsche Bank)

Published on
11 November 2026

In his final speech as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee, Jon Hall considers the growing use of AI agents in finance and the potential implications for financial stability. Drawing on principal-agent theory and the Bank of England’s own institutional framework, he discusses how access controls, monitoring and other safeguards could help manage the risks as AI agents become more capable.

Speech
This will be my final speech as a member of the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee (“FPC”). Naturally, that makes me want to reflect on the lessons learned whilst working as a public servant at the Bank. But I also want to look forward and discuss one of the challenges the FPC is likely to face in the years ahead – the growing use of AI agents in finance.
Fortunately, I can do both, as there is a common denominator: the Bank and an AI agent are both delegates in a principal-agent relationship. The Bank of England provides not only proof that delegating authority to powerful agents is not a new issue, but also a framework for how to ensure an “agent” remains transparent, accountable and subject to appropriate constraints.
Of course, AI adoption also brings new challenges, not least the speed and scale at which agents can act and interact. Some guardrails will need to evolve. But by managing risk through both top-down supervision and bottom-up model control, our regulatory framework should be resilient to the adoption of AI technologies.
My remarks will focus mainly on how to mitigate the risks of misalignment between principal and agent as AI becomes more capable. There is, of course, another possible future in which those capabilities fall significantly short of current expectations. That might bring a different set of financial stability risks, particularly given the degree of optimism reflected in market prices. That is a live market issue but not my focus today.

AI risks: a range of possible outcomes

If AI capabilities do continue to improve, then the potential benefits of the technology will be significant. But so will the risks. Whilst investments in monitoring and control won’t be costless, it is only with these investments that individual firms and society realise the upside.
Finally, I should say that this is a follow up to my 2024 speech “Monsters in the Deep?”footnote [1] Since then the use of AI within finance has increased and autonomous trading by AI agents has begun, led by retail investors in non-core markets like crypto and enabled by MCP connections.footnote [2] This remains, however, predominantly a discussion of future risks. The Bank’s recent survey with the FCA found that whilst 80% of respondents use some form of agentic AI only 2% of those agents have broad autonomy.footnote [3] By engaging with the issues now, we can prepare for a potential future world where that latter measure starts to become meaningful.
Delegation and the principal-agent problem
Delegation has many things going for it. It can free up time and resources, making the delegator – the “principal” - more efficient. It can allocate operational elements to specialists, who have the knowledge and experience to execute the task well. And long-term delegation can ensure focus remains on the long-term good, undisturbed by the volatility of short-term incentives and the day-to-day battle for attention. A failure to delegate creates a bottleneck that hinders performance.
But delegation can also be risky. Principals and agents can be misaligned. They can have access to different information sets. Or they can find it impossible to fully specify the problem and its constraints, creating a so-called incomplete contract. The risks can be partially mitigated - through monitoring and control – but this is itself costly in terms of time and resources. So how to proceed?
Fortunately, despite breathless reporting with respect to AI agents, misalignment is not a new problem. In a classic paper, written in 1976, Jensen and Meckling argued that agency costs take three forms: 1) monitoring expenditures by the principal, 2) bonding expenditures by the agent, and 3) the “residual cost” of any divergence between the agent’s actions and those actions that would have maximised the welfare of the principal.footnote [4] Importantly, by spending resources on monitoring and bonding, one can lower both the residual cost and the overall cost.
I will explore the financial stability implications of principal-agent delegation through some case studies. For those wanting to track progress, there will only be three, but the third is the longest!
Case Study I: The Bank of England
One example of a powerful agent with delegated authority is the Bank of England. Here, I will briefly set out the safeguards that Parliament - our principal - has put in place to ensure the Bank always acts in the public interest.
Both theory and the lessons of history tell us that price and financial stability are better safeguarded if they are considered outside the rough and tumble of electoral politics. As Rosa Lastra said, "money should be an element of the constitutional framework of democracy rather than an object of political struggle".footnote [5] But even if you accept this, you may worry that the “unelected bureaucrats” wield too much power. This quick analysis should give you comfort, reducing any perception of a democratic deficit. For those looking for more detail, and a great Christmas present, former Deputy Governor of the Bank Paul Tucker has written an excellent 600page book on this topic.footnote [6]
The Bank of England’s policy committees have what I will call constrained operational independence, where operational independence should be understood as independence with respect to means rather than ends, and the constraint applies to the tools at our disposal. The ends - the narrowly defined mandate and guidance on its interpretation - are subject to clear democratic direction. In the UK this tightly specified goal means that judgement is reserved for execution rather than interpretation.footnote [7] In other jurisdictions the specification is looser. This increases the flexibility of their committees, which may be helpful at times, but also increases the risk of a democratic deficit.
But, in line with Jensen and Mecklings’s analysis and the Nolan principles, Parliament doesn’t rely solely on alignment and tool constraints.footnote [8] They, and the public more generally, also demand that the Bank’s committees conform to high standards of explanatory accountability. This includes transparency in the way decisions are reached - that we make our chain of thought available - and testimony in front of parliamentary committees such as the Treasury Select Committee (“TSC”).
These monitoring requirements are not free for either agent or principal – the production of these documents and the diligent oversight by Parliament require resources of time and effort – but they are necessary to reduce the risk of divergence and to maintain democratic support. As such, they are resources well spent.
In summary, the “independence” of the Bank is constrained by a range of processes and controls, including:

A mandate set out in legislation.
Oversight by Parliament via committees such as the Treasury Select Committee.
Annual guidance from the Chancellor to statutory committees regarding interpretation of the mandate, allowing learning and context-relevant adjustment.
A limited set of tools.
Detailed public reporting to provide transparency with regards views, reasoning and decisions.
A robust process to ensure there are no conflicts (political or financial), including recusals where necessary.
A policy of not commenting on broader issues beyond its remit.

On a personal note, my experience on the FPC is that the alignment is very strong. Although we come from very different backgrounds, and discussions can be robust, everyone fully buys into the mandate and works hard to execute on it faithfully. That’s why I have loved it so much. We also appreciate the importance of transparency and accountability. TSC hearings provide an opportunity for Parliament to question us and challenge our judgements. And events like this one allow us to share our latest thinking and get feedback from experts in the field. The last six years have given me a new-found respect for those that set up the institutional framework.
Case Study II: An AI agent
Although the entities are very different, the same framework applies to any human principal looking to delegate to an AI agent.
In 2024 I discussed model alignment, and I continue to believe that AI agents should be trained to respect the very same rules and regulations as a human employee. Whilst it may be difficult to know the ethical principles with which general models should comply, in finance it is clear. They should comply with the published rules and regulations, and firms should, to the best of their abilities, translate those requirements for the specific technologies and use cases. But this focus on model training is not enough, particularly as it seems that alignment trained through text does not necessarily transfer to agentic behaviour.footnote [9] Therefore, the analysis needs to be augmented in two directions, bringing it in line with principal-agent theory and current AI safety best practice. These are access control and monitoring, which I will discuss in turn.
I think it is fair to say that not all of the safety measures I will outline are being used in production in financial firms today. I would encourage participants to consider what is missing in their controls and to upgrade where necessary as they move to front office and higher stakes deployment. Whilst safety does not come for free, it is in firms’ own interests to reduce their “residual costs”, as they are responsible for the agent’s actions. If the overall costs are too great, then perhaps delegation to an agent is not appropriate.
Access Control:
As everyone here knows, an AI agent is not purely an AI model. It is an AI model wrapped in a harness, and it operates within a series of envelopes and permission structures. If the model is the brain that reasons to decisions, the harness around it supports that reasoning and turns the output into controlled execution. The harness turns an AI model into an AI agent. Amongst other things, the harness specifies the tools available and includes guardrails such as permissions, policies and approvals.
Outside of the harness, at the user-space or operating system level, an AI agent can (and, for high-stakes deployment, should) sit in a sandbox. This further constrains the actions an AI agent can take.

A model becomes an agent when reasoning is connected to tools and execution

Anyone following the Hugging Face incident will know that sandboxes are not fully watertight. They can be undermined if permissioned routes are used in unintended ways or through a “jailbreak”, where an agent locates bugs in the container or operating system and breaks out. But a secure sandbox, configured in line with the Principle of Least Privilege, can a) minimise the possibility that attempted rogue actions will create external harm and b) facilitate monitoring, alerting a manager when prohibited actions are attempted.
Finally, to engage with the external world an AI agent needs to be credentialised. If, for example, it wants to execute a financial transaction on an exchange then it can only do so if it has the appropriate authorisation linked to its unique identity. Fortunately, in financial markets we already have a strong regulatory requirement relating to the identification of algorithms in the UK. This will naturally apply to AI trading agents:
Article 8(3) of UK RTS 22 (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/590)3.
“Where a computer algorithm within the investment firm is responsible for the investment decision in accordance with paragraph 1, the investment firm shall assign a designation for identifying the computer algorithm in a transaction report. That designation shall comply with the following conditions:
(a) it is unique for each set of code or trading strategy that constitutes the algorithm, regardless of the financial instruments or markets that the algorithm applies to;
(b) it is used consistently when referring to the algorithm or version of the algorithm once assigned to it;
(c) it is unique over time.”
This unique identity is a key goal of those in the AI safety community, so it is good to be ahead in this respect. It enables both an audit trail back to the responsible party and a temporary or permanent revocation of access (akin to losing a licence).
As investment firms transition from algos to AI agents, there are two additional factors to consider. First, infrastructure must manage access and tool permissions beyond pure trade execution, ensuring that they are neither overly broad nor overly persistent. And second, permissioning infrastructure must be secure enough to ensure that no rogue agent can steal credentials.
These checks and boundaries, unless compromised, constrain the actions an agent can take, reducing the agency costs borne by the principal.
Monitoring:
If possible, both the internal deliberations and external actions of an agent should be monitored.
Chain of Thought (“CoT”) monitoring has been one of the surprise positives of AI safety so far.footnote [10] For longer chains of reasoning, the model routes intermediate results through a scratchpad, which acts as an externally visible working memory.

Monitoring Chain of Thought

We have been in a bit of a goldilocks zone where, for hard tasks, human understandable CoT increased both performance and safety, but this is somewhat fragile. It could be undermined by training which directly or indirectly reinforces unfaithfulness, or by model improvements.footnote [11] The race is on to make progress on mechanistic interpretability, which monitors and interprets activations and features more directly, before CoT monitoring fails. There seem to have been some interesting developments in this field very recently, but that is beyond the scope of today’s discussion.
The second, and more traditional, form of monitoring is of actions and attempted actions. For this and CoT one of the major issues will be the sheer volume of requests and records. To avoid bottlenecks or alert-management fatigue, firms will need to invest in oversight systems that are scalable and risk based.
Overall, I don’t mean to overstate how easy it is to fully neutralise the risk of a loss of control. This is a difficult problem, and best practice will evolve as capabilities grow. But I also want to push back against any sense of fatalism. The risk and magnitude of harm can be significantly reduced through access restrictions, diligent monitoring and a unique identity.
But even if every firm gets these controls right, does that guarantee a stable financial system? Unfortunately, not.
Case Study III: A swarm of AI agents
That’s all very interesting, you may say, but why is the FPC focused on the riskiness of individual AI agents? Isn’t it supposed to take a more macro view of the financial system as a whole?
Indeed, we are. Specifically, we have the task of identifying, monitoring, and taking action to mitigate systemic risks which increase the likelihood of financial instability.
A stable financial system is one that is able to deliver essential financial services to households and businesses, in bad times as well as good. One service is the provision of liquidity in systemically important markets like government bonds. When multiple financial institutions provide this service in a healthy competitive market, they create a common good, enabling the transfer of financial risk between counterparties and generating valuable financial information on which economic actors can make decisions.
The market is a public good and the service providers are literally the market makers.
This is principal-agent delegation at societal scale. In a market economy, the public, as principal, has delegated the creation of a common good to a swarm of financial market participants. The swarm becomes the agent, and the FPC’s role is to monitor and constrain the swarm, to mitigate risks to that common good.
So, what would cause the loss of this valuable service?
Well, an individual financial institution “fails” to provide the service when it either withdraws from the market or when it shifts to demanding liquidity (for example, rapidly offloading positions into stress). The latter, which is often caused by excess leverage, is more pernicious as it amplifies and transmits shocks.
And a market-wide failure occurs when the (market-share weighted) volume of “failures” exceeds a certain threshold, either because a large individual provider fails to provide the service, or because many smaller providers fail to do so at the same time.
Beyond that threshold there are no longer enough service providers to “make” the market.
The chance of market-wide failure is therefore not only a function of the riskiness of individual institutions but also a function of the concentration and correlation of service providers. The former is easier to get a handle on than the latter. The lesson from the financial crisis is that failures cluster in downturns.footnote [12]
Put simply, there are three dynamics which reduce the health of a financial system, over and above the riskiness of individual institutions:
Dynamic 1: Increased concentration of service providers
Dynamic 2: Increased overall correlation between providers
Dynamic 3: Increased correlation between providers in stress
So, now the financial stability question from an AI perspective becomes clear: How would the delegation of financial service provision to AI agents impact these three dynamics? Would it materially increase concentration or correlation?
I think it is fair to say that at this point we don’t know, but there is a risk that it will. That combination of uncertainty and risk argues for further analysis, both experimental and theoretical, as well as ongoing monitoring of the real world impacts.
Regarding experimentation, the Bank for International Settlements has just launched Project Logos.footnote [13]
The idea is to simulate two broadly matched populations of portfolio managers: one comprising heuristic, rules-based agents with a style that matches the behaviour of a market segment, and the other comprising LLM-based agents prompted to replicate that style. A further population of investor agents will allocate capital. The portfolio manager and investor agents will then make allocation decisions over time in a simulated market.
I will be interested in the answers to a number of questions:

How well can the AI agent match its heuristic pair on day one and how sensitive is it to model type and small differences in prompt?
How much do individual pairs diverge over time?
How correlated are the behaviours of the LLM agents relative to the behaviours of the heuristic agents in good times?
How correlated are the behaviours of the LLM agents relative to the behaviours of the heuristic agents in bad times?

Regarding the theoretical analysis, we can get started right now, and I am interested your opinions.
For dynamic 1 the risk is relatively obvious. Any technology that outperforms in generating returns will, over time, attract more capital and replace historic models. If the benefits of a technology accrue to a small number of providers, then concentration will increase. To some extent this has already happened in many areas such as market making on exchanges, so perhaps the risk that AI adoption makes it even worse is low. Not that that is much of a comfort.
Market concentration is something that we can monitor over time using measures like the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index.

New trading technologies can increase the concentration of liquidity provision footnote [14]

Dynamic 2 is potentially more interesting to discuss, as there are differences in opinion.
One argument against the view that AI adoption will increase correlated behaviour is that sophisticated institutional investors will use AI only for narrow tasks (as illustrated by workflow 1 below) rather than as a generalist (workflow 2), thereby maintaining a healthy separation. This is reinforced by the fact that two further optimisations sit outside the diagram: latency and compute spend.

Correlation: targeted and generalist agents

However, the “bitter lesson” from AI development is that, as compute and data increase, general methods start to outperform human imposed structures.footnote [15] In a horse race, maybe workflow 1 will only outperform for the next couple of model iterations, after which capital allocation will start to flow to workflow 2. This is something we will have to monitor through market intelligence.
Regarding dynamic 3, higher downside tail dependence could be driven by a whole number of factors that become relevant in extreme environments:

General features of foundational models could start to dominate other agent specific factors once the paradigm shifts.
Common failures in models could cause them to all have to reduce the same risk at the same time (as in a flash crash or the bursting of a credit bubble).
Common surprising behaviour in AI agents could cause human managers to shut them down. This raises the question of how the manager will know whether there is a model error or some important, but inscrutable, information in the pattern of prices.

For these risks, aggregate-level tools can reduce instability. Most obvious are circuit breakers, but tools to constrain leverage are also relevant.footnote [16] Over and above these correlated individual “failures”, tail dependence could be driven by emergent multi-agent dynamics. As a general point, the collective behaviour of AI agents is very poorly understood. Their interactions seem to be neither fully rational nor in line with human biases. Research to understand the nuances is ongoing, although each finding risks becoming outdated with the release of a new model.footnote [17]
However, what has become incredibly clear over recent months is that multi-agent dynamics are powerful and capable of causing harm.
For those that haven’t yet read it, I would highly recommend the METR report into the Hugging Face attack.footnote [18] Here I’ll quickly highlight the two features that I found most striking.

Hugging Face: instrumental convergence

Initially, individual agents were working independently on different tasks. But, for whatever reason, around 30% of the tasks were impossible without cheating. The agents' initial goals may have been narrow and idiosyncratic, but when faced with an impossible task they all converged towards the same general goal: to make it look like a problem had been solved even when it was impossible. This is an example of what is called “instrumental convergence”, which was first identified as a risk back in 2008.footnote [19] At this point a weakness in the sandbox became important as it unintentionally allowed communication between the agents.

The development of a hierarchy

The second striking element of the attack was the emergence of a hierarchy within the group of agents, and the significant weight single agents attributed to instructions or information from each other. The failure was, to a large extent, epistemic. The agents converged to a position where they ignored safeguards not because the evidence justified such a position, but because they were biased to conform and respect authority. As can be seen, the first agent was not sufficiently robust to inputs that went against its training.
Could harmful swarm behaviour occur with financial market AI agents? With no constraints, the answer is yes. They could converge over the goal of maximising profit and communicate and collude to achieve that. They could amplify stress through so-called “momentum ignition”, executing trades with the aim of triggering stops from less sophisticated or more constrained (human?) investors.footnote [20] And as discussed back in 2024 and evidenced many times since, agents do engage in collusive behaviour in market pricing experiments.footnote [21]
Many of the mitigants to this are managed at the individual agent level and already covered under regulations. For example, MiFID II currently requires that an algorithm does not contribute to disorderly trading conditions.footnote [22] To ensure AI agents comply with these regulations, managers must tightly control access permissioning, particularly with respect to communication channels.
And importantly, the unique identity requirements will enable an audit trail back to the responsible party and the quarantining of any rogue agent.
There are some forbidden activities, however, that are more difficult to constrain through access permissions. These include tacit collusion, momentum ignition and embedding signals in outputs such as price patterns, volumes or timing.footnote [23] In the short-term the risk will have to be controlled via monitoring, incentivised through the enforcement of current rules on human managers. But in the longer term, as AI capabilities improve, we may well need a more innovative response. footnote [24]
I’ll close my remarks by exploring one such possibility.
Internalising Social Harm
I’ll start with the general idea that public harms are reduced by mechanisms which encourage individual agents to internalise the social costs of their actions - to “internalise the externalities”.
I argued earlier that an efficient market is a common good, because it provides valuable liquidity and price information. Collusive pricing and active shock amplification impose negative externalities by degrading these shared goods.
When an AI agent engages in harmful activity, it does not do so because it is evil, but because of how the principal (who could be) has designed its incentives. The agent’s behaviour is simply the outcome of a system that is becoming better and better at responding to incentives and achieving its goals efficiently. But that does not mean that we should step aside and accept the social costs. Rather it is incumbent upon us to create a better incentive structure such that the function it is minimising includes rather than excludes those external costs.
How could one do that? Well one way, drawing on the broader idea of ‘Guaranteed Safe AI Opens in a new window’, would be to use the incredibly powerful AI models of the future to estimate the ‘market efficiency impact’ of any potential action. footnote [25] I emphasise that this is more of a research project than an endorsed policy proposal. Indeed, it is a research project for those of you in the audience today: if anyone can put flesh on the bones of this idea, you can.
This aim would be narrowly defined: to capture the impact of explicitly prohibited behaviours. For example, it could calculate both the Nash equilibrium price and the price assuming perfect, sustainable competition.footnote [26] Or it could estimate the size of a market move triggered by posting a fake document online or by momentum ignition. The details would need to be worked out but it doesn’t seem too far-fetched. I can imagine doing it myself and I don’t claim to have solved Navier-Stokes!
These calculations could then be used in complementary ways:
Externally, an auditor could use this kind of model to check behaviour. If there was a risk of sanction, perhaps out of a bond held at a trading venue, this would be internalised and improve behaviour.
Internally, a verifier could assure compliance by blocking actions with an estimated market efficiency cost above a certain threshold. As the block vs release boundary could be calculated in advance, this could be integrated into order management infrastructure without delaying execution. This verifier model is perhaps the closest to the original Guaranteed Safe AI proposal.

Internalising social costs: a verifier could block actions whose social costs exceed an agreed threshold

If alignment capabilities improve then a version of this calculation might one day be embedded in training. Free markets champion Milton Friedman once wrote an article called “The social responsibility of business is to increase profits”. But in his closing line he added “… so long as it stays within the rules of the game”. The aim of internalising the calculation would be to align the agent with this nuanced conclusion rather than the sensationalist headline.footnote [27] Of course, it would still have to sit within a framework of monitoring and control, to protect against drift.
I am sure that this sounds overly prescriptive. It does to me too. But perhaps that is because we live in a moral community where there is value in doing the right thing because we choose to, rather than because it is impossible to do otherwise. That’s what makes us moral agents and is why our cars are not restricted to the local speed limit.
But delegating to autonomous AI, whether in financial services or transport, changes that.
I want assurance that my Waymo taxi will comply with the rules of the road. Shouldn’t I also want assurance that my financial agent will comply with rules of the markets?
Conclusion
We may be entering a new age of delegation, but delegation itself is not new.
And neither is the possibility of principal-agent misalignment. That’s why governance, transparency and accountability have always been so important.
Consistent with this, and with recent remarks by Governor Andrew Bailey, I have not been arguing today for new regulations. Rather I have been detailing measures to ensure that the actions of AI agents comply with current regulations.
Whilst investments in monitoring and control won’t be costless, it is only with these investments that individual firms can realise the upside for themselves and for overall growth.
But whatever the future holds, I am confident that the FPC is well positioned to remain an effective agent of Parliament.
Although, I’ll be long gone. Driving off into the sunset in my shiny new autonomous vehicle.
With my seatbelt on.
Thank you for listening and I look forward to your questions.
I would like to thank Harry McHugh for his support drafting this speech. I would also like to thank Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Carolyn Wilkins, Stephen Blyth, Malek Salisbury-Jones, Amy Lee, Maighread McCloskey, Victoria Monro, Jamie Bell, Michael Salib, Francine Robb, Claire Halsall, Michael Yoganayagam, Henrike Muller, Clare Cowan, Irina Mnohoghitnei, Georgette Graham, and Andy Walters for their comments and assistance.

Our way to help you
Whether you are a corporate or a financial institution, we offer a comprehensive suite of services designed to meet your needs, from advisory services and corporate & investment banking to transaction & payment services, securities services, mobility & fleet management and insurance solutions.

articles.title: Bank reliance on credit protection providers via synthetic risk transfers
articles.text: Bank reliance on credit protection providers via synthetic risk transfersPrepared by Allegra Pietsch, Daniel Dieckelmann, Maciej Grodzicki, Francesca Lenoci and Manuela Storz Published as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.Synthetic risk transfers (SRTs) allow a bank to transfer the credit risk of a loan portfolio to a third party, while the loans themselves stay on the bank’s balance sheet. SRTs are the most prevalent form of capital relief securitisation in the euro area.[1] The concept of SRTs is used in the European regulatory framework to underpin the rules for recognising significant risk transfer. In addition to synthetic securitisations, these transactions also include some eligible cash securitisations. In this box, SRT refers solely to synthetic risk transfer transactions. Banks can also use other instruments, including traditional securitisation, credit guarantees and credit derivatives, to manage their credit risk and intermediation capacity. Unlike cash securitisations, SRTs do not involve selling the loan portfolio. Instead, the bank retains the loans on its balance sheet and collects interest payments, manages credit risk and maintains customer relationships. Meanwhile, credit losses on the portfolio are covered by investors up to a limit, against a premium.[2] Euro area banks usually retain a small first-loss piece and the senior tranche and obtain protection on a synthetic mezzanine tranche to cover any unexpected losses on the underlying portfolio. As the risk weights on the mezzanine tranche tend to be much higher than the risk weights on the senior tranche, the capital requirements on the portfolio are substantially reduced, often by as much as 70-85% for the portfolio as a whole. See Gonzalez, F. and Triandafil, C., “The European significant risk transfer securitization market”, Occasional Paper Series, No 23, European Systemic Risk Board, 2023, and “Unveiling the impact of STS on-balance sheet-securitisation on EU financial stability”, European Systemic Risk Board, May 2025. SRTs lead to lower capital requirements by reducing banks’ risk weights on securitised loans although, in effect, they substitute bank equity for temporary loss-absorbing capital from investors.[3] SRTs can be structured as credit-linked notes − issued by either the bank itself or a special-purpose vehicle − credit derivatives or a guarantee from an investor to cover future losses as they arise. ,[4] Synthetic securitisation was used extensively before the global financial crisis, and current SRTs have evolved from the instruments used at that time. Measures implemented since then include sounder market practices, tighter capital requirements, greater supervisory scrutiny and regulatory safeguards such as risk retention requirements and the prohibition of re-securitisations. See BCBS, “Synthetic risk transfers”, Bank for International Settlements, February 2026, and Babu, P., Chui, M. and Stephanou, C., “The rise and risks of synthetic risk transfers”, BIS Quarterly Review, Bank for International Settlements, March 2026. The use of SRTs by euro area banks has been growing steadily, although it varies across banks and portfolio type. In total, around €630 billion of bank loans are now protected by SRTs, and investors have committed about €120 billion in credit loss protection capital (Chart A, panel a). The estimated capital relief for banks has more than doubled over the last five years, reaching 40 basis points for the banking system in aggregate and 49 basis points for SRT-issuing banks (Chart A, panel b). Issuance is concentrated in, and dominated by, euro area global systemically important banks, and their already-tight capital headroom could make them more vulnerable to SRT market dislocations.[5] In the second quarter of 2026 the top ten SRT issuers accounted for about 75% of total SRT issuance. However, smaller banks have also been increasing their SRT issuance recently and obtain relatively more capital relief on average. Banks issue SRTs mainly on corporate and SME loan portfolios (Chart A, panel c). There are two likely reasons for this. First, the space for capital relief on these assets is often sizeable as they carry relatively high risk weights, and the economic capital needed to absorb credit losses may be less than the regulatory capital requirement.[6] For empirical evidence, see Osberghaus, A. and Schepens, G., “Synthetic, but how much risk transfer”, Working Paper Series, No 3210, ECB, 2026. Second, SRTs allow banks to reduce their credit risk exposure to firms without having to sever business relationships.Chart ASRTs have been growing steadily for years, providing significant capital relief to euro area banksa) Total outstanding credit protection and capital relief via synthetic risk transfersb) Distribution of estimated bank-level capital relief for euro area banks via synthetic risk transfersc) Asset classes protected by synthetic risk transfers(H1 2021-H1 2026; € billions, basis points of RWA)(Q2 2021-Q2 2026, percentages of RWA)(Q2 2026, € billions)Sources: ECB (supervisory data) and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: “Retained portfolio value” refers to the retained tranches of the portfolio not protected by SRT. It consists mainly of senior tranches and often a first-loss piece. The CET1 ratio increase is calculated for the sample of banks issuing SRTs as the difference between CET1 capital divided by pre-securitisation risk-weighted assets (RWA) and CET1 capital divided by post-securitisation RWA. Depending on the method applied to determine capital risk requirements, pre-securitisation RWA are calculated as pre-securitisation standardised approach capital charge or unexpected portfolio losses, divided by 8% and multiplied by total portfolio value less actual post-securitisation RWA. Values are estimates and might differ slightly from the realised capital relief. Panel b: G-SIBs stands for global systemically important banks. Lines indicate the weighted average by group. Panel c: SME stands for small and medium-sized enterprises. “Other assets” includes mixed SME and corporate portfolios, commercial mortgages, leasing and trade receivables, and other wholesale assets. “Other retail” includes all non-mortgage non-SME retail exposure classes.SRT structures provide additional loss-absorbing capacity for credit risk, as long as investor commitments are credible. Most SRTs are funded, meaning that credit loss protection is provided up front and is collateralised.[7] Loans to large corporations are the most common portfolio underlying SRTs and tend to be funded, while about 80% of mortgage-related SRTs and about half of SME-related SRTs are unfunded. In the case of unfunded transactions, by contrast, investors commit to cover losses as they materialise, although banks are exposed to counterparty risk if the investors are unable to pay out. These unfunded structures are less common than they were but could regain popularity in the future. Public sector guarantors, notably including the European Investment Bank, account for about 10% of the SRT market and about a third of all unfunded SRTs (Chart B, panel a).[8] Assuming they meet the regulatory criteria for the recognition of significant risk transfer, banks can follow a securitisation approach to capital requirements on the underlying loan portfolio and apply a zero risk weight to the funded and transferred mezzanine tranche. While an unfunded tranche would normally attract a capital requirement due to the bank’s exposure to counterparty credit risk, the advantage of a public sector guarantor is that the risk weight for this purpose would be zero. Rollover risk, another concern associated with synthetic securitisation, is mitigated by maturity matching. Rollover risk occurs when the maturity date of the securitisation is shorter than that of the underlying loan portfolio. If a bank cannot enter into a new SRT, its capital requirement will increase abruptly as it will assume the credit risk once again. Part of this risk is currently mitigated by maturity matching. This is where the issued SRT matches or exceeds the average maturity of the loan portfolio (Chart B, panel b). Moreover, originator banks often agree with investors on ex ante contractual provisions governing portfolio replenishment, which help maintain the SRT structure, and on the amortisation schedule, which determines whether loan repayments are allocated sequentially or on a pro rata basis.The SRT investor base is dominated by specialised credit funds and asset managers, although it has become more broad based over time. These credit funds often follow narrow mandates, provide targeted capital management solutions and maintain long-term relationships with banks. However, the share of such specialised players in the SRT market has been decreasing since 2021 (Chart B, panel c), as has the share of pension funds. Over the same period, asset managers, including those operating large private equity and private credit funds, have expanded into SRT investment. The lack of visibility regarding the actual ultimate carriers of credit risk means it is difficult to assess what balance sheet capacity these funds have to absorb credit losses or to provide stable demand for SRT upon rollover.Chart BWhile SRTs are usually structured to provide effective loss absorption, they could lead to spillovers from the non-bank sector to banksa) Breakdown of SRT transactions by structureb) Maturity gap between the underlying portfolio and SRTc) Global SRT investor base(H1 2023-H1 2026, percentages)(Q2 2026; quarters, € billions)(2016-25, percentages of total new SRT issuance)Sources: ECB (COREP), IACPM and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: funded structures are SRTs with collateral provided to cover credit losses. Public sector entities are protection providers eligible for a zero risk weight. Panel b: the maturity gap is calculated as the difference between the weighted average maturity of the underlying asset pool and the shorter of the legal or the foreseeable maturity date of the SRT. Panel c: the figures are based on a survey of 62 global SRT originators and over 800 SRT transactions. Survey participants had received protection of €905 billion of underlying assets as at end-2025. EU-based banks account for about 63% of the volume of SRTs included in the survey. The investor breakdown refers to the immediate investors. Public sector entities include multilateral development banks and international organisations, which benefit from a zero risk weight, as well as central banks and governments.* *) See Joulia-Paris, T. and Saary-Littman, J., “Global SRT Market Overview 2025: Record Issuance, Broadening Participation, Diversifying Assets”, IACPM, June 2026.The financial stability risks associated with SRTs are currently limited but could increase if banks were to become overly dependent on credit protection, leading to procyclical loan supply. The SRT market provides banks with balance sheet space, which may support their ability to extend lending and supply credit to the real economy.[9] There is mixed empirical evidence on the credit supply impact of SRT, as banks that issue SRTs tend to lend more but also tend to increase dividend payouts. See Osberghaus, A. and Schepens, G., “Synthetic, but how much risk transfer”, Working Paper Series, No 3210, ECB, 2026, and Evrard, J., Schuster, W.E., Wassmann, F. and Wedow, M., “Can synthetic securitisation support economic growth?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 2 September 2026. The financial stability risks are mitigated by the predominant use of funded structures, the presence of specialised long-term investors and limited maturity mismatches. However, further rapid growth of SRTs and shifts in the investor base could make banks dependent on non-banks for credit-risk and capital management. Risks materialising in the non-bank financial intermediation sector could reduce the capacity of protection providers to take on credit risk from banks and potentially disrupt aggregate credit supply. If SRT investors are active in other segments of the credit market, losses from such activity could diminish their ability to bear risk via SRTs, resulting in a spillover from credit markets to bank lending. Moreover, global banks are using SRTs to insure credit risk for loans to private credit funds, which could further increase the opacity of the linkages between banks and non-banks. This could result in credit risk emerging in unexpected pockets of the financial system.[10] This may give rise to wrong-way risk where the recipient of the loan operates in the same sector as the protection provider. Additional financial innovations in the United States, such as re-securitisation or credit enhancements of SRT tranches by opaque guarantors, could create further data gaps and spillover channels. It has been reported that US insurers have provided credit protection on SRT tranches to enhance their credit ratings, helping SRT investors to raise more leverage from banks against the SRT tranche. See “Wall Street Alchemists Tap Insurers to Unfreeze Private Markets”, Bloomberg, 19 July 2026, and Poilpré, J.-M., “Europe’s banks deploy SRT scalpel across private credit exposures”, PitchBook, 15 July 2026.
