articles.title: Embedding sustainability into large-scale irrigated agriculture | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Agriculture
Embedding sustainability into large-scale irrigated agriculture

Link copied to clipboard

Through fertiliser optimisation trials and Regenagri certification, Macquarie is supporting Cubbie Ag in integrating sustainability into its day-to-day operations

Swipe for more

SectorAgricultureSub-sectorCroppingLocationAustralia

Opportunity

Cubbie Ag is one of Australia's largest irrigated cropping enterprises, producing cotton alongside wheat and chickpeas in southern Queensland.
As a major producer of food and fibre, the business seeks to balance productivity with the long-term health and resilience of the natural resources that underpin its operations.
For Australian broadacre cropping businesses, fertiliser is one of the largest direct costs, typically representing around 25 per cent of crop input costs.1 It is also a significant source of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions, representing approximately 60 per cent of Cubbie Ag’s Scope 1 emissions in 2025.2 Improving fertiliser efficiency therefore represents an opportunity to reduce emissions intensity while supporting operational productivity and lowering input costs.
At the same time, growing customer demand for sustainably produced commodities is increasing the commercial value of transparency and third-party certification across agricultural supply chains.

Approach

In 2024, Macquarie Asset Management Agriculture undertook a materiality-based review of its sustainability strategy, prioritising four pillars: Natural Resource Management, Climate Change, People and Community, and Animal Welfare.
Aligned with this strategy, Cubbie Ag has combined scientific research with regenerative agriculture practices to strengthen the sustainability and resilience of its operations. The business is now entering its third year of nitrogen inhibitor trials and second year of continuous nitrous oxide monitoring, helping to build one of Australia's most comprehensive datasets for irrigated cotton production. Conducted in partnership with research organisations and industry specialists, the trials are designed to better understand how fertiliser practices influence emissions, input efficiency and crop performance under irrigated conditions.
Alongside this work, Cubbie Ag is continuing to embed regenerative agriculture principles across its cotton production systems. It gained Regenagri certification in 2025, which provides independently recognised sustainability credentials for customers and supply chain partners.3

Outcome

Together, the trials and certification show how Cubbie Ag is embedding sustainability into everyday operations, delivering environmental, operational and commercial outcomes while helping support the long-term resilience of the business.
The fertiliser and nitrous oxide trials are providing practical insights to support Cubbie Ag’s emissions reduction and fertiliser management strategy. Early trial results have demonstrated reductions in nitrous oxide emissions of up to 35 per cent compared with conventional urea, although further monitoring and additional seasons of data are required to validate the consistency of these results across varying seasonal and field conditions.4 Findings to date are informing future fertiliser decisions, while supporting the broader assessment of enhanced efficiency fertilisers across the business.
Demand for Regenagri-certified cotton has also increased significantly as customers recognise the value of certified, sustainably produced fibre. A majority of Cubbie Ag's cotton is now sold under the Regenagri certification, attracting a small premium per bale and supporting greater product differentiation.

For Cubbie, it’s about understanding what our emissions look like under our own conditions. Building site-specific data helps us understand where the opportunities are and what’s working. Longer term, it also gives us the opportunity to demonstrate those improvements to our customers and create greater value from the cotton we produce.”
Cameron Brimblecombe
Cotton Production & Sustainability Manager
Cubbie Ag

articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

16 Nov 2026

US PCE nowcast – Broadening pressures lock in December rate hike

Our monthly PCE nowcast provides an early estimate of inflation trends ahead of official data releases, highlighting key drivers and implications for Federal Reserve policy.

Our nowcast is for headline PCE inflation to rise to 3.8% y/y in October, up from 3.6% y/y in September. The details suggest high energy prices are lifting food inflation and bleeding into core inflation. This will be discomforting to the Federal Reserve and bolster our expectation for a 25bp rate hike at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting; we think markets are overpricing the odds of a 50bp hike.

Recent declines in oil prices bode well for our forecast for headline inflation to peak in Q4, and the pass-through from higher energy prices to core inflation will ease over 2027. Muted equity markets, lower demand for homebuying, and modest wage growth should keep services inflation benign.

Each month, we replicate the Bureau of Economic Analysis’ (BEA) methodology to estimate the PCE deflator using the source data from the CPI, the PPI, and import prices. Because some underlying data and seasonal adjustments aren’t publicly available, there’s a small tracking error. Our average absolute errors since we began this approach are 3bps for headline and core PCE. Almost all the errors are in the core services ex-housing category, where the share of confidential data is the largest.

articles.title: Transparency and predictability: a foundation for future resilience − speech by Katharine Braddick
articles.text:
Transparency and predictability: a foundation for future resilience − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at the UK Finance Annual Dinner, London

Published on
18 November 2026

Katharine Braddick considers how the relationship between the PRA and regulated firms should evolve. She discusses how greater transparency and predictability can support effective supervision, and sets out how closer cooperation between regulators and industry can strengthen operational and cyber resilience of the financial sector.

Speech
Some of you will have heard my speech at the Mansion House last month in which I set out my vision for a PRA that is respected, trusted, and supports a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system.
The relationship between regulator and regulated entities is at the core of effective delivery of regulatory outcomes and will be central to the PRA’s delivery of this vision. This evening I want to discuss some thoughts about how that relationship should operate.
Regulatory transparency
As regulated firms you will be vividly aware that at the PRA we have deep and wide insight into the firms we supervise. We see Board and Exco papers, we understand and scrutinise your governance and controls, and we know your key projects and the detail of your balance sheets. We see your business strategies in development, at launch and through their life cycle. And we see that content for your competitors too. By contrast, of course, individual firms have detailed sight only of their own businesses, and quite limited insight into the PRA.
This results in an unavoidable information asymmetry between firms and the regulator. We must do what we can to narrow it. If we do not, Boards and management may spend valuable time debating the intention of our supervisory feedback, making changes that do not address our concerns, or add unnecessary layers of process and conservatism because they are uncertain about how we will react.
The PRA has a distinctive approach to prudential supervision. Rather than using in-depth on-site exams, our supervisors exercise their judgement on the key risks to firms’ safety and soundness on the basis of extensive discussions with firms. We then communicate our views qualitatively to firms’ leadership and Boards, and ensure that there is a credible plan with senior ownership to remediate those risks.
That approach depends on firms understanding not only what we expect of them, but the concerns and judgements that sit behind those expectations. At its worst, the sense that our actions cannot be predicted or easily interpreted risks creating cynicism or passivity about regulatory activity, which is corrosive for the compliance culture within regulated firms.
This is important more widely too. In practice, the majority of communication to investors about the UK’s regulatory regime does not come from the PRA but from the senior leaders of regulated firms themselves in their investor communications. Where the regime is poorly or partially understood, this undermines wider understanding, erodes trust in our regime and increases uncertainty, affecting investment decisions and the attractiveness of the UK’s business environment.
This is why we make significant efforts to ensure our intentions are clear. We publish and regularly update our approach to supervision. And we write to firms annually regarding our supervisory priorities and make them publicly available.
From next year, our new five-year strategy will supplement this. It will set out our longer-term priorities, increasing the transparency and predictability of our supervision, and provide Boards and senior leaders with greater visibility of where we intend to focus our attention, and why.
We will ensure firms continue to receive high quality supervisory feedback that clearly sets out the judgements our supervisors have taken, the reasons for those decisions, and what we expect of you. Where it is necessary for us to use our supervisory tools, we will ensure that the rationale and implications are clearly set out. And where we can help further contextualise our judgement – such as providing information on how you compare to your peers – we will do so. We will also ensure that firms receive feedback in a timely manner, helping you effectively address the issues we identify.
We should apply those same principles in how we regulate. I recognise, for example, the difficulties firms face when capital requirements change unexpectedly. We are significantly reducing the discretionary element of our capital requirements through Basel 3.1, making them more predictable. Similarly, uncertainty about our approach to firms’ buffer use can make it harder to conduct effective capital planning. We have already taken action to provide greater visibility and predictability in these areas, including for smaller firms, and we will consider if there are opportunities to go further for the sector as a whole.
In return, we expect firms to be candid and transparent with us, and to address our supervisory feedback in a timely and diligent manner.
In addition, we will prioritise more direct and regular engagement with investors in UK banks and insurers, as well as key market participants such as analysts and credit ratings agencies. This will be a two-way conversation: we want to foster a deeper understanding of the UK prudential regime among those making or influencing investment decisions, and we want to understand where greater clarity from us may be beneficial. We will also explore how our stakeholders perceive and engage with the PRA’s communications to ensure our approach is fit for purpose.
Operational and cyber resilience
Operational risk is the most rapidly escalating area of risk for the firms we regulate, and the way we work with regulated firms is evolving to address it.
The response to the global financial crisis necessarily relied on requirements set by authorities calibrated to the risks firms take. Non-financial resilience demands a different approach, founded in close co-operation between regulators and firms to share learning, identify gaps in system-wide resilience and agree priorities for the sector as a whole.
The last few weeks, let alone months, demonstrate the rapid increase in this work’s importance. Firms must increase attention to their operational and cyber resilience, and critically to their core cyber hygiene practices which remain the most significant mitigant to current risks. And we will give these issues a materially greater weight in our supervision.
Tomorrow, alongside the FCA, we will publish a consultation on cyber resilience. It clarifies how firms should demonstrate their resilience and preparedness, without trying to prescribe every aspect of how they achieve it. It draws on the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Assessment Framework, benefitting from our commitment to working with the NCSC and Government to enhance the UK’s cyber resilience.
I want firms to help us shape our approach through the consultation on these proposals. As we go forward in a risk environment that generates a new and startling news story every few days, and many more incidents that do not reach the public sphere, this is how we will work with the industry: engagement on the basis of the most up to date version of what is currently known, and adaptation in the light of experience.
It is vital for individual firms to increase their resilience, but this alone will not deliver resilience for the overall financial system. The financial system is increasingly interconnected, including through shared technology and third-party providers, a good deal of it outside the regulated perimeter. Disruption in one part of the system can have material consequences well beyond the firm in which it originates, and a material incident in the financial sector would require a co-ordinated approach to recovery across firms and authorities. While individual firm resilience therefore remains fundamental, there are vulnerabilities that we can only tackle effectively together.
As you will all know, we already have a highly effective and internationally well-regarded model in operation for this. The Cross-Market Operational Resilience Group, which brings regulators and firms together to improve resilience through practical guidance and targeted workplans, has been the foundation of the sectoral response to escalating risk from frontier technologies in the course of this year. I would like to take this opportunity to thank UK Finance for its leadership in that forum. That co-operation supplements our existing supervisory tools such as the targeted CBEST and STAR-FS cyber assessments.
As this approach has matured and the risk picture evolves, we intend to build on this success by providing a means for more strategic system-wide cooperation.
In the coming weeks we will therefore hold the first meeting of a new Systemic Resilience Council. Chaired by the Bank of England, this group will bring together authorities and CEOs of systemically important firms and financial infrastructure providers to identify the most pressing shared vulnerabilities facing the sector and agree the collective response. We will need to take significant and strategic decisions, and these are best made together. I am particularly pleased that UK Finance will be part of our first meeting next month, bringing their industry-wide insight to that discussion.
Our immediate priorities will be those areas where collective action can make the greatest difference. One of those will be the risks and opportunities posed by the latest artificial intelligence models for firms’ operational and cyber resilience, building on the work of our Frontier AI Information Sharing Forum established earlier this year. Another is how we gain greater assurance that firms can recover from severe cyber disruption, including scenarios that could require a material rebuild of their technology environments.
The Council will build on the capabilities, expertise and relationships already developed through CMORG and elsewhere, as we take this work forward. And CMORG will of course continue to play its vital role.
Conclusion
The PRA cannot deliver a resilient financial sector alone. Addressing the challenges that face us requires a greater level of understanding between firms and regulators. Although we will not always agree on every issue, we must continue to work together to identify risks to the financial sector and take action to ensure the sector remains resilient and able to provide the services on which the UK economy depends.
This is the relationship that I want the PRA to build with the firms that it regulates, and I look forward to working with you on this important agenda.
I would like to thank Aaron Schroeder-Willis and Ridheema Manek for their support in drafting this speech. I would also like to thank Sarah Breeden, Andrea Enria, Charlotte Gerken, Talib Idris, Rebecca Jackson, Metesh Patel, Dave Ramsden, David Soanes, John Taylor, Vicky White, as well as wider PRA colleagues, for their comments and assistance.

Deputy Governor
Prudential Regulation and CEO of the Prudential Regulation Authority

articles.title: Equity investment outlook: The great divides - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
We expect the current divergence between technology and non-tech stocks, as well as between hardware and software companies, to continue into 2027

While there is uncertainty over the long-term winners of AI development, earnings growth expectations are positive, offering potential opportunities for investors who can tolerate volatility

We believe equity markets can generate a positive return in 2027, driven by a supportive economic environment and the impact of AI, despite likely short-term fluctuations

The great divides that characterised equity markets in 2026 – first, between tech and non-tech stocks, and second within the technology sector between semiconductor/hardware and software stocks (including hyperscalers) – is likely to persist into 2027.

Returns for technology stocks fell into two phases in 2026: in the first half of the year, we saw a big rally in global semiconductor and hardware stocks, when they rose by 58% (local currency terms).1

This gain was partly mirrored by declines in software companies’ stocks including the hyperscalers, who were the principal customers of the semiconductor/hardware companies, or in those whose business models were themselves at risk from artificial intelligence technologies.

In the second half of the year, waning confidence in the capital expenditure outlook led to a reversal of performance, with semiconductor and hardware stocks declining 23%, while software stocks recovered their losses, rising 9%.2

Through all of this, non-tech stocks marched steadily higher (see Exhibit 1).

Growth despite earnings uncertainty

We expect these divides to persist, but the key question is, which pattern we will see?

Part of the high levels of volatility witnessed recently in tech stocks stems from the extreme uncertainty around how AI will develop, its impact on society, the economy and corporate profits. Views on who the winners and losers will be change almost daily with periodic ‘out of the blue’ surprises (like the launch of Chinese start-up DeepSeek’s AI model in January 2025) to shake things up even more.

This uncertainty can be seen in the big increase in the standard deviation of earnings estimates for tech stocks – showing how much analysts’ forecasts differ from one another. It has increased more than five times over the last two years, while for non-tech stocks it has been steady (see Exhibit 2).

Given the wide range of forecasted profits, any marginal news can have a big impact on stock prices. This dynamic is likely to remain part of the AI investment universe.

As for the pattern we may see next year, we anticipate semiconductor and hardware stocks posting good returns given the still very high levels of planned capital expenditures.

The performance of software stocks, including the hyperscalers, is harder to predict. There is intense competition between them, and it is unlikely all the investments being made today will generate a sufficient and timely return on investment.

Revenue generation, however, is increasing as companies learn how to incorporate AI into their operations and see meaningful productivity gains. Consumers, too, may be willing to pay more in the future for the benefits AI tools can provide.

Looking beyond volatility

Investors should not lose sight of the medium-term opportunity. It is essentially a question of how fast technology sector earnings will grow. Consensus estimates are for nearly 90% earnings growth over the next two years.

Even if it turns out to be ‘only’ 70%, that would still imply strong stock appreciation, particularly as valuations are currently below average. The z-score of the forward price-to-earnings ratio – which indicates how far valuations sit below their historical average – is around -0.2 for the Nasdaq 100 index and -1.4 for emerging market technology stocks. For all the volatility over the last few months, the earnings trajectory remains positive.

This dynamic, though, of high potential returns alongside high volatility, presents a challenge to investors who want to participate in the gains but are concerned by the wide swings in stock prices.

The slices of the AI ‘pie’ will continue to expand and shrink (and in some cases disappear). Some of the challenges ahead include higher financing costs, increasing competition (notably from China), and energy supply constraints. Nonetheless, we believe the pie will continue to grow over time. An investor who can accept the volatility may find there is potential for returns above those of the broad market over the medium term.

At the same time, the high volatility offers significant potential opportunities to portfolio managers who are able to identify the winners and avoid the losers.

The wider market

Of course, few investors would dedicate their entire portfolio to AI; the technology sector still only represents about 40% of the MSCI All Country World Index by market capitalisation.

Returns for the other sectors have been steadily positive, as Exhibit 1 illustrates. This has been driven by strong growth in the US and lower, but still steady, growth in Europe. The most recent earnings season saw double digit gains across many of the major equity indices and forecasts for next year are also good (18% for MSCI ACWI). We foresee this supportive economic environment continuing, even with interest rates likely to be higher on average in 2027 than in 2026, in our view.

The opportunity, however, may be in identifying those companies which are able to incorporate AI into their operations and accelerate profit growth. This is where the US may have an advantage.

To the degree that AI allows companies to reduce labour costs, US companies are among the quickest to adjust the size of their workforce, in contrast to those in Europe and Japan. This dynamic has its own implications for consumer demand depending on how quickly displaced workers move into new roles, but currently the US adult unemployment rate remains low and steady.

From a market perspective, the superior returns of the Russell Value index compared to other indices with a similar sector composition is perhaps evidence already of this phenomenon.

The potential for European companies may be best among those who are able to monetise the significant amount of funds behind the European strategic autonomy initiative in sectors such as defence and infrastructure.

The positive global macroeconomic outlook bodes well for equity returns in 2027. AI is likely to continue to play an outsized role in equity returns, with different dynamics between software companies and hyperscalers relative to semiconductor and hardware manufacturers. The medium-term outlook is positive, but it is unlikely to be a smooth path. Meanwhile, we expect non-tech sectors to see steady growth, with upside potential in those companies who are best able to leverage the AI revolution.

[1] Source: FactSet, BNP Asset Management.

[2] As of 5 November 2026.

What you need to know
We place restrictions on the use of physical and digital images of Bank of England banknotes. This is to stop the creation of banknote copies that could accidentally be used for, or accepted as, payment and to avoid banknote images being used in an offensive or inappropriate context, including distortion to the monarch's image.
We give you consent to reproduce our banknotes, or a part of one, if you comply with our reproduction conditions (you do not need to contact us for permission). These conditions apply whether you are using our approved images or creating your own.
If you do not comply with our conditions, this may result in legal action.
Banknotes and the law
It is an offence to:

reproduce banknotes issued by us, or part of banknotes issued by us, on any substance or to any scale without our consent. For the avoidance of doubt, consent for items marketed as ‘Movie’, ‘Prop’ or ‘Training’ items can only be obtained if such items meet our reproduction conditions. We have described these in more detail in the FAQ below.
deface Bank of England banknotes (including printing, writing or impressing words, letters or figures on them).
without the Bank’s consent knowingly and in the course of a business make for sale or hire, import, offer, exhibit in public, or distribute a copyright work. Copyright in Bank of England banknotes is owned by the Bank of England and also contains works which the Bank uses under licence from public and private sector bodies.
without the Bank’s consent apply to goods or packaging, to sell, expose or distribute goods with the Bank’s registered trade mark (or a sign likely to be mistaken for it) with a view to gain for himself or another, or with intent to cause loss to another.
commit fraud by false representation and misuse the Bank’s name as an instrument of fraud.

Counterfeit banknotes
It is also an offence to:

make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse or with the intention of passing or tendering it as genuine.
pass or tender or deliver to another a counterfeit banknote knowingly or believing it to be counterfeit.
have custody or control of a counterfeit banknote intending to pass or tender or deliver it as genuine or have in custody or control without lawful excuse.
have custody or control of anything intending to or allowing any person to use it to make a counterfeit banknote intending to pass it as genuine or make or have anything designed or adapted to make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse.

Find more about counterfeit banknotes

These offences are covered under sections 14-17 and 18 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981 Opens in a new window, section 12 of the Currency and Banknotes Act 1928 Opens in a new window, section 107 of the Copyright Designs and Patents Act 1988 Opens in a new window, section 92 of the Trade Marks Act 1994, and section 2 of the Fraud Act 2006.
In addition, civil liability attaches to infringement of the Bank’s copyright, moral rights, and trade mark rights.
The list is non-exhaustive. The content of this website is provided for general information purposes only and it does not constitute in any way legal advice. If you are seeking specific legal advice, you may wish to contact a qualified legal professional at your own expense.

all or part of a banknote

Inappropriate or novelty reproductions

As well as there being a risk of a reproduction offence, there is also a risk that a such notes may be counterfeit banknotes if they are reasonably capable of passing for a currency note.

Counterfeit banknotes

No, these are not Bank of England banknotes and no exchange for a Bank of England banknote can be made. Fortunately, such occurrences are extremely rare but please report any such cases to your local police.

Back to top

This page was last updated 01 June 2026

articles.title: AI isn’t just shaping biotech narratives, it’s shifting the market | RBCCM
articles.text:
How has the relationship between AI and biotech changed?
Rishi Jaluria: AI is no longer just shaping biotech innovation narratives. Increasingly, it may also be influencing biotech market performance. In our recent report, Does Healthcare Dream of Electric Sheep?, published as part of the RBC Imagine research series, we explored how developments in AI could influence biotech through broader market dynamics and capital flows, as well as innovation itself.
Leonid Timashev: We wanted to understand whether AI was influencing biotech performance in ways investors were not fully appreciating. Historically, AI and biotech tended to move together, but our analysis showed that the relationship had recently turned inverse. While biotech's strong performance could be explained by traditional factors such as M&A activity, FDA flexibility, reduced concern around drug pricing, and a more favorable policy backdrop, the data also pointed to capital rotating out of AI and semiconductor stocks and into biotech.
It's hard to know whether this is temporary or structural. What we do know is that the shift is recent and appears strongest among larger-cap biotech names, which may be better positioned to absorb fund flows. Whether it endures will depend on factors affecting both markets, including AI's ability to continue scaling, biotech's defensive appeal, and the impact of rates and policy.
Why do AI shocks ripple through biotech?
Jaluria: When the AI trade comes under pressure, capital can rotate out of the higher-volatility technology complex and into more defensive parts of the market. Biotech can benefit from that dynamic because its performance is driven by a different set of factors and offers investors diversification from AI-related exposures. If those capital flows persist, weakness in AI could continue to support inflows into biotech, reinforcing the inverse relationship that has recently emerged between the two sectors.
Timashev: Biotech and pharma account for about 12% of the S&P 500, compared with approximately 50% for AI-related companies. Because biotech represents a much smaller part of the index, even a limited rotation out of AI can have a more visible effect on biotech performance. Given biotech's traditional defensive characteristics, some of those flows may reflect investors seeking shelter from volatility rather than growing conviction around sector-specific fundamentals.
Jaluria: More broadly, investors are increasingly thinking across themes rather than sectors. When the same pool of capital is moving rapidly between technology, AI, and healthcare, sector boundaries matter less. Investors can no longer assess biotech solely through a healthcare lens; they also need to understand the forces shaping capital allocation across technology, AI, and the wider market.

"Investors can no longer assess biotech solely through a healthcare lens."
Rishi Jaluria, U.S. Software Analyst, RBC Capital Markets

Where can AI create the most value in biotech?
Timashev: In our view, AI can have its greatest impact early in the development process. It can support molecule discovery and novel chemistry, generate hypotheses, and analyze large biological and chemical datasets to identify ideas worth testing. AI can also improve productivity in areas such as regulatory documentation, where submissions to the FDA often involve significant amounts of text and forms.
That said, some expectations around AI's impact remain unproven. Biotech breakthroughs still depend on scientific research, experimental validation, and regulatory review. While AI can improve efficiency, it cannot accelerate timelines that are fixed by regulatory requirements, such as mandated toxicity studies. We see AI as an important enabler of innovation, but not a substitute for the scientific discovery process itself.

"A lot of the underlying science still has to be done and verified. By humans."
Leonid Timashev, Biotechnology Analyst, RBC Capital Markets

What should biotech investors be watching?
Jaluria: We identified several AI-related risk dimensions that biotech investors should monitor. One is the potential for diminishing returns from compute scaling. If hyperscalers begin to experience diminishing returns, biotech could benefit from a rotation of capital out of AI, potentially supporting gains of 15% to 20%. If performance continues to improve and commercial adoption accelerates, we would expect a gradual rotation back toward AI, potentially contributing to a 15% to 25% contraction in biotech.
Another key variable is the extent to which open-weight models challenge token-based pricing and the premium economics of the AI ecosystem. If open-weight adoption grows aggressively, it could pressure hyperscalers’ peak revenue expectations and support a rotation into biotech. Conversely, if regulatory restrictions reduce open-weight usage, stronger AI-related performance could contribute to capital moving back out of biotech.
Investors should also watch geopolitical, cybersecurity, regulatory, and capital-spending risks. A normalization in shipping could accelerate AI infrastructure investment and pressure biotech, while prolonged disruption could modestly benefit the sector. A rise in AI-related cybersecurity incidents could also increase regulatory scrutiny and potentially support biotech. In our analysis, a slowdown in AI capital expenditure could contribute to 10% to 15% upside for biotech, while continued or accelerated investment could create 5% to 10% downside pressure.

articles.title: Institutional Holdings of Bitcoin ETPs Reach New All-Time High
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Institutional Holdings of Bitcoin ETPs Reach New All-Time High

Research • November 19, 2026
Institutional Holdings of Bitcoin ETPs Reach New All-Time High
13F filings show wealth channel portion of ETP ownership reaches 40%.

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Bitcoin

Markets & Macro

Introduction Institutions returned to U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) as net buyers in the third quarter of 2026. Investment managers that file Form 13F with the SEC added the equivalent of 49,229 BTC, net of sales. That is the most since Q2 2025 and more than the 47,054 they had sold over the previous three quarters. Filers reported a record 356,491 BTC-equivalent ($29.78 billion) as of Sept. 30, 2026. Half of the net addition came from advisors and wealth platforms, which hold more of the funds than at any point since the ETPs launched in January 2024, both in bitcoin terms and as a share of institutional holdings. The continued accumulation in Q3 (July 1 through Sept. 30) occurred while bitcoin traded between its bear market low of $57,717 on July 1 and a Sept. 21 recent hit of $87,397. This report covers only holders of U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs, not foreign-issued vehicles.
Key Takeaways Advisors and wealth platforms are at record highs on every measure. The category, which covers registered investment advisors (RIAs), wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, reported 144,307 BTC-equivalent as of Sept. 30, 2026. That is 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin ETP holdings and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, and each figure is the highest in the series. Holdings have grown for nine straight quarters and are 3.3x their level on March 31, 2024; the one decline came in Q2 2024, the second quarter after launch. The category's share of 13F holdings has risen for five straight quarters, from 22.2% on June 30, 2025, after slipping in three of the earlier quarters. They have also been the steadiest buyers. Advisors and wealth platforms have been net buyers for nine consecutive quarters and account for 100,003 of the 179,300 BTC-equivalent that all filers added from Q2 2024 through Q3 2026. During the three quarters of net institutional selling that ended June 30, 2026, they added 32,706 while basis and relative-value hedge funds sold 54,683. The wirehouses drove the quarter. The category added a record 24,838 BTC-equivalent, of which 22,728 came from wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, led by Wells Fargo (+14,636), Bank of America (+7,201) and Morgan Stanley (+2,875). We then split those firms by business unit. Holdings at their advisor and brokerage arms rose to 43,583 from 30,978, and holdings at their dealer and trading units rose to 12,551 from 3,982, most of it at Bank of America. Wells Fargo is the largest 13F holder for the first time. It reported 30,553 BTC-equivalent ($2.55 billion), nearly double the 15,931 it held on June 30, 2026, and passed Jane Street, which led a quarter earlier. No wealth platform had ranked first before: Millennium Management was the largest holder in every quarter from Q1 2024 through Q1 2026. Breadth recovered, but a few large firms drove the net addition of bitcoin. The number of managers holding a spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline: 358 managers that held no position a quarter earlier reported one and 167 dropped out. The newcomers are small, with 9,554 BTC-equivalent among them. The 50 largest holders added a net 59,578, and all other managers combined, including those that left, were net sellers of 10,349. Form 13F filers hold 27.6% of the bitcoin in the ETPs. That is up from 24.8% on June 30, 2026, and just under the high of 27.7% on Dec. 31, 2024. The other 72.4% is held by investors that do not file the form, including individuals, advisors below the reporting threshold and most investors outside the U.S. Hedge funds hold less than a fifth, down from half. The three hedge fund categories together hold 19.0% of 13F-reported holdings, against 50.6% on Dec. 31, 2024. Basis and relative-value funds hold 34,053 BTC-equivalent, down from a peak of 101,826 on Dec. 31, 2024, although they and macro funds were buyers in the quarter (+9,184 and +10,492, respectively). BlackRock’s IBIT accounts for two-thirds of the institutional position. Filers hold 232,453 BTC-equivalent of IBIT, 65.2% of everything they reported, and the fund took 34,744 of the quarter's net 49,229. Filers' holdings of GBTC fell for the 10th straight quarter, and its sister fund, the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust, passed it for the first time. The reported holders are overwhelmingly U.S.-based. Managers in the U.S. hold a record 293,830 BTC-equivalent, or 82.5% of the 13F-reported total. The share held by managers outside the U.S. fell to 17.5% from 18.6% (the peak was 24.0% on Sept. 30, 2025) even though their holdings rose to 62,456 from 57,274, because U.S. managers added far more. What the filings cannot show. A Form 13F reports long positions at the quarter end, and only for accounts over which the manager has investment discretion. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, so ETP shares held by a market maker or a basis fund may be hedged, and client-directed brokerage accounts are generally absent, so we believe ownership through the wealth channel is understated. The filings are also a snapshot of Sept. 30, 2026. The funds' bitcoin holdings have since fallen by 38,531, to 1,252,139 on Nov. 16, 2026.
Q3 2026 by the Numbers For the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, 2,166 managers reported 356,491 BTC-equivalent ($29.78 billion) across 13 spot bitcoin funds, 191 more managers than on June 30, 2026. Measured in shares, to exclude the move in the bitcoin price, their net change was +49,229 BTC-equivalent, or about $4.11 billion at quarter-end prices. A total of 358 managers reported a position after holding none a quarter earlier, 167 that had held one reported none, and 1,808 held in both quarters.

Largest net additions Wells Fargo: +14,636, to 30,553 from 15,931 Brevan Howard: +8,606, to 12,686 from 4,082 Bank of America: +7,201, to 8,424 from 1,225 Millennium Management: +7,114, to 14,516 from 7,417 Jane Street: +6,180, to 23,167 from 17,007
Largest net reductions Walleye Capital: −3,270, to 370 from 3,642 Galaxy Digital: −2,721, to 4,786 from 7,519 Avenir Tech: −2,274, to 5,396 from 7,675 Cantor Fitzgerald: −1,680, to 1,949 from 3,650 Bank of Montreal: −1,632, to 1,014 from 2,648
Largest new holders Balyasny Asset Management: 1,782 D. E. Shaw: 1,075 SigFig Wealth Management: 884 Garda Capital Partners: 625 Symmetry Investments: 423 Figures are BTC-equivalent (see the methodology section for the calculations). They reflect 2,166 filings made through Nov. 17, 2026, the day after the reporting deadline. In past quarters, only 97.7% of filings were in by the end of the deadline day, so late filings and amendments could still move these numbers.
How Much Institutions Hold The charts in this section size the institutional position: its share of all the bitcoin in the funds, the number of managers behind it, and how it divides among the funds in bitcoin, in dollars and as a share of each fund.
Spot Bitcoin ETP Holdings by 13F Filer Group The spot bitcoin ETPs held 1,290,670 BTC, worth $107.81 billion, on Sept. 30, 2026. Managers that file Form 13F reported 356,286 of it, or 27.6%, up from 24.8% on June 30, 2026, and just under the high of 27.7% at Dec. 31, 2024. The other 72.4% (934,383 bitcoin) belongs to holders that do not file the form, a group that includes individual investors, advisors below the reporting threshold, and most investors outside the U.S. The 10 largest filers held 149,388 BTC-equivalent, which is 11.6% of all ETP bitcoin and 41.9% of what filers reported. That concentration was 59.4% on March 31, 2024, and fell as low as 34.2% at March 31, 2026, before large purchases by a few firms lifted it in the latest quarter. The other 2,154 filers held 206,898 (16.0%). The filings describe Sept. 30, 2026, and the funds have had net outflows since. The dashed line shows their bitcoin falling to 1,252,139 by Nov. 16, 2026, 38,531 below the quarter-end level, while the price of bitcoin fell to $64,943 from $83,580. How filers behaved during that decline will not be known until the next round of filings arrives in February.

Institutional 13F Filers Holding Spot Bitcoin ETPs The number of managers reporting a position in at least one spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline. The count is more than double the 1,009 that reported on March 31, 2024, the first quarter end after the funds launched, and is 85 short of the record 2,251 on Dec. 31, 2025. IBIT, BlackRock's fund, is by far the most widely held, with 1,648 managers, or 76% of all filers, which is 35 managers short of its own peak. GBTC (677), FBTC (665), the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust (511) and BITB (310) follow, and HODL reached a record 138. Most of these positions are small. Half of the 2,166 managers hold less than 10.4 BTC-equivalent, about $870,000 at the quarter-end price, and 215 hold less than one. The count of managers is therefore a measure of how widely the funds are used, not of how much bitcoin institutions hold.

BTC-Equivalent Held by 13F Filers by ETP Filers reported 356,491 BTC-equivalent across the spot funds, the most ever recorded and 2,192 more than the previous high of 354,299 on Sept. 30, 2025. The position has roughly doubled from 175,588 on March 31, 2024. IBIT accounts for 232,453 of the total, or 65.2%, although that is below the fund's own peak of 240,068 on Sept. 30, 2025. Fidelity’s FBTC is second at 41,429, its highest since June 30, 2025. The two Grayscale funds continued to move in opposite directions. Filers' holdings of GBTC (one of the oldest vehicles in the space, which converted from a grantor trust to an ETF in 2024) fell for the 10th straight quarter, to 15,842 from 68,449 on March 31, 2024. The lower-fee Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust rose for the sixth straight quarter, to 22,382, and for the first time holds more 13F-reported bitcoin than GBTC.

Quarterly Change in Count of 13F Filers by Fund The number of managers rose in 12 of the 13 funds, and only BRRR lost holders (two). IBIT gained 152, GBTC 65, the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust 39, FBTC 34 and BITB 34. That reverses the trend of the first half of 2026, when 12 of 13 funds lost managers in Q1 and 10 of 13 in Q2. Two details help in reading the chart below. The bars for Q3 sum to +390 while the number of distinct managers rose by 191, because a manager that adds a second or third fund counts once for each. And a fund can gain holders while losing bitcoin: GBTC added 65 managers in a quarter when filers reduced their GBTC shares by 5,897 BTC-equivalent.

New vs. Exiting 13F Holders This next chart splits the change in the manager count into arrivals and departures. In Q3 2026, 358 managers reported a position after reporting none a quarter earlier, 167 that had held one reported none, and 1,808 held in both quarters, for a net gain of 191. Both sides improved. Arrivals matched Q4 2025 as the most since Q2 2025 (379) and were more than double the 151 of Q2 2026. Departures were the fewest since Q3 2025 (135), after 316, 335, and 260 in the three quarters before. The new holders are small. Together they hold 9,554 BTC-equivalent, 2.7% of the total; only 15 of them hold 100 or more, and the median new position is 3.0. Breadth and volume are separate stories in this quarter: the count grew through many small accounts, and the bitcoin was added by a few large ones.

The Largest Holders The investment managers’ position in bitcoin ETPs is concentrated. The 10 largest filers hold 42.0% of everything reported, the 25 largest hold 60.8%, and the 50 largest hold 71.2%, so a small number of firms explains most of each quarter's change.
Largest 13F Holders of U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETPs Wells Fargo is the largest 13F holder of spot Bitcoin ETPs, with 30,553 BTC-equivalent worth $2.55 billion across 10 funds. That’s up from 15,931 on June 30, 2026. Wells Fargo passed Jane Street (23,167), previously the largest holder. Millennium Management, which ranks fourth with 14,516, had been the largest in every quarter from Q1 2024 through Q1 2026. The 15 largest holders are a cross-section of the institutional market. Three are wealth platforms (Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley, and Bank of America), five are market makers or bank trading desks (Jane Street, Goldman Sachs, Marex, Susquehanna, and JPMorgan Chase), three are hedge funds (Millennium Management, Brevan Howard, and Schonfeld), two are asset managers (Horizon Kinetics and BlackRock), one is a sovereign investor (Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala) and one is in the family office or corporate holder category (Avenir Tech). That mix matters for interpretation. The same number of shares can be a client allocation at a wealth platform, inventory at a market maker, or one leg of a hedged trade at a hedge fund, and a bank can hold all three under one filing.

Top 25 Holders and Their Quarterly Change The 25 largest holders reported 216,629 BTC-equivalent, 60.8% of the total. Of the 25, 17 added to their positions, six reduced and two made no change. Together they added a net 56,922, more than the 49,229 added by all 2,166 filers. The green segments show where the bitcoin came from. Wells Fargo added 14,636 (to 30,553 from 15,931), Brevan Howard 8,606 (to 12,686 from 4,082), Bank of America 7,201 (to 8,424 from 1,225), Millennium Management 7,114, Jane Street 6,180, Goldman Sachs 5,499, and Susquehanna 4,839. Those seven firms added 54,076 between them. The largest reductions among the 25 were at Galaxy Digital (2,721), Avenir Tech (2,274), and NEOS Investment Management (939). (Note that some firms may have adjusted how they hold exposure, such as by switching between spot, ETPs, or derivatives, depending on market circumstances and strategy). Mubadala (8,336) and Abu Dhabi Investment Council (4,653), both Abu Dhabi sovereign investors, reported no change.

Top 50 Holders and Net Quarterly Change The next chart widens the lens to capture the 50 largest holders, which together hold 71.2% of the total, and plots only the change. Of the 50, 30 added, 15 reduced and five were unchanged, for a net addition of 59,578 BTC-equivalent. All filers together added 49,229, so every other manager combined, including the 167 that left, was a net seller of 10,349. Managers that closed their positions account for about 7,689 of that reduction, and the 2,116 current holders ranked below the top 50 for about 2,660. The quarter's accumulation was the work of a few dozen large institutions; the long tail of smaller holders, taken together, did not add. Two of the 50 are new holders: Balyasny Asset Management (1,782) and D. E. Shaw (1,075), both classified here as basis and relative-value hedge funds. D. E. Shaw returned, having been among the 10 largest holders on Dec. 31, 2024. Below the top 25, the larger additions came from IMC (+1,550), Citigroup (+1,524), and Graham Capital Management (+1,048) and the larger reductions from Cantor Fitzgerald (−1,680) and Laurore (−906).

Who the Holders Are The charts in this section sort every filer into one of eight holder types and follow each type's holdings and flows. This is where the quarter's main story sits. Advisors and wealth platforms, the category that covers RIAs, wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, are the largest holder type by a wide margin and have been the steadiest buyers since the funds launched. Hedge funds, which held half of all 13F-reported ETP bitcoin at the end of 2024, hold less than a fifth. We believe the distinction matters because different investor types hold the funds for different reasons. A Form 13F reports long positions only, so the shares held by a basis fund or a market maker may be offset by futures or options that the form does not show. Holdings at advisors are more likely to be unhedged allocations in client accounts. The table below gives the category's record quarter by quarter.

Quarterly Bitcoin-Equivalent Holdings by Holder Type Advisors and wealth platforms reported 144,307 BTC-equivalent on Sept. 30, 2026, the most in the series and 3.3x the 44,053 they held at March 31, 2024. Their holdings have grown in each of the last nine quarters. The only decline in the series is Q2 2024, when the category fell to 40,155. That decline came entirely from wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms, whose holdings fell to 6,065 from 14,755; independent RIAs and wealth managers added in the same quarter. The category has been the largest holder type since Q3 2025. Before that it was basis and relative-value hedge funds, whose holdings peaked at 101,826 on Dec. 31, 2024, and have fallen by about two-thirds since, to 34,053. Market makers and bank desks rank second at a record 77,769. Asset managers (41,211) came in third, followed by basis and relative-value hedge funds (34,053), other hedge funds and crypto firms (16,933), macro hedge funds (16,656), pensions, sovereigns and endowments (16,545), and family offices and corporates (8,812). The decline at asset managers, from 42,361, is the first for that type.

Share of 13F Holdings by Holder Type This next chart restates the same holdings as shares of the total, which makes the change in the holder base easier to see. Advisors and wealth platforms hold 40.5% of 13F-reported spot Bitcoin ETP holdings, the highest in the series, against 24.3% a year earlier and 25.1% on March 31, 2024. The share has risen for five straight quarters, from 22.2% at June 30, 2025. It did not rise in every quarter before that. It fell in Q2 2024, when the wirehouses reduced, and again in Q4 2024 and Q2 2025, when advisors were buying but hedge funds and trading firms were buying more. Measured against all the bitcoin in the funds, including the part that no 13F filer reports, the category holds 11.2%, up from 5.3% on March 31, 2024, and that share has risen for nine straight quarters. The three hedge fund categories together hold 19.0%, down from a peak of 50.6% on Dec. 31, 2024. Basis and relative-value funds alone shrunk from 33.9% on March 31, 2024, to 9.6%. Market makers and bank desks have stayed between 16.8% and 23.7% throughout and held 21.8% at quarter end.

Net Quarterly Change by Holder Type The next chart isolates Q3 2026. Five of the eight holder types added and three reduced. Advisors and wealth platforms (+24,838) accounted for 50.5% of the +49,176 added by all filers across the 12 exchange-listed products, ahead of market makers and bank desks (+14,600), macro hedge funds (+10,492) and basis and relative-value hedge funds (+9,184). Pensions, sovereigns, and endowments were close to flat (+181). The types that reduced were other hedge funds and crypto firms (−5,295), family offices and corporates (−3,798,) and asset managers (−1,024). For family offices and corporates, it was the third straight quarterly reduction, and for asset managers it was the first net reduction in the series. One qualification applies to the largest bar. The advisor category includes the wirehouses, and the wirehouse unit breakdown table shows that their dealer and trading units, which behave more like the market makers and bank desks in the second bar, rose to 12,551 BTC-equivalent from 3,982 during the quarter.

Table of Net Quarterly Change by Holder Type (BTC-equivalent) The table below gives the numbers behind the holder type charts above and splits several holder types into their components. Three patterns stand out. First, among advisors and wealth platforms, the buying has shifted from independent firms to the large platforms. RIAs and wealth managers added in nine of the 10 quarters and account for 51,567 of the category's cumulative 100,003, but their flows in 2026 have been small (+2,492, −1,565, and +2,110). Wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms have added for nine straight quarters and at a rising pace: 3,998 in Q1 2026, 11,953 in Q2 2026 and 22,728 in Q3 2026. Second, basis and relative-value hedge funds are the only holder type with a negative cumulative total (−25,365). They have sold more since March 31, 2024, than they bought. Third, sovereign wealth and government holders added 13,142 between Q4 2024 and Q1 2026 and have not reported a net reduction in any quarter. They hold 13,101.

Wirehouses and Broker-Dealer Platform Holdings by Business Unit A bank or brokerage files one Form 13F for many subsidiaries, so a wirehouse's total can combine client accounts at its advisor arm with positions on its trading desk. This table uses each filing's own list of included managers to separate them. The 19 firms in the group hold 63,858 BTC-equivalent ($5.34 billion), up from 41,202 on June 30, 2026. Of that, 43,583 sits at advisor and brokerage arms, 12,551 at dealer and trading units, 5,256 at banks and trust companies, and 2,468 at asset management and other units. Holdings at the advisor and brokerage arms rose 41% in the quarter, from 30,978, so the main finding holds: the wealth channel itself is adding. But dealer and trading units more than tripled, to 12,551 from 3,982, and the advisor arms' share of the group fell to 68.2% from 75.2%. Counting only RIAs and these advisor arms, the wealth channel holds 124,032 BTC-equivalent, up from 109,548. That is more than the whole advisor category held at any earlier quarter end, though as a share of 13F holdings it slipped to 34.8% from 35.6%. Three firms hold 83.5% of the group's total. Wells Fargo's 30,553 is 85.1% at its advisor and brokerage arms (26,016, up from 13,219). Morgan Stanley's 14,354 is divided among advisor arms (7,141), dealer units (4,925) and asset management and other units (2,288). Bank of America is the exception. Of its 8,424, 7,626 sits at dealer and trading units, up from 421, and 16 at its advisor arms. We would read its increase as dealer positioning, not as demand from wealth clients. Form 13F covers only assets over which a manager has investment discretion. Client-directed brokerage accounts are generally not in these figures, so they understate what the firms' clients own.

Where the Holders Are The next charts place each manager at its principal office. A global bank or wirehouse counts at its headquarters, so this is a map of where the managers are, not of where their clients live. And because a manager outside the U.S. files Form 13F only if it manages at least $100 million in U.S.-listed securities, the figures for managers outside the U.S. are a floor.
Spot Bitcoin ETP Holdings of 13F Filers by Manager Region Managers based in the U.S. hold 293,830 BTC-equivalent, 82.5% of the 13F-reported total and the most in the series. Managers outside the U.S. hold 62,456, or 17.5%, across 111 firms. The U.K. and Crown Dependencies are the largest region outside the U.S. at 25,550, up from 16,699 on June 30, 2026, but about half the peak of 50,138 on Sept. 30, 2025. Asia-Pacific (14,938) has declined for three straight quarters from a peak of 24,353. The Middle East (14,525) is at a record and is the only region that has added in each of the last eight quarters. Canada (2,633), offshore financial centers (2,520), Europe outside the U.K. (2,000), and Latin America (290) are small.

Net Accumulation per Quarter by Manager Region U.S. managers added a net 43,961 BTC-equivalent in Q3 2026, their largest quarterly addition since Q4 2024 and 89% of the quarter's total. The U.K. and Crown Dependencies added 8,850, the region's first net addition after three quarters in which it sold a combined 33,338. The turn is largely one firm: Brevan Howard, which is placed in Jersey, added 8,606. The Middle East added 360 and extended its run of net additions to eight quarters. Asia-Pacific (−2,109) and Canada (−1,746) cut the most, and Asia-Pacific has been a net seller for three straight quarters. The chart also shows that the selling of late 2025 and early 2026 rotated from region to region. In Q4 2025 the U.K. and Crown Dependencies sold 20,206 while Asia-Pacific added 7,136. In Q1 2026 the U.S. sold 23,515. By Q2 2026 the U.S. had turned buyer (+13,494) while the U.K. and Crown Dependencies and Asia-Pacific were still selling.

Holdings Outside the U.S. by Country Four jurisdictions hold 76% of the bitcoin reported by managers outside the U.S. The United Arab Emirates is first with 13,842 BTC-equivalent (22.2% of the non-U.S. total), nearly all of it held by two Abu Dhabi sovereign investors. The island of Jersey is second with 13,149 after more than tripling in the quarter, from 4,121, reflecting the addition of Brevan Howard, which is based there. The U.K. (12,399) was little changed. Hong Kong (8,348) fell by about a third, from 12,408, as Avenir Tech and Laurore reduced. Australia (3,127), Singapore (2,997), Canada (2,633), and the Cayman Islands (2,219) follow. Canada has the most filers of any country outside the U.S. (27) but small positions, and continental Europe is thinly represented, led by Italy (735) and Switzerland (689).

13F Holdings in the U.S. by State Within the U.S., New York dominates. Managers there hold 138,825 BTC-equivalent, 47.2% of the U.S. total and 39.0% of all 13F-reported holdings, because most of the large hedge funds, market makers, banks and asset managers are placed there. The five largest states (New York, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Massachusetts) hold 74.3% of the U.S. total. The quarter's largest moves trace to single firms. California added 14,651 to reach 43,104, an amount almost equal to the addition at Wells Fargo (14,636), which is placed at its San Francisco headquarters. North Carolina more than quadrupled, to 9,794 from 2,315, on Bank of America's addition in Charlotte. Pennsylvania's gain of 5,234 comes largely from Susquehanna (+4,839). The managers are distributed differently from the bitcoin. California has the most filers (246), followed by New York (190), Texas (131), Florida (129), Pennsylvania (107) and Illinois (100), a spread that reflects where advisory firms are located more than where the largest positions are held.

Conclusion The most potent takeaway from Q3 is the relentless growth of advisors and wealth platforms as a distribution channel for bitcoin exposure through ETPs. In our October 2023 report Sizing the Market for a Bitcoin ETF, we argued that the wealth channel would be the most important segment for these products. The wealth management segment holds significant capital that has been unable to access bitcoin investments directly through traditional channels – with an approved spot ETF, financial advisors can start to direct their wealth clients to invest in bitcoin. Sizing the Market for a Bitcoin ETF. Galaxy Research, October 24, 2023. Now, more than 3 years later, that channel accounts for 40% of all institutional ownership of these products. The striking growth in Wells Fargo’s reported holdings – 85% of which come from its advisor and broker-dealer platforms – raises the possibility of the enactment of a systematic allocation strategy rather than simply a handful of very bullish clients. Bitcoin ETP holdings in this channel have exclusively increased every quarter since Q2 2024 regardless of market conditions. Because these accounts are longer term focused and utilize a target allocation per asset class in a portfolio, advisors are likely to buy when assets decline in value and sell when they appreciate, contributing to lower volatility and dampening downturns. We expect ETP ownership growth from this segment to continue.
Appendix: Definitions and Methodology
What is Form 13F? Institutional managers with investment discretion over at least $100 million in U.S.-listed equities and other Section 13(f) securities report their holdings to the Securities and Exchange Commission within 45 days of each quarter end. Filings for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, were due Nov. 16, 2026. This report reflects 2,166 filings made through Nov. 17, 2026. In past quarters 97.7% of filings were in by the end of the deadline day, so late filings and amendments can still change the figures.
What the form does not show A Form 13F lists long positions at the quarter end. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, and options positions are excluded here, so a long position at a market maker or a basis fund may be hedged. Only accounts over which the manager has investment discretion are reported, so client-directed accounts are generally absent. A parent and its sub-adviser can both report the same shares.
What is BTC-equivalent? A manager's shares in each fund multiplied by the fund's bitcoin per share at the quarter end. For six funds, the rate is equal to the trust's own reported bitcoin divided by its shares outstanding; for seven it is net asset value per share divided by the quarter-end price of bitcoin.
Net change The change in a manager's shares from the prior quarter end multiplied by the current quarter's bitcoin per share, adjusted for the share splits in ARKB, HODL and the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust. A move in the price of bitcoin therefore produces no net change. Dollar flows value the same share change at quarter-end share prices.
Two sets of funds Several charts and summary figures cover all 13 spot Bitcoin funds that filers reported, including the Osprey Bitcoin Trust, which trades over the counter (2,166 managers; 356,491 BTC-equivalent). Other charts cover the 12 exchange-listed funds (2,164 managers; 356,286 BTC-equivalent).
Holder types Each filing manager is assigned to one of eight types from its name, its Form ADV client mix, and a manual review of the largest filers. Wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms are counted with advisors and wealth platforms. We divide their holdings by business unit using the list of other included managers on each filing's cover page and the unit number on each line of its information table.
New and exiting holders A new holder reported a spot bitcoin fund at the quarter end and none at the prior quarter end. An exiting holder reported one at the prior quarter end and none at this one.
Geography Each manager is placed at its principal office, taken from the filing's cover page and other regulatory records, with registered-agent and mailbox addresses resolved by hand. A global bank or wirehouse counts at its headquarters. Primary data source: Galaxy Research, from Form 13F filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission and each fund's published holdings.

articles.title: AI governance for financial services firms
articles.text:
Developing robust frameworks

AI has transformed financial services, from optimising internal processes to managing different elements of the customer engagement and risk management lifecycles. According to the FCA and Bank of England (BoE), 86%opens in a new tab of firms now use AI. Banks have been embedding AI in their operational and wider risk management frameworks, for example in credit risk management and fraud detection, while insurers are increasingly using it in claims-handling. In the capital markets, AI is helping to optimise portfolios and analyse alternative data, and payments firms are using it to process customer behavioural analytics.While firms are benefitting from the opportunities presented by AI, FS regulators are alert to the risks it may present. A quick horizon scan of announcements reveals that AI risks are consistently high on supervisory agendas, with frequent speeches and warnings in the UK, EU, US and internationally (see AI Regulatory Radaropens in a new tab for more information). And yet, while AI risks attract significant attention, there are no regulatory regimes dedicated specifically to AI governance in financial services. Regulators have emphasised that existing frameworks should be used to manage AI risks and have stopped short of introducing new FS-specific policy or legislation. This is understandable: there are challenges in developing prescriptive regulation of a fast-paced technological change, and in an environment of growth, competitiveness and simplification, there is limited appetite from both firms and supervisors to develop additional regulatory regimes.However, relying on existing frameworks can present its own difficulties. As highlighted in the UK Mills Reviewopens in a new tab earlier this year, existing accountability, model risk management and consumer protection frameworks were designed for primarily human interactions. As AI becomes a core operational capability, firms should evolve their approaches and address AI risks such as model drift, data bias, hallucinations, AI agents, and other behaviours – many of which are not captured in traditional validation approaches. As highlighted by the UK Parliamentary Treasury Committeeopens in a new tab and the BoE’s Financial Policy Committeeopens in a new tab, there are potential consequences for financial stability and spillover effects into the wider economy if AI-driven FS risks crystallise, including financial impacts for consumers, policyholders and investors. Firms may therefore require more dynamic approaches to AI governance, and they are seeking practical guidance from regulators on how existing frameworks can help achieve this.At an international level the Financial Stability Board (FSB) has finalised Sound Practicesopens in a new tab for responsible AI-adoption. These are the closest development so far to an internationally-agreed AI governance approach specifically for FS firms, but the FSB is clear that while boards are ‘strongly encouraged’ to adopt the practices, they ‘do not constitute a binding international standard’.The FCA recently published good and poor AI practicesopens in a new tab on consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience. The publication includes case studies alongside guidance on how to apply the practices to smaller firms. The FCA has been clear that it supports innovation and will update its guidance as technology evolves.At KPMG in the UK, we often hear from firms that the lack of guidance around AI adoption can make it harder to manage risks appropriately, proportionally, and consistently with market peers. The FSB and FCA publications are therefore welcome interventions, and firms are likely to use them to guide their AI governance practices. Firms can also look to the AI Governance Principles for Boardsopens in a new tab developed jointly by KPMG International and INSEAD in 2026. Whilst these principles are sector-agnostic, they can be mapped neatly to the FSB sound practices, providing a prototype framework for AI governance in FS firms.

The FSB’s Sound Practices on Responsible AI Adoption

The FSB’s 12 Sound Practicesopens in a new tab were finalised on 15 October and cover responsible AI adoption by FS firms across the organisation and AI lifecycle. The FSB explicitly notes that the practices are ‘non-prescriptive’; instead, they are meant to ‘promote coordination, cooperation and information-sharing’ between FS stakeholders, and thus can be used by firms as a basis for AI governance. The FSB notes that the sound practices will evolve as AI technologies and understanding of their associated risks develop. For example, the finalised document includes greater consideration of agentic AI and multi-agent systems than the draft.Organisation-wide AI governance (sound practices 1-4)The FSB’s first four sound practices focus on organisation-wide AI governance and position boards and senior management at the centre of responsible AI adoption:1. Strategic direction and oversight – AI should be treated as a strategic business, risk and resilience issue, with boards ensuring that AI adoption aligns with the institution’s business model, risk appetite and long-term objectives.2. Governance and accountability – calls for clear governance structures and decision-making processes to oversee AI-related activities. This includes relevant approaches for centralised vs decentralised adoption, establishing cross-functional coordination and splitting responsibilities across the three lines of defence.3. AI risk management framework and effective documentation – highlights the need for robust policies, controls and documentation to identify, assess, monitor and manage AI-related risks across the organisation.4. Organisational adaptability – firms should develop the skills, resources and capabilities needed to respond to the rapid evolution of AI technologies and risks, including monitoring external developments that can surface early risk signals that internal processes may not detect.AI lifecycle management (sound practices 5-12)The remaining sound practices address the management of AI throughout its lifecycle:5. Materiality and risk assessments and6. Selection are important to assess the materiality and risk of AI use cases at the inception and thereafter, and to select models that are appropriate for their objectives and risk profile.7. Data governance – ensures that data used to train, test and operate AI systems is accurate, reliable and secure.8. Explainability and transparency – firms should understand differences in the explainability of various types of AI, implement controls if appropriate and provide transparency to different stakeholders.9. Performance management and10. Human oversight – call for rigorous testing, ongoing monitoring and oversight proportionate to the complexity, autonomy and risk of the AI application.11. Cyber and ICT risk management and12. Third-party risk management – firms should focus on strengthening operational resilience and managing risks arising from AI providers, including model performance, data quality, concentration, supply-chain and business continuity risks.

Mapping KPMG INSEAD principles to FSB sound practices

In 2026, KPMG International and INSEAD published a joint report on AI Governance Principles for Boardsopens in a new tab, highlighting five key principles to help companies evaluate the longer-term opportunities of AI while managing its risks:strategic oversight for long-term value creationactive technology and security oversightworkforce transformation and human accountabilitybuilding trustworthy AIthe work of the board.The FSB’s 12 sound practices can be mapped to the KPMG INSEAD sector-agnostic principles as follows:

Sources: AI Governance Principles for Boardsopens in a new tab and Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Final report - Financial Stability Boardopens in a new tab

In this way, FS firms can apply the KPMG INSEAD principles alongside the FSB’s sound practices, to help achieve appropriate and proportionate AI governance within their organisations.Applying these principles and sound practices involves translating them into proportionate governance, clear accountability and practical controls across the AI lifecycle, building on firms’ existing risk management arrangements.

How KPMG in the UK can help

KPMG professionals can work with firms to develop and strengthen AI governance processes, leveraging our Trusted AI assets and accelerators that have supported numerous organisations globally. This could include:Designing an FS-specific AI governance framework aligned with your business model, risk appetites and existing regulatory obligations, drawing on the FSB sound practices, KPMG INSEAD principles and emerging supervisory expectations.Clarifying board and senior management accountability by defining decision rights, committee responsibilities, escalation routes and management information needed to oversee AI strategy, risk and resilience.Assessing current AI governance maturity and identifying gaps across policies, controls, documentation, skills and oversight, benchmarking arrangements against evolving regulatory practice and relevant market peers.Helping to establish a risk-based AI inventory and classification approach to identify AI use cases, assess their materiality and apply proportionate approval, monitoring and control requirements.Strengthening lifecycle risk management across model selection, data governance, testing, explainability, human oversight, performance monitoring and the controlled retirement of AI systems. This includes working with business and technology teams to embed proportionate controls, define human oversight and permitted actions for generative and agentic AI, and establish monitoring, escalation and reassessment following material changes.Enhancing operational resilience and third-party oversight by assessing cyber, ICT, concentration, supply-chain, data quality and business continuity risks associated with external AI models and service providers.Supporting regulatory readiness and organisational adaptability through horizon scanning, regulatory mapping, scenario exercises, and board training.KPMG professionals can also support AI assurance readiness and provide independent assurance, with the scope and criteria tailored to the intended purpose. This could include:Assessing AI assurance readiness by determining whether suitable criteria, governance, oversight, controls, documentation and evidence needed to support future assurance are in place.Providing independent assurance over AI-related controls and systems through SOC 1, SOC 2 / SOC 2+ or ISAE 3000 assurance, where appropriate to the subject matter, agreed criteria and intended users, and subject to applicable independence requirements.

articles.text:
Finance and Economics Discussion Series (FEDS)

Twitter

RSS

November 2026

Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
Kabir Dasgupta, Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James, Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum

Abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.
Keywords: Drink-driving convictions, Criminal records and employment, Labour market effects of crime, Administrative data and causal inference

A house tipped on side after the 15 foot storm surge of the Galveston Hurricane of Sept. 1900. Shutterstock / Everett Collection

4 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
Karen Clark is a member of the Hutchins Center’s task force on reducing impact of extreme weather on insurance costs & availability. This paper was commissioned by the task force, which will issue a report in spring 2027.

Karen Clark and colleagues at Karen Clark & Co. use the firm’s model to estimate the reduction in property losses on the Texas coast in a hurricane as strong as the 1900 Galveston Hurricane if single family homes met the stiffest building codes. The bottom line: Stronger building codes can generate significant reductions in hurricane losses. The additional costs associated with stronger wind-resistant construction are often small relative to the resulting reduction in expected losses, particularly in high-risk coastal communities.
This map shows the territory on which the study focused.

The authors test four scenarios:
Scenario 1: All homes in coastal counties were built to the most recent building code in the year they were built.
Scenario 2: Only homes built in 1995 or after were built to the then-current building code. Under this scenario, approximately 40% of the replacement cost of houses in the coastal counties was upgraded.
Scenario 3: Only homes constructed after 2000 were built to meet then-current code. This corresponds roughly to the period following major advances in hurricane engineering and building code modernization in many jurisdictions. Under this scenario, approximately 30% of the replacement cost of houses in the coastal counties was upgraded.
Scenario 4: Only the newest building stock, i.e., those constructed in or after 2012, met the most recent building code during the year they were built. Under this scenario, approximately 16% of the replacement cost was upgraded.
This table summarizes the results.

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The authors then do a benefit-cost analysis, looking over 30 years with a discount rate of 4.25%. For most of the territory, the benefits exceed the costs, more in Galveston, which sits on the Gulf Coast, than for more inland areas, such as Houston. This table summarizes the results. (BCR means benefit-cost ratio. A ratio above one means benefits exceed costs. SFH means single-family home. IRC means International Residential Code.)
