articles.title: The debt financing of AI and its implications for financial stability
articles.text: The debt financing of AI and its implications for financial stabilityPrepared by Federica Bosio, Lara Coulier, Daniel Dieckelmann, Tina Emambakhsh, Maciej Grodzicki and Maria Leonor Puga[1] This box has benefited from data support provided by Chiara Scommegna and Fabian Wagner. Published as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.The investment needs of firms in the AI supply chain are unprecedented in scale. Cumulative capital expenditure by US big tech firms alone is forecast to reach about USD 5.5 trillion by 2030, although estimates vary widely. On an annual basis, overall AI investment needs would amount to more than 3% of US GDP between 2025 and 2032, which is considerably larger than the financing of other major innovations in the past.[2] The capital expenditure estimates for US big tech firms are based on broker estimates from the LSEG Data & Analytics platform on 26 October 2026 for Alphabet, Amazon, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle. Total annual capital expenditure figures are based on Van Nieuwerburgh, S., “Financing the AI Buildout”, NBER Working Papers, No 35865, National Bureau of Economic Research, October 2026. For comparison, annual capital expenditure for the development of the Northern Pacific Railway amounted to about 2.24% of US GDP between 1870 and 1890 and the internet boom between 1996 and 2003 took up 1.10% of US GDP. Investment in the AI buildout is highly concentrated among a small group of US firms, including hyperscalers and manufacturers of semiconductors. While these firms have in the past generated large free cash flows through their non-AI-related activities, free cash flows turned negative for most US hyperscalers in 2026, as capital expenditure on AI infrastructure exceeded operating cash flows.[3] At the same time, two large semiconductor firms, Broadcom and Nvidia, have seen their free cash flows soar on the back of strong demand for chips, including from hyperscalers. In response, these firms are increasingly turning to external funding from equity[4] See Dieckelmann, D., Franco, L., O’Gorman, P. and Scommegna, C., “Financial stability risks from large IPOs, equity issuance and passive investing”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, November 2026. and debt.Alongside debt from public and private markets, firms are increasingly using opaque off-balance-sheet structures to fund the AI infrastructure buildout. Public debt issuance by US big tech firms has surged within a very short period of time, in both the United States and other jurisdictions.[5] See Duquerroy, A., Furtuna, O. and Vaz Cruz, L., “Big tech’s growing presence in the euro bond market: implications for investors”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, November 2026. This issuance has been complemented by other sources of debt finance, based on expected future cash flows from monetising AI-related infrastructure. Specifically, hyperscalers contractually commit to use the AI-related infrastructure of data centre developers and advanced chip owners. Future cash flows from these commitments can be employed by owners of AI-related assets to secure borrowing from lenders like banks, bond investors or private credit funds.[6] Under US Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 842, a lease is not recognised on the balance sheet until the starting date of the asset’s use, even if the lease agreement was already signed prior to that date. Under ASC 440, any future obligations and significant contractual commitments must be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements. Such cash flow commitments are debt-like in economic terms, but they do not appear as liabilities on the balance sheets of hyperscalers under US accounting standards. Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than USD 4 trillion as of the second quarter of 2026 (Chart A, panel a), well in excess of their outstanding on-balance-sheet liabilities.The opaqueness of AI-related debt is further compounded by circular links in the form of mutual commitments and interlinked ownerships between firms in the AI supply chain. AI-related firms, such as cloud service providers and AI labs, purchase and lease chips from manufacturers to provide computing services. These purchases are often financed by the chipmakers. Such mutual finance commitments inflate the expected revenues of both the chipmaker and the service provider, because the reported demand of an involved firm is partly driven by that firm’s own financing decisions (Chart A, panel b). Hyperscalers are also connected to other firms in the AI ecosystem through lending and equity stakes. Valuation gains on private equity holdings, especially in AI labs, are increasingly contributing to hyperscalers’ earnings growth (Chart B, panel a).[7] “Other income” reported by Alphabet and Amazon comes from revaluations of private equity stakes in Anthropic, which are included in the reported earnings of these firms. Nvidia has acquired equity stakes in companies like CoreWeave, OpenAI and Anthropic. Chart ABig tech investments are increasingly being financed via debt issued outside of own balance sheets amid rising interlinkages within the AI ecosystema) Big tech firms’ total on- and off-balance-sheet liabilitiesb) Stylised example of circular financing risks in the AI ecosystem(2025, 2026; USD billions)Sources: Company SEC filings and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: GOOG = Alphabet, AMZN = Amazon, META = Meta, MSFT = Microsoft, NVDA = Nvidia, ORCL = Oracle, AVGO = Broadcom, ANT = Anthropic. Data for 2025 refer to the full financial year and data for 2026 refer to the most recent SEC filing. Data from Anthropic are based on its IPO filing (S-1). Fixed commitments refer to future lease payments or contractual purchases that are fixed. Contingent commitments include backstops and purchase obligations that become payable if pre-specified conditions apply, e.g. if the underlying counterparties experience financial distress. Data were extracted from the selected companies’ public SEC filings using an agentic AI model developed by ECB staff. The AI agent (using Open AI’s ChatGPT 5.6-Sol) was trained to replicate manually compiled and validated off-balance-sheet aggregates as of Q1 2026 from the sample of firms and instructed to identify the relevant balance-sheet information from the companies’ filings available on the SEC’s website for the other periods. The extracted data were subsequently cross-checked manually by ECB staff. Panel b: dashed blue lines indicate changes in valuation. Solid blue lines indicate flows of money. The yellow line indicates shock transmission. An AI lab is a company which develops, tests and applies AI technologies, including large language models (LLMs). SPV stands for special-purpose vehicle.Investors have become more attentive to risks associated with the volume and growth of the debt needed to finance the AI buildout, together with its opacity and circularity. There is a risk that hyperscaler earnings may not fully meet current expectations. This could be due to competition from cheaper open-source models abroad, supply-side factors – such as energy, chip and grid bottlenecks – or a shorter than expected lifespan of advanced chips.[8] The IMF estimates that the average implied useful life of graphics processing units (GPUs) and advanced chips is considerably shorter than more standard types of physical assets (two versus seven years) due to the speed of technological advancement in the AI field. See “Global Financial Stability Report”, International Monetary Fund, April 2026. In such a scenario, firm leverage metrics, and consequently their credit ratings, could deteriorate, as the full debt incurred for the AI buildout would gradually be recognised on balance sheets, while the value of assets may be impaired and income projections fall short of expectations. Circular relationships could amplify the impact and cause spillovers within the industry. The long duration of the debt (Chart B, panel b) exacerbates the risk of valuation losses if hyperscalers are not successful in monetising their investments. In essence, the maturity of hyperscalers’ outstanding debt exceeds the economic lifetimes of a substantial share of the physical capital funded by this debt, especially in the form of advanced chips.[9] Chips are not the only physical asset, and other assets like data centre facilities have longer economic lives. Given the long duration of the debt incurred, a significant mismatch likely remains. As issuance has increased, credit spreads on hyperscaler debt have widened relative to similarly rated corporate issuers, particularly at longer maturities (Chart B, panel c). This could be an indication that markets currently view rating agencies’ risk assessments as too benign.Chart BMarkets have started to acknowledge the rising debt levels of AI-related firms and the potential stranded asset risks stemming from a shorter than expected economic life of collateral assetsa) “Other income” as a share of total net incomeb) Hyperscalers’ cumulative outstanding debt securities, by residual maturityc) Difference between spreads on bonds of big tech firms and of equally rated US corporates(percentages)(left-hand scale: USD billions,right-hand scale: percentages)(Jan. 2024-Nov. 2026, basis points)Sources: Company SEC filings, Dealogic, a service of ION Analytics, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: “Other income” refers to revenue earned from activities outside a company's core operations and includes unrealised gains or losses from equity holdings as well as dividend income. Data for 2025 refer to the full financial year; data for 2026 refer to the most recent SEC filing, which is the annual financial statements in the case of Microsoft and Oracle and quarterly reports for the rest. Panel b: hyperscalers’ cumulative outstanding debt is calculated using the subset of issued debt that is in Dealogic. The last data point represents all outstanding debt. Market intelligence suggests that the economic life of AI equipment is between one and three years, as represented in the shaded area. The accounting life for servers and network equipment is taken from companies’ SEC filings between 2020 and 2025; most hyperscalers have increased this from three years in 2020 to six years in 2026. Data as at 10 November 2026. Panel c: the chart shows the difference between the credit spreads of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and SpaceX (i.e. the yield to maturity minus the maturity-matched yield of US Treasuries) and the credit spread of equally rated US corporate bond spreads (AAA, AA, A and BBB; again, measured against maturity-matched US Treasury yields). Credit spreads are weighted by US dollar amount outstanding. The chart shows the average across the eight firms and the respective minimum-maximum range.The rapid shift towards debt finance invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles and could lead to spillovers affecting euro area financial stability. Even if AI as a technology successfully transforms the global economy, the credit-driven AI boom may result in overcapacity, capital misallocation and credit losses for investors. Past episodes of technological disruption and financial exuberance provide historical parallels. The capital spending and technological aspects are reminiscent of the dotcom bubble of the early 2000s, which was characterised by overinvestment in infrastructure but only a shallow recession thanks to a large share of equity finance. So far, however, hyperscalers’ earnings have broadly kept up with expectations. That said, the rapid acceleration of debt financing raises concerns that the AI buildout might become debt-driven and unsustainable, with further risks added by circular financing, the use of off-balance-sheet transactions and opaqueness in private markets. Such dynamics were evident during the subprime mortgage bubble. Spillovers through direct and especially indirect channels could have significant adverse consequences in the euro area.[10] Direct spillovers would stem from holdings of AI-related debt and equity. They would expose institutional investors especially, but also households as direct investors in equity and indirect investors through funds, to valuation losses which could impair consumer confidence and spill over to the real economy. Indirect spillovers could come from a deterioration in global financial conditions, foreign demand or risk sentiment. Historically, credit booms that turned into a bust were associated with a significant and prolonged contraction in real GDP compared with pre-crisis trends. Such a shock to the US economy would likely result in a significant contraction in euro area GDP as well. This box has benefited from data support provided by Chiara Scommegna and Fabian Wagner. The capital expenditure estimates for US big tech firms are based on broker estimates from the LSEG Data & Analytics platform on 26 October 2026 for Alphabet, Amazon, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle. Total annual capital expenditure figures are based on Van Nieuwerburgh, S., “Financing the AI Buildout”, NBER Working Papers, No 35865, National Bureau of Economic Research, October 2026. For comparison, annual capital expenditure for the development of the Northern Pacific Railway amounted to about 2.24% of US GDP between 1870 and 1890 and the internet boom between 1996 and 2003 took up 1.10% of US GDP. At the same time, two large semiconductor firms, Broadcom and Nvidia, have seen their free cash flows soar on the back of strong demand for chips, including from hyperscalers. See Dieckelmann, D., Franco, L., O’Gorman, P. and Scommegna, C., “Financial stability risks from large IPOs, equity issuance and passive investing”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, November 2026. See Duquerroy, A., Furtuna, O. and Vaz Cruz, L., “Big tech’s growing presence in the euro bond market: implications for investors”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, November 2026. Under US Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 842, a lease is not recognised on the balance sheet until the starting date of the asset’s use, even if the lease agreement was already signed prior to that date. Under ASC 440, any future obligations and significant contractual commitments must be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements. “Other income” reported by Alphabet and Amazon comes from revaluations of private equity stakes in Anthropic, which are included in the reported earnings of these firms. Nvidia has acquired equity stakes in companies like CoreWeave, OpenAI and Anthropic. The IMF estimates that the average implied useful life of graphics processing units (GPUs) and advanced chips is considerably shorter than more standard types of physical assets (two versus seven years) due to the speed of technological advancement in the AI field. See “Global Financial Stability Report”, International Monetary Fund, April 2026. Chips are not the only physical asset, and other assets like data centre facilities have longer economic lives. Given the long duration of the debt incurred, a significant mismatch likely remains. Direct spillovers would stem from holdings of AI-related debt and equity. They would expose institutional investors especially, but also households as direct investors in equity and indirect investors through funds, to valuation losses which could impair consumer confidence and spill over to the real economy. Indirect spillovers could come from a deterioration in global financial conditions, foreign demand or risk sentiment. Historically, credit booms that turned into a bust were associated with a significant and prolonged contraction in real GDP compared with pre-crisis trends. Such a shock to the US economy would likely result in a significant contraction in euro area GDP as well.

The income produced by municipal bonds is typically exempt from income taxes at the federal level. Municipal bonds may also be exempt from state and local taxes based on where the investor resides.

In our view, there are many good reasons to invest in the municipal bond market now.
First, muni yields are as high as they've been in 15 years following two years of unprecedented interest rate hikes by the Fed.4
Second, municipal bonds have a long history of low defaults compared to corporate bonds because they fund essential American services.5
Third, the municipal yield curve is steeper than the Treasury yield curve. A steep yield curve means that there is value in duration. Municipal investors who own longer dated munis may be compensated much more than those in longer dated Treasuries.
Fourth, federal, state and in some places local tax rates are high and we don't see them going down. This may provide additional value to the muni tax exemption.

Our high conviction approach to investing aims to deliver a highly competitive yield by exploiting anomalies that exist in the high yield municipal market. The Invesco Municipal Bond team employs a bottom-up, research-oriented approach to generate income-driven total return. Our experienced credit research staff works to uncover value in non-rated bonds, which may offer the potential for higher yield and total return.

We believe in giving investors choices that work for their unique needs. Invesco Rochester High Yield Municipal ETF is an actively managed exchange-traded fund that seeks current income exempt from federal income tax.

We view risk from multiple lenses and manage it using both integrated and independent approaches. First, risk management is embedded within our investment process. Second, multiple governance structures provide independent oversight and monitoring. Third comes senior management and board review.

articles.title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Nomura London Macro Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Catherine L. Mann discusses how UK financial markets have priced in greater risk premia since the Middle East conflict intensified. She uses several models to uncover their sources and considers how monetary policy and communication can help reduce premia to ensure inflation returns to target.

Speech
Introduction
The conflict in the Middle East has generated significant volatility and financial market repricing in the UK, relating to uncertainty around the evolution of the conflict, the outlook for UK inflation, and our monetary policy response. Financial conditions are an essential mechanism through which monetary policy transmits and therefore form an important input into my monetary policy decisions. In this speech, I will evaluate the information that financial conditions provide about the current monetary policy stance and transmission, and carefully examine what they reveal about the types of risks driving recent moves.
Financial conditions
Let me start with a headline indicator of financial conditions, which summarizes how a broad range of asset price movements contribute to changes in nominal and real financial conditions. The effect of policy tightening since 2022 on nominal financial conditions in the UK is clearly visible, as the pink line in Chart 1 shows. Despite a modest loosening over 2025, this measure of nominal financial conditions resumed a slight tightening since the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East on account of higher short and long-term nominal interest rates.

Chart 1: Changes in UK financial conditions since 2020
Index points

Footnotes

Source: Burr (2023) Opens in a new window using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and LSEG.
Notes: The real financial conditions index uses real interest rate variables, exchange rate and equity prices – that is, net of inflation compensation. Latest observation: August 2026.

Nominal financial conditions incorporate inflation expectations and inflation risk premia, which may distort the signal about real tightness, particularly following an inflationary shock. The real financial conditions index in Chart 1 (white line) strips out the effects of rising inflation compensation following the start of the conflict in the Middle East at the end of February. This index suggests that real financial conditions loosened around the beginning of the conflict (consistent with inflation compensation measures rising significantly in March), some of which have since retraced, albeit with a notable compression in spreads.
Given that inflation has been well-above target for five years already and the conflict in the Middle East has contributed to further upside risks to inflation, real and nominal financial conditions need to remain tight. There are two mechanisms through which I can tighten real financial conditions: reducing measures of inflation compensation, and/or, raising nominal yields (and expectations), both of which can be achieved through an increase in Bank Rate. In my view, our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, which is why I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
As financial conditions indices summarize a range of underlying market dynamics, I will unpack some of their key drivers and explore what they reveal about what is priced in. This assessment concludes that the MPC cannot simply rely on policy restrictiveness coming from an upward shift in the nominal yield curve. At some point, we need to follow-through with Bank Rate rises – to maintain credibility, and to avoid policy expectations repricing downwards and inflation expectations repricing further upwards.
What does the gap between markets and participants imply?
Overall nominal financial conditions have remained relatively tight, but what are financial market expectations for the future path of monetary policy? We can gauge market expectations of the policy rate path from a variety of sources. For the UK, these are the yield curve, such as the overnight index swap (OIS) curve, and the Bank of England Market Participants Survey (MaPS).footnote [1]
Chart 2 plots the OIS curve across the UK, US and euro area (EA), and survey-based policy rate expectations from the respective central banks’ latest surveys of market participants. The survey-based measures should offer a cleaner read on policy rate expectations than the OIS curve, because they do not include risk premia or other market-based technical factors. As the differences between the light and dark solid lines in Chart 2 show, there are gaps between the two measures for all three jurisdictions, but the difference is largest for the UK.
If the OIS curve only reflected expectations for policy rate changes, it would imply almost 75 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the next 12 months, in contrast to a prolonged hold (and subsequent cuts) implied by the MaPS. I have plotted the OIS curve at the respective dates of survey closure. Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months. The swathes indicate the interquartile ranges of the survey-based distributions; however, taking that into account does only a little to explain the gap in the UK.

Chart 2: OIS curves and survey-implied expectations for policy rates
Percent

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: UK survey data shows the median response (solid light aqua line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded aqua area) to the September 2026 Market Participants Survey. US survey data shows the median response (solid light purple line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded purple area) to the July 2026 Survey of Market Expectations Opens in a new window. Euro area survey data shows the median response (solid light orange line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses to the September 2026 ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts Opens in a new window. OIS curves (dark solid lines) on the respective dates of survey closure (4th September, 20th July and 26th August). Survey measures typically ask for policy rate expectations (Bank Rate, Federal Funds Rate/Range and Deposit Rate Facility) for UK, US and EA respectively. These do not exactly match the interest rate underlying the OIS (SONIA, SOFR and €STR).

The UK seems to be an outlier internationally, but is the current gap also large by historical standards? Chart 3 shows how the average difference between the OIS curve and market participants’ median expectations for Bank Rate has evolved over a 3-year horizon (left panel). There has been a material increase in the gap since the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East, to levels last seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Because the survey-based measure only captures market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate, movements in the gap can be a crude measure of risk premia. The widening observed this year therefore suggests that investors are demanding greater compensation for UK risk.

Chart 3: Average gap between market-based and survey-implied expectations for policy rates over a 3-year horizon
Basis points

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: The height of the bar reflects the average gap between the respective survey’s median ‘most likely’ (modal) profile for the policy rate and the average OIS curve observed across the survey window over a 3-year horizon.

What risks are investors demanding greater compensation for? There is no single model that allows us to decompose this risk premium into its various sources and drivers. In the remainder of this speech, I will go through various hypotheses, using a variety of different models and data, to pinpoint the types of risks relevant to driving this gap.
The role of the term premium
Movements in nominal government bond yields can be decomposed into contributions from changes in expected interest rates and a term premium. The term premium is the additional compensation required by investors (above and beyond their interest rate expectations) to hold interest rate risk. Before discussing what the charts show, it is worth noting that the term premium, and risk premia in general, are unobservable. We rely on a suite of models to estimate them.
Chart 4 shows a model-implied structural decomposition of a 3-year nominal yield into these two categories across the UK, US and Germany. The model decomposition is an average of three term structure models: Malik and Meldrum (2016) Opens in a new window, Vlieghe (2016) and Andreasen and Meldrum (2015). For the UK, this structural model-based decomposition complements the survey-based evidence from MaPS on policy expectations.footnote [2] In both the UK and Germany, 3-year government bond yields have risen by around 100 basis points over the past year, but the drivers appear to be different.
According to this term structure model, higher term premia account for around 24 basis points of the increase in the UK, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany. This contribution has been increasingly positive in the UK throughout the year. In the US, a positive contribution from the term premium is only visible more recently, accounting for around 25 basis points of the 140 basis points rise in yields.

Chart 4: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year nominal yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

To compare results across different models I show, in Chart 5, a decomposition from a different model (Lengyel and Walker, 2026) that adapts a standard affine term structure framework to identify near-term risk premia more cleanly. Relative to classic models, which are typically calibrated to fit the yield curve as a whole, this approach uses OIS instead of government bond yields, allows for a richer factor structure, and directly incorporates survey-based expectations for Bank Rate. While term premia make a larger contribution to yields overall across the UK, US and EA, the result that its contribution is largest for the UK is robust.

Chart 5: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year OIS yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

In a historical and international context, it is somewhat unusual that the term premium has contributed significantly to the rise in short-term yields. The term premium is often defined as the additional compensation investors demand to hold a longer-term bond relative to a series of shorter-term bonds (Kaminska, Meldrum and Young, 2015 Opens in a new window). It is therefore common for the term premium to show up at the longer end of the yield curve. That is, the further into the future you go, the more uncertain the future path of interest rates is. So why is the UK term premium such an outlier, and such a significant driver of short-term yields?
Chart 6 plots the model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium between 2009 and today. Over this period, the 1-year and 3-year term premium have been negative throughout the 2010s and after the Russia-Ukraine shock. A negative term premium is not unusual. Joyce, Kaminska and Lildholdt (2008) discuss various drivers for the UK, including regulatory changes, excess liquidity, and “flight to quality” dynamics away from risky assets in times of uncertainty. This could also be explained by a negative inflation risk premium (Cieslak and Pflueger, 2023 Opens in a new window).

Chart 6: UK model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Lengyel and Walker (2026) using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations.
Note: Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

However, term premia rose at the start of the conflict in the Middle East and have recently turned positive. That is also true for the 3-year term premium, which stands out as particularly high in recent history, and was only exceeded during the post-GFC period and when Russia invaded Ukraine. The Middle East energy shock is notable, but not as large as the Russia-Ukraine energy shock.
Staff work finds that the UK term premium, especially at the short end, has become more volatile and responsive to news about economic and financial market developments. In part, this reflects higher sensitivity of (international) investors (Mann, 2026) and a different composition of demand for government debt, including a reduced role of preferred habitat investors such as insurance companies and pension funds, as Beltran and Li (2026) Opens in a new window also find for the US.
Lengyel and Walker (2026) argue that risk premia at the short end of the curve reflect the compensation investors require for uncertainty around the policy rate path. It is therefore important for monetary policymakers to understand whether changes in nominal yields reflect changing policy expectations or uncertainty around them – distinguishing between the two has important consequences on how to interpret the moves in financial conditions.footnote [3]
I explore the role of near-term policy uncertainty in the next section.
What is the role of uncertainty?
Chart 7 shows the option-implied distributions of SONIA (the risk-free overnight interest rate for sterling markets, and the rate underlying the overnight index swap) 12 months ahead, and its equivalents for the US (SOFR) and the euro area (€STR) based on the methodology of Clews et al. (2000).footnote [4] While the OIS rate shown in the earlier Chart 2 reflects a summary statistic of the underlying distribution, the full distribution in Chart 7 contains additional information. Prior to the conflict (orange), the distributions for all three jurisdictions are tight – implying little uncertainty, and high conviction, about the future path of policy rates. Since the conflict began, the distributions for all three have shifted to the right and widened. The UK distribution, however, has widened slightly more, implying that perceived risks and uncertainty about the future policy rate have increasingly been priced in by markets, and particularly more so for the UK.

Chart 7: Option-implied distribution of interest rates, 12 months ahead
For SONIA, SOFR and €STR

Footnotes

Source: ICE, CME and Bank calculations
Note: The underlying rate for the UK distribution is the 3-month SONIA rate 12 months ahead. Latest observation: 25th September 2026

Furthermore, the skewness of SONIA has turned sharply positive following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, which implies that upside risks to interest rates are perceived to be materially larger than downside risks. This degree of positive skewness was last observed following the post-Covid supply chain disruptions in 2021 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The increase in uncertainty and the positive skewness could simply reflect a repricing of the outlook for the economy – reflecting uncertainty about how the conflict in the Middle East could play out, how the resulting supply shock will affect the UK economy going forward, and how it is passed through to broader pricing dynamics. However, such trade-off inducing shocks (shocks that are inflationary but have contractionary effects on activity) also make it more challenging for monetary policymakers to set policy, and uncertainty about the policy rate path could also be higher.
Financial markets are trying to price in both: uncertainty about the economic outlook and uncertainty about the monetary policy response. There is no “textbook” monetary policy response to supply shocks, and therefore, the market’s understanding of how members of the MPC might respond (that is, our reaction function) could be incomplete or unclear. Given that inflation has remained above target for five years and is expected to increase further as the energy shock propagates, the market might be pricing in a reaction function that is not consistent with bringing inflation back to the 2% target sustainably in the medium-term.
Is there a monetary policy uncertainty premium?
Could uncertainty about the monetary policy response to the conflict in the Middle East have also contributed to the gap between the OIS curve and market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate? Research about the effects of monetary policy has generally focused on the effect of changes in the level of Bank Rate on the UK economy (see for instance Brandt et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; Braun et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Di Pace et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Uncertainty about future interest rates and its effects on financial markets and the real economy has received less attention.
Based on a methodology developed by Bauer et al. (2022) Opens in a new window, Raviraj (forthcoming) constructs a financial market-based measure of UK monetary policy uncertaintyfootnote [5] surprises that uses changes in the standard deviation of the option-implied distribution of SONIA around MPC announcement dates. Using the surprise series as an instrument for a monetary policy uncertainty shock in a structural VAR allows the author to causally identify the effects of monetary policy uncertainty on a set of outcome variables.
Let me start by showing what this monetary policy uncertainty variable looks like and how it relates to MPC announcements. On average across the sample period (1997 to 2026), a monetary policy announcement leads to a resolution of uncertainty about short-term interest rates, as the decrease in the aqua line following the day of an MPC announcement in the left panel of Chart 8 shows. Monetary policy and communications around MPC decisions have acted as a stabilizing force in the economy, resolving uncertainty around the future path of interest rates.

Chart 8: Changes in monetary policy uncertainty around MPC announcementdates
Percent (LHS) and factor score (RHS)

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: The solid aqua line in the left chart shows the average change in short-rate uncertainty on trading days around MPC announcements from June 1997 until July 2026. The pink line shows the change in short-rate uncertainty around the March 2026 MPC announcement. The shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval. In the right chart, monetary policy uncertainty factors are constructed by applying Varimax rotation to principal components of changes in short-rate uncertainty and first moment interest rates around MPC announcements.

However, there is one notable meeting where our decision and communications do not seem to have played that role. In the left panel of Chart 8, I also plot (in pink) changes in uncertainty around the March 2026 decision – the first monetary policy meeting after the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. One may argue that this simply reflects elevated levels of uncertainty following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. However, the identification strategy for the monetary policy uncertainty shock isolates changes in uncertainty on MPC announcement days – these changes should therefore largely reflect news associated with the monetary policy decision and associated communications. It strips out any first moment, level effects of monetary policy and captures shocks associated with MPC announcements beyond what markets had already priced in. I plot the estimated monetary policy uncertainty factor in the right panel of Chart 8, which shows that monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.footnote [6]
What are the implications of an increase in monetary policy uncertainty? Using the monetary policy uncertainty shock series, we can evaluate the impact of such a shock on financial market variables. The left panel of Chart 9 shows the impulse response function of short rate uncertaintyfootnote [7] to a one standard deviation increase in monetary policy uncertainty. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty also leads to a rise in the 1-year OIS rate, driven by both a higher term premium and higher interest rate expectations. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty tightens financial conditions.

Chart 9: Impulse response functions of short rate uncertainty, term premium and expected interest rates to a monetary policy uncertainty shock
Percentage points

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: Impulse response functions to a one standard deviation structural monetary policy uncertainty shock, proxied by the monetary policy uncertainty factor presented in the right panel of Chart 8. Shaded areas represent 68% and 90% confidence intervals.

Yet, why did such a clear signal, a unanimous decision to hold Bank Rate, result in higher uncertainty? It could be because our communication about the outlook for the economy, beyond what was already priced in by markets, was too focused on the uncertainty resulting from the conflict in the Middle East, rather than the underlying dynamics of the economy. Or our reaction function to the shock – the balance between looking through the shock and responding to signs of propagation – was not clearly articulated.
What does this mean for the role of monetary policy uncertainty in driving current risk premia? The committee’s vote splits in the past have revealed differences in views about both the economic outlook and the appropriate monetary policy response. The unanimous vote at the March meeting deviated from these previously communicated reaction functions in light of the conflict in the Middle East. Central bank communication – including our Monetary Policy Report, Monetary Policy Summary and minutes, press conferences, and speeches – is an important tool to explain past monetary policy decisions and to manage expectations about the economy and potential Bank Rate paths. Communication should provide clarity about our reaction function and reduce uncertainty around the future interest rate path (Blinder et al., 2008 Opens in a new window; Gebauer et al., 2024 Opens in a new window), even without having to provide explicit forward guidance.
Our communications in March highlighted larger uncertainties. Perhaps they were not clear on how the MPC’s reaction function would evolve with new information – it appeared we were in “wait mode”, which discounted our assurance to the markets that we would “act as necessary” to reach the inflation target. And, as discussed by my colleague Alan Taylor (Taylor, 2026), not publishing a baseline forecast in April most likely did not help either.
The March announcement and the uncertainty it reflected did trigger a strong upward shift in the OIS curve, contributing to the gap between OIS and MaPS. My concern is that this gap has continued to increase, and that one spike in monetary policy uncertainty may have had lasting effects, particularly in an environment with a higher sensitivity of term premia to shocks.
What about risk premia in other assets?
Risk premia and term premia are not synonymous. Term premia specifically refer to the additional compensation required for interest rate risk on risk-free bonds. Risk premia is a general term referring to the additional compensation required by investors for holding risky over risk-free assets.
One would expect uncertainty about the economic outlook arising from geopolitical and energy shocks to be reflected in risk premia for a range of assets. For example, the equity risk premium is the additional compensation for risk associated with holding stocks. Chart 10 plots model estimates of this risk premium (Kontoghiorghes et al., 2025). While there is a temporary spike following the conflict in the Middle East, equity risk premia do not appear elevated in historical context (other than in the US since 2020), likely driven by a robust demand for equities as an asset class in general, or reflecting lower perceived (relative) risk across asset classes.

Chart 10: Equity risk premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Kontoghiorghes et al. (2025).
Note: The measure used follows the lower-bound ERP estimate of Chabi-Yo and Loudis (2020) Opens in a new window over a one-year time horizon, and uses options on the FTSE 100, S&P 500, and EUROSTOXX 50 for the UK, US, and euro area, respectively. Latest observation: 16th September 2026.

But there is another source of risk premia that is of particular concern for an inflation-targeting central bank – the inflation risk premium. Chart 11 (left-hand panel) shows cumulative changes in the 3-year inflation swap since February, decomposed into contributions from changes in inflation expectations and inflation risk premia. It shows that the inflation risk premium has contributed significantly to the rise in the 3-year inflation swap this year. Rising CPI inflation expectations have also played a considerable role. This reduced slightly in June and July, when the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran was in place, but subsequently rose again following re-escalation of the conflict.

Chart 11: Decomposition of UK 3-year inflation swap rate (LHS) and 3-yearnominal yield (RHS)
Cumulative differences

Footnotes

Source: Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window for LHS, and Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations for RHS.
Note: The left panel is estimated using a model proposed in Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window. Latest observation: September 2026 (LHS) and 25th September 2026 (RHS).

The right-hand side panel shows that the contribution to the rise in 3-year nominal yields has been almost entirely accounted for by a rise in inflation compensation, which is a combination of inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium. This brings me back to my very first chart where I showed that while nominal financial conditions have tightened following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, real financial conditions remained looser.
Monetary policy strategy
What does all this mean for my monetary policy strategy?
The supply shock resulting from the conflict hit at a time when the disinflationary process from previous supply shocks was still incomplete, with nominal rigidities limiting the speed of normalization. Inflation has been above target for the last five years and the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027. This raises inflation above the attentiveness threshold of households and firms ahead of wage negotiations next spring.
Given rising upside risks to inflation, a risk management strategy to monetary policy is appropriate. When there is uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects, raising Bank Rate to commit to the inflation target can help ensure a sustainable return of inflation to the 2% target, with smaller losses to economic activity.
With the ‘sporadic continuance’ of the conflict in the Middle East, uncertainty around the outlook for the economy and inflation risks have remained elevated. Uncertainty about the MPC reaction function should not compound the problem. Ensuring that this communication is clear and that the reaction function is well understood is the purpose of collective communications. When a policy decision deviates from the collective, speeches such as this can provide additional clarity on the outlook, risks, and decisions.
Against this backdrop, as a monetary policymaker, I cannot take comfort from tighter nominal financial conditions when much of that tightening reflects a higher inflation risk premium and, possibly, a monetary policy uncertainty premium that our own decisions and communications may have contributed to. These premia raise nominal yields without necessarily tightening the real financial conditions that matter for demand and inflation. In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight. The appropriate response therefore is not to rely on risk premia to do the work of policy, but to reduce inflation risk and policy uncertainty through a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.
Acknowledgments
I would like to thank Natalie Burr and Christoph Herler for their help in the preparation of this speech.
I would also like to thank Harry Austin, Sofia Carollo, Alan Castle, Rohan Churm, Céline Gondat-Larralde, Iryna Kaminska, Alex Kontoghiorghes, Andras Lengyel, Clare Lombardelli, Rebecca Maule, Nades Raviraj, Tuli Saha, Martin Seneca and Bradley Speigner for their comments and help with data and analysis.

In parallel, heightened geopolitical complexity, from shifting tariffs and sanctions to evolving trade relationships, is prompting international energy companies to diversify their portfolios and look to the United States as a stable, strategically attractive market for investment.Successfully scaling U.S. operations, however, requires multinational firms to balance strong local execution with centralized treasury oversight and financial control. Citi's integrated suite of digital banking, treasury and trade finance solutions, including its CitiDirect platform, Citi Token Services and global trade finance capabilities, equips these companies with the visibility and agility needed to manage cross-border growth with confidence.Read the full articleDownload the PDF "Data Centers, Geopolitics, and Energy Demand"ServicesArtificial Intelligence (AI)GeopoliticsMore about Global Markets and EconomyRelated StoriesInsightsUnlocking the Data Center Supercycle with Trade FinanceThe rapid expansion of AI, cloud computing and digital infrastructure is driving a multi-trillion-dollar data center buildout, with Citi Research projecting $2.9 trillion in AI-related capital expenditure by 2030. Read more.SustainabilityAsia's Energy Market: Trends, Transformation and Treasury Best PracticesAsia's energy market is undergoing a significant transformation, driven by a long-term shift away from fossil fuels toward renewables and clean energy, alongside short-term volatility stemming from geopolitical developments and the impact of U.S. tariffs. While Southeast Asia has historically relied on coal, oil and gas for approximately 83% of its energy needs, the share of renewables in the region's energy mix has more than doubled since 2000, supported by growing investment in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and complementary technologies. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is playing a key transitional role, with many Asian nations now committing to purchase more U.S. LNG as part of evolving trade negotiations. Against this backdrop of rising energy demand — further accelerated by the growth of AI-driven data centers — energy companies face increasingly complex financing and liquidity challenges. articles.title: Central Bank independence in today’s world - Speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Central Bank independence in today’s world - Speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the SIAF Lecture Series, Zurich University

Published on
09 November 2026

In this speech Andrew Bailey argues that today’s shock prone world makes independent and accountable central banks more important than ever, both to control inflation and safeguard financial stability. Andrew is also optimistic about the potential benefits of AI to productivity and sustainable economic growth, but also outlines the financial stability risks posed by AI.

Speech
It is a great pleasure to be here in Zurich.
The main focus this evening is to have a discussion. I am just going to make a few opening comments across the subjects of central bank independence, financial stability and technology – as a prompt to get our discussion going.
We are living through difficult times. Imagine if any of us had been asked ten years ago what were the odds of major military conflicts in Europe and the Middle East at the same time. The economics of these events are supply shocks – which tend to push prices and inflation up and activity down at the same time. Such shocks are challenging for central banks, and particularly when they are large and more frequent. A shock prone world is more difficult.
At the same time, we are seeing growing signs of the beginnings of a positive supply shock coming from AI and the investment required for that. In the UK, economic activity is turning out to be more resilient than we had expected, and some of that is due to AI investment, particularly in the business services sector.
These are challenging times for independent central banks setting monetary policy and for the people we serve. These shocks push inflation away from our targets – our definitions of price stability. Our task is to set interest rates to bring inflation back to target. I do recognise that in Switzerland you have experienced a record of more subdued inflation.
When it comes to the independence of central banks, I would say two things. Yes, these conditions are more challenging. But, it is in the challenging times that we need robust institutions more than ever.
There is though an important further step in this line of argument, which may seem obvious but needs stating. As independent institutions, we are not independent of the people of our countries. We serve them and are accountable to them. This is our public legitimacy. And by this I mean the whole people. I think our independence and legitimacy depends on this – we don’t and shouldn’t select those whom we serve and we are therefore inherently plural in our approach to our societies. This is a critical feature of independence.
Let me turn now to financial stability and central bank independence. Monetary and financial stability are in my view inseparable as the core principles of central banks. They are both equally and firmly anchored around the stability of the value of money. But, notwithstanding this in my experience, the political economy of independence is different. When it comes to monetary policy, while there can be debate around the form and precise structure of the arrangements, the independence of the actual decisions on interest rates is not in doubt. But this does not carry over to financial stability, where the decisions are much more contested. The lobbying moreover is much louder, and the interests much more sharply defined I would argue.
This is illustrated by the current state of affairs. Memories of the financial crisis are receding. But it is contributing to pressure to ease back regulation. I don’t pretend that every one of our rules and regulations in the UK is perfect.
But, I do contend that sustained economic growth depends on financial stability. So, it matters. It also matters that so far we have come through the latest adverse economic shocks with a resilient financial system. That’s not an accident. The post crisis regulatory reforms have made a difference here. And, the final “it matters”, we are seeing the risks shift into new areas of the financial landscape.
Which brings me to my last subject – technology, and particularly AI. I am an optimist on AI, digital technology and most probably robotics too. They have the potential to lift the sustainable growth rates of many economies through raising productivity growth. That is a good thing.
But with that do come risks, the risks of how to come to terms with AI for instance. In our world, Frontier AI has increased the risk from cyber-attacks – something that was already prominent. More broadly, it has led to concerns which may call into question public trust in AI. This is critical. We must act promptly to identify ways to give the public the level of trust they want and deserve. To achieve this, we must be clear what public interest objectives we are pursuing and how we achieve them. A clear case for me is that we need more extensive model testing, pre and post release. This may lead us to conclude that we want more or different points or means of human user intervention in the operation of AI. We also certainly want better incident reporting, monitoring and follow up (to make sure we learn the lessons from them). The key point is that public trust will depend on assured human intervention. AI will succeed as a tool of humans.
Why does this matter for central banks you may well ask? It matters a lot I would argue. Let me briefly set out two reasons for this, which are closely interconnected, and linked to financial stability.
Throughout modern history there has been a close relationship between economic growth, the interest of businesses in fuelling that growth, and the public interest as defined and represented by governments and in some areas of public policy put into effect by institutions such as central banks. You don’t need to take any ideological position to believe in this nexus of connections – you could be Hayek, Keynes, Marx or Schumpeter.
The question we face today is whether AI poses a new and more forceful challenge to the nexus, in the sense that the risk of a loss of public trust requires a careful but determined response to underpin that trust and support the economic growth that we all want to see? My response to this question would be yes it does pose such a challenge. Put simply, if you say “very good things can come from this, but bad things may happen too”, you can’t leave it there. And, it deepens the dependency between commercial success and public policy.
But second, and finally, there is a powerful connection to financial stability here. There is a lot of speculation on the subject of whether there is an asset price bubble in AI, and the financial stability risks that go with that. Bubble spotting is an imprecise science. But, let’s recognise that such a risk exists, which we should do. How might the bubble burst and potentially cause a problem? Four arguments can I think be advanced here.
First, it is the job of financial markets to value uncertain future returns. The returns from AI may be good, but still markets may overvalue them. That’s in the nature of the task of valuing uncertainty.
Second, the returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted. This has been the case historically with big General Purpose Technology innovation – take Edison and electricity for instance. There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations.
Third, everyone is priced to be a winner, but history tends to tell us that this is not the case. Remember Netscape.
Fourth, the public trust point – there is a certain fragility created by this nexus. Arguably it is not new. A British Member of Parliament was killed by one of the earliest steam locomotives, people worried about the dangers of electricityfootnote [1]. I would argue that at present the argument seems more powerful with AI – but as I noted earlier, I treat that as a problem to be solved. But, until we have done so it could affect asset valuations.
So, there are clear financial stability risks here, and that’s without talking explicitly about cyber risks.
I said I would use my opening remarks to stir up some questions. Let’s see!
I would like to thank Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Clare Lombardelli, Dave Ramsden and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

The originally published speech mistakenly said that a British Prime Minister was killed. We’ve now corrected this.

Footnote [1]
The originally published speech mistakenly said that a British Prime Minister was killed. We’ve now corrected this.

articles.title: Who Sandwiches the Sandwichers? ‘MEV Bros’ Acquitted on Fraud Charges
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Who Sandwiches the Sandwichers? ‘MEV Bros’ Acquitted on Fraud Charges

Written by:

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

research • November 20, 2026

Who Sandwiches the Sandwichers? ‘MEV Bros’ Acquitted on Fraud Charges

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDOn Nov. 16, Judge Jessica Clarke acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of wire fraud and related charges, ending the first criminal case built around MEV, the profit available to whoever decides the order of transactions on a blockchain. In practice, that “whoever” means validators and the builders to whom they outsource. A whole industry of bots exists to pay them for favorable placement. The brothers set a trap for some of those bots, ones whose own business is jumping in front of other people’s trades, which makes for an unusual set of victims. Using a flaw in Ethereum’s block-building software, the pair saw what those bots were about to do, something the system was designed to prevent, and turned it against them. The brothers walked away with about $25 million in roughly twelve seconds, at the cost of a protocol penalty of about 1 ETH (worth ~$3,000 at the time).OUR TAKEThe judge did not say any of this was fine. She said wire fraud requires a lie, and the government never showed that the brothers told one. This relatively narrow ruling leaves a lot unresolved. Below, we walk through what the court found, then the questions it raises about manipulation law, sandwich trading, validator obligations, and whether code really is law.What the Court FoundSome background first, because this is not a simple case to wrap your head around. Validators are the participants chosen to propose new blocks on Ethereum. Most of them hand off the work of assembling those blocks to specialized builders, through intermediaries called relays. A relay keeps a block’s contents hidden from the network until the validator signs off on it. The targets here were sandwich bots, which buy just ahead of someone else’s pending trade and sell right after it. The brothers baited those bots with transactions built to look like ideal sandwich targets. The brothers’ own validator then signed off on a block with deliberately bogus fields. The relay checked that the signature was valid, but not those fields, and revealed the block’s contents. The brothers rebuilt the block, kept the bots’ purchases, and swapped out the bait for transactions that sold the same tokens into the prices the bots had just pushed up, leaving the bots holding the bag. Their validator was slashed about 1 ETH for the misdeed of proposing two blocks for one slot.The government outlined what it thought were two lies, and the court rejected both. The first alleged lie was the bait transaction. The court found no evidence that placing a transaction in the mempool, Ethereum’s public waiting room, conveys an agreement to be sandwiched. Nor does a transaction promise to be part of anyone’s bundle, or to land in any particular spot in a block, or any given block at all. Exploiting another market participant's expectations, even intentionally and profitably, doesn’t necessarily amount to a lie. The court drew that point from the Mango Markets case, United States v. Eisenberg. Avi Eisenberg pumped the price of Mango’s token and borrowed over $100 million against his inflated position. Mango had no terms of service, and the court found that Eisenberg’s borrowing made no promises, explicit or implicit.The second alleged lie was the signature on the bogus block. The government argued that by signing a block header with fields they knew were invalid, the brothers made a false statement to the relay. The court rejected the theory on two fronts. First, a validator’s signature is a commitment to publish the block or accept slashing, not a promise of anything else. Ethereum, and trustless blockchains more broadly, are systems where everyone expects validators to act in “their own rational self-interest—whatever that is.” Registering a validator with a MEV-Boost relay doesn’t come with any terms of use. Second, the relay wasn’t checking those fields at all. It would have revealed the block’s contents no matter what the brothers put there. The same bug that made the exploit possible also made the “lie” immaterial.Was Wire Fraud the Wrong Charge?Wire fraud requires deception. The Commodity Exchange Act, by contrast, separately prohibits manipulative trading and deceptive devices, so an artificial-price scheme can violate it without anyone telling a lie. Eisenberg’s wire fraud conviction fell for lack of a false representation, but his commodities fraud and manipulation convictions were vacated only because prosecutors brought them in the wrong venue, and the judge found the evidence on those counts sufficient. Judge Clarke, of the U.S. Court of the Southern District of New York, was similarly careful. She framed the question as whether the evidence supported wire fraud, not whether the brothers’ conduct was right, moral, or a violation of “uncharged crimes.” Neither ruling is a safe harbor for DeFi manipulation.Are Sandwich Attacks Legal?If manipulating prices through transaction ordering can violate the Commodity Exchange Act, sandwich trading itself starts to look exposed. The court observed that “no trader ... would agree to be sandwiched,” but it never decided whether the bots’ own strategy was lawful. The CFTC retains antifraud and anti-manipulation authority over spot commodity markets, digital commodities included.Slashing Is a Price, Not a ProhibitionThe validator half of the case raises a design problem more than a legal one. By reading the brothers’ signature as a commitment to publish a block or be slashed, the court treated slashing as a price rather than a prohibition. Ethereum’s guarantees hold only as long as deviating from expected behavior costs more than it pays, and here a 1 ETH penalty stood against a $25 million payoff.Code Is Law?Sort of. The Eisenberg case and the MEV brothers ruling both refuse to turn a developer’s intentions into binding promises without evidence. Terms and conditions could become the standard for protocols looking for legal recourse in the future, but a frontend popup gating access may not bind someone interacting directly with smart contracts. Following the code doesn’t protect you from anti-manipulation statutes either. The court rejected the idea that “undermining the spirit of a system alone constitutes fraud.” What it does say is that, for wire fraud purposes, expectations alone don’t create a promise, and absent an actual agreement, the code is the closest thing to one.Code isn’t law, but it is the closest thing to a contract you get when nobody signs anything else. The brothers read that contract more carefully than anyone on Ethereum, including the people who wrote the relay. If your protocol’s security depends on validators not doing the math on a 1 ETH penalty against a $25 million payoff, you don’t have a security model.
