articles.title: Will a UN Treaty on Autonomous Weapons Arrive Too Late?
articles.text: Source: GettyArticleCarnegie IndiaWill a UN Treaty on Autonomous Weapons Arrive Too Late?The final report by the Group of Governmental Experts is a key milestone toward a potential instrument regulating Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems and has garnered both accolades and criticism.Link CopiedBy Charukeshi BhattPublished on Nov 12, 2026On September 4, 2026, the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS), constituted under the United Nations’ Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), concluded discussions under its three-year mandate. The group has met twice every year since 2017, deliberating one of the most consequential and topical issues at the intersection of technology and security: the regulation of weapons that can identify and engage targets, and use lethal force, without human intervention.The group’s current mandate, as decided in the 2023 meeting of the High Contracting Parties (HCP) to the CCW, was to develop, by consensus, a set of elements for an instrument to address the issue of emerging technologies in the area of LAWS. The group produced a final report based on discussions held from 2023 to 2026, building on past work since 2017. The report will be tabled at the upcoming Seventh Review Conference of the HCPs to the CCW in November this year, making it the foundational text for any future discussion on regulation and governance of LAWS. As the primary UN body entrusted with implementing treaties to regulate the use of certain kinds of weapons, the CCW’s role is significant in shaping the instrument of regulation that the GGE has spent its mandate deliberating.The final report is a key milestone toward a potential instrument regulating LAWS and has garnered both accolades and criticism. The criticism is in part due to how long it took to conclude and the possibility that it may move to yet another round of such consultations when the Seventh Review Conference picks it up this month. Even so, it is useful to examine what the report was able to achieve. Examining the report will provide a clear sense of the threshold with which the CCW will begin its discussion on regulating the use of LAWS.The report is also important for national policymakers, as it sets the fencing around which future guardrails on LAWS will likely be built, notwithstanding discussions and subsequent modifications to the normative structure as the CCW process itself takes place. But there is a caveat: How long the subsequent process takes could impact the effectiveness of any future guardrails. The road toward this potential instrument could be as long as that of the final report. There is a need to be mindful of how a delay in this process could affect the governance of such technologies, and a stretched timeline leaves little room for negotiation.This article looks at the final report produced by the GGE, examines key tenets of the set of elements for an instrument on LAWS, and identifies gaps that remain unaddressed. It then looks at what’s next in the process toward an instrument of regulation and what the time delta between ongoing multilateral discussions and the eventual adoption of an international instrument could mean for the global governance of LAWS. As these weapons are increasingly used in combat, the risk is that an international instrument seeking to regulate their use might arrive too late.The Final Report: What Was Discussed and What Remains?Under its 2023 mandate, the GGE’s task can be broadly understood as the following:defining what constitutes as LAWS and what does notdetermining the scope of the application of international humanitarian law (IHL), among other various aspects of governing a kind of weapon systemascertaining where responsibility and accountability would lie in the context of human-machine interactionclarifying what obligations these tenets place on contracting partiesDiscussions and negotiations within the GGE since 2017 have contributed to the final report. This article compares the advance copy of the final report to the rolling text circulated in December 2025, which was the basis for discussions held under the two sessions of the GGE this year. This comparison might be helpful in understanding the changes introduced in the final draft.Characterization of LAWSIn the rolling text from December 2025, LAWS were described as a “functionally integrated combination of weapons and technological components capable of identifying, selecting and engaging a target without intervention by a human operator.” The text also clarified that humans setting target parameters did not exclude a system from the definition of LAWS. Meanwhile, the September 2026 report defined LAWS as systems capable of identifying, selecting, and engaging a target in a way that “results in loss of life,” without human intervention. The main change here was the emphasis on the weapon’s autonomous capability to cause loss of life, whereas the previous definition focused on the autonomous capability of a weapon to identify, select, and engage targets. This could narrow the scope of what constitutes LAWS, potentially excluding autonomous weapons that injure but do not kill.Application of IHLThe two documents maintain significant continuity when it comes to this tenet. Both maintain that IHL applies to international and non-international armed conflicts and governs “all weapons, means and methods of warfare.” The text also states that IHL applies fully to the development and use of LAWS and that obligations rest on states, parties to armed conflicts, and individuals, and not on machines. The rolling text from December 2025 however, placed stronger restrictions on states in that it specifically “prohibited certain LAWS whose effects could not be anticipated and limited as required by IHL and required states to refrain from manufacturing, acquiring, stockpiling and transferring such LAWS that did not comply with IHL.” The report of September 2026, while maintaining the applicability of the IHL to all LAWS, removes the restrictions placed on states with regards to manufacturing and stockpiling.Human-Machine InteractionWhile the two documents retain the central idea that human control and judgement are necessary for compliance with IHL, there is considerable weakening of the language when thinking of human-machine interaction and the transparency of a weapons system. As mentioned above, the obligations of IHL compliance rest on individuals and states. The December 2025 text mentioned “context-appropriate human judgement and control” and listed measures, including “responsible chain of command and control, human assessment of legal obligations and limits of the scale, types, duration and geographical scope of operations.” This rolling text was subsequently modified and shared in the first session of the GGE conducted in June 2026, where, in addition to the aspects of human control and judgement, the states’ responsibility to ensure that LAWS were “adequately predictable, reliable, traceable and explainable” to those responsible for their use was also added. The report of 2026 retains “human control (over LAWS) directly or indirectly, before and during use,” but it does away with “predictability, reliability, explainability and traceability” as a requirement for LAWS to comply with IHL. These requirements for AI systems are crucial for assigning human agency and accountability. Being able to ascertain why AI systems prefer certain outputs over others is key to identify where biases originate. In the context of weapons systems, such explainability is critical to ensure compliance with IHL principles of distinction and proportionality. In the absence of explainability requirements, there will be no consequence to a weapon system misidentifying a target group.How Far Are We From a Binding Instrument?The GGE’s recommendations will be taken up by the Seventh Review Conference of the HCPs scheduled for November 2026. The CCW convenes these conferences every five years as forums to review the different protocols, each of which ban or regulate specific kinds of weapons, asses their implementation, and make amendments. To keep the convention flexible and responsive to the changing nature of conflicts, weapons, and their technologies, Review Conferences also consider and discuss the creation of new protocols—as in the case of the Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons (Protocol IV) that was deliberated and drafted at the Review Conference concluded between 1995 and 1996, or the expansion of their existing scope of implementation.To be clear, the creation of a protocol will not automatically forbid the use of a kind of weapon. Protocols only apply to state parties to the Convention that have ratified them. Further, states also can denunciate their association with the Convention and its protocols via Article 9. The CCW remains important however, because it provides a framework for developing shared norms that prevent military interests from overriding humanitarian norms during times of conflict. Its value is in creating a moral and political suasion for states. It has also, in the past, addressed the risks of weapons before their full-fledged deployment. For example, Protocol IV prohibited blinding lasers before they became widely used. This preventive role is especially relevant when thinking of weapons powered by emerging technologies whose full effects are unknown as they continue to evolve. CCW can help establish norms for the use, transfer, and proliferation for such weapons before their harmful effects become entrenched.The final report of the GGE was endorsed by seventy-six members, seventy of which are HCPs of the CCW, meaning that they will likely participate in the proceedings of the review conference. This majority could make it easy to carry on the momentum of the GGE into the review conference, and for the set of elements of an instrument to be seriously considered for a draft text for a potential instrument.Possible PathwaysWith regard to the GGE’s final report, the Review Conference has a few possible ways forward. It may continue the GGE’s mandate to further discuss the issue of LAWS. Proposals being submitted to the Seventh Review Conference are already advocating for the need for more discussions on LAWS. However, the UN Secretary General’s 2026 deadline to conclude negotiations on a treaty on LAWS might pressure states to move toward the next steps.Alternatively, the Review Conference could begin formal proceedings toward negotiating a binding instrument. This seems likely because a majority of endorsers of the GGE report are HCPs participating in the Review Conference. Moreover, a cohort of countries represented by Brazil have extended support for the work done by the GGE and called the December 2025 rolling text sufficient to negotiate an instrument for LAWS. The urgency of beginning the process of negotiations is also echoed in the joint appeal made by the UN and ICRC in August this year to “establish specific prohibitions and restrictions on the use of autonomous weapons systems.” Strong support for a binding instrument is already visible both at the Seventh Review Conference, with proposals submitted for negotiating a protocol, and at the UNGA, with 163 states voting in favor of the resolution “to advance to negotiations on an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems.”The CCW may also exercise the option of abandoning the work concluded under the GGE. This could stem from disagreements over the necessity of a binding instrument that persisted within the GGE and reportedly even continued in the culminating session. It was in response to these differences that forums outside the GGE formed to address emerging technologies in the military domain. For example, the Responsible use of AI in the Military Domain (REAIM Process) was launched in 2023 by the Netherlands and the Republic of Korea. As part of the REAIM Process, a Global Commission was set up which concluded its mandate in September 2025. Its report, titled Responsible by Design, consists of guiding principles and recommendations for states, militaries, and industry when thinking of AI use in the military domain.The U.S.-led Political Declaration on the Responsible use of AI and Autonomy was the second track that emerged in 2023. It set out voluntary guidelines for the development and use of AI in the military. While the declaration did garner over fifty endorsements at the time of its launch, it was not a legally binding document. It was also launched during the Joe Biden administration and the current policy toward AI in and for the military domain seems to be more permissive. The Pentagon’s dispute with Anthropic over the use of its models for fully autonomous weapons points more directly to the shift in this policy and toward a more permissive stance.Moreover, these processes and platforms were only forums for discussions, seeking convergence around voluntary principles and responsible use-practices. None of them had the power to enforce a binding treaty.What Happens in the Duration of the Treaty’s Negotiation?As modern day conflicts witness increased deployment of AI-assisted weapons, with some being associated with autonomous behaviors, the governance process will become complicated. Longer negotiations will increase the risk of the final instrument reflecting the lowest common denominator among states. This is so because, as AI-assisted weaponry capabilities get more distributed among states, they will be more inclined to interpret concepts such as “human control,” meaningful human judgment, and acceptable levels of autonomy according to their interests. The draft report is already being dubbed by some experts as a weaker version of previous texts by the GGE.In the interval between the current deployment of AI-assisted technologies in conflict and the implementation of any binding instrument, companies building AI systems are setting their own red lines through contracts, deployment restrictions, and technical safeguards. These voluntary red lines, however, will be hard to maintain as companies try to balance market competition and ethical commitments. The Anthropic case is an example to consider in this regard. The U.S. Department of Defense’s subsequent contract with another AI firm points to the limitations of such redlines.First, these do not reflect universally agreed upon rules that bind other states or companies. And what could emerge is a fragmented regulatory space where acceptable military AI use and deployment vary according to the supplier.Secondly, market competition among rival technology providers will ultimately weaken the leverage of even one company willing to adhere to voluntary checks. In active conflicts, where procurement needs to happen quickly, states might look for comparable alternatives launching a race where suppliers might be disincentivized to even build voluntary guardrails for themselves. Over time, this could also weaken the incentives for states themselves to exercise restraint. If the state can secure technological capability through different vendors, then voluntary adherence to normative guardrails might be seen as bearing an unjustified strategic cost. Conflict and competition will reward vendors willing to maintain lower thresholds of regulation, and this may further pressurize other states and companies to reduce restrictions.ConclusionThe final report of the GGE is a result of a consensus-driven process and was able to bring together multifaceted differences across the technical, legal, ethical and the aspects of a potential instrument to govern LAWS. With the UN Secretary General re-iterating the need for an instrument of governance, the urgency of the matter is well established. The Seventh Review Conference is also likely to approach the report with some momentum since most of the states that endorsed the report are also HCPs to the CCW and will sit at the Review Conference.Still, a few concerns must stay in view. First, the timeline for an instrument cannot be stretched too far. A drawn-out negotiation will leave little room for effective control, especially as technology keeps advancing. Second, there is also the need to think about how to keep companies committed to voluntary guardrails, whether through incentives or reputational benefits. While this does not fall under the purview of the work that the Review Conference will undertake, engagement with industry will be critical to the designing of an instrument, specifically aspects of assigning human responsibility and the extent of control and judgement. This would help instill more trust and create moral suasion for industries to devise guardrails for technologies they build.About the AuthorCharukeshi BhattResearch Analyst, Technology and Society ProgramCharukeshi Bhatt is a research analyst with the Technology and Society program at Carnegie India. Her work focuses on the intersection of emerging technologies and international security.Recent WorkArticleIndia’s Stake in the Global Subsea Cable RaceCharukeshi BhattResearchFor People, Planet, and Progress: Perspectives from India's AI Impact Summit+3Nidhi Singh, Tejas Bharadwaj, Shruti Mittal, …IndiaTechnologyArms ControlCarnegie India does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from Carnegie IndiaArticleBuild, Not Buy: The Semiconductor Lesson that Indian AI Experts Must LearnAs AI grows more sophisticated, as the supply chains that power it become more contested, and as access to frontier models becomes geopolitically charged, India must begin to ask a different set of questions. articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

articles.title: Power outages and generators: the cost to developing economies
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

Power outages, generators, and firm performance

Joshua Wimpey

Phoebe Ishak

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

English

For many African businesses, generators are not backup but a second power system - and a routine cost of doing business. | © Shutterstock.com

Unreliable electricity is one of the most expensive constraints on businesses in the developing world. It does not arrive as a crisis. It arrives as a routine: machines and refrigerators stop, the payment terminal goes dark, and the working day is quietly shortened. Drawing on 292,581 firm interviews across 186 economies from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (2005-2025), this post asks two questions. How large is the cost of outages? And how far does buying a generator go in offsetting it?

A burden that falls on a handful of regions
Across all surveyed economies, 52 percent of firms experienced power outages in the last fiscal year, and 47 percent describe electricity as an obstacle to their operations. These averages hide extraordinary concentration. In Sub-Saharan Africa, 75 percent of firms report outages, averaging close to 8 a month, and costing an average of 5.2 percent of annual sales. In high-income OECD economies, the figures are 27 percent, 0.3 outages per month, and 0.2 percent of sales. The Middle East and North Africa and South Asia sit in between on incidence but at the top on frequency rankings, at roughly 13 to 16 outages a month.

Figure 1. Incidence, frequency and cost of power outages by region. World Bank Enterprise Surveys, 2005–2025.

Three bar charts comparing seven regions. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest share of firms reporting power outages (74 percent) and the largest sales losses (5.2 percent of annual sales). South Asia has the most outages in a typical month (16.9), followed by the Middle East and North Africa (10.7). High-income OECD economies have the fewest outages and losses on every measure.

Share of firmsreporting poweroutages (%)020406080Sub-Saharan AfricaSouth AsiaMiddle East & North AfricaEast Asia & PacificLatin America & CaribbeanEurope & Central AsiaHigh income: OECDOutages in atypical month(number)051015Annual sales lostto outages(% of sales)0246

Source: World Bank Enterprise Surveys, 2005-2025. Firm-level averages, weighted.

Where the grid fails, firms build their own
Roughly 30 percent of firms own or share a generator, rising to 42 percent among firms that experience outages. Among users, generators supply about a fifth of electricity consumption on average, and more than 70 percent for the top decile. For these firms, the generator is not a backup. It is a parallel power system and a standard cost of doing business.

Figure 2. Generator ownership rises with outage frequency. Most recent survey per economy with at least 50 firms surveyed.

Scatter chart of 182 economies: power outages in a typical month against the share of firms owning or sharing a generator. Generator use rises with outages (correlation 0.46). Many Sub-Saharan African economies, such as Nigeria, Chad and Ghana, combine frequent outages with generator ownership above 65 percent. Economies with almost no outages, such as Japan and Singapore, have low generator use.
Firms owning or sharing a generator (%)

Source: World Bank Enterprise Surveys; most recent survey per economy with at least 50 firms.
Marker size is proportional to the number of firms surveyed.

What changes when a firm buys a generator?
We followed more than 18,000 establishments across multiple survey waves (39,000 total observations), comparing firms that switched to owning a generator with firms that never own one, and controlling for firm and survey-wave fixed effects.

Figure 3. Difference-in-differences estimates of generator adoption on firm outcomes. Comparison group: firms that never owned a generator.

Dot plot of difference-in-differences estimates with 95 percent confidence intervals for five firm outcomes after buying a generator. Sales rise by 0.267, employment by 0.149, fixed-asset investment by 0.050 and sales lost to outages by 0.080; firm exit falls by 0.027. All confidence intervals exclude zero.

0.00.10.20.30.4Difference-in-differences estimate (95% confidence interval)+0.267Sales+0.149Employment+0.050Fixed-asset investment−0.027Firm exit (closure)+0.080Sales lost to outages

Note: firm and survey-wave fixed effects; standard errors clustered by firm. Comparison group is firms that never owned a generator.
Sales, employment and outage losses are in logs; investment and exit are shares.

After adoption, sales were about 31 percent and employment by about 16 percent relative to non-adopters, implying labor productivity gains of about 12 percent. Adopters are 5 percentage points more likely to invest in fixed assets and exit between survey waves falls by 2.7 percentage points from a base rate of 3 percent. Two caveats apply. Firms must survive long enough to report adopting a generator, which mechanically lowers measured exit among adopters. And firms may buy generators when they are already expanding. These results are best read as strong associations rather than precise causal effects.
However, adopting a generator does not reduce reported sales losses from outages, and adopters become more likely to call electricity an obstacle (+4.7 percentage points). Several explanations are plausible, including:

Timing: firms buy generators when grid supply is deteriorating.

Imperfect substitution: generators carry fuel costs and switching delays, and processes such as cold chains, continuous manufacturing, and payment systems are damaged by the interruption itself.

Measurement: lost sales are self-reported, and owning a generator may make firms more aware of outages or change how they estimate losses.

Generator ownership is a privilege, not ever firm can afford to self-insure
Generators are far from equally accessible. In the third of economies with the most frequent outages, 76 percent of large firms own or share a generator, compared with 40 percent of small firms. Elsewhere, the gap persists at lower levels: 41 percent versus 15 percent.

Figure 4. Generator ownership by firm size, in the most outage-prone economies and elsewhere.

Grouped column chart of the share of firms owning or sharing a generator by firm size. In economies with fewer outages the share is 15 percent for small, 26 percent for medium and 41 percent for large firms. In the most outage-prone economies it is 41, 61 and 76 percent.
Firms owning or sharing a generator (%)

Economies with fewer outages
Most outage-prone economies (top third)

01020304050607080Small(5-19 workers)15%41%Medium(20-99)26%61%Large(100+)41%76%

Source: World Bank Enterprise Surveys, 2005-2025. Outage-prone economies are the top third by average outages per month.

Finance also plays a role. In the most outage-prone economies, firms with a bank loan or line of credit are more likely to own a generator at every size: 47 percent versus 39 percent among small firms, 64 versus 59 percent among medium firms, and 81 versus 71 percent among large ones. A generator requires a lumpy, up-front investment with an ongoing fuel bill, so firms that struggle to borrow are less able to protect themselves. Credit constraints and infrastructure failures compound each other.

What does this mean for policy?

Grid reliability is not just energy policy; it is business policy. Reliable power is closely tied to firm growth and survival. Utility performance should be judged by what reliability it delivers for businesses, not only by generation capacity targets.

High generator ownership is not a sign of successful adaptation. It measures the depth of infrastructure failure and represents a costly, carbon-intensive duplication of capital that the grid was supposed to provide.

Where reliability cannot improve quickly, make coping affordable. Better access to credit and alternatives to diesel could help narrow a gap that affects firm survival. Banks and utility providers may find solutions in financing firm-level energy and storage investments that benefit both firms and utilities through improved grid reliability.

Measure the right thing. Lost sales from outages persist after generator purchase, making them a poor measure of electricity as a constraint. Survival, employment, and investment tell the story more accurately.

The bottom line
In Sub-Saharan Africa, power outages cost firms around 5 percent of annual sales, more than 25 times the burden in high-income economies. Generators appear to help firms grow, invest and survive, but they do not eliminate losses related to power outages: they offset part of the damage, at a cost only some firms can afford. Firms that can afford a generator pull ahead, while small and credit-constrained firms fall behind.

articles.title: Convenience yields and US safe haven status | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Convenience yields and US safe haven status

Robin Brooks

Robin Brooks

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

November 20, 2026

Shutterstock / Allan Wood Photography

10 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Introduction
In our previous edition of Global Currents, we discussed the concept of the U.S. convenience yield, which is the borrowing-cost advantage the U.S. enjoys because investors value the safety and liquidity of Treasuries. There are different ways to measure this. One way is to compare Treasuries to other domestic debt securities and look at how the difference in yields between these two has evolved. Another is to look at U.S. Treasury yields versus yields on government debt in other advanced countries. This is the metric we examined in the previous post.
The U.S. convenience yield by this measure has disappeared over time. In the early 2010s, the U.S. was able to issue 10-year Treasuries on average over 10 basis points below its peers across advanced economies. This has flipped to a premium of over 10 basis points, i.e., U.S. debt issuance is now more expensive than that of its peers once you hedge foreign yields back into U.S. dollars. This erosion of the U.S. convenience yield has not been sudden and correlates most obviously with greater supply of Treasury debt, i.e., which suggests this may come down to our large deficits that are eroding the scarcity and specialness of U.S. Treasuries. This is something that’s been documented elsewhere, including in Jiang et al. (2025).
However, the calculations underlying convenience yields are really just a transformation of underlying asset prices, and financial markets are famously volatile. What is true today may not be true tomorrow because financial markets change their mind. Today’s follow-up post compares the U.S. convenience yield with those of two other countries that are traditionally considered safe havens—Switzerland and Germany—to gain more perspective on what is going on with this metric. Both countries have low public debt. Switzerland stands just below 40% of GDP, while Germany is around 65% of GDP, but recently softened its debt brake to help finance rearmament in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. These debt levels are significantly below that of the U.S., which is approaching 130%. If rising public debt underlies the erosion of the U.S. convenience yield, this comparison may therefore offer some insight.
The comparison with Switzerland and Germany helps build intuition on how convenience yields behave. As eurozone debt worries have built this year, the convenience yield on Swiss government debt has unambiguously risen, while the picture for Germany is more complicated. Its convenience yield has eroded in recent years, especially since early 2025 when the debt brake was softened. More recently, the return of debt worries in the eurozone has lifted Germany’s convenience yield, but it remains low in historical perspective. In the recent escalation of sovereign debt concerns in Europe, the convenience yield (or premium) for the U.S. has been unaffected. This helps underscore that U.S. safe haven status is no longer what it once was.
A refresher on the U.S. convenience yield
Figure 1 shows the difference between the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and a trade-weighted average 10-year yield on government bonds in Germany (DE), Japan (JP), the United Kingdom (GB), Canada (CA), Switzerland (CH), Sweden (SE), and Australia (AU), where 10-year currency forwards are used to hedge yields on these government bonds into dollars. This differential is therefore purely in dollar terms and a good proxy for how “special” markets think Treasury debt is compared to debt from similarly advanced economies. When this difference is positive, it means the 10-year Treasury yield is above the trade-weighted average of its peer economies, signaling that there is no convenience yield on U.S. Treasuries. Instead, the opposite is the case: markets are demanding a premium to hold U.S. debt. If the difference is negative, the U.S. is able to issue 10-year debt more cheaply than its peers after adjusting for currency denomination differences.

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 1 shows that the U.S. used to issue on average over 10 basis points more cheaply than the trade-weighted average of the selected countries, but this convenience yield eroded steadily and turned positive in 2018, meaning the U.S. began to pay a premium over its peers. This erosion continued until 2022, after which the premium the U.S. pays stabilized over 15 basis points and has edged down to around 10 basis points since 2025. This is likely because the rise in global interest rates since COVID-19 has shone a light on the precarious state of public finances globally, with high-debt countries in Europe looking especially vulnerable. This is helping the U.S. look better on a relative basis, but—of course—this does not mean borrowing costs in an absolute sense are falling. They are rising, just that they are rising elsewhere too. Du et al. (2026) have documented the sharp erosion in the U.S. convenience yield in recent years, though they find that the convenience yield for the U.S. dollar remains robust, underscoring that U.S. status as an investment destination and potential safe haven remains intact.
The behavior of the U.S. convenience yield—or now premium—is simultaneously intuitive and counterintuitive. It has been clear for a long time that fiscal policy in the U.S. is on an unsustainable path, so the convenience yield’s gradual erosion of the and its transformation into a premium makes sense. The switch in sign to a premium suggests that foreign demand for Treasuries is weaker than it once was—all other things equal—which means potential upward pressure on U.S. borrowing costs. At the same time, it is somewhat counterintuitive that the premium has fallen in recent years, even though U.S. foreign and domestic policy have been quite erratic. You would have expected—all else equal—the risk premium on Treasury debt to keep growing and not compress as it has actually done.
Looking at the convenience yields of Switzerland and Germany
Figure 2 is the exact analogue to Figure 1 for Switzerland. It shows the difference between the 10-year yield on Swiss government bonds and a trade-weighted average 10-year yield on government bonds in Germany (DE), Japan (JP), the United States (U.S.), Canada (CA), the United Kingdom (GB), Sweden (SE), and Australia (AU), where 10-year currency forwards are used to hedge yields on these government bonds back into Swiss francs. So just like in the U.S. case, this metric is in local-currency terms and therefore an exact replica of Figure 1 for Switzerland.

Figure 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Swiss public debt stands below 40% of GDP, and the remarkable thing is that this metric suggests Switzerland has not generally had a borrowing-cost advantage relative to the countries in this sample. Figure 2 shows that there are two episodes when Switzerland did have a large convenience yield, i.e., in 2010 when the sovereign debt crisis in the eurozone first began and again in recent years as policy volatility in the U.S. increased and sovereign debt stress in the eurozone came back. This underscores two points. First, being a safe haven does not necessarily get you a convenience yield when global markets are calm. Switzerland has on average had to pay a premium on its debt issuance, which is quite remarkable. Markets don’t necessarily reward low debt and sound fiscal policy. Second, when the world becomes more volatile and demand for safe havens goes up, Switzerland benefits. The convenience yield in recent years has risen to near its historical highs.

Figure 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 3 is the same analysis for Germany and adds further intuition to the behavior of convenience yields, in particular, as the convenience yield for Switzerland has risen in recent years on greater volatility in global markets and the reemergence of debt stress in the eurozone. In contrast, Germany’s convenience yield has eroded in recent years, especially with the softening of Germany’s debt brake and large issuance needs to finance rearmament. It is true that the reemergence of sovereign debt fears in the eurozone has caused the German convenience yield to rise again this year, but it remains at historically low levels. This international comparison helps put the U.S. convenience yield (or premium) in perspective. The convenience yield is strongest for Switzerland where public debt is low and stable. It is on an eroding trend for Germany but the recent rise in debt worries has temporarily arrested that trend. In the U.S., the premium has not fallen further this year even as geopolitical risk has risen.
Conclusion
The international comparison in this post makes three big points on convenience yields. First, these measures are volatile, so—at any point—it is not the level that is informative but its evolution over time. In this regard, the trend has been unfavorable for the U.S., favorable for Switzerland, and a mixed bag for Germany. These differences map roughly onto the fiscal policy trajectories in the three countries.
Second, monetary tightening clearly plays a role in these measures. The COVID-19 hiking cycle penalized the U.S., driving the premium on 10-year Treasuries far above government debt elsewhere, while it benefited Switzerland and Germany. Monetary policy cycles therefore impact these measures on top of geopolitical and other risks.
Third, the fact that the U.S. premium has shrunk in recent years, which is counterintuitive, is effectively demonstrated through the lens of Switzerland and Germany, which, like the United States, are traditionally considered safe havens. Both countries saw their convenience yields rise as global uncertainty went up after 2022. This global uncertainty seems to have also benefited the U.S. to some degree, helping compress the premium it had been paying on Treasury debt in prior years.
The big takeaway from all of this leans in the direction that sound fiscal policy gets rewarded. That is why Switzerland and Germany have convenience yields and the U.S. pays a premium. It is also consistent with the erosion of Germany’s convenience yield in recent years as its debt brake has been softened. All that said, these measures are volatile because they capture financial market sentiment embedded in asset prices, which can vary from one day to the next.

November 19, 2026

For decades, oil price spikes were followed by U.S. recessions, but since the shale revolution the economic damage from oil supply shocks has weakened and, in recent years, often reversed into an expansion.
As the U.S. moved from a major petroleum importer to a net exporter, consumer spending, stock valuations (even in energy-intensive sectors like airlines), and employment have responded more favorably to oil shocks, pointing to broad income and demand effects rather than a mechanical rise in net exports.
The authors estimate that the 2022 oil price surge would have lowered industrial production by about 1% to 2% under the U.S. trade position of the early 2000s but produced an expansion under today’s, helping explain why it did not trigger a recession.

25 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

For decades, oil price spikes were followed by U.S. recessions. A new BPEA paper finds that this link has weakened as the United States shifted from a major petroleum importer to a net exporter, with consumer spending, stock valuations, and employment responding more favorably to oil shocks. On this episode of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity, Ben Harris talks to the paper’s authors, Diego Känzig of Northwestern University, James Stock of Harvard University, and Luca Zanotti of Northwestern University, about why oil shocks hit the U.S. economy differently now.

Transcript

[music]
EBERLY: Welcome to season nine of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity. I’m Jan Eberly, the James R. and Helen D. Russell Professor of Finance at Northwestern University. And this season, we’ll be listening to discussions about papers from the fall 2026 Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference, hosted by Brookings in September.
STEINSSON: And I’m Jón Steinsson, Marek Professor of Public Policy and Economics at the University of California, Berkeley. We are the co-editors of the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, a semi-annual conference and journal that pairs rigorous research with real-time policy analysis to address the most urgent economic challenges of the day.
EBERLY: Once again, we have a great lineup of timely topics, energy markets, inflation, migration’s effects on labor and housing markets, financing AI, and more. Over the course of this season, we’ll hear a lot more about the conference papers and importantly, how decision-makers should be thinking about the topics they explore.
[1:11]
On this episode, we’re diving into a paper on oil markets and the U.S. economy, a topic that feels perennial, but this one comes with a genuinely new twist. Ben Harris, director of the Economic Studies Program at Brookings, speaks with the authors, Diego Känzig of Northwestern University, Jim Stock of Harvard University, and Luca Zanotti of Northwestern University, about their new paper, “From Importer to Exporter: Oil Shocks and the U.S. Economy.”
STEINSSON: For much of the post-World War II period, spikes in oil prices have been strongly associated with recessions. As macroeconomist James Hamilton has documented, most of the major recessions since 1970 were preceded by large jumps in oil prices. But over the past decade or so, it seems as though this may have changed. Oil prices spiked in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and again this year when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, but no recessions have followed.
EBERLY: Yes. Traditionally, the U.S. has been heavily dependent on imported oil, but the shale revolution changed this. The U.S. has gone from being one of the world’s largest oil importers to being a net exporter. This transformation seems to have fundamentally changed how oil shocks affect the U.S. economy.
STEINSSON: Exactly. The much larger domestic oil industry in the U.S. means that many more people in the U.S. actually benefit from higher oil prices when it comes to employment and stock prices. These people consume more, which then benefits the broader economy. As a consequence, the overall effect of oil price spikes on the U.S. economy seems to have become much more muted relative to what it was 20 years ago.
EBERLY: Except, of course, that oil price spikes still lead to an increase in inflation.
STEINSSON: Yes, that’s true. That part unfortunately hasn’t changed as much.
EBERLY: Let’s turn it over to Ben.
[3:13]
HARRIS: Thank you, Jan and Jon. So, let’s say hi to our authors. Hey, Diego.
KÄNZIG: Hi, Ben.
HARRIS: Hey, Jim.
STOCK: Hi, Ben. It’s great to be here. Thanks.
HARRIS: Of course. And hello, Luca.
ZANOTTI: Hey, Ben.
[3:24]
HARRIS: So, let’s just dive right into your very, very interesting paper. I’m gonna start off by asking a question to Jim. So, Jim, for decades, an oil price spike meant a looming recession. This kind of gets to the conclusion of your paper from the outset, but why doesn’t this rule seem to hold anymore?
[3:42]
STOCK: Let me just just back up just a little bit and then underscore the main point there, which is that there really seems to have been a change in the business cycle dynamics associated with oil price shocks. So, back in the ‘70s, there were major oil price shocks, and there were substantial recessions. Right before the 1990 recession, there was the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, and that resulted in an oil price spike. There were oil price spikes later in the 2000s, including right before the, right before the dot-com bubble. And so those, there was this really established pattern that oil price spikes, typically from supply shocks, end up meaning that we’re gonna have a recession.
That just doesn’t seem to have happened in the last 15 years. So, there was the Arab Spring that jumped oil prices over $100 in December of 2010 and into 2011, yet that didn’t really result in a recession. And more recently, there was the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, and that jumped oil prices as well, and it didn’t seem to result in a recession.
Of course, there’s other things going on, so it could just be coincidence, but that’s why we had to sit down and look at the numbers and do some regressions and do some statistical analysis and try to sort that out.
[4:59]
So, to your point, yes, there does. The main purpose of the paper is to show that there has in fact been this change. And then the question is, why is that? We think that it is related to the shift of the United States from a net oil importer to a net oil exporter.
And this has been a really big shift from 10, 12 million barrels per day around 2005 of imports, to recently, it’s been in the five million barrels per day of exports. So, we have stopped looking like, say, Europe, and we started looking like an oil-producing country. And that just changes a lot.
It it means that there’s more, you know, reasons that oil is something that’s going to spur economic activity in the United States rather than retard it.
[5:50]
HARRIS: Thanks, and we’ll get to some of the explanations you guys advance later on, and some of the nuance which I think is really interesting. But Diego, maybe we can turn to you now and ask, looking at Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and then the war in Iran more recently, many expected these geopolitical events to cause a sharp economic downturn, if not a full-blown recession. So, what insight does your research provide on these two experiences?
[6:16]
KÄNZIG: Excellent. Yeah, no, that’s that’s exactly what motivated essentially our paper. Right? That we had, like, these big oil shocks in recent years, and if you were just guided by historical experience, we would have expected big consequences for the U.S. economy and for the global economy as a whole, but it just hasn’t happened. So, that’s why we really wanted to understand this and did a rigorous statistical analysis.
And one other piece of evidence I think that speaks a bit to our finding is if you look at the impact of oil shocks across countries, and there you also find that typically big oil-consuming nations, oil-importing nations, they are negatively affected if oil prices soar. But if you look at big oil producers like Russia, Saudi Arabia, Norway, these countries they typically benefit from higher oil prices.
So, that’s why when we looked at the U.S., and given the stark transformation, as as Jim has mentioned from petroleum importer, one of the biggest petroleum importers, to a net petroleum exporters, we wanted to see that is it actually the case that now, given that the U.S. is now the biggest oil producer in the world and net petroleum exporter, that it’s also positively affected by higher oil prices, similarly to other big oil producers across the globe. And and that’s actually the case.
And that has big implications for these recent episodes. Right? So, basically, oil prices soar. Now they’re again around $90, but we don’t see yet very severe consequences for the U.S. economy.
[7:46]
HARRIS: And so let’s let’s turn to Luca now to sort of elaborate on the point which you just made, which is that the U.S. is now a net oil exporter and may now benefit from higher oil oil prices. So, Luca, is the U.S. now more like Norway and Saudi Arabia in the sense that from a macroeconomic perspective, we should be rooting for oil price shocks?
[8:09]
ZANOTTI: Yes, thanks. So, as as Jim and Diego already said, our evidence points to a substantial change in how the U.S. economy responds to higher oil prices at the aggregate level. So if you compare it with the past, we see different responses by different measures of aggregate economic activity. We looked at industrial production, payroll employment, the unemployment rate, and the response does seem more muted.
And in fact, when we evaluate the response to higher oil prices of these variables at the 2025 U.S. petroleum trade position, we do see that actually these responses flip sign and they now respond positively.
So, the answer would be that, yes, at the aggregate level, the U.S. seems to respond a little bit more like Norway or Saudi Arabia might. At the same time though, it is true that this positive aggregate effect does not mean that every sector and everybody in the economy benefits from higher oil prices.
So, maybe we’ll get more into that. But so we do find that gains are fairly broad-based. They extend well beyond the oil sector and states that produce oil. But at the same time, it is true that there are several sectors in the economy that still are harmed by higher oil prices. So, we we see similar decline in consumption of energy goods and services that is the same now as it was in the past.
And for example, we also see the same decline in food consumption, consistent with the idea that food consumption is complementary to energy in household spending.
So, to go back to your your original question, probably at the aggregate level the answer seems to be yes, but these aggregate effects still mask substantial heterogeneity in the U.S. economy.
[10:01]
HARRIS: So, let me ask you a few follow-up questions. You model this around a 10% increase in oil prices, as an oil shock. So, for example, if, let’s say Brent, which is one of the global benchmarks around oil is at $70, and the shock means it goes up to $77.
But when we looked at least 2022, for example, the shock was much higher than that. The shock went from, I don’t quite remember, but you know, orders of magnitude larger. And in fact, at the time, there were bank notes like those coming out of Morgan Stanley that were projecting that if you saw a complete shutoff of Russian oil production we might be at around $285 per barrel, which was, like, a 300% shock to global energy prices.
So, how should we be thinking about your conclusion relative to the size of the shock? Does this hold for just a 10% shock or, you know, do you think it holds for for bigger shocks as well?
[10:52]
STOCK: I think we need to be careful econometricians, and for something like $285 oil, we haven’t been there. That’s not in our data. That would be an incredible shock to the world economy. Surely there would be major spillovers to the United States, massive disruptions. We haven’t run that experiment yet. But it would— I think that that’s, that’s beyond this.
But I think that, you know, the the scope of what we’ve seen, so what we’ve seen in Ukraine and what we’ve seen in the current episode with Iran is, you know, suggestive that these results of it being at least not recessionary and possibly expansionary are theirs.
[11:29]
HARRIS: And can I dig in a bit more on one of the figures in your paper? So, figure seven framed this trade-off between pre- and post-shale boom responses. And so, if you look at pre-2010, the way I would characterize it is you get a modest hit to industrial production, and then a slightly elevated rise in CPI for about 20 months, at which the shock turns negative. So, prices actually decline relative to baseline.
After the shale boom, you get just as large of a a change in industrial production, but it’s positive now. So, production goes up, but the change in CPI is elevated throughout the whole window, so, we’re talking about several years. And it’s, you know, markedly larger than the pre-2010 shale boom.
So, it seems like pre-2010, pre-shale boom, if I was gonna characterize a trade-off, I’d say you’re gonna produce moderately less, and you’re gonna have somewhat higher prices for about a year, and then lower prices thereafter. After the shale boom, you’re gonna produce somewhat more, but elevated prices are gonna be a bit of an issue for the next couple years.
Is that a fair characterization?
[12:45]
KÄNZIG: I think that’s that’s fair, even though the price response is not very precisely estimated. In fact, if you look at the difference across the two period, that’s not statistically significant, so, I think we have to be a little bit cautious.
We were actually surprised that we didn’t find much of a more of a difference between regimes in the price response. And I think one reason, and I think we’re gonna talk about this more, is is monetary policy, because we do find that monetary policy responds more in the more recent periods to these shocks by raising interest rates more, so, reacting to these inflationary pressures, and that helps contain prices.
[13:23]
STOCK: Let me just jump in with one overarching comment here, and this is, this echoes some wording that Luca used and some wording that Diego used, and then this particular question at hand. We try to be very careful not to use the words “good” or “bad,” like, this is, like, oil price shocks are now “good” for the economy or “bad” for the economy.
The word Luca used is things have “changed,” and our purpose is to document that change. So, oil price shocks are still inflationary, and folks who are at the gas station today, or certainly if you’re filling up your tractor with diesel today, boy, those are really high prices.
And we’re not saying that these oil price shocks are “good” for you. That’s not the purpose here. The purpose is really just to document these changes.
[14:11]
HARRIS: And so, maybe we can, we can dig into some of those nuanced changes, Jim, without without sort of prescribing any sort of value judgment to them. But in your paper, you find that it’s not just about rising exports, consumer spending, and even stock prices in energy intensive sectors like airlines respond better too.
I will say I found that airline finding quite surprising. I would have thought the exact opposite. So, can you maybe talk about the five hypotheses that you guys test and the and the one that you put the most value in? And so, that’s the first question. And maybe the second question is, can you talk about specifically the finding around rising stock prices in energy intensive sectors? I found that really surprising.
[14:53]
STOCK: Sure. I’ll start here, and then Luca and Diego, you should just feel free to jump in. So, we do consider five different mechanisms. One is just an accounting mechanism, which is that if you have more value of exports, you’re gonna have more net exports, and so, that is a interest positively in an accounting sense to GDP. We we looked at that. That doesn’t seem to be numerically anywhere close to the to a full explanation.
Second one is that there could just be regional shifts. So, because the oil sector is now producing more, maybe it’s great for regions that are producing oil, and it’s not so good for the other regions, but it’s now especially great for regions that are producing more oil.
But that doesn’t seem to account for it either. In fact, it’s quite interesting because employment, say employment in manufacturing, goes up both in regions that are oil exporters and in regions that are not oil exporters. So there really seems to be broad across the economy changes.
[15:53]
Another mechanism is a is a sectoral shift. Well, a sectoral shift between fossil fuel now. So that’s the the counterpart of the regional shift. So, it’s a sectoral shift where fossil fuel is outweighing the other sectors. But that’s not the case because these gains tend to be very broad-based.
I want to say it’s not like magic. There are certain sectors that you would think shouldn’t really change that much, like government employment, for example. And government employment didn’t used to change in response to oil prices, and it still doesn’t change in response to oil prices. So, it does kind of make sense.
We also look at whether the Fed policy seems to have changed, and maybe Diego can talk to that in a minute. The one that we settle on, because things are so broad-based and because there’s a large effect on stock prices, or a relatively large effect on stock prices, is that, you know, the U.S. has this oil, these oil reserves, these oil activities. U.S. is now gonna be better off in some net present value sense, and that then creates higher stock prices and a wealth effect that then filters through to consumption.
Not everybody’s gonna be consuming the same amount, but that would be an important mechanism.
I want to underscore that these are our thoughts, and, you know, we welcome more people doing more research on this. But Diego, maybe you want to say something about the Fed response part.
[17:07]
KÄNZIG: Yes, absolutely. Let me just add, like, uh, on, on the mechanism, I think it’s similar to what you expect also for other countries. For instance, in Norway, maybe it’s a bit more explicit because they have this wealth fund and some of these resources that can then get redistributed explicitly.
In the U.S., it’s more implicit because it happens through the market. Right? Because people have now more purchasing power, they can buy more foreign goods, so they’re better off than before. There may be impacts through the labor market because we do find sort of these reductions in unemployment and increases in employment, which benefits broad, parts of society. So, it’s just a bit more indirect. But basically it operates the same way as as basically in in Norway, where it’s much more explicit.
We also looked at monetary policy because historically that was also one of the main channels that people thought oil prices transmit to the economy. Because oftentimes central banks would would lean against these inflationary pressures, and that has also the consequence that this slows economic activity and may even cause a recession. So, this is, this is one big concern.
And and that’s a very challenging situation to be in for a central bank if if oil prices soar because it’s a stagflationary shock, or at least it used to be. Right? Because it creates these inflationary pressures and at the same time, it slows economic activity. So, this creates this trade-off on how to best respond to this type of shock. Should you lower rates? Should you raise interest rates?
[18:29]
But but now given that the transmission has changed so much, and actually these oil shocks transmit now more like demand shock in that activity increases and prices increase, monetary policy is no longer faced with this difficult trade-off. Right?
And that’s also what we find empirically. So, we find that in these more recent periods, the Federal Reserve seems to rise interest rates a little bit more when faced with these oil shocks than in earlier periods. Even though, I mean, I would also caveat these findings a little bit. They’re not super precisely estimated, but just looking at the at the baseline estimates, that seems to be the case.
[19:06]
HARRIS: So, let’s dig in a little bit deeper on this monetary policy question, Diego. Let’s say that you’re a staff economist at the Fed and you’re advising a governor on the board, and we get this 10% increase in crude oil prices owing to the Iran war. What’s your direct advice to the governor?
[19:28]
KÄNZIG: That, that’s a great question. I mean, to be able to respond to that, right, we need to be able to forecast what happens to to the economy when faced with, like, an increase in oil prices. And I think that’s, that’s where basically our evidence can be useful, because we show that the historical experience may not be the best guide to infer what happens after oil shocks in the U.S. economy today.
So, for the Fed, it’s just really important to to be able to forecast these prices, and I think maybe our paper can contribute a little bit to the understanding of how these shocks propagate through the U.S. economy. And then based on this evidence, obviously a governor can make a more informed decision.
[20:11]
STOCK: To put a to put a little bit more of a gloss on that than maybe Diego is willing to say, if you think about oil price shocks in the past, they’re the classic supply shock that’s stagflationary, and that just makes a really tough situation for the Fed because what are you gonna do? You, if you worry about the inflation piece, you raise interest rates, it’s gonna make the output side even worse.
And it seems to have changed so that the oil price shocks now are positive on output, and they’re also positive on inflation. And that kind of means these correlations are a little bit more like a demand shock in the sense of how monetary policy might be able to respond.
So, what that means is that perhaps monetary policy can respond a little bit more aggressively to to deal with the inflation problems in the context of an oil price shock.
HARRIS: So, the advice is 100% different than it would have been 15 years ago?
STOCK: Yeah.
[21:01]
HARRIS: So, can we maybe wrap up by going back to the question around equity prices for energy intensive stocks and the counterintuitive finding that oil price shocks raise equity prices for these for these industries. What’s driving that?
[21:20]
KÄNZIG: We were also surprised by that finding. I mean, it’s it’s quite striking, but I think it chimes well with some of the other results that we have that we just document these broad-based gains across sectors, across states.
So even in these sectors most exposed directly, obviously there is a negative effect for these because they pay more for their fuel and for these fuel expenses.
But there is an indirect effect because the U.S. economy now is doing better, so there is more demand. Maybe customers want to fly more, and obviously this this helps. And if this indirect effect is strong enough, it can even flip the sign, and that’s what we seem to find, at least in the very recent periods.
But yeah, definitely I think it’s a striking finding. But it underscores what we emphasize, that there are, like, these, these indirect effects that that operate through changes in demand, consumption demands that that affect basically also sectors that are very negatively impacted directly by this shock.
[22:17]
HARRIS: So, can I try to parse this out and and kind of give my summary, and you guys can tell me if you think it’s wrong? Which is that it seems like, as you guys point out, when we go from a net importer of oil of 5 million barrels a day to a net exporter of oil of 5 million barrels a day, and you get a shock that rises the price of oil by, let’s say, $10 a barrel, you’re talking about an extra $50 million flowing into the U.S. that wouldn’t have already happened, versus $50 million flowing out before the shale boom.
And that extra $50 million really drives everything. I mean, that’s a big wealth effect. We’re richer, and it overcomes any of the pass-through prices. It, well, it actually dominates any sort of negative employment impact that might happen from terms of trade. We’re just a wealthier country, and it seems like that wealth effect is really dominating everything.
Is that a fair kind of general summary, or am I being too blunt with my with my conclusion here?
[23:14]
KÄNZIG: More research needs to be done to basically get to the bottom of all the mechanisms that operate. But based on the analysis that we have done, that seems to be one of the dominant mechanisms. Yeah. That this creates basically this income and wealth effect.
So, so actually the terms of trade impact, that’s also a great point that you’re raising that because historically oil shocks, they transmitted to the U.S. economy as negative terms of trade effects. Right?
So, basically, export prices would raise less than import prices. Right? So, basically the terms of trade would fall, but now actually that response has flipped. So so, that means basically that you can afford more goods abroad.
HARRIS: So, let me just conclude by saying I think this is an incredibly important paper. I’ve had multiple stints in the White House, one of which was working for one of the best bosses that I ever had in Jim Stock. And that I think the policymakers will pay close attention to this. I mean, I’m sure, you know, as we’re having this podcast, there are probably people gathered in the White House and Treasury and maybe even the State Department who are wondering about the economic impacts of elevated crude prices associated with the Iran war.
And, you know, this is an incredibly counterintuitive finding that could alter the advice given to the cabinet and and top policymakers. So, I think this is really important, and I’m grateful that you guys wrote it. I thought it was a fascinating paper. It’s very careful and and like I said, I think it’s a really important paper.
So, let me just conclude by thanking the three of you for writing it, for being on this podcast, for being part of BPEA. So Diego, Jim, Luca, thanks so much. Appreciate you guys being on
STOCK: Thanks very much for having us.
KÄNZIG: Thanks so much, Ben. This was really fun.
ZANOTTI: Thanks. It was great. Thank you very much.
[music]
STEINSSON: Once again, I’m Jón Steinsson.
EBERLY: And I’m Jan Eberly.
STEINSSON: And this has been the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity. Thanks to our guests for this great conversation.
EBERLY: As always, you can find the full papers and the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference proceedings on our website at Brookings dot edu slash BPEA.
STEINSSON: And thank you to the team that makes this podcast possible: Ike Blake, supervising producer; Fred Dews, senior producer; Ranga Krishnamurthy, co-producer; Teddy Wansink, video editor; Chris Chang, audio editor. Chinese AI Faces The Nvidia Fallout

Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 19 Nov 2026

China’s artificial intelligence companies face a sharp squeeze amid the fallout of the Jensen Huang ouster and new US restrictions on their remote access to advanced AI compute. The rule compounds pressure from US frontier labs’ crackdowns on distillation and persistent difficulties turning model capabilities into revenues. The impact will depend on how Washington enforces the rule. Beijing is likely to take a measured view of this hawkish turn, tolerating some costs if tighter controls accelerate domestic chip adoption and reduce dependence on US technology.
