articles.title: Gamechangers - Tracking changing economies
articles.text:
Back to InsightsGlobal Investment ResearchGeneral Research InsightsDemographicsGamechangers - Tracking changing economiesBy James Pomeroy, Global Economist17 November 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterThe world continues to change dramatically each year, and as economists we spend much of our time focusing on the big-ticket themes that are driving economies and markets – such as geopolitics, energy prices and, of course, artificial intelligence.
But on top of these big themes, there are many more subtle changes to the global economy that are gradually changing the way we have to think about and track the economic data, and many of our previously crucial barometers of the economy have lost a lot of their value as a result of these shifts.
Policymakers are already flying blind and because of these shifts we would expect their vision to get murkier still. As a result, we need to think more about these changes and what they mean for both the economy and how we track it. We look at a variety of stories across three core themes:
1. Shortcomings in the economic data such as how manufacturing data is losing its relevance and the mismeasurement of services trade2. Changing population and consumption patterns including the rise of the ‘silver dollar’ and why this puts a floor under consumer demand, the growing size of the ‘off-peak’ economy, changing consumer spending models, with subscriptions on the rise and the impact of weight loss drugs and other medical breakthroughs3. The impact of new technologies including the changes in measured energy demand from the energy transition, the consumer benefits from new technology, the rising importance of robots and the tokenisation of assets and bank deposits.Across all these themes we can see subtle changes that could mean our traditional economic data is no longer fit for purpose. But why does that matter now? Simply – in a world of greater usage of AI – where more people are using AI-led models to analyse economic data or to build ‘black box’ models – these growing shortcomings with many of our economic data points become a much greater issue, as historical relationships may no longer hold as they once did and look set to weaken further going forwards.
This is a world in which understanding the nuances of economic data and key thematic overlays will be more important than ever. Knowing when to look at certain data points and what they are really telling you about the world will be a crucial skill for economists or anyone using economic data.
It means that although AI will likely lead to huge productivity gains for many pockets of the global economy in the coming years, when it comes to interpreting economic data, the role of AI may in fact be much more limited. Humans will need to stay in the loop in this process, as failing to read the data correctly could lead to mistakes when making key business or investment decisions.

articles.title: Is sulphur becoming more important to the energy transition? | Observations | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Observations
Is sulphur becoming more important to the energy transition?

Macquarie expert: Peter Taylor, Head of Commodities Desk Strategy, Macquarie Commodities and Global Markets

12 November 2026

Sulphur is a great example of how interconnected modern energy systems have become. Produced primarily through oil and gas processing but increasingly used in metals extraction,1 battery supply chains2 and industrial manufacturing,3 sulphur sits at the intersection of traditional energy markets and the technologies driving the energy transition. As demand broadens and supply chains become more connected, market participants are paying closer attention to a commodity that has traditionally attracted little attention.

How sulphur connects traditional energy and the energy transition

Most people don't associate sulphur with the energy transition.
Traditionally, sulphur has been viewed as a by-product of oil refining and natural gas processing, with fertiliser production accounting for much of the global demand. But its role is expanding.

It is increasingly important in the extraction and processing of metals such as copper, nickel and lithium,1 which are critical inputs for electrification, batteries and broader energy-transition infrastructure.
At the same time, most sulphur supply remains linked to the oil and gas sector.3 This creates an increasingly important connection between traditional energy systems and emerging clean-energy supply chains.
Why does it matter?
Sulphur highlights a broader shift taking place across global energy markets.
The energy transition is often discussed in terms of renewable generation, batteries or electric vehicles. But these technologies depend on complex industrial supply chains that span mining, metals processing, chemicals and commodity markets.
From Macquarie's perspective, sulphur is a reminder that energy is no longer a collection of separate markets. Developments in one part of the value chain can increasingly influence outcomes elsewhere. Demand for copper supports demand for sulphuric acid. Sulphuric acid production depends on sulphur. Sulphur supply depends largely on oil and gas processing.
Viewed through this lens, sulphur is more than an industrial commodity. It is part of the infrastructure that underpins both today's energy system and the technologies shaping tomorrow's.

What we’re watching next

Broader demand drivers emerge
Fertilisers are expected to remain the dominant source of demand for sulphur, but growing consumption from metals processing, battery materials and industrial applications could increase sulphur's strategic importance across multiple sectors.

Energy and industrial markets become more interconnected
Because most sulphur is produced through oil and gas processing while demand is linked to agriculture and industrial activity, changes in one market may increasingly affect the others.

Risk management and pricing tools continue to evolve
As the sulphur market matures and participants seek greater certainty around price exposure, demand for improved price discovery, liquidity and financial risk management solutions are likely to grow.

Webinar

Using economic impact evidence to get into the rooms that matter

Register Now

1 December 2026 – 11.00am CET (London)

online

Local decision-makers listen to the businesses they see as mattering to their economies. The question is whether they see yours that way.

In this webinar, we will show how quantifying your business’s economic impact, including the jobs you support across your supply chain, the output you generate and the tax revenues you stimulate, gives you the evidence to get into the rooms where decisions are made. We will also introduce new online tools that help businesses measure their economic contribution consistently and quickly.

Who should attend: Corporate affairs, public affairs, government relations, sustainability and communications teams.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Francesca Biagini

Lead Economist, Economic Impact

Pete Collings

Pete Collings leads Oxford Economics’ Economic Footprint and Sustainability Consulting teams. During his time at Oxford Economics, Pete has managed and conducted numerous large consulting projects including major global economic impact studies for the beer and tourism sectors, numerous footprint assessments encompassing Europe (for the European Space Agency, Rolls-Royce, Boeing and Huawei), as well as a large number of studies for major corporates and government elsewhere in the world.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics in 2009, Pete worked in the Fiscal Policy Unit of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, Zanzibar, on the ODI Fellowship Scheme. He has degrees from the University of York and the University of London.

articles.title: Insurance investment outlook 2027: Optimising portfolios amid shifting markets - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Higher and volatile bond yields are presenting insurers with investment opportunities but also challenges with regards to liquidity and interest rates risk mismatch

Tight credit spreads are prompting insurers to focus on shorter dated credit or to use the flexibility offered by derivatives

More complex regulatory regimes and volatile market conditions mean insurers must strengthen their investment and risk management frameworks to manage balance sheet liquidity and performance

The macroeconomic and market backdrop for insurers has changed significantly over the past year, chiefly because of the Iran conflict.

Soaring energy prices have helped push up Eurozone annual inflation from 2.2% in September 2025 to 3.8% in September 2026. And in the US, inflation rose from 2.13% in September 2025 to 3.74%, 12 months later.

A year ago, the European Central Bank was considering a normalisation of monetary policy, pausing the 2024-2025 interest rate cuts which had quickly followed a phase of rapid hikes between 2022 and 2024, thanks to inflation moving towards its 2% target.

Meanwhile, the US Federal Reserve was looking to enter an easing cycle, with four cuts expected at the time.

One year on and both, albeit at a differing pace, have hiked twice – and markets are expecting more: two additional hikes until the end of 2027 for both the ECB and the Fed.1

As central banks raised their policy rates, bond yields also rose, but the expected steepening of the long end of the yield curve didn’t really happen. In 2026, US and euro term premia barely increased, especially when put into historical perspective:

We believe this leaves room for considerably more steepening going forward, especially as unaddressed deficits and fiscal concerns – in the US, several eurozone countries, and in Japan – are fuelling the rise in global yields.

For these reasons we believe that, when entering in 2027, insurers are likely to focus duration purchases more on the short-and-medium-term end of the curve.

Managing liquidity

If higher yields should be good news for insurers, then this also presents several challenges. First, after several years of increasing reinvestment,cash flowing into the market may be scarcer with investment plans having already been accelerated or short-term maturities already refinanced. Here, repurchase agreements (repos) could offer the resources to aim for the desired exposure to higher-yielding investments.

Second – and still liquidity related – continuously increasing rates are imposing a strain on balance sheets: the marked-to-market value of fixed-rate receiving derivatives becomes more and more negative, while at same time, the value of high-quality assets – used for collateral purposes – decreases.

This means that, more than ever, insurers need to have a strengthened liquidity management framework and the appropriate infrastructure to meet their financial obligations in a timely and efficient way.

They need to measure and monitor liquidity needs and resources on an ongoing basis and under different market conditions. In practice, liquidity needs and resources must be projected at different time horizons and the value of derivatives and eligible collateral stress tested.

Repurchase agreements, again, can potentially allow insurers to manage cash shortfalls and to minimise cash buffers, reducing the opportunity cost. Bond Credit Support Annexes2 can potentially make collateral management even more efficient provided enough eligible collateral sits against derivatives positions.

Asset and liability management perspectives

From an asset and liability management perspective, higher yields can create a mismatch due to convexity (the pace of change of duration as interest rates change). Liabilities duration could decrease faster than that of assets, which is not a desirable outcome for insurers in such a market dynamic.

Addressing this issue requires either dynamically rotating fixed-income portfolios to shorter dated bonds – which may be challenging without diluting the portfolio’s overall yield unless the insurer accepts higher credit risk by incorporating lower-rated bonds – or using the flexibility offered by derivatives.

Payer swaps, where an investor can pay a fixed interest rate but receive a floating rate, could allow insurers to adjust the asset duration without realising undesired accounting losses.

Alternatively, payer swaptions – which give the option, but not the obligation, of entering into an interest rate swap – could hedge the still higher interest rates scenario by stabilising asset duration without impacting the portfolio’s bond holdings.

Also, persistent inflation can create a strain on liabilities for certain insurers (such as property and casualty insurers). In this context, real-yield assets that aim to generate returns above the rate of inflation, such as inflation-linked bonds, are relatively cheap and can act as valuable hedges to match these inflation-linked insurance obligations such as workers’ compensation.

Diversification and flexibility

The current environment highlights the importance of diversification within fixed income portfolios.

Huge investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, rising equity markets driven by high earnings expectations and global quantitative tightening – reducing central banks’ holdings of long-dated government bonds – are exacerbating an unprecedent competition for capital.

This, together with fiscal deficits, is likely to drive swap spreads wider.

Liquid investment-grade corporate credit spreads have been relatively resilient over the year, and alongside a solid forecast for economic activity, the market is expected to stay range-bound even if hyperscalers’ issuance volumes remain very high.

Against this backdrop of relatively compressed credit spread,managers of portfolios with profit-sharing (designated as VFA3 under IFRS) are increasingly adopting total return strategies to seek performance.

Another approach to aim to generate credit returns while mitigating risk is to invest in short-duration high yield bonds. These assets are particularly attractive for insurers as they may offer higher all-in yields and lower volatility than long-duration alternatives.

Interest rates derivatives, namely swaps, can again offer the flexibility to manage the interest rates risk factor more independently from the credit spread risk factor – that is, to maintain the desired duration while getting exposure through cash investments to shorter dated high-yield bonds. This could potentially offer an attractive return on capital, resulting in an overall portfolio optimisation.

Navigating bumps in the road

Equity markets have enjoyed, overall, a remarkable performance over the last two years, but in today’s volatile environment insurers may aim to minimise any significant downside through appropriate hedging derivatives overlays.

These could potentially help mitigate downside risk and bring valuable cushioning against equity volatility at moderate cost, ultimately improving portfolios’ risk profile and return on capital.

This could be beneficial, especially at a time where risk-based solvency regimes are being deployed across more jurisdictions and increasingly recognise risk mitigation techniques such as derivative overlays, as a way to aim to reduce capital requirements.

These solvency frameworks exhibit a converging trend toward being more ‘economic’, i.e. with capital requirements based on assets and liabilities’ actual market risk, rather than on fixed rules.

This is evidenced by the adoption of the Hong Kong Risk-Based Capital regime in 2024 and the entry into force of the Japanese economic solvency ratio ICS in 2027. Solvency II itself will evolve in 2027 when its official review is implemented.

The Solvency II Review emphasises the importance of proper matching/hedging by buckets of sensitivity. The introduction of the Credit Spread Sensitivity Ratio in the new Volatility Adjustment formula will require insurers to pay attention – depending on their respective allocation starting point – to the impact on solvency and liquidity of the bonds/swaps balance when managing long-end duration.

Among other noticeable changes that could create potential opportunities for insurers are the reduced capital charges for non-Simple, Transparent and Standardised securitisations, making them potentially much more interesting for European insurers (especially for AAA tranches).

Another notable alteration is a higher flexibility for applying the reduced 22% capital charge for long-term equity investments, opening potential opportunities for larger implementation.

Bumps in the road may well lay ahead for insurers, due to the fast-moving macroeconomic and financial environment, geopolitical uncertainties and changing regulations. We believe that strengthened processes and infrastructure remain critical to manage balance sheet liquidity, asset diversification and performance generation.

Insurers who take these steps are, in our view, more likely to be able to maintain a steady yet flexible path towards their goals, no matter the bumps in the road.

[1] As of 11 November 2026

[2] Credit Support Annexes set out the collateral required by both parties in a derivatives transaction, as a way to manage counterparty risk

[3] Variable Fee Approach

articles.title: London's safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research
articles.text:
Consulting Report

17 Nov 2026

London’s safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research

London’s safeguarded wharves play a vital role in keeping the capital supplied with the materials and goods it needs, while helping to take freight off congested roads and reduce transport emissions. But with pressure growing to release riverside land for housing and other development, how much wharf capacity will London need in the decades ahead? Commissioned by the Greater London Authority (GLA), this research by Oxford Economics examines the freight handled by London’s safeguarded wharves, identifies the factors driving future demand and forecasts the capacity required to 2050.

Drawing on ten years of freight data from the Port of London Authority, forecasts of industrial demand and interviews with wharf operators, the research provides a detailed picture of how the market could evolve. It examines seven commodity groups, from construction materials and agricultural bulks to metals, petroleum products and waste, and considers how demand will vary across the North East, South East and West regions of the Thames. The findings point to a potential capacity shortfall by 2050, with demand for construction materials alone forecast to exceed available capacity by 622,000 tonnes. The analysis also highlights important differences between regions, suggesting that the location of future capacity could be just as important as its overall level.

The findings have important implications for the future of London’s riverside infrastructure and its ambitions for growth. They highlight the need to consider not just how much wharf capacity the capital requires, but where it is located, which commodities it can handle and how efficiently it is used. The report also explores the uncertainties surrounding future demand and capacity, including the impact of major infrastructure projects, wharf closures and changing river connectivity. Together, the analysis provides an evidence base to inform decisions about the future safeguarding of London’s wharves and the role of the Thames in supporting a growing, more sustainable city.

articles.title: Market update - November 13th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Hot CPI puts a 50bp hike on the table, and Bitcoin holds its rangeBitcoin has spent another week grinding rather than collapsing, which in the circumstances is almost an achievement. October CPI came in hotter than expected, even if the headline monthly rate eased to 0.4% from September’s 0.6%.¹ More troubling was the composition. Food rose 0.5%, services remained firm and core CPI increased 0.3%, with services excluding rent, a gauge of domestic price pressure the Fed watches closely, rising 0.5%.¹ The inflation problem is therefore no longer easily dismissed as an oil story. Some of the earlier energy shock appears to have bled into the broader economy.The Fed’s hurdle, clearedMarkets responded in fairly predictable fashion. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped back towards 5%, expectations for tightening in December and into early 2027 rose sharply, and discussion quickly moved from whether the Fed hikes in December to whether 25bp is enough. Fed Governor Christopher Waller had rather unfortunately set the hurdle only hours before the release, saying that another core print around 0.3% or higher should put a half-percentage-point (50bp) move into consideration, arguing that a smaller increase could risk Fed credibility.² The October number landed almost exactly on that threshold.We remain sceptical that 50bp is the most sensible response. Inflation data are backward-looking, oil has fallen close to a fifth from its recent peak and financial conditions have already tightened considerably following last week’s equity sell-off. Three firm core readings make a case for persistence, not for an emergency, and the Fed has little precedent for treating them as one. September’s energy surge was significant, with gasoline up 9.1%,³ while October energy inflation slowed dramatically to 0.7%.¹ If that continues, some of the pressure feeding into services should begin to fade, although damage to refining capacity means a return to pre-Iran gasoline prices is unrealistic.Bitcoin absorbs the repricingBitcoin has reacted negatively to the repricing in rates, but once again the interesting feature is how little it has fallen relative to the scale of the macro shock. Our base case remains that Bitcoin trades broadly between US$60K and US$90k until something materially changes. There is no obvious catalyst for a sustained breakout at present. Monetary policy is moving in the wrong direction, whale selling has picked up again after a brief period of accumulation, and weaker sentiment across AI and technology is removing another source of risk appetite.The perverse upside: the bond marketThe slightly perverse upside scenario remains the US bond market itself. If yields were to move towards 6% or 7%, the fiscal consequences would become increasingly uncomfortable and pressure would mount for the authorities to intervene more aggressively in Treasury markets. At that point the conversation moves away from whether Bitcoin dislikes higher rates and towards whether investors trust the monetary response required to contain them. That would be a very different catalyst.Patience over predictionFor now, however, patience is probably required. Bitcoin’s resilience has been impressive, but resilience is not the same thing as a breakout. Without a meaningful change in Fed expectations, a sustained improvement in institutional flows or a return of whale accumulation, range trading remains the more plausible outcome.SourcesUS Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, October 2026, released 10 Nov 2026Federal Reserve Board, Governor Christopher Waller, speech on the economic outlook, 10 Nov 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, September 2026, released 14 Oct 2026

articles.title: 2026 Eastern Europe Crypto Adoption: $642.1B, Down 7.9%
articles.text:
This post is an excerpt from our 2026 Geography of Cryptocurrency Report. Download now. Summary
Eastern Europe’s crypto economy fell 7.9% to $642.1 billion, the weakest performance of any region we study.
Countries with larger Ukrainian populations send more retail stablecoin P2P to Ukraine, with the strongest flows coming from nearby neighbors like Romania and Poland.
Poland emerged as Eastern Europe’s crypto ATM leader amid uncertainty over national MiCA implementation. It was not alone: as of October 2026, neither Poland nor Romania had formally designated its MiCA competent authority.
Romania’s crypto users shifted away from centralized exchanges (CEXs) after a tax increase on crypto gains was announced in July 2025, with instant exchanges and decentralized exchanges (DEXs) seeing temporary surges.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Download your copyDownload your copy
Eastern Europe was the weakest-performing crypto region during the period studied. Its all-in crypto economy fell from $697.1 billion to $642.1 billion, a 7.9% decline compared to 1.6% globally. This drop was uniform across all categories within the crypto economy measure, except for domestic p2p volume, which saw a 330% increase period over period.Five of the ten Eastern European countries moved less than 2% in either direction: Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Moldova, and Ukraine. Belarus grew fastest at 27.6%, though as a heavily sanctioned market it represents a small share of regional activity.Despite the regional decline, retail-sized transfers (under $10,000) made up the largest share of service flows globally. Retail transfers made up 13.1% of the value Eastern Europeans sent to crypto services, ahead of Sub-Saharan Africa at 12.0% and well above the global average of 10.1%.The retail share rose because larger transfers fell. Retail value at services grew 8.3%, while transfers of $10,000 and over dropped from $591.5 billion to $488.6 billion. Eastern Europe’s crypto market is becoming more retail-weighted, even as its overall size contracts.Retail activity and cash-heavy services bucked the trendEven as the region’s overall crypto economy contracted, cash-heavy crypto services grew. Eastern Europe was the only region besides MENA where this service group expanded against a global decline.Crypto received by ATMs and P2P exchanges in Eastern Europe rose 1.5%, against a 25.6% decline worldwide. ATMs drove the growth, nearly doubling from $17.3 million to $33.9 million. Poland and Romania together accounted for 92% of the ATM increase.Crypto flows trace the paths of Ukrainian refugeesMore than four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s ties to its diaspora and refugee population remain visible on-chain. Wallet-to-wallet cross border stablecoin remittance flows into Ukraine totaled $12 billion this period, correlating strongly with the Ukrainian populations in the origin country.Across 36 countries in Western Europe, Eastern Europe, and North America, those with larger Ukrainian populations send more crypto to Ukraine. This includes both refugees who arrived since 2022 and the pre-war diaspora. The relationship is nearly proportional: a country with twice as many Ukrainian ex-pats saw roughly twice as many dollars-worth of crypto flowing to Ukraine.Canada had nearly 1.3 million residents of the Ukrainian diaspora before the war began, and took on nearly 300,000 more refugees after it commenced. It stands out as the largest sender, with $359 million in remittance-like transfers (under $10,000) flowing to Ukraine. Outliers like Germany and Poland exist, who have much larger refugee Ukrainian populations than Canada.Ukraine is the top destination for retail stablecoin flows from most of EuropeThe pull Ukraine exerts on regional crypto flows becomes even clearer when measured as a share of each country’s outbound transfers rather than absolute dollars. For 16 of the 21 markets on the map with $5 million or more of outbound retail stablecoin P2P, Ukraine was the top destination. For 19, it was in the top three. The median market sent 27.7% of its retail stablecoin P2P to Ukraine, more than three times Ukraine’s 8.2% share of global flows.The countries sending the highest share of their outbound crypto to Ukraine are the ones closest to Ukraine. Moldova sends nearly 45% of its cross-border wallet transfers to Ukraine. Estonia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, and Bulgaria all send between 23% and 40%.Poland’s regulatory standoff leaves crypto businesses in limboAs of October 2026, Poland does not have a national act implementing MiCA. The country’s president vetoed the implementing legislation three times between December 2025 and June 2026, and the Sejm failed to override the third veto in September. A presidential counter-draft and a separate members’ bill are now working through the legislature, but neither has been enacted.So, currently in November 2026, crypto businesses cannot obtain a MiCA CASP authorization in Poland because no national competent authority has been designated. The EU-wide maximum MiCA transitional period also expired on 1 July 2026, meaning that a legacy VASP registration alone no longer permits an operator to provide any regulated crypto-asset services. Operators must have a MiCA authorisation — including authorisation in another EU Member State passported into Poland — or another applicable MiCA route. Otherwise, they must cease those services in the EU.Poland emerges as Eastern Europe’s crypto ATM leaderPoland is one of Europe’s most digitally advanced payment markets. Cash accounts for less than 15% of transactions by value, payment terminal coverage has reached 98% of the market, and the homegrown BLIK system processed over 3.5 billion transactions in 2025. By most measures, Poland should be moving away from physical cash infrastructure, not toward it.Yet crypto ATMs in Poland more than doubled over the past year. Poland now accounts for 39% of Eastern Europe’s crypto ATM value and nearly three times the transaction volume of Romania, the next largest market.Poland accounted for half of Eastern Europe’s ATM growth over the past year, while growth elsewhere in the region stalled. Additionally, Poland now ranks third in ATM transactions globally, behind only the United States and Canada.Within Poland, ATMs were the fastest-growing way to convert crypto to cash. Transactions grew 120%, while centralized exchanges fell 5%. Every other off-ramp category either declined or grew modestly. Ninety percent of Poland’s ATM transactions involved stablecoins rather than bitcoin.Regulatory disruption may help explain the surge. As Poland’s MiCA transition approached its 1 July 2026 end, eligible legacy VASPs could still operate under national rules, but Poland lacked a domestic CASP authorisation pathway. After the deadline, those registrations alone were no longer sufficient; providers needed an applicable MiCA route, such as authorisation passported from another EU member state. ATMs are not exempt from MiCA or AML obligations, but offer a direct cash on/off-ramp. The timing is consistent with regulation shaping how users access crypto, but not with the claim that ATMs simply bypassed the rules.Platform risk may also be pushing users toward machines. Tristan Fong, Co-Founder of Localcoin, a Toronto-founded operator of crypto ATMs across Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong, told us that ATMs tend to draw users wary of online platforms. “Crypto ATMs typically attract customers that are nervous about web-based exchanges being unreliable, or even worse, fake scam websites,” Ahmed said. He added that ATM operators generally don’t hold customer funds; machines sit in retail locations customers already know, and phone support answers quickly. In his view, that builds trust and likely helps explain the ATMs’ success in Poland.The rest of the region saw ATM activity grow through early 2026 before leveling off. Poland’s growth was slower at first but more sustained, overtaking the regional average in April and continuing to climb through June, the same period when the third MiCA veto failed and the regulatory vacuum became entrenched. The data can’t prove causation, but the coincidence of timing is hard to ignore: as Poland’s path to crypto regulation closed, its crypto ATM usage surged.Stablecoins overtake bitcoin in peer-to-peer transfersPoland’s pivot toward stablecoins extends beyond ATMs. In wallet-to-wallet transfers, both domestic and cross-border, stablecoins quadrupled while bitcoin fell by a third. By March 2026, monthly stablecoin P2P had overtaken bitcoin for the first time, and the gap widened through the end of the period.“The volume of payments in stablecoins continues to grow steadily — separate infrastructure projects are already being built to support this, not just trading platforms,” said a spokesperson from WhiteBIT, a cryptocurrency exchange headquartered in Lithuania. “Today, stablecoin users are no longer just traders. We see ordinary users who use them to protect their savings from inflation, especially in markets with unstable national currencies.”Poland’s currency, the złoty, has been relatively stable compared to neighbors like Ukraine, so inflation hedging may be less of a driver. More likely, Poles are using stablecoins for what they do well: moving value quickly, cheaply, and without the volatility of bitcoin.Romanian crypto flows shifted to DeFi after a tax rise was announcedUncertainty over MiCA implementation is not unique to Poland: as of October 2026, Romania also lacked a formally designated MiCA competent authority. Romania’s shift toward instant exchanges, however, appears to have followed a separate policy signal. In July 2025, the government announced that tax on individuals’ crypto gains would rise from 10% to 16%, effective January 1, 2026. After the announcement, instant-exchange activity in Romania grew 59% over the period — the fastest growth in Eastern Europe among markets with meaningful volume.Romanians sent $41.8 million to instant exchanges in the 2026 period, up from $26.4 million. The next fastest growth among larger markets was Ukraine’s at only 9.9%. Most of the activity came in the second half of 2025, immediately after the tax announcement: $25.1 million, or 60% of the year’s total, flowed through instant exchanges between July and December leading up to the tax increase.Before the tax announcement, Romania’s exchange deposits were outperforming the region by more than any other market. Afterward, they underperformed more than any others.DEX, P2P exchanges, and instant exchange usage spiked temporarilyLooking at exchange alternatives more broadly, Romania’s share rose above the regional average only in the two quarters immediately following the announcement. In Q3 2025, Romania’s share of crypto going to exchange alternatives was 7.5 percentage points above the regional average. In Q4 2025, it was 4.4 points above. But once the tax increase took effect in January 2026, Romania’s activity returned to the mean.“Traders who use stablecoins as a unit of account and a tool for quickly rotating between assets,” as a WhiteBIT spokesperson described one user profile, may have been doing exactly that in Romania during the second half of 2025.A region adapting in real timeEastern Europe’s crypto story this year is less about growth or decline than about adaptation. Users are responding to what’s in front of them: Ukrainians abroad are using stablecoins to maintain financial ties with home; in Poland, users are converting crypto to cash at ATMs amid uncertainty over MiCA implementation; and in Romania — with the same MiCA implementation gap — users briefly turned to instant exchanges after a tax increase was announced.The common thread is flexibility. Across the region, people are responding to war, cross-border financial needs, tax changes, and uneven regulation by finding practical ways to access crypto that work for them.FAQsHow large is Eastern Europe’s crypto economy?Eastern Europe’s all-in crypto economy totaled $642.1 billion in the year ending June 2026, down 7.9% from the prior year. It was the weakest-performing of the eight regions we track.Which Eastern European countries are growing?Four markets grew: Belarus (+27.6%), Bulgaria (+0.6%), Ukraine (+0.2%), and Moldova (+1.6%). Five markets moved less than 2% in either direction.What happened to crypto activity in Romania after the tax increase?After Romania announced a tax increase on crypto gains in July 2025, exchange deposits fell sharply while instant exchange and DEX usage spiked. The shift was temporary, returning to normal once the new rate took effect in January 2026.How much crypto flows to Ukraine from abroad?Ukraine received $2.41 billion in retail stablecoin P2P from abroad in the year ending June 2026. It was the top destination for retail stablecoin flows from 16 of 21 nearby markets with significant outbound volume.

Global Key Themes 2027

Another year of resilience in the face of volatility

Despite all the tumult, the world economy looks on track to have expanded by 2.7% in 2026, which is in line with our forecast from last December.

For 2027, we expect a modest pick-up in world GDP growth to 3.0%, but the exact path and what it means for businesses and households will hinge on three themes.

Theme 1: The AI boom won’t turn to bust. Whether 2027 brings strong growth or something much weaker will depend on the durability of the AI boom. The recent stock market wobble probably isn’t the beginning of the end.

Theme 2: Inflation will grind lower. We expect the oil price to gradually decline to its pre-war path in 2027. But this is unlikely to trigger a dovish pivot by central banks.

Theme 3: AI will dictate the path for bond yields. The AI boom has been a key driver of this year’s rise in yields and should keep them elevated in 2027.

Charting the Year Ahead: Investment Ideas for 2027

Investors enter 2027 with a diversification challenge: Portfolios that look balanced across asset classes may be more concentrated in underlying risks than they appear.
War, an energy shock, higher interest rates, and political uncertainty repeatedly shifted the sources of market risks and opportunities during 2026, from stocks to bonds to commodities. Yet years of technology-led equity appreciation left many portfolios heavily tilted toward stocks, while the AI buildout has created less obvious connections across equities, credit, infrastructure, and real estate.
These shifts argue for analyzing risks and sources of return at the total portfolio level. Fortunately, global markets today offer many opportunities to diversify and restore balance across a portfolio.
We’ll explore five approaches to identifying potential hidden concentrations and broadening the investment opportunity set in 2027. We’ll provide a fuller update to our economic and fixed income views in our January Cyclical Outlook.

1. Look across a total portfolio to assess your full AI exposure

Investor takeaway:

Watch for unintended concentrations as equity, credit, and other investments may share the same underlying risks.

Seeing Through Asset-Class Labels

An investor may own leading technology companies through an equity index, lend to them through corporate bond markets, and gain further exposure through funds tied to data centers, infrastructure, utilities, or private credit. Each investment may make sense on its own, yet together they can create more concentration than traditional asset class labels suggest. Understanding these linkages across a total portfolio can help investors participate in AI’s potential while avoiding unintentional concentrations.
For example, analyst forecasts show hyperscalers’ capital spending increasingly outpacing their cash flow, boosting the companies’ reliance on borrowing to make up the difference and fund the AI buildout. As a result, tech companies, already an outsized share of equity indexes, are significantly changing the makeup of U.S. dollar (USD) investment grade (IG) and high yield (HY) corporate bond indexes as well (see Figure 1), with surging debt issuance also contributing to wider credit spreads in the sector.

Figure 1: Almost a quarter of 2026 USD IG non-financial debt issuance has been AI-related

Source: Bloomberg, PIMCO as of 11 November 2026

Lately, investors have begun to question the future returns on AI spending, and the U.S. midterm election results have further clouded the outlook. With data centers polling less favorably than nuclear power plants, many incoming local, state, and federal officials ran on platforms that included restricting data center development. In our view, we would expect some, if not many, of these politicians to deliver on their rhetoric once they take office in early 2027, although what that looks like will vary by locality and could range from full moratoria to tighter restrictions on data centers.
At PIMCO, we have been highly selective when participating in the AI buildout, preferring to focus on the infrastructure layer rather than letting performance and outcomes hinge on which AI applications may prevail (for more, see our 29 May 2026 commentary, “Investment Discipline Amid the AI Infrastructure Boom”). In our view, secured financing structures, backed by quality assets and contractual cash flows, offer stronger risk mitigation than unsecured debt or equity tied to the same theme.
For investors looking to diversify away from AI, asset classes such as agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and AAA rated nonagency residential MBS can offer more attractive credit spreads than IG corporate bonds without taking on corporate credit risk (for more, see the 9 November 2026 commentary, “The Credit Market Lens: Where to Seek Diversification From the AI Investment Theme”).

2. How broad is the exposure I’m getting from an equity index?

Investor takeaway:

Look beyond the market leaders as dispersion creates opportunities among investment factors, sectors, and individual companies.

Understanding Multi-Factor Strategies

An equity index reading only tells part of the story. Under the surface, valuations, earnings prospects, and balance sheet strength vary widely, creating potential opportunities beyond the market leaders.
Dispersion is becoming more common in today’s environment of geopolitical fragmentation and technological disruption (for more, see our 2026 Secular Outlook, “Rupture and Resilience”). Systematic approaches can seek to capitalize on these differences by evaluating factors such as value, momentum, and quality, potentially diversifying sources of return.
Individual companies respond differently to earnings, financing costs, the impact of AI, and changing demand. As the S&P 500 Index composition has grown more top-heavy with tech, the percentage of constituent companies with a negative correlation to the overall index has reached historically high levels (see Figure 2).

Figure 2: More S&P 500 constituents have exhibited a negative correlation to broad index returns

Source: Bloomberg data (quarterly) and PIMCO calculations as of September 2026

In our Charting the Year Ahead piece last year, we noted that equity valuations overall were near historical highs but value-oriented stocks remained attractively priced relative to historical averages – at an elevated value spread of about 1.24 as of November 2025, versus a long-term median of 1 – suggesting potential for mean reversion. Since then, the value spread has tightened (to 1.09 as of 6 November 2026) as value stocks have outperformed.Footnote1
Looking across equity factors lately, momentum – which picks up on AI sentiment – has been highly volatile in 2026. The value and low-volatility factors tended to rally during periods of momentum weakness. This further argues for diversification at a time when broad equity market sentiment can rise or fall with the latest tech IPO.
Today, more traditional sectors such as consumer staples, energy, and healthcare have been less correlated to tech and may offer comparatively healthier financial metrics and different valuation drivers.
For investors, the question is whether new equity allocations should add to existing concentration or pursue opportunities elsewhere in the market.

3. Look to quantitative and relative value strategies, which don’t depend on an entire asset class rising

Investor takeaway:

By seeking to benefit from differences among securities and markets, quantitative and relative value approaches can offer return drivers that complement stock and bond allocations.

Understanding Portable Alpha Strategies

Wide divergence in individual stock performance has created a favorable environment for equity dispersion strategies, combining attractive return potential with low correlation to the overall market. But the opportunity has the potential to extend well beyond equities. Divergence can also emerge across interest rate markets, commodities, currencies, and credit, creating opportunities to favor relatively attractive investments while reducing exposure to less attractive ones.
Looking at developed market sovereign bonds, heightened dispersion over the past few years has created greater fundamental relative value opportunities that active investing can seek to harness. For example, Australian 10-year government bonds have significantly outperformed U.S. 10-year Treasuries lately, moving from a yield advantage of about half a percentage point in September to trading at a nearly identical yield as of 13 November.
Among quantitative strategies, our interest rate models recently favored a long-duration position in the U.K. versus a short-duration position in the euro area. An investor in this trade may take no view on duration overall, only a relative value view between the two markets.
Today, our quantitative signals point to an unusually broad set of relative value opportunities. We measure how widely signals differ among investments within certain markets and compare that dispersion with its long-term history. The wider the gap between relatively attractive and less attractive investments, the greater the potential opportunity for relative value strategies. As Figure 3 shows, dispersion is currently high overall and elevated to varying degrees across the four major asset classes our quantitative signals track: equities, interest rates, commodities, and currencies.

Figure 3: Quant signals point to elevated relative value opportunities across markets

Source: PIMCO proprietary metrics as of 31 October 2026

Quantitative strategies can pursue such opportunities systematically to capitalize on dispersion. In general, we favor a diversified collection of quant signals but have lower conviction on any single trade, as these can change frequently.
These approaches can complement core stock and bond allocations by providing a differentiated source of potential return, while reducing reliance on any single market or economic forecast. For portfolios increasingly driven by a small number of risks, relative value strategies can help diversify not only what investors own, but how they generate returns.

4. How are higher interest rates pressuring corporate borrowers?

Investor takeaway:

Credit selection will be an increasingly important source of returns, with a focus on stronger balance sheets, more durable cash flows, and liquidity.

Understanding Corporate Bonds

The credit default cycle is already underway. Higher financing costs have led to tighter financial conditions while exposing vulnerabilities among more leveraged, lower-rated, and rate-sensitive borrowers. In public credit markets, CCC rated issuers are most at risk from a large increase in borrowing costs as these issuers start to refinance upcoming maturities (see Figure 4). There has also been an uptick in HY bonds trading at prices that indicate greater distress.

Figure 4: The lowest-rated high yield borrowers may face sharply higher refinancing costs

For illustrative purposes only. Figure is not indicative of the past or future results of any PIMCO product or strategy. There is no assurance that the stated results will be achieved. Source: Bloomberg, PIMCO as of 10 November 2026.

Higher refinancing costs aren’t just a problem for public markets. In recent quarters, investors have also started to withdraw money from less-liquid areas of private markets, particularly corporate direct lending, where many loans have floating-rate structures and thus feel the impact of higher front-end rates much more quickly.
One gauge of potential stress within less-liquid markets is the discount that some business development companies (BDCs) have seen in their price-to-book ratios relative to the performance of their bonds. These investment vehicles for corporate direct lending have come under pressure as investors worry about true underlying valuations against a backdrop of higher rates.
Investors considering private markets for diversification should look closely at what those allocations actually hold. Alternative investments can improve diversification when they bring genuinely different risks and economic drivers. But if private markets just add to existing sector exposures, or if they appear less volatile simply because private asset prices aren’t regularly marked to market, they may increase portfolio concentration rather than reduce it.
Overall, these dynamics can imply that issuer-level credit selection will become an increasingly important driver of performance for corporate credit investors. At PIMCO, we continue to favor higher-quality credits with relatively strong balance sheets and robust cash flows, while using a relative value lens to take advantage of temporary market dislocations.

5. What sort of diversification can commodities provide?

Investor takeaway:

Commodities are driven by different forces than stocks or bonds and can help diversify portfolios while potentially providing resilience to inflation, geopolitical disruption, and supply shocks.

Understanding Commodities

Diversification is about owning investments that respond differently to economic and market developments. Commodities have demonstrated that distinction amid repeated supply disruptions over the past decade, reacting directly to inflation and geopolitical shocks.
Across several recent multiyear periods, a portfolio with a 10% allocation to commodities has produced a higher Sharpe ratio – a gauge of risk-adjusted return – than a traditional 60% stocks/40% bonds allocation (see Figure 5). Looking ahead, geopolitical fragmentation, energy security, and growing infrastructure needs could continue to support the strategic case for the asset class.

Figure 5: A commodities allocation has improved risk-adjusted portfolio returns

For illustrative purposes only. Figure is not indicative of the past or future results of any PIMCO product or strategy. There is no assurance that the stated results will be achieved. Source: Bloomberg, PIMCO, Haver Analytics as of 31 October 2026. Uses Bloomberg Commodity Index Total Return as commodities proxy and 3-month T-Bill bid yield as the risk-free rate for Sharpe ratio calculation.

The diversification opportunity extends beyond any single commodity. Gold, energy, industrial metals, and agriculture have different drivers, so a broad allocation may provide more durable diversification than concentrating in whichever asset has performed best recently.
Gold surged in 2025. Oil became the main commodity story of 2026 after the Middle East war started in February. Looking ahead, we believe risks posed by this year’s unusually strong El Niño weather pattern could function as a tailwind for agricultural commodities, while demand from the AI buildout can support industrial metals.
Sizing also matters. The goal is to add a source of return driven by different risks.

Conclusion: Restoring balance without abandoning opportunity

Heading into 2027, investors and advisors face a practical question: Does my portfolio still reflect an intentional balance? Investments with different labels may be less independent than they appear, and years of strong equity returns have left many portfolios more tilted toward stocks.
Rebalancing does not necessarily mean selling appreciated stocks and realizing taxable gains, though some investors may choose to do just that given some of the extremes cited above. Investors can instead ask: Where is the best relative value for my next investable dollar?
The answer starts with understanding the risks and concentrations already evident in a portfolio, then being deliberate about where new capital goes. That could mean looking beyond market-cap-weighted indexes, using relative value strategies to capitalize on dispersion, becoming more selective in credit, or adding investments driven by different economic risks. With today’s elevated inflation-adjusted bond yields, fixed income markets can offer broadly attractive return potential (for more, see our 6 November 2026 video, “A Higher Starting Point.”)
There are further strategies beyond those explored here. For U.S. investors, the municipal bond market, private real estate, and certain other naturally tax-advantaged strategies provide interesting diversification options amid higher yields and a reset in valuations. For example, muni yields sit in the top decile of the past 15 years, with the Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index at a 4.23% yield to worst, or 7.14% on a taxable-equivalent basis, providing 114 basis points of taxable-equivalent spread over the Bloomberg U.S. Corporate Index.Footnote2
After a period when a narrow set of exposures drove returns, 2027 may favor portfolios built around a broader and more deliberate mix of return drivers.

Based on Compustat, Capital IQ, MSCI, and PIMCO calculations. Normalized value spread using PIMCO Value Composite, Developed Markets.Return to content↩
Source: Bloomberg as of 13 November 2026. Yield to worst (YTW) is the estimated lowest potential yield that can be received on a bond without the issuer actually defaulting. The YTW displayed above corresponds with the Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index. Taxable equivalent yield assumes a maximum tax rate of 40.8%.Return to content↩

articles.title: Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Proactive Monitoring of Markets and Institutions

Related Content

Federal Reserve Board finalizes rules that tailor its regulations for domestic and foreign banks to more closely match their risk profiles

Calibrating the GSIB Surcharge

The changing nature of risks and fluctuations in financial markets and the broader economy require timely monitoring of domestic and foreign financial markets and their effect on financial institutions. They even require monitoring of the nonfinancial sector to identify buildups of vulnerabilities that might require further study or policy action.

To this end, the Federal Reserve maintains a flexible, forward-looking financial stability monitoring program to help inform policymakers of the financial system’s vulnerabilities to a range of potential adverse events or shocks. Such a monitoring program is a critical part of a broader Federal Reserve System effort to assess and address vulnerabilities in the U.S. financial system. In the case of individual institutions, the Federal Reserve may take more direct action and in various ways.

Research Examining Causes, Effects, and Remedies for Financial Instability

A macroprudential approach to ensuring financial stability builds on a substantial and growing body of research on the factors that lead to vulnerabilities in the financial system and how government policies can mitigate such risks.

The Federal Reserve actively engages in financial stability research to improve understanding of issues related to financial stability and to engage with the broader research community on crucial policy matters. This engagement often involves collaboration with researchers at other domestic and international institutions.

Macroprudential Supervision and Regulation of Large, Complex Financial Institutions

Large, complex financial institutions interact with financial markets and the broader economy in a manner that may—during times of stress and in the absence of an appropriate regulatory framework and effective supervision—lead to financial instability.

The Federal Reserve promotes the safety and soundness of Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs)—including large bank holding companies and financial market utilities—through robust supervision and regulation programs that are informed by the macroprudential monitoring programs. In addition, the Federal Reserve serves as a “consolidated supervisor” of nonbank financial companies that the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) has determined should be supervised by the Federal Reserve Board and subject to prudential standards. Currently, there are no such firms that have been designated by the FSOC.

Monitoring Systemically Important Financial Institutions

The Federal Reserve actively monitors indicators of the riskiness of Systemically Important Financial Institions (SIFIs), both individually as well as through interlinkages in the broader network of financial institutions, to help identify vulnerabilities. It also imposes certain regulatory requirements on SIFIs in order to ensure that these large and interconnected institutions properly manage potentially risky activities and to mitigate spillover of distress into the broader economy. If a SIFI were to become distressed, disruptions in the financial system could arise from direct losses imposed on SIFI counterparties, contagion, fire sales effects, or a loss of critical services.

Recovery and Resolution Framework

During the 2007–09 financial crisis, the lack of effective resolution strategies contributed to the damaging spillovers of distress at or between individual institutions and from those institutions to the broader economy. The Federal Reserve, in collaboration with other U.S. agencies, has continued to work with large financial institutions to develop a range of recovery and resolution strategies in the event of their distress or failure. Improvements in resolution planning are intended to, among other things, diminish adverse effects from perceptions of certain institutions as “too big to fail” and contribute to more orderly conditions in the financial system if institutions face strains or fail.

International Financial Stability Monitoring

The U.S. dollar is the leading global funding and investment currency and is used widely for trade and other international transactions, and well-functioning dollar funding markets in the United States and abroad are critical in supporting these roles. Strains in these markets can adversely affect U.S. and foreign businesses, governments, households, and NBFIs that borrow in dollars. The Federal Reserve actively monitors the functioning and health of dollar funding markets and, in cooperation with foreign central banks, has worked to mitigate strains in these markets through the use of the Federal Reserve’s dollar liquidity swap arrangements.

The Federal Reserve actively monitors the resilience of foreign financial systems and potential transmission channels of foreign financial stress. An understanding of financial vulnerabilities abroad and how foreign shocks are transmitted to the United States is important for gauging the significant risks to the U.S. financial system.

articles.title: Daily: Treasury rally highlights the opportunity in bonds
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Equities: Industrials, health care, Eurozone, and quality AI (7 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Opportunities in high-quality bonds and select EM debt (5 mins)Thought of the dayThe S&P 500 fell for a fifth consecutive trading day on Wednesday, while US Treasuries gained for the third straight session. The US 10-year yield declined by 4 basis points to 5.06% amid lower oil prices, and a USD 16bn auction of 20-year Treasuries drew steady demand.The Treasury rally came despite minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October meeting showing that almost all officials agreed that further interest rate hikes would be needed if the US economy evolved as they expected. A few policymakers said that “a shift to a more restrictive policy stance” may be required, and two participants said a move larger than 25 basis points could be warranted if inflation proves more persistent.The minutes are consistent with our view that the US central bank will continue to raise rates into 2027. But more policy tightening is not necessarily negative for fixed income. In fact, we continue to rate the asset class as Attractive in our global portfolios and believe investors should rebalance toward bonds.Additional Fed hikes are already priced in, and a prolonged cycle appears unlikely. We expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points next month and again in March 2027, and acknowledge a higher risk of consecutive hikes following stronger-than-expected inflation data. But current fed fund futures suggest that markets have already priced in more than three additional rate increases from here. In our view, the cumulative impact of rate increases and tighter financial conditions is also likely to limit the need for a prolonged hiking cycle. This means Treasury yields have room to fall as markets reassess their Fed policy expectations, leaving scope for bond prices to move higher.Inflation should moderate in 2027, pointing to more measured tightening. While recent data point to still sticky price pressures, our base case is for underlying inflation to ease gradually next year amid favorable base effects. AI-related demand remains a risk factor for higher inflation, but lower oil prices and fading tariff effects should see disinflation resume. We forecast average inflation of 2.3% in the US in 2027, compared with 3.4% this year. This backdrop should support a more measured pace of tightening, a view recently backed by San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, New York Fed President John Williams, Boston Fed President Susan Collins, and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack.Bonds offer attractive portfolio income in an otherwise uncertain environment. Elevated starting yields are a key reason behind our Attractive view on fixed income, as they provide appealing opportunities to generate portfolio income even if interest rates or yields do not fall significantly. Historically, starting yields offer a good indication of subsequent total returns, and we think current yields can more than compensate for the risks of further yield volatility. For capital losses to offset one year of income, two-, five-, and 10-year US Treasury yields would need to increase by around 255, 113, and 65 basis points, respectively, from current levels, which we consider unlikely. Conversely, in a scenario where economic and equity market risks intensify, quality bonds would likely rally, helping insulate portfolios.So, we think investors should review their bond allocations and consider adding exposure. We see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, and within fixed income, we see the best return opportunity in emerging market and high yield bonds. We favor an intermediate average duration, generally through maturities of around two to 10 years, with a preference for shorter-dated bonds in the more growth-sensitive credit segments.

What do you need to know?

US inflation rose by 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% the market had been expecting. Though it was a slowdown from September’s 0.6%, the data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates in December. An annualised figure was not released due to the government shutdown in October 2025. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, increased by 0.3%, for the third consecutive month. Separately, the MSCI World Index rose 2% in the week to Thursday’s close with the Nasdaq rebounding 4% from the previous week’s fall*.

*In US dollar terms. Source: FactSet, data as of 12 November 2026

Around the world

China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026, well above the $964.8 billion recorded in the same period last year, driven by global demand for artificial intelligence-related products. The figure puts the country on track to reach a record level for the full year. Elsewhere, eurozone GDP grew 0.4% in the third quarter, the official second estimate showed, down from 0.6% in Q2. In addition, the UK economy grew 0.7% on a quarterly basis in Q3, its fastest pace for more than two years.

Figure in focus: 35%

A new global pledge aims to increase the use of electricity to 35% of total energy consumption by 2035, up from around 23% today. The “35 by 35” target was officially endorsed at the United Nations climate change conference COP31, taking place in Turkey from 9-20 November. The goal includes increasingly moving from fossil fuels to electricity for sectors including transport, buildings and industry, to reduce carbon emissions and costs, as well as enhancing energy security.

Chart of the week

US consumer confidence has recovered slightly in November, according to the University of Michigan’s initial estimate – though the index has fluctuated at low levels for a year. Meanwhile, the eurozone index has failed to recover sustainably since its drop in March and April. Although consumer confidence is usually only loosely correlated with spending, purchasing power erosion due to rising energy costs is sufficiently pronounced to modify consumption habits. Additionally, widespread uncertainty is expected to deter households from major spending.

Words of wisdom: Singles’ Day

Singles’ Day started in China as a celebration of being single, taking place on 11 November – the date was chosen as the numerals represent individuals. It has grown into one of the largest global online shopping events, with retailers offering sizeable discounts to rival those of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sales around Singles’ Day are viewed as a barometer of China’s economic activity – this year sales rose 4.8% to 1.78 trillion yuan (US $267 billion) from the year before, according to reports citing data provider Syntun.

What’s coming up?

On Monday, the eurozone reports industrial production data, followed by the US on Tuesday. The Reserve Bank of Australia publishes the minutes of its last interest rate-setting meeting on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the eurozone and UK each publish their latest inflation data, while the Federal Reserve issues the minutes of its last monetary policy meeting. It opted to keep rates on hold at 3.75%-4.0% in October.
