articles.text:
Insights / Research / Weekly Research Brief: Anthropic IPO, ‘MEV Bros’ Acquittal, Solana Breakpoint

Research • November 20, 2026 • 18 mins
Weekly Research Brief: Anthropic IPO, ‘MEV Bros’ Acquittal, Solana Breakpoint
This week, Alex Thorn breaks down the market ramifications of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO; Thad Pinakiewicz examines the acquittal of the “MEV brothers”; and Lucas Tcheyan shares takeaways from Solana’s annual Breakpoint confab.

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Lucas Tcheyan
Vice President, Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

AI

Bitcoin

Ethereum

Markets & Macro

Solana

Weekly Research Brief

Welcome to Galaxy Research's Weekly Research Brief. Subscribe to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.This week, Alex Thorn breaks down the market ramifications of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO; Thad Pinakiewicz explains the acquittal of the “MEV brothers”; and Lucas Tcheyan shares takeaways from Solana’s annual Breakpoint confab.
Anthropic Prices Record IPO in a Market – and World – on Edge WHAT HAPPENEDAnthropic completed the largest IPO in history on Wednesday evening, pricing at $83 per share, after updating its prospectus last week with an expected price range of $70 to $78. Strong demand led the AI company, best known for its Claude chatbot, to upsize its offering, selling about 980 million shares and raising $81.3 billion, up from the 825 million originally planned. That figure surpasses Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June, and Anthropic's IPO price implied a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion for a company founded barely six years ago. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal, as they did for SpaceX. Ahead of the open, Cboe’s JJ Kinahan said demand was running almost seven times the offering, and CNBC sources reported that retail demand was the largest in history.Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT at 11:48 a.m. ET on Thursday. The first print was $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, which briefly gave the company a market capitalization of $2 trillion. The stock hit its intraday high of $114.99 in the minute after the first trade and then spent the rest of the session fading. By the afternoon it was trading in the mid-$90s, at $94.67, up about 14% from the offering price, as of 2:18 p.m. ET. The decline from the open was unusually steep. Of 20 big US IPOs since 2008, only Coupang was doing worse at the same point in its first day, according to Yahoo Finance; the group’s average was up about 3.5%. The broader market also sold off as soon as the stock opened. Stocks fell to their session lows the moment Anthropic began trading, and chip stocks including Nvidia and Broadcom erased their gains. Listed ANT options are set to start trading on Monday.Onchain, Hyperliquid showed the success of its pre-IPO perp market yet again. Its markets correctly called the deal pricing, with the perp trading well above the $70-78 range for weeks, signaling that demand was stronger than the underwriters’ original target. The perp ultimately undershot the open by about 7%, with the contract trading around $103.67 at 8:40 AM ET, roughly 25% above the $83/share offer price. Thursday morning’s perp price was roughly in line with market consensus (Cboe’s Kinahan said the first trade should land around $103 or $104), but ultimately both the perps and the pros were off with the first trade ultimately printing at $111.50. But the perp nailed where the stock ended up trading. For most of the week before listing, the perp sat in the mid-to-high $90s. It was about $96.93 as of Nov. 17 and $98.83 on the hourly chart the night before pricing, having briefly fallen below $94 during the earlier tech selloff. After the opening pop faded, the stock traded right back into that band, around $94–$97 by the afternoon. One could argue the perp’s week-long equilibrium was a better estimate of “fair” first-day value than the opening print, which looked like a short-lived demand spike.OUR TAKEThere was something strange about watching Anthropic’s staff clap on the Nasdaq floor as they IPO’d a company whose primary media narrative is that AI might kill us all. This week has been the most doomer week in recent memory, coming off the back of Microsoft’s O365 outage Thursday, the nationwide FAA ground stop Friday, bank outages on Monday, even the NSA’s internal comms system reportedly disrupted (twice?). Costco reported a wave of panic buying, people pulled cash out of banks, and prepping content went viral on social media. Chatter among traders included tips on which types of solar-powered batteries to buy, how to store substantial amounts of dry food in a New York City apartment, and which are the best routes to escape the city in the event of a grid collapse. So maybe it’s only fitting that this week’s blockbuster IPO was one in which the S-1’s risk factors included “the end of humanity.” (Although we are not equity analysts, we agree that the end of humanity could materially affect Anthropic’s earnings.)Since Oct. 1, the S&P 500 is down 7%, gold is off 12.2%, and BTC is in the red 25%. Treasuries have depreciated, inflation is hot, rates are expected to rise, commodities are falling, and the Democrats swept to power largely on calls to solve the “affordability crisis.” Our own Bitcoin fear & greed index is printing near all-time lows (meaning “extreme fear”), the VIX is trading at levels comparable to those from the breakout of the Iran War in March, though not quite the level from the “Tariff Tantrum” in April 2025. Stanley Druckenmiller said he is “more uncertain than ever after 50 years of investing” and that his firm’s equity positions are “basically flat.” Another Wall Street luminary, Howard Marks, argued in a Nov. 11 memo entitled “A Layman Thinks About AI” that the breakneck speed of AI development is a big risk, even for Anthropic. Paul Tudor Jones said in mid-October that “2027 is going to be a really difficult year for the stock market.” So it’s fair to say the stock market intelligentsia is uneasy.

Some have theorized that recent risk asset headwinds were enhanced by the liquidity drain caused by allocators pulling assets to buy the Anthropic IPO. This does feel intuitively right, though there’s not much evidence to directly support it. Bitcoin’s price did behave similarly when it traded poorly into the SpaceX IPO in June and made its current bear-market low on July 1 ($57,717 on Coinbase). Whether BTC and other risk assets will receive some respite now that ANT is a public stock remains to be seen. The reality is that Americans are fearful and psychologically traumatized. Polarization has long been a characteristic of the American political landscape, but the Democratic sweep was so dramatic that big swings are expected on things like tax policy, AI policy, legislative priorities, and more. Layer on the never-ending drumbeat of cyber vulnerabilities and a spectrum of AI outcomes that is so wide it contains both the possibilities of permanent utopia and impending obliteration of the species, and it’s easy to see why markets are unsteady. There’s a sense that one more piece of big bad news could tip markets over the edge – a major cyber-attack, an escalation of the Iran or Ukraine wars, an outbreak or substantial natural disaster. Alternatively, a major peace deal or initiative emanating from Trump’s visit with Xi and Putin, cessation of major regional conflicts, or a legislative breakthrough in Congress could assuage the fears. As they say, if you’re going through hell, keep going. The only way out is through. Everything is different, yes, but everything is fine. Bitcoin keeps producing blocks uninterrupted, and I just coded a slick new dashboard to monitor the situation. – Alex Thorn

Who Sandwiches the Sandwichers? ‘MEV Bros’ Acquitted on Fraud ChargesWHAT HAPPENEDOn Nov. 16, Judge Jessica Clarke acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of wire fraud and related charges, ending the first criminal case built around MEV, the profit available to whoever decides the order of transactions on a blockchain. In practice, that “whoever” means validators and the builders to whom they outsource. A whole industry of bots exists to pay them for favorable placement. The brothers set a trap for some of those bots, ones whose own business is jumping in front of other people’s trades, which makes for an unusual set of victims. Using a flaw in Ethereum’s block-building software, the pair saw what those bots were about to do, something the system was designed to prevent, and turned it against them. The brothers walked away with about $25 million in roughly twelve seconds, at the cost of a protocol penalty of about 1 ETH (worth ~$3,000 at the time).OUR TAKEThe judge did not say any of this was fine. She said wire fraud requires a lie, and the government never showed that the brothers told one. This relatively narrow ruling leaves a lot unresolved. Below, we walk through what the court found, then the questions it raises about manipulation law, sandwich trading, validator obligations, and whether code really is law.What the Court FoundSome background first, because this is not a simple case to wrap your head around. Validators are the participants chosen to propose new blocks on Ethereum. Most of them hand off the work of assembling those blocks to specialized builders, through intermediaries called relays. A relay keeps a block’s contents hidden from the network until the validator signs off on it. The targets here were sandwich bots, which buy just ahead of someone else’s pending trade and sell right after it. The brothers baited those bots with transactions built to look like ideal sandwich targets. The brothers’ own validator then signed off on a block with deliberately bogus fields. The relay checked that the signature was valid, but not those fields, and revealed the block’s contents. The brothers rebuilt the block, kept the bots’ purchases, and swapped out the bait for transactions that sold the same tokens into the prices the bots had just pushed up, leaving the bots holding the bag. Their validator was slashed about 1 ETH for the misdeed of proposing two blocks for one slot.The government outlined what it thought were two lies, and the court rejected both. The first alleged lie was the bait transaction. The court found no evidence that placing a transaction in the mempool, Ethereum’s public waiting room, conveys an agreement to be sandwiched. Nor does a transaction promise to be part of anyone’s bundle, or to land in any particular spot in a block, or any given block at all. Exploiting another market participant's expectations, even intentionally and profitably, doesn’t necessarily amount to a lie. The court drew that point from the Mango Markets case, United States v. Eisenberg. Avi Eisenberg pumped the price of Mango’s token and borrowed over $100 million against his inflated position. Mango had no terms of service, and the court found that Eisenberg’s borrowing made no promises, explicit or implicit.The second alleged lie was the signature on the bogus block. The government argued that by signing a block header with fields they knew were invalid, the brothers made a false statement to the relay. The court rejected the theory on two fronts. First, a validator’s signature is a commitment to publish the block or accept slashing, not a promise of anything else. Ethereum, and trustless blockchains more broadly, are systems where everyone expects validators to act in “their own rational self-interest—whatever that is.” Registering a validator with a MEV-Boost relay doesn’t come with any terms of use. Second, the relay wasn’t checking those fields at all. It would have revealed the block’s contents no matter what the brothers put there. The same bug that made the exploit possible also made the “lie” immaterial.Was Wire Fraud the Wrong Charge?Wire fraud requires deception. The Commodity Exchange Act, by contrast, separately prohibits manipulative trading and deceptive devices, so an artificial-price scheme can violate it without anyone telling a lie. Eisenberg’s wire fraud conviction fell for lack of a false representation, but his commodities fraud and manipulation convictions were vacated only because prosecutors brought them in the wrong venue, and the judge found the evidence on those counts sufficient. Judge Clarke, of the U.S. Court of the Southern District of New York, was similarly careful. She framed the question as whether the evidence supported wire fraud, not whether the brothers’ conduct was right, moral, or a violation of “uncharged crimes.” Neither ruling is a safe harbor for DeFi manipulation.Are Sandwich Attacks Legal?If manipulating prices through transaction ordering can violate the Commodity Exchange Act, sandwich trading itself starts to look exposed. The court observed that “no trader ... would agree to be sandwiched,” but it never decided whether the bots’ own strategy was lawful. The CFTC retains antifraud and anti-manipulation authority over spot commodity markets, digital commodities included.Slashing Is a Price, Not a ProhibitionThe validator half of the case raises a design problem more than a legal one. By reading the brothers’ signature as a commitment to publish a block or be slashed, the court treated slashing as a price rather than a prohibition. Ethereum’s guarantees hold only as long as deviating from expected behavior costs more than it pays, and here a 1 ETH penalty stood against a $25 million payoff.Code Is Law?Sort of. The Eisenberg case and the MEV brothers ruling both refuse to turn a developer’s intentions into binding promises without evidence. Terms and conditions could become the standard for protocols looking for legal recourse in the future, but a frontend popup gating access may not bind someone interacting directly with smart contracts. Following the code doesn’t protect you from anti-manipulation statutes either. The court rejected the idea that “undermining the spirit of a system alone constitutes fraud.” What it does say is that, for wire fraud purposes, expectations alone don’t create a promise, and absent an actual agreement, the code is the closest thing to one.Code isn’t law, but it is the closest thing to a contract you get when nobody signs anything else. The brothers read that contract more carefully than anyone on Ethereum, including the people who wrote the relay. If your protocol’s security depends on validators not doing the math on a 1 ETH penalty against a $25 million payoff, you don’t have a security model. – Thad Pinakiewicz
Solana’s Institutional BreakpointSolana's annual Breakpoint conference took place Nov. 15–17 in London under the theme "Token Supercycle," showcasing the network's growing ambitions in payments, tokenization, and institutional finance. The event also marked Solana's graduation from "mainnet beta" to Mainnet 1.0, following a series of infrastructure upgrades that halved target block times to 200 milliseconds (ms) and reduced target finality to approximately 150 ms through the Alpenglow consensus protocol.Institutional adoption dominated the announcements. Zelle, the bank-owned payments network that processed more than $1.2 trillion in 2025, demonstrated a $1.25 million confidential stablecoin transfer and outlined plans to launch ZelleUSD on Solana for international payments. Global remittance giant MoneyGram and wallet provider Solflare announced USDC-to-cash conversions across 170 countries and territories, while fintech lender SoFi highlighted Solana as a preferred network for stablecoins and tokenized assets.Tokenization was another major theme. The DTCC outlined plans to connect its Tokenization Service to Solana in the second half of 2027, while wealth management platform Allfunds, banking giant BNY, and investment manager Baillie Gifford highlighted initiatives bringing traditional investment products onchain. Other announcements spanned tokenized equities, regulated derivatives, decentralized compute, and agentic payments, reflecting Solana's efforts to expand beyond its established strengths in retail trading and decentralized finance.OUR TAKE Solana's evolution since 2023 has created a growing disconnect between how the network is perceived and what its ecosystem is attempting to become. For less engaged observers, Solana remains synonymous with memecoin speculation and the sometimes unsavory activity that accompanies it. For those following the ecosystem more closely, however, the network is increasingly positioning itself as infrastructure for payments, tokenized assets, and other forms of financial activity that could bring considerably larger pools of users and capital onchain.These two identities are not mutually exclusive. Solana's success as an onchain casino has been a powerful engine for attracting users, developers, liquidity, and investment. Its ability to support high-frequency, low-value financial transactions at scale helped establish a competitive advantage in a market where speed, cost, and usability were often sufficient to win. However, the conditions that allowed Solana to dominate that segment are materially different from those governing the next phase of adoption. Payments, tokenization, and agentic commerce are increasingly attracting the attention of the world's largest financial institutions, payment providers, and technology companies. These players have considerably greater resources and distribution than crypto-native startups, and Solana is one of several networks they are exploring, alongside proprietary infrastructure they can develop and control themselves.For institutions, performance is increasingly a prerequisite rather than a differentiator. Privacy, compliance, operational accountability, distribution, and access to pools of liquidity are equally consequential. Solana's realistic opportunity, at least in the near term, is therefore less about becoming the universal settlement layer for global finance and more about establishing itself as a leading neutral venue for the subset of financial activity that benefits from shared, composable, high-performance public infrastructure.A recent paper from J.P. Morgan's Kinexys and MIT's Digital Currency Initiative illustrates the challenge. Financial institutions recognize the appeal of public blockchains as shared infrastructure that no single participant controls, the paper notes. But their requirements for confidentiality, compliance, governance, and other operational necessities can conflict with the characteristics that make these networks valuable in the first place. Accommodating those requirements often means reintroducing intermediaries, permissioning, or centralized controls, potentially undermining the neutrality and interoperability that distinguish public blockchains from traditional systems. Yet building proprietary networks creates its own challenges, particularly when competing institutions must coordinate across fragmented systems. The likely outcome is not a wholesale migration from private to public infrastructure, but a gradual and selective adoption of public networks where their advantages are sufficiently compelling.Breakpoint offered evidence of the opportunity and its limitations. Zelle's confidential-transfer demonstration, DTCC's planned integration, and initiatives from major asset managers suggest that Solana is increasingly being considered for financial activity well beyond its crypto-native base. Its presence in tokenized-equity trading also demonstrates that the network can attract meaningful activity in emerging asset classes. Solana accounted for approximately 42% of onchain tokenized-equity trading volume between January and September 2026. But there is an important distinction between being selected as a supported network and becoming the primary venue where liquidity, users, and economic activity ultimately concentrate. DTCC's integration, for example, forms part of a broader multichain strategy rather than an exclusive commitment to Solana. Nor is Solana entering these markets without crypto-native competition. Hyperliquid remains a formidable competitor in onchain perpetual derivatives, while the emerging agentic economy has yet to produce a clear winner or a compelling reason why payment and coordination infrastructure must concentrate on Solana. Privacy tooling is improving, but its maturity, regulatory compatibility, and institutional adoption remain important questions. These dynamics make the ecosystem's ability to attract and retain builders particularly consequential. Solana's dense developer culture and willingness to experiment have been central to its recovery and growth, and preserving those characteristics will matter as the network courts institutional capital.Solana has made substantial progress in addressing the technical limitations that once threatened its credibility. The more difficult task ahead is translating that progress into durable distribution, liquidity, and institutional dependence in markets where performance alone is unlikely to determine the winner. Breakpoint demonstrated that Solana has earned a place in those conversations. Whether it can turn that position into an enduring advantage, rather than remain one capable option in an increasingly competitive and multichain financial system, is the more consequential question. -Lucas Tcheyan

As of Sept. 30, the financial services giant held the equivalent of 30,553 BTC, worth $2.55 billion, across 10 funds. That’s up from 15,931 on June 30. Wells passed trading firm Jane Street (23,167), previously the largest holder.

The 15 largest holders are a cross-section of the institutional market: wealth platforms, market makers, bank trading desks, hedge funds, asset managers, one sovereign wealth fund, and one crypto investment firm. That mix matters for interpretation. The same number of shares can be a client’s allocation at a wealth platform, inventory at a market maker, or one leg of a hedged trade at a hedge fund. How the oil market could move from famine to glut
Supply growth is coming through higher than expected

How the oil market could move from famine to glut

Opinion
14 March 2018
Can conventional oil projects compete with L48 oil?

View Harry Paton's full profile

The constraint of Gulf crude exports since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March pushed Brent prices above US$100/bbl for much of the past nine months, triggering soaring fuel prices, rising inflation and weaker economic growth.
Senior VP Alan Gelder and the wider WoodMac Macro Oils team foresee the potential for much lower prices when flows of exports resume on a peace agreement, reversing these knock-on effects. Importantly, it may not be a fleeting downturn. Additional supply is set to arrive on the market that could contribute to prices trading below our previous long-term forecasts well into the early 2030s. I asked Alan about the new analysis.
Why have you lowered your near-term price outlook?
We believe that the oil market is headed towards substantial oversupply. Much depends on how the Iran war plays out. The key assumption in our new Base Case is that the US and Iran reach a peace agreement late in 2026, but with no breakthrough in the Russia-Ukraine war. Crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz normalise progressively through 2027, allowing fundamentals to play a greater role in shaping the market once again.
We expect demand to bounce back in 2027, but the growth in supply will be much more substantial. The significant change in our supply data is the addition 1million b/d in 2027 and another 1.8 million b/d in 2028 – even as Middle East ‘legacy’ production rapidly returns to pre-war levels and beyond. Just over half of the additional volumes come from the US (including gas production-related NGLs and tight oil), the UAE, Brazil and Venezuela. Plentiful supply not only meets higher demand in 2027 but allows the rebuilding of global observable inventories – which reduced by 1 billion barrels this year – to pre-war levels of over 7 billion barrels by mid-2028.
We forecast Brent will track down over the next two years, averaging US$84/bbl in 2027 and US$55/bbl in 2028.
What happens if the crisis doesn’t end this year?
The next two years are very different in our US-Iran Stand-off scenario. The scenario assumes that the realignment of US politics after the midterm elections rules out a return to military conflict. Without a credible threat of attack, Iran waits out the rest of President Trump’s term. Strait of Hormuz transits do not fully normalise until after 2028 and Middle East crude output stays around 3 million b/d below our Base Case through 2027-28.
Supply growth outside the region would keep the crude market on the long side, but inventories rebuild more slowly. In the scenario, Brent averages US$105/bbl in 2027 and US$91/bbl in 2028.
The underlying fundamentals won’t change, though. Whenever peace comes – by the end of the year in our Base Case or later as in the scenario – an agreement ending the threat to flows through the Strait could mark a shift from famine to glut.
Could Brent be lower-for-longer?
Yes, because there are more low-cost barrels coming into the future supply stack. We base our longer-term price outlook on the marginal cost of the barrel needed to meet demand. Demand growth and declines in producing fields lead to a supply gap of 20 million b/d in 2036. As ever, this gap must be filled by supply from existing fields (reserves growth), new fields, yet-to-find and other technical discoveries.
What’s changed is that our asset-by-asset data shows there are more lower-cost barrels available through 2036 than in our previous analyses. These barrels are from a variety of sources, including the UAE and Iran, along with higher NGLs. The marginal cost is now nearer US$60-65/bbl compared with US$70-75/bbl previously.
Implied OPEC spare capacity remains broadly unchanged at 8 million b/d through this entire period, suggesting ample available supply will dampen the potential for price upside from geopolitical risk.
Won’t OPEC cut production to support prices?
We think they will have to before the decade ends if a serious price crash is to be avoided. Balancing the books is one consideration in favour of a cut, given several OPEC countries have a fiscal breakeven of above US$80/bbl (Brent). OPEC, along with its OPEC+ partners, had success in pursuing its price-driven strategy before the war. Holding substantial volumes off the market was a material factor in Brent averaging US$90/bbl from 2021 to 2025.
The coming years, though, may prove tougher. With the UAE now outside OPEC, there are fewer remaining members to share the burden of cuts. Moreover, OPEC may baulk at production cuts that support prices and so help recent departees, which are free to increase production.
How could lower prices affect corporate strategies?
Oil and gas companies are looking to strengthen portfolios to offset production declines in the mid-2030s. With the midterm oil demand outlook robust, that won’t change. The mindset of the industry is still based around capital discipline and resilience, both portfolio-wise and financially. Much of the US$0.75 trillion net cash flow windfall in 2026 will be used to strengthen balance sheets, helping businesses to navigate any commodity price downturn.
Any shift in business development will be to sharpen the existing focus on low-cost opportunities that can be resilient as prices fall. A dip in oil prices could present M&A opportunities for the financially strong. Players, though, may be in no hurry to deal if oil prices remain high, preferring to wait for the right time to make a counter-cyclical move.

articles.title: European Strategic Autonomy in 2027: Where are we? Where are we going? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Two years after Mario Draghi’s 2024 competitiveness report, implementation of recommendations is uneven; while security and defence have seen significant progress other sectors have advanced more slowly

There is substantial investment growth across several strategic areas, including a rising defence budget and €21.1 billion earmarked for critical raw materials projects

The focus is transitioning from policy announcements to execution, where the primary challenge for investors is identifying which companies and issuers can successfully convert increased EU spending into sustainable earnings and durable economic returns

In September 2024, former European Central Bank President, Mario Draghi presented a landmark report on the future of European competitiveness.

The report diagnosed structural weaknesses in productivity, investment and industrial capacity relative to the US and China and set out 383 recommendations spanning several sectors.

Its central thesis is that Europe must mobilise substantially higher public and private investment – originally estimated at between €750 billion and €800 billion annually – and streamline decision-making if it is to safeguard strategic autonomy.

The agenda has since become a reference point for European Union industrial and security policy.

Two years on, the so-called Draghi Implementation Index shows that 15.7% of the recommendations have been fully implemented, with the combined strict-plus-partial rate – a measure of how much of Draghi’s competitiveness report has been turned into binding law – at 41.3%.1

Progress is uneven but tangible in security-linked areas. Defence has reached 78.6% (strict-plus-partial), but digitalisation and advanced technologies (29.8%), pharmaceuticals (27.8%) and energy (21.7%) have advanced more slowly. These results indicate that delivery has been strongest where competitiveness overlaps with security imperatives.

Addressable markets are expanding

In defence, EU member states spent €418 billion in 2025 and are projected to reach €454 billion in 2026, with trends indicating further growth toward as much as €547 billion by 2029.2

A substantial share of equipment and investment spending flows to European industry, generating multi-year opportunities measured in the high hundreds of billions of euros. Additional demand for non-traditional defence suppliers could reach up to €500 billion over 2026–29.3

Major joint programmes can be tricky to agree on as Germany and France have showed recently: the next-generation fighter Future Combat Air System and the Main Ground Combat System initial plan have been cancelled which will reduce economies of scale.4

In space, the Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite – IRIS constellation – with a total cost of €15.6 billion, has moved into the implementation phase.

Major manufacturing contracts awarded in August–September 2026 cover the bulk of the 348-satellite programme, with first launches scheduled for 2029.5

Furthermore, space sovereignty has moved higher up in Europe’s strategic agenda: Thedisruption to Starshield connectivity in Ukraine on 14 October 2026 has highlighted Europe’s dependence on US space infrastructure.

While Eutelsat OneWeb satellite and IRIS provide European-controlled alternatives, Europe still lacks Starlink’s scale and a sovereign space-based missile-warning capability. Limited launch capacity remains another vulnerability.

This urgency is strengthening political support for Project Bromo (proposed consolidation of the satellite-manufacturing activities of Airbus, Thales and Leonardo).

Further spending on secure communications, missile warning and Earth observation should support the order pipeline. However, without greater launch capacity, Europe risks developing sovereign satellite capabilities while remaining reliant on US infrastructure to deploy them.

Raw materials and clean tech bolster backdrop

Critical raw materials offer a growing project pipeline: the 46 new strategic projects selected in October 2026 under the Critical Raw Materials Act are expected to mobilise around €21.1 billion in public and private investment, advancing capacity in lithium, nickel, cobalt, rare earths and related materials for batteries, defence and permanent magnets.6

Clean technologiesand the energy transition continue to present large-scale opportunities, in our view. Draghi’s original framework of roughly €750 billion to €800 billion in annual additional investment needs remains a useful reference, while McKinsey analysis highlights multi-trillion-euro global cleantech capital expenditure by the mid-2030s, with substantial accessible value for European players in e-mobility, grids and related technologies.7

Digitalisation and advanced technologies offer long-term markets linked to AI and industrial connectivity.

Industrial policy measures are reinforcing these dynamics. The EU steel measure, effective from 1 July 2026, establishes a duty-free quota of 18.3 million tonnes with a 50% out-of-quota duty, supporting domestic capacity utilisation.8 Strategic designations for critical materials and refinements to battery local-content rules further strengthen the operating environment for European producers.

Equity valuations in exposed sectors have adjusted from earlier peaks, creating interesting entry points alongside still-elevated earnings growth expectations in defence.

Fixed-income markets continue to see increased issuance linked to defence and infrastructure, new issuers mainly in euro are paving the way, the market is broadening and new eastern European and Nordic companies are now using the euro bond market to fund their needs. The EU money injections are driving a whole ecosystem all over Europe.

2027: From policy ambition to investment execution

Europe’s strategic-autonomy agenda is increasingly translating into tangible investment across defence, energy infrastructure, space and critical supply chains. For investors, however, the opportunity is becoming more selective.

In equities, the focus is shifting from policy announcements and order intake towards companies able to convert larger backlogs and capacity investment into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

In fixed income, higher investment creates additional issuance opportunities but also requires greater differentiation. Sector selection is key and rating agencies are really segregating between companies that are benefitting from the EU umbrella (upgrades such as in the defence sector) and those losing momentum in the face of fierce global competition.

The key investment question for 2027 is therefore no longer simply whether Europe will spend more, but which companies and issuers can translate strategic autonomy into durable economic returns.

articles.title: Making the economic case for your university
articles.text:
Webinar

Making the economic case for your university

Register Now

2 December 2026 – 11.00am CET

online

Universities across Europe are feeling a squeeze. Costs are rising while funding per student is falls in real terms, and the pressure to demonstrate value to stakeholders has never been greater. Demonstrating economic contribution across local, regional and national economies can help make the case for supporting institutions at every level.

In this webinar, we will show how universities can measure the economic impact of their operations, student spending and visitor spending, in terms of jobs, economic output and tax revenues, and use that evidence to cut through with stakeholders and strengthen funding cases. We will also introduce new online tools that help universities do this consistently and quickly.

Who should attend: University leadership, strategy, external affairs, communications and estates teams

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Aoife Pearson

Aoife works in Business Development for Oxford Economics’ Consulting division and is based in our London office. She is responsible for new business growth and the management of ongoing client relationships across various sectors and geographies.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics in 2015, she held roles in Account Management and Marketing for a FTSE 100 company. Aoife holds a first-class degree in Geography from Newcastle University.

Senior Business Development Manager

Patrick Deshpande

Patrick is a Lead Economist in the Cities and Regions team, specialising in economic impact model development, socio-economic profiling, and bespoke modelling on consultancy projects. Patrick is a UK Office for National Statistics Accredited Researcher. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Patrick was a Senior Economist in the Economic Development team at AECOM.

Patrick has a BA in Economics from the University of Leicester and an MSc in Economics from Trinity College Dublin.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsHow Will Higher-than-Expected Inflation Data Impact the Fed's Next Rate Decisions? Nov 13, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyYouTubeAppleDownload TranscriptWhile a smaller hike remains more likely, October’s hotter-than-expected inflation data may open the door to a 50-basis point rate hike at the Fed’s December meeting, says Muhammad Qubbaj, co-head of North America Interest Rate Product Sales and Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. A recent drop in oil prices is unlikely to give the Fed cover to look past the CPI number without becoming more aggressive in the inflation fight, Qubbaj says on this episode of The Markets podcast. He also explains why his base case is for the 10-Year Treasury yield to remain below recent highs.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, November 12th, and we're here on the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Muhammad Qubbaj, who is co-head of North American Interest Rate Sales and Trading within FICC and Equities. And today, we're going to talk about how a hot CPI print this week is impacting rates and bonds markets, and how that has a carryover effect to other markets around the world.
Q, thanks so much for joining us.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Thanks for having me.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's start with the CPI print. It came in hot this week. What did you make of the market's reaction? How do you think the Fed is going to respond?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Well, there's no rest for the wicked when you look at the sources of volatility in the market, whether it's geopolitics, whether it's the Fed, whether it's AI.
We felt we almost had a little bit of a respite, maybe for five minutes, and all of a sudden CPI comes to the forefront and changes the board a little bit, too, and the Fed walks right back into the building. CPI affected us in three ways. First, I would say that it was unacceptable number, .3, third time in a row.
Strong across all categories. The Fed has to reckon with that number, and the market priced that accordingly. Two, it wasn't just about the CPI level, it was about the Fed reaction function. We woke up that morning, Waller had made a speech and put 50s back on the table. He basically asked a question, and CPI answered.
He said, "Contingent on .3, 50s could be on the table." And-
Chris Hussey: And by 50s on the table, what you mean is that we could do a hike of 50 basis points, not 25.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Exactly. So it just, again, underscored a hawkishness to the Fed and opened up the distribution to 50s, which was definitely a surprise that morning, before we even walked in and got the CPI number.
The third thing was we spent almost a month executing a hike compression. We took out almost 50 basis points of hikes in the next one year, and some of this is a give back. So in terms of the market reaction, unwind of positioning and the high compression, a reaction to the strength of the CPI, the third one in a row and a re-understanding of the Fed's reaction function and opening up the distribution for 50s.
Chris Hussey: All right, so it wasn't trivial. That's interesting. But you also talk about a Fed reaction function, and one of the things they have to react to is oil, I would imagine, because, this was an October report, but for the month of November, oil prices are now down 15%. How does oil factor into the rates market?
Muhammad Qubbaj: We can't basically say that the causality between oil and rates is a one-for-one thing. They're definitely a participant. They definitely have a feed through to CPI, and they definitely show up into, basically, core CPI and how the Fed takes that number so that they can adjust policy.
But, the sell-off wasn't just about oil when we had the big sell-off in the year. At one point it was about corporate earnings and growth. At another point it was a debate on the Fed reaction function uncertainty because they removed forward guidance term premium on the back of bond supply and CapEx supply, convexity hedging or the convexity profile of the market where we saw a lot of selling and positioning.
Oil coming off in the last couple of weeks is definitely affects the level of rates, but you can't expect a full refund just based on the oil movement.
Chris Hussey: Okay. Another thing that's changed since that October CPI print was the midterms. We got the midterms in early November. How does a change in Congress, if at all, have any impact on the rates market?
Muhammad Qubbaj: I think a couple of things. One is the Fed's not a political body. It should not affect the Fed path, first order. It affects oil, obviously, based on the vote on the geopolitical outlook of the Iran war. Midterms affect oil, CPI affects the Fed. We've had almost triple the move based on the CPI morning print that we did in rates for the entire of midterms week. So I think that's where the focus is.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's expand the conversation to 10-year bond yields. They have such an impact across markets. We were up at 5.3% not too long ago. They've come back to 5%. Are the conditions still in place, though, for us to eclipse the recent highs?
Muhammad Qubbaj: You have to look at basically what took us to the peak in rates. There were several different factors. One, we had this new reaction function from the Fed, no forward guidance, the debate on how the Fed's reaction function will evolve under a Warsh leadership.
You had the debate on term premium. You had the debate on Government issuance compounded by AI CapEx-related supply. You had a positioning situation in the market. You also had convexity selling in the market. All of those things contributed to the sell-off. So, I don't think that you're going to have that same set of circumstances reassert itself on the market again and push yields to the high, high level that we saw in October.
Furthermore, you have two new breaks in the system: a Fed that is actively hiking, a hike lands in the front end but flattens the curve. Two, we had some sort of reflexivity that's been put onto the market in Warsh's last speech. He specifically tied the level of rates to the level of AI CapEx financing.
So what happens when you do that is basically saying that you have a self-balancing system. If rates go up too much, then it can slow down the AI CapEx build-out, and it will almost have a self-balancing system from that perspective. But let us remember that if -- Do I think it's going to be a rate sell-off can happen again driven by positioning or term premium or supply worries or convexity selling?
No. If we have a reassertion of strong earnings and I think that can give us some room.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, a little bit of a growth-driven thing. Can I ask you to define one thing? Convexity selling, what is that?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Convexity selling is a situation where, as the market sells off, people have more to sell.
At its core, it means as things are getting worse, your flows are going to make it even worse.
Chris Hussey: Right. It's a little technical factor. All right, let's talk about the competition between stocks, bonds, and credit.
Cause that's always part of the equation here, I would imagine. How do you see that shaping up here? You talked about the growth equation being such a big one for where yields go from here.
Muhammad Qubbaj: When we look at yields as it pertains to credit and as it pertains to equities, we have to look at it from a couple of lenses.
What drives higher yields? Is it growth? Is it earnings? Then that should be good for the credit complex, and should be good for the equity complex. Is it driven by term premium worries and a supply absorption worries? Then you have a capital markets problem, and that's where they could be negative for equities, and it could be negative for credit.
That's one factor. The other factor is the amount of leverage that we're talking about. When you're looking at a bond that is a corporation that is on the lower side of the spectrum of leverage, then higher rates affects the discount factor. When you look at a bond that's on the other side of the leverage spectrum, higher rates is a funding bill.
It's a funding problem. So you can't... You have to be a little bit more nuanced when you say how do higher rates affect the equity market or credit market. It's a function of how did we get there, and how levered are the companies that we're talking about? And that's basically where you get your answer.
Chris Hussey: All right, lot to digest. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Muhammad Qubbaj: I like to think of it from a serenity prayer perspective.
Chris Hussey: Ah, the serenity prayer.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Accept the things you cannot change. It is a one-factor market.
It's all about mega-cap tech. Once you accept that, you realize that's the bet you're going to be making. Now, where do you have control? Where can you make some changes on the edges? One is how much of a size of a position you're going to take. It depends on how you hedge your portfolio. Two, the amount of leverage and what's the expression you take on mega cap to see basically how much exposure you have and how much factor risk you have.
So we have discussed the risk. Now let's discuss the hedges. When you look at the hedges, you basically have out-of-the-money dollar puts. You have out-of-the-money equity puts. Delta one is favorable in the level of rates. A combination of those, you can build a carry neutral or positive carry hedge portfolio, and you can size it up and down depending on the amount of risk and leverage you're taking on the mega-cap tech.
Now, you wanna own the factor, and you wanna rent the insurance.
Chris Hussey: And by owning the factor, you want to own stocks.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Yes.
Chris Hussey: And by renting the insurance, you wanna maybe own some puts as well.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Exactly.
Chris Hussey: All right, what are you looking for in the weeks ahead?
Muhammad Qubbaj: Three sources of volatility we mentioned in the market. Oil, let's continue to see how the geopolitical, situation unfolds. The Fed, we are going to look at Fed speak and the Fed minutes and basically try to read the tea leaves and to see how hawkish the Fed is right now so we can get a feeling for the size.
While, we're confident on the direction of which way the Fed is going. It's about size and timing right now. And the third factor is the AI economy. Anything, whether it's a capital market situation or an earning situation, anything that can continue to give us confidence or allow us to re-rate the level of risk in the market as it pertains to the AI economy.
Chris Hussey: That's terrific. Q, you're always just a fountain of knowledge for us. Really appreciate you joining us.
Muhammad Qubbaj: Thank you for having me.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.

Marc Seidner, Gregory Hall

11/20/2026

Greg Hall: Hey, everybody, welcome to another episode of Accrued Interest, PIMCO's podcast dedicated to serving financial advisors, their clients and the wealth management community at large. As usual, I'm your host, Greg Hall. I lead the wealth management business for PIMCO here in the United States, and back by popular demand, Marc Seidner, our CIO of nontraditional strategies. Hey, Marc, thanks for joining us this morning.
Marc Seidner: Always a pleasure, Greg. Good to be in the room with you this time.
Greg Hall: It's nice to be here in Newport Beach with you. It is Anthropic Thursday. So we do anticipate the listing of the latest AI wonder story this morning in markets. And it's a great, I think, a great backdrop to be discussing the topic that lies ahead of us today.
So, folks, we have Marc on not just because he's a terrific guest to have and a good friend and always a good friend of the podcast, but he's just published a piece. This is the second annual edition of this piece. We decided to start putting this out last year. It's called Charting the Year Ahead. It's available at pimco.com in the US or wherever you access us if you're listening in another country. And it's a piece that I think it offers, and Marc, you'll opine on this, I think it offers a nice opportunity for us to step back from macroeconomic forecasting and the interest rate environment, and really just sort of take a little bit of a broader lens to investing. And one of the things I like about this piece is it's, you know, it's your creation.
It's the things that are capturing your attention in markets, and it's built around the charts and the visuals that demonstrate that. And so, you know, with that as our intro, we're going to talk about that piece, give you guys a little bit of a preview, and then we would encourage you to go read it for yourselves.
So, do you want to get into it? How do you want to frame the themes of the piece this year?
Marc Seidner: You know, Greg, it's obviously a very interesting market and macroeconomic and political and geopolitical environment. And as you said, you know, in my opinion, PIMCO is excellent, if not outstanding, in putting forth our secular macroeconomic and market views, our cyclical macroeconomic and market views and ongoing market commentary. And as you noted, the purpose of this piece is really to open up the aperture.
I mean, I think we're well known for our views on the attractive starting point of yields in fixed income markets, that we're well known for our views on the economy and inflation and diversification of benefits of bonds, income and the like. This piece, as you say, really does try to widen the aperture and scratch the surface a little bit.
You know, so much focus by investors, whether they be institutional or retail, you know this from your conversations, I know this from my conversations, from our engagement with clients, really is on some high-level topics, right? You know, technology, AI as a theme, the Federal Reserve as a theme, politics and geopolitics as a theme. And not only is that, you know, the engaging part of a lot of client conversations these days, but it seems to be all the media wants to focus on, right? Like, what, as you say, you know, today is Anthropic Thursday. And so what will it do? What does it mean for tech?I mean, it's been up and down throughout the year. I mean,
Greg Hall: Yeah
Marc Seidner: It’s kind of striking that the Nasdaq, you know, as of last night, was only up something like 5% for the year.
Greg Hall: Yep
Marc Seidner: And obviously there have been plenty of gains compounded in recent years, but not much of a story this year. And our purpose of this piece really is to scratch the surface, to dig a little bit deeper than what, you know, the headlines would draw your attention to and look for opportunity beyond these wide rivers, major, major themes. And one of the observations, and the highest-level observation that we've made in the piece, is, you know, just when you look at concentrations in market indexes and clients' and individual portfolios, there really is a need to take a higher-level look, not just at what things are called,
Greg Hall: mmm hmm
Marc Seidner: but what the underlying risks are and what theme they're capturing. And I'm sure we'll walk through the details of the piece.
But, you know, as we all learned in, you know, our first-year macroeconomic classes or finance classes, diversification is, you know, the one free lunch that we all have. And when you end up with concentration, concentrated benchmarks and concentrated portfolios, it's incumbent upon folks like us to point out areas where there are opportunities to diversify.
And it's not to say, hey, sell everything and buy something else, because that's not efficient and that's not practical. But as wealth continues to grow and compound, what do you do with the marginal dollar? Where does it go? Do you rinse, repeat and do what you have been doing? Or do you, as I said a moment ago, open up the aperture and think a little bit more broadly, scratch the surface, get outside of the news headlines and find some interesting opportunities?
Greg Hall: Yeah, I mean, I think there's so much to unpack there. I know.
Marc Seidner: Really? Sorry, sorry.
Greg Hall: I mean, as usual, you know, you have a nice way of speaking in paragraphs. And so, but I do think, you know, the Nasdaq up 5%, but so much roiling underneath the surface of that sort of placid headline. And then I think, you know, the point you're making, I think implicitly, is that it may be that advisors listening, certainly some of their clients, maybe don't quite realize the discrepancy in underlying returns, the components of that index. We had
Liz Ann Sonders, who is Schwab's investment strategist, she was on a couple of weeks ago.
Marc Seidner: She's excellent.
Greg Hall: Excellent, excellent. And she's really able to frame the issues through the lens of their clientele, many of whom are, you know, individuals. And so, you know, her concern is just that, you know, these big concentrations are building up in equity indices so that to own the S&P, to own the Nasdaq, is essentially to be all in on AI.
And then also starting to see some of that exposure creep into bond indices, creep into other areas of the market. So maybe we can, I think your first point is about some of the issuance in the tech AI space, and how it's influencing investment-grade indices.
Marc Seidner: Well, I agree with everything you said except for creep into credit indices. I mean, I'll, we can talk about, you know, the corporate bond issuance this year, which, again, as you know, I've been doing this for 38, 39 years. You know, going back over the course of my career, you could probably count on one hand the number of $20 billion corporate bond issues in any day.
And, you know, September felt like it was a $20 billion corporate bond issue every day. And so it really was quite, quite profound in that regard. And you're right, I think we all know that there's nobody who's going to listen to this and say, you know, I didn't know that, you know, 40% of the S&P 500 is held in a handful of names.
What's becoming increasingly interesting about corporate exposure is that if you go back two or three years, and we have this chart in the piece, which is, you know, again, hopefully this piece has a few gee-whiz-type charts that capture people's eyes and imagination and start conversation. But if you go back two or three years, tech companies, particularly the high-quality tech companies, didn't borrow in the corporate bond market. They didn't have to. They didn't, they didn't have to. They generated so much free cash flow. Microsoft bought Activision, and I think they paid, what, $78 billion? They funded it by rolling commercial paper. They didn't issue debt because they knew that they were going to generate so much free cash flow that they could pay it back within a few quarters.
It's obviously very different now. And, you know, the hyperscaler cohort is no longer free cash flow positive, and they're funding their massive investment in AI through debt issuance. So if you go back two or three years, tech-related issuance as a percentage of non-financial corporate issuance was about 3 or 4%. This year it's going to be 25 or 30%.
I mean, that is such a dramatic sea change in the environment. So that's one of our points, right? I mean, I think investors, and your point on Liz Ann, know that they've got, if you own the S&P 500, you've got pretty decent concentration in this theme and this trade. But increasingly, that is finding its way into your corporate bond exposure.
It's also finding its way into potentially your real estate or infrastructure or private credit portfolio. And that's, again, why we would suggest folks take a, you know, a top-down, you know, portfolio approach to thinking about risks and positioning and risk management.
Greg Hall: Isn't it the case? I mean, I think that, you know, when we think about things creeping in in a sort of unintentional way, we're obviously talking about the passive indices and less about what we do in the active space. But that being said, one of the pieces you make in the points is just how selective we have been.
It's not that we eschew any involvement in AI financing. Quite, quite the contrary. We've done some very large transactions ourselves, but they're not all created equal. Talk to me about the active-passive dynamic and what you're likely to end up with if you're not being vigilant about which of these exposures you're taking on and not taking on.
Marc Seidner: Well, I think the statistic, at least the high-level statistic, is something like we've done two out of 100 deals that we've looked at, and there's an awful lot of transactions. Well, what we want to focus on is really longer-duration assets, higher-quality assets, certainty of cash flow, certainty of execution.
And what I mean by that is certainty of an ability to complete a project, whether it be through, you know, permitting, whether it be through entitlements, whether it be through, you know, securing power and the like. And then we also want to get paid for the risk. And so that's sort of our compass, our true north, if you will, in terms of deploying capital in the space.
And there are plenty of opportunities to, you know, step outside, you know, your generic corporate issue and deploy. Now, the AI theme is certainly getting more interesting, right? I mean, there are AA-rated companies, one comes to mind, we can mention if you want, but, you know, they're issuing bonds at 160 to 200 basis points spread.
Yeah, you know, that's probably three or four times where they would have been a year ago in terms of risk premium. So the market's charging a premium, or is beginning to charge a premium. There's some discipline creeping back into the corporate bond market.
Greg Hall: And this is a result of, obviously, the Nvidia situation, the sort of the concern around the lack of the, what they call the AI central bank, in the wake of Jensen's scandal.
Marc Seidner: Yeah, it even goes back a bit before that. Again, it's this need for free cash flow. You know, it's this need for debt-financed investment, because free cash flow isn't supporting, you know, the scale and scope of the investment any longer. But if you look at a AA company that's issuing bonds at a spread of 160 to 200 basis points, that's, you know, that's global financial crisis, that's COVID-type levels.
And so, you know, the opportunity certainly is increasing. And, you know, in our minds, you know, that, once again, not to sound like a bond manager, is saying if you can get fixed-rate coupons of six and a half, seven and a half percent, that's a pretty attractive, that's a pretty attractive starting point, and minimizes the uncertainty of trying to pick, you know, winners and losers and whether or not equities are undervalued or overvalued.
So, you know, that dynamic really is becoming quite interesting. But the point you made earlier, which is the one of active versus passive, this is an unbelievably ripe environment for the active manager because there is a healthy degree of dispersion. There is a healthy degree of differentiation. And that's what's so exciting about the environment that we're in.
Greg Hall: I think one of the things that I found interesting, touring around the country, talking to advisors and then, you know, going to conferences and just sort of seeing how the AI theme umm titrates you know percolates into other investment areas. We've talked about equities, talked about the fixed income landscape and the indices. And then you mentioned real estate, infrastructure, private credit.
It is very interesting. I think advisors listening, one of the questions you have to ask yourself is just how much AI leverage, or how much do I want my portfolio to be leveraged to the AI theme? And then where do I want it? Do I want it in stocks? Do I want it in bonds? Do I, and then also want it as a data center holding in my real estate, diversifying exposure? And then, given the dynamic that you just mentioned, a AA company trading 160, 200 basis points wide, surely that credit crunch is going to find its way into the middle market.
Surely the private credit money that's been raised over the last ten years will, you know, these are lenders looking for borrowers. I'll get off my soapbox here in a second.
Marc Seidner: you can stay I'll join you.
Greg Hall: Yeah, but you can see a situation, right, in which this theme is so appealing that virtually every asset class, virtually every asset manager, tries to find their way in, and then portfolios become a lot less diversified than they think they are.
Marc Seidner: Look, let's be clear. The AI revolution, if you will, is a critical investment theme. There's no doubt about it. And this is not a, you know, a rallying point to say that it's not a valid investment. Yes. I mean, this is revolutionary technology. This is adoption at a pace that probably hasn't been seen since the onset of humankind.
I mean, people compare it to, you know, railroads and assembly lines and how revolutionary it is.
Greg Hall: Maybe it's more like fire and clothing, right? Like, it's—
Marc Seidner: Yeah, I mean, it comes about pretty quickly, right? And so it's not a call to, you know, minimize the theme. It's an important theme. It's a call to say there's a lot of other things that are interesting that's going on, that are going on in the market if you scratch the surface. Absolutely. You know, we can touch on a couple of the themes.
But, you know, even for equity indices, when you look at the S&P 500, we have another interesting chart in the piece. I think it's something like 30% of the S&P 500, 30% of the names in the S&P 500, have negative correlation with the S&P 500, right?
Greg Hall: Yes
Marc Seidner: And, you know, and that has spiked this year.
And so, you know, absolutely, you know, equities are a critical and should continue to be a major, major component of wealth creation, compounding and the like. But the AI theme becomes this momentum-oriented theme. And we know that momentum can turn very quickly. Beyond momentum, there are plenty of other equity risk factors that look quite attractive.
Value is often talked about. Quality is another one, low beta. And it doesn't mean that those, and in fact, we pointed out in the piece, we called out this time last year that, yeah, maybe it is time to diversify away from momentum AI into quality value. And that has certainly worked. The relationship was, you know, at a reasonable extreme this time last year. It has mean reverted to some degree, but there's still opportunity there. And the surprise of this year, when you look at the various factors, is how quality, how low beta, how value have performed well. And in months where the momentum theme, the AI theme, has faced its challenges, right, has been a wonderful diversifier in terms of a broad portfolio context. And that sort of, you know, again, the gee-whiz moment is that 30% of the S&P 500, of the individual names, is not correlated with the S&P 500, and it doesn't mean it doesn't go up.
It can still go up, but it has that diversification benefit. And so, you know, the marginal dollar, sure. I mean, I hope everyone got an allocation to Anthropic today. I'm guessing some are looking at their reports this morning or a little bit disappointed. We'll see how it trades. SpaceX is interesting. I mean, he came with much flurry earlier in the year, traded up a lot, and then it's been kind of dead money since then. While there are a lot of stocks that have done very, very well, let's see how Anthropic does. But that theme of what do you do with the marginal dollar, where can you find a home for it, is critically important. And that's what we're doing in our asset allocation portfolios.
That's what we're doing in our quantitative, you know, in our quantitative strategies as well.
Greg Hall: I'm glad you brought that up, because I think you mentioned in the piece, you know, our quantitative strategies. And that strikes me as, you know, it's a little bit of a self-hedge, right? It's a, by definition, unemotional way of allocating to things that screen as attractive relative to alternatives. Classic relative value investing through a quantitative lens.
And that has been, I've been surprised to see the take-up of those strategies, not just here in the US, but with some of our wealth groups internationally as well, investors actively seeking this automatic diversification, you know, that, like, hey, take the wheel and let's make sure that we're rotating exposures into things that screen more attractive on a very, you know, active basis.
So I think that's good advice for advisors. It's a nice part of the piece.
Marc Seidner: Well, let's face facts. We're all human beings. We're all emotional. And, you know, in terms of broad portfolio diversification, even taking some of the emotion out of it and allocating to something that is completely unemotional and has, you know, and works well in some environments, has periods where it may not. But, again, even diversifying between emotion and complete sort of, you know, quantitative rigor and discipline, that's a moment of diversification as well.
Greg Hall: One of the things you point out in the piece, and it's something that we're, you know, the road here has been a little bit bumpier than we might have liked, but you pointed it out as we started, we certainly enjoy the higher yields that we're earning in high-quality fixed income. And we think that that sets up investors in our space for good long-term returns.
Historically, that's, you know, tended to be the case. That being said, high rates put a little bit of pressure on levered companies. And so I'm curious if you're at all worried. We talk a lot, we talked a lot already about credit and leverage in the AI space. Or are you worried about the incumbent economy when it comes to borrowing and financial conditions?
And is that something that you think investors ought to be looking at?
Marc Seidner: Absolutely. I could give you the short answer and just say yes, absolutely.
Greg Hall: It'd be a very short podcast if we did that.
Marc Seidner: To be, might be more interesting.
Greg Hall: Be very efficient. We promise the advisors efficiency.
Marc Seidner: We'd be—
Greg Hall: Here's Marc Seidner for five yes-or-no questions.
Marc Seidner: Yes. Maybe. Yes. Yes. No. Look, we already touched on this with talking about, you know, sort of credit issuance patterns and some very high-quality companies trading at, you know, for their quality or for their rating, quite wide spreads and cheap to what we would assume some form of fair value analysis.
When you go down in quality to the high-yield part of the market and, probably by extension, with less transparency, less data and less availability in pricing, certainly to private credit markets, specifically sponsor-led direct lending, there is absolutely a credit cycle going on, and there has been significant, you know, this notion of, you know, 30% of the single names, the individual names in the S&P 500, trading with negative correlation to the index itself.
That's true with credit as well. I mean, if you take the high-yield index, single B, double Bs, single Bs have been relatively well contained. I mean, spreads have widened a little bit, but they're still historically quite narrow. CCCs have come under an incredible amount of pressure. And so there's absolutely a credit cycle that is going on.
The stressed, distressed component of the market is going up. Now, those are interesting statistics. When you look forward, if the entire universe of CCCs were to have to refinance today, you're talking about 15 or 16% borrowing costs. Now, they don't have to, because, but again, you know, most of—
Greg Hall: The clock's ticking.
Marc Seidner: The clock is ticking. Most of the borrowing, you know, where companies locked in low yields, low spreads, happened three, four or five years ago. And we know the average maturity is, you know, 6 to 10 years, probably 7 to 8 years on average. And so that moment is coming up in the next few years.
And unless something changes fundamentally, that refinancing risk is going to be really, really significant. And I think, again, that speaks to, you know, your question earlier about active versus passive. I mean, even through all the questions that you've asked, you know, you'd say, you know, active versus passive on the fundamental, on the credit, on the high-quality credit selection.
You'd say active versus passive for sure, driven by quantitative strategies. You'd say active versus passive for sure down in credit quality, and certainly for stocks as well. And I think that would be the battle cry. The battle cry is for those that are stuck in passive indices where, you know, the risks are mounting and the correlation and sort of the concentrations are increasing.
Yeah, that's where you want to think about true diversification. And, you know, again, what you would do with the marginal dollar, the next dollar, or how you could possibly rebalance and give yourself a safer portfolio that may very well not sacrifice return.
Greg Hall: Right. Yeah, autopilot does feel like an increasingly dangerous place to be in this type of environment.
Marc Seidner: Yeah, I think that's well said.
Greg Hall: So we've talked a lot about the performance, or the performance discrepancy between underlying asset classes. Of course, you know, the inescapable reality for a lot of our advisors here in the US is taxes. And how do you, you know, whenever we have a rebalancing or a reallocation conversation, you've got to tackle taxes as an issue. It's a frictional cost to moving assets around.
It's an important one. Good advisors take it very seriously. And as, you know, as professionals, they try to minimize the tax consequences for their clients when they're moving assets around. And as a result of this tax sensitivity, one of the places that we're always talking to advisors about is the municipal bond market. We haven't talked about it yet today, Marc, but it just, it struck me as interesting, with yields where they are and with maybe some of the concerns about concentration in the AI theme or maybe some underlying credit quality issues, are munis a respite here?
Are they a haven for folks looking to capture yield without, you know, increasing their concentration in some of these themes?
Marc Seidner: Yeah, no doubt. I mean, in fact, you know, we get this question quite, quite a lot, right? Which is, hey, you know, the debt and deficit dynamics for the US government, how does that affect the states? And, you know, our basic assessment is that the states are fundamentally very sound. I mean, unlike the federal government, they are required to run a balanced budget in most states. And with yields, you know, moving higher this year, that has once again created, you know, incredibly interesting opportunity to deploy money in the municipal market, particularly the high-quality market.
There's a lot of risks, not unlike the credit risks that we've talked about, in lower quality. And by the way, that concentration theme, we see a lot. Maybe I shouldn't talk about our competitors, but we see a lot of our competitors have highly concentrated positions in lower-quality muni names. You don't have to do that. You don't have to take that risk, because there is definitely downside in the high-yield segment of the market.
But when a high-quality muni portfolio potentially offers you, you know, four, four and a quarter percent yield, which translates into a tax-equivalent yield of seven, 7.5%, that's, you know, an opportunity to be tax efficient that absolutely cannot be ignored. I mean, many advisors take advantage of it. But again, we've been talking about the marginal dollar of capital deployment, seven, 7.5% tax equivalent in the muni portfolio you know, seems, you know, hate to sound like an old-school bond manager, but it seems really, really compelling.
Greg Hall: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. No, no, I mean, I think the theme you raised there too is, you know, this focus on nominal yield regardless of credit risk. And that has been something that we've had to, when we talk to advisors, it's just, understand your fully loaded cost of holding this risk. And the problem with credit risk is it often shows up well after you've made the initial investment.
Everything's really exciting at the outset. And then whether it's because of, you know, degrading financial conditions or it's because of mark-to-model accounting or whatever the function is, the fully loaded cost of holding that yield can show up a lot later.
Marc Seidner: Yeah. As we've said, you know, repeatedly now, this is an active versus passive market. This is, or environment. This is not, this is by no means a set it or forget it, or set it and forget it, type of environment. And so, you know, your starting point may be an attractive starting point, but as portfolios evolve, it does really require some hands-on management.
Greg Hall: Terrific. One of the last, the last thing you bring up, and speaking of kind of other areas that offer return and have been a big story this year, is the commodity markets. And of course, you know, we haven't seen resolution, full resolution to the conflict in Iran. We have a different political and geopolitical environment that we're dealing with now versus earlier in the year.
And I'm glad you just took the moment to remind folks that, you know, commodities are, you know, very interesting portfolio diversification opportunity. What do you see in those markets right now that strikes you as interesting?
Marc Seidner: Well, I mean, we just show the numbers, right? I mean, your 60/40 portfolio, if you alter it just 10%, that doesn't mean the 10% is the right number because of, you know, various portfolio constructions, but you increase the Sharpe ratio of those portfolios by adding a bit of broad-based commodity exposure. And again, it's a theme that has, I think, some legs, in the sense that, you know, gold was the, was the shining star.
Yes, pun certainly intended, was the shining star in 2025. The energy complex and oil was absolutely, you know, I mean, it'll end up as, you know, the oil complex will end up being, you know, the top-performing asset, you know, broad-based asset for 2026. There are plenty of themes that could be in play in 2027.
I mean, there's, you know, here we are in Southern California today and it's supposed to rain, and it's not supposed to rain in Southern California. It's—
Greg Hall: Cold and rainy. I want my money back. I flew in from New York yesterday.
Marc Seidner: Well, you're welcome to go home. I mean, you know, it's cold in New York too, right? Yeah. So, folks, unseasonably cold for this time of year. So folks have to turn their heating on early. And so, you know, whether it's the El Niño effect that's affecting weather patterns that will have impact on commodity prices, and potentially for both the energy complex and agriculture, or whether it's the AI theme and the construction and the build, right, you know, industrial metals. And again, as we look at it in a more complicated world of greater political, geopolitical and other risks, as we show in the piece, you know, if you can diversify your portfolio and actually improve your Sharpe ratio by adding a little bit of commodity exposure, broad-based commodity exposure, not picking something or one versus another, broad-based commodity exposure, that's a very easy diversifier, right? And certainly fits the theme that we just discussed of sort of, you know, ongoing conflict, ongoing geopolitical risk, weather patterns, you know, supply-demand and the like.
Greg Hall: Yeah. How to make volatility work for you, how to take advantage of dispersion across asset classes, within indices, within asset classes. I think that's the predominant theme of this year's paper, and it's a great read. I hope everybody will click through and take a look at it as they, you know, look to prepare for their next client meeting.
Marc, thanks for giving us a preview of the piece today, and hopefully you'll incite more people to go read your work. With that, we're going to leave you for now. This will be a quick one for us. We did not do yes-or-no questions, but we got through it in pretty good time. Thanks for being with us, Marc.
Thanks, everybody, for listening. If you have a moment and you've enjoyed what you've heard here, please do hit like and subscribe. If we know you're out there, it helps us continue to bring you great content, which you hopefully agree is great. If you visit us at pimco.com or the PIMCO website in your country of residence and you identify yourself as a financial advisor, you'll be taken to Advisor Forum.
That is our one-stop shop for you to get what you need from PIMCO, digest it as quickly and practically as possible, and get back out visiting with your clients and holding their hands through interesting, exciting and volatile markets. We will see you next time. Thanks so much!

From This Episode

Against that backdrop, Marc Seidner identifies five investment ideas for building more deliberate diversification in 2027, including extending duration and emphasizing higher-quality assets; rebalancing into municipal bonds for attractive after-tax income; and seeking differentiated return potential through quantitative and relative value strategies. He and Greg Hall explore how advisors can help clients put their next dollar to work.
