articles.title: My workers or ours? How labor sharing shapes hiring in urban firm clusters: Guest post by Zachary Kuloszewski
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

My workers or ours? How labor sharing shapes hiring in urban firm clusters: Guest post by Zachary Kuloszewski

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the 11th in this year’s series of posts by PhD students on the job market.
“Who do you work for?” usually has a simple answer: a business, a shop owner, or a family member exclusively hires a worker for an agreed-upon duration. But if you ask this question in a busy workshop, you may hear the names of many different firms or owners. In my job market paper, I break down why the answer to this question can be a bit more complicated in dense, informal labor markets.
Small, informal firms, which employ the majority of workers in sub-Saharan Africa, face many challenges hiring and maintaining an appropriately sized workforce. Worker ability is hard to judge before a worker is on the job, so vetting a new hire is slow and costly. Demand from consumers can vary widely week to week. Firms confronting both issues face the difficult choice of carrying idle labor during slow periods or being left unprepared for peaks in demand. In high-income countries, firms turn to formal temporary agencies. What do firms do in the absence of these formal intermediaries?
In urban Uganda, I survey over 500 firms and 1,000 of their workers to show that firms rely on labor sharing, borrowing workers directly from their competitors, to cope with both high hiring costs and shifting demand. By offering on-demand workers who come pre-verified by a neighboring firm, labor sharing provides flexible capacity, allowing hiring managers to reach across the firm boundary and meet their spikes in demand without sacrificing quality. In effect, skilled workers have a “home firm” but are frequently reallocated to others nearby. In the paper, I combine detailed hiring data with stated choice experiments to estimate an equilibrium model investigating how labor sharing changes hiring and the impacts of labor market policies.
What is labor sharing?
Labor sharing is a distinctive kind of exchange used for temporary work, organized through firm-to-firm relationships rather than an open market. These exchanges have a common structure; they are reciprocal, uncompensated, and owner-coordinated. When one firm receives a large order, the owner requests workers from other same-industry firms nearby, with the borrowing firm paying the shared worker’s wages for the duration of the job, which is often less than a week.
Labor sharing is common and frequently used in the carpentry and metalworking sectors of Kampala, with 80% of firms reporting borrowing a worker from a competitor, and the average sharing firm borrowing or lending about once every ten days. Beyond Uganda, it has been qualitatively documented in Tanzania and Indonesia, where urban markets also feature dense firm clusters. Thus, questions of its structure and impact are important to understanding how small firms (collectively) function in low-income markets.
Labor sharing carries a quality signal and is available on demand
As in many low-income labor markets, workers lack credible signals of quality or skill. Permanent hiring is slow, taking over 4 days to screen a new worker. To examine labor sharing’s role in addressing this screening friction, I elicit firm beliefs about worker characteristics by asking firm owners about worker quality, screening time, and supervision needs. Owners expect 6.3 of 10 hires through labor sharing to make sellable products without further training, higher than any other hiring channel, including social network referrals (p<0.001). Owners report the least time to screen new shared workers and the fewest hours of supervision, consistent with the idea that borrowing workers avoids high hiring costs, cited by 58% as an advantage of sharing.
Shared workers are also valuable because they are a timely response to short-term, firm-specific demand shocks, which come in the form of large orders. A busy month brings in five times the revenue of a slow month, and over half of owners report that their first response to unexpected demand spikes is to hire via labor sharing.
I combine these market features in the design of stated choice experiments where firms face hypothetical demand shocks and choose between potential extra hires to add to their staff. The experiments show how much firms value specific worker attributes [Figure 1]. I find firms are willing to pay a wage premium of roughly 53,000 Ugandan shillings per week ($14) for a shared worker over a similar walk-in worker. This premium is equivalent to about five years of industry experience, or a third of the median weekly wage.
Figure 1

In stated choice experiments for workers, I measure worker preferences by presenting hypothetical job offers varying the worker’s personal connection to a new firm, along with other attributes. I find that workers value opportunities through labor sharing about the same as other types of referrals, but more than jobs at firms where they have no prior connection. The worker choice experiments importantly show that workers positively value being lent out through labor sharing despite the implicit uncertainty or adjustment costs. Over 90% of workers are paid piece rate and earn little in slow periods, so being shared acts as a form of earnings insurance across firms and improves worker capacity utilization.
What sharing does to the labor market
Firms and workers both make staffing and employment decisions internalizing the presence of labor sharing as an additional hiring margin. Before knowing their demand from consumers, firms face a choice to hire now or borrow later. Borrowing brings assurances of skill for an additional cost, such as future lending obligations, which I measure in total from the choice experiments above. I formalize these trade-offs in an equilibrium model of hiring where workers choose firms based on wages and amenities (including the ability to be shared), and firms hire under uncertainty about consumer demand and worker skill.
Compared to an economy where firms hire only via walk-ins and referrals, the economy with labor sharing creates 7.0% more surplus, benefiting skilled workers and firms. This economy also supports more, smaller firms, as it reduces the carrying costs of slack labor. The gains are driven by improved allocation of workers across demand states [Figure 2, top panel]. When firms can share, the fraction of skilled-worker time spent at busy firms doubles, leading to increased profits for firms and higher earnings for shared workers.
However, labor sharing changes who hires and holds permanent workers. With labor sharing, permanent jobs shift toward lower-productivity firms [Figure 2, bottom panel]. In effect, the ability to share separates hiring costs from worker utilization. Lower-productivity firms screen and hire workers, then lend them out to higher-productivity firms, which are more likely to meet their labor demand by borrowing than by permanently hiring. In the model, top-tercile firms use 46% of busy-week skilled work and produce over half of the economy’s output, while holding only 29% of permanent skilled jobs.
Figure 2

Lessons for policy
One of the key roles of the firm in these markets is to match customer orders to the right workers. Labor sharing is a market adaptation which helps firms collectively achieve this goal, but it also provides a degree of skill verification. So, it may interact with commonly implemented skill policies, such as certification or training. In my model:
Certification makes hiring skilled workers through walk-ins or referrals comparatively cheaper and concentrates gains among low-productivity lending firms (+4% profits) at the expense of high-productivity borrowers (-17%).
Training increases the supply of skilled labor and enables high-productivity firms to hire permanently instead of relying on borrowing, leading these firms to grow.
Taken together, these findings suggest existing informal institutions can determine who gains from labor market policy. Policymakers seeking to improve firm efficiency and worker outcomes in low-income markets should account for firm-to-firm interactions when considering and designing policy tools.
Zachary Kuloszewski is a Ph.D. candidate in Economics at the University of Chicago. On Twitter/X: @ZachKulos.

Emerging Markets: Key Themes for 2027

1-2 December 20262 sessions:1 December 2026 – 2.00pm GMT (London/ 9am EST)2 December 2026 – 10.00am HKT (Hong Kong/ 1pm Sydney)

online

On consumption, it’s energy spikes versus AI and easing trade pressures. We think inflation will be tolerable, implying EM central banks will avoid a broad-based tightening cycle. We remain constructive on AI, despite setbacks.

Productivity gains and increased trade will dominate our concerns over employment and next year’s negative impulse. The politics of maintaining debt sustainability are a thorny medium-term issue: But despite major concerns across numerous markets, time is on the side of those with political support for adjustment.

The panel will focus on regional differences and key country calls and will deliver market implications. We’ll also reveal our top EM and regional risks for 2027.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Gabriel Sterne

Gabriel delivers macro-economic products tailored for corporates and financial markets, as head of a team that integrates EM macro and strategy views. In recent years he has published wide-ranging research including on stagflation risks, monetary policy credibility, global savings, demographics, Covid scarring, risks and resilience in emerging markets, and sovereign crisis resolution. He joined from investment banking boutique Exotix in May 2014, following 20 years of public sector experience, including at the Bank of England and International Monetary Fund.

Head of Emerging Markets

Joan Domene

Joan Domene is the Chief Economist for Latin America and is responsible for developing Oxford Economics’ view on the region. Joan is responsible for producing macroeconomic forecasts for Mexico. He manages a team of economists who produce regional and country-specific research on over 30 countries. Joan’s work also involves presenting the outlook to clients and liaising with the media. Joan joined Oxford Economics in 2019 as Senior Economist after 5 years at a Mexican private bank.

Chief Latin America Economist

Louise Loo

Louise Loo is the Head of Asia Economics at Oxford Economics. She leads the firm’s macroeconomic research and forecasting efforts on Greater China.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, she was a senior economist at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. At Goldman Sachs, she was also a long-term advisor to China Ministry of Finance and the China-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) with regards to their sovereign credit ratings.

Louise is a regular contributor to various international financial news outlets and has earned Economics and public policy degrees with Sheffield University and Columbia University.

Head of Asia Economics

Sergi Lanau

Sergi’s research focuses on emerging and frontier markets. He joined Oxford Economics in 2023. He previously worked on emerging markets and the eurozone at the Institute of International Finance and IMF. He began his career at the Bank of England.

articles.title: Diverging developments in euro area residential real estate markets: risks and policy considerations
articles.text: Diverging developments in euro area residential real estate markets: risks and policy considerationsPrepared by Giorgia De Nora, Barbara Jarmulska and Cristian PeralesPublished as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.Since 2022 residential real estate (RRE) price growth has diverged significantly across the euro area. While one group of euro area countries is currently experiencing strong RRE price growth and has had price levels remaining relatively high since 2022, another has seen more subdued RRE price dynamics over the same period (Chart A, panel a). This box examines the factors underlying this variation in RRE price developments, with the aim of shedding light on the channels through which possible vulnerabilities may be building up.Chart ARRE price developments differ markedly across countries, with multiple factors driving the recent price boom in some countriesa) One-year nominal RRE price growthb) Cumulative contributions to RRE price growth(Q4 2021-Q4 2025, percentages)(Q4 2021-Q4 2025, percentage points)Sources: ECB and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: all euro area countries are split into two groups, depending on whether they are above or below the median one-year nominal RRE price growth rate in Q4 2025 of the country sample used in panel b (for consistency between panel a and panel b). As a result, one-third of countries are in the lower RRE price growth category and two-thirds in the higher category. The solid lines depict the median for each group of countries, while the shaded areas around the solid lines represent the interquartile range. Panel b: averages of cumulative shock contributions to house prices are estimated using country-level Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR)(2) models for nine euro area countries (Germany, Ireland, Spain, France, Italy, Netherlands, Austria, Portugal and Finland). The nine euro area countries in the sample are split into two groups, depending on whether they are above or below the median one-year nominal RRE price growth rate in Q4 2025. The variables included in the BVAR(2) models are residential investments, real disposable income, house prices, the euro area shadow rate*, lending rate on household loans, outstanding mortgage loans and the consumer price index. The estimation sample covers the period Q1 2003-Q4 2025. Five of the seven structural shocks are identified through zero and sign restrictions (for the impact of the identified structural shocks on house price growth, see Chart A, panel b).*) See Krippner, L., “Measuring the stance of monetary policy in zero lower bound environments”, Economics Letters, Vol. 118, Issue 1, 2013, pp. 135-138, and Krippner, L., Zero Lower Bound Term Structure Modeling: A Practitioner’s Guide, Palgrave Macmillan, New York, 2015.Diverging price developments reflect both differences in the drivers of house price growth and differences in how common shocks pass through to national housing markets.[1] See also Di Casola, P. and Grothe, M., “Housing wealth and monetary policy transmission: cross-country evidence”, Working Paper Series, No 3204, ECB, 2026, who find that the response of house prices to monetary policy shocks is uneven across advanced economies and related to housing and mortgage market characteristics. In the group of countries experiencing price growth above the median, house prices continued to rise between the end of 2021 and the end of 2025, driven by three main factors: (i) favourable mortgage supply conditions, i.e. changes in the price or availability of mortgage credit that are not directly related to changes in the monetary policy stance (a broad concept capturing factors such as bank funding costs, risk appetite and credit standards);[2] See, for example, Gambetti, L. and Musso, A., “Loan Supply Shocks and the Business Cycle”, Journal of Applied Econometrics, Vol. 32, Issue 4, 2017, pp. 764-782. (ii) stronger housing preference, with housing increasingly seen as an attractive investment; and (iii) constrained housing supply (Chart A, panel b). The same three main factors listed above exerted a downward pressure on prices in countries with RRE growth below median, with mortgage supply shocks contributing most to the difference between the two groups. Monetary policy weighed on prices in both groups, but the drag (as the stance was tightened) was around twice as large in the group with lower RRE price growth.[3] These results reflect average dynamics within each group and should not be seen as identifying the drivers of house price developments in individual countries. Since the same monetary policy stance applies across the euro area, this gap stems from how changes in policy rates impact each national housing market rather than from the policy itself. This in turn depends on the market’s structural features across countries, which is considered next.The structural features of the RRE and mortgage markets shape the impact of interest rate hikes on house prices. These features vary substantially across the euro area, which can help explain why house prices in various countries responded differently to rising interest rates during the hiking cycle that started in 2022 (Chart B). In countries where fixed-rate mortgages predominate, for example, rate hikes had a stronger impact on house prices. This would be consistent with the notion that house prices can be highly sensitive to interest rates even when most outstanding mortgages have fixed rates, because changes in financing costs for new buyers can have a substantial effect on housing demand and prices.[4] A vast literature exists on the strength of the impact of interest rates on house prices depending on whether fixed- or variable-rate mortgage lending is more common. Many papers show prices reacting more strongly to monetary policy when variable-rate lending predominates (see Calza, A., Monacelli, T. and Stracca, L., “Housing Finance and Monetary Policy”, Journal of the European Economic Association, Vol. 11, 2013, pp. 101-122; Fonseca, J. and Liu, L., “Mortgage Lock-In, Mobility, and Labor Reallocation”, The Journal of Finance, Vol. 79, Issue 6, 2024, pp. 3729-3772; and Fonseca, J., Liu, L. and Mabille, P., “Unlocking Mortgage Lock-In: Equilibrium Effects in a Spatial Housing Ladder model”, NBER Working Paper Series, No 35237, National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026). However, other literature shows a stronger reaction of house prices to interest rates in countries where fixed-rate lending predominates (see Dieckelmann, D., Hempell, H.S., Jarmulska, B., Lang, J.H. and Rusnák, M., “House prices and ultra-low interest rates: exploring the nonlinear nexus”, Empirical Economics, Vol. 68, 2025, pp. 1001-1037) and that house price responses to monetary policy can be particularly strong in a US housing market dominated by fixed-rate lending (see Musso, A., Neri, S. and Stracca, L., “Housing, consumption and monetary policy: How different are the US and the euro area?”, Journal of Banking & Finance, Vol. 35, Issue 11, 2011, pp. 3019-3041). At the same time, theoretical research highlights the importance of pass-through to new fixed-rate mortgage rates (see Kinnerud, K., “The Effects of Monetary Policy through Housing and Mortgage Choices on Aggregate Demand”, Quantitative Economics, Vol. 16, Issue 2, 2025, pp. 659-703). Moreover, house prices were more sensitive to rising rates in countries without binding loan-to-value (LTV) limits. An LTV cap in place for first-time buyers is used as a proxy for the leverage of a marginal buyer[5] Limits on loan-to-income (LTI) or debt-to-income (DTI) would have been a closer proxy for the leverage of the marginal buyer. However, LTV caps were chosen instead due to their prevalence across euro area counties, with LTI/DTI caps activated in only four countries. While the LTV caps may be a good proxy for the LTV of marginal buyer in most of the countries, this does not automatically mean that, in all countries without strict LTV caps in place, a marginal buyer will be more leveraged than in countries with strict LTV caps in place. ; the result obtained could reflect how marginal buyers in countries without binding LTV limits tend to be more leveraged than those in countries where binding LTV caps are in place. This means their capacity to purchase a property would decline more when interest rates go up.[6] This finding is consistent with the literature which, however, looked at actual prevailing LTVs and not LTV caps (see Calza, A., Monacelli, T. and Stracca, L., “Housing Finance and Monetary Policy”, Journal of the European Economic Association, Vol. 11, 2013, pp. 101-122, and Rubaszek, M., Stenvall, D. and Uddin, G.S., “Rental market structure and housing dynamics: An interacted panel VAR investigation”, International Journal of Finance & Economics, Vol. 30, Issue 1, 2025, pp. 781-802). In addition, markets that were substantially overvalued at the peak of the house price cycle experienced sharper price corrections than markets that were not. This likely reflects the tendency of prices to revert to sustainable levels more quickly the more they previously deviated from them. By contrast, countries with high levels of house purchases not financed by mortgages showed less sensitivity to interest rate changes, consistent with the idea that buyers were less affected by changes to mortgage rates.[7] The strength of this effect is likely to depend on the presence of non-household buyers in the housing market in a given country. The estimates of shares of non-mortgage purchases could include purchases by institutional investors and/or state entities such as local authorities which could be debt-financed, and hence also dependent on prevailing interest rates. Lastly, higher home ownership rates were linked to weaker price adjustments, probably because part of the adjustment to rising interest rates occurred through reduced transaction volumes, thereby limiting the extent of price declines.Chart BInterest rate elasticity of house prices(Q4 2021-Q3 2025, elasticity)Sources: National central banks, Eurostat, ECB and ECB calculations.Notes: ARM stands for adjustable-rate mortgage; LTV stands for loan-to-value. The interest rate elasticity of house prices measures the percentage change in house prices associated with a 1% change in interest rates, holding other factors constant. The elasticity estimates come from an econometric model with the log real index of house prices regressed on the log interest rate variable (calculated as a logarithm of the following expression: the real long-term interest rate minus the long-term rent growth plus a risk premium of 6%) with relevant demand-side control variables, following Dieckelmann et al.* The analysis focuses on the period Q4 2021-Q3 2025 for 20 euro area countries (Bulgaria is not included as the variable capturing the supply of housing is not available). The model was augmented with interactions between the interest rate variable and country dummies (fixed in time) based on the structural characteristics considered, with the interactions added one at a time. The country dummies are constructed as follows: (1) high ARM shares indicate countries where shares of variable-rate mortgages and mortgages that reprice in the following year in the stock in Q4 2025 exceed 20%; (2) countries with binding LTV caps are those where LTV caps were in place in H2 2025, calibrated at a maximum of 90% for the first-time buyers; (3) countries with high overvaluation are those where the deviation in the house price/income ratio from the mean in Q2 2022 (peak of the house price cycle) was higher than 25% (acknowledging that this is an estimate of an unobservable category and different methods may yield different estimates); (4) countries with a high share of non-mortgage property purchases are those where estimates (based in some cases on expert judgement rather than empirical evidence) coming from national authorities and/or industry reports are at over 30% of purchases; and (5) countries with a high share of home ownership are those where the ownership rate is over 70%. The results are robust to different cut-offs for country dummies. The impact of tax incentives to purchase property and supply-side shortages was also tested, but the results were not robust. A model excluding the supply of housing among the explanatory control variables but including Bulgaria yields similar results. The analysis focused on the period Q4 2021-Q3 2025 as the structural features which we consider could affect the interest rate elasticity of house prices differently depending on the period analysed, e.g. during a period of higher or lower interest rates.*) Dieckelmann, D., Hempell, H.S., Jarmulska, B., Lang J.H. and Rusnák M., “House prices and ultra-low interest rates: exploring the nonlinear nexus”, Empirical Economics, Vol. 68, 2025, pp. 1001-1037.Common macro-financial shocks can have markedly different implications for residential RRE markets and the build-up of vulnerabilities across euro area countries. The findings in this box suggest that strong house price growth does not always reflect the same vulnerabilities. From a financial stability perspective, credit-driven price growth warrants the closest attention, as it fuels household leverage and might heighten banks’ credit risk. Structural features of national markets also shape how house prices and borrowers respond to changes in interest rates. This is particularly relevant at the current juncture, as financing conditions are tightening again. Identifying the dominant factors helps explain why housing markets respond differently to common shocks, makes it easier to interpret housing market indicators and supports the early detection of risks. It also informs macroprudential policymaking, as the effectiveness of policy measures depends on the channels through which vulnerabilities build up.[8] See Fell, J., “House price booms and policy choices: insights from a meta-regression analysis”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, May 2026. In addition, understanding these dominant factors may help policymakers decide whether other housing market measures, such as housing-related taxes and levies, may be the appropriate policy response.[9] See Kholodilin, K.A., “The Impact of Governmental Regulations on Housing Market: Findings of a Meta-Study of Empirical Literature”, Discussion Papers, No 2113, Deutsches Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung, 2025. See also Di Casola, P. and Grothe, M., “Housing wealth and monetary policy transmission: cross-country evidence”, Working Paper Series, No 3204, ECB, 2026, who find that the response of house prices to monetary policy shocks is uneven across advanced economies and related to housing and mortgage market characteristics. See, for example, Gambetti, L. and Musso, A., “Loan Supply Shocks and the Business Cycle”, Journal of Applied Econometrics, Vol. 32, Issue 4, 2017, pp. 764-782. These results reflect average dynamics within each group and should not be seen as identifying the drivers of house price developments in individual countries. Many papers show prices reacting more strongly to monetary policy when variable-rate lending predominates (see Calza, A., Monacelli, T. and Stracca, L., “Housing Finance and Monetary Policy”, Journal of the European Economic Association, Vol. 11, 2013, pp. 101-122; Fonseca, J. and Liu, L., “Mortgage Lock-In, Mobility, and Labor Reallocation”, The Journal of Finance, Vol. 79, Issue 6, 2024, pp. 3729-3772; and Fonseca, J., Liu, L. and Mabille, P., “Unlocking Mortgage Lock-In: Equilibrium Effects in a Spatial Housing Ladder model”, NBER Working Paper Series, No 35237, National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026). However, other literature shows a stronger reaction of house prices to interest rates in countries where fixed-rate lending predominates (see Dieckelmann, D., Hempell, H.S., Jarmulska, B., Lang, J.H. and Rusnák, M., “House prices and ultra-low interest rates: exploring the nonlinear nexus”, Empirical Economics, Vol. 68, 2025, pp. 1001-1037) and that house price responses to monetary policy can be particularly strong in a US housing market dominated by fixed-rate lending (see Musso, A., Neri, S. and Stracca, L., “Housing, consumption and monetary policy: How different are the US and the euro area?”, Journal of Banking & Finance, Vol. 35, Issue 11, 2011, pp. 3019-3041). At the same time, theoretical research highlights the importance of pass-through to new fixed-rate mortgage rates (see Kinnerud, K., “The Effects of Monetary Policy through Housing and Mortgage Choices on Aggregate Demand”, Quantitative Economics, Vol. 16, Issue 2, 2025, pp. 659-703). Limits on loan-to-income (LTI) or debt-to-income (DTI) would have been a closer proxy for the leverage of the marginal buyer. However, LTV caps were chosen instead due to their prevalence across euro area counties, with LTI/DTI caps activated in only four countries. While the LTV caps may be a good proxy for the LTV of marginal buyer in most of the countries, this does not automatically mean that, in all countries without strict LTV caps in place, a marginal buyer will be more leveraged than in countries with strict LTV caps in place. This finding is consistent with the literature which, however, looked at actual prevailing LTVs and not LTV caps (see Calza, A., Monacelli, T. and Stracca, L., “Housing Finance and Monetary Policy”, Journal of the European Economic Association, Vol. 11, 2013, pp. 101-122, and Rubaszek, M., Stenvall, D. and Uddin, G.S., “Rental market structure and housing dynamics: An interacted panel VAR investigation”, International Journal of Finance & Economics, Vol. 30, Issue 1, 2025, pp. 781-802). The strength of this effect is likely to depend on the presence of non-household buyers in the housing market in a given country. The estimates of shares of non-mortgage purchases could include purchases by institutional investors and/or state entities such as local authorities which could be debt-financed, and hence also dependent on prevailing interest rates. See Fell, J., “House price booms and policy choices: insights from a meta-regression analysis”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, May 2026. See Kholodilin, K.A., “The Impact of Governmental Regulations on Housing Market: Findings of a Meta-Study of Empirical Literature”, Discussion Papers, No 2113, Deutsches Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung, 2025.

How can investors navigate financial markets in 2027? Where are the potential opportunities, and the risks?

Our 2027 Investment Outlook explores the key factors we believe will drive economies as well as equity and fixed income markets over the coming year.

We break down the key challenges facing investors today and highlight the areas where we see the most potential for growth.

Download our Investment Outlook

Macro and markets

The global economy enters 2027 with stability and renewed momentum but economic growth is likely to be uneven and numerous risks remain.

Sustainable returns will depend on active selection, disciplined risk management, and the ability to identify those investments most capable of converting structural change into sustainable value creation.

Macroeconomic outlook

We expect global economic resilience to be tested in 2027. Europe enters the year with fresh momentum.

US growth is expected to remain robust even as some of the tailwind from the artificial intelligence boom is expected to fade China, meanwhile, faces a slowing recovery while across emerging markets, growth should remain buoyant but uneven.

Global inflation and political uncertainty remain concerns however, driven by geopolitical tensions in Iran and upcoming elections in Europe.

Read more

Bond markets are mixed

Bond markets are entering 2027 from a very different position than a year ago. Inflation and fiscal concerns are weighing on the outlook for government bonds. Meanwhile US and European corporate bonds are currently attractive.

Read more

Equity markets continue to diverge

Equity markets continue to witness a divergence between technology and non-tech stocks’ performance. While there is uncertainty over the long-term winners of AI development, earnings growth expectations are positive.

articles.title: Daily: Rising yields raise the portfolio appeal of bonds and diversified investing
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: The AI sell-off and US midterms: Live at the UBS Disruptive Tech Summit (6 mins)
CIO Live Replay: CIO Asia equity strategists on the AI sell-off and opportunities (30 mins)Thought of the dayHigher global bond yields on recalibrated interest rate expectations and a rebound in appetite for stocks have hurt investors with existing fixed income positions. At the time of writing, the policy-sensitive German 2-year yield stood roughly 17bps higher on the week and was on course for its sharpest weekly rise in two months. And Japanese 10-year yields climbed to their highest levels since 22 October in Asian trading, in tandem with higher US government yields on news that President Trump was not seeking a peace deal with Iran and as investors weighed comments from Federal Reserve President Waller around the possibility of a 50bps rate hike at the Fed's December meeting.But elevated starting yields have restored rather than diminished the appeal of the traditional balanced (60% stock, 40% bond) portfolio. While equities can provide long-term growth, high-quality bonds once again offer meaningful income, potential capital appreciation if growth slows, and a cushion against some equity market declines.Bonds have returned to the core The reset in yields has materially improved the role bonds can play in portfolios. After the global financial crisis, low interest rates left fixed income offering limited income and relatively little protection against an equity market drawdown, while exposing investors to the risk of rising yields. Current higher starting yields matter in several ways. They increase the income available from bonds and provide a greater cushion against negative returns in case rates increase further. They also create scope for capital appreciation if inflation moderates, economic growth weakens, or central banks eventually reduce interest rates. The portfolio role of bonds extends beyond expected returns. High-quality bonds can help preserve capital and may diversify equity exposure when economic growth disappoints. Their senior position in the capital structure also generally makes them less risky than equities issued by the same company.60/40 is stronger, but not invulnerable. The revival of bond yields improves the case for a 60/40 equity-bond portfolio. But it is not guaranteed that bonds will offset every equity decline. The diversification benefit depends partly on why equity markets are falling.High-quality bonds have historically been more effective equity diversifiers during periods of low or stable inflation. If growth weakens and inflation moderates, bond prices may rise as equities come under pressure. If inflation remains elevated and interest rates rise, stocks and bonds can decline together. That distinction is important at present, as investors face several plausible paths for growth, inflation, fiscal policy, energy prices, and geopolitical risk into the year ahead.Completion assets can address different risks. Uncertainty and the need to think in terms of market scenarios makes the case for completion assets stronger. Completion assets can earn their place by doing a specific job that the core may not perform consistently. That might include generating differentiated returns, providing income, reducing sensitivity to equity markets, or helping preserve purchasing power during periods of elevated inflation.Hedge funds may provide alternative sources of return when equities and bonds face pressure at the same time. Real assets can address a different set of risks. Commodities have historically displayed relatively low correlation with traditional asset classes and may benefit when physical supply is constrained or inflation remains elevated. And private infrastructure may offer relatively predictable and potentially inflation-linked income, while providing exposure to long-term investment in electricity networks, data centers, electrification, energy security, and more resilient supply chains.So, the return of meaningful bond yields has made the traditional balanced portfolio relevant again. A diversified mix of equities and high-quality bonds can provide a more credible combination of growth, income, and capital preservation than it could during the low-yield era.We currently rate high grade and investment grade bonds as Attractive. We favor exposure to short- to medium-duration high-quality bonds, while remaining more cautious on longer maturities given fiscal concerns and elevated issuance. We also rate high yield and emerging market bonds as Attractive, supported by elevated yields and, in aggregate, resilient fundamentals.However, 60/40 is a foundation, not a complete answer. We believe investors should also look at commodities, real assets, and select structured strategies as ways to enhance returns, improve portfolio resilience, and best match specific goals with portfolios, subject to careful risk management. Private investments in particular can involve illiquidity, limited disclosure, uncertain cash flows, leverage, capital calls, and blind-pool risk.Finally, portfolio discipline matters as much as portfolio design. A 60/40 US equity-bond portfolio invested in 2020 would have drifted to about 80/20 if left untouched, reflecting the stronger performance of equities. Regular rebalancing helps restore the intended risk profile, reduce unintended concentrations, and prevent recent outperformers from determining the portfolio’s future behavior.

We turned more cautious on the stock market and expected buying opportunities after the midterm elections. We got more of a buying opportunity than we bargained for, as the S&P 500 dropped from 7,585.73 on September 15 to 6,910.39 on Friday. It is down 11.6% since its October 6 record high of 7818.93 (chart). We expected a pullback. It has turned into a correction. articles.title: The footprint of hedge funds in euro area sovereign bond markets via repo markets
articles.text: The footprint of hedge funds in euro area sovereign bond markets via repo marketsPrepared by Carlos Miguel Aguiar da Glória, Maurizio Michael Habib, Andrea Sante and Michael SchmidtPublished as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.The sudden unwinding of large hedge fund positions in sovereign bond markets can pose risks for financial stability. Understanding hedge funds’ behaviour during periods of market stress is increasingly important, given the rapid growth of the sector and its substantial exposure to US and European sovereign bonds. Hedge funds now account for a sizeable share of trading activity in euro area sovereign bonds.[1] See Ferrara, F.M. et al., “Hedge funds: good or bad for market functioning?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 23 September 2024. These funds typically use flexible trading strategies that rely heavily on leverage, particularly when trading such bonds. These include relative value strategies such as basis trades, swap spread trades and auction cycle arbitrage, as well as directional strategies such as yield curve arbitrage or sovereign spread trades.[2] See Monin, P.J., “Decomposing Hedge Funds’ U.S. Treasury Exposures”, FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 22 June 2026; “Vulnerabilities in Government Bond-backed Repo Markets”, Financial Stability Board, 4 February 2026; Bassi, C. et al., “Financial stability risks from basis trades in the US Treasury and euro area government bond markets”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, May 2024; and Linzert, T., Nguyen, B., Pelizzon, L., Poinelli, A. and Tomio, D., “Elastic in Cash, Inelastic in Repo: Hedge Funds in the Treasury and Repo Markets”, SAFE Working Papers, No 492, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, August 2026. Although hedge funds may support market liquidity in normal times, tighter financing conditions or internal risk limits during periods of stress can force them to quickly unwind their positions.[3] See Kruttli, M.S., Monin, P.J., Petrasek, L. and Watugala, S.W., “LTCM redux? Hedge fund Treasury trading, funding fragility, and risk constraints”, Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 169, Article 104017, 2025. Such actions can dry up market liquidity, disrupt benchmark asset prices and further exacerbate market turmoil.[4] See Kashyap, A.K., Stein, J.C., Wallen, J.L. and Younger, J., “Treasury Market Dysfunction and the Role of the Central Bank”, Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2025, pp. 221-265. The objective of this box is to analyse how global hedge funds adjusted their exposures to euro area sovereign bond markets via the repo market, focusing on the March 2026 period of bond market volatility triggered by the start of the latest conflict in the Middle East. This unexpected geopolitical event provides a unique opportunity to analyse how hedge funds responded to a large shock in these markets.[5] The analysis is based on data reported under the Securities Financing Transactions Regulation, which makes it possible to monitor hedge fund activity in repo markets collateralised by euro area sovereign bonds. The concentration and offshore location of hedge funds raise additional financial stability concerns for the euro area. Hedge fund activity in euro area sovereign bond and derivatives markets is highly concentrated, accounted for by a small number of funds (Chart A, panel a). This raises the risk that disruptions involving a single entity could have a systemic impact on these markets. Moreover, the large majority of the hedge funds trading euro area repos and derivatives are domiciled in offshore financial centres such as the Cayman Islands. This offshore location limits the ability of euro area supervisory authorities to monitor risks and adopt macroprudential measures (Chart A, panel b). The exposures of EU banks to hedge funds also tend to be concentrated in entities domiciled in the Cayman Islands, raising additional wider concerns around cross-border and cross-sectoral contagion to the EU financial system.[6] See “Financial stability risks from linkages between banks and the non-bank financial intermediation sector”, ECB/ESRB workstream on financial stability risks from bank-NBFI linkages, ECB/ESRB, February 2026. Chart AHedge fund activity in repo and derivatives markets is concentrated in a small number of funds located outside the euro area – their footprint is most visible in the repo marketa) Share of top five hedge funds relative to total outstanding positions of all hedge funds, by market segmentb) Domicile of hedge funds active in the euro area, by market segmentc) Total share of outstanding hedge fund positions, by market segment(Jan. 2026, percentages)(Jan. 2026, percentages)(Jan. 2026, percentages)Sources: ECB (SFTDS, EMIR) and ECB calculations.Notes: EGB stands for European government bond. Panel a: market share held by the top five hedge funds within each market segment, relative to the total outstanding positions of all hedge funds in that segment. The top five hedge funds are those with the largest outstanding positions in each market segment at the beginning of January 2026. Panel b: domicile decomposition is calculated from all active hedge fund transactions recorded in the SFTDS (repos) and EMIR (EGB futures and interest rate swaps) datasets. Panel c: the market shares refer to the gross notional outstanding of hedge fund transactions against all sectors as reported in the SFTDS and EMIR datasets. Note that derivative volumes in particular might be underestimated due to the exclusion of transactions that do not involve an EU counterparty.Hedge funds have a substantial footprint in repo markets, while the visibility of their activities in derivatives markets linked to euro rates or sovereign bonds is more limited. Hedge funds account for a notable share of repo markets using euro area sovereign bonds as collateral, representing 14% of total volumes outstanding. This increases to 27% if centrally cleared transactions (primarily inter-dealer trades) are excluded.[7] Hedge funds are generally not clearing members of European central counterparties. Their activity in European repo markets is concentrated in the bilateral market. By contrast, their market share in derivatives markets linked to euro area sovereign bonds, involving instruments such as futures and interest rate swaps, is much smaller (Chart A, panel c). According to data reported under the European Market Infrastructure Regulation (EMIR), hedge funds account for only around 2% of total volumes outstanding in these markets. However, this figure may underestimate their true market share because EMIR data lack visibility for offshore transactions that do not involve an EU counterparty.[8] For instance, trades between hedge funds domiciled outside the EU (such as a fund located in the Cayman Islands) and non-EU counterparties (such as the subsidiary of a global bank or dealer located in London) are not captured by EMIR data. Hedge funds had built up large gross positions in the euro area repo market over the previous two years but deleveraged when bond market volatility soared in March 2026. At the time when the conflict broke out in the Middle East in February 2026, hedge funds had accumulated a gross repo position against euro area sovereign bonds of around €640 billion, against the background of limited bond market volatility in the previous months. This represents an increase of over 60% since the beginning of the previous year, much greater than the pace of accumulation by other financial institutions such as banks, dealers, investment funds and money market funds (Chart B, panel a). As euro area interest rate volatility rose following the start of the Middle East conflict, hedge funds reduced their positions in repos collateralised by euro area sovereign bonds. Hedge fund positions contracted by 13% in March 2026, which was a faster retrenchment compared with that of dealers and other financial institutions (3%). At the same time, banks actually increased their gross repo positions over the same period.[9] These financial intermediaries and institutions, together with hedge funds, account for almost 95% of repo volumes in the euro area. In repo markets, hedge funds actively borrow cash to take long positions, often procyclically, in euro area sovereign bonds. Over the past year, hedge funds have used the repo market to borrow around €73 billion on average in net terms, maintaining in aggregate a net long position in most euro area sovereign bonds. During the surge in bond market volatility seen in March 2026, however, hedge funds reduced their net cash borrowing by approximately €50 billion, down from a peak of more than €105 billion in February (Chart B, panel b). This sharp deleveraging varied across sovereign issuers but was particularly pronounced in the case of repos collateralised by Spanish and Italian sovereign bonds. Notably, the timing of this reduction aligns with the peak in euro area interest rate volatility, as measured by the Merrill Lynch 1-Month EUR Swaption Volatility Estimate Index. As interest rate volatility eased during the summer, hedge funds began rebuilding their net cash borrowing positions in the repo market (Chart B, panel b). These trends suggest that hedge funds exhibit risk-off behaviour during periods of market stress, consistent with their characterisation as procyclical investors who adjust their exposures in response to changing market conditions.[10] Kerry W., Lewrick, U. and Schmieder, C., “Understanding hedge fund leverage targeting and fire sales”, SUERF Policy Brief, No 1342, SUERF, 15 January 2026. Chart BHedge funds have been building up large positions in the repo market, borrowing cash to take a long position in Spanish, French and Italian sovereign bonds procyclicallya) Growth rate of gross repo positions outstanding, by market participantb) Hedge fund net repo cash borrowing position, by collateral country(Jan. 2025-Feb. 2026, Mar. 2026; percentages)(Jan. 2025-Nov. 2026, left-hand scale: € billions, right-hand scale: index)Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P., ECB (SFTDS, EMIR) and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel b: the hedge fund net repo cash borrowing positions are calculated as the difference between the total nominal outstanding of hedge fund cash borrowing and cash lending transactions. Net notional amounts are calculated weekly, taking into account only repo transactions where the underlying is a sovereign bond issued by Germany, Spain, France or Italy. Negative positions indicate that hedge funds have lent out more cash than they have borrowed by using the sovereign bonds of a certain issuer country as collateral. SMOVE is the Merrill Lynch 1M EUR Swaption Volatility Estimate Index. The right-hand scale is inverted.To conclude, hedge funds are swift, procyclical investors, adjusting their exposures unevenly across euro area sovereign issuers in response to market stress. It is still an open question whether their substantial footprint in euro area repo markets, combined with their reliance on leveraged trading strategies, could amplify market volatility during periods of turmoil. The concentration of hedge fund activity in a small number of entities and their offshore domiciliation – primarily in financial centres outside the euro area – makes it harder for euro area authorities to monitor and mitigate any potential risk. This reinforces the need for cross-border cooperation between financial stability and supervisory authorities. Such authorities should share aggregate data on leverage in key non-bank sectors on a best-efforts basis and use harmonised data and metrics where possible when exchanging information, following the recommendations of the Financial Stability Board.[11] See “Leverage in Nonbank Financial Intermediation – Final report”, Financial Stability Board, 9 July 2025. See Ferrara, F.M. et al., “Hedge funds: good or bad for market functioning?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 23 September 2024. See Monin, P.J., “Decomposing Hedge Funds’ U.S. Treasury Exposures”, FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 22 June 2026; “Vulnerabilities in Government Bond-backed Repo Markets”, Financial Stability Board, 4 February 2026; Bassi, C. et al., “Financial stability risks from basis trades in the US Treasury and euro area government bond markets”, Financial Stability Review, ECB, May 2024; and Linzert, T., Nguyen, B., Pelizzon, L., Poinelli, A. and Tomio, D., “Elastic in Cash, Inelastic in Repo: Hedge Funds in the Treasury and Repo Markets”, SAFE Working Papers, No 492, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, August 2026. See Kruttli, M.S., Monin, P.J., Petrasek, L. and Watugala, S.W., “LTCM redux? Hedge fund Treasury trading, funding fragility, and risk constraints”, Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 169, Article 104017, 2025. See Kashyap, A.K., Stein, J.C., Wallen, J.L. and Younger, J., “Treasury Market Dysfunction and the Role of the Central Bank”, Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2025, pp. 221-265. The analysis is based on data reported under the Securities Financing Transactions Regulation, which makes it possible to monitor hedge fund activity in repo markets collateralised by euro area sovereign bonds. See “Financial stability risks from linkages between banks and the non-bank financial intermediation sector”, ECB/ESRB workstream on financial stability risks from bank-NBFI linkages, ECB/ESRB, February 2026. Hedge funds are generally not clearing members of European central counterparties. Their activity in European repo markets is concentrated in the bilateral market. For instance, trades between hedge funds domiciled outside the EU (such as a fund located in the Cayman Islands) and non-EU counterparties (such as the subsidiary of a global bank or dealer located in London) are not captured by EMIR data. These financial intermediaries and institutions, together with hedge funds, account for almost 95% of repo volumes in the euro area. Kerry W., Lewrick, U. and Schmieder, C., “Understanding hedge fund leverage targeting and fire sales”, SUERF Policy Brief, No 1342, SUERF, 15 January 2026. See “Leverage in Nonbank Financial Intermediation – Final report”, Financial Stability Board, 9 July 2025.

articles.text:
Investment Outlook

Artificial Intelligence

Equity

Diversification

AI in 2027: greater scrutiny on returns

Outlook 2027 - AI in 2027: greater scrutiny on returns

AI has absorbed a disproportionate share of global capital, earnings growth, and investor attention. The returns debate is not new, but it should sharpen in 2027: as free cash flow thins and leverage rises, every additional dollar of investment will face greater scrutiny. The narrative is shifting from who can invest the most to who can capture the highest returns. EPS leadership and market leadership may increasingly diverge as valuations and expectations become more demanding. EPS concentration will not necessarily translate into equity performance: how companies will deliver relative to expectations is more crucial than ever.

Global earnings will depend more on AI

Although earnings breadth is improving, with more MSCI ACWI constituents expected to deliver higher net income in 2027 than in 2026, the IT sector will account for 70% of growth in net income across the entire index, up from around 40% in 2026, led by semiconductors and hardware. Energy and communication services are expected to detract from growth, and consumer discretionary is likely to make only a modest contribution. Several major US hyperscalers sit within communication services and consumer discretionary.

The cycle is past its early innings, but not overThe cycle is real, and supply constraints remain genuine, but warning signs are accumulating: leverage is rising along with huge off-balance sheet commitments, the hyperscalers’ core business results are coming under scrutinity as investors’ patience for return on investment wears thin, quality and cyclical names are starting to diverge, and the remaining funding pipeline will increasingly test capital markets’ capacity to absorb new issuance and be a real test for frontier-model economics.The risk is not an abrupt end to the cycle, but a widening gap between capital deployed and returns generated. AI adoption may accelerate even as returns on AI infrastructure remain contested, particularly as the cost of external financing rises. Volatility is likely to stay, but three considerations make us believe the cycle is maturing and has further to run:Public equity issuance is increasing, but it has not reached the excesses of past issuance-heavy cycles;Hyperscalers’ AI revenue map is richer than the infrastructure-only framing suggests. As both enablers and adopters, they have monetisation levers that pure infrastructure plays lack;Hyperscalers external financing and capital deployment are surging, but remain far below the levels seen in other market segments, like real estate and utility companies, thanks to high operating cash flows.

In 2027, the market will stop paying for capacity and start asking to be shown the returns.

From build-out to payback: own the bottlenecks, not the spending dependents

US hyperscalers’ free cash flow (FCF) is likely to trough in 2027, with capex above operating cash flow. The market will care more about why it recovers than when, demanding early evidence that the monetisation curve is bending upward. Renewed commitments would confirm the cycle has room, while any wavering on spending guidance or disappointing earnings risk a sharp re-rating of the entire AI infrastructure complex.For us, being selective in 2027 follows a simple rule: limit exposure to industries requiring further commitments. Spending dependent names (above all neoclouds, data centre developers, and colocation REITs) may face direct revenue impairment if spending plateaus. Real infrastructure plays (power equipment, electrical grid, networking, chip fabrication) are more insulated, even though physical scarcity and technological disruption remain meaningful risks. Supply is constrained, backlogs extend beyond 2027, and physical bottlenecks remain.

Mind the middle: facilitators could see monetisation firstThe market frames AI as a two-horse race between enablers, which build infrastructure, and adopters, which put it to use. That misses the middle layer. Facilitators, comprising the IT services and software firms that turn AI capacity into enterprise workflows, are structurally positioned to monetise earlier and face a much lower bar of expectations. While AI is simultaneously a revenue opportunity and a structural headwind (which translate into dispersion and limited optimism in aggregate), the transition to consumption-based pricing, the acceleration of agentic AI adoption, and the structural role of IT services as implementation partners point to a monetisation inflection that is closer and less priced in than that in the infrastructure layer.backlogs extend beyond 2027, and physical bottlenecks remain.

The challenger from the other bloc: China sits outside most portfolios, but inside the returns debateWeaponised economic policy has split the AI supply chain into two blocs: a US-led network under the Pax Silica umbrella, and a Chinese ecosystem pushing for self-sufficiency as Washington restricts access to advanced compute. Chinese AI names have only a small weight in global portfolios, but their influence on the AI trade is far from marginal. Open-weight models compress frontier pricing power, parts of the stack are commoditising, and efficiency gains achieved under compute scarcity question the capex intensity the US build-out assumes. Of all the risks, this is the one that challenges the returns thesis itself, not just its timing.China is not simply a challenger to US AI leadership; it offers a different economic model for AI deployment. Compute constraints and competitive open models will accelerate efficiency and adoption while putting pressure on monetisation across parts of the global AI value chain. Opportunities may extend beyond model developers into industrial automation and production beneficiaries.

As AI investment becomes more capital intensive, financing structures will matter as much as tech leadership. The goring involvement of debt and private capital creates new transmission channels between AI valuations, credit conditions and investment spending.

Diversifying AI risks with a greater focus on dividends and on selecting corporates with evident return of investmentAI exposure remains vulnerable to a range of risks that could affect returns before fundamentals have time to differentiate, from concentration and valuation risk to funding stress, which would first hit spending-dependent names. In addition, physical constraints such as power shortages, grid bottlenecks, packaging limits, and permitting delays could push payback further out. Policy and security risks, including export controls, tariffs, or even a major cyber incident, could also disrupt supply chains, margins, and adoption.As AI investment shifts from capacity expansion to return generation, portfolio construction should place greater emphasis on cash flow visibility, capital discipline, valuations and sustainability of profits in semiconductors.Dividend income and attractive valuations can provide complementary returns, particularly if market leadership broadens beyond the capital-intensive segments of the AI trade. This can help dampen volatility and provide a steadier return stream, including in a sticky inflation environment, while also diversifying sector exposure.

Key Investment Implications

Selective exposure, taking into account physical bottlenecks, power equipment, grid infrastructure, and selected semiconductor supply-chain names.

Emerging opportunities in AI facilitators that show monetisation and attractive valuations.

Broadening potential into industrial automation and productivity beneficiaries across Europe, Japan, and China.

Caution on spending-dependent infrastructure businesses and highly leveraged operators.

Portfolio diversification through quality cash flow, sustainable dividends, and selective equity exposure.

Explore the 2027 Outlook

Our 2027 outlook, “The Price of Power”, focuses on the costs and trade-offs of a macro regime shaped by five powerful forces and what they mean for investors.Go to Investment Outlook 2027 →

articles.title: A policy roadmap for better retirement outcomes
articles.text:
Expert insight

A policy roadmap for better retirement outcomes

November 18, 2026

As Congress begins to consider the next generation of retirement savings legislation, Vanguard is advocating for policy changes that could help millions of Americans build greater financial security. Drawing on extensive client, industry, academic, and government data, Vanguard researchers have identified key friction points in the U.S. private retirement system—from gaps in automatic enrollment coverage, to challenges when workers change jobs, to the complexity faced by retirees who need to convert accumulated savings to dependable income.

In this Q&A, Fiona Greig, global head of Policy and Research, and Ben Barasky, head of U.S. Advocacy, discuss what the data reveal about where the retirement system falls short and how policy solutions could create better outcomes for investors.

The retirement system works well for those who have access to it, but Vanguard’s new policy paper, Six Big Ideas for Improving U.S. Retirement Outcomes, shows that significant gaps remain. Fiona, what part of the research surprised you the most?

Greig: I was struck by how many people still aren’t in employer plans with automatic enrollment. It’s a major focus at Vanguard—61% of the plans we administer automatically enroll their participants. Nationally, that figure is only 42%.1 Another 16.6 million workers could benefit from automatic enrollment, so the opportunity is significant.
I was also surprised by the cumulative impact of what I’d call “fine print” in plan design. Many people switch jobs every year, and when you add up all the little frictions—low default saving rates, lack of immediate eligibility, vesting requirements—there are just so many ways people’s savings journeys lose momentum with every job change. We knew the fine print mattered, but the magnitude of how many people were affected is striking.

What are the prospects for legislative action, Ben?

Barasky: Retirement savings policy remains one of the last bastions of bipartisan agreement in Washington, D.C. We saw it with the SECURE Act and SECURE 2.0 Act, and we’re optimistic that will continue. That said, congressional attention is spread across many priorities. It’s somewhat peculiar that the first SECURE acts passed just three years apart. Before that, you’d have to go back to the Pension Protection Act in 2006 for the last truly meaningful bill. We think Congress will start working on SECURE 3.0 in earnest, but it could be a few years before something moves from introduction to enactment.

Individual retirement accounts hold more assets than workplace plans, and many IRA investors are stuck in cash. Why does that matter?

Greig: We have these two vehicles for retirement savings—defined contribution plans and IRAs—and we’ve designed all these automatic features in DC plans that help get people into default investment alternatives. There’s no reason we shouldn’t be able to automatically invest contributions and rollovers into IRAs as well.
What’s surprising is seeing so much cash in accounts dedicated for retirement, especially among those with lower balances and younger investors. These are the people with the longest investment horizons who ought to be thinking about higher equity allocations. We believe that qualified default investments could help young people save almost $60,000 more by retirement age by avoiding cash drag.

Some of Vanguard’s retirement proposals build on existing policies while others introduce new concepts. How does that affect the path to enactment?

Barasky: This body of research spans both wholly new ideas and areas where we’re building upon existing policy that works. It can be easier to enact something when an idea is already on the books and you’re just adjusting the dial.
For example, automatic enrollment isn’t new—SECURE 2.0 required it for new plans, and Vanguard’s data shows its immense impact versus voluntary enrollment. Applying that to all plans will benefit a broad range of people. That’s building on proven policy.
Ideas like a retirement income paycheck or bringing default investments to IRAs are newer concepts. We’ll need to help policymakers and investors understand why we’re advocating for these changes and how they’ll help people. That’s why we quantify the impact on an individual investor basis and share the background on why these policies would help them.

The research highlights retirement income as another opportunity area. Fiona, can you explain the tax benefits of a retirement paycheck approach?

Greig: Sure. Many retirees rely on Social Security for five to 10 years before IRS rules require them to start taking minimum distributions from their IRAs and employer-sponsored retirement plans at 73. Required minimum distributions are generally taxable, and they can bump people into higher tax brackets.
The lifetime tax obligations are lower if you smooth income across all those years, taking some distributions from retirement accounts in your 60s and early 70s, before they become required. That approach limits the income step-up when RMDs begin. It also aligns better with spending patterns. National survey data shows that early retirees spend a lot in the so-called go-go years, but then spending naturally declines in later retirement as people’s capacity to spend decreases. The current behavior pattern loads spending at the wrong phase of retirement.

Ben, this is an ambitious set of proposals, which you and your advocacy team now have to “sell.” How does Vanguard’s approach to policy advocacy differ from that of other firms in the industry?

Barasky: Vanguard’s mission is to take a stand for all investors, to treat them fairly, and to give them the best chance for investment success. Our policy advocacy is one way we take a stand. We use the power of our data to demonstrate how policies like automatic enrollment for all plans could benefit savers over their lifetime. And we do it on a nonpartisan basis, reflective of our 50 million individual investors.
There may be providers who have concerns about the cost of these ideas or what they might mean to their business model and fee structures. The through line in our advocacy work is not how a policy affects Vanguard, but how it affects the end investor. That’s the privilege of our mission.

Editor’s note: Taken together, Vanguard’s six ideas offer policymakers a path to strengthen the retirement system across the full retirement journey. Explore the full paper with our recommendations and research to learn more.

1 Sources: How America Saves (Vanguard, 2026), for the share of Vanguard plans with automatic enrollment; Using Large Language Models to Measure U.S. Retirement Plan Design at Scale: Methods and Evidence (2026 working paper by Taha Choukhmane, John Dedyo, Cormac O’Dea, and Lawrence D. W. Schmidt), for the national figure.

Gregory Hall

11/17/2026

Share via Email

PIMCO Accrued Interest
CBS News’ Jill Schlesinger on Advice AI Can't Replace
