GREG HALL: Hey, everybody. Welcome to another episode of Accrued Interest, PIMCO's podcast dedicated to serving financial advisors and their clients. As usual, I'm your host, Greg Hall. I run our wealth management business here in the United States. I am super excited to be joined in the studio today with one of my new favorite people. And I keep trying to call you doctor. I really…
JILL SCHLESINGER: I would love that.
GREG HALL: I understand...
JILL SCHLESINGER: I mean, I feel like it's such a letdown to my entire family that I'm the only person without a graduate degree. So, you know, I'm only an undergrad. That's it.
GREG HALL: Hey, we all disappoint our families at some point. But, you know, accrued interest is about truth. And I am not gonna give you a false accreditation. I am joined by Jill Schlesinger. Jill, you may know and probably do know, started her career as an options trader, ran, co-ran and operated in the investment function of an investment advisory firm for 14 years, and then switched and moved into media where she could broaden out the advice that she gives everyday investors. You can see her, I think, all over CBS News. Right. I mean, I think all over, basically, if you turn on CBS, you're on there talking about money.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Totally. I am the face of money and, no, I'm just kidding. Usually on the morning show, sometimes evenings.
GREG HALL: And you've got Jill on Money, which exists, I believe, as a podcast. Was on a radio show. You're on Substack under that moniker.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah.
GREG HALL: If I'm not mistaken. And then I think there's another podcast that you do.
JILL SCHLESINGER: New show.
GREG HALL: This is Money Moves.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yes. That's since I met you. That has come to fruition.
GREG HALL: Wow.
JILL SCHLESINGER: So, yeah. That just launched the end of June.
GREG HALL: And both of your shows, I think, are really special because it's not just about your views and your insights or your partner's insights on the shows, but then you have callers calling in actually with their money issues, and you get to tackle real life problems kind of in real time. Right?
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. It's very old school. It is based on the old-time calling radio, like sports radio. You know, long time listener, first time caller. And we started this as a radio show 15 years ago through CBS and CBS lent me one of the radio producers and writers to help launch the show. And then five years after that, we turned towards podcasting, and Jill on Money became a podcast. So, we had a radio show podcast.
Earlier this year, the radio show ended, and it was kind of intense. Like I was a little bit thrown, not so much because I didn't understand the financial wherewithal and the viability of radio. But, you know, I just, I love spoken word, but then CBS came to me and they said, hey, you own Jill on Money on the outside of work, and we have nothing to do with that.
Would you launch a new show for us? That would be a YouTube show. And that was Money Moves. And, you know, it was tough because Jill on Money has a very loyal audience, but it tends to be kind of a different demo. They said, do something really different.
So I pitched them the idea that I wanted to be kind of like Aunt Jill to the 25- to 45-year-olds who had money questions and do it on YouTube and, you know, basically make it a little bit more of a robust show in terms of the pacing of it and some other features.
And so, yeah. We've been on the air since I think June 30th was our launch date. And it's been fun. It's really, it's a new skill for me to really move that show along and not wanna do an actual financial plan in real time for people.
GREG HALL: Yeah. Well, I mean, I've caught a few episodes and you talk about the difficulty of attaining a mortgage in a rate environment, like what we're seeing with housing prices, where they are, you talk about what to do about the AI slowdown, people call in and you get some good banter going with a, wait a minute. You know, how long have you been married, and, you know, like it's a really nice concept. We should think about it for accrued interest, but I think the questions might be a little too difficult.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. Well, I mean, I am not afraid to say that. I don't know. Something that, I mean, I think that one of the nice things is after doing this for so long, that if someone comes on the air and asks me something, and I really don't know, I'm like, you know, I don't know, but let me find out for you.
And we do always get back in touch with them. You know, someone asked a really weird question about like, what about if I'm a US citizen, but then I end up retiring abroad and I get paid this much, and what's the tax implication? I'm like, I’m not a CPA and we have a treaty with the UK I think it's all right, but like, someone knows this. I don't know this.
GREG HALL: Okay. Well, I teased your bio a little bit on the way in and you and I had the opportunity to have a conversation like this one back in June when PIMCO for Pride Month asked you to come and maybe talk to a bunch of our folks. And that was the first time you and I had met, and …
JILL SCHLESINGER: It was a great first date.
GREG HALL: It was so fun.
JILL SCHLESINGER: I mean, it was like, there were a lot of people who were on the date with us, but it was awesome.
GREG HALL: It was, yes. It was a weirdly public first date. But we ended up having this rolling rollicking conversation. And my favorite part of it was actually you kind of talking about your journey to where you are today. So, can you take us back to the options exchange, you know, the floor in the eighties?
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yes.
GREG HALL: How you found yourself there. And then maybe walk us through kind of how you got to where you are today.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Sure. I'll try to do this efficiently because you know, it's a weird story. First of all, I am not of the current, you know, younger generation that has, you know, sort of planned out my career. My career has taken twists and turns, and often it has just been random how I've taken one job versus another.
And I think that's sort of the luxury of graduating into a bull market is that you're like, oh, let me try this. But my dad was a trader on the floor of the American Stock Exchange. His best friend was a specialist on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. So, my summer jobs as growing up in the suburbs of New York, I was a clerk. And these were physical exchanges where you did things like order that was complete, a paper order.
You put the paper orders down on you, you sort of saw the big post on the exchange, and in the back, there was a copying machine, and you made copies of the orders, you put it into a tube, the tube went shooting off. And both sides were apprised of what happened. So that's kind of like my roots. I got to college. I got very excited about broadcasting.
And I was an intern at the local NBC affiliate, and I was like the sports intern. I played sports in college, and I was fun. I thought I was gonna do that. And the summer after my junior year, I had half the summer where I was clerking for my dad's firm. And the other half of the summer is working for a communications company. Communications company paid you gave you 15 subway tokens, and that was your pay, basically. And when, you know, it was…
GREG HALL: That's not bad.
JILL SCHLESINGER: It was awesome. You know, it was, I think it was 85 cents a ride. And maybe you got a lunch every now and again. And listen, I was a clerk during a bull market. There was a frenzy. Everyone was making money. At the end of the summer, I got a $5,000 bonus out of nowhere. Because the firm was making so much money. And my father's like, don't give Jill a bonus. And his partners were like, we're not doing that. We don't like exclude her just because she's your daughter.
GREG HALL: It's great to work for your dad, isn't it?
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. Don't give her that. She doesn't need that.
GREG HALL: The toughest job of my life. You know, by far working for my dad.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. So, when I came out of school out of college, I went to work on the floor of the commodities exchange for a company that no longer exists called Spear Leads in Kellogg. It was subsequently absorbed or bought out by Goldman Sachs. And they said, they were a clearing firm. And so, they saw the activity on all the major exchanges, and they saw on the commodities exchange were people making a lot of money.
And it is a little bit of the Wild West, if anyone who's listening, who sort of understands that commodities exchange is open outcry, whereas these other floors or have specialists. But it was regulated loosely. But there was something called dual trading. You could act as a broker and you could also trade for yourself on the same day.
That is not allowed on other exchanges. So, there was a lot of money being made. So, Spear said, let's go hire some young kids and throw them on the floor and we'll put some money in the account. So, we got hired as intern as clerks first 15 grand was the salary. As soon as you went on your seat, as soon as you started to trade, you went up to 30, and then you got a bonus. And that was it. And it was a brutal place to learn anything.
It was, you know, I thought I understood how a trading floor works. When we're, it didn't work like that on the commodities exchange. There we were also walking onto an exchange where there were a lot of people who paid dues, and we paid like zero dues, but had, you know, badges. So, we had our own trading badge. We, someone bought a seat for us on the commodities exchange.
GREG HALL: Were you the first generation? Okay, so this was a new program.
JILL SCHLESINGER: New thing
GREG HALL: And who are these kids who've just shown up with these?
JILL SCHLESINGER: It was tough. The pace of everything that was happening was like this transformation of a very active market that hadn't been transformed electronically yet. And so, a lot of what we did was by hand. And, but we were coming into using technology to help us, and we would have printed out trading sheets that would show fair values of options.
And, you know, I am a little bit of a math nerd, so I did like that. They threw me in the gold options ring and the silver. So, I traded gold, silver, and copper options. And, you know, it was great. And then after one month of trading, the crash of 1987 occurred. And it was insane. And gold was going limit up then limit down. And there was like a lot going on. And my father's firm was like, going broke because they got caught long and all these things were happening.
And at the end of the day, it was like pretty, it was like we got quite the six of us who got hired. We got an amazing experience. After six months, there were three left, and after 12 months, there was one left.
GREG HALL: Was that because they were pushed out because the firm had become less profitable or did people opt out for their own sanity?
JILL SCHLESINGER: Three people opted out. And at the end of the first year, I left because I got a nice bonus and I just said, what do I need to trade for them for? I'll trade for myself. And so, I bought my own seat and then traded for another few years on my own.
GREG HALL: Pretty gutsy for somebody in their early twenties.
JILL SCHLESINGER: I had so little to lose, I had very little to lose. You know, it's like, you know, you could open an account with a hundred grand in it and be like, okay. And so, I got a good bonus. It was fun. I kept trading, you know, it was like a vicious place. 8 women, 800 men.
There’s no room for like emotions and you win over trust, and there's all these things that are happening on the floor. At the end of the day, I actually realized that the thing that I thought was so awesome about trading, which was that it was like a sport became kind of boring to me. And I, what I learned was that, well, you know, it's a weird thing. All you're doing is making money. Like in a great day, you're making money.
And on a bad day, you're losing money. But there's like, there's nothing else. And I, maybe I didn't like making money, or maybe I didn't make, I wasn't good enough to be making so much money. So, there was a month, like in the summer, and my dad was over at my apartment.
We were meeting my mom and my sister for dinner, and he was looking at my trading sheets, and he's like, oh my God, you're such a great July. And I'm like, yeah. And then there was like a pause and he just looked at me. He goes, honey, this is it. Like this is all there is.
GREG HALL: Yeah. If you're not excited about this, then the job doesn't hold anything else for you. And is that because it just wasn't activating kind of other, you'd mentioned you were already interested in broadcasting. It was, it just not?
JILL SCHLESINGER: I wish I could tell you that I would. It just, I didn't know what it was, but it wasn't providing me with that sense of real satisfaction. And you know, I'm highly competitive, but, you know, it wasn't like you're all on the same team. Even if you worked for a firm, you were really your own person, you know, and you're out there and you're trading and you have friends and you help friends out who blow out and you do those things.
But it was not doing it for me. My dad said to me very clearly was, if you can't get excited in a month like this, you know, there are gonna be a lot of bad months ahead of you. And also, like, it's a job that he went, he went into this thing trading, and his father thought it was like beneath them.
He thought my grandfather was very disappointed that my father went to Wall Street. He thought that was very anti-intellectual choice. And, you know, don't you wanna be a lawyer or go into corporate finance and like do something a little bit more elitist? And my dad was a rebel, and he's like, no, I wanna do this. And also, I get home by four o'clock to watch every one of Kim and Jill's activities and do whatever I want.
And my dad basically said to me, it was huge for him to have a job where he could be done. When I was little, the hours of the New York Stock Exchange were 10 to 2. My father was home sometimes before I got home from school. And then the hours went from 10 to 2 to 10 to 3 to 10 to 4. 9.30 to 4, 9.30 to 4, the options goes. But my dad did not miss one game of my high school soccer career in four years.
GREG HALL: I'm sensing the beginnings of a through line here, given how much of your time today you spend helping people balance their personal, their career, their financial ambitions. It seems like you lived that almost in extremes, right? At this time period, because it might've been 10 to 2, but that was a wild 10 to 2. That you all lived at the time.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. And I think that when I really got down to it, you know, I was a young 20 something in New York City, and the thing that was the most meaningful time every single week, I volunteered at Sloan Kettering, the cancer hospital. And I was in the pediatric cancer unit and I was like, wow, this one hour a week is the best hour of my week. And I mean, I'm not so altruistic, I'm not gonna be a doctor, unfortunately. But there was something very satisfying.
And that was what was missing. And I think that that's, so that was a long part of my early story, which is then I ended up going back up to Providence, Rhode Island, because even though I celebrated Pride Month with you, there was a man involved. And so, I was dating somebody who was in medical school at Brown.
And I went up to Providence. I didn't really know what to do. And I had, you know, I bounced around a little bit. And then I met a guy who had a small financial planning firm. And, you know, honestly, I didn't know anything about retail investing.
When I told my father, my mom didn’t know anything about this. And by the way, my mother, nice Jewish lady in the suburbs was like, when I moved back to Providence, she was like, as if I moved to the moon. And what do you mean you're moving outta New York? Why would you do that? It's okay for college, but why would you do that now? And I'm like, I'm okay.
GREG HALL: That prejudice is alive and well in New York City today.
JILL SCHLESINGER: It's crazy.
GREG HALL: It hasn't gone away.
JILL SCHLESINGER: So, I went back up to New England and I joined this guy who had a financial planning firm because he said, just come spend a few days with me in the office and you'll see what I do. And he was really early. It's like the mid-nineties. He's doing financial plans. He was a certified financial planner. By the way he was using some PIMCO bond funds. Just wanna say.
GREG HALL: Well, we'd appreciate his support.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Shout-out to PIMCO bond funds. And by the way, also, we were using early on, you know, we were using some of the universal life policies. Because the tax world was so different. Right because capital gains were the exact same rate as ordinary income. So, it was a whole different ball game. So, I learned how to do it. I liked it a lot.
I really did. So, I went and worked for this in this teeny tiny company. And we ended up at the end of a year, he said to me, you know, you kind of act like an owner you wanna buy in part of the business. And I'm like, all right, how much? And I wrote a check and I did it. And I'm like a reluctant business owner. I didn't love it. We did it for 14 years.
We grew the firm because we hosted a call and radio show, and that was the beginning of my broadcasting. And when I was in Rhode Island is the size of, you know, like a peanut in terms of a community. And it was very open and warm community. So, we hosted a radio show. The guy who hosted the Today Show lead in on television called me up one day and said, hey, you know, I'd love it if you came on TV. Ever think about TV.
I said, funny thing, I used to be an intern at your TV station years ago. So, things go full circle. I started doing TV there. And throughout my 14 years when I was running this company, I was the Chief Investment Officer. And really, you know, like, honestly, we went through a lot of different eras where, you know, it was like commission base because that's what you did.
And then we went to fee-based because that's what you did. And then we went from, you know, instead of doing active, we did more passive funds. So, we did evolve quite a bit as the times changed. And it was great. And at the end of the day, we had sold the company a few years earlier. And then, you know, I sort of was facing this idea of like sticking around as an earn out and do that. And then, you know, I was just kind of done with Rhode Island, so my mother may have been right which I don't. I hope she's not listening.
GREG HALL: You said you gave it a good amount of time. It's run great state.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Great state, great food.
GREG HALL: It held your attention for a nice long time.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. And it was a good place to grow a company. That's really what I can say. That it was just like very — it's almost like it's so small that everybody has to work with everybody. And so, you know, and the few that don't, you just don't work with them. And so, what ended up happening was that I started going back and forth to New York, where I am from.
And I was doing some media in New York in the 2000s because someone in Rhode Island knew about that I was from New York, and that I was dating someone in New York now. And I was going back and forth, and they said, oh, I'm gonna send your stuff to a friend of mine at Fox, and, you know, let's go. And so, I was able to go on Neil Cavuto's show and Shep Smith's show, and when they launched Fox Business, they wanted me to go on.
So, I went on and I did that. And then someone from CNN saw it. And so I went on CNN, and then in 2007, is that right? Is that where the Bear Stearns funds blew out?
GREG HALL: The hedge funds Yeah.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah, so they blew out in 2007. I was on the air and on either CNN or Fox, I can't remember. Someone from CBS called me and said, “Hey, I know this is weird, but I could have sworn, I heard your voice when I was driving with my family to Cape Cod.
And, but then I see you on TV, like, where are you?” I'm like, “Well, I'm based in Rhode Island, but I come to New York a lot. Are you exclusive to those places?” “No.” And this guy said to me, like, “I'm the producer who does all the business content. You talk like a normal person, not like a weird wonky dude.”

And I say, why are you coming onto a podcast and asking me?
GREG HALL: Right.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Okay. Because sometimes I think advisors believe they have a stronger relationship with a client than they do.
GREG HALL: Or maybe an exclusive relationship.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. Your colleague.
GREG HALL: Which is not…
JILL SCHLESINGER: You're not in a monogamous relationship there.
GREG HALL: Yeah.
JILL SCHLESINGER: We're all in it. We're like a throuple. And I don't say that to be like they're —I getting them, but I will say, what did your advisor say? I would say, my advisor said this. Well, what's going on? I got a funny feeling. Well, did you talk to your advisor about it? Well, I don't want it to be insulted.
GREG HALL: Yeah.
JILL SCHLESINGER: I think that one of the big problems that advisors have is that, you know, you're really busy. You're doing a ton of things. Take a moment and look at your client and say, how are you feeling about this? People don't love feeling. I'm living in feeling world. Okay. And I noticed that my own doctor who was like previously an overburdened doctor now is concierge doctor.
And I told her like, you're really bad at this concierge part of it which is like, you wanna have conversation, but you're also like, let me get to the bottom of this right now. And it's just taking a breath and like, how do you feel about this?
GREG HALL: Yeah.
JILL SCHLESINGER: And if you ask that question, they'll tell you, give them permission to say that. And especially if you are an advisor and you're working with a couple and you're really like, you talk to the woman, not to the husband, or you talk to the husband and not to the woman. Go meet with the person, the uninvolved spouse, meet with that person without the involved spouse there go like, have a relationship. Do you wanna hold onto the relationship when someone dies? Have a relationship with both?
GREG HALL: Yeah. Yeah. That's really interesting. You can't escape emotion. We're all human. And one of the things that we've embraced here, and we tend at PIMCO to be a very, you know, hyper articulation, right? We, we talk, we debate. We're very specific about, you know, words have meanings and we use the right word for the right.
But that feeling, which you can't articulate, that you can't quite express in the room, is a debate. It has informational content for you and just because you can't quite set out what it means doesn't invalidate it. Right. And that's, it's a really good point of advice.
JILL SCHLESINGER: And it is one of the downsides to having relationships that are two dimensional. Like you're having Zoom meetings rather being in a room. And looking at someone's eyes and having, you know, to some extent understanding what are the cues, you know, when you're doing this a long time and you've been a manager for a very long time. So, you know this where some, you say to one of your folks and you say, well, what's going on? I'm fine. You like that? Not fine.
GREG HALL: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Not fine. Like, you can scratch a little bit beneath the surface.
GREG HALL: I’m trying to being a parent, you know, like how is school? Fun.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah, exactly. And I think that sometimes these relationships, we wanna— you know, I have another friend who's a surgeon and I made some comment to her like…
GREG HALL: You got some really qualified friends.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yeah. I'm the bottom of the barrel. And, I remember when she was like, we were talking about surgery and I was like, I don't know, like I'm in a young advisor and she's doing her surgical residency at NYU and she's like, people just don't do the things that you'd want them to do.
And she said, yeah, of course. She's like, every day I tell people not to drink, not to smoke, not to, but she's like, they just can't get out of their own way. And like, just have some grace. It's okay. And I said, well, you know, no one's convinced. She basically was like, no one's convinced by the science. And she said, you know, even when you think about like being a doctor, she said, everyone thinks it's all science.
JILL SCHLESINGER: She goes, I'm a surgeon. It should be like technical. Right. She's like, it's really, it's half science and it's half art. And she goes, if I get the science right part then I only have half a chance to screw it up. And I kind of feel that way with advising. Like, we fall back on models and we fall back on performance and doing the plan. And it's all like, that is the science, the math part.
You have half a chance to screw it up if you don't understand the art of the human being in front of you. And that's the goal. Like, you did not become a financial advisor and you would've been sitting in a room, you know, running numbers and working someplace on one, you know, in a different part of this industry.
If that's what really motivated you. You like people, I mean they're a pain in the ass sometimes. I get it. Client business is really hard. But lean into that part because that's the part that AI can't touch and that's the part that many people don't want to go near.
GREG HALL: Alright. That is the perfect note to end on.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Done.
GREG HALL: You have successfully defended the financial advice industry from the onslaught of AI.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yes.
GREG HALL: You heard it here on accrued interest. Everything's fine. The robots aren't coming for us.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Not today.
GREG HALL: Not today. Dr. Jill.
JILL SCHLESINGER: Yes mam.
GREG HALL: Thank you so much for being with us. This was just a wonderful journey through your life, through your experiences getting all of, well, I don't wanna say all of because we're gonna have you back.
JILL SCHLESINGER: That’s fabulous. And I'll have you on my podcast.
GREG HALL: Oh, well. You may have a few more listener than the little old fixed income podcast here.
JILL SCHLESINGER: There you go.
GREG HALL: But thank you everybody for listening today. We're really glad you could join us. We so hope that you'll go check out everything that Jill does on her own and with CBS and we'll include links in the show notes to whatever we can. Check out her books. Listen for me on her podcast, when that happens. Anything that we talked about from a market perspective or a fixed income perspective that you found interesting, please do visit pimco.com here in the US or our local site.
If you happen to be listening in another country, if you identify yourself as a financial advisor, you'll be taken to Advisor Forum. That's our one stop shop for you to get what you need from PIMCO to get a great digest on what's going on in markets on the way to or in between your client meetings where you're doing exactly what Jill hopes you will do, which is embrace the human connection that you've worked so hard to create with them and to give them good advice. We will be back with you soon. And until then, good luck in the markets.

From This Episode

Through all of it, Jill has helped everyday investors make sense of their money in all types of markets. Her prescription for advisors: lean into the thing no algorithm can do. That means understanding how clients really feel, keeping them disciplined when markets run hot, and building a plan that changes with their lives, not the headlines.
Show notes:
(5:20) From the options floor to CBS: Jill's career
(21:35) Then vs. now: fear, greed and today's markets

articles.title: Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code
articles.text:
Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code

The Bank of England chairs the Money Markets Committee, which has endorsed the voluntary UK Money Markets Code setting out best practice for participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets.

In this section

Fair and Effective Markets
Foreign currency reserves
Market intelligence
Bank of England Market Operations Guide
Settlement and collateral management
SONIA interest rate benchmark
Transition from LIBOR to risk-free rates

On this pageMoney Markets CommitteeUK Money Markets Code CommitteeSecurities Lending CommitteeMoney Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo CommitteeUK Money Markets Code

Money Markets Committee
The Money Markets Committee (MMC) is a senior-level forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to discuss issues concerning the UK unsecured deposits and funding market, the securities lending market and the repo market.
The MMC is chaired by the Bank of England.
The committee meets quarterly and also has two permanent sub-committees: the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee and the Securities Lending Committee.
Objectives of the Money Markets Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK money, repo and securities lending markets.
Where appropriate, to propose responses to any issues identified.
To aid understanding and enhance monitoring of the functioning of the UK money markets.
To endorse and facilitate continuing market-wide adoption of the UK Money Markets Code, a voluntary code of good practice for the money and securities financing markets.
To identify and address any high-level issues concerning contingency planning in the UK money markets and payment systems, having regard to international developments.

Increasing diversity in our committees
The UK Money Markets Code includes an expectation that market participants will promote the development of a diverse and inclusive within their money market teams. This includes working to create a diverse pipeline of potential future Committee members.
We also aim for diversity within the Money Markets Committee and its Sub-committees, in order that they can best represent the people of the United Kingdom. Diverse membership means that these Committees benefit from diversity of thought, which bring different viewpoints and help to ensure well-informed decision-making.
We work with members from the Money Markets Committee to diversify its membership. As part of this, we provide opportunities for members to bring observers to Committee meetings, in order that these observers can gain a better understanding of the Committee, and to help identify potential future diverse candidates.
You can find out more about ‘Meeting Varied People’ – our initiative to increase the diversity of the market contacts that we engage with – on the Market intelligence page.

UK Money Markets Code Committee
The project to update and revise the former codes for non-foreign exchange market products in the UK market led by a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee is a permanent sub-committee of the MMC, and is co-chaired by, and made up of, senior market participants. The sub-committee meets regularly to ensure that the code remains relevant and up to date as markets evolve.

Terms of reference for the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee
UK Money Markets Code Committee current membership list (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

UK Money Markets Code Committee minutes

Letter to Signatories of Statement of Commitment to UK Money Markets Code (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

Securities Lending Committee
The Securities Lending Committee (SLC) is a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The SLC is chaired by a market participant. It is a forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to meet to discuss issues concerning the UK securities lending market, including all collateral activities.
Objectives of the Securities Lending Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK securities lending market.
To discuss legal, regulatory, trading, settlement, infrastructure, tax, disclosure and other related developments in this market.
Where appropriate, it will propose responses to these issues.
To aid the understanding and enhance the monitoring of the functioning of this market.

Working Group on Settlement Efficiency
The Bank of England Securities Lending Committee has established a Working Group to examine the issue of settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. It provides a senior-level forum for market participants to meet to identify root causes for settlement issues in the UK securities lending market and suggest best practices.
The Working Group will examine drivers and impact of fails and determine potential solutions to settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. Part of this work will be to advocate best practice in the securities lending market.
Membership of the group will reflect a diverse group of market participants with relevant expertise, perspective and knowledge. It is chaired by Tim McLeod (Blackrock, Inc.). The Bank of England will participate as Ex-Officio members and provide administrative support.
Please note that views and outputs of the Working Group do not constitute guidance or legal advice from, and are not necessarily endorsed by, the Bank of England (including the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)).

Money Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo Committee
The Money Markets Committee was formed in March 2017 to replace previous markets committees, the Money Markets Liaison Committee (MMLC) and Securities Lending and Repo Committee (SLRC).
Please see the National Archives for historic MMLC and SLRC minutes.
The National Archives Opens in a new window
UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code is a voluntary code written by market participants. It incorporates revised relevant sections of the Non-Investment Products (NIPs) Code, and also a revision and update of the Gilt Repo Code and Securities Borrowing and Lending Code.
The UK Money Markets Code was published on 26 April 2017.

The UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code: explanatory notes

Voluntary codes of best practice can help to establish the basis on which financial markets function, ensuring trust between participants. This in turn creates an environment so that a fair, effective and transparent market can flourish and in which, by adhering to such codes, high standards of behaviour can be assured.
The code sets out such standards and the best practice expected from participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets in the UK. It supersedes previous guidance for participants in these markets provided by the NIPs Code, the Gilt Repo Code and the Securities Borrowing and Lending Code. By bringing these together it will more clearly establish the framework for transacting in UK money markets. The code is endorsed by the Money Markets Committee and will be updated regularly.
The Money Markets Committee has also established a Public Register of Institutions who have signed a Statement of Commitment or a Statement of Support to the Code. The purpose of the Register is to further restore trust in financial markets by making it easier to see which institutions have taken the important step of committing to the principles set out in the Code.
UK Money Markets Code: Public Register
The UK Money Markets Code Committee and the Association of Corporate Treasurers have produced this guide to promote and encourage wider adherence to the Code among the Corporate sector.

The UK Money Markets Code, along with the FX Global Code and the Global Precious Metals Code, replaces the Non-Investment Products Code.

articles.title: Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin
articles.text:
Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin

Speech to be given at DAMA Data and AI Conference Europe 2026

Published on
04 November 2026

In this speech Ben Martin explores how the Bank is transforming its use of data, analytics and AI. From building stronger data foundations to safely adopting new AI capabilities, he explains how the Bank is enabling, equipping and empowering colleagues to make the most of these tools.

Speech
Good morning. It is a great pleasure to be here today at the DAMA Data & AI Conference. This event is about sharing practical experience of building trusted, responsible and effective data and AI capabilities, so I thought it would be a good opportunity to share some of the work we are doing on this at the Bank of England.
In recent years, my colleagues at the Bank have spoken publicly about the implications of AI on the wider economyfootnote [1] footnote [2]. Today, I want to talk about this from a slightly different perspective: what data and analytics transformation means for the Bank of England itself, as an organisation.
But first, let me introduce myself: my name is Ben Martin and I am the Bank’s Chief Data Officer. I took up this role just under a year ago, following a career across the Bank’s economics, markets and supervision areas. This experience gave me a deep understanding of the Bank’s data needs. Taking on the CDO role has allowed me to bring those perspectives together at an enterprise level. It has been encouraging to see how much progress we have made – and continue to make – in improving our data, analytics and AI capabilities. Even though we are making good progress, this is by no means job done. The pace of change in this field is rapid, and our ambitions need to keep pace with it. So today, I want to reflect on the journey we have been on, where we are now, and some of the opportunities and challenges that lie ahead.
Our mission at the Bank of England is to promote the good of the people of the United Kingdom, by maintaining monetary and financial stability. Across our offices in London and Leeds, our people are working to deliver that mission. Central to this is our ability to make the best possible decisions using the most effective data and analytics to achieve our public policy objectives. Data and analytics are integral to our work. They support our understanding of the economy, our supervision of the financial firms within it, and the operations through which we fulfil our responsibilities.
A couple of years ago, we published our Data & Analytics Strategyfootnote [3]. Our overarching aim is to make the best use of data and analytics to fulfil the Bank’s mission. Our ambitions are summarised by three missions.

First, making it easy for people in the Bank to work with and analyse data.
Second, bridging data gaps to increase the value of what we collect and share.
Third, enabling safe and effective innovation, including artificial intelligence.

Those missions rest on two foundations: a modern enterprise data platform on the cloud; and investment in business change, skills and culture to embed this.
That combination is important. We are not simply replacing systems. We are seeking to change how people find and use data, how they collaborate on it with each other, and how they develop new analytical tools and techniques to gain the best insights to make good decisions.
Today I want to focus on how we are enabling, equipping and empowering our organisation to deliver this strategy. Let me give a quick overview before we dive into each in more detail later on.
First, what do I mean by enablement? This covers the work we are doing to build solid foundations by providing transformed systems and high-quality data for our colleagues.
Second, we are equipping our colleagues with new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails and associated training, so they can safely achieve new insights.
Last, but by no means least, I will cover empowerment – our approach to supporting colleagues to make the most of the investment we have made and to have the confidence to explore these new tools.
I am a big fan of the television programme Grand Designs, watching people use exciting, modern solutions in an innovative way to build something truly special – not just special on paper or to look at, but special for the people who live there. I sometimes think about our strategy in the same way. We are using modern techniques and the latest thinking on how to use data, but not as an end in itself or to wow anyone. Instead, the point is to deliver the Bank’s mission effectively and to make sure our colleagues can flourish. We are enabling colleagues by putting the foundations in place, equipping them with new capabilities to continue building on those foundations and empowering them to make the most of those new capabilities. Thankfully, the one thing we don’t have is Kevin McCloud turning up every few months to see how we’re getting on!
I will say a bit more about the work we are doing on these three Es – enable, equip and empower – at the Bank of England.
Enable – by building solid foundations
As I have said, we are building solid foundations, so we can enable our colleagues by providing effective systems and high-quality data as the bedrock of good analysis. At the Bank, we are part way through a multi-year investment programme to build solid data foundations. This includes investing in new systems and technology, but also continuing to invest in the ‘bread and butter’ of good data management: quality, governance and trust. AI may be grabbing the headlines, but AI runs on data. This audience knows well enough that without high-quality, well-governed and trusted data, even the most sophisticated AI will struggle to deliver. So I will share some reflections on how we are bringing together the new systems and the good old basics to ensure solid foundations.
New systems
At the foundation of our Data & Analytics Strategy is a new Enterprise Data Platform, or EDP. This is our central, cloud-based data and analytics ecosystem. It will bring together a wide range of data needed across the Bank’s responsibilities, including macroeconomic and financial market data we bring in from partners, and the regulatory and statistical returns we collect directly from the financial sector. But the EDP is about much more than storing data. It provides a structured and governed way of bringing data into the Bank, and transforming it into trusted, reusable data that can be readily used for analysis. Alongside this, the EDP provides modern analytical tools and capabilities, including access to approved AI models, helping colleagues to work with data more effectively and strengthening analysis and decision-making across the Bank.
Earlier this year, we deployed the core of the platform. We are now migrating data services and data systems onto that foundation in stages. Those new data systems are being completely transformed from the legacy systems we are retiring. Alongside this technology, we are building the operating model needed to support it. Together, the platform and its operating model are intended to help us move beyond data silos, establish a shared foundation for future data initiatives, and make greater use of cloud-native capabilities to develop new products and services.
The word ‘enterprise’ really matters here. The Bank of England brings together a number of different responsibilities within one institution, in part because of the connections and synergies between them. Our approach to data should reflect that same principle. Data collected or created for one purpose can often have value elsewhere, and insights can be richer when we are able to connect information from across the organisation. So rather than recreating a collection of separate systems, we are building shared data and analytical capabilities that can be used right across the organisation to support delivery of the Bank’s mission.
Good basics
Now, there is no point in building new systems but immediately filling them with poorly managed data. I know that data management is familiar territory for this audience. DAMA gives us a useful way of thinking about it: not as a standalone control, but as the coordinating mechanism that connects ownership, quality, metadata, architecture and use. For us, the real test is whether those disciplines show up in the everyday experience of colleagues working with data. That is why, since launching our Data & Analytics Strategy, we have focused on putting those practical data management foundations in place.
We have an organisation-wide data management policy and an ownership and stewardship framework, alongside data management learning within our wider data fluency programme.
We have numerous Data Owners and Stewards across all areas of the Bank who support over 2,000 registered data assets. These arrangements combine accountability for data with the day-to-day work needed to manage it.
These are important foundations helping us improve consistency, transparency and trust across an increasingly complex data estate. But the existence of a policy, a register, or an assigned owner, is far from being the end of the task. Our objective is that data can be found, accessed, trusted, understood and used, where data management acts as an enabler, not a barrier.
That is the practical test of data management. Does it help someone coming with fresh eyes establish what a dataset contains? Or understand whether it is appropriate for their purpose? Do they know who can answer their questions about it? And can they use it with confidence?
Like other long-established institutions, we face particular challenges in modernising our data estate. The Bank has a long history and with that comes years of accumulated data, systems and processes. Recent independent reviews by the Independent Evaluation Officefootnote [4] and Dr Ben Bernankefootnote [5] have reinforced the importance of tackling these challenges. It is clear we cannot simply build something new and expect all that complexity to disappear. Our Enterprise Data Platform is a good example – as we move datasets across, we are ensuring we look carefully at what we are bringing with us, to improve our data quality and embed those enduring data management basics from the outset. To stick with the theme of houses, this is a bit like moving house. If you live somewhere for a long time, you inevitably accumulate things along the way, which get shoved in drawers or the loft. Moving gives you the opportunity to decide what you really need, tidy things up and organise them better, rather than simply packing everything into boxes and recreating the same clutter in your new home.
Equip – by providing new capabilities
Next, we want to equip our colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
New capabilities
Much of the focus on data tooling over the past couple of years has been around the opportunities from new AI capabilities. We have been open about our approach to using AI at the Bank of England, which we outlined in our AI strategy that was published last yearfootnote [6]. To support a consistent and coherent approach to AI across the Bank, our AI strategy rests on a set of principles that set the tone for how we approach AI. Although frontier AI models and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past year, these principles are enduring. The principles are embodied in the ‘TRUSTED’ framework, which is for our AI solutions to be:

Targeted on tightly defined use cases that have a clear business purpose.
Reliable with high performance standards and grounded in high-quality data.
Understood in the context of their intended purpose.
Secure so we protect ourselves from risks such as unauthorised access.
Tested thoroughly for their technology standards and impact on behaviour.
Ethical including being beneficial and scientifically rigorous, fair and inclusive, transparent and secure, and compliant and accountable.
Durable so they remain effective despite changing conditions and usage patterns.

To bring this to life, I thought I would share some examples of how we have implemented this framework in practice. Our approach combines broad access to general purpose tools across the Bank with a more tailored applications for specific business needs.
A significant milestone has been the organisation-wide rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Nearly all colleagues at the Bank use it each week. Some colleagues also use GitHub Copilot to support code development. As colleagues have become more confident, this has extended to the creation of many custom Copilot agents over the past year, typically to improve personal productivity in day-to-day tasks or to help navigate internal services. Many began as experiments, but some are now being used more widely across the organisation. For example, our ‘AskHR’ agent provides answers to questions on leave, pay and our people policies. Another agent, called ‘AskTech’, helps with technology-related questions and can direct colleagues to further support where needed. As you can see, our approach to naming them has been slightly less experimental!
Alongside these general-purpose tools, we are also developing bespoke AI applications for important business processes.
One example is our Agency Retrieval and Insights App, known as ARIA. The Bank’s regional Agents, based in 12 agencies across the nations and regions in the UK, maintain close relationships with businesses of all sizes, providing the Monetary Policy Committee with real-time insight into economic conditions and perspectives from across the country. Those relationships and the judgements of our Agents remain at the heart of that work, but ARIA complements this by helping them make sense of this wealth of intelligence they gather, using capabilities such as theme detection and quantitative analysis to identify patterns and draw out insights. It is a good example of technology augmenting human expertise and strengthening one part of the evidence base that supports the MPC in making its policy decisions.
Another example is called GRACE, which provides retrieval-augmented AI to enable colleagues to draw deep insights from large and trusted internal knowledge repositories. But what I particularly like is that it does this through an email interface, a tool colleagues already know how to use every day. They can send off a query, get on with something else and come back to the response when it arrives. The interaction is also captured naturally in the email chain. It is a simple example of designing AI around people and the way they work, rather than the other way round. These applications address different needs. What connects them is the effort to make technology useful within the work people already do.
Effective training
The pace of technology change can be dizzying, and with new capabilities emerging all the time, it can be difficult to know where to start. That is why we need to equip colleagues not just with the access to these tools, but to also equip them with the confidence and skills to use them safely and effectively. We want to help them feel confident navigating that change and so we have maintained a focus on training which is one of the two foundations of our Data & Analytics Strategy. It focuses on business change, skills and culture, recognising that successful adoption requires practical support, as colleagues move to new services and learning that goes beyond narrow technical training.
To put this in practice, we have a dedicated data and analytics learning function. To date, I am proud to say it has delivered more than 250 courses to many colleagues across our data science and analytical toolset.
Our aim is not simply to provide more training. It is to make learning more relevant to the work people need to do. On Copilot, we began with introductory learning to establish a common baseline for everyone. Many colleagues then attended application-based deep dives. We have subsequently introduced clinics offering more personalised support for local and role-specific use cases.
That progression from training course to back at the desk matters. General awareness can help people get started. Practical support helps them move from experimenting with a tool, to using it effectively and achieving results.
But formal learning is only part of the picture. We have a thriving Data Community, with almost 2,000 members. It actively supports collaboration, sharing and peer-to-peer learning. During our ‘Data & Analytics Fortnight’ in June, over 1,000 colleagues turned out to one of our events, which included a wide range of internal and external presenters sharing their expertise. Beyond this, the community also organises regular hackathons which have turned out some brilliant solutions.
Bringing people together is incredibly important but the value of a community is not only in the events it organises. It is in the opportunities it creates as a place for people to ask questions, share experience, and learn from colleagues who have faced and overcome similar challenges.
Beyond catalysing an organic approach to building capacity, we are also developing more structured pathways for embedding data skills professionally.
We launched the Data Profession last November, bringing together colleagues from across the Bank whose work involves data into a single professional community. It covers disciplines including data science, data analytics and data governance, helping us take a more joined-up approach to the data skills we need, how we recruit and develop people, and the career pathways and support available to them.
Building our capabilities also means broadening access to opportunities. I am pleased to say that our recently established partnership with Women in Data helps this through a range of initiatives supporting our commitment to greater representation and inclusivity in the workplace.
Like our data tools and technology, our learning approach must also keep evolving. We are working to understand shifting skills requirements across different time horizons, using a role-based approach to assessing skills profiles to help us to map the work different colleagues need to do, against the skills required to do it effectively, and the most appropriate ways to support them in addressing any gaps.
So, we are equipping colleagues to safely achieve new insights by using new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails, and by providing the right training.
Empower – by supporting colleagues to innovate
Investing in equipping and enabling our people is important, but to unlock its full potential, we need to empower colleagues to try innovative new approaches in their roles. This is not just about doing what we already do more efficiently. It is also about opening up new possibilities, helping colleagues work differently and undertake types of analysis that simply were not possible before. Ultimately, it is about giving people the tools and confidence to evolve with the world around us.
Support
Like many organisations, we want to reduce the costs to trying new innovative approaches and to avoid the risks of this happening in siloes. To do so, we are bringing together a dedicated team of experts from both our data and technology functions to act as an innovation hub for the Bank as a whole. The aim is to support colleagues to understand the range of tools available to facilitate innovative work and to support them to bring insights from across different teams. The idea is not that we try to do the innovative analytical work centrally, but instead to be a centre of excellence and smooth the way for the innovative work that the various business functions of the Bank want to achieve. This includes a forum where local business and central support functions’ representatives can meet, share developments, and to prioritise work to achieve the biggest benefits.
Culture
Finally, we need a culture that gives colleagues the confidence to try something new. Sometimes trying something new feels daunting. We want colleagues to feel that innovation is part of their role – that they are empowered to question how something is done today, explore whether there might be a better way, and have a safe environment in which to test new approaches, which can be supported by the innovation hub. It gives colleagues somewhere to experiment with the right support and safeguards around them, reducing some of the barriers to trying something new. Of course, the design of this needs to be appropriate for the evolving culture of the Bank, just like a well-designed house needs to work in the place where it’s built and for the people who live there.
Senior leaders have an important role here too. We need to visibly take the lead in encouraging people across the organisation to innovate, make space for them to do it, and celebrate the examples that demonstrate what is possible. Over time, that is how we make innovation feel more like a natural part of how we work, and why we are launching in the coming months a new leadership programme focused on leading in an increasingly digital, data and AI enabled world.

Conclusion
Let me conclude by returning to the main theme of my remarks today. Data and analytics transformation is not primarily about technology for its own sake. It is about making sure the Bank of England can continue to fulfil its mission effectively in a world where the volume of data, the sophistication of analytical tools, and the pace of technological change are all increasing rapidly.
For us, that means doing three things together. First, we need to enable colleagues by putting the right foundations in place: modern platforms, well-managed data, clear ownership and the enduring disciplines of data management. Those foundations matter because high-quality analysis, effective decision-making and responsible AI all depend on trusted and accessible data.
Second, we need to equip people with new capabilities and the confidence to use them safely. That includes making general-purpose tools such as Copilot available at scale, developing more tailored applications where there are specific business needs, and applying clear guardrails through our AI framework. But it also means investing in training, communities and professional pathways, so that people can use these tools well and understand their limits.
Third, we need to empower colleagues to innovate. The opportunities from data, analytics and AI will not be realised by a central team alone. They will come from colleagues across the organisation identifying better ways to do their work, experimenting responsibly, sharing experience, and building on each other’s successes. Our role centrally is to reduce the friction, provide expertise and make it easier for good ideas to move from the drawing board to practical use.
We cannot stand still and our job is not done. At the Bank, our ambition is to build on the progress we have made and keep moving forward: enabling colleagues with trusted foundations, equipping them with safe and effective capabilities, and empowering them to innovate in support of the public good.
The technology around us will continue to evolve and expectations of what is possible will continue to rise in the era of AI. But keeping pace is not just about technology. It is also about continuing to learn from one another. The work of communities such as DAMA has a vital role to play in bringing people together, sharing practical experience as we are today, and ensuring that even as technology moves quickly, the standards underpinning our data remain strong. Thank you.
And if Kevin McCloud is in the audience, ignore what I said earlier – you're welcome to come to the Bank any time you want!

I would also like to thank, Nay Assassa, Karen Bassett, David Bradnum, Jane Cathrall, Benjamin Crampton, Elizabeth Hall, Rachel Heppinstall, Alan Hicks, Rebecca Jackson, Sarah John, Neil Kisserli, Georgios Kyriakopoulos, Leslie Lambert, Clare Lombardelli, Phillippa Loveridge, Pat O'Connor, Arshadur Rahman and Paul Robinson for their input and helpful comments.

articles.title: What Is a 401(k)? Key Facts About Saving for Retirement | BlackRock
articles.text:
What is a 401(k) plan?

A 401(k) is an employer-offered retirement account. Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-ups must be Roth. Traditional 401(k)s use pre-tax dollars; Roth 401(k)s use after-tax dollars.

Key takeaways

01

Understand the rules around eligibility and contributions
Plans may require age 21 and 1 year of service, though some allow earlier entry. In 2026, the limit is $24,500, plus $8,000 at 50+ if permitted, or $11,250 at ages 60–63. If prior-year wages exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be Roth (after-tax).

02

Know the differences between traditional and Roth 401(k)s
Traditional 401(k) plans use pre-tax dollars, while Roth 401(k) plans use after-tax dollars. Traditional plans require taxes to be paid upon withdrawal, whereas Roth plans offer tax-free withdrawals under certain conditions. Roth accounts are also not subject to required minimum distributions during your lifetime.

03

Look into your employer’s matching and vesting policies
Employers often contribute to employees' 401(k) accounts through matching contributions. The specifics of matching and vesting rules vary by employer, and employees should consider these provisions before changing jobs to avoid missing out on extra savings.

401(k) plans

What is a 401(k) plan and who is eligible?

A 401(k) plan is an investment account offered by your employer that allows you to save for retirement. If your company offers a 401(k) plan, it may have certain eligibility requirements. While these requirements vary by company, some employees may be excluded from participating if they are not at least 21 years of age or have not completed a year of service with the company.
If you’re considering a job offer, be sure to ask about the company’s retirement plan, including any waiting period.
How much can I contribute to a 401(k) plan?
401(k) plan accounts have higher contribution limits than individual retirement accounts (IRAs). For 2026, you can contribute up to $24,500 of your salary to a 401(k). This limit applies to your combined contributions across all 401(k), 403(b) and SIMPLE plans in which you participate, not to each account separately. Employer contributions don't count toward this limit.
To boost your contributions even further, you might consider catch-up contributions, if your plan offers them. If you are 50 or older, you can contribute an extra $8,000 (up to $32,500 total in 2026). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. These increased limits can help boost your savings as you near the retirement finish line. But you don't actually have to be "behind" in your savings to take advantage of catch-up contributions.
What is the difference between a traditional and Roth 401(k) plan?
Many 401(k) plans let you make traditional contributions, Roth contributions, or both. These plans have some similarities: They are subject to the same annual contribution limit and may offer the same investment options. However, traditional and Roth 401(k) plans differ in terms of the tax benefits they offer.

Traditional

Roth

Contributions

Made on a pre-tax basis

Made on an after-tax basis

Withdrawals

Subject to income tax

Tax-free after age 59 ½*

*A withdrawal is qualified if at least five taxable years have passed since your first Roth contribution to the plan, and it is made after you reach age 59½, because of disability, or to a beneficiary after your death. Source: IRS.gov. Date as of Aug 2026.
A traditional 401(k) plan is sometimes referred to as a pre-tax 401(k) plan. You contribute to the plan with before-tax dollars. Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. This structure could be an advantage if you’re in a high tax bracket today but expect to be in a lower one when retired.
With a Roth 401(k) plan, the opposite is true. You save after-tax dollars in the account. Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you’re saving, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as both of the following criteria are met:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½, because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

How does 401(k) plan matching work?
One major benefit of 401(k) plans is that employers often contribute to your account and “match” what you save. Each employer has its own methods and rules for how it makes matching 401(k) plan contributions. Importantly, a match does not necessarily mean that an employer matches your contributions dollar for dollar. Instead, employers typically match up to a certain percentage of your salary or your contribution.
If your company offers a match, be sure to consider taking advantage of this benefit. It could be a simple and effective way to boost your retirement savings.
One important note: Employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.
When can I withdraw from my 401(k) plan?
59½, although your plan's rules determine when withdrawals are available, particularly while you're still working for the employer. Taking out your savings before that age could cost you an extra 10% federal tax on top of the regular federal and state income taxes you'd normally pay, unless an exception applies (for example, if you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55).
When it's time to start using your savings, be sure to consider the tax implications. In addition, you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) from pre-tax 401(k) savings at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire. Roth 401(k) accounts are not subject to RMDs during your lifetime.
401(k) plans can be very useful tools in saving for retirement, particularly if you take advantage of features that your plan may offer to help maximize your savings. And the sooner you start saving in your 401(k) plan, the longer any investment earnings have to produce earnings of their own.

Wrap up

Top questions about 401(k)s

First, you don’t have to actually be “behind” in your savings to take advantage of this benefit. If you are 50 or older and your plan permits catch-up contributions, you can contribute an extra $8,000 to your 401(k) account in 2026 (up to $32,500 total). Participants who turn 60 through 63 during 2026 have a higher $11,250 catch-up limit (up to $35,750 total). Beginning in 2026, if your prior-year wages from your employer exceeded $150,000, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth (after-tax) basis. Catch-up contributions can help boost your savings as you near retirement.

Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. Note that you generally must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) at age 73 (age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later). If you're still working for the employer that sponsors the plan, you may be able to delay RMDs until you retire.

The money you contribute from your own paycheck is always yours. However, employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.

Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you contribute, your withdrawals are considered “qualified” distributions and won’t be taxed as long as you meet both of the following criteria:

It has been at least five years since your initial Roth contribution to the plan.
Distributions are made after age 59½ because of disability or to a beneficiary after your death.

Saving for retirement can be complicated – but it doesn’t have to be. Arm yourself with the information you need to make the best decisions for your financial future.

Keep learning

Retirement is more complex than ever. We’re helping make it easier, more accessible, and more affordable by providing education, insights and solutions, no matter where you are on your journey.
