articles.title: The AI boom’s critical next phase
articles.text:
Economics and markets

The AI boom’s critical next phase

November 19, 2026

Commentary

Regional outlooks

Commentary

Regional outlooks

In this global outlook summary, Joe Davis, our global chief economist, highlights the top-level findings of Vanguard’s full 2027 economic and market outlook to be released in December.

Key takeaways

A capital spending boom, led by AI and broadening beyond the tech giants, underpins Vanguard’s above-consensus forecast of around 3% U.S. growth in 2027, but the greater risk lies in the transition from building AI to broad adoption.

Interest rates are likely to stay above pre-pandemic levels as AI investment and government borrowing compete for a limited pool of capital.

Strong earnings should support stocks in 2027 despite higher rates, but with a narrower margin for error. Many investors may own more of the AI buildout theme than they realize, leaving portfolios exposed to a potentially bumpy transition from buildout to broad adoption.

Position for diffusion: As was the case last year, we see greater opportunity in reasonably value-oriented companies (the AI adopters) than in the AI producers. And in bonds, we favor high-quality government debt for both attractive inflation-adjusted returns and as a hedge against an eventual slowdown in AI investment as the cycle eventually shifts from buildout to diffusion.

AI capital spending is on track to become the largest investment cycle in U.S. history. Transformative technologies—such as what we expect AI to become—often unfold in two phases: buildout, when money pours into new infrastructure, followed by diffusion, when adoption broadens and productivity gains spread through the economy. That second phase can be both transformative and disruptive.
We expect the AI buildout to remain strong in 2027, and we are increasingly confident that AI will eventually transform and disrupt the broader economy in profound ways. We are more cautious, however, about the timing of the transition from buildout to diffusion, which could test the resolve of investors who may be unprepared.
AI investment drives our above-consensus forecast of near 3% U.S. growth in 2027, with broader economic strength providing an additional tailwind. Such an environment would support double-digit earnings growth (and therefore asset prices) even as interest rates remain high. Over the next several years, we expect AI’s benefits to spread well beyond today’s technology leaders and further into the economy at large.

The AI transition is where the risks rise

Past technology cycles strongly suggest that investment can temporarily stall before widespread adoption and productivity gains take over. Stock markets, in our view, do not fully reflect those risks. Strong near-term growth can coexist with greater uncertainty ahead.
For investors, the message can be simple: Stay invested and broaden out.
In other words, participate in today’s AI buildout, diversify against an uncertain transition, and position for broader adoption. Investors can maintain exposure to the “AI complex”—the companies building and supplying AI infrastructure, including many of today’s market leaders—while directing new money toward reasonably valued stocks outside of the AI complex in the U.S. and developed international markets, as well as high-quality government bonds. We hold this differentiated thesis with high conviction, given how today’s risk landscape is evolving. (We discuss this approach in the “Portfolios: Stay in, broaden out” section below.)

Vanguard’s 2027 economic forecasts

Notes: Forecasts are as of November 19, 2026. For the U.S., growth is defined as the fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter change in real (inflation-adjusted) GDP compared with the previous year. Core inflation is the year-over-year percentage change in the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, excluding volatile food and energy prices. Unemployment rate is as of year-end. Monetary policy is the rounded midpoint of the Federal Reserve’s target range for the federal funds rate at year-end. For the euro area, growth is defined as the annual change in real (inflation-adjusted) GDP compared with the previous year. Unemployment rate is as of December. Core inflation is the year-over-year change in the Harmonized Indexes of Consumer Prices, excluding volatile energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco prices, based on the fourth-quarter average for each year. Monetary policy is the European Central Bank’s deposit facility rate at year-end. For Japan, growth is defined as the annual change in real (inflation-adjusted) GDP compared with the previous year. Core inflation is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index, excluding volatile fresh food prices, as of December. Unemployment rate is as of December. Monetary policy is the Bank of Japan’s year-end target for the overnight rate.
Source: Vanguard.

The economy: Powering through higher rates

The AI boom should continue through 2027, with capital spending a key driver of our above-consensus U.S. growth forecast. Outside the U.S., some economies will benefit more than others. Asia supplies the “picks and shovels” for AI through its chip, hardware, and equipment industries.1 In the U.K., AI and related services are becoming an important source of growth. Higher commodity prices and German government spending shape Europe’s outlook, rising wages and stronger demand support Japan, and weak consumption and a continued housing slump weigh on China.
At the same time, the world is competing for a limited pool of capital. The AI buildout requires enormous investment just as governments are borrowing more for defense, infrastructure, and social spending. Technology giants that once funded expansion largely from their own cash are becoming major bond issuers. The result is greater competition for money and another reason we reaffirm our view that interest rates will stay higher than investors grew accustomed to pre-pandemic.
Inflation should moderate in 2027 but remain above target in many economies. In the U.S., we believe the Federal Reserve—after an anticipated December 2026 rate hike—will be close to having raised rates enough if supply shocks to inflation continue to ease as we expect. Stronger-than-expected demand and a resulting economic tightening present the key risk to this assessment. In Europe, we expect the European Central Bank to raise rates to 3.0% to contain inflationary pressures from higher commodity prices. In Japan, meanwhile, the challenge has flipped from generating inflation to containing it, creating upside risk to our 2.0% policy-rate forecast.

Capital markets: Pricing the transition

Higher yields have restored bonds’ appeal. Investors can once again earn attractive income without having to rely on falling interest rates to generate returns. But high fiscal borrowing and lingering inflation will keep long-term rates volatile. We see more opportunity in high-quality government bonds than in corporate debt, where prices leave less room for upside and borrowing is increasing.
For stocks, strong earnings should remain supportive across the U.S., Europe, Japan, and emerging markets in 2027, but a higher cost of capital leaves a narrower margin for error. Earnings expectations remain high, particularly for the AI complex, reflecting in part the continued strength of the AI buildout. Strong profit growth could help companies grow into today’s prices. But elevated valuations leave little cushion if earnings disappoint.
Our concern is less about near-term earnings than what could happen during a potentially turbulent transition as the AI buildout gives way to broader adoption. A smooth transition could sustain markets, although such historical precedent is rare. A rougher transition is much more likely, which could bring a sharp correction that investors are not fully prepared for. For this reason, we expect more modest annualized U.S. stock returns of 5%–8% over the next three to five years.
The key risk is whether AI providers can generate enough revenue soon enough to justify today’s stock prices. Higher borrowing costs, slower AI revenue growth, rapid data-center chip obsolescence, and cheaper competing models could all undermine the earnings growth those valuations require. The central danger is a timing mismatch: AI capacity arriving sooner than end users are willing to pay for it.
Reasonably valued stocks outside the AI complex, in both the U.S. and developed international markets, offer a hedge against AI-driven volatility. Such stocks are less dependent on the AI buildout and offer earnings growth from a broader mix of industries, often at more attractive prices. In private markets, meanwhile, cheap borrowing is gone, making the price investors pay and the managers they choose increasingly important.

Portfolios: Stay in, broaden out

Investors need not choose between believing in AI and protecting against its risks. Because no one knows exactly when the buildout will give way to broad adoption, diversification matters now, not just when the transition becomes obvious. Rather than trying to perfectly time the buildout, transition, and diffusion, investors should prepare for all three:

Participate in the buildout. The AI complex, concentrated in the U.S. and in emerging Asia’s chip and hardware makers, continues to drive earnings, and abandoning these companies altogether could mean missing significant upside. But their prices already assume strong growth, and many investors may own more of this AI buildout theme than they realize. The goal is to size it knowingly, through awareness of fund holdings, and not to hold it blindly.

Cushion the transition. Hedging needs to be in place before volatility arrives. This is not a bet against AI. Even if AI ultimately transforms the economy, a slowdown in earnings or a reassessment of today’s expectations could hurt the AI complex most. Developed-market stocks outside the U.S., especially in Europe, offer attractive return potential driven by non-AI economic forces. In addition, short- and intermediate-term high-quality government bonds offer meaningful income and hedging if growth weakens unexpectedly. At today’s yields, investors holding these bonds no longer have to sacrifice much potential return.

Position for diffusion. AI’s biggest long-term winners—companies that use rather than build AI to cut costs, gain market share, disrupt incumbents, and build new platforms—may look quite different from today’s market leaders. But simply adopting AI will not guarantee success. The winners will be those that turn AI into a durable competitive edge, placing a greater premium on management teams that can harness it decisively. As some firms adapt far better than others, dispersion should widen, creating greater opportunities for skilled active investors. For those who prefer not to pursue active investing, broad diversification spanning regions offers another way to participate in AI’s gains from eventual diffusion.

The objective is not to time the transition. It is to stay invested in today’s AI buildout while broadening toward the opportunities that come next.

Notes:

1 The phrase “picks and shovels” derives from the California gold rush in the mid-19th century, when companies that were selling picks and shovels to gold miners benefited from supplying the essential tools and equipment, regardless of which individual miner struck gold.

articles.title: The great wealth transfer: Not just for the rich
articles.text:
Better Vantage podcast

The great wealth transfer: Not just for the rich

November 17, 2026

Video length: 22 minutes 5 seconds

Read the transcript

Christine Kashkari: The greatest wealth transfer in human history is underway. Roughly $124 trillion is set to pass from Baby Boomers and the Silent Generation to their heirs over the coming decades. Most families are unprepared and the opportunity cost could easily be tens of thousands of dollars, if not more.
Welcome to Season 3 of Better Vantage by Vanguard, a podcast series hosted by Custom Content from WSJ and Vanguard. I'm Christine Kashkari, editorial director at WSJ Custom Programming and with me, as always is my co-host and our resident expert, Joe Davis, global chief economist at Vanguard. Joe.
Joe Davis: Great to be here.
Christine: Great to be with you again. Today, in addition to covering the strategies families should consider to streamline their wealth transfer, we'll also address another critical component, the conversations that families should be having today to prepare.
Joining us are Joel Dickson, global head of advice strategies, and Alisa Shin, senior estate and trust specialist, both at Vanguard.
Joel, Alisa, welcome.
Alisa Shin: Thank you.
Joel Dickson: Thank you. It's good to be here.
Joe: Full disclosure, I've known both of these leaders, individuals for over for well over 20 years. They've helped me personally, they've helped my family and most importantly, they are industry leading thought leaders and experts in areas of estate planning, trusts, wealth planning, taxes. So, I'm really excited about today--actionable insights. Let's bust some myths today. We have two of the best experts in the industry that can help us do that.
Christine: Absolutely. So, Joel, is wealth planning really just for the ultra wealthy?
Joel: Not at all. I do think we need to get out of this thinking of people say estate planning and thinking, well, it's just that death and what happens with assets and so forth. It's only for the really rich and it's to avoid these things called estate taxes or death taxes or whatever. I prefer to think of it as legacy planning, you know, what are you going to do? And this, it matters for everyone that you know, $100,000, $10,000, a million, $10 million, right?
Alisa: Absolutely.
Joe: Expand on that more. It's a much broader conversation in issue.
Alisa: People work hard for their money that they've earned and they've saved, and they have thoughts about who should get it, why they should get it, how it should be used. And so, even in worlds where the estate tax exemption is as high as is today, the $15 million number, what can be passed tax free at the federal level, people want to be intentional about where their wealth goes to their family and what that family can use that money for. So, estate planning, having a will, having a revocable trust, having powers of attorney to plan for incapacity are all still really important regardless of net worth.
Christine: And is that urgency amplified because of the great wealth transfer that we were just that I just mentioned at the open?
Joel: What I think is a little bit different, say over the last couple of decades or so, is people have now a little bit more gotten used to being responsible for saving for their own retirement. But with that has come, they tend to have more financial assets in terms of their overall wealth and things that may survive their death.
Whereas, you know, you think about income like a defined benefit plan or your Social Security and that doesn't really survive your death in the same way. So what are you going to do with those assets? There's this thing that I call the rise of the unintentional bequest that has happened where it's sort of like, well, I have these assets, they're going to fund my retirement, but I might have money leftover. I'm not really planning for it, but I might well okay. Even in that case, what's your plan? What do you want done with that?
Joe: That’s right. You talk to hundreds of families, hundreds of experts across the industry. What is being underestimated or is applying to more individuals and families now more than ever?
Alisa: There's been such uncertainty with the estate tax laws over the last decade plus. This is the first time in a while that we've had certainty. There is no sunset with the estate tax laws. For the last 10 years, people have been so focused on what if the exemption is $15 million, what if it's $5 million, what if it goes to a million? Those are big differences and have big consequences if it does go down. So, people were really focused on that, and people are taking a step away from thinking about their foundational plan. Do I have the right will in place? Do I have the right revocable trust in place in case something premature happens to me? And so right now, clients are spending. We're trying to encourage clients to spend more time thinking about what am I doing? Why am I doing it? What is the purpose of my wealth? And with that knowledge, is what I've done still make sense?
Joel: Yeah. Along those lines, I kind of conceptualize this in the following way. Legacy planning and thinking to me is more about the principle for your assets as opposed to the principal of your assets.
Joe: I like that.
Joel: Okay, what's the plan? What are the basics? What do you want that money to do? Not how much is that money?
Joe: Well, I got to admit, sometimes I've spent so much on the math and some of the numbers and we're going to get into what I should be doing, the execution. I am acknowledging I have not done nearly as much at the top of the funnel and the legacy and the plan and the purpose.
Alisa: The purpose.
Joe: Maybe it's because I spent my whole life just still accumulating, right? I haven't even given myself a license to think about the next stage.
Alisa: Everyone's so busy working, saving, raising their family, helping their children out, helping their beneficiaries out.
Joel: Avoiding. Sometimes it's avoiding the conversation.
Alisa: That's right.
Christine: That's another big part of our conversation.
Alisa Shin: That's right.
Christine: But when after you've realized your purpose, what's the next step?
Alisa: So, then the next step is to make sure you have a plan in place that aligns with the purpose, right. So, when we think about purpose, in reality, there's really only three places your wealth can go, right? One is to individuals or to a trust for their benefit, two is to charity, and three is to the government in the form of taxes. Right? Everybody's pie looks different.
Joe: I like the first two more than the third.
Alisa: Exactly.
Christine: We want to minimize the third.
Alisa: That's right. You want to minimize the third. But you know, so I think people understanding what that pie looks like and how big each of those pieces should be. Now people are numbers might change, but their philosophy generally doesn't change. Are they trying to get every dollar they've earned to their family or to their beneficiaries? Or is there are they overly philanthropic? They want something more to go to charity. That philosophy probably won't change. So, once they define that, to your point, Christine, the next step is really to develop a plan that if something happens to you or when something happens to you, you pass away, making sure those assets go in accordance with that plan.
Joel: The only thing I would add to that is I think another part of the plan is do I wait until I die for that to kind of pass
Alisa: That’s step two right. So, to Joel's point, you know, when's the right time to do that? Should you be making gifts today? There is a lot of research being done right now showing that there is a true mistiming of when people receive their inheritance with people living longer, living into their 80s, 90s. That means their kids aren't getting the inheritance until they're in their 50s, their 60s, and 70s. When they really need the help, it's probably when they're in their late 20s, thirties.
Joe: That’s when I needed it for a downpayment. Just got married, grad school, student loans.
Alisa: And so being really thoughtful of making sure one, I've always told all of our clients the most important things that you're saving for your own retirement. I can always find a bank to lend money to your children to send their kids to school. I won't find a bank who's going to lend money to you to retire. But to Joel's point, a lot of people are saving enough for retirement and have a little bit extra that they can help their family out and thinking strategically when to do that.
Joel: I would add, I think one of the things that I see from kind of an asset standpoint is there is so much what I'll call noise in the system around this. People here gift tax, estate tax, death tax and they think everyone is paying tax when somebody dies when in fact almost no one is paying tax because of death.
Joe: Seriously?
Joel: Seriously. Now that's not to say there aren't things that you should do from a tax standpoint to transfer more after-tax wealth in the ways that you want it. But the actual death that occurs or gifts that most people give during their lifetime are not subject to any tax, especially at the beneficiary level. Now, state taxes can be, there's some complication with individual states, but by and large, no one, a little overstated, but no one pays a tax upon death at the federal level.
Christine: So why does that persist? That misconception.
Joe: So then what’s the issue? Where does that come from?
Joel: Well, I think a lot of it is just the discourse that's been out there. I mean, categorizing estate taxes in the political domain as death taxes. And everyone's like, oh my goodness, I don't want to pay that. But even 25 years ago, 2001, the estate exemption was $675,000. It's $15 million today per person.1 Six hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars, even then only 2% of people that passed away were paying some form of estate tax on their estate at the federal level.2
Alisa: At the federal level.
Joel: Today, it is less than 1%, much less than 1%, but yet there's all this noise and so forth. And, and it, it stops people from doing things that might be more efficient. We talked about things like giving during your lifetime, what you can give in excess of $19,000 a year. You might just have to report it, but there's not likely to be any tax liability with it.
Alisa: Absolutely. That's right.
Joe: So, we talked a little bit about planning, maybe we'll go there because you mentioned taxes, right. So, where is the value least being captured or value being destroyed either that advisors could help clients with or self-directed. Like, what comes to mind?
Joel: I see the mistakes that people make in this area as things that they don't know. It's lack of awareness and they don't know and it actually destroys wealth rather than preserves wealth. And I'll give you an example. People be like, hey, look, I'm getting my parents are getting into, you know, later years worried about things like cognitive decline, their ability to access their accounts and so forth. But the parents will say, we're going to put you, my kids, as a joint owner on some asset might be an investment account, it might be the house and so forth. As opposed to doing something like having what we would call principal agent, you know, authorization, where you've got power of attorney, you know, and being able to make monetary decisions for example. The act of making somebody a joint owner may completely screw up how those assets are transferred upon death in a tax efficiency.
Joe: That simple change?
Joel: That simple change. Don't do transfer on death (TOD). Do power of attorney if you need to, you know, have access? And I'll give you an example if this happened with my mother, even though I was telling her to do it a different way. You know, there were other issues going on, but you know, she had a will. Good had it designated how she wanted the assets doled up and so forth. But she had also put my brother and I as 50/50, you know, transfer on death beneficiaries on all of her investment accounts here at Vanguard. Well, that was the vast, vast majority of her total assets. The will is only in play after all of those other transfer on death things have happened. So, what was left, literally, was about $1000 in what was not, you know, it was kind of home possessions, right? There was only about $1,000 that the will would actually distribute. But it says, hey, I want $15,000 going to the church. You know, I want this amount of money going here. And so now that actually then became a conversation between me and my brother about how do we fulfill these wishes of the will with what are now our assets, not the estate’s assets. So now we have to use things like our own gifting.
Alisa: To fulfill your mom’s wishes.
Joel: To fulfill our mom’s wishes. So, that's where this transfer on death can really change the plan, right?
Alisa: Well, I think, I mean, your lawyer can only do so much if they only know a certain amount. Your financial investment advisors, your financial planners can only help you so far if they only know this amount. Client success with their wealth plans. One of the key things is making sure all of your advisors are at least figuratively, if not literally, around the same table on the same page and everyone knows everything. Because then the lawyer would could say to Joel's mom, don't do the TOD because her advisor could say, we put a TOD on this. This is who the beneficiary is of lawyer could say, oh, no, that's going to mess that up. So, keeping your advisory, well, creating an advisory team, one, right. And then two, keeping your advisory team completely, you know, fully informed so that you could do holistic planning is really key to make this successful.
Christine: How do you get that started? Because it's really hard. Nobody wants to talk about their mortality.
Alisa: It's hard. Yeah.
Christine: Nobody wants to face it.
Alisa: That's right.
Joel Dickson: The vast majority of people aren't even thinking about it, Christine, for some of that very reason, I don't want to think about the death. Oh, you know, it's whatever. I'm not planning to leave anything. But you know, if it is, they'll figure it out. So it's that lack of preparation that is really throughout all of this. I mean, a vast majority of people.
Alisa: Nobody likes to think about their mortality. It's not fun, It's hard. It is hard work. And then to try and communicate that to your kids or to your nieces and nephews, whoever it's going to receive, that's even harder. They don't like to think about it. It can be very uncomfortable.
Like as my dad was aging, he tried to have certain conversations that I was just like, I can't do this dad. And fortunately for me, I did some of it. But fortunately for me, even more so, he wrote down his thoughts on an app on his phone. So, after he passed suddenly away, my sister and I were going through the phone and surely, he had information there that was like, oh, thank God he told us this. So, now we know it. And some of it was account numbers, where the money was. And some of it was just like family history, right? Like where he came from, the fact that his family escaped from North Korea. Like that family history is so important and some of it was what he hopes my sister and I and our children use this money for that they'll eventually inherit.
Joe: Wow.
Christine: Wow, that family is …. so moved. It's like a letter wishes, right?
Alisa: Absolutely. And I don't think he thought about creating it, but that's what he did. And I think that's one of the most important things where people understand there is not a one-size-fits-all recipe. Family meetings, letter wishes, they take all sorts of forms and it's what's comfortable for you. You don't have to verbalize everything. You could write it. It doesn't have to be an actual letter, could be little notes. And I do think future generations understanding the family history, understanding where the wealth came from will hopefully increase the chances of family members remaining productive individuals and being good stewards of that family wealth.
Christine: So how do you align those?
Alisa: There's no recipe that I could say. When your kids are X age, this is what you should do. When you're X age, this is what you should do, right? So, it's got to be what's comfortable. Every family's unique. The dynamics are unique. The clients who are more open to collaborate with their kids to get their insight right. It's a better chance for the wealth planning to be successful because it's not just about transferring the wealth and not losing wealth to taxes. I also think it's really important that, and I've said to many of my clients, if after you die your children start fighting and they don't talk to each other, I would personally feel like I completely failed your family. Like keeping that family and the dynamics and the relationships intact for many families is the foremost, the primary purpose of what they're doing. The wealth is a nice safety net, but keeping those dynamics, the relationships intact.
Joe: So that would be a reason to have them into the even if it's uncomfortable at first.
Joel: You don't want it to be a surprise at the time of death. Even if you've set up, you've written a letter and all the thoughts down. It still becomes a surprise. Think of all of the emotions that are happening at the time of death and so forth. And you know, the financial advisors and so forth will say, hey, have a 30, 60, 90 day plan post death. Crying out loud, throw that out the window. You're not thinking in terms of objective 30, 60, 90. You're dealing with grief, you're dealing with maybe anger, you're dealing with, you know, pent up emotions.
Joe: So definitely earlier if possible.
Alisa: Yeah, doesn't mean you have to tell your family your net worth and how much they're getting right. But there's certainly conversations. I think it's good for them to hear from you directly versus reading it, you know, and they might have some thoughts as well. And I think that's all important.
Joe: Let's go back a little bit to estate, I'm thinking ETT--estates, taxes trusts, right? What are the areas where you two may disagree? Is this agreement on is this agreement on everything?
Joel: By the way, we don't we don't really disagree on the philosophy. No, but as a tactic, I come at it from a, do you want to do this from a tax standpoint first and then think about the exceptions. Alisa, I'm not going to put words in her mouth but she'll come at it from the kind of control and how do you think about this perspective and then think about the tactics of the tax pieces of it. So, where I'm going with this is that especially with, at the federal level, all of the huge estate tax limitations where pretty much no one pays, you know, estate tax. The role of trusts as a tax avoidance, if you will, approach is much, much attenuated relative to say a few decades ago. Now there are plenty of state reasons, there's plenty of control and access reasons to think about it. But the use of trust, everyone just give me it goes, oh, I need to save on taxes, so I need to set up a trust. No, that's not the reason to set up a trust in my opinion.
Alisa: That's where we do differ. Because I look, because I look beyond just the first generation, the wealth creator. I think when the mistakes clients make and financial advisors make is not thinking about the next generation. What are they doing? Are they able to support themselves? Are they able to save for their own retirement? And if your kids, your nieces, and nephews of those who your beneficiaries are able to do that, the chances of them needing to use your money to live on or you know, it's probably greatly diminished. And so, if they got that money outright, in addition to subjecting that money now to a person's future creditors, which includes a divorcing spouse, you're also subjecting it to likely to estate taxes. So, the use of trust, I agree to avoid taxes at mom and dad's death may not be necessary, but to avoid estate taxes or potential estate taxes when your kids die, so more go to your grandchildren could be a valid use of a trust.
Joel: I worry a lot. That in the name of tax avoidance, we create wealth avoidance. There's the potential that the costs of the trust, whether it's annual taxes, whether the set up costs, the ongoing maintenance, the ongoing reporting and all that kind of stuff could be more than the tax savings that you're getting. So that's where you know, it just it's important to talk what those possibilities are.
Alisa: I think that's right.
Joel: Is there any guidance you would give or for those that may be inheriting the wealth or they may be sandwich generations? So, they have the parents, but again, I'm thinking more for the generation that's younger versus those that will be transferring the legacy. So any guidance there?
Alisa: I think as your parents age, for sure, and if they have not had a conversation with you, asking questions of do you have a power attorney in place? If you're a Vanguard client, have you signed an agent authorization? Do you have a trusted contact named here? Do we have our ducks in a row?
Joe: I think those are all fair and appropriate.
Christine: So, what will be your main take away? You've both shared a lot, but if there's one thing that you want an advisor or a wealth generator to do or an heir, even a potential heir, what is that one thing that just do it now?
Alisa: Lean in and have that conversation, have that hard conversation, bring it up somehow.
Joel: I'm just going to plus one that.
Joe: It's that important. That's been the theme.
Joel: The basics here are what are important.
Christine: Well, thank you so much, Alisa and Joel. And that's it for today's episode. Next time, we're turning to fixed income and asking whether investors chasing higher yields today fully understand the risks they're taking. Join us for that conversation and all upcoming episodes.
If you enjoyed this episode and found it helpful, subscribe and share.

Roughly $124 trillion is set to pass from Baby Boomers and the Silent Generation to their heirs and to charity over the coming decades. But in this episode of Better Vantage, Joel Dickson, global head of advised strategies at Vanguard, and Alisa Shin, senior wealth planning strategist at Vanguard, say that most families are unprepared for this wealth transfer, and the opportunity cost could easily reach tens of thousands of dollars.
Almost no one pays federal estate tax when someone dies—the current exemption stands at $15 million per person.1 Yet Dickson and Shin say persistent noise around "death taxes" keeps families focused on the wrong problem.
The actual challenges? With people living into their 80s and 90s, inheritances land when beneficiaries are in their 50s, 60s, or 70s—decades after they could have used help with things like down payments on homes and student loans. And the vast majority of families avoid these conversations entirely, creating consequences beyond money, such as surprise distributions that can fracture relationships and leave heirs unprepared.
The foundation is straightforward: have a will, establish powers of attorney, and ensure your advisory team is coordinated. Your wealth ultimately goes three places: to individuals or trusts, to charity, or to the government in taxes. Being intentional about that distribution matters.
Dickson and Shin’s advice for getting started? "Lean in and have that conversation." The wealth transfer is happening whether families plan for it or not.

articles.title: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
articles.text:
Oil can help achieve SDG 7

Globally, over 666 million people do not have access to electricity. If those without electricity were a country, they would be the third most populous on earth. There is no shortage of ‘how-to guidance’ on addressing this human tragedy. Much of it comes from the UN, in tracking progress on Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7), which aims to achieve universal access to electricity by 2030. Such advice is framed, however, almost exclusively, in the language of solar and wind power, grid access, storage and financing. Most reports omit any role for hydrocarbons in closing the electricity access gap. The opposite is the case. Hydrocarbons are predominantly referred to in such documents in terms of how they can be phased out and removed. Two goals are pursued simultaneously: universal electricity access while restricting electricity generation by certain fuels. With just four years remaining to achieve the goal of universal energy access, perhaps it is time to acknowledge a fact borne out by realities. Never, in human history, have a group as large as 666 million people achieved access to electricity in a four-year time frame by generating electricity through a restricted number of energy sources. The scale is unprecedented. The timeframe is unprecedented. The policies aimed at achieving it, with two seemingly contradictory goals, are unprecedented. Furthermore, there is no historical example of hundreds of millions of people gaining access to electricity without hydrocarbons. Large jumps in access have always come through a mix of fuels and technologies. Texts and progress reports on SDG 7 never suggest oil can play a positive or practical role in closing the electricity access gap. While statistically oil constitutes a small percentage of global electricity generation, roughly 3%, in the bid to achieve universal access, no fuel should be dismissed. There are specific circumstances when oil is appropriate for electricity generation. Three points illustrate this. The first is remote settlements, or those with no grid connection. In such cases, bringing in generators and fuel is simpler than building new lines or facilities. This is why island nations often generate a high proportion of their electricity from oil. For example, the EU country with the highest proportion of electricity generated by oil is Cyprus. The majority of those without electricity live in remote areas, 84% of the 666 million live in rural areas. These are predominantly low-income regions, often in fragile security situations and with weak infrastructure. In such cases, diesel-powered generators can be the right solution. Secondly, diesel-powered generation often has low upfront costs and simple deployment. This avoids the need for large loans that, for example, some well-designed solar mini grids at community scale may require. As climate financing from developed countries has not come close to the levels developing countries require, short-term bridge solutions, like diesel-powered generators, may become more necessary to improve electricity access. The third case when oil plays a crucial role in electricity generation is in terms of emergency backup generation. Diesel generators are known as the ‘default workhorse’ backup generators for critical infrastructure, airports, emergency operation centres, defense facilities, data centres, hospitals and much more.This is because of how promptly they can start operations, their ability to function well in harsh weather conditions and their capacity to sustain power supply for long periods. Many authorities and emergency planners pre-stock diesel generators as part of continuity and civil protection plans.This is not restricted to developing countries. One large survey has found that about 85% of backup generators in commercial buildings and critical facilities in the US run on diesel, and another report suggests that the share worldwide is over 60%.An illuminating example of this is the backup generator system in the largest hospital in Vienna, the Allgemeine Krankenhaus. If the public grid were to fail, within just 15 seconds, a diesel-powered emergency generator would take over the hospital’s power supply, ensuring critical, life-saving equipment keeps functioning. This diesel emergency power plant can maintain power for the entire hospital for 48 hours of autonomous operation and, with shed loading, this can be extended further.These points underscore the fact that there are circumstances when oil powered electricity is an appropriate option. Given that electricity demand is expected to increase by a massive 85% by 2050, perhaps an expanded role of oil in meeting this demand should be considered. In the 1990s, oil constituted around 10% of total electricity generation globally. With technological innovation improving its environmental credentials, oil’s role in future electricity generation cannot be discounted. This important role for oil in electricity generation depends on a secure and stable supply of crude oil, and this is fundamental to all OPEC’s actions and activities. Oil should not be dismissed, nor should any energy source, as the SDG 7 2030 deadline for universal access to electricity looms ever nearer.

Growth outlook

Key findings

Leader perspective

Our insights

What will drive the next era of banking and capital markets growth?

Banking CEOs that took part in the KPMG CEO Outlook survey are optimistic about growth, and realistic about the challenges ahead. AI is emerging as one of the most important growth enablers, driving investment, operational redesign, and workforce transformation. At the same time, rising regulatory demands, escalating cyber threats and near-universal concern over fraud are forcing leaders to rethink resilience.The 12th edition of the KPMG CEO Outlook, based on insights from 1,400 CEOs, offers a perspective on their mindset, strategies, and planning approaches. This report focuses exclusively on the 120 Banking and Capital Markets CEOs surveyed between 11 August and 21 September 2026, representing commercial banking, capital markets and investment banking, retail banking, and organizations operating across multiple segments, including retail, commercial, and investment banking.

Key findings

The confidence to grow

82% of respondents expect annual earnings growth of 2.5% or more over the next three years, up from 61% in 2025

Unlocking AI's benefits

78% of banks surveyed say AI is a top investment priority.

Building resilience in an AI world

64% of respondents have increased investment in cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience.

Protecting trust in an era of escalating fraud

98% surveyed are concerned about fraud detection and prevention as a risk to their cybersecurity.

Redesigning operations for growth

69% of respondents say AI is having a transformational or significant impact on risk management and regulatory compliance.

Transforming the workforce of the future

93% of respondents are retaining and retraining high-potential talent in response to AI.

articles.title: Too few formal jobs, or a preference for informal work? What Brazilian workers do when offered a formal contract Guest post by Carla Srebot
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

Too few formal jobs, or a preference for informal work? What Brazilian workers do when offered a formal contract Guest post by Carla Srebot

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the 12th in this year’s series of posts by PhD students on the job market.
If workers could leave informality, would they? That choice may depend on what changes when their job becomes formal: take-home pay, working hours, access to labor and social-security protections, or the flexibility to balance work and family responsibilities. With 58% of workers worldwide holding an unregulated job, understanding these trade-offs matters for policies that aim to reduce informality. Yet observing workers in informal jobs tells us little about whether their situation reflects a market failure that limits access to formal employment or workers’ preferences for informal work. In my job market paper, I bring new evidence from Brazil to a simple question that is surprisingly hard to answer empirically: if an informal worker’s own employer put a formal contract on the table, would the worker sign it—and what would shape that decision?
Take Brazil as an example, where 38% of workers are informally employed. About a third of these workers are salaried employees without a signed contract, and roughly half are self-employed without tax registration. For employers, the cost of hiring formally is high, and until the 2017 labor reform, formal contracts offered little room for flexible working hours. My paper focuses on salaried workers without a signed contract. Many already work for formally registered firms, a pattern also observed in other countries in the region, such as Mexico and Peru. Growing evidence on informality has pointed to two driving explanations: workers are informal for “opportunity” reasons—the voluntary informality wherein workers prefer informal jobs—or for “necessity” reasons—the involuntary informality due to a lack of formal job offers. This distinction is usually drawn for the choice between self-employment and salaried work, but it applies similarly to a salaried worker deciding whether to work under a formal contract. For workers, a formal contract can mean less money to take home and less flexibility to change their hours. Workers have to pay 7.5–14% of their gross wages in social security contributions. If employers also offer lower wages to cover some of their own payroll costs, take-home pay can fall even further.
Which of the two explanations dominates has first-order policy consequences: the remedy for too few formal job offers is very different from the remedy for formal contracts that workers do not find worth accepting.
Separating preferences from access is empirically challenging: the formalization rate is an equilibrium object that reflects the decisions of workers and firms as well as the labor market’s ability to match a firm willing to offer a formal job with a worker in search of such an arrangement. What we need to observe is whether informal workers would accept a formal contract if their current employer offered one. I approximate this setting through two complementary approaches: labor inspections in Brazil that require employers to register informal workers, and a survey experiment that elicits acceptance under a guaranteed formal offer.
Do informal workers want to formalize?
When Brazilian labor inspectors detect workers without a formal contract, they require the employer to register them under the social security system—that is, to formalize them. I use novel inspection data that record labor-code violations, penalties imposed on firms, and the exact number of informal workers detected, separately by gender. Using a matched difference-in-differences design that compares inspected firms to observationally similar, never-inspected firms within the same labor market, I measure take-up of formal employment as the inspection-induced inflow of new formal hires divided by the number of informal workers subject to the formalization requirement.
Most informal workers formalize immediately: within six months of the inspection, new formal hires correspond to 78% of detected informal men and 68% of detected informal women (Figure 1). Declining does not mean staying informal at the inspected firm: the employer remains liable for fines and back payments. A worker who does not sign has to leave, potentially for another informal job.
One limitation of the inspection approach is that I observe formal registrations but not the offers made to individual workers. To complement these results, I surveyed 1,501 Brazilian workers and focus on the 942 who have held an informal job. Respondents consider a vignette that mimics a real labor inspection and answer whether they would accept their employer registering their existing job. When employee social-security contributions lower take-home pay, 57% of women accept, compared to 66% of men—a gender gap comparable to my estimates from actual inspections. The vignette also includes a scenario that I cannot observe in the administrative records, in which the employer raises gross pay to cover the contribution and take-home pay stays the same. Acceptance climbs to 77% among women and 81% among men, and the gender gap shrinks to a third of its size and is no longer statistically significant (Figure 1). Women are not more likely to reject formal employment per se; they are more sensitive to its immediate monetary cost. The two scenarios differ only in whether take-home pay falls, and that difference alone moves women’s acceptance by 21 percentage points, compared with 15 points for men.
Figure 1. Formalization Rates following Inspections

What drives formalization?
The 10-percentage-point gender gap from actual inspections conceals substantial heterogeneity across workplaces: women are 8 percentage points more likely to formalize than men in female-dominated industries, whereas in male-dominated industries they are 18 points less likely. What makes a workplace a more appealing place to formalize—in particular, for women?
To answer this, I model the decision of an informal worker who, after the inspection, compares the terms of the offered formal contract with those of an informal job alternative within the same labor market, and I estimate the model at the firm level, separately by gender. Men and women respond similarly to wages: a 10% increase in the firm’s formal wage premium increases take-up of the formal job by around 10%. Gender differences appear in the valuation of non-wage attributes. Women value leave provisions and flexibility and part-time arrangements at about 19% and 18% of their formal wage, compared with only 4% and −8% for men (Figure 2). The survey’s choice experiment, where job attributes are randomly assigned, shows the same ordering: women’s valuation of parental leave reaches 42% of the wage, against 27% for men. Moreover, increasing provisions on maternity and childcare, leave, harassment and discrimination, and flexibility and part-time work to the sample mean at firms below it raises women’s predicted formalization by about 3 percentage points, while leaving men’s unchanged. Higher wages thus raise take-up for both genders, while better non-wage terms can also narrow the gender formalization gap. Yes, better workplaces for women increase their chances of accepting a formal contract. But do women prefer flexible arrangements, or do they face constraints that lead them to choose these job terms?
Figure 2. Valuation of Non-Wage Job Attributes: Flexibility and Leave

What deters formalization?
I examine two possible explanations for why women have lower take-up of formal employment. First, using the survey data, I find that 27% of the gender acceptance gap is explained by household and caregiving constraints, where women bear most of the burden. Second, I measure preferences for gig-style work—schedule flexibility, on-call pay, and working offsite—relative to formal-sector protections, as a proxy for preferences for informal work. Workers with a higher gig-style-preference index are less likely to accept the formal offer in the inspection vignette, although the estimates are noisy. These results suggest that household constraints and preferences for job attributes associated with informal employment help explain why some workers decline formalization and why women are less likely than men to accept it.
If workers say yes to formal jobs, why does informality persist—and what can policy do?
In the final part of my job market paper, I ask how often workers have a chance to formalize outside the inspection setting. Using Brazil’s household labor-force survey, I measure six-month transitions from informal to formal employment with the same employer. These transitions are substantially less frequent than formalization following inspections. This contrast suggests that low formalization in the broader labor market cannot be explained by workers turning down formal contracts alone: a back-of-the-envelope calculation shows that limited access to formal offers accounts for a substantial part of persistent informality and of the gender gap in formalization.
Where does this leave policy? Informality in Brazil does not persist because workers reject formal contracts: when an offer reaches them, most sign. Policies aiming to reduce informality therefore need to address both access to formal offers and the terms that shape workers’ willingness to accept them. Higher wages increase take-up of formal employment for both men and women, while flexibility and leave provisions can also narrow gender differences in formalization. Yet making formal jobs more attractive may have limited effects when informal workers rarely receive an offer. The overall impact of these policies also depends on how employers adjust hiring, wages, and working conditions—a response that goes beyond the partial-equilibrium changes considered here.
Carla Srebot is a Ph.D. candidate in Economics at the University of British Columbia. @CarlaSrebot

News Release
Virtual power plant capacity expands 25.9% year-over-year to reach 47.2 GW
VPP growth outpaces deployments, programs and offtakers

18 November 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

The virtual power plant (VPP) market grew rapidly over the last year, reaching 47.2 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity, according to a new report from Wood Mackenzie.

The report, “2026 North America virtual power plant market report”, finds that the VPP market deepened more than it broadened this year, as capacity expanded 25.9%, outpacing growth in the number of company deployments, unique offtakers, and market and utility programs monetized, which each expanded less than 15%.
“Escalating turbine costs, affordability concerns and slow supply response to large loads are driving more interest in VPPs,” said Elham Akhavan, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie.
Akhavan noted that with heavy-turbine capex expanding more than 80% since 2020, BESS VPPs now win on cost per kW in 2026. Distributed BESS retained its position as the most cost-effective in this time frame.
Market maturation accelerates in some sectors
The largest jump in VPP wholesale market capacity recorded in the residential market, with 155% expansion year-over-year.
"Residential’s share of wholesale-market VPP capacity more than doubled, reflecting opt-out enrollment and retailer-led battery growth," said Max Issokson, senior research analyst, Wood Mackenzie.
Storage and EV penetration relative to thermostats experienced impressive growth as well, displaying a 19.7% YOY growth and outpacing 2025’s growth. The only portion that contracted was economic participants in the market, with growth shrinking 13.5% YOY.
Evolving markets
PJM and ERCOT remain the regions with the greatest utility commitments to data center capacity, also have the greatest disclosed VPP offtake capacity.
Emerging markets such as MISO, as well as activity in Arizona, Illinois and Virginia are demonstrating opportunity for more growth.
Summer capacity prices rose significantly in MISO this year, from $30 to $384-424/MW-day, but aggregation rules still limit growth.
“Arizona, Virginia and Illinois are building new programs that may increase capacity,” said Akhavan. “California has been a strong market in the past, but its future growth depends on SB 913 versus one-off DSGS funding.”
Data centers and the competitive frontier
The 2026 report identifies a new signal in the market, with VPP providers disclosing a 1 GW pipeline of capacity specifically targeting data center load, a category that did not appear in last year's scorecard, demonstrating that VPPs are increasingly positioned as a direct response to the infrastructure demands.
Competition among commercial and industrial aggregators is tightening as well, with battery ownership and optimization emerging as key points of differentiation.
“Financiers are divided on how to account for VPP revenue, with some pricing it directly into storage leases, while others pass it through to customers as a bill credit or direct incentive,” said Akhavan. “How that revenue is treated is becoming a defining competitive variable.
At the same time, the report cautions that deployed storage does not automatically translate into VPP capacity. Opt-out enrollment has demonstrated it can shift capacity overnight, while opt-in models and data access barriers continue to constrain growth.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesEuropeWhy European Companies Are Forecast to Have Robust Earnings GrowthNov 13, 2026Share Strong earnings growth has helped European stocks absorb higher bond yields, elevated energy prices, and subdued domestic economic growth over the last year. European earnings are growing significantly faster than the euro area’s economic growth rate: Goldman Sachs Research forecasts STOXX 600 EPS to grow 18% in 2026. The equity market is a “distorted mirror” of the economy, with some sectors representing a higher proportion of earnings in the stock index compared with their contribution to overall economic activity. Listed companies now generate most of their revenues outside their country of domicile, and the euro area’s share of STOXX 600 sales has fallen from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today.European company earnings are growing rapidly—and at a faster pace than the euro area economy. The strong earnings have helped the stock market absorb higher bond yields, elevated energy prices, and subdued domestic economic growth, writes Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist for Goldman Sachs Research, in a report.
What is the forecast for STOXX 600 index earnings?

Our analysts expect earnings per share for the STOXX 600 index of European stocks to grow 18% in 2026 and 7% in 2027. Meanwhile, euro area nominal GDP is forecast to grow 3.3% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027.
“This raises an important question,” Bell writes. “Why are European earnings proving more resilient than the domestic economy would suggest?”
Are listed companies an accurate representation of the economy?

Investors often use domestic GDP growth to gauge company earnings growth, Bell observes. “But this relationship is far from mechanical and can vary significantly over time,” she adds.
For example, the two were roughly aligned in 2025 when euro area nominal GDP grew around 3.7% while STOXX 600 earnings growth was 2.4%. This year, though, earnings are expected to considerably outpace economic growth. (The STOXX 600 benchmark reflects a broader European footprint than the euro area, spanning companies domiciled in the UK, Switzerland, and Denmark, among others.)
One possible reason why earnings of listed European companies appear to be decoupling from domestic economic growth could be the composition of sectors represented among Europe’s biggest stocks.
“The equity market is a distorted mirror of the economy,” Bell writes. GDP measures value across the entire domestic economy, whereas aggregate market earnings reflect the profits of a concentrated group of large listed companies.
For example, companies in the financial sector account for more than 30% of EURO STOXX earnings (an index of euro area stocks), but only 10% of euro area economic activity. Energy and technology are also more important to listed earnings, while real estate, retail, and industrials have much larger weights in the economy relative to the European stock market.
Why does global growth matter more than domestic growth for European companies?

Country exposure also helps to explain the divergence between European earnings and the domestic economy. Listed companies now generate most of their revenues outside their country of domicile, and the euro area’s share of STOXX 600 sales has fallen from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today.
At the same time, exposure to the US, Asia, and emerging markets has increased steadily, Bell observes.
“With more than half of STOXX 600 revenues now generated outside Europe, global rather than domestic growth is increasingly more relevant for listed companies.”
Goldman Sachs Research captures this with sales-weighted GDP growth, which weights regional growth by the geographic breakdown of companies’ revenues in the prior year. This measure has exceeded euro area growth in most years since the early 2000s. It is also the dominant driver of earnings: A 1 percentage point acceleration is associated with roughly 10 percentage points of higher STOXX 600 EPS growth.
Currency also matters. A weaker euro raises the translated value of overseas profits, a meaningful share of which is denominated in US dollars, and improves the competitiveness of European companies.
Can higher energy prices support company earnings?

Europe is a net energy importer, so higher prices squeeze households and raise corporate costs. But the economy's sensitivity to oil prices has declined as the euro area economy has become less dependent on oil.
The market's composition also provides a cushion: companies involved in energy and basic resources benefit directly from higher commodity prices, while chemicals companies and many industrial companies can pass costs on to customers.
The cushion may not last. Sustained high energy costs can weaken company profit margins as growth and pricing power fade. The negative impact of higher costs can take time to appear in margins: After the 2022 energy shock, earnings for energy companies rose quickly while easing supply bottlenecks supported autos and chemicals companies; six to 12 months later, earnings estimates for energy and chemicals companies began to fall as commodity prices normalized and cost pressure became more visible.
The current Middle East shock could follow a similar sequence, with margins outside financials and commodities coming under pressure if demand slows and pricing power fades.
Given that our economists do not expect significant changes in euro area economic growth momentum, Bell’s team is more cautious than the consensus of financial analysts when it comes to European companies’ profit margins. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts broadly flat margins for STOXX 600 companies until 2028 after financials and commodities are excluded. On the other hand, the consensus of analysts expects margins to expand by more than 100 basis points to 10.1% from 8.7%.

articles.title: European Strategic Autonomy in 2027: Where are we? Where are we going? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English

Two years after Mario Draghi’s 2024 competitiveness report, implementation of recommendations is uneven; while security and defence have seen significant progress other sectors have advanced more slowly

There is substantial investment growth across several strategic areas, including a rising defence budget and €21.1 billion earmarked for critical raw materials projects

The focus is transitioning from policy announcements to execution, where the primary challenge for investors is identifying which companies and issuers can successfully convert increased EU spending into sustainable earnings and durable economic returns

In September 2024, former European Central Bank President, Mario Draghi presented a landmark report on the future of European competitiveness.

The report diagnosed structural weaknesses in productivity, investment and industrial capacity relative to the US and China and set out 383 recommendations spanning several sectors.

Its central thesis is that Europe must mobilise substantially higher public and private investment – originally estimated at between €750 billion and €800 billion annually – and streamline decision-making if it is to safeguard strategic autonomy.

The agenda has since become a reference point for European Union industrial and security policy.

Two years on, the so-called Draghi Implementation Index shows that 15.7% of the recommendations have been fully implemented, with the combined strict-plus-partial rate – a measure of how much of Draghi’s competitiveness report has been turned into binding law – at 41.3%.1

Progress is uneven but tangible in security-linked areas. Defence has reached 78.6% (strict-plus-partial), but digitalisation and advanced technologies (29.8%), pharmaceuticals (27.8%) and energy (21.7%) have advanced more slowly. These results indicate that delivery has been strongest where competitiveness overlaps with security imperatives.

Addressable markets are expanding

In defence, EU member states spent €418 billion in 2025 and are projected to reach €454 billion in 2026, with trends indicating further growth toward as much as €547 billion by 2029.2

A substantial share of equipment and investment spending flows to European industry, generating multi-year opportunities measured in the high hundreds of billions of euros. Additional demand for non-traditional defence suppliers could reach up to €500 billion over 2026–29.3

Major joint programmes can be tricky to agree on as Germany and France have showed recently: the next-generation fighter Future Combat Air System and the Main Ground Combat System initial plan have been cancelled which will reduce economies of scale.4

In space, the Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite – IRIS constellation – with a total cost of €15.6 billion, has moved into the implementation phase.

Major manufacturing contracts awarded in August–September 2026 cover the bulk of the 348-satellite programme, with first launches scheduled for 2029.5

Furthermore, space sovereignty has moved higher up in Europe’s strategic agenda: Thedisruption to Starshield connectivity in Ukraine on 14 October 2026 has highlighted Europe’s dependence on US space infrastructure.

While Eutelsat OneWeb satellite and IRIS provide European-controlled alternatives, Europe still lacks Starlink’s scale and a sovereign space-based missile-warning capability. Limited launch capacity remains another vulnerability.

This urgency is strengthening political support for Project Bromo (proposed consolidation of the satellite-manufacturing activities of Airbus, Thales and Leonardo).

Further spending on secure communications, missile warning and Earth observation should support the order pipeline. However, without greater launch capacity, Europe risks developing sovereign satellite capabilities while remaining reliant on US infrastructure to deploy them.

Raw materials and clean tech bolster backdrop

Critical raw materials offer a growing project pipeline: the 46 new strategic projects selected in October 2026 under the Critical Raw Materials Act are expected to mobilise around €21.1 billion in public and private investment, advancing capacity in lithium, nickel, cobalt, rare earths and related materials for batteries, defence and permanent magnets.6

Clean technologiesand the energy transition continue to present large-scale opportunities, in our view. Draghi’s original framework of roughly €750 billion to €800 billion in annual additional investment needs remains a useful reference, while McKinsey analysis highlights multi-trillion-euro global cleantech capital expenditure by the mid-2030s, with substantial accessible value for European players in e-mobility, grids and related technologies.7

Digitalisation and advanced technologies offer long-term markets linked to AI and industrial connectivity.

Industrial policy measures are reinforcing these dynamics. The EU steel measure, effective from 1 July 2026, establishes a duty-free quota of 18.3 million tonnes with a 50% out-of-quota duty, supporting domestic capacity utilisation.8 Strategic designations for critical materials and refinements to battery local-content rules further strengthen the operating environment for European producers.

Equity valuations in exposed sectors have adjusted from earlier peaks, creating interesting entry points alongside still-elevated earnings growth expectations in defence.

Fixed-income markets continue to see increased issuance linked to defence and infrastructure, new issuers mainly in euro are paving the way, the market is broadening and new eastern European and Nordic companies are now using the euro bond market to fund their needs. The EU money injections are driving a whole ecosystem all over Europe.

2027: From policy ambition to investment execution

Europe’s strategic-autonomy agenda is increasingly translating into tangible investment across defence, energy infrastructure, space and critical supply chains. For investors, however, the opportunity is becoming more selective.

In equities, the focus is shifting from policy announcements and order intake towards companies able to convert larger backlogs and capacity investment into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

In fixed income, higher investment creates additional issuance opportunities but also requires greater differentiation. Sector selection is key and rating agencies are really segregating between companies that are benefitting from the EU umbrella (upgrades such as in the defence sector) and those losing momentum in the face of fierce global competition.

The key investment question for 2027 is therefore no longer simply whether Europe will spend more, but which companies and issuers can translate strategic autonomy into durable economic returns.

articles.title: US Key Themes 2027
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

21 Nov 2026

US Key Themes 2027

Our highest-conviction call for 2027 is that economic growth will be comfortably above the consensus.

The US economy heads into 2027 after absorbing an energy price shock, a hawkish shift from the Federal Reserve, and a change of control in Congress. We expect GDP growth to strengthen to 2.5% from 2.4% in 2026, well above the consensus forecast of 2.1%. That resilience masks an economy that’s reliant on a single engine.

Four themes will shape how 2027 unfolds; together, they describe an expansion that’s strong but one where risks are building. We doubt those vulnerabilities will cause major problems in 2027, but they’ll determine how painful the next downturn proves to be.

Theme 1: The AI buildout has more room to run. We expect the non-AI economy to rebound in 2027, but reliance on continued strength in AI isn’t going anywhere. Growth is broadening across industries, while households’ high exposure to AI stocks will support consumer spending.

Theme 2: Inflation will remain sticky. Repeated shocks and bottlenecks, along with a solid underlying economy, mean core inflation will remain above the consensus in 2027.

Theme 3: Fiscal policy mostly adds noise, but it could fuel growth and inflation. Divided government will bring bruising fights over shutdowns and the debt limit, while doing little to curb tariff, immigration, and geopolitical uncertainty. A deficit-financed bipartisan deal could lift defense and healthcare spending ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Theme 4: The seeds of the next recession are being sown during a strong expansion. A debt-financed surge in investment, weak hiring by small businesses, and a postponed labor-market adjustment to AI mean we expect the next downturn, when it arrives, to be more painful, with less cushion from fiscal policy.

articles.title: Daily: Tech sell-off puts AI investment case to the test
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Data with Donovan | 25bps or 50bps Fed hike in December? (3 mins)
Video: The AI Show | Latest on NVIDIA and how the AI investment is reshaped (6 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US stocks fell on Monday amid renewed tech sector volatility ahead of a key earnings report from NVIDIA, while the Trump administration's move to restrict Chinese companies' remote access to advanced AI chips and servers added to the selling pressure. The S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, and Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed 1.9%, 2.7%, and 5.3% lower, respectively.The Bureau of Industry and Security issued a new rule that marks a significant shift in how the US restricts access to advanced computing power. According to the new measure, data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need to obtain a US government license before buying from US chipmakers, as it aims to restrict China and other US rivals from accessing offshore computing power that uses American-designed processors.Markets also digested a speech from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh that added a macroeconomic dimension to existing concerns about AI investment returns. Warsh described AI as a potentially transformative technology that could lift productivity and economic growth. But he also identified the possibility that substantial capital investment and stock-market gains could be followed by disappointing returns and falling equity valuations, producing an economic slowdown and a more pronounced rise in unemployment.Selling broadened beyond the largest technology companies, with almost all S&P 500 sectors declining. With risk-off sentiment on the rise, bonds rallied and the yield on the 10-year US Treasury fell 1 basis point to 5.13%.What do we think?
In our view, the market reaction reflects a further positioning adjustment as investors reassess whether AI demand, utilization, and monetization can support elevated capital spending and market expectations. Recent volatility does not yet change our conviction in the structural AI opportunity or our constructive view on diversified equities.Underlying demand for computing capacity remains robust. Recent earnings have shown accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders, and we forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027, and USD 1.5tr in 2028. Most spending is concentrated in large, generally well-funded technology platforms, which should limit the direct impact of financial stress among more leveraged infrastructure providers on overall investment. Project delays, repricing, and consolidation appear more likely than a broad collapse in AI spending.However, as the cumulative investment in the AI build-out moves into trillions of US dollars, investors are placing greater weight on how this spending translates into revenue, free cash flow, utilization, and sustainable returns. NVIDIA’s results will therefore be assessed not only for chip demand, but also for evidence on data-center utilization, margins, order visibility, supply constraints, and customers’ capital-spending plans. Evidence that computing capacity is being absorbed by rising usage would support confidence in the investment cycle. Weaker utilization, slowing customer commitments, or greater difficulty converting investment into revenue could renew concerns about overcapacity and prospective returns.The new chip restriction could affect 5-10% of next year’s AI demand, according to our estimates, but the revenue impact on US chipmakers should be limited as supply remains tight and displaced capacity can be sold elsewhere. Major US hyperscalers also appear relatively insulated, given the scale and diversity of their cloud businesses. While we see impact on smaller cloud and regional data center operators as well as standalone Chinese AI labs, the greater concern is that the rule adds to pressure on elevated 2028 capital spending and earnings expectations.Warsh’s speech also reinforces the unusually wide range of economic and market outcomes associated with AI. The bar for performance is rising, and greater differentiation across the AI ecosystem is likely to make sharp market moves more common at this stage of the cycle.Still, for the sell-off to indicate a lasting deterioration in the AI investment cycle, we would need to see weakening compute demand, slowing AI-related revenue growth, poor capacity utilization, or tighter financial conditions constraining spending by the largest technology platforms. The breadth of selling will also matter. Concentrated weakness in chips, data-center companies, and other highly valued growth stocks would remain consistent with a valuation and positioning adjustment. A sustained spread into financials, industrials, and other cyclical sectors, accompanied by weaker economic, credit, or earnings data, could indicate a broader reassessment. Current evidence does not yet support that conclusion.We therefore continue to see potential for gains in broad equity markets over the next six to 12 months, supported by resilient economic growth and corporate earnings. Near-term volatility reinforces the importance of selectivity and disciplined portfolio construction rather than a broadly defensive stance.How to invest?
We believe investors should remain engaged with the structural AI opportunity while ensuring that portfolios are not overly dependent on a single company, sector, or catalyst. Diversification across the AI value chain, other equity sectors, regions, and asset classes can help investors participate in further growth while reducing sensitivity to company-specific setbacks.Retain diversified exposure to AI. Investors should avoid abandoning the structural opportunity in response to short-term volatility. We favor established technology platforms with tangible AI revenues, existing computing capacity, strong balance sheets, and the ability to finance investment internally. Within semiconductors and hardware, investors should emphasize competitive positioning, reasonable valuations, and lower exposure to excess capacity. Defensive technology businesses can complement more cyclical AI holdings.Reduce excessive concentration. Investors with outsized positions in individual technology companies should use periods of market strength to reduce concentration relative to technology-sector and broad-market benchmarks. Diversifying across compute, foundries, platforms, applications, power infrastructure, and other enabling technologies can reduce dependence on a single bottleneck or business model. Investors whose overall technology allocation has moved above its intended weight should also consider rebalancing into other sectors. Our preferred US sectors include health care and industrials.Broaden portfolios across regions and asset classes. We remain positive on Eurozone equities, where valuations are lower and the earnings outlook is supported by a manufacturing recovery and structural investment. Investors with significant bond underweights should consider rebuilding exposure to short- and medium-maturity high-quality bonds, where elevated starting yields offer attractive income and diversification potential. Broad commodities and select alternatives can provide additional return drivers for investors able to tolerate their specific risks. A strong multi-asset core can help investors remain positioned for equity gains while limiting the impact of further technology volatility.
