There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesOutlooksThe Global Economy Is Forecast to Grow 2.8% in 2027 as Oil Prices DeclineNov 13, 2026Share Goldman Sachs Research forecasts steady global economic growth in 2027: The US, Japan, and the UK are projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates. Energy prices are expected to flip from an economic headwind to a modest boost next year. AI spending is projected to keep boosting global economic growth in 2027. Our analysts expect nominal global AI investment to rise to $1.8 trillion next year. The risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast “are tilted to the downside”: Tensions in Iran, fiscal deficits, and lower-than-expected AI capex could result in slower global GDP growth.Goldman Sachs Research expects steady global economic growth in 2027, as lower energy prices and still-strong capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy.
What is the outlook for global GDP growth in 2027?

Global GDP is predicted to increase 2.8% in 2027, up from 2.7% this year, Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. The economies of the US, Japan, and the UK are among those projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates.
As has been the case for the last several years, our economists are more optimistic than consensus on US economic expansion owing to resilient investment. They are more downbeat on the European growth outlook amid tighter financial conditions and their expectation that higher energy prices will start to bite this winter. Goldman Sachs Research also forecasts continued robust economic expansion in South Korea and Taiwan, reflecting another year of strong AI exports.
While growth is expected to be solid, the risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for global GDP growth “are tilted to the downside,” Hatzius writes. Renewed escalation in the Iran war could result in another energy price surge. Large fiscal deficits could push up long-term yields more sharply, especially in France. AI capex could be lower than expected because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress, or weaker demand, and Hatzius also sees early signs that AI adoption is weighing on the job market.
“We expect another year of solid but unremarkable GDP growth in 2027, but several of the impulses that shaped global growth in 2026 will look different,” Hatzius writes.
How will oil and energy prices affect GDP growth in 2027?
The headwind from the energy supply shock will likely flip next year as energy prices normalize. The baseline forecast from Goldman Sachs Research’s commodity strategists is that continued Middle East supply adaptation will lower Brent prices to $78 per barrel by the end of 2027, with a similar normalization in global prices for liquefied natural gas.
At the same time, Goldman Sachs Research sees an ongoing drag from energy prices in Europe from delayed energy cost pass-through to consumers.
How financial conditions and the fiscal outlook will affect GDP growth
Lower energy prices should outweigh the effect of tighter financial conditions and a smaller fiscal impulse to GDP expansion in 2027, Hatzius writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s Financial Conditions Index implies a moderate drag on growth over the next few quarters.
While our economists do not “expect meaningful fiscal consolidation” in 2027, the large fiscal expansions of the last few years are fading. The main exception is in Japan, where consumption tax cuts, increased defense spending, and the government’s investment plans are forecast to boost GDP growth by 0.7 percentage point.
“We also expect modestly positive impulses in Germany and the US—where the Democratic victory in November’s US election suggests some of the spending cuts from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will be reversed,” Hatzius writes. Our economists project a continued fiscal drag in the UK that leaves the fiscal impulse in developed markets “only slightly positive.”
Will AI boost the global economy in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research expects AI capex to boost global economic growth again next year. Our analysts forecast that nominal global AI investment will rise to $1.8 trillion in 2027 from $1.1 trillion this year, mostly driven by an increase of over $500 billion in hardware spending in the US. The investment surge is projected to be frontloaded, with the year-over-year change in investment as a share of GDP peaking in the first half of 2027.
“Even with the expected slowdown, the impact on GDP growth will be sizable,” Hatzius writes. Our economists estimate that AI investment will boost GDP growth by 0.4 percentage point globally. In the US, Goldman Sachs Research estimates AI investment will give a 0.6-percentage-point boost to "true" GDP growth after accounting for continued undercounting of semiconductor investment and chip-related intellectual property exports.
The transition to an AI-enabled economy, meanwhile, is occurring in two phases, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The first phase involves an investment boom that raises both corporate profits and global GDP growth but features only limited productivity gains. The second phase involves less hardware investment but more business reorganization, as well as more substantial productivity gains and labor market disruption.
Goldman Sachs Research has argued that AI is likely to displace some jobs and cause a temporary increase in the unemployment rate. Our economists’ baseline expectation is that AI adoption will only have a small effect on the labor market in 2027 and there will be more notable effects in 2028-2029.
What is the outlook for China’s economic growth in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research forecasts China’s GDP to grow 4.5% in 2027, compared with the consensus estimate of 4.4%. This “reflects very robust expectations for Chinese exports and a further increase in China’s trade surplus,” Hatzius writes.
By contrast, domestic demand growth is predicted to remain weak next year owing to a drag from the property sector and weak underlying consumer spending.
This is expected to result in a modest headwind of 0.1 percentage point to the rest of the world’s GDP growth, with larger drags on growth in manufacturing-heavy economies such as Germany (headwind of 0.3 percentage point) and Central Europe (headwind of 0.2 percentage point).
What is the forecast for inflation in 2027?
Under Goldman Sachs Research’s baseline commodity forecasts for a steady decline in energy prices next year, inflation should slow in 2027, Hatzius writes.
The case for disinflation is particularly strong in the US because the price boosts from tariffs should fully drop out of the year-over-year inflation statistics next spring, he writes. With tariff effects fading and a much smaller inflation boost from the war in Iran, our economists expect core PCE inflation to slow to 2.4% at the end of 2027 from 3.2% at the end of 2026.
“We forecast a steady decline in year-over-year core inflation in the US and a more delayed decline in other major economies once the energy price shock is fully digested,” Hatzius writes.
What is the outlook for the Fed and other central banks in 2027?
Goldman Sachs Research expects “incremental policy tightening” through early 2027 in most major economies, but its economic forecasts support a dovish view on rates next year. Central banks could either deliver gradual normalization cuts later in 2027 as inflation comes down, or they could pivot to cuts sooner if economic growth is slower than projected.
The US Federal Reserve is expected to hike rates in December and March in response to lingering inflation pressures. But our economists say softer inflation data should allow the Fed to cut once in December 2027, followed by three more cuts in 2028 to a terminal rate of 3.25-3.5%.
“Furthermore, we see more dovish rate risks in the US than in most other economies, both because US inflation drivers look more clearly temporary and because the US is most exposed to a downturn in the AI cycle,” Hatzius writes.
Our economists’ views on other major developed markets also skew dovish. The European Central Bank is forecast to deliver its final hike in December, before starting to normalize back toward a 2.25% terminal rate in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Goldman Sachs Research expects a final hike from the Bank of England to 4.25% in February before a hold for the remainder of 2027. Our economists forecast normalization cuts from the BoE to a 3.25% terminal rate, but not until 2028.
“The main outlier to our forecast of only modest further policy tightening is Japan,” Hatzius writes.
Goldman Sachs Research expects the Bank of Japan to hike rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting recent communication from the central bank highlighting both upside inflation risks and the impact of higher global interest rates on the Japanese yen. With core CPI (excluding fresh food but including energy) likely to rise above 3.5% through next summer, our economists now expect that the BoJ will follow through with additional hikes in March and June for a terminal rate of 2%.

PERSPECTIVES: Economic and asset class update – March 2026

Ready to talk?

×

Robust economic growth is expected due to solid consumption and sizeable investment, although geopolitical tensions could act as a drag. We see stable sequential quarterly growth in the US in 2026, while in the Eurozone extensive German fiscal stimulus should keep growth near potential. In Japan, the government’s pro-growth policy will help sustain robust economic activity. Policy support for strategic industries and households will continue in China.

On investment, we argue that discipline will continue to beat drama. Equities started the year on a strong footing and, despite recent reverses, are still on track for future gains. A strong earnings outlook is supportive and sectoral strength is broadening. On fixed income, deficits are keeping the US long end elevated but investment grade is steady despite AI disruption risks. Recent events in the Middle East and investors’ reactions have underlined the case for gold; oil remains fundamentally well-supplied but more short-term price spikes are possible. In FX, previous USD weakness has not been sustained but future possible headwinds from asset diversification are still relevant.

articles.title: Beverage prices ease as supply prospects improve
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Beverage prices ease as supply prospects improve

John Baffes

Kaltrina Temaj

November 19, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Improving coffee and cocoa supplies are helping ease beverage prices, though El Niño continues to pose risks to production and market stability. / Image: Shutterstock

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here.

The World Bank Group’s beverage price index edged down in the first half of November, following a 20 percent increase in 2026Q3 (q/q). Cocoa and coffee prices declined amid improving supply conditions, while tea prices remained broadly stable. The index is projected to fall by 24 percent in 2026, largely reflecting recovering coffee and cocoa supplies, before rising marginally in 2027 as cocoa prices strengthen and then stabilizing in 2028.
Coffee prices ease as supply prospects improve. After rising by about 8 percent in 2026Q3 amid weather-related supply disruptions, coffee prices edged down in November as supply prospects improved. In October, Arabica averaged about $7/kg, 17 percent below its year-earlier level, while Robusta approached $4/kg. Despite weather concerns, global coffee output is expected to rise by 6 percent to a record 190 million bags in 2026–27, marking a fourth consecutive annual increase. Reflecting stronger supplies, Arabica prices are projected to decline by 13 percent in 2026, followed by smaller declines in 2027 and 2028. Robusta prices are projected to fall by 21 percent in 2026 before stabilizing in 2027–28. Weather-related risks remain substantial. The ongoing strong El Niño could disrupt production through drought and heat in Viet Nam and Central America, erratic rainfall and higher temperatures in Brazil and Colombia, and crop diseases triggered by heavy rains in Brazil.

Cocoa prices stabilize following a sharp increase. Cocoa prices were broadly stable in the first half of November, following a 46 percent increase in 2026Q3 (q/q) amid concerns that El Niño could disrupt supplies from Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the world’s leading cocoa producers. Higher production in both countries is estimated to have lifted global output by 7 percent in the 2025–26 crop season, which ended in September, raising the stocks-to-grinding ratio to 43 percent, above its long-term average of 41 percent. However, the market is expected to tighten in 2026–27 as adverse weather and lower pod counts weigh on West African crops. Following a projected 37 percent decline in 2026, prices are forecast to rise by 10 percent in 2027 and stabilize in 2028 as supply and demand move broadly into balance. Weather is the main risk as El Niño has historically reduced yields by bringing drier conditions to rainfed cocoa-growing areas in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana.

Tea prices edge down amid weak demand and ample supplies. The three-auction average edged lower in November after remaining broadly unchanged in 2026Q3 (q/q). Kolkata prices fell sharply, following a seasonal pattern, amid weak export demand and strong production. Colombo prices also eased as subdued demand outweighed weather-related output declines. Mombasa prices were little changed and stood 8 percent above their year-earlier level as softer demand offset lower production in Uganda and Tanzania. Despite adverse weather in southern India and Sri Lanka, rising output in northern India, Bangladesh, and Kenya has kept the global market well supplied. Tea prices are forecast to rise by 4 percent in 2027 and 2 percent in 2028 as demand recovers, particularly in the Middle East. Prolonged Red Sea shipping disruptions pose a downside risk by raising costs and dampening demand in the Middle East and North Africa, a key market for East African tea. Conversely, El Niño poses an upside risk if it reduces tea output and quality in Bangladesh and parts of India.

articles.title: Unwinding of corporate spread compression: implications for euro area market repricing
articles.text: Unwinding of corporate spread compression: implications for euro area market repricingPrepared by Mar Domenech Palacios, Martina Jančoková, Paraic O’Gorman and Chiara ScommegnaPublished as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.Euro area corporate bond spreads have started to widen after a period of steady compression in recent years. Spreads peaked in October 2022 when disruptions to the supply of energy following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, high inflation and rapidly tightening monetary policy gave rise to fears of a recession. Thereafter they narrowed substantially in both the investment-grade and the high-yield segments to levels well below their long-term averages (Chart A, panel a). This compression took place despite elevated geopolitical tensions, renewed inflation concerns linked to the conflict in the Middle East, growing debt issuance by AI hyperscalers and subdued growth prospects, all of which could have weighed on risk sentiment and corporate fundamentals. In recent weeks, however, corporate spreads have widened alongside rising government bond yields and tighter monetary policy. This box examines what is driving this widening and how a further repricing of risk would affect euro area borrowers and investors.Chart AThe compression in euro area corporate bond spreads due to high levels of risk taking by investors may now be reversinga) Euro area corporate bond spreads and long-term averagesb) Decomposition of euro area non-financial corporate bond spreads(3 Jan. 2005-10 Nov. 2026, basis points)(4 Jan. 2019-6 Nov. 2026, basis points)Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Moody’s and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: corporate bond spreads for the ICE BofA Euro High Yield and Investment Grade Indices are calculated over the six-month EURIBOR curve. The dashed lines indicate long-term averages. Panel b: excess bond premia are calculated following the baseline specification in Gilchrist and Zakrajšek*. The explanatory variables include distance to default, duration, amount outstanding, coupon rate, an indicator variable that is equal to one if the bond is callable and zero otherwise, and country, industry and rating fixed effects. The estimation is based on senior unsecured bonds with maturities above one year.*) Gilchrist, S. and Zakrajšek, E., “Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations”, American Economic Review, Vol. 102, No 4, June 2012, pp. 1692-1720.The recent changes in spreads mainly reflect shifts in investor risk appetite, with credit quality playing a secondary role. Corporate bond spreads can be decomposed into a component that may be explained by credit risk fundamentals and a residual excess bond premium (EBP). The EBP is the additional (or missing) compensation investors require to hold corporate bonds above (or below) the amount implied by the issuer’s own default risk.[1] Following Gilchrist, S. and Zakrajšek, E., “Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations”, American Economic Review, Vol. 102, No 4, June 2012, pp. 1692-1720, option-adjusted spreads on euro area non-financial corporate bonds are regressed on distance to default, the logs of duration and amount outstanding, the coupon, the rating and dummies for industry, country and callability. Given that the EBP reflects investor sentiment, it is sensitive to sudden shifts in risk appetite, whether they are global or euro area-specific. According to this decomposition of corporate bond spreads, less than one-fifth of the decline between October 2022 and September 2026 can be attributed to fundamentals, while the remainder reflects a falling EBP (Chart A, panel b). In October 2024 the average euro area EBP turned negative, with almost 90% of bonds trading at spreads tighter than those implied by their fundamentals for much of 2026. This suggests that risk appetite and risk-bearing capacity in the financial sector was unusually strong, with similar negative EBP levels last seen when corporate bond purchases by the Eurosystem were exerting downward pressure on spreads.[2] See, for example, De Santis, R.A., Geis, A., Juskaite, A. and Cruz, L.V., “The impact of the corporate sector purchase programme on corporate bond markets and the financing of euro area non-financial corporations”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB, 2018. At the same time excess bond premia compressed most for the riskiest borrowers, which is fully consistent with “search for yield” behaviour (Chart B, panel a). In recent weeks, the average EBP has risen close to zero, with this component accounting for almost all of the recent widening of spreads. By contrast, the fundamentals component has remained broadly unchanged, indicating that the widening is being driven primarily by shifts in risk sentiment rather than by changes in underlying credit fundamentals. In the United States, the EBP is still firmly in negative territory, implying that while the earlier compression of spreads was driven, at least in part, by global factors, the recent unwinding has a strong euro area-specific component.[3] See Domenech Palacios, M. and Jančoková, M., “Challenges to the resilience of US corporate bond spreads”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB, 2025. Chart BDespite solid credit fundamentals, riskier firms are most exposed to the recent repricing of risk and higher rollover costsa) Median excess bond premium, by distance-to-default quintileb) Expected default frequencies for euro area non-financial corporations c) Rollover costs for euro area corporate bonds, by distance-to-default quintile(14 Oct. 2022-6 Nov. 2026, basis points)(Jan. 1990-Oct. 2026, percentages)(1 Jan. 2019-6 Nov. 2026, percentages)Sources: Moody’s, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and ECB calculations.Notes: Panel a: quintiles are constructed weekly on distance to default. Quintile 1 contains those bonds whose issuers are furthest from default and quintile 5 contains those closest to default. The dates 14 October 2022 and 10 July 2026 indicate a recent peak and trough in the average EBP respectively, while “Latest” refers to 6 November 2026. Panel b: the expected default frequency is a market-based measure developed by Moody’s KMV which indicates the probability that a company will default within one year. Panel c: face value-weighted average difference between yield to worst and coupon rate of individual bonds. Quintiles are as defined in panel a. Diamonds show the rollover cost in an EBP repricing scenario which is similar to the repricing seen between August 2021 and July 2022.Improving fundamentals have helped to contain rising spreads to a moderate extent. The component of spreads explained by fundamentals now stands at around the levels seen just before the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 (Chart A, panel b). The rating mix has shifted favourably, with a shrinking share of high-yield bonds in the outstanding stock.[4] Part of the rating mix shift may reflect the migration of weaker borrowers to private credit and leveraged loan markets rather than a genuine strengthening of corporate credit quality. The median expected default frequency remains close to historical lows, although the proportion of risky borrowers remains at the elevated 2022 levels (Chart B, panel b). Moreover, the average duration of bonds has declined from over five years in 2020 to close to four years today, which lowers spreads mechanically. At the same time, the euro area bond market has become significantly more integrated since the sovereign debt crisis.[5] Country of domicile explains less of the variation in spreads than rating, industry or distance to default. More specifically, univariate regressions of log option-adjusted spreads on each characteristic in turn give an R² of 5% for country of domicile, against 28% for rating, 18% for industry and 13% for distance to default. Earlier research finds there was deep financial market fragmentation in the euro area corporate bond market during the sovereign debt crisis. See De Santis, R.A., “Unobservable country bond premia and fragmentation”, Journal of International Money and Finance, Vol. 82, 2018, pp. 1-25. The risk of further abrupt repricing appears elevated in light of previous stress episodes. Both the 2020 and the 2022 episodes show that the EBP can move by more than 100 basis points within a quarter. Repricing has a disproportionate effect on the riskiest borrowers, whose premia are generally the most cyclical[6] See Domenech Palacios, M., “Firms’ risk and monetary transmission: revisiting the excess bond premium”, Working Paper Series, No 3118, ECB, September 2025. and are also the most sensitive to global risk shocks.[7] A global risk shock passes through to high-yield spreads around 4.7 times more strongly than it does to investment-grade spreads. This is the median impulse response based on a BVAR model containing German ten-year bond yields, euro area and US stock prices, the USD/EUR exchange rate, the spread between German and US ten-year yields and either investment-grade or high-yield euro area non-financial corporation spreads. Shocks are identified using sign restrictions, following Brandt, L., Saint Guilhem, A., Schröder, M. and Van Robays, I., “What drives euro area financial market developments? The role of US spillovers and global risk”, International Journal of Central Banking (forthcoming). The model is estimated using daily data between January 2006 and 13 August 2026, building on the BEAR toolbox; see Dieppe, A., Legrand, R. and van Roye, B., “The BEAR toolbox”, Working Paper Series, No 1934, ECB, July 2016. Shorter bond durations mean that higher borrowing costs pass through faster, as a larger share of corporate debt will be refinanced over the coming years. A further shock to the EBP of the magnitude experienced in 2022 would increase refinancing costs for most borrowers, especially those in the riskiest segment. However, rollover costs would remain below their 2023 highs, given that a significant amount of debt had already been issued at elevated rates (Chart B, panel c).Beyond higher costs for borrowers, a further repricing would imply losses for euro area investors, notably investment funds and insurance corporations. Of the euro area non-financial corporate bonds held by euro area residents, investment funds held 39% and insurance corporations 20% as of the second quarter of 2026. A repricing of the EBP on the scale of that seen in 2020 or 2022 would result in a mark-to-market loss of up to 4% on the outstanding stock of euro area corporate bonds. With spreads offering little compensation for the risk of such losses, a shift in risk sentiment could have consequences well beyond the corporate bond market. Following Gilchrist, S. and Zakrajšek, E., “Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations”, American Economic Review, Vol. 102, No 4, June 2012, pp. 1692-1720, option-adjusted spreads on euro area non-financial corporate bonds are regressed on distance to default, the logs of duration and amount outstanding, the coupon, the rating and dummies for industry, country and callability. See, for example, De Santis, R.A., Geis, A., Juskaite, A. and Cruz, L.V., “The impact of the corporate sector purchase programme on corporate bond markets and the financing of euro area non-financial corporations”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB, 2018. See Domenech Palacios, M. and Jančoková, M., “Challenges to the resilience of US corporate bond spreads”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB, 2025. Part of the rating mix shift may reflect the migration of weaker borrowers to private credit and leveraged loan markets rather than a genuine strengthening of corporate credit quality. Country of domicile explains less of the variation in spreads than rating, industry or distance to default. More specifically, univariate regressions of log option-adjusted spreads on each characteristic in turn give an R² of 5% for country of domicile, against 28% for rating, 18% for industry and 13% for distance to default. Earlier research finds there was deep financial market fragmentation in the euro area corporate bond market during the sovereign debt crisis. See De Santis, R.A., “Unobservable country bond premia and fragmentation”, Journal of International Money and Finance, Vol. 82, 2018, pp. 1-25. See Domenech Palacios, M., “Firms’ risk and monetary transmission: revisiting the excess bond premium”, Working Paper Series, No 3118, ECB, September 2025. A global risk shock passes through to high-yield spreads around 4.7 times more strongly than it does to investment-grade spreads. This is the median impulse response based on a BVAR model containing German ten-year bond yields, euro area and US stock prices, the USD/EUR exchange rate, the spread between German and US ten-year yields and either investment-grade or high-yield euro area non-financial corporation spreads. Shocks are identified using sign restrictions, following Brandt, L., Saint Guilhem, A., Schröder, M. and Van Robays, I., “What drives euro area financial market developments? The role of US spillovers and global risk”, International Journal of Central Banking (forthcoming). The model is estimated using daily data between January 2006 and 13 August 2026, building on the BEAR toolbox; see Dieppe, A., Legrand, R. and van Roye, B., “The BEAR toolbox”, Working Paper Series, No 1934, ECB, July 2016.

articles.title: Is deglobalisation reshaping where energy infrastructure gets built? | Observations | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Observations
Is deglobalisation reshaping where energy infrastructure gets built?

Macquarie expert: Danish Aleemullah, Head of Renewables Infrastructure, ANZ, Macquarie Capital

17 November 2026

Short answer: Yes. As nations reassess the resilience of their supply chains and reassert sovereignty over energy and data, the geography of infrastructure investment is fundamentally shifting.

Investment is rising across critical energy infrastructure
Global energy investment by sector, 2015 and 2026 estimate, billion USD (2025, MER)

Source: IEA, World Energy Investment 2026. Licence: CC BY 4.0.1
Many nations are now actively reducing their exposure to international trade disruption by reshoring critical manufacturing and building domestic energy capacity. The shift is no longer theoretical: US industrial production grew at a 2.1 per cent annualised rate in Q1 2026, with reshoring commitments accelerating after the April 2025 tariffs.2
Energy technology manufacturing is rebalancing globally, with the IEA noting shifts in solar PV, battery and wind investment patterns across geographies.3
But shifting imports away from one market doesn't automatically mean production reshores domestically. Supply chain gaps upstream remain a real constraint and closing them requires capital, advisory capability and deep sector knowledge across the full infrastructure ecosystem.
Why does it matter?
The implications reach well beyond trade policy. For investors, the significance lies in understanding where three converging forces intersect:
The energy transition continues to reshape how power is generated, transmitted and consumed.
Digitalisation has turned connectivity, compute and data storage into essential services.
Supply chain reconfiguration is bringing production closer to end markets, while some legacy assets show signs of underinvestment.

As Macquarie Capital's infrastructure supercycle perspective highlights, the most compelling opportunities are emerging at the intersection of the major forces reshaping markets, rather than within any single trend alone. As infrastructure systems become more interconnected and capital requirements continue to grow, investors will need partners with the capability to advise, finance and invest across the full infrastructure ecosystem.

What we're watching next

Commitment vs capacity

Whether reshoring ambitions and energy transition investments can be translated into operational capacity. Supply chain constraints, permitting timelines, workforce availability and financing structures all have the potential to slow delivery.

Energy security as industrial policy
Clean energy supply chain strategy is now a formal policy priority, with governments identifying where they have competitive advantage or are most vulnerable.

AI infrastructure demand

Demand forecasts for AI compute continue to rise, but the pace at which hyperscalers can build and energise new capacity remains uncertain. The speed of deployment will influence power demand, grid investment and broader infrastructure planning.

The Credit Market Lens: In a Slower AI Buildout, Who Captures the Scarcity Premium?

Key takeaways

Election results are more likely to stretch the AI buildout than shrink it. Permitting frictions could slow development, but ongoing demand for computing power means the longer-term need for capacity and financing remains substantial.
Scarcity favors strong balance sheets. Diversified hyperscalers appear best positioned to benefit from scarce existing compute while absorbing delays and redirecting investment. In credit, a slower financing calendar should provide an additional technical tailwind.
Existing data center debt could benefit disproportionately. Slower construction should limit new data center supply, generally supporting spread compression versus hyperscalers’ senior unsecured debt.
For leveraged infrastructure providers, scarcity is only half the equation. Investors must weigh today’s economics against future recontracting risk, GPU residual values, and a longer, less certain monetization timeline.

The U.S. midterm election results will likely reshape the pace of the AI buildout without fundamentally changing its ultimate size (see the 4 November 2026 article, “With Echoes of 1974, a Decisive Victory for the Democratic Party”). More permitting friction, higher costs, and longer development timelines may slow capex and therefore reduce near-term financing needs.
The potential exposure to such a slowdown is significant. Data compiled from Cleanview suggest that roughly 45% of planned U.S. data center capacity is located in states where tighter restrictions could emerge, with Texas alone representing roughly one-quarter.
That said, 45% exposure does not necessarily mean 45% is at risk. Projects may be delayed, relocated, or redesigned rather than canceled; some of today’s backlog would probably never have been built anyway. The ultimate impact will depend on the scope and timing of new restrictions and the permitting status of individual projects.
Perhaps more importantly, unless the underlying demand for compute changes materially, the long-term need for capacity – and the financing behind it – should still be substantial.
For now, however, we expect a longer, and less linear, AI buildout rather than a materially smaller one.
We don’t expect that path to be smooth. The past two weeks have seen plenty of noise across the AI ecosystem. The NVIDIA governance change, CoreWeave’s upside earnings surprise, and the macro implications of the midterms are among a confluence of catalysts driving substantial volatility in both equity and credit.
Once the dust settles, we expect the underlying differentiation to reassert itself: A slower AI buildout should favor the players best able to absorb delays, while others may struggle amid uncertainty.

Scarcity favors those that can afford to wait

With their generally strong balance sheets and varied earnings sources, diversified hyperscalers appear well-positioned to withstand a slower investment cycle.
Slower deployment extends the scarcity of existing compute, supporting utilization and pricing while reducing the risk of eventual overcapacity. Their balance sheets, diversified cash flows, and geographic flexibility also give these hyperscalers more options to redirect investment as permitting conditions change.
However, diversified hyperscalers are not completely immune to an AI slowdown. Physical delays do not necessarily delay financial commitments. GPU purchases, leases, and infrastructure obligations remain in place even if revenue gets pushed further into the future. And hardware bought for delayed sites could depreciate before it is fully monetized. The impact on free cash flow therefore depends on how much spending can be genuinely deferred versus how much is already committed.
This tension creates an interesting asymmetry between equity and credit markets. Equity tends to absorb both the upside from prolonged scarcity and the potential drag on investment returns. Credit can benefit from a less front-loaded AI financing calendar and therefore a slower pace of issuance. Even if cumulative financing needs remain large, stretching them over a longer period reduces the near-term technical pressure from supply.
The same logic is likely to favor existing hyperscaler-tenanted data center debt, particularly issues with strong structural protections for bondholders. If slower construction reduces data center issuance more than senior unsecured issuance, the ensuing technical tailwind should support spread compression between hyperscaler-tenanted data center bonds and the senior debt of their tenants (see Figure 1). For bondholders, the strongest structures are those where contractual protections keep the tenant economically responsible even when construction is delayed.

Figure 1: If slowing data center issuance materializes, spreads vs. senior debt of the tenants may compress further

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 10 November 2026. Chart encompasses major investment grade hyperscaler-backed data center deals, equally weighted. The option-adjusted spread (OAS) is a measure used to compare the yield of a bond with embedded options relative to a “risk-free” benchmark, such as US Treasuries.

Scarcity offers breathing room, but it is no panacea

The calculus is very different for more leveraged infrastructure providers.
On one hand, existing powered capacity benefits from scarcity. On the other hand, these businesses also have less balance sheet flexibility and rely more heavily on continued access to financing. Leases, GPU commitments, and interest expenses may continue while construction and revenues are delayed; a slower issuance calendar provides little comfort if existing capital remains tied up for longer than planned.
This creates a tension between scarcity value and valuation. Scarcity can support utilization, rental rates, and near-term cash flows. But investors still need to value cash flows beyond the initial contract, where economics depend on future demand, recontracting rates, GPU residual values, and access to financing.
A slower buildout can allow older GPU capacity to be renewed at more attractive prices, but it raises a key question for equity and credit investors: What will that capacity be worth several years from now as customer requirements and technology evolve?
Therefore, for leveraged business models, the risk is that the scarcity premium may be more than offset by a valuation discount for recontracting risk and a longer, less certain monetization timeline.

Slower does not mean smaller

Before the election, consensus forecasts pointed toward another extraordinary period of AI investment, with hyperscaler capex estimates of roughly $1.2 trillion in both 2027 and 2028 and investment running ahead of operating cash flows (see Figures 2 and 3). Those forecasts may now be revised lower or, more likely, pushed further into the future.

Figure 2: Hyperscaler capex expectations reached roughly $1.2 trillion in both 2027 and 2028

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 11 November 2026. Hyperscalers include Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle. Aggregate consensus estimates are derived from the average of analysts’ expectations.

Figure 3: The levels of expected capex are set to outpace operating cash flows

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 11 November 2026. Hyperscalers include Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle. Aggregate consensus estimates are derived from the average of analysts’ expectations.

For credit portfolios, a slower AI buildout may reduce the flow of new issuance, but it does not make the concentration challenge disappear, as we discussed in the 3 November 2026 article, “The Credit Market Lens: Where to Seek Diversification From the AI Investment Theme.” The stock of AI-related exposure is already substantial, and the eventual financing requirements could remain large even if they arrive over a longer horizon.
The U.S. election outcome may slow the AI buildout, but it’s unlikely to stop it. For investors, the key post-election questions are who earns the scarcity premium in the interim, who bears the cost of delay, and who has the balance sheet capacity to bridge the two.
Michael Puempel and Gabriel Cazaubieilh contributed to this report.

Economic uncertainty, geopolitical fragmentation and AI-driven workforce changes are reshaping the conditions in which businesses and investors operate. Inequality is central to understanding these challenges and modelling effective responses: rising and persistent inequalities can undermine societal stability, macroeconomic health and financial stability - these effects can, in turn, have consequences for business performance and long-term resilience. This paper explores how scenario analysis could help businesses and investors examine these connections and assess how social and inequality-related risks and opportunities may influence strategy, business models, resilience and financial outcomes. It also considers the practical challenges involved and the shared scenarios, data, methods and organizational capabilities needed to make the analysis more consistent and decision-useful.

How the oil market could move from famine to glut
Supply growth is coming through higher than expected

19 November 2026
6 minute read

Email
Share by email

Simon Flowers, Chairman, Chief Analyst

Alan Gelder, SVP Refining, Chemicals & Oil Markets

Gavin Thompson, Senior Vice President, Research

Harry Paton, Senior Research Analyst, Oil Supply

Show more

Chairman, Chief Analyst

View Simon Flowers's full profile

Close

Alan Gelder
SVP Refining, Chemicals & Oil Markets

View Alan Gelder's full profile

Senior Vice President, Research

View Gavin Thompson's full profile

Close

Harry Paton
Senior Research Analyst, Oil Supply
Harry is a member of four oil supply research team. His focus is developing oil price models and benchmarking assets.

Latest articles by Harry

The Edge
19 November 2026
How the oil market could move from famine to glut

Opinion
14 March 2018
Can conventional oil projects compete with L48 oil?

View Harry Paton's full profile

The constraint of Gulf crude exports since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March pushed Brent prices above US$100/bbl for much of the past nine months, triggering soaring fuel prices, rising inflation and weaker economic growth.
Senior VP Alan Gelder and the wider WoodMac Macro Oils team foresee the potential for much lower prices when flows of exports resume on a peace agreement, reversing these knock-on effects. Importantly, it may not be a fleeting downturn. Additional supply is set to arrive on the market that could contribute to prices trading below our previous long-term forecasts well into the early 2030s. I asked Alan about the new analysis.
Why have you lowered your near-term price outlook?
We believe that the oil market is headed towards substantial oversupply. Much depends on how the Iran war plays out. The key assumption in our new Base Case is that the US and Iran reach a peace agreement late in 2026, but with no breakthrough in the Russia-Ukraine war. Crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz normalise progressively through 2027, allowing fundamentals to play a greater role in shaping the market once again.
We expect demand to bounce back in 2027, but the growth in supply will be much more substantial. The significant change in our supply data is the addition 1million b/d in 2027 and another 1.8 million b/d in 2028 – even as Middle East ‘legacy’ production rapidly returns to pre-war levels and beyond. Just over half of the additional volumes come from the US (including gas production-related NGLs and tight oil), the UAE, Brazil and Venezuela. Plentiful supply not only meets higher demand in 2027 but allows the rebuilding of global observable inventories – which reduced by 1 billion barrels this year – to pre-war levels of over 7 billion barrels by mid-2028.
We forecast Brent will track down over the next two years, averaging US$84/bbl in 2027 and US$55/bbl in 2028.
What happens if the crisis doesn’t end this year?
The next two years are very different in our US-Iran Stand-off scenario. The scenario assumes that the realignment of US politics after the midterm elections rules out a return to military conflict. Without a credible threat of attack, Iran waits out the rest of President Trump’s term. Strait of Hormuz transits do not fully normalise until after 2028 and Middle East crude output stays around 3 million b/d below our Base Case through 2027-28.
Supply growth outside the region would keep the crude market on the long side, but inventories rebuild more slowly. In the scenario, Brent averages US$105/bbl in 2027 and US$91/bbl in 2028.
The underlying fundamentals won’t change, though. Whenever peace comes – by the end of the year in our Base Case or later as in the scenario – an agreement ending the threat to flows through the Strait could mark a shift from famine to glut.
Could Brent be lower-for-longer?
Yes, because there are more low-cost barrels coming into the future supply stack. We base our longer-term price outlook on the marginal cost of the barrel needed to meet demand. Demand growth and declines in producing fields lead to a supply gap of 20 million b/d in 2036. As ever, this gap must be filled by supply from existing fields (reserves growth), new fields, yet-to-find and other technical discoveries.
What’s changed is that our asset-by-asset data shows there are more lower-cost barrels available through 2036 than in our previous analyses. These barrels are from a variety of sources, including the UAE and Iran, along with higher NGLs. The marginal cost is now nearer US$60-65/bbl compared with US$70-75/bbl previously.
Implied OPEC spare capacity remains broadly unchanged at 8 million b/d through this entire period, suggesting ample available supply will dampen the potential for price upside from geopolitical risk.
Won’t OPEC cut production to support prices?
We think they will have to before the decade ends if a serious price crash is to be avoided. Balancing the books is one consideration in favour of a cut, given several OPEC countries have a fiscal breakeven of above US$80/bbl (Brent). OPEC, along with its OPEC+ partners, had success in pursuing its price-driven strategy before the war. Holding substantial volumes off the market was a material factor in Brent averaging US$90/bbl from 2021 to 2025.
The coming years, though, may prove tougher. With the UAE now outside OPEC, there are fewer remaining members to share the burden of cuts. Moreover, OPEC may baulk at production cuts that support prices and so help recent departees, which are free to increase production.
How could lower prices affect corporate strategies?
Oil and gas companies are looking to strengthen portfolios to offset production declines in the mid-2030s. With the midterm oil demand outlook robust, that won’t change. The mindset of the industry is still based around capital discipline and resilience, both portfolio-wise and financially. Much of the US$0.75 trillion net cash flow windfall in 2026 will be used to strengthen balance sheets, helping businesses to navigate any commodity price downturn.
Any shift in business development will be to sharpen the existing focus on low-cost opportunities that can be resilient as prices fall. A dip in oil prices could present M&A opportunities for the financially strong. Players, though, may be in no hurry to deal if oil prices remain high, preferring to wait for the right time to make a counter-cyclical move.

articles.title: More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales
articles.text:
More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales

Given at Association of Financial Mutuals Annual Conference 2026

Published on
05 October 2026

Speech
Opening remarks
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.
Having been in my role for a few months, I have been reflecting on the insights it has given me into how firms operate. One thing that has stood out about mutuals is not just that they are owned by their members, but how that ownership shapes the decisions they make. We can see this in the important role they play in serving parts of the market that may otherwise be underserved.
Against this background, you can understand why the Mutuals Landscape Report sets out our ambition to support the sector’s sustainable long-term growth. What that means will differ from one mutual to another. Many mutuals will continue to operate sustainably. Some will grow organically, while others may pursue acquisitions.
For some mutuals, the strategic challenge is different. They have told us that their current business models may not be sustainable over the longer term. The reasons for this include high levels of competition, keeping pace with technological change, and responding to rapidly-changing economic pressures. Some of these firms are responding by adapting their strategies and exploring new opportunities. Others are considering whether a solvent exit, including through transferring some or all of their business to another firm, may provide the best outcome for their members.
Where the firm being acquired is a friendly society, the transaction will take place through the Part VIII transfer process under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, with the PRA being ultimately responsible for deciding whether a transfer should proceed. While that process is grounded in legislation, we heard feedback that firms would benefit from having a clearer understanding of both the process itself and the factors that inform our decisions. In the Mutuals Landscape Report, we committed to providing more clarity, and CP12/26 (the CP) fulfils that promise. It sets out proposals intended to make our approach clearer and gives firms a more structured sequence of steps to follow. And alongside that, we are also improving the way we manage these transactions internally.
With these initiatives, we aim to promote a dynamic market and support sustainable growth of the mutuals sector.
But the PRA is not the only one working to make this process more efficient. We have also observedfootnote [1] practical approaches developed by firms to improve how these transactions are managed. Today, I want to provide an overview of the Part VIII process. As I do so, I will weave practical insights on how we have seen firms successfully navigate that process, so that others can benefit from the experience of previous transactions.
Reflections from a recent mover
Before turning to those insights, let me take a step back and explain why the process matters.
A Part VIII transfer can offer significant strategic benefits, such as realising economies of scale, improving service standards, and becoming more resilient. All of these improve outcomes for members. But it also requires firms to commit considerable time and resources, with the costs ultimately borne by members. At the PRA, we are very conscious that if a transfer cannot be confirmed, those costs may still have been incurred without the expected benefits being realised. That’s why we work with firms to try to help them build the evidence needed to demonstrate that the legislative requirements have been met.
Meeting those requirements is not just about ticking a legal box. Members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, to protect their interests.
So, how should firms approach the Part VIII process?
While no analogy can fully capture the significance of a Part VIII transfer, particularly for mutuals with long histories and strong member communities, it may be helpful in illustrating the process itself, especially for those who are less familiar with Part VIII transfers. The decisions surrounding a transfer are often complex and significant. But when it comes to the process, it has some parallels with moving house. Driving the moving van into your new driveway may feel like the culmination of the journey, but a successful move depends on everything that happened beforehand. You need to understand why you are moving, weigh up the options, complete the necessary checks, and prepare carefully for what follows.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer.
As the slide shows, we have split that journey into five parts. Let me take each in turn.

Chart 1: Part VIII Transfer Process

Part A: Planning and preparation
Let me start with planning and preparation.
Every house move begins with a reason for moving. When my wife and I bought our home, we spent as much time discussing why we wanted to move as we spent choosing the house. Did we need more space? Or a shorter commute? Once we were clear about our objectives, many of the decisions that followed became easier.
A1: Intention to transfer, A4: Details of transfer plans
When similar questions are considered in the context of a Part VIII transfer, firms may have many avenues to explore. To help firms navigate these factors, the CP highlights the matters the PRA is likely to focus on early in the process, including members' interests.
Of course, firms will generally pursue a transfer because they believe it will deliver better outcomes for members. However, those benefits may not be shared equally between all members, and they may emerge at different times. It is possible that in some circumstances, particular groups of members could be worse off. The key question then is whether the transfer is in the interests of the members of each friendly society participating in the transfer.
Part of answering that question comes from how the benefits are expected to arise. Where a proposal relies on cost savings, operational changes, or integration programmes, those assumptions help explain how the combined business is expected to operate after the transfer. They can provide an important indication of whether there is a credible strategy and a realistic plan to deliver the expected benefits to members.
We have also found it helpful to consider the proposal from another perspective: in what circumstances might some members be worse off? Firms often undertake careful analysis of that question to understand whether potentially adverse impacts have been appropriately considered.
We can work with you as you develop your thinking in this area, which will help with later stages of the transfer. For example, some benefits may depend on integrating the two firms and could take several years to emerge. Whilst there are different ways to ensure that members will be protected in the meantime, the PRA can work with firms to establish what evidence could help show that the legal test has been met. These discussions could inform the transfer documentation, actuarial analysis, and communications with members.
A2: Preparations, updating rules, and applying for permission
Moving on to the preparations step, we have seen firms take a careful and considered approach to the practical aspects of the process. That includes considering whether the acquirer has the necessary regulatory permissions. This matters because permissions do not transfer with the business.
As an extra check, some firms have used the FCA’s register to compare the transferring society’s permission with the acquirer’s permission. This has allowed the acquirer to confirm whether it has identified and addressed any gaps in its permission.
This has also helped firms explain why a permission will no longer be required to cover specific regulated activities and, in doing so, show that the relevant statutory test has been met. These checks may appear relatively small. But when carried out early, they help the wider process run more efficiently.
A3: Considerations of overseas members and regulators
Turning to overseas members, this relates to one of the statutory tests, where the PRA must assess whether there is a substantial risk that the acquirer will be unable legally to carry on the business being transferred. This is usually relatively straightforward for members in the UK, but firms have found it more challenging for members based overseas.
Much of that work begins with a simple question: where are your members based? Maintaining up-to-date member records has helped firms with this work. There are other useful ways of checking those records. Some firms may find it helpful to consider payments to and from non-UK bank accounts to identify any other overseas members.
With that information in hand, firms can consider their overseas members in the context of the legal test and develop a reasoned explanation of why the legal test is met. There is a range of different forms of evidence to consider, from local legal advice to the relevant EIOPA recommendationfootnote [2]. The CP highlights engagement with overseas regulators, which firms may find to be a practical and cost-effective way of exploring the position.
While these steps should help, we recognise that firms continue to face challenges in this area. Indeed, we engaged with the Law Commission on the issue ahead of its recently published proposals. At our recent roundtablefootnote [3], firms also suggested ways in which the PRA could help firms with the overseas member part of the process. We are considering if we can further clarify what information we might need from firms in order for the PRA to assess the legal test under the existing legislation. We will, of course, consider this feedback alongside any responses we receive to the CP.
A5: PRA’s approach to special resolution: consent for Part VIII transfers
Let me turn to the final part of planning and preparation: what many firms call the dispensation process. This is where the acquiring society can seek the PRA's consent for the transfer to be approved by its board, rather than through a special resolution voted on by its members.
Giving the acquirer’s members the opportunity to vote is an important safeguard, so it is not a requirement the PRA will dispense with lightly. But we also recognise that holding a vote comes at a cost, which is ultimately borne by members.
In the past, firms have told us that this is one of the less predictable parts of the process, so we have added more clarity on our approach in the CP. It provides some reference points for how the PRA is likely to consider whether to consent to a dispensation. One of these is that firms will also need to show that the transfer is in the interests of the acquirer’s members and that there are no factors likely to lead a material number of them to vote against it. Firms are likely to benefit from discussing this with their transfer partner and considering this point together.
For example, that collaboration may bring to light a history of tension between the societies that could influence how members would vote if they were given the opportunity. Factors like this don’t necessarily mean that consent couldn’t be granted. But open discussions on such matters can help the PRA understand the position more quickly and reduce the need for further questions.
Part B: Recording and analysing the transfer
Let me move on to recording and analysing the transfer.
Once my family had decided which house to buy, our attention turned to the practicalities. The paperwork began, surveys were commissioned and the important decisions had to be documented.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer. Once firms have developed their proposal, the focus shifts to documenting the terms of the transfer and analysing its effects.
B1: Instrument of Transfer
Once firms are clear about the purpose and structure of the transaction, that understanding must be captured in the Instrument of Transfer. Producing the Instrument is a statutory requirement, but it can also provide important protections for the members of both firms.
The Instrument can cover a wide range of matters, from service standards to membership rights. We have seen firms benefit from bringing together legal, risk, and actuarial specialists to develop it. It has also helped firms consider not only what is needed to give effect to the transfer, but what additional protections could be provided to members, both now and over the long-term.
Those protections will depend on the circumstances of each transfer. We have seen firms consider important safeguards for the management of transferred funds, appropriate governance arrangements, and commitments about the future treatment of policyholders.
Where with-profits policies are involved, firms have found it helpful to specify the fund to which those policies will be allocated and how expenses will be apportioned. They have also considered what support may be available from other funds, particularly where this could affect the receiving fund’s investment strategy. Setting out these details in the draft Instrument can then provide a clear basis for the actuarial analysis supporting the transfer.
B2: Internal actuarial reports, B3: Independent actuary report and supplementary report(s)
The actuarial analysis is an important part of the process. Internal actuarial reports help boards and regulators understand how a proposed transfer is expected to affect members. Clear and balanced reports can also provide a strong foundation for communications with members, particularly where outcomes are uncertain or depend on judgement. The more useful reports explain the assumptions, evidence, and reasoning behind the conclusions they reach.
In our experience, the more complete internal actuarial reports consider how members are expected to be affected before the transfer, immediately after the transfer, as well as after any integration of the two businesses. This helps all of us – including members – understand both the destination and the journey to get there.
The firms’ own analysis is important. However, in some cases, the process also requires an independent perspective. Much as an independent surveyor provides an objective assessment when someone is purchasing a property, the Independent Actuary provides independent scrutiny of the firms’ analysis. The CP provides greater clarity on when we are likely to require a report from an Independent Actuary. We hope this will help firms better understand the likely costs of a transfer.
Where an Independent Actuary provides a report, the legislation requires it to address the likely effects of the transfer on members who are long-term policyholders. We have found that reports are most useful when they explain both the positive and adverse effects, how those effects may differ between groups of policyholders, and the basis for any conclusions about materiality. Of course, this balanced analysis helps members understand the proposal. But it also supports the PRA’s assessment of whether the transfer is in members’ interests, alongside the FCA’s consideration of fairness.
As an aside, we have found that it is often a good idea for firms to also consider any FCA requirements that apply to the transaction (for example, if the FCA's reattribution rules for with-profits business apply).
There is also an important relationship between the internal actuarial reports and the Independent Actuary’s report. If an internal report contains material information that is not reflected in the summary of the Independent Actuary’s report included in communications sent to members, firms will need to consider whether members have received all the information they need to understand the proposal and make an informed decision. This is one of the statutory tests the PRA must assess. In previous transfers, we have worked with firms to understand how they have met it.
Even where an Independent Actuary is not appointed, another form of independent review may still be valuable. We have seen firms benefit from independent peer review of their internal actuarial analysis and key judgements. This can strengthen the overall assessment and give members greater confidence in the analysis, particularly where they are considering whether to make representations about the proposed transfer.
Part C: Member engagement and member vote(s)
Having considered the key documents supporting a transfer, the next stage is to translate them into communications that members can understand and engage with.
When my family moved house, it wasn’t enough for me to know the plan. Everyone needed to understand what was happening, why it was happening and what it means for them (or, in our case, who was getting the biggest bedroom). Member engagement is similar. The technical analysis may be robust, but it only serves its purpose if members can understand what the transfer means for them.
C1: Member engagement: general approach, C2: Member engagement: Schedule 15 statement, C3: Resolutions
Member communications play an important role in informing how members vote. So, as you would expect, the FCA considers them through the lens of the Consumer Duty, with a focus on ensuring that they are clear and easy to understand. What makes the Part VIII transfer process slightly different is that the PRA also has a statutory role in reviewing one of the key communications sent to members: the Schedule 15 statement.
The CP provides more details on what the PRA considers as part of that review. I want to reflect on some practical approaches that we have seen work well in previous transfers.
The more developed Schedule 15 statements are those that clearly explain what the transfer means for members. They present the key considerations fairly and help members reach their own view. One approach that could work well is testing communications before they are finalised. We have read documents that include all the relevant technical details, but it is not always clear whether these messages are framed in the best way for members to fully understand them. To ensure that the proposed messages can be understood, it may be helpful to run the proposed communications past a colleague who has not been involved in the transfer or seek feedback from a small group of members.
We have also seen the value of careful and balanced drafting. The stronger summaries of the Independent Actuary’s conclusions tend to be those that faithfully reflect the full report while focusing on the matters most relevant to members’ decisions.
Of course, even the clearest communication is only effective if it reaches the people for whom it is intended. The legislation requires the Schedule 15 statement to be sent to all eligible voting members. Where firms have faced challenges contacting members, we have seen a range of practical approaches, including tracing exercises, updating records, using alternative contact methods, and contacting members directly to confirm their details. Firms have also used press notices and other engagement channels to raise awareness of the transfer and the voting process. In some cases, firms have supplemented this with dedicated webpages containing information about the transfer.
Although I have focused on the Schedule 15 statement, we have seen firms engage with their members in different ways. This includes with letters, frequently asked questions, presentations, webinars, and online material. The aim is to help members understand the proposed transfer and give them a genuine opportunity to engage with the proposal before casting their vote. Where members are effectively engaged, it helps firms address issues and reduce the likelihood of unexpected representations arising later in the transfer process.
Part D: Formal application, public notices, and representations
When buying a house, arguably the most important stage is the period leading up to the exchange of contracts. During that stage, surveyors, solicitors, mortgage brokers, and banks can all raise questions, identify risks or challenge assumptions underlying the proposed purchase.
D1: Formal notice of the application
The formal notice of the application plays an important role in the period leading up to the transaction, bringing it to the attention of interested parties and ensuring that those affected have an opportunity to engage with the process.
Firms will submit the formal notice after the member vote. So, whilst the progression of these tasks remains subject to member approval, there is preparatory work we can do ahead of that. In previous transfers, firms have provided draft notices for our review.
The PRA will also direct firms to publish the notice in the London, Edinburgh, or Belfast Gazettes as well as other newspapers where appropriate. However, firms can suggest which Gazette(s) and newspapers they feel would be the most appropriate.
D2: Approach to representations, D3: Representations Hearing
Once the formal notice has been published, the representations period begins. It gives members and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the transfer.
But the representations process is about more than formal representations submitted directly to the PRA. Firms also consider whether concerns, complaints, or queries received through their own channels raise issues that are similar in nature to a formal representation. These interactions can provide valuable insight into the matters that are most important to members.
Part E: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s) and related processes
The final stage of buying a house is exchanging contracts and moving into the property. By that point, much of the hard work has already been done. The legal issues have been addressed and the financing agreed. What remains is to finalise the purchase arrangements. The same principle applies to the final stage of a Part VIII transfer.
E1: Preparations for the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s), E2: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
The Preclusion Grounds Analysis sits at the heart of this stage. It explains why none of the statutory grounds that would prevent the PRA from confirming the transfer have been met. The stronger submissions tend to be balanced and leverage the evidence already generated throughout the transfer process and present it in a thorough and structured way.
Let me give you an example. When looking at the solvency ground, some firms carefully consider whether the acquiring society will maintain an adequate margin of solvency after the transfer. They bring together the evidence supporting that conclusion, such as post-transfer financial projections, actuarial analysis, audited financial information, and any material changes since the latest valuation date.
We have seen a similar approach taken when considering whether the members’ vote was representative. Firms’ analysis usually explains why the requirements of the legislation and the relevant society rules have been met. The more developed analyses also consider factors such as how voting turnout compares with previous member votes and whether the outcome would have changed under different assumptions. For example, where some members could not be traced despite reasonable efforts being made to contact them, firms could consider whether the outcome of the member vote would have been different if those members had voted against the transfer.
Perhaps the area where we have seen the greatest variation is the assessment of whether the proposed transfer is in the interests of the members of both societies. The more developed analyses bring together actuarial, risk, and legal evidence to consider factors such as benefit security, benefit expectations, service standards, and membership rights. They also identify situations in which some members may be disadvantaged and explain how those risks have been assessed and mitigated.
In considering firms’ post-transfer target operating models, we have taken a proportionate approach, with discussions often centred on three related questions.

How will the enlarged business operate immediately after the transfer?
What is the target operating model?
How does the firm intend to move from one to the other?

E3: The PRA’s decision, E4: Processes after the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
After the PRA has reached its decision, it is not the end of the journey. There are a few procedural steps left including issuing the decision notice and registering the Instrument of Transfer.
Firms will also continue implementing aspects of their target operating model after the transfer has completed. Boards should continue to satisfy themselves that members are seeing the expected benefits from the transfer.
Closing remarks
I appreciate that this statutory process may feel a long and complex journey. But members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, so it’s right that we approach the statutory requirements with care.
At the same time, we recognise that members ultimately benefit from an efficient process. CP12/26 sets out our proposals to make our approach clearer, more transparent, and easier to navigate. Your engagement has already informed those proposals, and I would encourage you to respond to the consultation so that we can continue refining our approach together.
I don’t want to close without recognising the important work being undertaken by the Law Commission to modernise the legislative framework for friendly societies. We have engaged with the Law Commission as it has developed its final report and draft bill Opens in a new window. Should any legislative changes be made, the PRA stands ready to update its approach and guidance as necessary.
I hope that what I’ve shared today will highlight that a successful transfer is not simply about completing a transaction or changing an address. It’s about finding the right long-term home for a friendly society’s members.
I am grateful to Hannah-Kousar Rashid for preparing these remarks. I am also grateful to Abi Batchelor, Alex Tapp, Giles Woodruff, Nozipho Gazi, Robert Kipling, Robyn Dwyer, Sanjeev Chandran, and Wayne Snow for their support and comments.

The observations shared in this speech are based on a range of firms and transfers at different times. They are illustrative of the general approach taken. articles.title: Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)
articles.text:
Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)

Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+) analysis was originally developed in 2007 to bring clarity to the evolving cost dynamics of various generation technologies at a time when no industry standard approach existed. It remains a widely cited resource grounded in Lazard's extensive industry expertise and client relationships.

Produced by Lazard’s Power, Energy and Infrastructure advisory group, the LCOE+ gives the sector a common, transparent yardstick for comparing the economics of different power sources. After nearly two decades of annual editions, it offers insight into how technology costs, financing conditions and market pressures shift over time.This 2026 report explores key aspects of energy generation, energy storage and system-level considerations, while reflecting on developments over the past 12 months.

Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ ReportLazard's 2026 LCOE+ report highlights that, despite rising and inflationary cost pressures across all generation technologies, renewables remain the most cost-competitive form of new-build generation on an unsubsidized basis (i.e., without tax subsidies). The report also emphasizes that meeting unprecedented power demand will require both a diverse generation fleet and a thoughtful acceleration of permitting and approval processes. At the same time, rising new-build costs and execution challenges have made replacement capacity more expensive and harder to deliver while load growth drives increased utilization of existing assets, improving their marginal cost relative to new-build LCOEs. Storage costs have also risen this year, reversing recent declines.Read the Report

2026 LCOE+ Report

In today's energy landscape, the relevance of data-driven cost analysis has never been greater. The LCOE+ captures a market defined by unprecedented demand growth, rising costs across every generation technology and an intensifying focus on reliability — making objective, real-world benchmarking more critical than ever for the stakeholders, policymakers and investors shaping the industry's future.

George Bilicic
Managing Director

Dive deeper into lazard's 2026 lcoe+George Bilicic joined the Redefining Energy Podcast to discuss Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ Report and the real cost of power.

Listen Here

We’ve entered a speed-to-power era—demand is outpacing supply, costs are climbing across every technology, and value is shifting to whoever can deliver capacity the fastest, renewables remain the lowest-cost and quickest to deploy resource, but meeting this moment will require a diverse generation fleet.

Samuel Scroggins
Managing Director

Frequently asked questions

BulletShares are a suite of defined maturity exchange-traded funds (ETFs) designed to help investors build targeted fixed income portfolios. Each fund holds a diversified basket of bonds that all mature in the same calendar year, helping investors target specific maturity timelines, risk preferences, and investment objectives. By combining the precision of individual bonds with the structural benefits of ETFs, BulletShares offer diversification, transparency, and liquidity. The funds typically distribute income monthly.

A bond ladder is built with individual bonds of varying maturities. As the bonds mature, the anticipated proceeds can be used for income needs or reinvested in new bonds that mature in subsequent years. Investors may use bond ladders to help create some predictability and stability regardless of market volatility and interest rate environments. Since they have specific maturity dates, investors can use BulletShares to build bond ladders without the time and expense of using individual bonds.

BulletShares can provide investors with an efficient way to establish potential protection from rising rates because the duration of the fund slowly rolls down to zero over the life of the ETF. Most traditional fixed income mutual funds and ETFs typically have a perpetual duration target, making them more sensitive to rising interest rates. Investors using BulletShares in bond ladders can also take advantage of rising interest rates by reinvesting the proceeds at maturity into BulletShares that mature in subsequent years and invest in bonds with higher interest rates.

BulletShares provide targeted exposure to investment-grade corporate bonds, high-yield corporate bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds and treasury bonds.

BulletShares have defined maturities to simulate the investor experience of buying and holding individual bonds to maturity for use in bond ladders and other strategies. BulletShares have designated years of maturities that are included in the fund’s name. Each BulletShares is designed to terminate in December of the designated year and make a final distribution at maturity. At each fund’s expected termination, the net asset value (NAV) of its assets is distributed to investors without any action on their part.

As BulletShares approach maturity, their durations decrease. In the last six months of the ETF’s maturity year, it is anticipated that the bonds in the portfolio will either mature or be called. Proceeds for these events will then be held either in cash or in cash equivalents such as US Treasury bills or commercial paper.

As your BulletShares mature, you may want to consult with an investment professional and explore having the distribution proceeds invested in a BulletShares ETF in a subsequent maturity year.
