Title: Why build a bond ladder with BulletShares ETFs
Description: Our BulletShares ETFs offer a flexible and cost-effective solution to help you achieve your income goals now and — and in the future. Our Head of Fixed Income and Alternatives ETF Product Strategy Jason Bloom explains why.
Hello, I’m Jason Bloom head of the Fixed Income ETF Product Strategy team.
Having a flexible and resilient income strategy is crucial because markets are everchanging. Bond ladders are a solution and our BulletShares ETFs offer a convenient and cost-effective solution to implement a ladder to help you achieve your income objectives now — and in the future.
Here’s how.
Think of a bond ladder as a series of bonds on rungs on a ladder with each bond maturing at a different time. As each bond matures, you can use the proceeds to either meet specific financial needs — such as college tuition or an upcoming tax bill — or reinvest the proceeds into new bonds with longer maturities and maintain the ladder.
There are two key reasons why bond ladders can be advantageous:
First, they can provide a predictable and steady income.
Second, you have the flexibility to tailor your portfolio’s maturity and duration profiles and adjust for interest rate changes. If interest rates increase, you can reinvest any proceeds from maturing bonds at higher future interest rates. If interest rates decrease, only a segment of your laddered portfolio has to be reinvested during the low-rate period.
BulletShares ETFs can help make building bond ladders easier and more efficient. They have designated maturity years and cover a range of bond types, including investment-grade corporate, high-yield corporate, and municipal bonds. This allows you to build a bond ladder that matches with your financial goals.
They also combine the best of both worlds ­— the benefits of individual bonds and the advantages of exchange-traded funds.
Like individual bonds, BulletShares offer the potential for monthly income and a final distribution at maturity. You choose your portfolio’s maturity, yield, and credit quality.
As ETFs, BulletShares provide enhanced diversification, liquidity, transparency, convenience, and cost-effectiveness.
Whether you’re looking to generate steady income, customize your portfolio, or insulate against interest rate fluctuations, BulletShares ETFs provide a robust and versatile tool for building bond ladders.
Let’s build a stronger financial future together.
Before investing, investors should carefully read the prospectus/summary prospectus and carefully consider the investment objectives, risks, charges, and expenses. For this and more complete information about the Fund call 800-983-0903 or visit invesco.com for the prospectus/summary prospectus.

During periods of rising interest rates, an issuer may exercise its right to pay principal on an obligation later than expected, resulting in a decrease in the value of the obligation and in a decline in the funds’ income.
An issuer’s ability to prepay principal prior to maturity can limit the funds’ potential gains. Prepayments may require the funds to replace the loan or debt security with a lower yielding security, adversely affecting the funds’ yield.

For example, at times the funds may make distributions at a greater (or lesser) rate than the coupon payments received, which will result in the funds returning a lesser (or greater) amount on liquidation than would otherwise be the case. The rate of fund distribution payments may affect the tax characterization of returns, and the amount received as liquidation proceeds upon fund termination may result in a gain or loss for tax purposes.

20 November 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Staying diversified,adding US mega caps
AI-related concerns continue to weigh on equities, especially with new US restrictions on third-country access to advanced American semiconductor chips. Renewed volatility across the AI ecosystem drove the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) back above 25.
However, two major event risks this week turned out to be less concerning – Nvidia’s Q3 revenue and earnings exceeded expectations, while Anthropic’s record initial public offering was priced above its indicative range.
Our quant models are not signalling a strong buy signal yet. However, with VIX spiking above 25 and investor positioning and sentiment indicators suggesting limited downside, we see value emerging in the US mega caps segment following its recent underperformance.
We add an opportunistic idea on US mega cap equities, which we see benefitting from scale, financial strength and potential industry consolidation.

How will US chip restrictions impact the technology sector?

What are the implications of the Fed’s latest meeting minutes on bonds?

Do you see opportunities in gold after the latest selloff?

Charts of the week: Oil’s disinflation effect

Falling oil and fuel prices likely to support disinflation in 2027; bonds are starting to offer greater diversification benefits

Projected* y/y change in crude oil and gasoline prices by quarter

21- and 126-day rolling correlation of global equities and bonds

Source: US Energy Information Administration, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *EIA projections
Editorial

Staying diversified, adding US mega caps

Strategy summary. AI-related concerns continue to weigh on equities, especially with new US restrictions on third-country access to advanced American semiconductor chips. Renewed volatility across the AI ecosystem drove the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) back above 25. However, two major event risks this week turned out to be less concerning – Nvidia’s Q3 revenue and earnings exceeded expectations, while Anthropic’s record initial public offering was priced above its indicative range.
Our quant models are not signalling strong buy signal yet. However, with VIX spiking above 25 and investor positioning and sentiment indicators suggesting limited downside, we see value emerging in the US mega caps segment following its recent underperformance. We add an opportunistic idea on the segment, which we see benefitting from scale, financial strength and potential industry consolidation.
Opportunistically adding US megacaps. Asian equities led declines this week, led by Taiwan, China and Korea, after new US export controls targeted access to advanced AI computing through overseas data centres. Licensing requirements focus on capacity supplied to restricted customers, with additional controls affecting regional hubs. These measures increase compliance burdens and financing uncertainty, potentially weighing on AI capital expenditure. We expect the market’s AI capex estimates for 2027 to be cut towards our own more-conservative projections. Established cloud operators (hyperscalers) may be better equipped to manage customer checks than smaller providers. We initiate an opportunistic idea on US mega caps as we see a catch-up opportunity, given their established franchises, strong cash generation and relatively resilient earnings prospects (see page 7 for details).
Diversifying beyond the AI trade. Although positive cross asset and sector correlations returned this week, sector rotations earlier this month reinforces the importance of maintaining exposure to different drivers of equity returns. Our preferred US sectors remain technology, healthcare, financials and materials, combining technology participation with opportunities beyond AI. Beyond the US, we like Euro area and Japanese banks, which are benefitting from elevated interest rates, actively managed global dividend strategies for income

.

opportunities, and Indian equities due to their low correlation with the AI trade.
Allure of high dividend equities. While global dividend yields remain historically low, attractive pockets persist. The Swiss equity market yields almost 4%, versus 1.6% for global equities. Euro area (3.6%), Australia (3.5%) and Singapore (3.4%) are other leading dividend paying markets. Taiwan offers almost a 2% yield, combining income with structural growth opportunities. We favour active management over simply chasing yield, avoiding value traps. Dividend equities can complement bonds within a diversified portfolio, balancing income opportunities with broader exposure across markets.
Increasing diversification offered by bonds. The one-month correlation between global stocks and bonds has turned negative after more than a year. This means bonds are offering greater diversification benefits amid the equity drawdown. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting suggest policymakers are likely to hike rates further. However, we remain dovish vs. markets on the Fed’s 12-month rates outlook (we see Fed target rate at 4.25% by end-2027 vs. market pricing above 4.5%) as lower oil prices and fading tariff effects lead to noticeable disinflation by H2 2027. Thus, we see particular value in the 3-7-year maturity bucket, with a preference for BB-to-BBB segment corporate bonds, which have resilient balance sheets and offer attractive yield pick-up. We see the US 10-year government bond offering value if the yield rises above 5.25%.
Dollar appears overbought; potential for gold upside: The USD index (DXY) has jumped over 2% in the past two weeks after stronger-than-expected US jobs and inflation reports for October revived Fed rate hike bets. Nevertheless, crude oil prices have slumped almost 20% this month as the Republican party’s heavy losses in the US mid-term elections raised the prospects of de-escalation in the Middle East conflict. Forward markets are pricing US crude oil below USD 75/bbl by Q3 next year. Lower oil prices are likely to support disinflation next year. With DXY technically overbought and Fed policy expectations excessively hawkish, we expect a pullback in USD. Conversely, gold looks oversold. We see an upside for XAU/USD, despite revising lower our 3- and 12-month targets (see page 7).
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as neutral for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Strong US retail sales; ongoing peace talks(-)factors: Broad-based China slowdown; hawkish central banks

Top client questions

How will the new US semiconductor restrictions impact the technology sector?

Our view: While compute is likely to remain a bottleneck for AI, greater US regulatory restrictions could weigh on AI capex.
Rationale: The US has announced broader restrictions on overseas computing capacity used by Chinese and other restricted-country companies, extending controls beyond physical chip shipments to remote access through data centres. This could delay data centre deployments and raise financing costs, as affected operators may defer expansion plans until licences or replacement customers are secured. Lower spending could weigh on chip and hardware orders, bringing consensus capex estimates closer to our forecasts. While we expect AI capex to rise 50% to USD 1.2trn in 2027, supported by projects already under construction, the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2027 and 2030 is likely to moderate to c.12%.
We therefore favour broadening technology exposure beyond semiconductors through our US Information Technology (IT) opportunistic idea, which also includes hardware and software industries. Investors should also consider diversifying into our other preferred sectors, such as US healthcare and financials.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

AI capital expenditure (capex) should continue to rise, but growth is expected to moderate from 2028
Global AI capex (USD bn)

Source: Company reports, Standard Chartered

How were Chinese technology giants’ Q3 2026 earnings?

Our view: Chinese tech giants’ Q3 earnings highlight growing demand for AI, but heavy spending is pressuring margins and cash flow, underscoring the need for stronger AI monetisation.
Rationale: Heavy AI capex continues to weigh on profitability, compressing near-term margins and deepening negative free cash flows, with share dilution a riskas tech giants may have to tap into equity markets for the AI buildout. Cloud growth points to genuine AI demand, but the AI-related revenue contribution remains small relative to the cost base. AI monetisation remains challenging, with competition set to intensify. Weak consumer spending was a common thread contributing to revenue misses. Major players reiteratedthe need for more tangible investment returns amid aggressive AI investments.
In the near term, investor sentiment remains weighed down by tightening US restrictions targeting China’s access to advanced chips, introducing downside risks to 2027 AI cloud revenue. While this could hamper the development of next-generation AI models, accelerating domestic AI chip adoption should benefit local semiconductor companies as China pushes for technological self-sufficiency.We expect rising AI adoption to benefit China’s IT sector over time, though we prefer diversifying our China equity exposure across preferred sectors, such as financials and healthcare.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

China’s technology sector valuation remains inexpensive at 12.9x, falling 1 standard deviation below the mean
Hang Seng Technology (HSTECH Index) 12-month forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What are the implications of the October Fed meeting minutes for the rate path forward and short-dated bonds? Do US 10-year government bonds now offer a good re-entry point?

Our view: October’s Fed meeting minutes maintained a hawkish-hold narrative. We continue to expect the Fed to raise rates by 25bps at its 8-9 December meeting. However, with short-dated US government bonds having largely priced in three hikes by June 2027, we see any spike above 5.25% in the US 10-year bond yield as an opportunistic bullish entry point.
Rationale: The hawkish-hold tone of the Fed’s October meeting minutes suggests the December Fed meeting is ‘live’. The market is currently pricing in three hikes by year-end 2027 (vs. our expectation of two hikes by H1 2027 followed by a potential cut in H2 2027). Short-dated government bond yields – using the US 2-year yield as a proxy – have largely priced in three hikes, and we do not expect the hawkish minutes to have a material impact on them.
Should the US 10-year government bond yield spike above 5.25%, the near-term risk-reward would become favourable, in our opinion. As we expect inflation to moderate in H2 2027, we see scope for the Fed to pivot towards easing, and we would turn more constructive on short-dated government bonds. We expect the US 2-year government bond yield to decline to 4.00-4.25% in 12 months, contributing to yield curve steepening.
— Ray Heung, Senior Investment Strategist

US short-term government bond yields have largely priced in 2-3 Fed rate hikes
US government bond yield curve, current and three months ago

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Is it time to add exposure to the EUR after its recent slide against the USD?

Our view: Yes, we are bullish on EUR/USD and favour gradually adding EUR exposure in the coming weeks. Markets are pricing in more Fed tightening than we expect. Lower oil prices support the Euro area and are likely to ease the Fed’s inflation concerns on a forward-looking basis.
Rationale: Lower oil prices are a double positive for EUR/USD, as they ease costs for Euro area households and businesses and temper US inflation, reducing the need for the Fed to tighten as much as markets expect.
Markets are pricing in a terminal Fed funds rate close to 4.63%, down from 4.72% a week ago, with the yield curve now also pricing a rate-cutting cycle after the September 2027 peak. We expect the bullish near-term USD momentum to linger until markets’ peak rate expectations converge towards our view. EUR/USD’s relative strength index (RSI) is below 30, and consolidation above 1.0950 points to oversold conditions. We expect a rebound towards 1.11 to confirm our recovery view in the next three weeks.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist

EUR/USD oversold; near-term rebound risk grows
EUR/USD and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What could support a sustained recovery in the AUD?

Our view: We believe a sustained AUD recovery requires a combination of domestic resilience and fading USD momentum.
Rationale: AUD/USD has been pressured by two key external headwinds: hawkish Fed repricing and weaker AI-related risk sentiment. A reversal in either could provide scope for recovery.
Softer US economic data or less hawkish Fed communication could ease upward pressure on US government bond yields, narrow rate differentials and weaken the USD. At the same time, a stabilisation in AI and broader equity sentiment could restore demand for the risk-sensitive AUD, particularly if Asian equities recover.
Domestic fundamentals remain a relative source of support. Still-elevated inflation should constrain the RBA’s ability to turn dovish quickly, while exporter and real-money demand for the AUD could cushion the downside. However, Australia’s rising unemployment raises the prospect of RBA rate cuts in H2 2027, potentially eroding the AUD’s carry advantage over time. With AUD/USD technically oversold, we see scope for a rebound from 0.6600, with 0.6830 as the key resistance level.
— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

Looking for a near-term AUD/USD rebound
AUD/USD and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

How will the improving oil supply-demand balance shape crude oil prices over the coming quarters?

Our view: Improving supply-demand balances should support inventory rebuilding and ease oil prices over time, despite persistent geopolitical risks, supporting disinflation in H2 2027.
Rationale: Crude oil’s recent retreat marks an important transition: expanding physical supply is finally asserting control over headline geopolitical noise. With non-OPEC production resilient, Gulf exports recovering and alternative transit routes adapting, markets are steadily pricing in an approaching supply surplus.
However, high freight costs and extended voyage times keep significant crude oil volumes tied up at sea rather than refilling local storage tanks. Crucially, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve’s crude inventories have fallen nearly 33% from pre-conflict levels, leaving a thinner buffer against renewed supply disruptions.
For investors, improving fundamentals point to gradual price normalisation as trade routes adapt, despite persistent geopolitical volatility. We expect near-term West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil to range between USD 80/bbl and USD 90/bbl. Softer energy prices should provide some relief to headline inflation, but are unlikely to materially alter the Fed’s near-term policy trajectory.
— Anthony Naab, Investment Strategist

Gulf crude flows have recovered to nearly 70% of their pre-conflict levels, easing supply constraints
Gulf crude oil exports (mb/week)

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Are there any tactical opportunities amidst the equity drawdown?

Our view: We introduce US mega cap equities as a new opportunistic idea, favouring their scale and financial strength amid heightened volatility and potential industry consolidation.
Rationale: We believe the mid-cycle backdrop favours large companies with strong cash generation, established competitive positions and the financial capacity to invest through periods of uncertainty. US mega caps’ forward P/E has fallen well below its two-year average and the -2x standard deviation level, offering a more attractive entry point into US market leaders.
A potential reset in AI capex expectations could also accelerate industry consolidation, favouring established leaders with the balance sheets, infrastructure and customer reach to sustain investment and capture market share. Key risks include a sharper-than-expected economic slowdown, weaker returns on AI investment, regulatory pressures, key man risks and concentration in a few dominant companies.
— Robin Xie, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

We introduce US mega caps as a new opportunistic idea, favouring their scale and financial strength amid heightened volatility and potential industry consolidation
Equity opportunistic ideas: Adding US mega caps

Source: Standard Chartered. * Denotes new idea, with performance measured based on the S&P Top 20 Select 35/20 Capped Index

Do you see opportunities in gold after the recent sell-off?

Our view: We are lowering our gold price targets to USD 4,000/oz (three months) and USD 4,500/oz (12 months). Despite gold’s recent drop below our revised three-month price target, we continue to believe the precious metal can rebound in the medium term.
Rationale: Several factors have been driving down gold prices. A combination of stronger-than-expected US jobs, consumer inflation and producer inflation reports since early November has reinforced the case for Fed tightening. This, in turn, brought renewed hawkish Fed rhetoric, driving up the repricing of Fed rate-hike expectations. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold, while also strengthening the USD – a double headwind for bullion. In addition, recent volatility in the equity markets has raised liquidity needs for leveraged investors, causing some of them to sell gold to cover their losses.
However, at current levels, gold has undershot even our newly revised three-month price target for the precious metal. Emerging Market central banks remain structural buyers of gold as they continue to shift away from USD-denominated reserves. The US fiscal outlook remains dire, and with political gridlock now having returned to Washington, persistent fiscal deficits with no reforms will likely remain entrenched for the next two years at least. Confidence in US government finances and the USD is expected to weaken into 2027, and investors are likely to once again turn to gold as a store of value, informing our 12-month price target of USD 4,500/oz.
— Jonathan Liang, CFA, CIO, Fixed Income and FX

articles.title: First Meeting with a Financial Advisor | Wells Fargo Advisors
articles.text:
Day One With Your Financial Advisor

Preparing for your first meeting

Your first meeting with your Financial Advisor marks the beginning of an important professional relationship. Just as you rely on your doctor with your health and your mechanic with your car, you’ll be entrusting your Financial Advisor with something of great value too — your financial goals.

call out

Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client.

end call out

Our Financial Advisors work with many types of investors and value their diversity. Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client — so he or she can understand the best way to help you with your investment needs and life goals.

The right fit

Meeting with a Financial Advisor for the first time, you should expect a friendly, casual conversation — you’re just getting to know each other. There’s no obligation, no pressure, no judgment — and no cost for your first meeting. You should be candid about your level of investing experience, overall financial situation, and financial goals. You should also feel comfortable asking as many questions as you’d like.
It’s important you choose a Financial Advisor who listens to your concerns, understands your financial needs, and values your input. The relationship between you and your Financial Advisor is a critical one — through the years, you should have many sensitive, private conversations. The relationship may even expand to include friends and future generations of your family.

Getting ready

Before the meeting, your Financial Advisor should send you a checklist of items to bring. Your privacy is a top priority, and your Financial Advisor is committed to maintaining strict confidentiality.
A good Financial Advisor will want the right fit for you as much you seek the right fit in him or her. Before your first consultation, you’ll want to reflect on and be prepared to discuss:

Your values about money and your vision for your future
What life events are happening or could potentially happen
Short- and long-term life and financial goals
Investment questions
Your current financial situation
Preferred account management style

Remember, the more you share about your financial picture, investment goals, and risk tolerance, the better your Financial Advisor will be able to recommend strategies and create an investment plan. You’ll find the initial meeting with your Financial Advisor will set the stage for many conversations to come.

Next steps

Think about how you prefer to work with your advisor and what types of investments you’re interested in.
Gather the necessary documentation for your initial meeting and prepare answers to questions your advisor may ask.

articles.title: Measuring Active Risk Under the Total Portfolio Approach | BNY
articles.text:
Risk management

Measuring What Matters: A Practical Guide to Active Risk Under the Total Portfolio Approach

As plan sponsors move from Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) to Total Portfolio Approach (TPA), wider flexibility demands a new approach to measuring active risk.

alarm

6 minutes read

calendar_today

20 Nov, 2026

Key Takeaways

TPA replaces rigid asset-class targets with a broader reference portfolio and a wider active risk budgetForward-looking ex-ante risk analytics become essential for managing total portfolios effectively under the TPA frameworkBNY Risk View uses a full-revaluation security-level approach to build confidence in portfolio risk outputsBest practices start with the risk question and measure ex-ante risk to course correct in real time

A Wider Budget Demands a Sharper Lens

As more U.S. plan sponsors move from Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) to a Total Portfolio Approach (TPA), they gain greater flexibility to allocate capital to the opportunities they view as most attractive on a risk-adjusted basis. This flexibility helps them respond more effectively to changing market conditions in pursuit of greater alpha across the plan. However, it also carries a wider active risk budgets, making forward-looking risk measurement more essential to managing the portfolio.
But measuring active risk under TPA is not simply a matter of widening the budget. It requires a different lens — one that decomposes risk across the total portfolio, stress-tests decisions before they’re made and treats analytics as an input into allocation, not just a report on it.

The Shift from SAA to TPA

The key difference is flexibility, and that shift changes how we measure and manage risk.
Under SAA, teams operate within board-approved asset class targets and ranges, with limited scope for tactical positioning within those parameters. Active risk, typically measured as tracking error, the expected volatility of returns relative to a benchmark, stays tightly bounded. The board and investment teams manage it at two levels: a total-plan budget of 2–3%, and narrower risk budgets at the asset-class budget level.
Under TPA, the emphasis shifts from “Are we close to our strategic weights?” to “Are we taking the right risks across the total portfolio to generate additional alpha in pursuit of our objectives?” Instead of managing against a traditional policy benchmark, the plan may adopt a broader reference portfolio; for example, 75% MSCI ACWI IMI Net / 25% Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate. The team still operates within an active risk budget, but it may be wider, for example 4–5% versus 2–3% under SAA, giving investment teams greater flexibility while preserving disciplined oversight of total portfolio risk.

Same Portfolio, Different Lens

The same portfolio shows a 1-year ex-ante (forward-looking) tracking error of 2.3% against an SAA policy benchmark — but 4.0% against a broader TPA reference benchmark. The portfolio itself has not changed. What has changed is the lens through risk is measured.

The example also illustrates why looking beyond allocation weights matters: a relatively smaller portfolio allocation can account for a disproportionate share of active risk.

Why Risk Analytics Is Critical under TPA

Greater flexibility makes robust risk measurement more important, not less. A team operating with a wider active risk budget and greater discretion needs confidence in its ex-ante view of risk today — rather than waiting years for realized ex-post (backward-looking) tracking error to show, after the fact, how those risks played out.

4 Questions Every Team Should Answer Continuously

#1
How much active risk are we assuming?
#2
Where is that risk coming from?
#3
Which positions, managers, and asset classes are driving it?
#4
What happens to portfolio risk if we reallocate capital, add a new investment or appoint a prospective manager?

Under TPA, risk analytics move beyond measurement and become an input into portfolio construction. Teams can decompose ex-ante active risk at the manager, asset-class and total-plan levels — and run what-if analysis to test allocation decisions before implementing them. In practical terms, this reframes the question from simply measuring risk to asking: “If we make this investment decision, what happens to our total portfolio risk?” These capabilities are valuable under either framework but become increasingly important as investment teams gain greater flexibility to allocate across the total portfolio.

Confidence in the Risk Engine Matters

Investment decisions are only as good as the risk analytics that support them. At BNY, our risk framework — BNY Risk View, developed in partnership with Innocap — employs a complex risk methodology (a full revaluation) security-level approach to calculate risk. BNY Risk View uses Axioma’s Multi-Asset Class risk model as the core model is a holdings-based, scenario-driven security level risk model. BNY Risk View supports Monte Carlo, Historical, VaR and Relative VaR methodologies, along with deep-sensitivity and stress-testing capabilities.
The reason this matters is practical, not theoretical: a full-revaluation, security-level approach gives investment teams the granularity and transparency to understand risk down to the position level. That, in turn, helps build confidence in the risk outputs that inform portfolio construction, active risk budgeting and investment decisions.

Best Practices: A Checklist

Best Practices for Asset Owners under TPA

Start with the risk question, not the tool. Define the decisions the team needs to make — decomposing risk, testing allocations, stress-testing — and let those requirements drive the framework choice.
Measure ex-ante risk to make investment decisions — don’t wait for ex-post risk to be realized. Forward-looking tracking error lets teams course-correct in real time; waiting years for realized results turns risk management into an autopsy.
Decompose risk to its sources. The total number is necessary but not sufficient — teams need to see which positions, managers, and asset classes are driving it.
Treat risk analytics as an allocation input, not just a report. The most valuable use is pre-decision: running what-if analysis before reallocating, not measuring the outcome after.
Demand sufficient transparency and granularity for more robust Monte Carlo simulations. Security-level analysis can help teams understand what is driving risk and build confidence in the numbers informing allocation decisions.
Anchor accountability in human judgment. Analytics inform decisions; they don’t make them. The team — not the engine — owns the allocation.

Looking Ahead

The transition from SAA to TPA is not a binary one; it runs along a spectrum. What unites every plan along that spectrum is a common imperative: as investment flexibility increases, the analytics used to measure and manage risk must keep pace.
The plan most likely to succeed will pair broader discretion with equally robust risk analytics — understanding how much forward-looking active risk they are taking, where that risk comes from, and how individual decisions may change it. Whether operating under SAA or TPA, or transitioning between the two, the practical question is the same: “Do we have the robust risk measurement capabilities and tools in place to use our flexibility deliberately to create alpha?”.
That is the question every plan sponsor should be asking, and the answer requires analytics that can decompose risk to the position level, stress-test decisions before they're made, and keep pace with the flexibility TPA demands.

Continue Exploring Best Practices for Asset Owners

From risk to data management, our Best Practices series explores the practical capabilities asset owners need to navigate change and make confident decisions. Next, explore A Different Lens on Data: Driving Innovation and Insight Through Data Best Practices

articles.title: Cybersecurity & Fraud: Protecting Your Information | KKR
articles.text:
Security and Fraud Awareness
KKR prioritizes the security of our clients’ information and assets and is committed to ensuring that clients and employees are made aware of fraudulent schemes and activities when communicating with KKR. Fraud is an issue that companies may face regardless of size, industry, or country.
While we maintain robust cybersecurity measures, cyber criminals may seek to impersonate or claim affiliation with KKR and create fraudulent websites, email domains, applications, and social media accounts. Fraudsters may pose as legitimate organizations and send emails or make phone calls to extract personal data that can be manipulated for the use of financial crimes. These scams are complex as the perpetrators may use real employee names and replicate proprietary documentation.

articles.title: The next big asset class could come from emerging markets
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

The next big asset class could come from emerging markets

Ajay Banga

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma

November 13, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

Español

中文

English

Français

Español

中文

A KIOO employee in Tanzania checks glass bottles for inconsistences or defects. Copyright: World Bank Group

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, but their economies are expected to create only around 400 million jobs. That 800 million gap could have implications for poverty, migration, and stability. But, with the right ingredients, this generation can drive growth and prosperity at home and around the world.
It is an objective that cannot be met with public finance alone. Much progress has already been made in building public-private partnerships that deliver the resources needed to realize growth in emerging markets and developing countries.
We can therefore build on progress. For instance, the World Bank Group has grown private capital mobilization from $35 billion in 2022 to $112 billion last year. Comparatively, all OECD countries mobilized approximately $600 billion between 2012 and 2024.
It is the product of a workplan and a model that we believe should be replicated among governments and development banks working together with the private sector to multiply their impact by using their own resources to attract far more capital than they could provide alone.
Most of this has been done through individual deals, and this gets us only so far. The next frontier is bringing institutional capital into development at scale. Institutional capital is invested in almost everything, from government bonds and office towers to private credit and renewable energy. Yet one enormous investment opportunity remains largely untapped: investing in businesses across emerging and frontier markets.
We want to change that.
For decades, multilateral development banks have held loans they provide to finance businesses and infrastructure on their own balance sheets. They have accumulated financial assets, expertise and hard-won knowledge of how these investments perform. Now, rather than keeping those assets, development banks are making them available to institutional investors. Transferring those assets to long-term investors frees up capital for new projects, multiplying the impact that development banks have with the resources available.
The Netherlands and the World Bank are working together to further unlock these opportunities. The World Bank brings investments, country knowledge, and experience in managing risk. The Netherlands has a strong development tradition, financial expertise and institutional investors that see value in investing in emerging markets. This leads to concrete results. For instance, ILX invests capital on behalf of Dutch and Danish pension funds alongside the IFC in sustainable forestry in Uruguay. This allows for expansion of sustainable forestry while reducing waste and enhancing exports, leading to more jobs and growth in Uruguay while supplying sustainably sourced wood for construction in Europe and elsewhere.
The opportunities are already available, but further scaling-up institutional investments requires changing how assets reach the market. Pension funds need scale, diversification, reliable information and familiar structures. They cannot assess thousands of individual loans, each with different terms and documentation. That is why the World Bank Group and five other multilateral development banks are working on common ways to assess, document, package and transfer investments. Done well, this can attract more investors and release development bank capital for the next generation of projects.
We know that institutional investors often consider emerging markets to be risky investments, but the data shows that this is not the case.
The Global Emerging Markets Risk Database, or GEMs, draws on decades of lending experience of multilateral development banks (MDB) and development finance institutions (DFI) originated private debt. With 30 years of information on loans, it provides a clear picture of credit performance. It shows that the average default rate of EM market private debt is comparable to developed markets. However, recovery rates are above many global benchmarks. Crucially, the default patterns are only weakly correlated with developed markets, making emerging market investments with MDBs/DFIs a compelling diversifier in institutional portfolios.
The World Bank Group has demonstrated what can be achieved. Dutch investors have shown that institutional capital can participate. Now the ambition is to make that participation commonplace. If only 1% of the USD 100 trillion assets under management from global institutional investors and pension funds would go to emerging and frontier markets in the coming years, this would mean USD 1 trillion extra in investments in clean water, energy transition, healthcare and jobs. It would also mean that institutional investors gain access to attractive markets, and we build new ties between countries. A triple win worth investing in together.
And if we get this right, a young boy can go to school to realize his dream of becoming an engineer. A woman can grow her business into an international business. This will shape the economic future of a generation.

Ajay Banga

President, World Bank Group

articles.title: View from the markets: The next chapter for monetary policy and the bond market - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Alessandro Tentori, Senior Market Strategist, Europe

Former US Federal Reserve Chair, Ben Bernanke, once quipped that “monetary policy is 98% talk and 2% action”. But recently, central banks have tried to shift more towards action, primarily through strategy reviews – focusing on the modelling framework and repeated references to the incoming data landscape.

Still, semantic nuances and almost imperceptible variations in tone make fascinating fare for watchers and investors alike.

We’ve lived through many shocks and surprises this year, but the economy has remained resilient thanks to a technological innovation – namely artificial intelligence – that promises to affect our productivity beyond the scale experienced in the mid-1990s.

At the same time, inflation has surprised to the upside. These two variables merit our attention.

Measuring the AI effect

There is a tremendous effort to measure AI’s contribution to output and economists will undoubtedly receive more information as the technology spreads to all sectors of the economy.

The adoption process takes some time – in 1987 Nobel Prize winning economist Robert Solow famously said “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics” – but we can rely on a solid theoretical framework which allows us to put technological change, potential growth and the natural rate of interest into one box.

And that is exactly what central bankers have done in the past 12 months, as they’ve realised that monetary policy’s neutral range might have shifted upward owing to an unprecedented productivity boost.

Neutral rate – where art thou?

Of course, if you ask two central bankers where they see the neutral interest rate – the theoretical real interest rate which neither stimulates nor restricts growth – you will most likely hear three different answers. This is where the art of central banking is required, and where the wording and the nuances matter most.

In retrospect, we could say that both the Fed and the European Central Bank have done a tremendous job in not scaring the financial markets, by describing their actions as a step-by-step search for the neutral interest rate. In doing so, they have smartly avoided the risk of sparking a painful discussion about a tightening cycle.

Market-based expectations at the beginning of 2026 were for two rate cuts by the Fed and the ECB standing pat. Instead, the Fed has already hiked once and is expected to deliver another 25 basis points in December. Similarly, the ECB has already increased rates twice and will most likely add a third hike in a few weeks’ time.

This is a significant U-turn in monetary policy, which under normal circumstances might have triggered fears of a recession. Not in 2026, though, and the reason might again be technological change and central banks’ wise guidance on the neutral interest rate.

The next chapter: Inflation

I think we are within reach of the neutral rate, both in Frankfurt and in the US. The question is therefore about the next chapter in this monetary policy story, which leads us straight to inflation.

Since the Middle East crisis, inflation has accelerated almost everywhere due to both direct and indirect effects. On the other hand, there is little evidence – indeed, arguably none – of so-called second-round inflation, which is primarily associated with inflation expectations and requires an asymmetric inflationary shock to be both deep and long-lasting.

Therefore, central banks are managing the risk of second-round inflation rather than inflation itself, as recently suggested by Bank of England Chief Economist, Huw Pill.

Looking ahead, the risk is that the current above-target inflation mutates into entrenched inflation. Growing inflation expectations should be on everybody’s radar screen as this would constitute another significant surprise for market participants after this year’s policy U-turn.

Concretely, the risk is about central banks having to switch from their storyline of “reaching neutral” to one of a “policy tightening cycle”, thus hitting both risk premia and corporate valuations.

As Exhibit 1 shows, the market is not pricing in a hiking cycle for the Fed or the ECB beyond the next two to three rate hikes. In other words, a policy path that diverges significantly from whatever neutral level the central bankers have in mind would definitely take investors by surprise.

Source: Bloomberg, 18 November 2026

Government bond markets: More than just inflation and rates

Equally, the bond universe is not immune to such a scenario. Market-based inflation expectations have orbited slightly above target for the past four years, thus confirming both central banks’ credibility and a striking contrast with survey-based inflation measures.

However, the discussion about government bond markets is more subtle than just inflation and interest rate expectations.

According to the International Monetary Fund’s Fiscal Monitor, expansionary fiscal policy in an environment of increasing yields will require ever-increasing bond issuance by governments in developed markets for the next five years.

And as the demand side can no longer rely on infinitely elastic balance sheets (i.e., quantitative easing), the question suddenly becomes: Who will buy all these bonds, and at what price?

If there is one certainty in a world of uncertainty, it is that there will be more government bonds tomorrow than there are today.

articles.title: After the Blue Tsunami: Getting rid of Trump’s tariffs
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

After the Blue Tsunami: Getting rid of Trump’s tariffs

Alan Wm. Wolff (PIIE)

Date
November 16, 2026 12:25 PM

Photo Credit: Sipa USA via Reuters/Matthew Kaminsky

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Can we expect the House and Senate Democratic majorities taking office in January to quickly succeed in rolling back very unpopular policies like President Donald Trump's tariffs? It is far from easy, but not impossible. Passing anti-tariff legislation will be difficult because the incoming Congress will need enough votes to override a likely presidential veto. For the next two years, absent a concerted effort, the likely outcome will be a legislative stalemate on most of the tariffs, leaving hopes for removing them pinned on the courts.
Trump, whose term lasts into January 2029, likes tariffs. He believes in the correctness of his tariffs. They are hallmarks of his administration. The likelihood of Trump signing a bill lifting the tariffs is about zero. Overriding his veto requires the votes of at least 290 House members and 67 senators. Though votes are still being counted as of this writing on November 16, the Associated Press(link is external) reports that Democrats will hold at least 256 House seats and 55 Senate seats (including two independents who caucus with the Democrats)—solid majorities, but not enough to override a veto. Vetoes are hard to override. Congress has overridden only 112(link is external) of the 2,599 presidential vetoes made since George Washington took office in 1789.
Options before the incoming Congress
The new congressional majorities have a few tools they can use. They can add a blanket repeal of the tariffs Trump imposed to a must-pass(link is external) bill like the National Defense Authorization Act(link is external) (NDAA). Otherwise, they can offer a standalone bill expecting his veto but forcing him and his congressional supporters to own the tariffs' costs to consumers and small businesses. A third possibility for the Democrats is to scale back the level of their ambition and attempt to lift the most recent anti-Canada tariffs by repealing the statute on which they are based (Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930) and by supporting North American free trade. This could succeed for a few reasons: The 1930 statute invoked as authority for the tariffs is no longer in force anyway. Moreover, Trump's tariffs against Canada, a close neighbor and ally, are harmful to US businesses and are particularly unpopular(link is external). But while canceling those tariffs would be a step in the right direction, they apply to only $20 billion of US imports. Trump's tariffs target a large share of total US imported goods from all sources, on track to be worth $3.8 trillion to $3.9 trillion in 2026.[1] Congress might have a better shot at a veto override on a Canada bill, but even that narrower result is not guaranteed.
From Canada's point of view, the more damaging US tariffs are those imposed on Canadian goods, including steel, aluminum, lumber, copper, auto parts, and other products, for purported national security reasons under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. These goods were not excused under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) from paying Section 232 tariffs and accounted for a large share of the $10 billion in duties the US collected on Canadian imports in 2025.[2] One way to lift those tariffs would be for Congress to legislate that Canada, historically the closest US ally, is to be exempt from Section 232 duties. Trump's animus toward Canada (his 51st US state) is such that his likely veto of this measure would still have to be overridden.
Can a broader anti-tariff bill pass with a veto-proof margin? The new majority could forbid the use of trade statutes for economic coercion against an ally or neutral country, requiring a congressional vote to initiate a trade war or take hostile trade actions against an ally. Such legislation would have at least three problems: First it would require defining an ally and a neutral country, which would likely involve making contentious political judgments. Second, it would mean the end of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which has been used by this and prior administrations to threaten tariffs in response to foreign trade practices deemed unfair. Third, there are vested interests who welcome protection and would oppose the bill.
During both the Trump and Biden administrations, the largest share of US tariffs has been applied to imports from China. In any general tariff rollback addressing affordability, a bill could include a more rational approach to tariffs on Chinese goods—namely, excluding those goods that clearly are a net benefit to the US economy. The legislation might garner votes from the US farm belt if as a result the Chinese market were fully opened once again to US agricultural exports. The difficulty for proponents is that appearing weak on China could be politically costly. Would a China-focused bill get enough votes to override a veto? Not at all likely, but Congress should test how much bipartisan support might exist for such a measure.
There are numerous legislative proposals to add conditions to the use of tariff authorities. All of these would be Trump veto bait if effective. The White House might accept technical changes with low economic impact, but that would not achieve the goal of rolling back Trump's unpopular tariffs and lowering consumer prices. The AP Voter Poll (link is external)found that almost 50 percent of respondents said the cost of living was crucial to their vote for Congress. The tariffs fed inflation, making life in this country less affordable.
The incoming Congress must assert its constitutional role of controlling the nation's tariffs. Moreover, the recent midterm elections have created an expectation for change. For example, Congress could legislate a new fast track procedure that would require congressional agreement before the president can impose tariffs for any reason. Once again, however, the bill would need enough bipartisan support to override a veto.
However, Congress does have some leverage. Senate confirmation is required for new appointments to most senior positions in the Trump administration and to the federal judiciary. Appropriations must be passed into law. The Trump administration may even need occasional congressional support or forbearance that can be used as trading stock. As noted above, some bills are considered "must pass" and cannot effectively be vetoed. But these powers are not always readily deployable. Members of the incoming Congress have more than tariff reform on their wish lists of policies and measures, and they will have to use their leverage selectively.
Cooperation between Trump and Congress on tariffs cannot be ruled out entirely. Quick tariff relief for consumers and small businesses over the next two years, cannot be solely at the discretion of the president even if hard for the incoming 120th Congress to achieve.
Working toward a better future
Greater cooperation is needed between the legislative and executive branches. Under the US constitution, only the president can negotiate trade agreements that mutually benefit the signatories while only Congress can implement agreements that require changes in US law. Lawmakers realized this during debates leading to the enactment of the Trade Act of 1974. To facilitate interbranch cooperation, under the 1974 Act's procedures—known as "fast track trade negotiating authority," later renamed Trade Promotion Authority (TPA)—Congress mandates negotiations, transparency, and consultations; in return, it gives up its weapons of delay and amendment to block an international trade agreement. Prior administrations (including the first Trump administration) benefited from this arrangement from 1975 to 2021, but the current president and his immediate predecessor did not ask Congress to renew the TPA when it expired in July 2021.
Even Trump needed Congress to allow him to implement USMCA, which he heralded(link is external) as "the largest, fairest, most balanced, and modern trade agreement in the history of our country." The next president, whether Democrat or Republican, could discover the merits of working with Congress on trade.
Notes
1. Author's calculations using US Census data(link is external) for monthly imports and extending it to the full year, as recent months are higher than the average.
2. According to US Census data(link is external), in 2025, the US imposed duties on about 15 percent of US imports from Canada by value (about $56 billion total), with a total of $10 billion(link is external) in calculated duties (compared with $0.4 billion in 2024).

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsThe Outlook for Retail Stocks as Black Friday ApproachesNov 20, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptSolid retail sales data and a positive start to retail earnings reporting are demonstrating the strength of the US consumer heading into Black Friday, says Scott Feiler, consumer sector specialist in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Low jobless claims and declining gas prices also suggest resilient consumer spending, which is showing up in sales for experiences and giving a boost to hotel and cruise-line stocks. At the same time, Feiler says on The Markets podcast that it will be important to monitor how higher material costs flow through to corporate margins and retail prices in 2027.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, November 19th. And I'm joined from our Dallas office by Scott Feiler, who is a consumer sector specialist within FICC and Equities. And this week we're going to discuss a retail sales report we got earlier in the week, what it means for the consumer, how earnings are shaping up, and what the setup into next week's Black Friday is for the entire consumer space.
Scott, thanks so much for joining us.
Scott Feiler: Thanks for having me, Chris
Chris Hussey: Okay, Scott, I was looking back at my notes. We had you on exactly a year ago. Why not? Get you right ahead of the Black Friday and also in the middle of earnings season. Back then, you were a little bit cautious on the consumer, though. Where are you falling out on the consumer in the year ahead?
Scott Feiler: Yeah, I mean, you could use a couple different words. The consumer is fine. The consumer is resilient. Most of the companies that we've heard from so far sound good. Things are just steady. It's hard for me to pound the table and tell you that everyone is doing well, nor are we seeing the deceleration in the consumer that everyone expected we were going to see when gas prices were high and inflation was sticky.
The consumer is fine. Obviously, you hinted the retail sales report. The October retail sales report beat again. September, last month, beat and was revised higher. So, from a top-down perspective, consumer spending is good, and from a bottoms-up perspective, the corporates generally sound steady and while that's not amazing, it's certainly a lot better than people feared a couple months ago
Chris Hussey: All right. I want to talk a little bit about our strategist, Ben Sneider. He's made a very big call on consumer staples as a defensive. You're making a little bit of a call, though, talking about the consumer being strong here. Do you want to play the consumer for defense or do you want to play the consumer for offense?
Scott Feiler: I mean, historically it's one or the other, right? But recently consumer discretionary and consumer staples equal weight have had a positive correlation. That's very rare. So you don't necessarily have to pick one or the other. Ben has certainly had an out of consensus call by being constructive on staples.
And it's been a good call. And the group has obviously acted quite defensive as the market has gotten choppier, and if the market remains choppy, that's going to continue to work. I'm a little more constructive on consumer discretionary right now though, simply because corporates are telling us that things are fine.
Jobless claims are at the recent lows, and spending is accelerating a little bit into fourth quarter, and we think Black Friday's going to be good. So, we'd be selectively constructive on consumer discretionary right now
Chris Hussey: Let me explore one of those aspects of that call. You talked about gasoline prices maybe on the decline, and that is part of the inflation call here. Affordability has become a big buzzword in the economy today. How is the consumer sort of hanging in there with all the inflation they're seeing, and how are corporates that are in this space hanging in with all the inflation they're seeing? How are they keeping margins up?
Scott Feiler: We got another weekly jobless claims number that was down around 200 today. So the consumer is employed and wage growth is still strong, and so they just have confidence in their job still. So, that's number one.
Gas prices have come off peaks, and so the consumer has probably responded to that. Savings are still, obviously still just more elevated than most people realized, and we just haven't seen the givebacks from the tax refunds that we had earlier in this year. So, the consumer is sort of spending through those temporary inflation headwinds that we had over the last few months.
And so yeah, I mean the consumer holds in. We're not in the clear yet. I do think companies still could pass on more prices. They're not fully giving the consumer back all of the tariff refunds that they've got. These corporates could continue to pass on prices into next year, though.
Chris Hussey: There's also an energy lag though on that corporate side, especially in the consumer staples side, but it's also flowing through some of the retailers who deal in apparel and things like that. Are you concerned at all that you're going to see input cost inflation rise so fast that they're not going to be able to pass it on to the consumer through price?
Scott Feiler: I don't think we're out of the woods yet in terms of some of the raw material costs. Even though energy prices have begun to come down, corporates are almost certainly going to have margin pressures from raw material costs next year as new contracts come up.
And so there are going to be margin pressures next year. Most of the companies that we have heard from who have talked about 2027 have hinted that margins are likely to be lower next year on a year-over-year basis and below consensus. And so, we do think corporates will try to raise prices to offset some of the raw material costs that they're going to see next year on the freight side and other raw material costs.
It's going to come down to who has pricing power and who doesn't. Some companies have pricing power, some companies don't. But we do think corporates are going to try and pass through prices to offset some of the raw material increases that they are going to see next year.
Chris Hussey: Well, we're getting an update on that pricing power right now, cause I'm catching you right in the middle of earnings season for the retailers, maybe the heart of earnings season. What are you learning so far? Whats coming out of the earnings season that's catching your eye?
Scott Feiler: Consumers are still spending on travel and experiences. The travel group is up 10% the last month. Hotel RevPAR is incredibly strong still. Everyone was expecting trends to fade after the World Cup, and they've accelerated further. Cruise lines sound really good. So, consumers are still spending on experiences and that is showing up in stock prices as well.
So that's number one. And then number two is you're not seeing perfectly linear strength in trends week to week, but you are seeing the consumer remain generally resilient. The corporates we have heard from who have spoken about fourth quarter, quarter to date, the few weeks before Black Friday, have generally told us that fourth quarter has started stronger than 3Q ended.
So, the consumer is still showing up and feels like it's going to be fine into Black Friday.
Chris Hussey: One more question here on Black Friday, because we're going to be going into Black Friday as well here. What is your outlook for Black Friday? How much does it matter?
Scott Feiler: I mean, the consumer always shows up for Black Friday or for any event for that matter. And given the consumer is employed and given sentiment has picked up off the lows in the sentiment readings, we think the consumer is going to show up next week and on Black Friday as well. They always do.
November historically is very strong for the retail group. The retail group has outperformed nine of the last 10 years in a row in November, and most of that outperformance comes the last two weeks of November around Black Friday because the holiday reads we always get are generally good. And given the corporates that we've heard from over the last couple weeks have told us that things are accelerating into fourth quarter, we think that's going to continue into next week and we think retail outperformance is probably going to continue and be strong next week
Chris Hussey: Yeah, it's the Cindy Lou Who economy. No matter what happens, Christmas came, Christmas came just the same. All right, good stuff. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Scott Feiler: We talked on it briefly already, but I think you're supposed to buy all sorts of dips in anything travel related. Hotels, cruise lines. Hotels are going to do well. In an agentic world where people are going to book more direct through hotels as opposed to potentially through other ways, hotels do well in that world.
It's a higher margin business for them. So we like hotels on any sort of pullbacks. We like cruise lines as well. Net yield growth is going to accelerate into next year. And so we like those two parts of travel. And then there's select single names that we like as well. Some discretionary names that are value, that are discounted valuations, that are quality companies that have seen real pullbacks.
There's a lot of single stocks that we really like specifically that are levered to apparel, that are trading at pretty deep discounts to history.
Chris Hussey: Okay, a lot coming up. What are you watching for next week and beyond?
Scott Feiler: We're going to get a lot of earnings next week, over the next couple weeks. In addition to obviously we're getting Black Friday, we're going to hear from department stores and off-price companies. These are less idiosyncratic stories and more just reads on consumer health. So we're going to get those the next couple weeks.
The last few weeks has been about idiosyncratic stories. The next couple weeks are going to be about consumer bellwethers and how these companies are sounding around the consumer through the first three weeks of November, and we think that's going to be incredibly important to hear from. So, next week's earnings are going to be important.
Department stores and off-pricers, that's who we're watching next week, and we think it'll be generally good
Chris Hussey: All right, I can't let a conversation with Dallas, go without this. Dallas Cowboys off to a tough start though, but are they going to make the playoffs anyway?
Scott Feiler: I don't think so. I mean, I might get tomatoes thrown at me for saying that, but I just don't think it's going to happen unfortunately. We're just finding ways to lose games that we should win. We're just not closing it out in the fourth quarter. We're just not a fourth quarter team unfortunately
Chris Hussey: Well, Scott, I appreciate that. Thank you for taking time with us this week.
Scott Feiler: Thanks very much, Chris
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.
