articles.title: Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins
articles.text:
Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins

Given at Queen’s University, Belfast

Published on
15 September 2026

In her speech, Carolyn Wilkins draws on historical experience of private money issuance to explore whether private digital money can operate safely at scale. She also considers what could happen if US dollar stablecoins become widely used, and what that could mean for the future of international monetary power.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me. It is a pleasure to be here at Queen’s University in Belfast to talk about payment innovations, and what they mean for international money and power.
I’ll focus on stablecoins. They have some affinities with the local banknotes issued here. And while stablecoins are often presented in very dry terms - blockchains, tokens, settlement layers - the bigger questions are about money and power.
Payment means and systems are like electricity grids. When they are working, they are in the background, and when they are not, there can be widespread disruption. And, payment systems can be used by governments to enforce economic sanctions, as we saw after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. They can also be used to monitor financial flows and to project influence. That has made the infrastructure of money and payments an increasingly important part of economic statecraft.
The strategic issue here is what role stablecoins will play in a system where money, payments and geopolitical power are becoming increasingly intertwined. We want to know which forms of digital money will ultimately succeed, and which currencies and institutions will become embedded in the next generation of payment infrastructure. It is early days, so the answers are honestly unknown. But we can learn a lot by considering three questions.
First: can private digital money work safely at scale?
Second: what happens if US dollar stablecoins really do scale?
Third: what would that mean for international monetary power?
These questions are top of mind for me because the Bank of England recently published a framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins.footnote [1]
1. Can private digital money work safely at scale?
Let me start with what a stablecoin is.
A fiat-backed payment stablecoin is a privately issued claim designed to maintain a fixed value against sovereign money - usually one stablecoin for one dollar.
There is a familiar analogue here in Northern Ireland. Private banks issue their own sterling banknotes, which circulate pound-for-pound with other sterling money and are fully backed by ring-fenced assets, but the basic monetary promise is familiar: a privately issued claim that people expect to maintain its value at par.
One way to see what stablecoins add is to compare them with Bitcoin. Bitcoin showed something fundamental: value can be transferred globally and continuously without a central intermediary. Bitcoin is not backed by reserve assets, and its value can move enormously.
In 2010, two pizzas were actually bought for 10,000 bitcoins - about $40 at the time. Today, 10,000 bitcoins would be worth about $770 million. Those are probably the most expensive pizzas in history.
Figure 1 shows the underlying problem more systematically. Bitcoin is far more volatile than the major payment stablecoins, making it poorly suited to everyday payments.
Stablecoins were designed to address that problem by backing the monetary promise of a stable value with reserve assets, while retaining some of the features of crypto technology. Transfers can take place continuously, often across borders, and transactions can be programmed using smart contracts.

Figure 1: Volatility of Bitcoin, USDT and USDC

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

There is a real demand for this innovation, particularly where payments systems are slow, expensive and difficult to access.
For now, they are used mainly inside the crypto ecosystem, as a settlement asset for trading and lending, as collateral, to provide liquidity, and as a way of moving between crypto markets and conventional money.
The market has grown very quickly. Stablecoins in circulation reached roughly $300 billion by mid-2026, up from less than $5 billion at the beginning of 2020 (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Stablecoins in circulation by market capitalisation

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

As much as the blockchain technology seems avant-garde, the economic structure of stablecoins is very familiar.
Private institutions have issued money-like claims for centuries. Those systems repeatedly had to solve the same basic problems: can the issuer make good on the promise to redeem; will claims issued by different institutions be accepted and settled at the same value; and what happens when many people want to redeem at once?
The nineteenth-century history of private money is a useful place to start.
In the United Kingdom, private banknotes circulated alongside Bank of England notes. Scotland developed a relatively stable system built around large branch networks, stronger shareholder liability and regular clearing among banks. If a bank issued too many notes, other banks returned them for settlement and it lost reserves. That imposed discipline in normal times.
England had a more fragile structure. Many country banks were small and poorly diversified. This weakness was reinforced by the Bank of England's monopoly on joint-stock banking within London, which limited the development of larger banking institutions. Dozens of banks failed in the crisis of 1825. Parliament responded by allowing larger joint-stock banks outside London.
But stronger banks did not solve the problem of liquidity in a crisis. Reserves and crisis management became increasingly concentrated around the Bank of England. The Bank Charter Act of 1844 tied note issuance more tightly to gold, yet crises followed in 1847, 1857 and 1866. Each time, the statutory limit on note issuance was temporarily relaxed so that the Bank could lend into the panic.
So the UK experience points to two conditions for success. Private money needs mechanisms that keep different claims trading at par in normal times. And it needs a way to provide liquidity when the system comes under stress.
The United States learned much the same lesson, but through a more turbulent route.
During the Free Banking era, banks issued their own notes, and those notes did not necessarily trade at face value. Their value depended on the assets backing them, the reputation of the issuing bank and even the distance from the place of redemption. There were catalogues telling people what different banknotes were worth.
So a dollar was not always simply a dollar.
The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 tried to fix that problem by requiring national banknotes to be backed by US government bonds. The notes became more uniform and the collateral improved.
But another problem remained. The supply of currency could not expand easily when demand for liquidity rose. The panics of 1873, 1893 and 1907 exposed that weakness.
Private clearinghouses tried to fill the gap by providing emergency settlement liquidity. In 1907, J.P. Morgan and others also organized extraordinary support. But the system still depended on improvised private cooperation.
The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 eventually put those crisis-management functions on a permanent national footing.
Across these historical experiences, several conditions for success stand out.
Private money needs credible convertibility, so holders are confident they can redeem at par, and high-quality, transparent backing that makes that promise believable. It also needs a sufficiently uniform regulatory perimeter, so that similar monetary claims are subject to consistent standards, and clearing and settlement arrangements that keep those claims exchanging at par. Finally, there must be credible arrangements for crisis management and loss allocation when the system comes under stress.
Together, these conditions support what Gary Gorton and Jeffery Zhang call the “no questions asked” property of money.footnote [2] A monetary claim works well when people can accept it at face value without having to assess the issuer every time they use it.
Stablecoins have already provided a useful test of that principle.
When Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, Circle - the issuer of the stablecoin called USDC - had about $3.3 billion of reserves deposited there.
Holders suddenly had reason to question whether USDC could still be converted into one dollar. Redemptions accelerated and USDC lost its peg (Figure 3). The peg recovered after US authorities guaranteed all of Silicon Valley Bank’s deposits.footnote [3]

Figure 3: USDC around the failure of Silicon Valley Bank
Deviation from par value (per cent)

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

The episode showed how a weakness in the institutional structure behind a stablecoin can quickly affect confidence in the token itself.
Regulatory frameworks are now trying to address those weaknesses.
In the US, Congress passed the GENIUS Act in July 2025, creating a federal framework for all payment stablecoins.footnote [4] The Act sets rules for who can issue a stablecoin, what assets must stand behind it, and what happens when a holder wants their money back.
It requires at least one dollar of eligible reserves for every dollar of stablecoins issued. Those reserves can include Treasury securities, bank deposits and other short-term liquid assets. It also strengthens disclosure and gives stablecoin holders priority in insolvency. One implementation challenge will be maintaining consistent standards across its federal and state regulatory regimes.
That goes a long way toward answering one question: are the assets there? The trickier question is: can they be turned into cash quickly when everyone wants to redeem at once?
We saw why that distinction matters during the “dash for cash” at the onset of the pandemic in March 2020. Even the US Treasury market came under severe strain, and the Federal Reserve had to intervene on a very large scale. Assets that are safe and liquid in normal times can become much less liquid in a crisis.footnote [5]
The Federal Reserve has also proposed a new, limited form of account that would allow eligible firms to connect more directly to its payment system. That could make day-to-day settlement more reliable. But it would not allow them to borrow from the Fed, which means there is no pre-established source of emergency liquidity in a run.
The Bank of England’s framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins, which will be finalised at the end of this year, goes further on some of these issues.footnote [6] It is more restrictive about reserve assets and puts more weight on liquidity contingency planning, payment-system access and arrangements for failure. It also allows for the possibility of central-bank liquidity under appropriate conditions.footnote [7]
This framework applies only to systemic stablecoins and is more demanding than the US framework. I think this is appropriate because it gives greater weight to the liquidity and crisis-management problems that recur in the historical record.
Let’s not forget that cross-border use makes these issues even harder. In some regimes, a stablecoin may be issued in one jurisdiction, hold its reserves in another, use a custodian in a third and serve holders in many more.footnote [8] Redemption rights, insolvency treatment, supervision and crisis-management responsibilities do not automatically travel with the token.footnote [9]
International banking spent decades developing home- and host-country responsibilities, common standards and supervisory cooperation. That said, stablecoins may become global much faster than the institutional framework around them.
So, my answer to the first question is a qualified yes. Private digital money can work at scale, but the historical record is clear about the conditions required to make that possible.
2. What happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale?
This brings me to the second question.
Today, about 98 percent of stablecoin value is denominated in US dollars.footnote [10] The dollar therefore has a considerable first-mover advantage as stablecoins move beyond their original role in crypto markets.
The US administration sees this as a strategic opportunity. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued explicitly that dollar stablecoins can reinforce the dollar’s international role and increase demand for US Treasury securities.
There are three main channels through which wider use could matter.
The first channel is settlement. Stablecoin transactions can take place around the clock and cross borders without passing through every link in a correspondent-banking chain. They do not eliminate intermediaries, but they can reduce reliance on traditional banking links. Recent work presented at Jackson Hole just a few weeks ago argues that this could make settlement faster or cheaper where cross-border banking is slow or costly.footnote [11] In 2024, sending a USD 200 remittance cost around 6.4% on average globally, while costs in Sub-Saharan Africa averaged about 8.5%.footnote [12]
The second channel is digital dollarisation. If your local currency is unstable or access to dollar banking is difficult, a dollar stablecoin can put a dollar-linked asset on your phone without requiring a US bank account. Recent work finds that the advantage can be significant in some emerging-market payment corridors with capital controls or segmented foreign-exchange markets, although limited liquidity still constrains scale.footnote [13] This could extend the use of the dollar into new digital markets.
The third channel is demand for US safe assets.
Stablecoin issuers hold reserves against their liabilities, and the GENIUS Act requires reserves to be held in specified highly liquid assets, including short-dated US Treasury securities.footnote [14]
USDT and USDC together held almost $150 billion in Treasury bills at the end of 2025. Their net purchases in that year were around $33 billion (Figure 4).footnote [15]

Figure 4: Holdings of US T-bills Q4 2025, US$ Billions

Footnotes

Source: Ahmed, R. and Aldasoro, I. (2025, revised 2026), Stablecoins and Safe Asset Prices, BIS Working Papers No. 1270; authors' calculations.

Those amounts remain small relative to the Treasury market as a whole, but they make the largest stablecoin issuers meaningful participants in the short-term market.
That additional demand can affect Treasury prices. Recent evidence suggests that stablecoin inflows put modest downward pressure on short-term Treasury yields, consistent with issuers adding to demand for safe and liquid assets.footnote [16]
Of course, the overall effect will depend on where the money comes from. If investors move from a Treasury money-market fund into a stablecoin whose issuer then buys Treasury bills, the net increase in demand for US safe assets is limited. If stablecoins attract funds that would otherwise be held in another currency or another asset class, the effect is larger. If stablecoins instead draw materially from bank deposits, they could also affect bank funding costs and credit supply.
At sufficient scale, these channels could reinforce one another – creating a positive feedback loop. Greater use of dollar stablecoins expands dollar settlement. Issuers hold more Treasury securities. Deep and liquid dollar markets make dollar stablecoins more attractive to users and platforms.

Figure 5: Positive feedback loop

But the same balance sheet can work in reverse. Inflows mean reserve purchases; redemptions mean asset sales.
Remember, like deposits or money market fund investments stablecoins are demandable claims. They can trade around the clock, and holders can seek redemption quickly. Issuers therefore need to turn reserve assets into cash when redemptions rise.
If several large issuers had to sell Treasury bills at the same time, particularly into an already stressed market, they could amplify moves in yields and market liquidity. We saw a similar feedback mechanism in the UK gilt market during the LDI episode in 2022.
And the stress need not begin with the stablecoin. Concerns about US inflation, fiscal sustainability or institutional credibility could weaken demand for dollar assets, with stablecoin redemptions adding to the selling pressure.

Figure 6: Negative feedback loop

The stablecoin sector is not currently large enough for this mechanism to pose a major threat to the Treasury market or a material financial stability risk in UK. However, a major de-pegging episode could also damage confidence in regulated stablecoins more broadly.
US policy is intended to provide space for the sector to grow substantially. If successful, the balance-sheet link between stablecoins and the rest of the dollar system will matter more over time.
Scale therefore brings both benefits and vulnerabilities. Dollar stablecoins could extend dollar settlement, support digital dollarisation and add to demand for safe US assets. At greater scale, they would also create a stronger link between confidence in privately issued money and conditions in the markets where the reserves are held.
3. What would that mean for monetary power?
That brings me to the third question.
When I talk about monetary power, I do not mean only the dollar’s share of reserves or international trade.
I mean control of the system itself. Who provides the monetary anchor, who provides liquidity in a crisis, who writes and enforces the rules, and who can control access to the financial network.
By conventional measures, the dollar remains in a strong position in global finance, although its share of global reserves has declined since the beginning of the century.footnote [17] Its share of disclosed foreign-exchange reserves has fallen from a little over 70 percent around 2000 to about 57 percent in the first quarter of 2026. The decline has been gradual and spread across a range of currencies. The euro remains near 20 percent, while the renminbi accounts for a much smaller share. At the same time, the dollar was on one side of 89.2 percent of over-the-counter foreign-exchange trades in April 2025.footnote [18]

Figure 7: Official Foreign Exchange Reserves by Currency

Footnotes

Source: IMF Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER) Survey.

Since the end of Bretton Woods in the early 1970s, there has been no promise to convert dollars into gold. The anchor instead has rested on confidence in the fiscal and monetary policies of the United States, as well as in its institutions and legal systems and judiciary.
The sheer economic and geopolitical weight of the US has traditionally reinforced those advantages.
Network effects have made the US more powerful. Firms tend to invoice in currencies widely used by their counterparties. Financial institutions value currencies with deep markets and liquid hedging instruments. US Treasuries provide a large stock of safe assets that are used as reserves, collateral, stores of value and pricing benchmarks.
That safe-asset advantage has historically been valuable to the United States. Investors have been willing to accept lower yields on Treasuries because they are safe and liquid; one influential estimate put that advantage at about 70 basis points.footnote [19] But recent evidence suggests it has weakened. The advantage attached specifically to Treasury securities has fallen sharply, even turning negative at longer maturities, while the broader international advantage of the dollar remains strong.footnote [20]
This financial infrastructure also gives the United States strategic leverage.
Because many international transactions depend on institutions subject to US jurisdiction or on access to dollar markets, US authorities can monitor financial flows, impose sanctions and restrict access to important parts of the financial network. Secondary sanctions can extend those effects beyond US institutions.
The sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine made the strategic importance of financial infrastructure particularly visible. More broadly, the use of financial sanctions has strengthened the incentive for some governments to develop alternative channels for international payments.
China is the most important example. This is not because the renminbi is close to displacing the dollar, but because China has the economic scale to develop alternative infrastructure.
It has expanded the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, for renminbi-denominated international payments. China has also participated in mBridge, which has experimented with cross-border settlement using wholesale central-bank digital currencies.
These arrangements remain much smaller than the dollar-centred financial system. Their importance lies in the development of additional payment routes that rely less heavily on traditional dollar-based correspondent banking.
This points to an important distinction: the currency and the rails can change at different speeds.
The dollar could remain the leading reserve and financing currency while more cross-border payments move through regional or digital networks that are less centred on the United States. This form of monetary multipolarity does not require another currency to replace the dollar. But it could still reduce US direct control over the infrastructure through which some international payments are made.
Stablecoins can contribute to both sides of this process. Dollar stablecoins can extend dollar settlement into new digital networks. Other countries can use digital currencies, stablecoins or new payment platforms to develop alternative networks.
This competition can improve efficiency and encourage innovation. It can also create fragmentation if systems are not interoperable or if legal, regulatory and liquidity arrangements diverge sharply across jurisdictions.footnote [21]
The strategic question therefore concerns both the currency people choose to use and the infrastructure through which they use it.
The US position remains strong because no competitor currently offers the same combination of deep and liquid capital markets, a large supply of safe assets, convertibility, legal credibility and established global use.
History nevertheless shows that network advantages are persistent rather than permanent.footnote [22]
Sterling is the clearest example.
Before the First World War, sterling bills financed international trade far beyond transactions involving the UK. London was the leading international financial centre. Imperial trade links and the sterling area reinforced a powerful network even after the UK’s relative economic position had begun to weaken.
The transition away from sterling took decades.
War debts strained the UK’s fiscal capacity. The commitment to gold became harder to sustain. Britain’s relative economic weight declined, and its ability to provide international liquidity weakened. At the same time, the United States became a larger economic and financial power.
The shift reflected changing economic strength and changing confidence in the institutions supporting the currency.
That history matters for the current questions about stablecoins and US dollar dominance.
Network effects can reinforce an international currency for a very long time. But, ultimately, they sit on top of fundamentals.
For the dollar, as for any currency, those fundamentals are the same ones I mentioned earlier: sustainable fiscal capacity; credible institutions and policies, including monetary policy; predictable legal institutions and the rule of law; deep and liquid capital markets; and a demonstrated ability to provide liquidity when the financial system is under stress.footnote [23] General government gross as a percent of GDP has been on an upward trend and is projected to increase further, particularly in the US and China (Figure 8).
These are fairly old-fashioned foundations of monetary power. Digital technology does not make them less important.

Figure 8: General government gross debt (per cent of GDP)

Footnotes

Source: International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Economic Outlook Database, April 2026. Chart shows total gross general government debt on an internationally comparable basis. Separately published country measures can use different methodologies.

4. Conclusions
Let me close by returning to my three questions.
First, can private digital money work safely at scale? Yes. History shows that it can, but only when the institutions around it make redemption credible, support exchange at par and provide a way to deal with stress.
Second, what happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale? They could extend dollar settlement, deepen digital dollarisation and add to demand for US safe assets. But greater scale would also create stronger links between stablecoins and the markets in which their reserves are held. This could create financial stability risks that extend past US borders.
And third, what does this mean for international monetary power? History shows that network effects can sustain a dominant currency for a long time, so stablecoins could help reinforce the dollar. At the same time, global payments systems could become more multipolar. But technology cannot secure dollar dominance on its own. As sterling’s experience ultimately showed, that rests squarely on monetary credibility, fiscal capacity, deep capital markets and the rule of law.
Acknowledgements and notes
These remarks draw on joint work that I have undertaken with Michael Bordo, entitled “Money and Power: Historical Lessons for Stablecoins and U.S. Dollar Dominance Opens in a new window,” Hoover Institution. I would like to thank Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Pavel Chichkanov, Clare Lombardelli, Sarah McDonnell, Raakhi Odedra, Francine Robb, James Talbot, and Michael Yoganayagam for their assistance in preparing these remarks.
These remarks reflect my views and not those of the Financial Policy Committee or other Bank of England colleagues.

The Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) is the Bank of England’s committee for financial market infrastructure regulation and is responsible for setting the regulatory framework for systemic stablecoins. The Financial Policy Committee (FPC), of which I am a member, welcomed publication of the Bank’s policy statement and draft rules in June 2026.

Gorton, G B and Zhang, J Y (2023), ‘Taming Wildcat Stablecoins Opens in a new window’, University of Chicago Law Review, Vol. 90, No. 3.

Circle (2023), ‘$3.3 Billion of USDC Reserve Risk Removed, Dollar De-peg Closes Opens in a new window’.

United States Congress (2025), ‘Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act of 2025 (GENIUS Act) Opens in a new window’, S. 1582.

Liang, N (2025), ‘Stablecoins: Issues for regulators as they implement GENIUS Act’ Opens in a new window, Brookings Institution; and Liang, N and Dudley, W (2026), ‘Next Steps for GENIUS Payment Stablecoins’ Opens in a new window, Brookings Institution. The authors note that the GENIUS Act leaves capital, liquidity and risk-management requirements to implementing regulation and argue that prudential standards are needed to ensure stablecoins remain convertible at par during periods of stress.

Bank of England (2026), ‘Bank of England launches policy statement and draft rules on regulating systemic stablecoins’.

The comparison is not entirely like-for-like since the GENIUS Act establishes the US framework for payment stablecoins generally, whereas the Bank’s regime applies only once a stablecoin is recognised as systemic and focuses primarily on sterling-denominated systemic stablecoins.

The UK framework deliberately limits this problem for systemic sterling stablecoins by requiring an overseas issuer to establish a UK entity and by locating key safeguarding arrangements in the UK.

When it comes to stablecoins based on decentralised systems such as permissionless blockchains, there are important questions about who is legally accountable and which jurisdiction’s laws and regulations apply across borders.

Aldasoro, I, Frost, J and Ito, H (2026), ‘The impact of stablecoins on the international monetary and financial system Opens in a new window’, BIS Papers No. 170.

RESEARCH | BARCLAYS GLOBAL OUTLOOK

Barclays Global Outlook Q1 2027: A correction, not a collapse

Lead contributors: Ajay Rajadhyaksha, Venu Krishna, Michael McLean & Anshul Pradhan

19 Nov 2026

Recent AI weakness raises a key question for 2027: is this a turning point or reset? Despite volatility, the S&P 500 is still up 9-10% year to date, company earnings have grown around 30% y/y and AI has added more than a percentage point. Returns and overcapacity are real risks, but longer-term ones, not signs the cycle is breaking. Our team’s outlook is more cautious, but still constructive.

Client log-in for full report

Key takeaways:

Markets are correcting, not collapsing. Global growth is forecast at 3.4% in 2026, and recent weakness looks like a mid-cycle reset in valuations, not the end of the cycle.
AI fear, real demand. Cloud providers remain compute-constrained, yet cloud revenue growth is strong, and AI has added more than a percentage point to US growth this year.
Investors will reward delivery over narrative in 2027. With valuations elevated, strong earnings may no longer be enough. Good numbers increasingly need to become great ones.
Market leadership is broadening. Investors are rotating into cyclicals, healthcare and defence rather than abandoning equities.
The market outlook is more cautious, but still constructive. AI returns and overcapacity are longer-term risks, not signs the cycle is breaking. Barclays Research remains overweight equities versus fixed income.

Markets are navigating a mid-cycle correction

Markets have repriced, but the fundamental backdrop has not broken, according to Ajay Rajadhyaksha, Chairman of Research at Barclays. Rajadhyaksha’s team forecasts global growth at 3.4% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027. The US grew 2.7% through Q3, with Q4 tracking toward 3.4%.
Even after the recent sell-off, the S&P 500 remains up 9-10% this year. Investors are rotating into cyclicals, healthcare and defence rather than abandoning equities. This looks more like a reset in valuations and positioning than a break in the cycle, according to Rajadhyaksha.

Double click here to edit Flourish Column Chart component

Barclays Research forecasts global GDP to be 3.4% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027. Forecasts for 20 developed and emerging economies are also presented.

AI fears capture headlines, yet underlying demand is real

The path will stay volatile, particularly around AI capex, returns and the risk of eventual overcapacity, according to our Research analysts. But today's fundamentals point to demand, not excess. Last quarter, revenue grew 48% at Azure, 103% at Google Cloud and 39% at Amazon Web Services (AWS), while major cloud providers remain compute-constrained and ASML’s lithography machines that make chips are sold out through 2028.
That matters because AI has already contributed more than a percentage point to US growth this year, with spillovers extending into power, construction and manufacturing. The eventual returns remain uncertain, but there is little evidence that the investment cycle itself is breaking.

Related content

Podcast: Chips, chokepoints and the battle for AI supremacy

AI investment is accelerating, but semiconductor chokepoints and geopolitical pressures are creating a new strategic reality.

Double click here to edit Flourish Column Chart component

AI investment is set to more than double from $767bn (estimated) in 2026 to nearly $1.7tn (estimated) by 2028, led by Alphabet and AWS.

The bar has moved beyond earnings

Strong earnings growth may no longer be enough to lift all areas of the market, according to Venu Krishna, Head of US Equity Strategy and Equity Linked Strategies (ELS) at Barclays.
In Q3, 83% of S&P 500 companies beat expectations. Earnings have grown around 30% year-on-year, and the 2027 consensus points to a further c.15% increase. Yet markets are not rewarding this strong performance. With AI expectations still high, good numbers increasingly need to be great ones. For the AI buildout, the challenge has moved beyond generating demand to the cost of funding supply.
2027 is likely to bring a more selective market, where delivery matters more than narrative. Barclays Research is more nervous, but not bearish, and remains overweight equities versus fixed income for another quarter.

Important content disclosures

Frequently asked questions

What is the outlook for Europe's economy in 2027?

According to Barclays Research, Europe has outperformed expectations, with Q3 growth of 0.4% led by Germany and Spain, but it remains roughly a 1% growth economy. Higher rates, high energy costs and French fiscal uncertainty weigh on the outlook. German defence and infrastructure spending and lower oil prices offer some support.

What is the outlook for China's economy in 2027?

China's headline growth looks respectable, with 2026 forecast at 4.6%, but Barclays Research expects it to slow to 4% in 2027. AI and high-tech exports are strong, but consumer demand, property, credit and household confidence remain weak, and a large new stimulus looks unlikely.

Will the Bank of Japan keep raising rates in 2027?

Barclays Research expects the Bank of Japan (BoJ) to raise rates in December, March and July, taking the policy rate to 2%. Underlying inflation has reached 2.4%, close to target for the first time in a generation. But once a consumption tax cut pulls measured inflation lower later in 2027, further hikes will likely be harder to justify. Therefore, most of the tightening is likely to come in the first half of the year.

Will the US midterm results slow the AI data centre buildout?

The US midterm results may add friction but are unlikely to derail the AI data centre buildout. Texas accounts for almost a third of planned US data centre projects, and its governor-elect campaigned on a moratorium. However, existing permits will be honoured, which covers most planned spending through 2027 and into 2028. Barclays Research has not cut its forecasts for growth or for hyperscaler borrowing.

Is overbuilding of AI infrastructure a risk?

In the long run, possibly, but Barclays Research does not expect it in 2027. The concern echoes the railroad crash of 1873: many individually rational decisions to build added up to a system that was overbuilt. Whether AI capacity overshoots on a three-to-five-year horizon remains genuinely uncertain. For now, demand backlogs and supply constraints are real. ASML, for example, is pre-sold through 2028.

News Release
Malaysia's CRESS Acceleration Package improves project economics, but execution remains the critical test
New analysis finds revised grid access framework competitive against utility tariffs, but compressed 2028 deadline will separate market leaders from the rest

17 November 2026
4 minute read

Email
Share by email

Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS)’s revised grid access framework improves project bankability and keeps renewable procurement cost-effective against utility tariffs. But with a hard commissioning deadline of 31 December 2028 and no extensions on the table, Wood Mackenzie says the window for action is narrowing fast. For developers and offtakers without a credible execution plan, the revised economics are beside the point.
On 18 September 2026, the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation (PETRA) announced the CRESS Acceleration Package, reducing the System Access Charge (SAC) for developers from MYR200/MWh (US$49/MWh) to MYR140/MWh (US$34/MWh). While this initially appeared to be a straightforward cost reduction, the Energy Commission later clarified that green consumers must pay an additional MYR40/MWh (US$10/MWh) charge, which is subject to revision under future Regulatory Period tariff reviews. This brings the effective grid access charge to MYR180/MWh (US$44/MWh).
The fixed MYR140/MWh developer charge offers lenders and project sponsors predictable cash flow for the first ten years of operations. The variable MYR40/MWh consumer charge shifts tariff reset risk to offtakers during this period. As RP4 ends in December 2027, a ten-year agreement will cover multiple tariff review cycles. If future guidelines maintain the 15% cap on adjustments, the green consumer charge may rise by about MYR20–30/MWh (US$4.9–7.3/MWh) over the contract term.
"The most significant design feature is the revised structure’s reallocation of risk" said Alvin Tan, research analyst, Southeast Asia power and renewable at Wood Mackenzie. Now, developers gain ten years of cost certainty. Offtakers absorb the exposure to future tariff resets. Commercial discussions will increasingly focus on how that risk is shared.
Beyond the near-term window, Wood Mackenzie said that many Corporate Power Purchase Agreements (CPPAs) run for 15 to 21 years, extending well beyond the fixed-rate window. PETRA has not clarified how the SAC will be treated after year ten, and we expect developers and lenders to build post-year-ten cost assumptions into long-term return assessments regardless.
CRESS total delivered costs remain below High Voltage and Ultra High Voltage tariffs through 2038
CRESS total delivered costs remain competitive against utility tariffs. Comparing the SAC to conventional network charges alone is misleading, Tan warned. On this basis, Wood Mackenzie estimates CRESS procurement costs at US$95/MWh in 2026, making it competitive with both High Voltage (HV) and Ultra High Voltage (UHV) electricity tariffs. Despite periodic network tariff reviews, procurement costs are projected to increase by only around 8% through 2038, underscoring the role of renewable generation costs as the primary driver of CRESS competitiveness.
Comparison of UHV and HV ToU tariffs with estimated CRESS procurement costs in 2026, 2029 and 2038 (US$/MWh)

Source: Southeast Asia end-user tariff dataset 2026; Asia Pacific levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) 2026 Dataset. Estimated CRESS costs comprise the new-build LCOE, fixed SAC and variable SAC components, assuming the maximum permitted 15% increase at each RP review over the 10-year contract tenure. Energy charge outlook for UHV ToU and HV ToU are displayed in US$ real terms.
Project readiness will determine who benefits
Project readiness is emerging as the key constraint. Although 3,148 MW has been registered across 11 developers and eight buyers, the maturity of these projects remains unclear. With only 26 months until the 2028 COD deadline and utility-scale solar projects typically requiring 18-24 months from construction to commissioning, developers face a narrow window to secure permits, land, financing and grid access.
This structural difference is compounded by competition: CRESS developers must identify grid injection points and cover network reinforcement costs. Competition with the Large Scale Solar (LSS) programme for land and transmission capacity further increases this pressure, Wood Mackenzie noted.
“The lower SAC improves project economics, but it does not create additional land or transmission capacity,” said Tan. “Developers with secured sites and a clear path to grid connection are best positioned to deliver. For offtakers, delaying procurement is not a neutral decision. The most advanced projects will be secured quickly, and negotiating leverage will follow.”

articles.title: Fixed Income: Let Income Do the Heavy Lifting | BlackRock
articles.text:
Fixed Income

Nov 17, 2026

Rick Rieder

There are plenty of reasons to love long weekends. Rest, travel, time with family. But at today's yields, there's one more: your portfolio keeps working while you're away. As a simple illustration, at a 7% annual yield, a $1 million portfolio generates roughly $575 over a single three-day weekend.1 Markets close, prices stop moving on screens, but interest can continue accruing.
For years, investors had to stretch for returns, venture further out on the risk spectrum, absorb more volatility, and extend duration just to generate meaningful income. But with yields across high-quality fixed income at levels we haven't seen in a generation, the question has fundamentally changed. It's no longer how much risk can we take. It's how much risk do we actually need to take?
Fixed income: Getting paid to take less risk
The power of starting yield is difficult to overstate. Take another illustration, $10 million invested in U.S. investment grade credit generates approximately $30,300 of carry across 21 calendar days (seven long weekends), 2.7 times the 2021 level.2 All without needing to reach into obscure corners of the market, it's simply what high-quality fixed income pays today.
Beyond generating income, today's starting yields have fundamentally changed the recovery math. In the early 2020s, it would have taken nearly four years of income to offset a modest rise in two-year Treasury yields. Today, higher starting yields mean that same loss could be recovered in just 28 days.3 The cushion is substantial across fixed income: Take another illustration which shows yields would need to rise 147 basis points on the U.S. 5-year, 91 basis points on investment grade and 232 basis points on high yield before a full year of carry is erased.4 Higher yields may provide more information to help offset potential price declines if interest rates rise.
Across the global markets, real yields look as compelling as they have in more than a decade. The U.S. 10-year real rate sits at its 100th percentile since 2010.5 Australia, the U.K., and Germany are all near or above their 90th percentile.6 For years, investors were penalized for holding safe assets. That penalty has been inverted. Today, investors may get paid handsomely for sitting in real rates.
Days of carry needed to recover from a 20-basis-point rise in two-year U.S. Treasury yields

Source: Bloomberg, as of Oct. 21, 2026. The chart shows how higher bond yields have dramatically shortened the time needed for interest income to offset losses from a modest rise in two-year Treasury yields, from nearly four years in 2020 to just 28 days today.

Growth is strong, but the engine is narrow
Make no mistake: the U.S. economy continues to perform. Implied nominal yields based on historical growth and rate ratios suggest the current yield curve is fairly pricing a regime of solid real growth alongside persistent inflation.
But the composition of that growth matters, and it has become strikingly narrow. Virtually all the strength is concentrated in rate-insensitive nonresidential investment, primarily AI and infrastructure-related capex. Residential investment contracted at an annualized rate of 4.9% over the past two quarters.7 Goods consumption is barely positive.8 The growth engine is running on one extraordinarily powerful cylinder, but it's still just one cylinder.
Meanwhile, the relationship between growth and labor continues to decouple in a staggeringly clear way. Third-quarter nominal GDP is tracking near 7% year-over-year while compensation growth has stalled at around 5%. Profit per employee has surged back to 20%+ growth.9 The labor market is stable but unimpressive, and growth may increasingly come at the expense of labor, not alongside it.
Economic growth is outpacing compensation growth

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and Bloomberg, as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Inflation, too, remains stickier than many expected. Core consumer price index (CPI) inflation on a 3-month annualized basis has ticked back up, and even shelter inflation is showing renewed firmness. The Fed faces a difficult policy trade-off, with the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%. The challenge is that the Fed is essentially operating a house with one thermostat but very different temperatures in every room. Cyclical, rate-sensitive components of inflation appear relatively well controlled, but the hot spots, including energy, insurance, healthcare, education and shelter, are areas where another 25-basis point increase in the federal funds rate is unlikely to have much effect. In fact, a good deal of the shelter pressure exists precisely because mortgage rates are too high to build homes and unfreeze the housing market. Turning the thermostat down further may make the rooms that are already cool even colder, without doing much to cool the ones that remain hot. Hawkish rhetoric and patient policy can coexist, and we think they should.
The AI investment cycle: massive, magnificent, and increasingly concentrated
Hyperscaler capital expenditure (capex) is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2026 and $1.7 trillion in 2027, with upside risk.10 Financing this expansion increasingly requires significant issuance across debt and equity markets.11 The scale of that issuance is immense: total AI-related capital raising is projected at roughly $1.1 trillion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.12 AI-related debt outstanding is expected to be larger than the entire U.S. high yield market by the end of 2027.13 This surge in AI financing is reshaping fixed income supply dynamics in real time.
Just 10 companies now account for 40% of S&P 500 market capitalization and over 40% of its net income. Twenty stocks account for approximately 92% of the year-to-date increase in index EPS estimates (92%!). Expected EPS growth for the S&P 500 is 27%, but strip out the top 10 and it drops to 11%. Remove the largest 200 and you're at 5%.14
Concentration isn't just a valuation concern; it's a structural sensitivity. Using a hypothetical illustration, 50% moderation in the top companies' earnings growth rate would bring S&P 500 net income growth from roughly 32% down to around 20%,15 a significant swing driven by a handful of names all exposed to the same theme.16 High AI growth expectations and continued capital investment leave increasingly little room for any change in trajectory or disappointment, particularly given all the debt, equity, and rollover financing required from here.
The key question going forward is which companies can turn strong demand into lasting profits that justify the cost of their investments, and whether investors are better positioned in their stocks, bonds or both. So far, the largest increases in AI debt financing have come from companies with low leverage and high return on invested capital (ROIC). But as financing costs rise, the margin for error narrows.
A handful of companies account for much of S&P 500 net income growth17

Source: Bloomberg, as of Oct. 16, 2026. The chart shows that a relatively small group of large companies, led by Alphabet, Nvidia and Amazon, accounts for a substantial share of the S&P 500's earnings growth, highlighting how concentrated corporate profit growth has become. These companies were selected because they are the largest individual contributors to S&P 500 net income growth, highlighting how a relatively small group of companies drives overall earnings growth.

The case for rebalancing: it's in the data
The equity risk premium sits at its 7th percentile over the last three decades, meaning investors are getting paid very little incremental compensation for taking equity risk over fixed income. U.S. household equity allocations are at a record 71% of liquid assets while fixed income sits at just 8%, the lowest level in more than 40 years. Each percentage point of that liquid pool represents approximately $1.1 trillion.18
History is unambiguous here. Across U.S. and European credit, subsequent five-year annualized returns have historically tracked starting yields remarkably closely. Today's combination of strong economic growth alongside high available yields has historically tended to be one of the most favorable setups for forward fixed income returns.19
The recent equity rotation underscores this. Many AI names have unwound sharply since June while defensive sectors outperformed. When stocks start at higher valuations, returns can vary widely, even when corporate earnings are growing strongly. Historically, when S&P 500 earnings have grown by more than 10% and stocks were trading at more than 20 times earnings, market returns have ranged from losses of roughly 30% to gains of 50%.20 But that cuts both ways. High multiples certainly don't mean equities can't deliver very attractive returns, particularly with growth still solid and productivity gains helping margins. In fact, we think the next 12 months could be quite good for equities. We just expect a bumpier ride, with a much wider range of winners and losers along the way.
Meanwhile, fixed income offers a very different proposition today. With starting yields across the spectrum materially higher than in the prior decade, we believe there may still be an opportunity for investors to generate income without depending on price appreciation to drive returns. And the breadth of the market provides an opportunity to diversify that income across issuers, sectors and structures, while maintaining a focus on credit quality. In our view, the combination of higher starting yields and the potential diversification benefits of bonds makes fixed income a consideration in portfolio construction.
Fixed income offers a much broader opportunity to diversify

Sources: Bloomberg and BlackRock, as of Oct. 16, 2026. The chart shows that just 21 companies account for half of the S&P 500’s total market value, compared with nearly 2,200 bonds in the U.S. investment grade bond market, highlighting how much more concentrated the stock market has become.

The other side of selectivity: Credit quality matters more here
Headline spreads in high yield mask notable dispersion. A record share of bonds in the index now offer relatively little additional yield to compensate investors for credit risk, while the gap in yields between lower-rated B bonds and riskier CCC bonds is approaching levels seen during past financial crises. In this environment, we believe investors should be cautious about taking on significant exposure to riskier debt.
The risk of refinancing existing debt at higher interest rates is significant. Companies with B credit ratings that need to refinance in 2027 could face substantially higher borrowing costs, while those rated CCC face even greater challenges. Historically, companies with B-minus ratings have defaulted at an annual rate of roughly 8.3% when inflation-adjusted interest rates are high, compared with 4.9% when rates are low.21
At the same time, while security selection can’t assure positive results, we believe there's no shortage of idiosyncratic opportunity in asset-backed securities (ABS), commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) and emerging market (EM) local markets for investors willing to do the work on security selection. But a long weekend is only relaxing when your portfolio is built to withstand the unexpected. We believe the opportunity is to source income from quality and breadth, not to stretch for an extra 50 basis points.
Lower-rated credits face greater default risk in high real-rate environments

Sources: Bloomberg, Deutsche Bank, and BlackRock, as of Sept. 30, 2026. Chart shows that since 1980, companies with lower credit ratings have been more likely to default on their debt, particularly when inflation-adjusted interest rates are high.

Bottom line: Let your portfolio work so you don't have to
By way of illustration, if you are able to generate a 7% annual yield, a $1 million portfolio earns approximately $575 every three-day weekend. That covers roughly half the cost of an average three-day trip from New York, generated almost entirely from high-quality assets.22
The regime has shifted. Fixed income yields are at historically attractive levels. Real rates are positive across the globe. The equity risk premium is paper-thin, and equity market concentration creates fragility that investors don't need to accept. We believe today's starting yields give investors a much greater opportunity to generate meaningful income and diversify portfolios without relying exclusively on equity appreciation.
We believe this is a moment for investors to consider:

Anchor portfolios in high-quality, short-to-intermediate duration income.
Being patient about adding interest rate risk, particularly beyond five years, where the extra yield doesn't compensate for the incremental loss potential.23
Use fixed income's breadth as a structural advantage (just 21 stocks account for half the S&P 500's value; while more than 2,000 bonds account for half of the investment-grade index).
Be selective in lower-quality credit, where spreads mask a meaningful repricing of rollover and default risk.
Stay constructive on equities, with solid growth and productivity supporting another potentially good year, but be prepared for greater volatility and dispersion.

The markets will close again this Friday. The screens will go quiet, but interest can keep accruing. Enjoy the weekend.

articles.title: A Big Week For Markets
articles.text:
A Big Week For Markets

Will Denyer

Gavekal Research | 16 Nov 2026

This will be an eventful week for markets. On Tuesday, Nvidia will report its third-quarter earnings, diverting attention—even if only briefly—from former CEO Jensen Huang’s amorous affairs to what will be seen as an important healthcheck for the state of the AI capex boom. Then on Wednesday, Anthropic will price its IPO, before its shares begin trading Thursday. Meanwhile, after Friday’s air traffic control system failure grounded commercial flights throughout the US, President Donald Trump is calling on Congress to greenlight funds for an early upgrade, even as he is demanding immediate approval for an additional US$350bn in military spending.All this adds up to a lot of demand for capital, at a time when—as BlackRock CEO Larry Fink put it in October—the US is “seeing genuine shortages of capital,” and when the US Federal Reserve is poised to tighten monetary policy, with the futures market pricing in a certain rate hike in December and another probable increase in January. This is an ugly combination for bond markets, and helps explain why 10-year US treasury yields have risen 32bp from their November 5 low to trade at 5.14% early Monday. The forces keeping the US Federal Reserve in monetary tightening mode have not faded. Diesel and petrol prices remain high, artificial intelligence-driven inflation has not eased, and the labour market remains resilient. Housing market weakness and the recent wobble in AI optimism may make the Fed cautious, but core inflation is still skewed to the upside.

Listen to the article

Play00:00…Volume

Asian central banks have typically followed the Fed’s rate increases. However, it may be different this time unless the Fed’s hikes cause significant exchange rate depreciation in the region.

US inflationary pressures remain

The underlying inflation dynamics in the US have not changed much since the Fed’s rate increase in September. Global energy prices have remained high and tight diesel markets have boosted diesel price inflation (see Exhibit 1). Diesel prices are pivotal to the pass-through to broader inflationary pressures due to the fuel’s widespread use in transport, manufacturing and farming.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged recently that tighter financial conditions (due to the rise in bond yields) had helped the Fed to contain inflationary pressures. However, he also stressed that the Fed’s job was to ensure that sector-specific price shocks do not broaden out and that inflation expectations would not be unanchored. So, rising bond yields do not necessarily stand in the way of further rate hikes.

Asia is different

The Fed has already raised rates once in September. October’s stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation has increased the markets’ conviction of another Fed rate hike in December. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% month-on-month versus the consensus forecast of 0.3% and core CPI was 0.3% versus consensus expectations of 0.2%.

The European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada have also hiked their rates since September. In Asia (excluding Japan), the picture is more diverse. While a couple of central banks have hiked rates, most have stood pat.

Recent monetary policy cycle experience shows that Asia has not always followed the Fed’s rate moves in lock-step or has followed them with a lag unless the Fed’s hikes triggered sharp exchange rate depreciation. Why is that?

Firstly, Asian central banks have a wider set of policy targets than the Fed. They do not follow the Fed if its moves are inconsistent with their own domestic policy needs. Both market experience and Bank for International Settlements research1 show that Asia’s regional central banks have ‘unwritten targets’ including the exchange rate, economic growth and bond yields.

These factors, in turn, affect domestic inflation. Furthermore, the regional authorities also target headline inflation alongside core inflation. All these are different from the Fed-style dual mandates that put core inflation and maximum employment on an equal footing.

Exchange rate is paramount in Asia

Among these policy targets, the exchange rate is of primary importance for Asian authorities. Fed rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential between Asia and the US and if exchange rates depreciate markedly, this could amplify the inflationary effects on the region’s economies and financial conditions. To contain that potentially greater impact, the regional central banks will follow the Fed or even react more strongly than the Fed’s original move.

However, other than Indonesia and the Philippines, most of Asia’s economies have large current account surpluses (see Exhibit 2) that provide strong support for the region’s exchange rates, thus lessening the pressure to follow the Fed’s rate hikes. The recent downward pressures on Asia’s exchange rates mostly reflect a risk-off sentiment arising from the speed and breadth of the global rates sell-off rather than poor fundamentals and wider interest-rate differentials.

Secondly, despite nine months of high oil prices, core inflation has remained close to, or even lower than, target in most Asian economies, with the notable exceptions of Vietnam and the Philippines (see Exhibit 3). Subsidies have so far helped Asia to contain oil price-induced inflation and the region’s central banks to stay put at low fiscal costs to their treasuries.

However, if the oil shock lasts longer, fiscal pressure will increase and eventually prompt Asian governments to let fuel prices adjust accordingly, unleashing inflationary pressures. This would, in turn, likely prompt regional rate hikes in the wake of those by the Fed.

The bottom lines

The macroeconomic backdrop suggests that Asia is far from being in a broad-based interest-rate hike cycle. Policy rates are currently being driven by the impact of rising oil prices on domestic inflation.

A hawkish Fed may lead to a potential tightening bias in Asia, but it will not likely prompt widespread rate hikes unless interest-rate differentials between Asia and the US result in large and persistent regional exchange-rate depreciation.

Data sources: CEIC, Trading Economics, as of 10 November 2026 (unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

[1] The Expansionary Lower Bound: Contractionary Monetary Easing and the Trilemma, Bank for International Settlements, 2019.

articles.title: What is happening to the convenience yield on US Treasuries? | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

What is happening to the convenience yield on US Treasuries?

Chesapeake Dowdy and

Chesapeake Dowdy

Research Assistant
- Economic Studies, The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy

David Wessel

David Wessel

Director
- The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy,

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

November 20, 2026

Shutterstock / christianthiel.net

6 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The convenience yield compares a U.S. Treasury security’s yield to an otherwise comparable asset—such as a AAA-rated corporate bond or another advanced economy’s sovereign debt—with a similar maturity, risk, and payment profile.
When the convenience yield is positive, the U.S. government will pay less to borrow than others. In the past, estimated convenience yields for U.S. Treasuries were significant and positive because Treasuries were regarded as the ultimate safe asset: The market is large and liquid, and they’re widely accepted as high-quality collateral. But lately the estimated convenience yield on U.S. Treasuries has been shrinking.
Why do convenience yields matter?
Because the U.S. government is such a large borrower, even small increases in interest rates add up to a big number. Already, 15% of all federal spending goes to interest payments. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that if interest rates over the next decade are half a percentage point higher than it currently projects, the deficit would be $1.9 trillion larger over 10 years.
How do economists measure the convenience yield?
To measure the convenience yield, economists want to compare the yield on U.S. Treasuries to other risk-free assets, but there aren’t any precisely comparable assets. One approach is to compare the yield on Treasuries to the yield on AAA corporate bonds, adjusted to account for risk and for differences such as a corporation’s ability to call a bond before maturity. But only two corporations (Microsoft and Johnson & Johnson) are currently rated AAA by the two largest credit rating agencies. One alternative is to construct a measure of a risk-free asset from market interest rates using interest rate swaps or certain trading strategies designed to completely hedge risk. Another alternative is to compare the yield of Treasuries to the yield of debt issued by other governments, adjusted for differences in exchange rates.
What has been happening to convenience yields? Why?
The Treasury convenience yield has been declining since the Great Recession of 2007-2008 and turned negative in the early 2010s for longer-maturity Treasury securities. Following the COVID pandemic in 2020, the convenience yield fell further. In other words, Treasury yields are closer to the yield on risk-adjusted AAA corporate bonds and currency-adjusted G10 sovereigns than they were before the Great Recession.
A measure by Wenxin Du of Harvard, Ritt Keerati of the Federal Reserve Board, and Jesse Schreger of Columbia shows that the convenience yield for 5-year Treasuries compared to G10 government bonds of the same maturity has declined by 17 basis points, from -11 basis points on average from 2012-2020 to -28 basis points on average from 2021-2025.

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

There are different explanations of the erosion in the convenience yield. Among them:

Some researchers say the increase in U.S. Treasury debt issuance and fiscal concerns after the U.S. borrowed heavily to support the economy during the Great Recession and the COVID pandemic may have pushed the convenience yield on Treasury securities down. Bondholders may be getting less confident in the U.S. government’s ability or willingness to pay back the sums it has borrowed. Investors increasingly see U.S. Treasury debt as risky rather than safe, says Hanno Lustig of Stanford, due to worries that the government will not be able to collect enough revenue to repay it. He argues that central bankers and financial regulators haven’t grasped this new reality.
Du, Keerati, and Schreger find that the more borrowing by foreign governments relative to U.S. borrowing, the more attractive U.S. Treasury securities, and thus the bigger the convenience yield estimate, and vice versa.
Paul Cochran and co-authors at the Federal Reserve Board note that regulatory and other risk management constraints could limit dealers’ willingness to intermediate in Treasury markets. As Treasury supply grows relative to intermediaries’ capacity, Du and co-authors Benjamin Hébert of Stanford and Wenhao Li of USC argue, the convenience yield on Treasury securities declines.
Treasuries traditionally have been a hedge for stock market investors; when stock markets fall, Treasuries rise in value. But after 2021, Viral Acharya and Toomas Laarits of NYU note, stock and bond markets have moved in the same direction, weakening demand for Treasury securities as a hedge, and pushing down the convenience yield.

Is the declining convenience yield a sign of the U.S. dollar falling out of favor with global investors?
No.
Demand from global investors for other dollar-denominated assets, such as equities and corporate bonds, has remained strong—largely because of the dollar’s dominant role in global payments and financing.
Despite the declining Treasury convenience yield following the Great Recession, dollar yield convenience has remained positive. Even following “Liberation Day” tariff announcements in April 2025 that were associated with a depreciation of the dollar and decline in Treasury convenience yields, the convenience yield on the dollar rose.

articles.title: Is This a Bear Market? Bitcoin and Equities, Nov 2026
articles.text: November has been rough for digital assets and technology stocks. Bitcoin fell to a four-month low near USD 62k on 14 Nov 2026, and equities have sold off since Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s chief executive. Is this a bear market, or a correction? We asked our Head of Research, James Butterfill, and our Index Fund Manager, Alexandre Schmidt, for their readings. Both views and mentioned data date from 18 Nov 2026.Crypto: a continuation, not a new startIs this volatility an opportunity or the sign of a bear market? We asked our Head of Research James Butterfill and our Index Equity Analyst Alexandre Schmidt their takes on the current situation. A note provided on Wednesday 18 November 2026. For James Butterfill, the view is clear: Bitcoin was already in a bear market. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he says. “Bitcoin is still working through the whale selling that weighed on prices from late 2025, while expectations of higher interest rates and weakness in technology stocks have kept buyers cautious. Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease. Geopolitics will have a considerable say in that. A sustained breakout would likely require a change in the policy outlook, renewed whale participation or both.” As he wrote in our latest 13F report, which compiles the quarterly holdings disclosures of US institutional investors, “Institutional adoption continues”, yet “it cannot cancel out restrictive liquidity.” Equities: a correction, with crypto-linked shares as the exception In equities the picture is more nuanced, because valuations remain high. “Sentiment in equity markets has turned negative in recent weeks following concerns about the financing capabilities of major players in the AI trade, currently one of the main sources of US growth. While Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has thrown further uncertainty into the mix, the sell-off has so far been deemed a correction, with lofty valuations prevailing throughout,” Alexandre Schmidt says. “Broader equities remain in positive territory, with the S&P 500 up 7% YTD, but blockchain-related names are feeling the pressure, with bellwether names such as Coinbase and Strategy down 49% and 36% YTD respectively (as of 18 November 2026).”That gap is the point: blockchain-related shares are trading with crypto, not with the wider market. “Given that blockchain equity fundamentals are closely related to that of cryptocurrency markets, a breakout is likely to be triggered by an appreciation in Bitcoin and other digital assets or broader adoption of blockchain technology in other applications, especially asset tokenisation,” Schmidt adds. “Put simply, blockchain equities’ bear market is a mirror of crypto’s, and it is likely to end only when crypto sees a path to a sustained recovery.”Both researchers point to the same hinge: a change in the outlook for crypto itself, whether from policy, from large holders returning, or from wider use of blockchain technology.

articles.title: Transforming safety performance across transport infrastructure | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Infrastructure
Transforming safety performance across transport infrastructure

Link copied to clipboard

Through active ownership, MAM supported Odinsa to strengthen safety governance, accountability and culture, delivering improvements in safety performance

Swipe for more

SectorInfrastructureSub-sectorTransportLocationColombia and Ecuador

Opportunity

In 2022, a fund managed by Macquarie Asset Management (MAM) acquired a 50 per cent stake in Odinsa's transport platform, bringing together four roadway concessions and two international airports across Colombia and Ecuador.
The platform spans 774 kilometres of roads and two airports serving more than 52 million passengers annually, supported by more than 8,000 employees and contractors across diverse terrains, climates and regulatory environments.
Managing workplace health and safety (WHS) within a geographically dispersed transport network presented a complex challenge, particularly while major construction continued alongside live road and airport operations. Safety practices were also at varying stages of maturity, creating an opportunity to establish a more consistent approach to safety management, strengthen governance and accountability and reduce incidents in both operating and construction activities.

Approach

Leveraging specialist safety expertise and global best practices, MAM supported Odinsa to implement a platform-wide safety improvement plan focused on building a stronger and more consistent safety culture.
This included aligning Odinsa's practices with MAM's minimum safety expectations and supporting the formation of a joint WHS Committee, with Board-level representation from both organisations. The Committee provides dedicated oversight of safety performance, rigorous review of incidents and ongoing accountability against a refreshed risk strategy.
A comprehensive assurance framework spanning internal and contractor operations was also established, providing greater visibility into field-level operations and the platform's operational risk profile. Partnering with external consultancy advisers, Odinsa also launched initiatives including the ‘11 Life-Saving Rules’ and comprehensive training for leaders, frontline teams and contractors to identify and manage the precursors of serious harm injury.1
To drive accountability at the leadership level, WHS metrics were incorporated into management's short-term incentive plan, directly linking safety performance to reward.

Outcome

Odinsa's commitment at Board level, supported by the joint WHS Committee and technical guidance from MAM safety specialists, has helped drive a significant improvement in safety performance across the platform.
As of December 2025, the Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate (LTIFR) across Odinsa's roads and airports stood at 0.08, down from 2.70 in 2023. This was achieved while active construction programs continued alongside ongoing operations.2
Beyond the reduction in injuries, the platform has demonstrated that consistent safety standards can be embedded across geographically diverse assets with differing operational risk profiles. The strengthened governance model has deepened collaboration between MAM and Odinsa while creating safer outcomes for employees, contractors, road users and airport passengers.

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.
The safety and protection of data and information is a priority for Lazard, and we appreciate your careful attention and diligence.

Parsys 3

AI is moving quickly from assisting with individual tasks to agents capable of orchestrating increasingly complex workflows. But for financial services, turning that potential into meaningful outcomes at scale requires more than access to the latest technology.
Host Ronnie Wexler sits down with Barclays Co-Chief Operating Officer Anne Marie Darling to explore how AI could reshape customer journeys and the way businesses work, and what it takes for emerging use cases to move from experimentation into production. They discuss the importance of infrastructure, governance, resilience and human oversight as AI becomes increasingly capable of taking action on behalf of humans.
The conversation also looks beyond the technology itself to what this shift means for people and businesses, including why curiosity, critical thinking and deep domain expertise could become even more valuable as automation advances.
Listeners can also explore the topic further in previous Barclays Brief episodes:​​

Chips, chokepoints and the battle for AI supremacy
Pacing the Frontier: What’s next for AI?
AI goes economy-wide
Rise of the humanoid robots

Related content

Podcast: Chips, chokepoints and the battle for AI supremacy

AI investment is accelerating, but semiconductor chokepoints and geopolitical pressures are creating a new strategic reality.

Important non-Research content disclosures
