Transcript

Patrick Coffey
Think about how much more you're using AI today than even a year ago. It’s changing the way work, they way we think, and the way we solve problems. And for businesses, the opportunities are enormous. But turning that potential into reality, particularly at scale is far from straightforward.
To explore this more, Ronnie sat down in New York with Anne Marie Darling, our Co-Chief Operating Officer at Barclays, who helps run the technology strategy and implementation.
I hope you enjoy their conversation.
Ronnie Wexler
Anne-Marie, welcome to the Brief.
Anne Marie Darling
Thanks for having me, Ronnie.
Ronnie
Your first time, I have a feeling. Won't be your last, though. Especially with how quickly technology is moving, how fast the world is moving. We're clearly in a time of enormous change. We're going to speak a lot about that. But why don't we, before we kind of get into the here and now, fast forward in our minds: If we're sitting here in three years, how has the banking industry changed in your mind? How has the way we serve our customers changed in your mind?
Anne Marie
It’s tough
Ronnie
We had to start somewhere
Anne Marie
It's impossible to predict the future, given how quickly the pace of change was over the past six months.
Ronnie
Right.
Anne Marie
However, there's real structural shift happening. First of all, from a customer perspective, the opportunity isn't another chatbot. It's really agentifying the customer journey and workflows. And that will mean simpler, seamless, personalized and proactive experience that will really differentiate firms. The second is around colleagues. Everyone's using AI assist, I’m sure, you use it in your personal life and now it's moving to agentic.
So how do they think about the workflows? What does that mean, managing human and digital across complex workflows that you now have to orchestrate between the two? And all of that is really changing significantly. The other thing that really stands out is re-engineering businesses. So it's not about just making the horse go faster, it's about transforming a transportation system.
So the firms that differentiate themselves will be the firms that really reimagine the workflow and have a significant step function change. And the last is ruthless discipline on execution.
Ronnie
So it's all moving fast, hard for most people, sometimes me to keep up. How do you think about the way you prioritize our path forward and the way you prioritize the way we scale this technology?
Anne Marie
That's a great question. What we're really first focused on is enabling experimentation and innovation, because we really need that to happen to have those great ideas surface. But we then need to take that, put it as a proof of concept in a pilot. Is it working? Is the agent performing like we're expecting it to? Is it appropriate against the evals [evaluations] that we've set out?
And then do they earn the right to scale? And scale really goes against ‘do we have the right infrastructure in place to do that?’, ‘Do we have the right adoption?’ And importantly, ‘how are we prioritizing the high value AI initiatives?’, ‘Does that impact the customer where we want it to?’, ‘Is it reducing risk for the firm and is it increasing resiliency?’
And of course, ‘is it driving efficiency?’ which we've already seen to date. But that's what's really driving our overall prioritization.
Ronnie
So you mentioned experimentation earlier. You even brought the personal element of it. I have an interesting confession to make. Just this week I gave my own personal AI access to all my financial information, to my personal email. It was like very terrifying to do.
Anne Marie
You’re better than me Ronnie, I’m not there yet!
Ronnie
It was terrifying to do. But I have to tell you, it's liberating. Now that I have this, I can't stop and the work that it can do for me and just I feel so much more in control of my personal life. I feel like I have my hands on the wheel in a totally different way, and I, and I can see how this experimentation, this risk taking is just going to cause all these breakthroughs and everything that we do. And I'm excited about it. But you mentioned agents as well as we move into the agentic phase, so AI taking action on our behalf, on our businesses’ behalf, on our behalf as individuals and our personal life.
How do you think about risks and controlling those in that world where we're headed?
Anne Marie
Yeah, ultimately, you could do a lot more in your personal life than you can in our regulated environment. There's really four things that we're focused on. The first is the foundation. So do we have the right infrastructure in place? The right harness around the model, the right evals, and importantly, the right way to measure and look at the guardrails.
The second is around each AI use case and the life cycle. ‘What is the business outcome that you're trying to define?’ So start there, it's not about the technology
Ronnie
Right.
Anne Marie
Do you then have the right risk and controls around that outcome?’ How you then deploy that safely into production?
And we're very focused on that life cycle. The two other things we're focused on is enterprise. So how do these different AI use cases create dependencies across each other? Are we thinking about the resiliency across the firm? And do we have flexibility to move from different models if we were required to?
And then the last is really about soundness and scalability more broadly. And that's everything we put in place around our governance, transparency, observability and really linking each agent to a personal identity and access management. So we know exactly who it's tied to and the guardrails in place in terms of what it's allowed and approved to do.
Ronnie
Well, you spend a lot of time with AI leaders out there. Do you think they understand the magnitude issues of deploying this technology in a regulated fashion in a regulated industry like ours? And then also, what are some of the lessons of being at the forefront of this with those tech leaders? And how can we maybe apply some of that to what we do here?
Anne Marie
First of all, I think there's two sides to that. One: these technology companies are bringing innovation. They’re on the tip of the spear from a frontier perspective, and so we could learn a lot from that. And really developing our partnerships allows us to benefit. But the second is, as you know, our environment is quite regulated.
Ronnie
Yeah.
Anne Marie
And so to industrialize that technology, it has to be done in a certain way to ensure the safety and soundness of our customers data, all the money movement that happens across the firm to ensure we're doing that in the appropriate way. And so both sides can really learn, and that's a journey.
Ronnie
Let's move this to the lens of markets. A lot of what we do around here, what are some of the things around this phase shift in this journey that you think they should be acutely focused on right now?
Anne Marie
Well, the first is around compute. Obviously there's been a lot of discussions around compute. And so we should pay close attention to the supply around that, the demand, how we can access that and what that means over the next 3 to 5 years. So that will be a significant part of the equation. The second is around capabilities, right. This is moving quite quickly. I would say it's just like AI is similar to electricity, right? It's getting cheaper and there's more access, but it doesn't mean our consumption is going to go down. It really means how do we deploy it in so many different ways we haven't thought about. And so that capability as it evolves will be very important.
And then the other thing we're really thinking about is where do we build versus buy.
And so there's lots of benefits to get to market quickly by partnering with someone. But you also have to do it in the right way to ensure its industrialized in a regulated environment.
Ronnie
So you're at the forefront of major technological change. How has it changed the way you work personally?
What are some things that are different today versus maybe a year ago in your own workflow?
Anne Marie
So for me, I used to obviously do what everyone else did, efficiencies on email, drafting, helping me write a speech. Maybe not quite to the level you are in terms of bank accounts.
Ronnie
You'll get there, you'll get there.
Anne Marie
But what I'm spending a lot of time on is more the critical thinking. So if I have a hypothesis or an idea, what are the risks I haven't thought about? Where am I potentially not being as, where I'm more biased in my approach? How do I think about that? How is somebody pushing back on me? I mean, you should think about A, B and C. And I find that to be quite helpful. Now we're going to move into a world where I'm going to have the agents that are orchestrating much more complex workflows for me, where I will be delegating things to. Of course, I will be in the loop, but that's the part I'm really excited about.
Ronnie
So let's spend a little bit of time on the advice you would give to folks in the broader business world. There's a lot of anxiety around this change and how quickly it's happening. What advice would you give broadly to people in the professional world on how to embrace this technology and make the most of it?
Anne Marie
Yeah, there's a couple of things I would think about for me personally, and then more broadly. The first is curiosity is the most important, you need to experiment, innovate, you need to be hands on.
Ronnie
Yeah.
Anne Marie
Otherwise you're going to get left behind. The second is, cultural. As leaders, if we're not driving this and setting a good example, it's going to be pretty hard for anyone else in your team to change their behavior.
And then the third part is can you drive real change and have impacts? And that's the part that's most exciting.
Ronnie
Let's end on the next generation. My kids are young, they're in first and third grade, but they're constantly coming home asking about AI, asking about why it's such a big deal to everybody, asking about what it means for them. How do you advise them on how to make the most of this in their lives?
Anne Marie
Let's be honest. They're advising me and they're further ahead, as I really say.
Ronnie
That's probably that's probably comforting, right?
Anne Marie
I think that's a generational thing.
Ronnie
Good.
Anne Marie
I love learning from my kids. But what I what advice would you give them is, is similar like, be very curious. Right. You need to innovate and continue to learn and evolve not as it relates to just the technology – in general. The second is have deep domain expertise. Right? Because this technology is going to automate some parts of the workflow.
But the individual who's really deep and has domain expertise is going to leverage the automation to have a better outcome. And then lastly really think about overall leadership and how you're thinking about your team members around that and bringing them along the journey.
Ronnie
That's great. It's very bullish to me to see that the next generation is already way ahead of us.
Anne Marie
They’re passing us, Ronnie
Ronnie
And embracing this means that means there are some very good things to come. This was amazing. I really enjoyed spending time with you here. Thank you for all your insights.
Anne Marie
Great. Thanks for having me

About the experts

Anne Marie Darling

Group Co-Chief Operating Officer and Co-CEO of Barclays Execution Services

Anne Marie Darling is Group Co-Chief Operating Officer (COO) and Co-CEO of Barclays Execution Services (BX) and is a member of the Group Executive Committee. She co-leads Barclays’ global operations and technology teams, driving innovation and growth across the organization and delivering seamless experiences for clients worldwide.
Leading a global team of 60,000+, Anne Marie drives operational excellence and spearheads digital transformation, harnessing technology and AI to unlock new revenue streams and elevate client experience.
Prior to joining Barclays, Anne Marie was a Partner at Goldman Sachs, where she held senior leadership roles over a 25-year career, including Head of Marquee Digital Distribution Strategy, Head of Global Multi-Asset Platform Sales, Head of Global FICC Execution Services and COO of Global Securities Client Strategy. She played a key role in shaping strategy and digital client solutions and served on several firmwide committees. She was named Managing Director in 2007 and Partner in 2012.

Anne Marie serves as an Independent Non-Executive Director on the Nasdaq Exchange Board and on the Presidential Leadership Council for both Columbia and Brown Universities. In addition, she is deeply committed to advancing diversity and inclusion as Co-Chair of the Diversity & Inclusion Advisory Council for Brown University.

She graduated from Brown University with a degree in Engineering and holds an MBA from New York University’s Stern School of Business.

Ronnie Wexler

Global Head of Equities Distribution

Ronnie Wexler is the Global Head of Equities Distribution based in New York and a member of the Global Markets Management Committee. Ronnie has more than two decades of leadership experience in the financial services industry. He joined Barclays from NYDIG, where he served as Global Head of Business Development. Prior to this, he spent 19 years at Goldman Sachs where he held several leadership positions across Securities Division distribution, most recently as Partner and Co-Head of Americas Equities Distribution & Execution. In this role, Ronnie was responsible for all client facing functions across execution services, derivatives and research sales. He joined Goldman Sachs in 2001 and was one of the founding members of their Cross-asset Sales desk. Ronnie graduated from Cornell University and serves on the Board of Directors for Teach for America New York.

articles.title: Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation Disclosures
articles.text:
Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation Disclosures

Integration of Sustainability Risks into Investment Decision-Making ProcessAs a global macro multi-asset manager, our investment process is rooted in a deep understanding of how economies and markets work. Because environmental, social, and governance dynamics often impact global economies and markets, we deeply research these issues and integrate that research into our investment process in a manner that is consistent with our systematic way of managing money. Our approach seeks to understand how ESG considerations impact the financial objectives of return and risk. As a result, any research insight related to environmental or social issues that we believe would have material impact on financial performance flows through to each portfolio consistent with its objectives.Our research process is designed to continually adapt to include and prioritize new topics as they arise. The list of environmental, social, and governance dynamics we are looking at, and our assessment of their materiality continues to develop and evolve. Below we provide examples of different ESG topics with clear macro implications that we’ve researched and how we’ve incorporated the insights from that research into our investment decision-making with the aim of increasing returns and reducing risk.Remuneration PolicyBridgewater’s remuneration policies are consistent with its approach to the integration of sustainability risks into the investment decision making process. As sustainability risks can be a type of financial risk, Bridgewater acknowledges that failure to consider such risks could have an adverse impact on the performance of investments. Pursuant to its remuneration practices, Bridgewater typically awards fixed and variable remuneration to staff. Variable remuneration is awarded on a discretionary basis and takes into account the performance of an individual employee and the performance of the strategies managed by Bridgewater. Accordingly, to the extent that sustainability risks have an adverse impact on performance of the strategies that Bridgewater manages, this is likely to be reflected in the overall level of variable remuneration awarded to staff.Principal Adverse Impact PolicyBridgewater does not consider the principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factors as contemplated by article 4 of SFDR, as the nature of these investment products do not provide for the consideration of such adverse impacts. However, as noted above Bridgewater does incorporate so-called sustainability factors that it believes have material financial (risk/return) relevance into its investment process for all products it offers.EngagementBridgewater’s Stewardship and Corporate Engagement Policy is set, implemented, and overseen by the Sustainable Investing Committee, and it covers our approach to proxy voting, corporate engagement, industry collaborations with a broad range of industry actors, including data providers, research institutions, industry partners, and our clients, as well as external affiliations. The policy adheres to the guidelines of the Principles for Responsible Investing (PRI) and aligns with the recommended framework of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).Bridgewater Associates, LP — 2022 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2023 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2024 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2025 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factors

articles.title: Consumers Can Handle a Stock Crash
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Consumers Can Handle a Stock Crash

Jason Furman (PIIE)

Date
November 17, 2026 10:15 AM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Jeenah Moon

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org(link is external) website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website(link is external) for details).

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
This is the third in what I expect will be a series of five posts on the vulnerability of the economy to a collapse in what could be an AI bubble. The first(link is external) used the Fed’s large-scale macroeconomic model, FRB/US, to estimate the contribution of the AI boom to the economy and the second(link is external) assessed the magnitude of possible stock market declines. Future posts will look at the broader financial system and the system’s shock absorbers.

How bad would it be for the economy if AI is a bubble and it bursts? In my last post(link is external) I looked at how far the stock market might fall. This post is a deep dive into one channel through which a bear market would hurt the economy: consumers cutting back their spending if the stock market falls, aka the wealth effect. In the course of working on it I learned two relevant things that surprised me. The first is that the 2001 recession was barely a result of consumer spending cutbacks after the market fell; in fact, it was the least consumer-driven recession in both relative and absolute terms in the postwar period. The second is that consumers, in aggregate, have been surprisingly prudent in spending the recent stock increases—spending only about 1 cent of every dollar the market has gone up, meaning they would not need to cut their spending back dramatically on the way down.
This post examines the three scenarios that I justified in more detail in the previous installment. The baseline is a 25 percent decline in the market. But “baseline” should not be thought of as a base case—in fact, market pricing puts the probability of a decline of this magnitude sustained through the end of 2027 at less than 10 percent. A bad case is a 35 percent decline. And the severe case—which I view as very unlikely (market pricing puts it at about 2 percent; I would go above that but not by much)—is a 50 percent decline.
The bottom line of this analysis is that spending cutbacks if there is a bubble that bursts are expected to reduce economic growth by about 0.6 percentage point over the next year according to my preferred specification (Table 1), looking only at the effect of the stock market decline on consumption and ignoring other channels that could either exacerbate or mitigate the effect. The magnitude could be as large as 3.4 percentage points, but I view that happening solely through the wealth effect on consumption—the sole subject of this post—as a very remote tail risk.

In the remainder I start with what history says about stock market falls, move to the current context and then discuss what it means for economic growth.
Stock market declines called 17 of the last 9 recessions
Paul Samuelson famously quipped(link is external) that the stock market “predicted nine out of the last five recessions.” The current tally is 17 of the last 9 since 1946 for declines of 20 percent or more in the U.S. stock market(link is external) as a whole (Figure 1). Stock declines also missed three recessions that came without a decline of that magnitude.

In almost every case the market fall and the recession arrived at roughly the same time—the stock market decline was more a coincident indicator of recession than a leading indicator. Many of the stock market declines were not the cause of the recessions but instead were caused by the same forces that brought the recession. To take an extreme example, the big decline in the market in 2020 did not cause the COVID recession; both were caused by the pandemic.
One of the most clear-cut exogenous declines in the stock market was the 20.5 percent fall in the S&P 500 on October 19, 1987—a seemingly random event triggered in part by the release of worse-than-expected data on the trade deficit. In the year following that decline, real GDP grew 3.8 percent and real consumer spending grew 4.6 percent. (It helped that the Fed immediately said it stood ready to provide liquidity, and that the market had risen nearly 40 percent earlier in the year, but those are precisely the type of factors that could be operative if a bubble bursts today.)
As an aside, the stock market is not the only source of wealth. Housing is even more important for the majority of households and also affects consumption. Since 1976 the correlation between real changes in stock prices and house prices over a year has been just 0.16, and nominal house prices fell in only one of the ten big stock declines since 1980 shown in Figure 1 (2007–09), though adjusted for inflation they also fell substantially in 1980–82 and 1989–90. As a result, the hypothetical scenarios in this post just model stock market declines without considering any propagation or mitigation through the housing market.
Consumer spending held up after the 2001 bubble burst
The common analogy for the current situation is the dot-com bubble, which burst starting in March 2000, with the market falling by half and a mild recession starting a year later—followed by a painfully slow jobs recovery. That recession, however, was primarily about a dramatic reduction in investment: real business investment fell for eight straight quarters, dropping 12 percent from the end of 2000 to the end of 2002. Consumer spending slowed but it never went negative: during its worst four quarters it still grew 1.8 percent.
In fact, the 2001 recession is the only recession since 1950 in which consumer spending subtracted less from growth than business investment did (counting the back-to-back 1980 and 1981–82 recessions as one), accounting for only 21 percent of the shortfall in output growth—compared with 44 percent in the median of the other postwar recessions. Moreover, the absolute drag from consumer spending in 2001 was smaller than in any other postwar recession, as shown in Figure 2: only 0.5 percentage point, compared with a median drag of 2.0 points in the other recessions. (Note, you can see these plus many more comparisons of the sources and consequences of post-World War II U.S. recessions on the new Econvitals Recession Explorer(link is external).)

The surprise that drove the 2001 recession was almost entirely in investment. In December 2000 the Fed staff(link is external) had already marked down its forecast for consumer spending “as the effects of the lower stock market feed through,” and consumers did about what the staff expected: it forecast 3 percent growth in 2001, and spending grew 2.5 percent according to the latest data. It expected business investment to grow 7.1 percent; instead it fell 6.9 percent, as shown in Figure 3.

(And note, this slowdown in consumption spending growth is not a clean test of the wealth effect. Spending was held back by more than stocks: unemployment rose from 3.9 percent at the end of 2000 to 5.7 percent a year later, and 9/11 shook confidence. On the other side several factors helped spending: the Fed cut interest rates from 6.5 percent to 1.75 percent, housing wealth rose and the government sent tax rebates to households. Of course many of these same mechanisms could be expected if there is another large fall in stock prices—so the clean wealth effect is probably not the right prediction for what would actually happen.)
The biggest risk if there is a bubble that bursts is that the stock market is much bigger today…
The total value of the U.S. stock market(link is external) has grown from an average of 65 percent of GDP from 1952 to 1995, to 187 percent at the peak of the dot-com bubble in early 2000, to a record 286 percent in the middle of 2026, as shown in Figure 4. At the same time, an increasing share of the U.S. market is held by foreigners—from 8 percent in 2000 to 24 percent in 2026. But even the stock held by U.S. households, directly and through mutual funds, 401(k)s and IRAs, is much higher than it was in 2000, rising from 137 percent of GDP to 227 percent of GDP. (The household figure includes the foreign stocks Americans own, so it is not simply the part of the U.S. market that foreigners do not own.)

Part of the increase reflects the increased internationalization of the stock market. U.S. companies earn a lot of their profits abroad, and those profits show up in their stock prices but not in U.S. GDP. Mickey Levy estimates(link is external) that about one-third of the revenues of S&P 500 companies come from abroad, and an even higher share of their profits. Another cause is higher profits at home as income has shifted from labor to capital. Finally, multiples on earnings have increased(link is external)—which could be a sign of a bubble.
Regardless of the causes, the fact is that a 25 percent decline in the stock market today would wipe out about as much household wealth, relative to the size of the economy, as the halving of the market did after 2000: about 57 percent of GDP if foreign shares fell as much as U.S. ones, compared with the 61 percent households actually lost from early 2000 to late 2002. That is the best case for worrying.
…But households have spent only about 1 cent of every dollar of their recent stock gains
Historically people have increased their spending by about 3 cents for every $1 increase in their stock wealth (e.g., see this study by Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, Plamen Nenov and Alp Simsek(link is external)). There is no clear evidence that the effect is larger or smaller when the stock market is falling than when it is rising. The evidence on whether the wealth effect was shrinking over time is also mixed and uncertain (see the online appendix(link is external) by Claude for a literature review).
In the current stock market boom, however, it appears as if people have spent something more like 1 cent of every dollar of their gains—and possibly even less. This is very different from the housing bubble where people made purchases and leverage decisions based on the expectation of continued house price appreciation. If anything, it is as if people have either not had time to ratchet their spending up or are nervous enough about it lasting that they have been conservative in their spending.
The idea that people are being prudent and conservative with their spending may seem at odds with headlines about increasing financial stress, for example rising delinquencies, as people have tried to maintain consumption in the face of rising prices. The way to square the two is to note that much of consumption, and even more of wealth, is concentrated among households at the very top. In mid-2026, the top 0.1 percent of households owned 25 percent(link is external) of the stock and mutual funds households hold outside 401(k)s and pensions—up from 15 percent in 1989—and the top 10 percent owned 88 percent.
To take an extreme example, according to Forbes(link is external) the wealth of the 10 richest Americans in fall 2026 is $2.5 trillion higher than it was in fall 2019. While we do not have data on their consumption, I am willing to bet they did not increase their annual consumption expenditures by $7 billion each (which is 3 percent of their average wealth gain). Similarly, if the market crashes, they will not cut their spending by anything like that amount.
So let’s dive into the 1-cent number. There are four complementary ways to get at it:

A simple back-of-the-envelope calculation: Before COVID, from 2015 to 2019, consumer spending averaged 90.5 percent of disposable income. So far in 2026 it has averaged 91.6 percent—about 1 percent of income higher. Over the same period, the stock that households own rose from 1.8 times their annual income to 2.8 times—an increase worth about a full year of income. An extra year’s income in stock wealth bringing an extra 1 percent of income in spending is 1 cent per dollar—and probably less, since home values rose too. I use the five years before COVID rather than a single year because single years can mislead: 2019 had an unusually high saving rate and 2022, as people spent down their pandemic savings, an unusually low one. If you average over longer periods you get a similar or even smaller answer. (You can see other options for this comparison in the online appendix(link is external).)
The Federal Reserve’s model has a wealth effect of roughly 1 cent per dollar—and it matches post-COVID consumption data well. Figure 5 shows the prediction of the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US large-scale macroeconomic model, which is what I used in the first post in this series(link is external). The model has a marginal propensity to consume out of wealth of 0.9 cents per dollar in the short run and 1.4 cents in the long run. Its prediction is within a fraction of a percent of actual spending in 2026—which suggests it could be a reliable basis for predicting what would happen if the bubble bursts. If anything, it suggests FRB/US could overstate the wealth effect on the way down because it still overpredicted cumulative consumption on the way up—with households never making up for the spending they missed during COVID.
The prediction from a simple consumption function: Figure 5 also shows actual consumer spending against what a simple consumption function predicts—one that relates spending to income, wealth, unemployment and interest rates, estimated with data from 1955 to 2019 (it is explained more in the online appendix(link is external); it puts the marginal propensity to consume at about 2 cents out of stock wealth and 4 cents out of housing wealth). Actual spending is well below what this model predicts assuming households were in equilibrium in 2019: the actual spending rate is 2.1 percent of income lower than predicted, or $510 billion a year. Assuming instead that spending was in equilibrium on average from 2015 to 2019, the shortfall is 3.6 percent of income, or about $870 billion. The cumulative prediction errors are even larger because consumers never made up for all of their reduced consumption during the pandemic (adding up to about 15 percent of a year’s income since the start of 2020). Adjusting the 2-cent marginal propensity to consume out of stock wealth prediction for these prediction errors takes it down to 1 cent or lower.

Estimates of the marginal propensity to consume are much lower once the years since 2019 are included. If you estimate the same consumption function over rolling 20-year periods, the marginal propensity to consume out of stock wealth was about 2 to 3 cents in the periods ending between 2012 and 2019—but when you include data after 2019 it falls precipitously, to only 0.6 cents for the 20 years ending in 2026 (1.2 if you exclude 2020 and 2021), as shown in Figure 6.

How much would a bubble burst affect GDP?
All of this is a long way of saying I would not assume that stock declines take 3 cents off consumption for every dollar that is lost. Using the FRB/US model or a 1-cent marginal propensity to consume roughly matches the recent data—so is a reasonable and possibly even conservative guide to what would happen if the stock market falls. The consumption function I estimated based on data through 2019 is also reasonable, although the fact that actual consumption has risen less than it would predict suggests that it could fall less than it would predict. I also show a 3-cent rule of thumb as a downside risk case—it is certainly reasonable to consider the parameter that has historically governed behavior in the face of wealth shocks.
Table 1 at the top of this post puts these pieces together under the three stock market decline scenarios. Figure 7 shows the time series impact on consumption for a 25 percent decline in the stock market under the different assumptions—and you can see many more versions of the FRB/US simulation on the Econvitals Macroeconomic Simulator(link is external).

The bottom line, so far
If the stock market is a bubble that falls by 25 percent, then a decline in consumption of about 0.8 percent over the next year is plausible—which would mean about a 0.6 percentage point reduction in GDP growth assuming no other economic changes. Cutbacks in historic levels of business spending on data centers and the other pieces of the AI buildout would further hurt growth—but probably by only about 0.3 percentage point, as discussed in the first post(link is external) in this series, much less than the drop in investment itself, because about three-quarters of that spending is imported.
This analysis leaves out two other factors. The first is the degree to which other problems in the financial system—including in credit markets and banks, bank runs, capital flight or just a general increase in the risk premium—could reduce lending to other sectors, greatly exacerbating the data center investment reduction and consumer spending reductions. On the other hand, shock absorbers like monetary policy, fiscal policy and a shift in activity to other sectors—like housing—could mitigate the economic damage. The next two posts in this series consider these issues.

Data Disclosure

Note: This post was written by Jason with title, edits and fact checks by Claude. The data work was done interactively with Claude. An online appendix(link is external) by Claude has a literature review and the details of the estimates. A replication package(link is external) is available on Econvitals.

articles.title: Research funding and fellowships
articles.text:
Research funding and fellowships

There are several funding channels and fellowships available at the Bank of England, which support and further our research agenda.

In this section

Bank of England Agenda for Research, 2025-2028
Research datasets
Researchers
The digital pound
Fintech
Research Visitor Programme

Houblon-Norman and George Fellowships
Houblon-Norman and George Fellowships are awarded to promote research into and disseminate knowledge and understanding of the working, interaction and function of financial business institutions in the UK and elsewhere and the economic conditions affecting them.
The Houblon Norman Fund (registered charity 213168) is administered by trustees, on the advice of an expert committee.

Fund trustees
One of the fund trustees must be a current Bank of England Governor or Deputy Governor. The current trustees are:

Clare Lombardelli, Chair (appointed 2024)
Anne Glover (appointed 2019)
Nathanaël Benjamin (appointed 2023).

Fund advisory committee
The advisory committee is appointed by the trustees. It is made up of three people who have the academic standing and knowledge to make recommendations on who is awarded a fellowship.
The committee is currently made up of:

Professor Julia Black, Chair (appointed 2021)
Huw Pill (appointed 2021)
Professor Alan Taylor (appointed 2025).

Who is eligible for a fellowship?
Our fellowships enable successful applicants to engage in research on an economic or financial topic of their own choice, preferably one that would particularly benefit from being studied at the Bank of England. Applicants are encouraged to consult the Bank of England Agenda for Research. When assessing applications, the trustees will place particular emphasis on the relevance of the proposed research to current issues in economics and finance.
Senior fellowships are awarded to tenured full or chaired professors. Fellowships are also open to applicants at all other career stages, including postdoctoral researchers or those with equivalent experience. The duration of the fellowship is flexible, typically ranging from one month to one year.
The total amount distributed in any year rarely exceeds £120,000. Awards are provided as a per diem allowance, to cover subsistence costs such as travel, accommodation, and incidental expenses incurred during the fellowship. These allowances do not cover salary and should not be considered a substitute for remuneration.
Fellows will not be able to carry out teaching or other paid work during their fellowship without prior approval from the trustees’.
Applying for a fellowship
Please note applications for 2027/28 are now open. The closing date for applications is Monday 7 December 2026. Applications should be submitted via e-mail to MA-HNGFund@bankofengland.co.uk.
Application form Opens in a new window
For queries about the fellowships, you can email MA-HNGFund@bankofengland.co.uk.
History of the fellowships
The Houblon-Norman Fellowship was established in 1944 to celebrate our 250th anniversary. It is named after the first Governor of the Bank, Sir John Houblon, and the Governor at the time of the anniversary, Montagu Norman.

The George Fellowship was established in 2003 to recognise former Governor Sir Edward George’s lifelong service to the Bank, and his role as the first chair of our Monetary Policy Committee.

articles.title: Daily: Building resilience for 2027
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)Thought of the dayToday, we launched our Year Ahead 2027 outlook, "Sustaining resilience." Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of economies, corporate profits, and financial markets. In 2027, successful investing may depend more on deliberately building resilience into portfolios.The economic backdrop remains broadly supportive. We expect global growth to stay close to trend, while corporate earnings should rise further, and demand for computing capacity is likely to sustain investment in AI infrastructure. Easing inflation should also allow bond yields to decline modestly later in the year.But the range of potential outcomes is wide. Sticky inflation, elevated government debt, and geopolitical risks could drive bond yields higher and equity markets lower. In another risk scenario, execution and monetization risks could undermine confidence in attractive AI returns across the value chain.After a multi-year bull run, we therefore see a more balanced risk-reward for global equities in 2027. Our earnings forecasts remain constructive, but elevated expectations, index concentration, and uncertainty around the AI investment cycle leave less room for disappointment. We have downgraded global equities from Attractive to Neutral. Across asset classes, we see the most favorable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash as our least preferred asset class.Equities: Refocus rather than retreat. AI investment is accelerating, but so are the risks. We expect global AI-related investment to rise from USD 1.0 trillion in 2026 to USD 1.5 trillion in 2028, supported by constrained computing capacity and strong demand. Yet, cumulative US technology investment could approach USD 5.0 trillion by then. Revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5 trillion by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return, and while this is possible, not every company may reap the rewards. Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. External financing is also becoming harder, while market concentration, regulatory, and company-specific risks could increase volatility.This evolving nature of the AI trade is important for our S&P 500 outlook as the top 10 firms, most of which are exposed to AI, comprise 39% of the index, adding concentration risk. Beyond AI concerns, the risk of stickier inflation, higher Federal Reserve policy rates, and higher bond yields could contribute to additional uncertainty about the outlook. We believe the market may start to apply a lower multiple to future earnings to account for rising risks.We think investors should refocus equity exposure and diversify away from concentrated positions in technology. Regionally, the Eurozone is our preferred equity market. We forecast earnings growth of 15% in 2027, comparable with the S&P 500 but from a lower starting valuation and with a broader range of earnings drivers. At the sector level, we favor industrials and health care, while equal-weight strategies in the US can help reduce technology concentration. Since the start of June, the equal-weighted S&P 500 index has outperformed the market-cap-weighted index by around 7 percentage points.Bonds: Rebalance toward income and diversification. Elevated starting yields provide attractive income and a cushion against further increases in market rates. Quality bonds can also offer portfolio protection if economic or equity-market risks intensify. While we see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, within fixed income we see the best return opportunity in emerging market (EM) and high yield bonds. Improved external positions and fewer distressed issuers support EM bonds, although selection remains key. US high yield also looks resilient: 60% of the market is rated BB, expected defaults are around 2%, and only 3% of the universe matures over the next year. Across fixed income, we favor an intermediate average duration, generally through maturities of around two to 10 years, with a preference for shorter-dated bonds in the more growth-sensitive credit segments.Broaden returns with commodities, currencies, and alternatives. Commodities can help protect portfolios against geopolitical disruption, inflation, and constrained supply. We upgrade gold to Attractive: structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields should support a recovery toward USD 5,000 an ounce by December 2027. Oil should remain supported in the first half of the year, while copper is our preferred industrial metal given demand from electrification, power networks, data centers, and AI infrastructure.We think policy and interest rate shifts are creating attractive currency opportunities in 2027. Sterling is our preferred G10 carry opportunity, while select emerging market currencies may benefit from high yields and relatively contained volatility. In alternatives, our favored areas include hedge fund strategies that exploit market dispersion, operationally focused private equity and secondaries, and infrastructure with visible cash flows. Manager selection, underwriting discipline, liquidity, and position sizing remain important to manage risks including illiquidity and higher complexity.Our central message for 2027 is not to retreat from markets, but to take risk more deliberately. Putting excess cash to work, addressing portfolio concentration, rebalancing toward fixed income, and adding differentiated return drivers can help portfolios continue to compound even when markets depart from the base case.

Without these Cookies, services you've asked for (such as internet banking) can't be provided. These Cookies don't gather information about you that could be used for marketing or remembering where you've been on the internet. These Cookies can be disabled through your browser or device settings but to do so would prevent our Websites from working properly, e.g. we cannot guarantee the security during your visit.First Party PerformanceAlways ActiveThese Cookies collect information about how you use our Websites, for example which pages you go to most often and if you get error messages from certain pages. These Cookies enable us to count visits and traffic sources so we can improve our website and its features but don't gather information that identifies you, as information collected by these Cookies is aggregated. Performance Cookies are not used to target you with online advertising. You can disable them, but then we will be unable to see how our Websites are performing and make relevant improvements to enhance your browsing experience.First Party FunctionalAlways ActiveThese Cookies allow the Websites to remember choices you make (such as entering your user name, selecting your language or the region you're in) and tailor the Websites to provide enhanced features and content for you. For example, they can be used to remember certain log-in details and changes you've made to text size, font and other parts of pages that you can customize. They may also be used to provide services you've requested like watching a video or commenting on a blog. These Cookies may also be used to ensure that our services and communications are relevant to you. The information collected by these Cookies cannot track your browsing activity on the internet. Without these Cookies, our Websites cannot remember choices you have previously made to personalize your browsing experience, meaning you would have to reset these for every visit to our Websites. In addition, some functionality will not be available if this type of Cookie is disabled. First Party TargetingAlways ActiveWe set these Cookies to gather information about your browsing habits, for example the cookies may remember that you've visited a particular website. This is to provide you with tailored online advertisements that are more relevant to you and your interests. These cookies may be set on our website to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other websites. Although these Cookies can track your visits to other websites, they don't usually know who you are. If these Cookies are disabled, online advertisements will be less relevant to you and your interests.Third Party PerformanceAlways ActiveThese cookies come from third-party organizations with which BNY partners and are used to collect information about how you use our websites, for example which pages you go to most often and if you get error messages from certain pages. These Cookies count visits and traffic sources to improve websites and features but do not usually gather information that identifies you, as information collected by these Cookies is usually aggregated. Performance Cookies are not used to target you with online advertising. You can disable them, but this will impact our ability to make relevant improvements to enhance your browsing experience.Third Party FunctionalAlways ActiveThese cookies come from third-party organizations with which BNY partners and allow websites to remember choices you make, such as entering your user name, selecting your language or the region you're in, and tailor the websites to provide enhanced features and content for you. For example, they can be used to remember certain log-in details and changes made to text size, font and other parts of pages that you can customize. They may also be used to provide services you've requested like watching a video or commenting on a blog. Without these Cookies, our websites cannot remember choices you have previously made to personalize your browsing experience, meaning you would have to reset these for every visit to our websites. In addition, some functionality will not be available if this type of Cookie is disabled.Third Party TargetingAlways ActiveThese cookies come from third-party organizations with which BNY partners, including social media providers, and gather information about your browsing habits, for example the cookies may remember that you've visited a particular website. This enables third parties to provide you with tailored online advertisements that are more relevant to you and your interests. These cookies may be set on our website by third parties to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other websites. articles.title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks -  speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the Central Bank of Turkey, İstanbul Economic Forum

Published on
08 October 2026

Andrew Bailey says that although the financial system has remained resilient through repeated geopolitical and economic shocks, weaker growth, persistent supply disruptions, rising sovereign debt, leveraged markets and expanding AI-related exposures create risks. Policymakers should therefore pursue sustainable growth, maintain credible monetary and fiscal frameworks, and strengthen core financial markets so they can absorb future shocks without amplifying them.

Speech
The financial system has so far weathered the latest period of uncertainty. But lower growth, repeated supply shocks and changing market structures mean that resilience cannot be taken for granted.
The conflict in the Middle East has created major uncertainty about growth, inflation and interest rates. Existing vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets, credit markets and asset valuations could crystallise together. The rapid expansion of financing connected with artificial intelligence has created new exposures, while incidents involving frontier AI have underlined the associated operational, cyber and financial risks.
However, an important part of the story so far is economic resilience in the sense that recent supply shocks have hit the world economy at the same time as the potential growth dividends from AI have become clearer.
Moreover, the story of the financial system so far has been one of resilience. Banking systems generally remain well capitalised and we are not seeing funding stress. Despite a succession of economic shocks and heightened volatility, most financial markets have continued to function without a major breakdown in liquidity or trading conditions.
Financial markets have so far withstood significant increases in sovereign bond yields, and most market adjustments have remained orderly. This resilience owes much to the reforms introduced after the global financial crisis. Those reforms are sometimes criticised as burdensome. Today, their value is clear.
But we cannot be relaxed. Experience teaches us that specific problems can emerge even when the wider system appears stable. The lesson of the global financial crisis is that such problems are much easier to manage when the wider system is resilient and the authorities are committed to keeping it that way.
The deeper economic challenge
Behind the immediate risks lie two longer-term developments.
The first is weaker potential growth, driven in many economies by slowing productivity, which determines how rapidly national income and living standards can rise.
The second is the frequency of large negative supply shocks. Covid, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have each disrupted the supply capacity of economies. Covid was also both a supply and demand shock, with the balance changing over time. But all these episodes were exceptionally large, and they followed one another with unusual speed.
Are repeated shocks the new normal? Central bankers should be wary of becoming political soothsayers. But a more multipolar world, in which economic policy is increasingly an arena for geopolitical competition, may produce more frequent disruptions. We should therefore prepare for a world in which larger shocks are not rare exceptions.
This creates a particular difficulty for monetary policy. A negative supply shock pushes inflation and output in opposite directions, producing weaker output but higher inflation.
The textbook response is to look through a one-off increase in the price level. Interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and monetary policy affects the economy with long lags. But looking through a shock is possible only if inflation expectations remain well anchored.
If households and businesses begin to incorporate higher inflation into wage demands and pricing decisions, a temporary shock can become persistent. These second-round effects are slower to emerge. Central banks must make forward-looking judgements and update them as the evidence changes.
The difficulty becomes greater when shocks arrive in quick succession. A recent history of higher inflation can cause people to expect further inflation. The sequencing of Covid and the invasion of Ukraine have made this risk particularly acute.
The interaction with financial stability
Supply shocks can also create tension between monetary and financial stability. Interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens. Debt-servicing costs increase just as household incomes and corporate earnings come under pressure. Asset prices can fall, reducing the value of collateral and restricting the supply of credit.
This is why resilience before a shock is so important. Strong banks and sound household and corporate balance sheets give policymakers room to respond without turning an economic adjustment into a financial crisis.
Fiscal policy faces a related challenge. Lower growth and repeated supply shocks weaken the public finances while increasing pressure on governments to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and weaker growth raise debt-to-GDP ratios. If markets begin to doubt the fiscal trajectory, bond yields can rise further, tightening monetary and financial conditions.
Governments can ordinarily use their balance sheets to cushion a severe downturn and rebuild fiscal space when conditions improve. That is the principle of countercyclical policy. But when shocks become more frequent, underlying growth is weaker, and the succession of shocks leads to a higher level of government debt, this becomes much harder to sustain.
A changing market structure
Global government bond markets have also changed profoundly. They were once dominated by long-term investors, often described as “real money” and “price insensitive”. Today, leveraged investors play a much larger role, while traditional demand for long-duration debt has declined, partly because of changes in pension provision and ageing populations.
This new structure has so far increased the capacity of markets to absorb the additional supply of government debt. But greater absorption has come with greater fragility. Leveraged positions can be unwound rapidly. Losses can trigger margin calls, model-driven repricing and stop-outs, producing further forced selling that can amplify market moves. The buyers are typically more price sensitive.
The same funds may hold large leveraged positions across several countries and asset classes. Deleveraging that begins in one market can therefore spread quickly to others.
The policy response must have several parts.
First, we must pursue sustainable growth. There is no single solution, but major technological advances have historically lifted productivity. Artificial intelligence and robotics can drive scientific discovery, improve efficiency and raise prosperity. Financing that investment is essential. But greater financial exposure to AI also creates risk. If earnings expectations or confidence in the pace of AI adoption were sharply revised, the consequences could spread through equity, credit and sovereign markets. AI safety and financial stability are therefore becoming increasingly connected. Safely deployed, we should see AI as a growth opportunity.
Second, monetary and fiscal frameworks must remain credible. For monetary policy, that means an unwavering commitment to returning inflation to target. I remain sceptical of unconditional promises about future interest rates. The world is too uncertain. But central banks should explain clearly how policy would respond under different economic conditions.
Fiscal policy must likewise be directed towards stability and be seen by markets as credible. Clear frameworks, including fiscal rules, can help contain risk premia when shocks occur.
Third, we must strengthen the resilience of core markets. Greater central clearing, appropriate minimum haircuts and stronger risk management all merit consideration.
There is no quick fix. But the direction is clear: raise sustainable growth, maintain credible policy frameworks, and ensure that financial markets can absorb shocks without amplifying them.
The system has been resilient. Our task is to make sure it remains so.
I would like to thank Nat Benjamin, Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Andrea Rosen, Vicky Saporta and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England

articles.title: Take Two: US inflation rises - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
What do you need to know?

US inflation rose by 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% the market had been expecting. Though it was a slowdown from September’s 0.6%, the data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates in December. An annualised figure was not released due to the government shutdown in October 2025. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, increased by 0.3%, for the third consecutive month. Separately, the MSCI World Index rose 2% in the week to Thursday’s close with the Nasdaq rebounding 4% from the previous week’s fall*.

*In US dollar terms. Source: FactSet, data as of 12 November 2026

Around the world

China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026, well above the $964.8 billion recorded in the same period last year, driven by global demand for artificial intelligence-related products. The figure puts the country on track to reach a record level for the full year. Elsewhere, eurozone GDP grew 0.4% in the third quarter, the official second estimate showed, down from 0.6% in Q2. In addition, the UK economy grew 0.7% on a quarterly basis in Q3, its fastest pace for more than two years.

Figure in focus: 35%

A new global pledge aims to increase the use of electricity to 35% of total energy consumption by 2035, up from around 23% today. The “35 by 35” target was officially endorsed at the United Nations climate change conference COP31, taking place in Turkey from 9-20 November. The goal includes increasingly moving from fossil fuels to electricity for sectors including transport, buildings and industry, to reduce carbon emissions and costs, as well as enhancing energy security.

Chart of the week

US consumer confidence has recovered slightly in November, according to the University of Michigan’s initial estimate – though the index has fluctuated at low levels for a year. Meanwhile, the eurozone index has failed to recover sustainably since its drop in March and April. Although consumer confidence is usually only loosely correlated with spending, purchasing power erosion due to rising energy costs is sufficiently pronounced to modify consumption habits. Additionally, widespread uncertainty is expected to deter households from major spending.

Words of wisdom: Singles’ Day

Singles’ Day started in China as a celebration of being single, taking place on 11 November – the date was chosen as the numerals represent individuals. It has grown into one of the largest global online shopping events, with retailers offering sizeable discounts to rival those of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sales around Singles’ Day are viewed as a barometer of China’s economic activity – this year sales rose 4.8% to 1.78 trillion yuan (US $267 billion) from the year before, according to reports citing data provider Syntun.

What’s coming up?

On Monday, the eurozone reports industrial production data, followed by the US on Tuesday. The Reserve Bank of Australia publishes the minutes of its last interest rate-setting meeting on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the eurozone and UK each publish their latest inflation data, while the Federal Reserve issues the minutes of its last monetary policy meeting. It opted to keep rates on hold at 3.75%-4.0% in October.

articles.title: Outlook 2027: Investment implications - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
The global economy enters 2027 with renewed momentum, although growth remains uneven and threatened by political uncertainty, inflation, and high debt costs

In equities, we see potential opportunities in technology and in Europe’s drive towards strategic autonomy

In fixed income, we favour inflation-linked bonds as well as European investment-grade corporate bonds

The global economy enters 2027 with stability and renewed momentum but economic growth is likely to be uneven and numerous risks remain.

The International Monetary Fund recently raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from the 3.0% it projected in July but kept its 2027 forecast unchanged at 3.4%.

The US economy has been resilient, and inflation appears likely to slow. Europe’s growth outlook is more positive than it has been for some time despite a backdrop of political uncertainty.

In China, growth is likely to slow as consumption and property investment remain subdued. Elsewhere in emerging markets, we expect growth to remain resilient albeit uneven in 2027.

From a markets perspective, we expect the technology sector will remain a key driver of equity markets, though the other sectors have seen steady gains, particularly in the US.

Within fixed income, inflation and debt concerns are weighing on the outlook for government bonds. Inflation-linked bonds can potentially offer a hedge against further escalation in the Middle East. Meanwhile US and European corporate bond yields look attractive, but investors should remain selective.

Central investment themes for 2027

AI shifts from experimentation to adoption

Artificial intelligence’s economic impact could become increasingly visible in the year ahead, marking a shift from technological possibility to real-world adoption and monetisation. Advances in physical AI are beginning to translate into real-world automation, initially in factories and warehouses, alongside AI-enabled wearables such as smart glasses. This could bring notable return on investment for companies at the forefront of new AI-related products and services.

Implementation idea – Disruptive technologies

Rationale: AI infrastructure demand is expected to outpace supply through 2027, especially as innovation opens new opportunities. Companies that can translate AI investment into sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on capital should emerge as the long-term winners.

2027 could be the year that cloud service providers demonstrate the return on investment for their unprecedented AI infrastructure spending, but the software sector will require increasingly careful navigation to distinguish AI beneficiaries from those vulnerable to disruption.

The AI safety and regulation debate will continue in 2027 meaning cybersecurity and governance will play a critical role, with stocks in this sector remaining potentially attractive despite premium valuations.

Europe’s strategic autonomy drive

As Europe aims to grow its economy while safeguarding its own interests, it is placing greater focus – and investment – in areas ranging from defence and manufacturing to energy, food and health.

Security concerns have accelerated investment in areas such as defence while digitalisation is advancing more slowly. Even so, technology remains a cornerstone of European sovereignty, which is shaping not only European policy but also presenting significant opportunities for investors. Companies capable of translating the drive for European strategic autonomy into cash flow and sustainable revenue growth could well emerge as the long-term winners.

Implementation idea – European equities

Rationale:

European strategic autonomy is driving potential opportunities for equity investors in high-growth sectors such as technology, renewable energy and energy infrastructure. Meanwhile government and corporate bond issuance is likely to increase to fund the required support, meaning potential new opportunities for fixed income investors.

At the same time, it is becoming more important for investors to be selective and distinguish between companies benefiting from policy support and increased demand, including the prospect for stable cash flows and long-term contracts, and those struggling against global competition.

Navigating inflation volatility

Geopolitical tensions, energy insecurity and rising AI investment are reshaping the inflation outlook. As the global economy moves away from the price stability of the pre-pandemic decade, investors are facing a world where inflation is likely to be more elevated and less predictable. We believe investors need to shift to a more strategic approach to inflation protection.

While inflation-linked bonds have historically been used as short-term tools, they now offer an attractive option as a long-term portfolio component. Valuations of inflation-linked bonds have become more appealing, and they can potentially provide a buffer against unexpected price shocks while preserving purchasing power.

Implementation idea – Inflation-linked bonds

Rationale:

The shift toward a more volatile inflation backdrop strengthens the case for inflation-linked bonds within fixed income or multi-asset portfolios. Unlike conventional bonds, inflation-linked bonds have cash flows that are adjusted in line with inflation, aiming to provide a structural hedge against the erosion of purchasing power.

However, because inflation dynamics vary by region, as seen in the differing impacts of US tariffs versus energy shocks in Europe, an active, global approach is essential. This can allow investors to diversify across markets and potentially manage the interest rate sensitivity of their bond portfolio while aiming to capture inflation protection.

Capitalising on Europe’s corporate resilience

The European investment-grade bond market has shown remarkable resilience against a highly uncertain backdrop. Corporate fundamentals remain healthy, with solid cash-flow generation providing a strong foundation.

Looking toward 2027, we expect volatility to persist, but we believe the European credit outlook remains constructive. Attractive bond yields and robust corporate earnings offer a potentially attractive entry point for investors, suggesting that demand for the asset class will remain supportive despite short-term market fluctuations.

Implementation idea – European investment grade bonds

Rationale: The combination of attractive yield levels and strong corporate balance sheets makes European investment-grade credit a potentially attractive addition to diversified portfolios. While higher interest rates have raised concerns, the ability of high-quality issuers to maintain profitability and manage funding costs likely limits the risk of significant rating pressure.

However, as the market becomes more differentiated, a one-size-fits-all approach is no longer sufficient. Security selection is critical, and an active approach allows investors to target potential returns in other areas such as higher-quality high-yield bonds.

Opinions draw on investment team views and are not intended as asset allocation advice.

articles.text:
Consulting Report

19 Nov 2026

How can tax and finance leaders prepare their function for an AI-enabled future?

In collaboration with EY (Ernst & Young)

Transforming tax and finance requires more than applying AI to existing processes. Functions have to adapt to rising regulatory demands while providing greater strategic value. We surveyed 1,600 tax and finance executives globally, spanning 22 industries, to dig deeper into these themes, examining how leaders can combine technology, trusted data, and human judgement to build more responsive operating models.

Amidst geopolitical instability, shifting trade policies, and the expansion of digital tax administration, tax and finance teams are under growing pressure. Leaders must manage increasingly complex compliance requirements while responding quickly to changes across the markets in which their organisations operate.

At the same time, businesses expect tax and finance functions to look beyond their traditional responsibilities. Teams are being asked to identify emerging risks and contribute more directly to strategic decision-making. Our findings suggest that AI can help create the capacity needed to meet these expectations, but technology alone will not deliver transformation.
