articles.title: Market update - November 20th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Bitcoin’s bounce meets a Fed that has not finished tighteningA bit of green is welcome after the last few weeks, although we would be cautious about declaring victory just yet. Bitcoin’s recovery towards US$64,000 looks largely tied to improving risk appetite around Anthropic’s IPO. The deal was heavily oversubscribed and priced above expectations, while results from the likes of Nvidia have also helped steady sentiment towards AI after a challenging few weeks. Investors clearly have not lost their appetite for the theme, although they have become rather less forgiving about valuations.There has been plenty of discussion about AI drawing capital away from crypto, and there is probably something in that. But the relationship works both ways. The recent deterioration in AI sentiment has been damaging for Bitcoin as part of the wider risk trade, so a recovery there can also help crypto. What neither market escapes, however, is the Fed. Improving sentiment around an IPO does little to alter the cost of capital.Wednesday’s FOMC minutes1 were more hawkish than Warsh’s press conference had suggested. Almost all participants judged that further rate increases would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks. Most supported holding rates in October, but a few of them regarded the decision as a close call. A couple of participants said a move larger than 25bp (a quarter of a percentage point) could warrant consideration in December if inflation data disappointed. For now, 25bp remains the central case, with the more important issue increasingly whether further tightening follows in January and March.The minutes also contained an interesting warning on AI itself, with the staff highlighting the rapid growth in AI-related debt, off-balance-sheet leases and circular financing arrangements, and the risk that losses could be amplified if investment returns disappoint. Most participants observed that much of this borrowing sits in complex and opaque structures. That is another reason we struggle to see the case for a 50bp move unless the inflation data deteriorate materially. There is already plenty of leverage sitting inside the most rate-sensitive part of the equity market.Retail sales have not made the Fed’s job any easier. Headline sales rose only 0.2% in October, but excluding autos they increased 0.6%, while the control group, the core measure used in GDP calculations, also rose 0.6%.2 September’s headline increase was unchanged at 0.8%. Consumers appear more selective rather than meaningfully weaker, which supports the case for another hike even if it does not justify an aggressive one.We believe markets are becoming a little too pessimistic on inflation. Inflation is a lagging indicator: oil has fallen from roughly US$113 to around US$92 per barrel over the last couple of weeks, and that will eventually feed through. The more important question is whether the Fed gets ahead of that disinflation or waits for it to appear in the backward-looking data. History suggests the latter is more likely, and that is probably the larger risk for markets now.Crypto sentiment remains poor. Long positions have been unwinding, liquidity is thin, and even the bid-ask spread on IBIT, BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF, has widened to around 17 to 19bp, which is about as close to peak bearishness as market plumbing usually gets. Momentum indicators such as the relative strength index also show markets oversold at present, so it is worth being cautious about extrapolating the current weakness indefinitely.Gold’s sharp fall adds another useful perspective. Bitcoin has held up relatively well by comparison, although it may simply be that gold is catching up after having run much harder earlier in the year. Either way, Bitcoin’s refusal to break materially lower despite hawkish rate expectations, weaker risk appetite and persistent outflows is notable.There are increasingly bearish calls for Bitcoin to revisit US$40,000, usually based on applying the drawdowns of previous cycles to the current one. We believe this is too simplistic. Institutional ownership is much larger than in prior cycles and is providing a degree of structural support that simply was not present before.US$60,000 therefore remains a very important psychological level. Our outlook still assumes Bitcoin spends much of the period trading between roughly US$60,000 and US$90,000. A decisive break in either direction probably requires a much more aggressive change in monetary policy or liquidity conditions than we are seeing today.The AI relationship is slightly more complicated over the longer term. Technology equities have historically had a strong relationship with money supply because they are long-duration, rate-sensitive assets, and AI is very much part of that trade. Bitcoin is also sensitive to liquidity, although it often moves earlier. If the AI investment cycle eventually suffers a more serious leverage-driven correction, Bitcoin would probably be hit with it initially and may even lead the move. We would also expect it to recover faster once investors start distinguishing between a leveraged capex cycle and an asset whose monetary characteristics are rather different.Waller’s speech this week was constructive in that respect. He described the convergence between blockchain and traditional finance as clearly under way, with tokenised stocks, bonds and commodities (issued as digital tokens on a blockchain) increasingly moving on-chain. Stablecoins, tokenised deposits and money-market funds could coexist with conventional payment rails, while traditional firms and decentralised finance (DeFi) businesses compete across multiple models. His caveats were around governance, custody and legal certainty rather than the direction of travel.So sentiment has improved slightly, but the rates problem has not gone away. The market is probably too pessimistic on some parts of the inflation story and too optimistic about how quickly the Fed will acknowledge that. Until that tension resolves, Bitcoin looks more likely to grind around within its range than embark on a clean trend.Sources1 Federal Reserve, Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee, 27 to 28 October 2026, published 18 November 20262 US Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade Report, October 2026, released 17 November 2026

articles.title: A breakdown of China's government revenue and tax history over nearly 75 years
articles.text:
PIIE CHARTS

A breakdown of China's government revenue and tax history over nearly 75 years

Navneeraj Sharma (Asian Development Bank) and

Arvind Subramanian (PIIE)

November 12, 2026

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Chart Embed

Description
This chart shows China's government revenues from taxes and other sources during 1952–2024.
The overall level of revenues averaged about 30 percent of GDP before China's then-leader Deng Xiaoping's 1978 "Reform and Opening Up" policies. Revenues declined sharply thereafter in the 1980s, increased sharply from the mid-1990s, reaching a peak of about 28.5 percent of GDP in 2015. When adding land sales and retained profits from state-owned enterprises (SOE), revenues peaked at 39 percent in 2018.
The composition of revenues has changed dramatically. In the pre-reform period, a substantial share of overall revenues came as profits of SOEs. Compulsory production quotas at off-market prices, financial repression in favor of SOEs, and strict quotas on consumer goods imports diverting demand to consumer goods produced by SOEs were all implicit ways of extracting revenues, which were reflected in the profits of SOEs.
After the mid-1990s, and consistent with the turn to markets, more modern tax levers have been used, including value-added taxes (VAT), personal and corporate income taxes, and social insurance contributions. Distinctively, revenues from land sales have accounted for a substantial share of revenues since 2003. Throughout its history, therefore, China has generated a substantial share of revenue from sources other than taxes on its people, which is surprising for a communist state.
Regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for most of the last decade; for example, taxes (excluding social insurance contributions) have collapsed by nearly 5.5 percentage points, from 18.4 percent of GDP in 2012 to 13.0 percent in 2024, and revenues including land sales and retained SOE profits fell 6.5 percentage points, from 39.0 percent of GDP in 2018 to 32.5 percent in 2024. These tax levels are associated with a struggling, lower middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower.
How much of this decline is attributable to growth that is even slower than headline numbers indicate and how much to the tax cuts enacted over the last decade is difficult to say. But it also seems that the government was so reliant on non-tax sources that, once they dried up, it became politically difficult to turn around and impose taxes on the population.
ADDITIONAL NOTES

Subsidies to loss-making SOEs are spending, as in the International Monetary Fund's system of fiscal accounting. China's budget subtracted them from revenue in 1985 to 2006; they are added back here. Before 1985 they were also subtracted, but the amounts were not published, so they cannot be added back; the broadest measure is broken between 1984 and 1985 for this reason, and most of the rise of the bars in 1985 comes from it. Without the add-back, 1985 would be 25.0 percent of GDP, against 25.2 percent in 1984.
Not available, and so left out: subsidies to loss-making SOEs before 1985; social insurance contributions, 1984 to 1988 (they were 0.9 percent of GDP in 1989); the social insurance funds' own income, 1998, 1999 and 2010; government funds inside the budget, 1997 (2.2 percent of GDP in 1998); local state capital budgets, 2007 to 2011 (central government only); and retained SOE profits before 1996.

articles.title: How Far Could Stocks Fall?
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

How Far Could Stocks Fall?

Jason Furman (PIIE)

Date
November 15, 2026 9:30 AM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Jeenah Moon.

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org(link is external) website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website(link is external) for details).

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
This is the second in what I expect to be a series of five posts that chart the consequences of the AI boom and the risks of it deflating. The first post(link is external) used the Federal Reserve’s large-scale macroeconomic model to estimate the consequences of the AI boom. This post is about the risks of a stock market decline. The next post will discuss how much a given fall in the stock market would affect consumption and economic growth. After that I plan to tackle the financial system and the economy’s shock absorbers.

One critical piece in understanding the risks we face in the economy today is understanding how much stocks could fall if it turns out we are in a bubble. It is hard to answer how much the stock market would decline if there is a bubble that bursts because my normal presumption is that I cannot outguess the market, and thus that it is not actually a bubble now. That is why I keep the bulk of my financial investments in the broad stock market (Vanguard's VT specifically, which effectively holds all of the world's stocks). I am not currently making an exception to that rule, so, putting my mouth where my money is, a decline is not my central expectation.
That said, if forced to answer the question of how much the stock market would fall if it is in a bubble, I would use a number of methodologies. A 50 percent decline in the biggest AI stocks would by itself mean an 11 percent decline in the broader market, not counting any knock-on effects on other sectors. Another method is to look at various valuation metrics and combine them with assumptions about earnings declines. These give answers in the range of 18 to 41 percent. All of these declines are much larger than what options markets treat as likely; in fact, options pricing suggests an unusually low chance of a large market decline—but, of course, if the market is misvalued these options may be too. Regardless, anything like the 50 percent decline seen when the dot-com bubble burst is a very low-probability tail risk, and if forced to pick a baseline I would choose 25 percent.
Just because many past technologies have ended in bubbles does not mean it is a bubble now
Bubble proponents note that, historically, exciting new technologies often lead to bubbles, like railroads, radio and the internet. This is not actually always true—jet planes and smartphones were not bubbles. Regardless, even if major new technologies are eventually bubbles, that does not provide much insight about whether it is in a bubble at any given moment. If the stock market rises a lot before losing some of its gains, then calling a bubble today would have been wrong—as the 1996 test below shows.
Being early to call a bubble is not prescient—it is wrong. I first personally called the Tesla bubble in April 2017 (the call was made to friends, not in writing). That is when Tesla's market value exceeded both Ford's and General Motors'. At the time, Tesla was making about 76,000 cars a year, Ford about 7 million and General Motors about 10 million. It was an obviously insane valuation. And yet Tesla is up about 1,800 percent since I made that call. During this period I mentally shorted Tesla several times—but fortunately never acted on it and kept my money in Vanguard index funds. And yes, Tesla may fall one day, but unless it falls about 96 percent or more—which I do not think even their biggest critics expect—my call will have been wrong.
One model of a technology explosion is a process where each year there is an 85 percent chance of a 30 percent increase and a 15 percent chance of a 50 percent decline. The expected return is 18 percent—a good investment—but it is also inevitably the case that a 50 percent decline will happen and a bubble caller will be superficially vindicated.
Or consider another process, which could be operative today, which is that there is a small probability of a massive return to a company. It is easy to imagine that with Anthropic or OpenAI. In this case, it could be that in the majority of the cases the bubble callers will be vindicated—and not just superficially—but on average they will still be wrong and it could still be worth investing.
But let's get more concrete on where we are today and how it compares to 2000.
Today does not appear to be 2000
Since the end of 2019 the S&P 500(link is external) has risen about 135 percent while its companies' earnings have risen about 125 percent. The biggest drivers of today's stock market boom are mature companies with very high revenue that is growing very quickly like Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia. Over just the last three years, Nvidia's revenue has risen more than ninefold, and Alphabet's and Microsoft's have each risen about 60 percent. Driving much of this is the emergence of AI, a technology that has been adopted faster than anything we have seen before—including the personal computer and the internet(link is external).
The demand is also different. Much of the late 1990s investment boom was in building out the fiber network for the internet. Much of it was based on a "build it and they will come" theory that was not quickly vindicated—by one widely cited estimate(link is external) only 5 percent of the fiber was lit in the early 2000s, although others put it closer to a third. Today the investment boom is in data centers and so far basically all the chips are being used to the max—in fact there is so much excess demand that the price of renting an Nvidia H100(link is external) has risen more than 50 percent since last December.
You can see the large difference from 2000 by comparing some of the leading stocks of the dot-com bubble(link is external) with the leaders now (Table 1): their prices relative to both current and expected earnings were much, much higher in 2000 than they are now. Cisco, for example, was trading at 213 times its trailing earnings as compared to 21 for Nvidia today. Or comparing to expected earnings, Cisco was at 102 then (on earnings two years ahead, which flatters it) as compared to Nvidia at 13 today.

The aggregate market tells a similar story. The ratio of stock prices to expected earnings over the next twelve months(link is external) is 18.3, the 77th percentile of its history since 1979 (Figure 1). This is well below the 24 to 25 of 1999 and 2000.

Of course, the expected earnings may themselves reflect bubbly forecasts. Another measure is Robert Shiller's cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio(link is external) (aka CAPE) which compares stock prices to inflation-adjusted earnings averaged over the previous ten years. The advantage of this measure is that it averages over business cycles so it does not extrapolate too much from what might be a temporary boom in earnings. The disadvantage is that if there are genuine changes in earnings over time it can be slow to update based on them. This measure stands at 40 today, the 99th percentile of its range since 1881 but still a bit below its 1999–2000 peak of 44 (Figure 2).

The high stock market is about profits, not multiples
The high valuation of stocks has been more a story of rapidly rising profits (which is missed by the Shiller CAPE measure, which is very lagged) than of increases in multiples on these earnings. You can see this in the profit share (Figure 3), which had been stable for decades after World War II but has been steadily rising since 2000 and recently has reached a new record.

Note this too is very different from 2000, when the profit share had been falling—from 7.9 percent of GDP in 1997 to 6.0 percent at the stock market's peak in early 2000.
This suggests that the recent run-up in stock prices has been more about earnings than multiples. So the biggest worry going forward is less about a dramatic decline in future earnings growth than it is about a dramatic decline in actual earnings.
Although one should also be worried that multiples fall. In some ways the steady multiple itself is a puzzle given that alternative investments to stocks have gotten more attractive. The real interest rate, as measured by 10-year TIPS, has risen from generally being less than 1 percent in the years prior to COVID to above 2 percent for the last six months.
The next section considers both falling earnings and falling multiples to size the potential fall if a bubble bursts.
How far would the stock market have to fall to get back to "normal"?
Notwithstanding the high and rising revenue of tech companies, it is not hard to imagine a large stock market decline. The valuations of AI-related stocks are premised on both an increase in productivity from the technology that makes it desirable to businesses and consumers and also the ability to monetize that by building moats. The second assumption, especially, is at best uncertain.
Relatedly, the companies could be victims of their own success. The more the models improve, the more people can use older, cheaper models—including extremely cheap open-weight models. In fact, there are some signs(link is external) that revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic is no longer increasing as fast as it was: The Economist estimates that the AI developers' three-month revenue growth slowed from 80 to 90 percent in the spring to 12 percent in October, although not every indicator agrees. I personally find my token usage has fallen over the last few months as models have become more efficient and I am now considering cancelling one or even two of my four Claude Ultra plans.
If it is a bubble that bursts then by how much will the market fall? Table 2 considers several ways of sizing the fall in the market as a whole(link is external), measured from where it closed on November 13, about 3 percent below its record high on August 13.

If Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom and Oracle all fall by 50 percent then the market as a whole would fall by 11 percent. On the one hand, a 50 percent decline is very large for many of those companies because they are large, established companies with substantial profit flows unrelated to AI. On the other hand, if they fell it is likely other AI-related stocks and even other unrelated stocks would fall too—although it is possible there would be a countervailing increase in software stocks, which have fallen 14 percent since their peak in September 2025 on fears that AI would replace them.
To look at the broader market, one thought experiment is that the forward price-earnings ratio falls from its current value of 18.3 to its average since 1979, 15.0. That would mean an 18 percent decline in the market. If that reset was accompanied by 20 percent lower expected earnings, that would be a 34 percent decline in the market.
If the Shiller CAPE returned to its average since 1979, 23.6, that would be a 41 percent decline in the market. Finally, if the excess growth of the stock market over nominal GDP since 2019 was reversed, that would be a 34 percent decline in the market. Note this is similar to assuming a counterfactual in which the stock market had normal returns over the last seven years—nominal GDP has grown at a 6.2 percent annual rate(link is external) since 2019—a bit below the roughly 7 percent a year that stock prices have grown over the long run.
Would these yardsticks have worked in the dot-com bubble?
How would these methodologies have worked in predicting the magnitude of the dot-com decline? It is tempting to ask what they would have predicted about the magnitude of the decline on March 24, 2000 (the S&P 500's peak). But that analysis assumes you already know the date the bubble will burst, something that is only clear in hindsight. If earnings and stock prices continue to rise before the bubble bursts then the trough, measured from today, could be much less of a fall than using today's metrics would imply. To that end, I also apply this analysis to a "placebo" date, which I choose as December 5, 1996, when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan gave his famous "irrational exuberance" speech(link is external).
Table 3 runs the same yardsticks on those two dates and compares them with what actually happened.

This analysis suggests that if we are at the peak of the bubble today, then the metrics are reasonable. They basically called the magnitude of the dot-com bust correctly: the actual fall, 51 percent, was near the mild end of their range of 49 to 59 percent. That leads me to think that if we're at the peak now (or just below it, since prices are already down a little), then the 18 to 41 percent range is reasonable—and that one should shade that down, not up.
But we do not know we are at a peak, and the 1996 test suggests that, judged in advance, this analysis could be hopeless—massively overstating future stock losses if earnings grow more before the potential bubble deflates.
What options markets say
Finally, another way to estimate the probability of stock market declines is by looking at the pricing of options on declines in the S&P 500(link is external). Table 4 shows these for options that expire in December 2027.

These are the chances that the index ends up at least that far down on the day the options expire, not that it falls that far at some point along the way. By that measure, options put the chance of the S&P 500 being 20 percent or more lower in December 2027 at 11 percent, and the chance of its being down by half at 2 percent. The chances of declines this large at some point before then, including ones followed by some recovery, are higher.
Figure 4 shows the history of a closely related measure since 2007, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis(link is external): the chance options put on the S&P 500 being 20 percent lower a year later. The pricing of that risk is near the low end of its range: at 8.5 percent at the end of October, it was lower than in 86 percent of the weeks since the series began in 2007. (That is a bit below the 11 percent in Table 4 because it covers 12 months rather than 13 and was measured before stocks fell in early November.)

This history also shows that in one sense even an implied 8.5 percent chance that the market will be down 20 percent a year later is too high. Investors are paying for insurance and so willing to lose in expected value for securities that pay off in bad times. That is why since 2007 options have priced the chance that the S&P 500 would be 20 percent lower a year later at 13 percent on average, while that actually happened about 5 percent of the time.
That said, if you think the market is irrationally overpriced then these contracts are too. Historically options pricing has not been particularly prescient. It turns out it has been more of a coincident than a leading indicator, only sounding a warning once a decline is under way. In fact, it was below average in October 2007, February 2020 and February 2025—all just before large market declines.
Bottom line: a baseline of 25 percent
Based on all of this—and if one is willing to ignore actual market pricing of the level and risk of market changes—a reasonable baseline for the "if it is a bubble and it bursts" case is a 25 percent decline. I would consider a bad case to be a 35 percent decline in the broader market. A severe—and highly unlikely—case is 50 percent.
Even the baseline case would be a big hit to household wealth: a 25 percent fall would wipe out about $19 trillion of the stock that households own directly and through mutual funds and retirement accounts. Whether that would cause a recession—through consumers cutting back, and through the financial system—is the subject of my next posts.

Data Disclosure

Note: A partial replication package(link is external) is available on Econvitals: the code for every figure and table and the public data behind them. The licensed data are described there but not included.

articles.title: Macro Signposts | The Rent ‘Catch-Up’ Is Over – What’s Next for Shelter Inflation? | PIMCO
articles.text:
Tiffany Wilding, J. R. Scott

11/18/2026

| 8 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

All the presented audio appears as text.

PIMCO Pod
The Rent ‘Catch-Up’ Is Over – What’s Next for Shelter Inflation?

0:00
/
15:07

Seek

Volume

Playback Speed

Key takeaways

The post-pandemic rent “catch-up” that kept U.S. shelter inflation elevated is largely over. We expect shelter inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to continue moderating through 2027, settling around 3% or slightly below.
Owners’ equivalent rent (OER), a major component of shelter inflation, may cool more gradually. It increasingly reflects single-family rents, which remain firmer than multifamily apartment rents amid high mortgage rates and limited supply.
Shelter should remain a source of broader disinflation, but its contribution is likely to diminish. As the multifamily supply wave recedes, the scope for further declines may narrow approaching 2028.

For the past several years, shelter inflation has been one of the most persistent sources of overall U.S. inflation, and a major affordability challenge for many households. We have argued that much of that persistence reflected the unusual mechanics of the post-pandemic rental market: New-lease rents surged in COVID’s immediate aftermath, while rents for existing tenants adjusted much more gradually. That left a large gap between market rents and the average rents captured in the Consumer Price Index (CPI); the gap narrowed as lease renewal rents slowly “caught up” to market rates. (Details in the 11 February 2026 Macro Signposts.)
In late 2026, the gap between new-lease and renewal rents has mostly normalized, and shelter CPI inflation has fallen dramatically from its 2023 peak. Adjusting for distortions related to last year’s government shutdown, shelter CPI inflation was 3.3% year-over-year in October 2026, down from more than 8% at its peak.
But the end of the rent catch-up story does not necessarily mean every category of rent is headed sharply lower from here. Owners’ equivalent rent (OER), which estimates how much homeowners could expect to be paid if they rented out their primary residence (even if they don’t actually do so), is a major component of shelter CPI calculations – and OER inflation isn’t decelerating as quickly as some other shelter inflation measures. This is largely because single-family rent growth, which is increasingly represented in OER, continues to outpace rental inflation in larger multifamily housing units as post-pandemic preferences for more space and higher mortgage rates keep would-be homeowners in the market for single-family rentals. This segmentation appears especially pronounced in large cities, where new single-family rental supply is limited.
Family preferences, along with our outlook for the Federal Reserve to keep rates higher for longer – we are expecting two or maybe three more hikes from here, followed by a prolonged pause – plus the greater supply of multifamily housing still coming to market in the Sunbelt after the post-pandemic building boom are likely to support divergent trends within rental markets and keep shelter CPI inflation around 3% or just slightly below.

The great rent catch-up

The origins of the current trends in the U.S. rental market trace back to the pandemic. COVID delivered an extraordinary shock to U.S. housing demand. Remote work and disruptions to in-person schooling increased households’ demand for space, household formation accelerated, and historically low mortgage rates and strong household balance sheets (fueled in part by government stimulus) amplified purchasing power, all while the supply of housing was slow to respond.
The result was a rapid rise in home prices – followed closely by a rise in rents – in 2021 and 2022, as more households competed for a relatively fixed stock of housing. Research from the San Francisco FedFootnote1 estimates that the shift to remote work and resulting preferences for more space alone accounted for more than half of the pandemic-era increase in house prices, with similarly large effects on rents.
The adjustment within the housing market wasn’t uniform; renters in particular felt the shock at different speeds. New tenants experienced the rent spike almost immediately. For example, Zillow’s measure of market rents rose at double-digit rates during the COVID boom, peaking at 17.2% year-over-year in February 2022; by October 2022, rents were nearly 27% above their October 2019 level.
Existing tenants experienced the shock much more gradually as leases expired over time and landlords were slow to reset rents on existing tenants. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), only about 20% of renters move in a typical year, while research published by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)Footnote2 estimates that rents for continuing tenants close only about 20% of the remaining gap between the old rent and current market rent when leases are renewed. Because that adjustment applies to the remaining gap rather than the original gap, convergence is slow: After five years, roughly 70% of the original gap has closed.
As a result of these dynamics, OER inflation lagged other U.S. market-rent measures by about one year. It recorded a lower peak in the post-pandemic era, but it also took much longer to normalize (see Figure 1).

Figure 1: Owners’ equivalent rent didn’t surge as much as other U.S. rental inflation measures, but it took longer to normalize

For illustrative purposes only. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Zillow, Cotality, and CoStar as of October 2026

Now, roughly six years after the initial pandemic shock, the significant divergence between market rents and the rents paid by existing tenants has greatly diminished. For example, the gap between OER inflation and Cotality’s single-family rent index, which approached 10 percentage points in early 2022, had returned to its pre-pandemic average by late 2025. The rent gap that sustained shelter inflation for several years is therefore no longer the dominant force driving its outlook.

Which definition of market rent should OER follow?

With the post-pandemic rent catch-up largely complete, the next question is which measure of market rents OER should follow.
Not all rental markets behave alike. Research by BLS and Cleveland Fed economists finds that rent inflation for apartments and detached homes can diverge materially even within the same neighborhood, evidence that rental markets are segmented by structure type. That finding is important for OER: While OER is intended to measure the rental value of the owner-occupied housing stock, the rental sample underlying the index historically contained more apartments and fewer detached homes than would be representative of the owner-occupied housing stock.
In January 2023, BLS changed its methodology, reweighting rental observations used to calculate OER to better match the structure-type composition of the owner-occupied housing stock. This adjustment gave additional weight to detached rental homes where they were underrepresented. In January 2024 alone, the OER weight on single-family detached homes increased by roughly 5 percentage points.
More recently, market-rent measures that historically moved relatively closely together are now sending quite different signals. Zillow and Cotality’s measures of rents for single-family housing units are rising between 2% and 3% year-over-year, compared with roughly 1% to 0% increases reported by CoStar and Apartment List national rent measures, both of which primarily measure rents in multifamily units.
There are good economic reasons for this divergence to persist. Multifamily construction surged after the pandemic, particularly across Sunbelt markets, pushing apartment vacancies higher and restraining rent growth.
But newly constructed apartments are imperfect substitutes for large single-family units. A family looking for more space, a particular school district, or a suburban three-bedroom home may compete for a single-family rental even when apartment supply is abundant elsewhere. High mortgage rates reinforce that segmentation by keeping would-be homeowners in the rental market and supporting demand for properties that are closer substitutes for owner-occupied homes.
Geography compounds these differences. In markets with a large supply of multifamily units, such as Austin and Seattle, landlords tend to offer substantial concessions, while townhomes and other specialized rental products in the same cities can experience materially stronger rent growth. Large, supply-constrained cities can also look very different from markets with more space to build that experienced the largest post-pandemic construction booms.
These geographic differences are increasingly apparent in the official inflation data. OER inflation in the 12 largest U.S. metropolitan areas was running at 3.5% year-over-year in October 2026, compared with 3.0% elsewhere, reversing the pattern observed as recently as mid-2025 (see Figure 2). At the same time, the multifamily supply wave itself is beginning to recede as the number of new units completed has fallen sharply from its 2024 peak.

Figure 2: Owners’ equivalent rent in the largest U.S. cities now outpaces the average elsewhere

For illustrative purposes only. Source: BLS, Haver Analytics, and PIMCO calculations as of October 2026

Shelter disinflation still has further to run, but probably not forever

The implication of greater market segmentation and OER’s detached housing measurement focus is that multifamily apartment rents may no longer be the best forward indicator of OER. The end of the post-pandemic catch-up should continue to pull OER inflation lower, but there is no reason OER must converge all the way to the near-zero inflation currently reported by some multifamily rent indices. The relevant rental markets are segmented by structure type, geography, household characteristics, and affordability, and today’s data increasingly reflect those differences.
Putting these pieces together, our outlook is for U.S. OER inflation to settle around 3% (maybe a touch below) and stay there throughout 2027. Across 40 forecasting models,Footnote3 including time-series, leading-indicator, rent-gap, and structural lease-renewal approaches, the average forecast points to shelter CPI inflation moderating to slightly below 3% by the end of 2027 (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: Economic models support a forecast of gradually moderating shelter inflation

For illustrative purposes only. Source: BLS, forecasting models, and PIMCO calculations as of October 2026, with forecasts through September 2027

As an aside, published inflation data may temporarily obscure this underlying disinflation. Because of distortions associated with the October 2025 government shutdown, year-over-year shelter inflation could approach 3.5% over the coming months, even as the underlying pace continues to moderate. These base effects should largely unwind by April 2027.

Bottom line for inflation

In 2024 and 2025, the key question was how long OER would take to catch up to the enormous pandemic increase in market rents. Today, that adjustment is largely behind us. The question now is what inflation rate the underlying rental market will sustain.
We expect shelter inflation to continue cooling through 2027, settling just under a 3% pace and providing an important offset to inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy. But we would be cautious about extrapolating multifamily rent weakness directly into OER, or assuming shelter inflation will simply keep falling. OER increasingly reflects a single-family rental market that remains supported by expensive homeownership and constrained supply, while the enormous wave of new multifamily supply is beginning to recede. As a result, the scope for further shelter disinflation should diminish as we approach 2028.
The pandemic rent catch-up may be over, but that does not mean shelter inflation will converge to softer trends for multifamily rentals.

articles.title: What is the federal debt ceiling? | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

What is the federal debt ceiling?

Sage Belz,

Sage Belz

Former Research Analyst
- Hutchins Center on Fiscal & Monetary Policy, The Brookings Institution

Sophia Campbell,

Sophia Campbell

Former Senior Research Assistant
- Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy

Lorae Stojanovic, and

Lorae Stojanovic

Former Senior Research Assistant
- Economic Studies, The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy

David Wessel

David Wessel

Director
- The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy,

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

November 18, 2026

12 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
This explainer was originally published in August 2017 and has been updated several times since.

The recurring need to lift the ceiling on overall U.S. Treasury borrowing is always a political hot potato. The U.S. government’s borrowing hit the debt limit ($36.1 trillion) on January 1, 2025. The Treasury then initiated what are known as “extraordinary measures” to conserve cash. On May 9, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Congress that unless Congress acted, the Treasury probably wouldn’t be able to pay its bills in full and on time beginning in August. Congress did act. In the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, Congress raised the debt ceiling by $5 trillion, to $41.1 trillion. Because the federal government continues to run deficits, the debt has risen since then. The Bipartisan Policy Center projects that the debt will hit the ceiling in February or March 2027 and that the Treasury will have enough cash and maneuvering room to pay the government’s bills for another six to nine months after that.
What is the debt limit, and why do we have one?
When the federal government runs a deficit—that is, spends more than it collects in revenue—it borrows money to cover the difference, usually by issuing IOUs in the form of U.S. Treasury securities. The debt ceiling is a legal limit on the amount of borrowing the Treasury can do.
Before 1917, each loan issued by the Treasury required authorization from Congress. When the U.S. entered World War I, however, Congress changed the law to allow the Treasury to sell war bonds (Liberty Bonds) as needed, provided that bond sales didn’t exceed a specific amount—the debt limit.
Over the last three decades, the limit has precipitated political battles during which some legislators have used the vote on the debt ceiling to try to slow the growth of federal spending. In 2011, for instance, an impasse was resolved when President Obama and Congress agreed on the Budget Control Act, which raised the debt ceiling and set limits on future spending.
When Congress is faced with a decision about the debt ceiling, it can either choose to raise the debt ceiling by a fixed dollar amount or to suspend the debt limit for a specified period of time. When Congress raises the debt ceiling, the Treasury can continue to issue debt as needed until it reaches the new debt level. For example, in December 2021, Congress raised the debt ceiling from $28.9 trillion to $31.4 trillion, allowing borrowing to proceed until the total government borrowing reached this new limit (which finally happened on January 19, 2023). On the other hand, when a suspension period ends, the debt limit is reinstated at a level that accommodates the federal borrowing that has occurred up until then. For example, in August 2019, the debt ceiling, then at $22.0 trillion, was suspended for 24 months. During this period, the Treasury borrowed an additional $6.4 trillion. When the suspension period expired in August 2021, the debt limit was reinstated at $28.4 trillion—the sum of the previous limit and the additional borrowing.
After a debt limit is reached or a debt suspension period ends, the U.S. Treasury is no longer authorized to borrow additional funds. At that point, the Treasury can and often does take what are known as “extraordinary measures” (explained below) to keep the debt subject to the limit from rising until Congress acts.
The most recent round of extraordinary measures began in January 2025, when the debt ceiling of $31.4 trillion was reached. With mere days remaining before the projected X-date—the day that even extraordinary measures would not provide enough cash for the government’s activities—the White House and Congress cut a deal. The debt limit was suspended until January 1, 2025. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen informed Congress that a new debt limit would be set on January 2 at the level of the debt outstanding the day before. But the debt was projected to decrease temporarily on that date, so she said Treasury anticipated that it would delay implementing extraordinary measures until sometime between January 14 and January 23, 2025. In a January 17 follow-up letter to Congress, Secretary Yellen announced that extraordinary measures would begin January 21, 2025, and “will continue to be evaluated on an ongoing basis.”
Does raising the debt ceiling allow the government to spend more money?
Raising the limit does not authorize the government to increase spending beyond the level Congress has approved. Rather, it allows the government to meet its existing obligations to citizens, vendors, and bondholders.
What happens when Treasury hits the debt ceiling?
First, the Treasury employs a series of cash-saving tools known as “extraordinary measures.” These maneuvers suppress the level of intragovernmental debt (Treasury securities held by other government agencies) to create space for public debt. One way to achieve this is by suspending the daily reinvestment of certain government funds. When the federal government sets up a fund—for retirement plans, currency exchange, or other government transactions—it invests a portion of that fund in special Treasury securities that mature and are reinvested daily. Preventing that reinvestment lowers Treasury’s total amount of debt and allows it to legally issue debt to the public once again. In August 2021, for example, the Treasury reported that suspending reinvestment of the G Fund (a retirement fund for Federal employees with a portfolio of U.S. Treasury securities) could free up $270 billion in debt which the Treasury could use to raise cash and pay bills. In the ensuing period of extraordinary measures, it borrowed $262 billion from the G Fund, which was paid back in full in December 2021.
Extraordinary measures buy time but aren’t large enough to prevent the government from reaching the debt ceiling eventually. Unless Congress raises the debt limit, these extraordinary measures will generate enough cash for a limited time, at which point the U.S. government’s ability to pay its bills will be limited by the amount of revenue it collects each day. The date on which the government won’t have enough cash to meet its obligations is hard to predict precisely because it depends on the flow of revenues and spending, which depend, among other things, on the pace of economic growth.

The blue line in the above chart shows the federal debt subject to the limit. Congress has suspended the debt limit five times since January 2016 (the periods shaded in gray). At the end of the suspension period, the limit is reinstated at a level that covers all borrowing during the suspension period—but the Treasury must undertake “extraordinary measures” (the periods shaded in blue) to prevent additional borrowing until Congress raises or suspends the limit once more. The debt is currently approaching the $41.1 trillion limit that Congress set in July 2025.
What does it mean for the Treasury to run out of cash?
Every day, the Treasury collects revenues from taxes and pays its bills—everything from Social Security benefits to utilities in federal buildings to interest on the debt. When expenses exceed revenues, and the Treasury cannot increase its borrowing because of the debt ceiling, it can cover expenses only to the extent that there is cash coming in. There will be enough money coming into the Treasury to pay some—but not all—of the government’s bills and obligations.
Why is raising the debt ceiling so controversial?
The debt limit—although technically unrelated to the level of government spending—has become a flash point for debate about the size of the federal budget. Politicians who want to reduce deficits or restrain the size of government have used the debt limit to negotiate for spending caps or budget restrictions in the past—a tactic that has proven successful on occasion, as it was in 2011.
Some view “fiscal brinksmanship” as irresponsible and argue that raising the limit ought to be routine. Congress has already lifted, temporarily extended, or revised the definition of the limit 78 times since 1960, the Treasury says, and ought to do so again. Others, including a number of former Treasury secretaries from both parties, have argued for abolishing the limit altogether. Voices in this camp claim the limit imposes unnecessary costs on taxpayers, puts the solvency of the U.S. government at risk, and does little to rein in federal spending. Others argue that forcing Congress to vote to raise the debt limit is a useful lever to impose fiscal discipline in Washington.
What if Congress doesn’t act?
Unable to meet all its obligations, the Treasury would have to choose which bills to pay. Failure to pay Social Security or other benefits on time would have obvious political ramifications. During the 2021 round of extraordinary measures, Treasury Secretary Yellen warned that running out of cash would put “[e]very Social Security beneficiary, every family receiving a Child Tax Credit, every military family waiting for a paycheck or small business owners receiving a federal loan … at risk.” In addition, a failure to make interest or principal payments on time—a default—is likely to damage the way the markets view U.S. government debt, perhaps increasing the interest rates that investors demand when they buy Treasury bonds. But Congress has never failed to act in time, so no one knows with certainty what the consequences would be.
Transcripts from an August 2011 Federal Open Market Committee meeting reveal that officials at Treasury and the Federal Reserve had planned to prioritize interest payments on the debt over other government bills if Congress didn’t raise the ceiling. Their objective was to discourage investors from fleeing Treasuries and inciting volatility in capital markets. Even with the promise of interest payments, however, Fed officials noted that a debt breach could make rolling over matured debt—a crucial part of cash flow—difficult. Rollover occurs when short-term securities mature, but the proceeds are either reinvested by the original owner or other investors put their money into Treasury securities. If investors react poorly enough to a debt breach, the Treasury could have a hard time finding buyers for those short-term securities, and in turn, would suddenly have to make payments on a portion of its debt. In short, the debt situation could escalate very quickly depending on how investors reacted to the first breach.
For more on what might happen if the debt ceiling isn’t lifted before the Treasury runs out of cash, see “How worried should we be if the debt ceiling isn’t lifted?”.
As long as Congress acts, even at the last minute, is everything OK?
No. There’s evidence from a 2013 debt ceiling impasse—when Congress waited until the last minute to raise the debt ceiling— that investors dumped Treasury securities that had maturity dates around the projected limit date. In turn, rates on those securities rose sharply, and liquidity in the Treasury securities market dropped. In fall 2017, yields on short-term Treasury bills spiked leading up to the projected limit date, as investors signaled they were worried about the possibility of default. Because many financial transactions rely on Treasuries for collateral and for low-risk investment, those effects ripple throughout financial markets. Beyond that, higher yields on Treasuries have a direct cost on taxpayers because they make federal debt more expensive. A Government Accountability Office study estimated that the 2011 debt limit showdown raised Treasury borrowing costs for debt that matured in 2011 by $1.3 billion.

articles.title: The Economic Importance of Motorcycles to Europe
articles.text:
Consulting Report

17 Nov 2026

The Economic Importance of Motorcycles to Europe

A Report for the European Association of Motorcycle Manufacturers (ACEM)

In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported an estimated €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. These figures capture the sector’s own operations, its supply chains and the wider spending it supports, including spending by employees and visitors attending motorcycle events.

The analysis covers motorcycle manufacturing, sales and repairs, as well as accessories, sports and promotional events. Drawing on official statistics, industry data and economic modelling, it traces how these activities support businesses across the economy. For every €1 of GDP generated directly by the sector, a further €2.30 was supported elsewhere.

International trade is another important part of the picture. Around half of EU motorcycle and parts production was exported in 2024. The report examines Europe’s position in global markets and how trade barriers, growing competition and regulatory complexity affect the industry’s opportunities to invest and expand.

The study also explores how motorcycle use can reduce commuting times, operating costs, emissions and demand for urban space. Around 6.4 million people across the EU and the UK already commute by motorcycle. Under a modelled scenario in which 5% of car commuters switched to motorcycles, the report estimates potential annual savings of 28 million days of commuting time and 2.6 million tonnes of CO₂. It also considers how motorcycles can complement public transport and other modes within urban mobility plans.

articles.title: Response to CSA Consultation Paper 51-406 Modernizing the Regulation of Public Companies | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
We refer to the Canadian Securities Administrators (CSA)’s consultation on modernizing the regulation of public companies. We appreciate the opportunity to contribute our perspective.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is the investment management division of the Norwegian Central Bank that manages the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global. We work to safeguard and build financial wealth for future generations. As of 30 June 2026, we managed approximately CAD 3.3 trillion (USD 2.3 trillion) in assets, with CAD 106 billion invested in Canada. We held shares in 149 Canadian public companies with a combined value of about CAD 54 billion.
As a long-term, diversified financial investor, we rely on companies' disclosures to inform our investment decisions, risk management and shareholder voting. We have an interest in disclosure regimes that surface material, investor-relevant information in a consistent and comparable format, without imposing undue cost or duplication on reporting companies. We support the CSA's aim of a balanced and responsive regime that maintains strong investor protection and disclosure quality.
We highlight four points from our response. First, we support removing undue cost or duplication while retaining the material, consistent and comparable disclosures investors rely on for their decision-making wherever relief is applied. Second, consistent with our view on optimizing corporate reporting frequency, we support giving companies the option to report semi-annually, but suggest a measured approach, with appropriate safeguards to retain disclosure quality in and between filings. Third, we stress the importance of maintaining strong shareholder protections and regulatory stability through any modernization process to support a competitive Canadian market. Finally, we encourage the publication of a roadmap for aligning with the standards of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) for reporting financially material sustainability-related information.
Our responses to selected consultation questions are set out in Annex 1. They draw on our published positions and refer to our submissions to other regulators and standard-setters where relevant. We thank the CSA for considering our perspectives and remain at your disposal should you wish to discuss these matters further.
Yours sincerely,

Snorre GjerdePolicy Lead

articles.title: Daily: Market volatility reinforces case for portfolio resilience
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Equities: Industrials, health care, Eurozone, and quality AI (7 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Opportunities in high-quality bonds and select EM debt (5 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US equities fell again on Thursday as concerns about the AI trade combined with a more hawkish interest rate backdrop. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed down 2% and 2.3%, respectively, and the sell-off continued in Asia on Friday. The Nikkei 225 slid over 5%, while Taiwan's benchmark index was 6.2% lower.The market weakness was relatively broad. All major S&P 500 sectors traded lower, while declining stocks substantially outnumbered advancing stocks on both the NYSE and Nasdaq. Recent selling has followed persistent pressure on chipmakers and cloud companies as investors question the scale of investment required to build AI infrastructure.Monetary policy uncertainty has added to fragile market sentiment. Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting indicated that nearly all policymakers expected further tightening to be necessary if the US economy evolves as anticipated. Markets were pricing a near certainty of a 25-basis-point increase in December, with persistent inflation pressures also supporting the US dollar. US two-year and 10-year Treasury yields fell 4bps and 2bps, respectively, while the US dollar held recent gains. Higher rate expectations and dollar strength weighed on gold, which fell to a 14-month low of around USD 3,575 an ounce at the time of writing.Without taking single-security views, sentiment was also dented by reports from the Financial Times and newswires that investigative research house Hunterbrook had published a short-sell report on AMD (-7.7%) over fears that its business with China may be affected by stricter US chip restrictions; NVIDIA (-3.3%) also extended its recent losses despite having issued an upbeat revenue forecast earlier in the week.What do we think?
As outlined in our recently published Year Ahead publication, we do not think that the economic expansion, corporate earnings cycle, or structural AI investment story has broken. Our base case for 2027 remains for economic growth close to trend, rising corporate profits, further growth in AI investment, and moderating inflation later in the year. We still expect this combination to support additional equity gains and positive fixed income returns.But the risk-reward in equities has become more balanced. We recently downgraded global equities from Attractive to Neutral, reflecting elevated expectations, high index concentration, and a wider range of potential outcomes around AI. In particular, the AI debate is shifting from whether investment will continue to whether it can generate sufficient revenues and shareholder returns. Today's price action supports this shift in focus.Cumulative US technology investment in AI infrastructure could approach USD 5tr by the end of 2028. But we estimate that AI model and application revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5tr by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return. While this is possible, it is unlikely that every company will reap the rewards from this: Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. Financing, regulatory, and company-specific risks also add to uncertainty.Tighter monetary policy expectations add another source of volatility. While we foresee further near-term rate increases (namely 25bps hikes in the US in December 2026 and March 2027), we do not anticipate a prolonged tightening cycle. The cumulative effects of higher rates look set to weigh on consumer demand, while we believe base effects will contribute to a moderation in underlying inflation.How do we invest?
In our base case, we expect upside for equity markets in 2027. But the range of potential outcomes is broader. The challenge for investors in 2027 is constructing portfolios that can prove resilient across a variety of scenarios.Refocus equity exposure. In our base case, we expect corporate earnings growth to support equities, with around 15% S&P 500 earnings growth in 2027. But with the top 10 companies accounting for 39% of the index, relatively small changes in expectations about a handful of AI-linked businesses can have an outsized effect on returns.The Eurozone is our preferred equity region, with 15% earnings growth forecast for 2027, a lower valuation than the US, and earnings drivers spanning manufacturing, defense, infrastructure, and electrification. At a sector level, we favor industrials and health care, while equal-weight strategies in the US can be a convenient way to help reduce technology concentration.Within US technology, we favor financially strong hyperscalers with visible AI monetization, alongside select leaders in compute, foundry, semiconductor equipment, and infrastructure software. We remain cautious on leveraged capacity providers, lower-quality suppliers, and companies whose valuations depend on persistent bottlenecks or distant cash flows.Rebalance into fixed income. Elevated yields offer an attractive combination of income and potential portfolio resilience, while providing a return cushion even if rates do not decline materially. We favor intermediate duration, broadly two to 10 years. We see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, and within fixed income, we see the best return opportunity in emerging market and high yield bonds. EM sovereign and corporate bonds currently yield roughly 7.1% and 7.0%, respectively, while US high yield offers around 8.3%.Use volatility, rather than fear it. Investors should prepare for volatility instead of trying to predict every setback. Structured strategies can help investors build exposure in more tailored ways, potentially limiting losses, generating additional income, or allowing more measured market participation. Higher implied volatility, all else equal, may raise the appeal of such approaches. However, investors must understand the potential trade-offs, including capital loss, issuer, liquidity, and opportunity-cost risks, so we favor diversification and careful sizing of structures.To read our views in more detail, please see Year Ahead: Sustaining resilience and Monthly Letter: Sustaining resilience.

articles.title: Technology investment outlook 2027: AI moves from promise to proof
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | ARTICLE – 7 min read
Technology investment outlook 2027: AI moves from promise to proof

By
PAMELA HEGARTY, DEREK GLYNN 19.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Personal AI agents go mainstreamAI moves into core enterprise workflowsAI safety and cybersecurity remain top of mindPhysical AI and edge computing build momentumSector outlookValuations bolster environmentThe next stage

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

Pamela Hegarty, Co-Portfolio Manager of the Disruptive Technology Fund, Derek Glynn, Co-Portfolio Manager of the Disruptive Technology Fund

AI shifts from promise to measurable return on investment: 2027 should see AI move further from experimentation toward monetisation, productivity gains, and demonstrable returns, particularly across cloud and enterprise applications

AI infrastructure spending remains strong: Demand for GPUs, custom silicon, optical networking, data center power, and other infrastructure should remain robust, with supply constraints persisting in several areas

A constructive outlook balanced by rising risks: Technology valuations remain broadly supportive, but higher interest rates, debt-financed AI capex, geopolitics, and AI safety concerns could create periods of volatility

After several years of rapid innovation, the year ahead could mark the point at which artificial intelligence’s economic impact becomes increasingly visible.

The conversation is likely to shift from technological possibility to real-world adoption, monetisation, and return on investment.

Personal AI agents, enterprise automation, physical AI, and cloud infrastructure are all moving from experimentation toward broader deployment at scale.

The companies best positioned to monetise new products and distribute this innovation should be the primary beneficiaries of the AI cycle’s next phase.

Personal AI agents go mainstream

2027 could be the year that agentic AI transitions from an emerging technology to a mainstream consumer product.

Rather than simply answering questions, personal AI agents will increasingly perform tasks on a user’s behalf. Common use cases could include prioritising email messages, booking travel, scheduling appointments, managing subscriptions, and coordinating household services.

Improvements in reasoning, memory, and tool use should allow these agents to operate across applications and websites with minimal user input.

Adoption will likely be driven less by model breakthroughs and more by convenience, reliability, and integration into products consumers already use. Over time, personal AI agents could become a new interface layer for the internet.

AI moves into core enterprise workflows

Enterprise AI use cases will expand beyond coding assistants and customer service into agentic capabilities that augment core business workflows.

Organisations will increasingly deploy AI across functions such as finance, sales, human resources, and supply chain management. The next stage of the AI cycle will be defined not only by model capabilities, but also by the ability to deliver useful intelligence at an attractive cost.

Smaller models are likely to handle routine tasks, while larger models are reserved for more complex reasoning. Increasingly sophisticated orchestration software will manage these interactions behind the scenes, making AI more seamless for end users.

As adoption broadens, the focus should shift from experimentation to measurable productivity gains.

AI safety and cybersecurity remain top of mind

The AI safety debate will continue in 2027. Many industry experts fear a major cybersecurity breach or biohazard attack by bad actors using AI models. It is increasingly clear that cybersecurity, governance, and observability software will play a critical role going forward.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and others have advocated for deterministic supervisory software monitoring each AI model to build in policy guardrails for governance, compliance, and security.1

Other suggestions by industry experts include third-party auditing of training workloads and independent testing of models before public release. There is a growing consensus that governments need to regulate the industry, but also significant disagreement over how such regulations should be formulated.

Physical AI and edge computing build momentum

Next year could be a pivotal period for physical AI and edge computing – where data processing and storage is physically closer to the data source – as advances in AI begin translating into real-world automation.

Adoption is likely to accelerate first in structured environments such as factories, warehouses, and logistics networks, where intelligent robots can improve productivity and help address labour shortages.

Likewise, AI-enabled wearables, such as smart glasses, could emerge as an important new computing category by bringing contextual intelligence into everyday activities.

Humanoid robots may also make meaningful technical progress, but large-scale adoption likely remains several years away. Taken together, 2027 may represent the beginning of a new phase in which AI expands beyond software and digital workflows into the physical world.

Sector outlook

Semiconductors and hardware: Demand continues to exceed supply

We expect AI infrastructure demand to continue to outpace supply through 2027. Demand remains strong with hyperscalers and other customers providing suppliers with orders stretching through 2027 and beyond.

Optical components, semiconductors, and power for data centres will continue to be key constraints on the supply side. Leadership will continue to diversify as investors look for the next area of investment to support training and inferencing applications, especially as model innovations open new opportunities.

One key risk to monitor is access to capital at an economic cost, especially in a rising interest rate environment. It is unreasonable to expect the buildout to proceed in a linear fashion, but it is hard to know the timing of any digestion period or interruption in the AI infrastructure race.

Given the magnitude of outperformance of technology infrastructure names particularly during the first half of 2026, it would not be surprising to see continued volatility through 2027 as investors debate the relative merits of software versus semiconductors.

Cloud service providers: Return on investment comes into focus.

2027 could be the year that cloud service providers prove the return on investment for their unprecedented AI infrastructure spending.

Cloud service providers are uniquely positioned to monetise AI given their unmatched data centre footprints, access to graphics processing units, rapidly expanding custom silicon programmes, and highly profitable core businesses which support funding needs.

Investors should become more constructive as cloud revenue growth accelerates, capex growth moderates, and cloud margins remain healthy. Together, these factors could provide compelling evidence that AI infrastructure can generate attractive long-term returns rather than simply support an arms race.

Software: Careful navigation required

The software sector will require increasingly careful navigation as investors distinguish between AI beneficiaries and companies vulnerable to AI disruption.

Broad-based scepticism toward application software should give way to a more nuanced assessment of which companies can leverage AI to expand their total addressable markets and strengthen their competitive positions.

While AI monetisation is likely to accelerate across the industry, it will still represent a relatively small portion of revenue for most software companies in 2027.

We remain constructive on cybersecurity and infrastructure software, where AI is driving both increased demand and new product opportunities, though we are mindful of premium valuations given strong performance in 2026.

The first wave of frontier AI IPOs arrives

The potential public listings of leading frontier AI labs in the year ahead would mark a significant milestone. The initial public offerings would likely represent some of the most notable technology debuts since the emergence of the cloud service providers.

Beyond expanding the investable universe, these listings could provide investors with direct pure play exposure to the development and monetisation of frontier AI models, potentially attracting significant capital flows and reshaping technology indices.

More broadly, due to public market scrutiny, these companies will be under pressure to demonstrate sustainable revenue growth, scalability, margins, and returns on capital.

Valuations bolster environment

Valuations across much of the technology sector remain supportive, providing a constructive backdrop for investors.

While select AI beneficiaries continue to command premium multiples, many software, semiconductor, and hardware names trade at levels that appear reasonable relative to their growth and earnings outlooks.

The average forward price-to-earnings ratio for the semiconductor industry has declined to below 19 times (as of mid-October 2026) compared to the five-year average closer to 25, and the software sector’s enterprise value-to-sales ratio is moderately below its long-term average.2

Semiconductor stock valuations look reasonable given earnings momentum. In the semiconductor industry group, valuations are compelling, but for companies in commodity markets for standardised components like memory chips, investors are hesitant to put high multiples on what could prove to be peak earnings expectations

Valuations remain compelling for select application software companies that can monetise AI and defend their competitive positions against disruption.Outside of application software,widely perceived AI beneficiaries including certain data management and cybersecurity companies now command premium valuation multiples. Meanwhile, the cloud service providers appear undervalued, particularly if further evidence emerges that AI investments are generating attractive returns

Select hardware stocks are undervalued. Optical and other data centre infrastructure stocks have pulled back on concerns about the sustainability of supply shortages and of demand, and perhaps in relation to the prospects of a Democratic sweep in the US (which we believe would not in and of itself have a major impact on data centre approvals); select stocks look compelling

The long-term opportunity created by AI remains significant, but investors should remain mindful of several risks that could slow adoption or pressure valuations.While these risks are worth monitoring, the balance of evidence continues to support a constructive outlook for the sector. Key risks include, but are not limited to:

High interest rates could result in valuation pressure for long duration assets and could raise the cost of capital for financing AI infrastructure

The geopolitical environment is uncertain and makes it more likely that there will be competing AI ecosystems, inefficient supply chains, and physical risks to AI infrastructure

AI safety concerns could slow development, particularly if there is a cyber or biological attack by a bad actor, and/ or if there are more breaches by AI agents going rogue

Financing challenges could slow AI investment, especially as a higher portion of capex is being debt financed

Trends could give rise to the formation of an AI bubble, including circular relationships, increasing use of debt financing and off-balance sheet vehicles, lax regulation, private market valuations moving into the public markets with IPOs, and rising interest rates (which could pop a bubble)

However, mitigating factors include investor scepticism, encouraging AI adoption trends in consumer and enterprise applications which demonstrate paths to positive return on investment, and reasonable valuations that are not yet at dotcom bubble levels.

The next stage

The next phase of the AI cycle is likely to be defined less by technological breakthroughs and more by execution, adoption, and monetisation.

Companies that can translate AI investment into sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on capital should emerge as the long-term winners.

While periodic volatility is inevitable, we remain constructive on the technology sector and the opportunities created by the ongoing AI transformation.

articles.title: Daily: Stay invested as volatility tests market fundamentals
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: Jump Start | NVIDIA earnings, Fed minutes, and European equities(5 mins)
Video: Data with Donovan | 25bps or 50bps Fed hike in December? (3 mins)
Video: The AI Show | Latest on NVIDIA and how the AI investment is reshaped (6 mins)Thought of the dayThe S&P 500 rose 2.5% last week, its first increase in five weeks and the largest gain since August as investors weighed market fundamentals against developments in technology, inflation, and geopolitics.This week’s calendar could further test market expectations. NVIDIA is set to report its third-quarter results, an AI developer will begin trading on the Nasdaq, and multiple Federal Reserve policymakers are scheduled to speak. Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russia’s leader Vladimir Putin are expected to meet on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Shenzhen.These events could keep market volatility elevated, but we also believe fundamentals remain constructive for investors to stay in the market.AI investment remains compelling, but selectivity matters. Beyond the headlines surrounding NVIDIA’s leadership, investors will be looking for evidence that overall AI demand remains strong and can generate sufficient returns to justify higher spending on infrastructure. Without taking any single-name views, we retain our conviction in the structural AI opportunity. We forecast aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1tr this year and USD 1.4tr in 2027, and expect cloud revenue growth to accelerate further. At the same time, uncertainty over chip restrictions and ongoing financing and execution risks argue for greater selectivity and diversification.Higher yields continue to favor quality bonds. While US consumer prices rose more than expected in October, producer price inflation offered some relief. Core producer prices rose 0.3% month over month, slowing from an upwardly revised 0.8% increase in September. That said, the latest set of inflation data still increases the risk that the Federal Reserve could shift from gradual quarterly hikes to consecutive 25-basis-point moves. We believe comments from a broad range of Fed officials speaking this week may be more balanced than the recent hawkish remarks from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Fed Governor Christopher Waller. Our view remains that current elevated yields offer meaningful return potential for high-quality fixed income.Portfolio resilience matters amid geopolitical risks. Significant geopolitical breakthroughs appear unlikely in the immediate term, and we have long held the view that investors should not make major portfolio adjustments solely in response to geopolitical developments. Instead, portfolios should be sufficiently resilient to volatility driven by geoplitics. Exposure to broad commodities, hedge funds, and select real assets may help limit sensitivity to fresh shocks, as they provide differentiated sources of return.So, while volatility is likely to persist in the near term, we think investors should stay engaged with markets through a well diversified portfolio across sectors, regions, and asset classes.
