articles.title: Daily: Building resilience for 2027
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)Thought of the dayToday, we launched our Year Ahead 2027 outlook, "Sustaining resilience." Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of economies, corporate profits, and financial markets. In 2027, successful investing may depend more on deliberately building resilience into portfolios.The economic backdrop remains broadly supportive. We expect global growth to stay close to trend, while corporate earnings should rise further, and demand for computing capacity is likely to sustain investment in AI infrastructure. Easing inflation should also allow bond yields to decline modestly later in the year.But the range of potential outcomes is wide. Sticky inflation, elevated government debt, and geopolitical risks could drive bond yields higher and equity markets lower. In another risk scenario, execution and monetization risks could undermine confidence in attractive AI returns across the value chain.After a multi-year bull run, we therefore see a more balanced risk-reward for global equities in 2027. Our earnings forecasts remain constructive, but elevated expectations, index concentration, and uncertainty around the AI investment cycle leave less room for disappointment. We have downgraded global equities from Attractive to Neutral. Across asset classes, we see the most favorable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash as our least preferred asset class.Equities: Refocus rather than retreat. AI investment is accelerating, but so are the risks. We expect global AI-related investment to rise from USD 1.0 trillion in 2026 to USD 1.5 trillion in 2028, supported by constrained computing capacity and strong demand. Yet, cumulative US technology investment could approach USD 5.0 trillion by then. Revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5 trillion by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return, and while this is possible, not every company may reap the rewards. Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. External financing is also becoming harder, while market concentration, regulatory, and company-specific risks could increase volatility.This evolving nature of the AI trade is important for our S&P 500 outlook as the top 10 firms, most of which are exposed to AI, comprise 39% of the index, adding concentration risk. Beyond AI concerns, the risk of stickier inflation, higher Federal Reserve policy rates, and higher bond yields could contribute to additional uncertainty about the outlook. We believe the market may start to apply a lower multiple to future earnings to account for rising risks.We think investors should refocus equity exposure and diversify away from concentrated positions in technology. Regionally, the Eurozone is our preferred equity market. We forecast earnings growth of 15% in 2027, comparable with the S&P 500 but from a lower starting valuation and with a broader range of earnings drivers. At the sector level, we favor industrials and health care, while equal-weight strategies in the US can help reduce technology concentration. Since the start of June, the equal-weighted S&P 500 index has outperformed the market-cap-weighted index by around 7 percentage points.Bonds: Rebalance toward income and diversification. Elevated starting yields provide attractive income and a cushion against further increases in market rates. Quality bonds can also offer portfolio protection if economic or equity-market risks intensify. While we see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, within fixed income we see the best return opportunity in emerging market (EM) and high yield bonds. Improved external positions and fewer distressed issuers support EM bonds, although selection remains key. US high yield also looks resilient: 60% of the market is rated BB, expected defaults are around 2%, and only 3% of the universe matures over the next year. Across fixed income, we favor an intermediate average duration, generally through maturities of around two to 10 years, with a preference for shorter-dated bonds in the more growth-sensitive credit segments.Broaden returns with commodities, currencies, and alternatives. Commodities can help protect portfolios against geopolitical disruption, inflation, and constrained supply. We upgrade gold to Attractive: structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields should support a recovery toward USD 5,000 an ounce by December 2027. Oil should remain supported in the first half of the year, while copper is our preferred industrial metal given demand from electrification, power networks, data centers, and AI infrastructure.We think policy and interest rate shifts are creating attractive currency opportunities in 2027. Sterling is our preferred G10 carry opportunity, while select emerging market currencies may benefit from high yields and relatively contained volatility. In alternatives, our favored areas include hedge fund strategies that exploit market dispersion, operationally focused private equity and secondaries, and infrastructure with visible cash flows. Manager selection, underwriting discipline, liquidity, and position sizing remain important to manage risks including illiquidity and higher complexity.Our central message for 2027 is not to retreat from markets, but to take risk more deliberately. Putting excess cash to work, addressing portfolio concentration, rebalancing toward fixed income, and adding differentiated return drivers can help portfolios continue to compound even when markets depart from the base case.

articles.title: Global pension trends for 2027: The new retirement paradigm - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
The pensions industry is shifting to further focus on delivering sustainable, long-term retirement income and managing longevity risks

Investment strategies are evolving towards total portfolio management, while scale is becoming increasingly important

Governance, sustainability and AI are helping drive more resilient and outcome-focused retirement systems

The global pensions industry is entering a new phase of development. Having spent much of the past two decades focused on pension accumulation, deficit recovery and investment returns, attention is shifting towards the delivery of sustainable retirement income and the management of retirement risks.

Several structural trends are converging. Pension liabilities continue to migrate towards insurers and specialist consolidators through buyouts, longevity hedging and other risk-transfer solutions, while collective risk-sharing arrangements are re-emerging to address the limitations of purely individual retirement systems.

Scale is becoming increasingly important as pension providers seek access to private markets, technology and retirement-income capabilities. At the same time investment strategies are evolving towards whole-portfolio management, supported by greater exposure to private assets and renewed interest in fixed income.

Meanwhile, stronger governance, artificial intelligence and financially material sustainability practices1 are enhancing decision-making and risk management. Together, these developments are creating a more integrated, resilient and outcome-focused retirement system. Below, we outline the areas which we believe will dominate the pension landscape in the coming year.

1: Risk transfer and risk pooling

A defining theme of the 2027 pensions market will, in our view, be the simultaneous growth of risk transfer and risk pooling.

Improved funding levels, supported by the higher interest rates that we have seen between 2022 and 2025, have enabled many defined benefit schemes to move beyond deficit repair and focus on endgame strategies.

Buy-ins, buyouts, longevity swaps, superfund2 transfers and run-on approaches are becoming increasingly common, with insurers assuming a larger role as pension liabilities migrate from corporate balance sheets.

The debate, however, is no longer whether risks should be transferred, but which risks should be retained. For some well-funded schemes, selective retention of liabilities through run-on strategies may offer greater value than full insurance transactions.

At the same time, policymakers are revisiting collective approaches to retirement provision. Collective defined contribution schemes, target benefit plans, shared-risk models and longevity pools are attracting renewed interest as mechanisms for sharing investment and longevity risks without recreating traditional defined benefit guarantees.

Together, these developments reflect a more sophisticated approach to retirement risk allocation.

2: Scale, consolidation and the retirement ecosystem

Retirement systems are becoming increasingly concentrated and interconnected.

As pension risk transfers accelerate and retirement income solutions expand, insurers, pension funds and asset managers are operating within a more integrated retirement ecosystem. Scale is emerging as a key competitive advantage, providing access to private markets, technology, internal expertise and lower operating costs.

This is driving consolidation across UK defined contribution schemes, Australian superannuation funds, Canadian pension plans and European pension institutions. By 2027, smaller schemes are likely to face growing pressure to demonstrate superior member outcomes or seek consolidation.

3: The retirement income revolution

After decades of focusing on accumulation, the industry is turning its attention towards retirement income.

Across developed markets, policymakers increasingly recognise that successful saving does not guarantee successful retirement outcomes. Individuals are expected to manage investment risk, inflation, longevity and withdrawal decisions simultaneously, despite limited expertise.

As a result, managed retirement income solutions, deferred annuities, lifetime-income products, longevity pools and blended drawdown structures are gaining momentum. The next major battleground for pension providers will be retirement-income delivery rather than accumulation – especially for the emerging Asian middle class that has benefitted from a very rapid asset accumulation.

4: Asset allocation

Pension investing continues to evolve from asset-class optimisation towards whole-portfolio management.

The Total Portfolio Approach (TPA), where instead of managing individual asset classes the portfolio is managed as a whole, is gaining wider adoption as asset owners focus on long-term outcomes, governance efficiency and portfolio resilience. At the same time, higher interest rates have restored fixed income as a potentially meaningful source of income, diversification and liability matching.

Governments are also encouraging pension funds to direct their capital to support infrastructure, energy transition, housing and digital development. The challenge for trustees is balancing these opportunities with fiduciary obligations and member outcomes.

5: Asset classes

Private markets are now core portfolio holdings rather than specialist allocations.

Infrastructure, private credit and real assets continue to attract capital because of their potential for long-duration cash flows, diversification benefits and inflation protection. Meanwhile, investors are reassessing the role of concentrated equity portfolios as a means of improving stewardship, transparency and customisation, although concerns regarding concentration risk remain.

The return of attractive bond yields has also improved the investment case for fixed income and strengthened retirement income and insurance solutions.

6: Risk management

Risk management is becoming broader and more forward-looking. Investors are focusing less on short-term volatility and more on resilience across liquidity, valuation, climate and demographic risks. As private market allocations expand, governance, liquidity management and valuation discipline are becoming increasingly important.

Sustainability considerations are also being assessed primarily through a financial materiality lens, with climate, nature-related and transition risks integrated into portfolio construction and oversight. At the same time, longevity risk is re-emerging as populations age and retirement periods lengthen.

7: Governance, AI and sustainability

Governance is becoming one of the most important differentiators among pension institutions. Competitive advantage increasingly stems from decision-making quality, oversight and execution rather than investment complexity alone.

AI is beginning to reshape pension administration, member engagement, actuarial modelling, portfolio construction and risk management. Here, its greatest long-term potential could lie in delivering more personalised retirement solutions tailored to individual circumstances and objectives.

Sustainability is also entering a more pragmatic phase. Rather than focusing primarily on disclosure and compliance, pension investors are increasingly evaluating climate, biodiversity, human capital and governance factors for their impact on long-term cash flows, liabilities and portfolio resilience.

The combination of strong governance, AI-enabled decision making and financially material sustainability practices is likely to distinguish the leading pension organisations of the future.

The emergence of a new pensions era

As such, the defining feature of the pension landscape in 2027 is the convergence of multiple structural transformations.

Risk transfer is accelerating, collective risk-sharing is re-emerging, retirement-income solutions are becoming central, and investment strategies are evolving towards more integrated portfolio management. At the same time, scale, governance, technology and sustainability are reshaping how pension institutions operate.

The most successful organisations will recognise these developments not as isolated trends, but as elements of a broader transition.

The industry’s objective is no longer simply to maximise pension wealth. Increasingly, it is to deliver resilient, inflation-aware and lifelong retirement income. That shift is likely to define the global pensions market for the remainder of the decade.

[1] Financially material sustainability refers to the sustainability and environmental, social and governance factors that could have direct consequences for a company’s financial performance. It seeks to identify those issues, such as regulatory risks, climate-related costs, or supply chain disruptions, which could influence a company’s key financial metrics.

[2] Pension superfunds are pension scheme consolidators which aim to make a profit and are a relatively new development in the UK. When a pension scheme transfers to a UK superfund, the employer no longer guarantees the pension payments. Instead, the superfund takes over, using a capital buffer (assets held in reserve) to provide security. If the scheme struggles to pay pensions in the future, the capital buffer can be used. The capital buffer might come from investors looking for profit, payments from the employer who wants to end their guarantee, or existing surplus funds within the pension scheme (Source: Pensions: defined benefit superfunds – House of Commons Library).

articles.title: View from the markets: The next chapter for monetary policy and the bond market - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Alessandro Tentori, Senior Market Strategist, Europe

Former US Federal Reserve Chair, Ben Bernanke, once quipped that “monetary policy is 98% talk and 2% action”. But recently, central banks have tried to shift more towards action, primarily through strategy reviews – focusing on the modelling framework and repeated references to the incoming data landscape.

Still, semantic nuances and almost imperceptible variations in tone make fascinating fare for watchers and investors alike.

We’ve lived through many shocks and surprises this year, but the economy has remained resilient thanks to a technological innovation – namely artificial intelligence – that promises to affect our productivity beyond the scale experienced in the mid-1990s.

At the same time, inflation has surprised to the upside. These two variables merit our attention.

Measuring the AI effect

There is a tremendous effort to measure AI’s contribution to output and economists will undoubtedly receive more information as the technology spreads to all sectors of the economy.

The adoption process takes some time – in 1987 Nobel Prize winning economist Robert Solow famously said “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics” – but we can rely on a solid theoretical framework which allows us to put technological change, potential growth and the natural rate of interest into one box.

And that is exactly what central bankers have done in the past 12 months, as they’ve realised that monetary policy’s neutral range might have shifted upward owing to an unprecedented productivity boost.

Neutral rate – where art thou?

Of course, if you ask two central bankers where they see the neutral interest rate – the theoretical real interest rate which neither stimulates nor restricts growth – you will most likely hear three different answers. This is where the art of central banking is required, and where the wording and the nuances matter most.

In retrospect, we could say that both the Fed and the European Central Bank have done a tremendous job in not scaring the financial markets, by describing their actions as a step-by-step search for the neutral interest rate. In doing so, they have smartly avoided the risk of sparking a painful discussion about a tightening cycle.

Market-based expectations at the beginning of 2026 were for two rate cuts by the Fed and the ECB standing pat. Instead, the Fed has already hiked once and is expected to deliver another 25 basis points in December. Similarly, the ECB has already increased rates twice and will most likely add a third hike in a few weeks’ time.

This is a significant U-turn in monetary policy, which under normal circumstances might have triggered fears of a recession. Not in 2026, though, and the reason might again be technological change and central banks’ wise guidance on the neutral interest rate.

The next chapter: Inflation

I think we are within reach of the neutral rate, both in Frankfurt and in the US. The question is therefore about the next chapter in this monetary policy story, which leads us straight to inflation.

Since the Middle East crisis, inflation has accelerated almost everywhere due to both direct and indirect effects. On the other hand, there is little evidence – indeed, arguably none – of so-called second-round inflation, which is primarily associated with inflation expectations and requires an asymmetric inflationary shock to be both deep and long-lasting.

Therefore, central banks are managing the risk of second-round inflation rather than inflation itself, as recently suggested by Bank of England Chief Economist, Huw Pill.

Looking ahead, the risk is that the current above-target inflation mutates into entrenched inflation. Growing inflation expectations should be on everybody’s radar screen as this would constitute another significant surprise for market participants after this year’s policy U-turn.

Concretely, the risk is about central banks having to switch from their storyline of “reaching neutral” to one of a “policy tightening cycle”, thus hitting both risk premia and corporate valuations.

As Exhibit 1 shows, the market is not pricing in a hiking cycle for the Fed or the ECB beyond the next two to three rate hikes. In other words, a policy path that diverges significantly from whatever neutral level the central bankers have in mind would definitely take investors by surprise.

Source: Bloomberg, 18 November 2026

Government bond markets: More than just inflation and rates

Equally, the bond universe is not immune to such a scenario. Market-based inflation expectations have orbited slightly above target for the past four years, thus confirming both central banks’ credibility and a striking contrast with survey-based inflation measures.

However, the discussion about government bond markets is more subtle than just inflation and interest rate expectations.

According to the International Monetary Fund’s Fiscal Monitor, expansionary fiscal policy in an environment of increasing yields will require ever-increasing bond issuance by governments in developed markets for the next five years.

And as the demand side can no longer rely on infinitely elastic balance sheets (i.e., quantitative easing), the question suddenly becomes: Who will buy all these bonds, and at what price?

If there is one certainty in a world of uncertainty, it is that there will be more government bonds tomorrow than there are today.

articles.title: Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice
articles.text:
Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice

Bridgewater Associates, LP (“Bridgewater”) is a premier asset management firm, focused on delivering unique insight and partnership for the most sophisticated global institutional investors. We have recently become aware of an increase in fraudulent schemes in which unauthorized third parties (often operating through fake websites, social-media profiles, unsolicited e-mail or social media messages, text messages, telephone calls, or other communication platforms) misrepresent themselves as employees, agents, or affiliates of Bridgewater. These bad actors may attempt to obtain confidential personal information, solicit investments (including cryptocurrency investments), offer investment advice, induce the transfer of funds under false pretenses, or may target job seekers purporting to offer jobs at Bridgewater. The fraudulent activity is sophisticated, constantly evolving and frequently mimics the look and feel of genuine Bridgewater communications, and may reference accurate-looking logos, executive names, marketing materials, and the official Bridgewater.com website. We issue this notice to alert current and prospective clients, counterparties, vendors, job applicants, and the general public to these unlawful practices. The actions of these unauthorized persons are in no way associated with Bridgewater.Bridgewater communicates only through official channels, including with its clients, counterparties and job applicants. Bridgewater’s official website is: https://www.bridgewater.com, and our email address ends strictly in “@bwater.com”. No other websites or email domains are authorized by Bridgewater. The only social media accounts authorized by Bridgewater are LinkedIn and Meta (Facebook and Instagram). We only use these authorized social media accounts to issue informational postings. Please be aware that Bridgewater does not conduct business activities, financial transactions, solicit investments or provide investment advice through social-media direct messages, personal e-mail domains, encrypted messaging apps, or public chat platforms, such as Telegram, WeChat, or WhatsApp, or other public platforms. Bridgewater does not hire from social media or conduct interviews via text or messaging services, nor will Bridgewater request any form of payment in connection with the hiring process.Some of the warning signs or red flags that may indicate a scam include: (a) phishing websites that have the look and feel of the official Bridgewater website, (b) variations in email domains that appear to have come from a Bridgewater email address, (c) fraudulent mobile device apps which purport to be an official Bridgewater app, and (d) time bound offers which pressure you to invest immediately.If you have any questions about this notice or the legitimacy of any communication purportedly from Bridgewater, please email our Legal Department at LRG_FraudAwareness@bwater.com. If you believe you may have been the victim of internet crime or fraudulent activity, please report it to law enforcement in your jurisdiction.

The strategic role of the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector

The EU fuel manufacturing and refining industry remains a strategic pillar of Europe’s economy and industrial base.

Our report explores the industry’s strategic importance to the EU, the role it can play in enabling industrial transformation, and the economic risks that could emerge if refining capacity contracts faster than the transition can be delivered.

In 2025, the sector supported €200 billion in GDP, 1.8 million jobs, and €83 billion in tax revenues across the EU, while supplying the fuels and feedstocks that underpin transport, manufacturing, petrochemicals, agriculture, and household activity. However, the analysis also highlights the risks of a continued decline in refining capacity. A faster-than-expected contraction could reduce EU GDP by almost €25 billion, eliminate around 120,000 jobs, lower government revenues by €14 billion, and increase the EU’s reliance on imported fuels by 2035, with implications for competitiveness, energy security, and the transition to low-carbon fuels.

articles.title: New horizons: the legal and commercial frontier of digital assets − speech by Sasha Mills
articles.text:
New horizons: the legal and commercial frontier of digital assets − speech by Sasha Mills

Given at Hogan Lovells and Global Digital Finance Digital Assets Summit

Published on
01 October 2026

In this speech, Sasha Mills sets out five ways the Bank will continue to support responsible innovation. It will focus on outcomes, support testing and growth, clarify its processes, bring firms together and work with overseas authorities. Together, these steps will foster innovation while protecting financial stability.

Speech
Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to be with you today. Thank you to Hogan Lovells and Global Digital Finance for bringing together financial institutions, policymakers, regulators and technology innovators at a moment when the digital-assets debate is changing in an important way.
For several years, much of this debate has been about technical possibility. Can a security be issued on a distributed ledger? Can a smart contract automate an event in its lifecycle and embed AML/KYC checks? Can cash and assets move together across different systems? Increasingly, the answer is yes.
The harder question is whether those possibilities can become trusted, widely-used and commercially sustainable. We must ask not only whether the technology works, but who owns the asset; which record is authoritative; when settlement becomes final; what happens on insolvency; who is accountable; where the regulatory perimeter falls; and whether the service solves a problem that customers are willing to pay to solve.
Those are not peripheral questions. They mark the difference between an interesting experiment and working part of the financial system's infrastructure. Technology can create a token in an instant. Creating a trusted market around it is the more consequential task.
There is a useful parallel in the history of medicine. When Alexander Fleming observed the antibacterial effect of penicillin in 1928, the scientific insight was extraordinary. But the observation in a petri dish was not yet a medicine that could improve outcomes at scale. Other researchers had to turn that insight into a stable treatment. Manufacturers had to find ways to produce it reliably and in large quantities. Clinicians needed evidence and confidence to use it. A breakthrough became transformative only when a wider system developed around it.
I do not want to stretch the analogy too far. Financial markets are not medicine. But the lesson is helpful. Discovery matters. So do trial and error, evidence, standards, production, distribution and trust. Innovation succeeds when invention becomes everyday practice.
That is the journey I want to discuss today: how useful innovations in digital finance, led by industry with convening and coordination from the authorities where appropriate, can move from possibility to practical use, and from practical use to permanence.
Innovation founded on stability
For the Bank, financial stability is the foundation. But stability and innovation are not opposing objectives. Confidence in the system enables firms to invest, users to adopt and new approaches to achieve scale. Our secondary innovation objective recognises that innovation, pursued safely, can improve efficiency, strengthen resilience and support broader economic growth. We therefore support innovation in ways that preserve, and may ultimately reinforce, financial stability.
Our ambition is to create conditions in which new entrants and incumbents can explore responsible change, and in which successful initiatives can progress from experimentation towards scale. The secondary innovation objective has applied to the Bank’s regulation of central counterparties and central securities depositories. The Government has proposed extending that statutory focus to the Bank’s regulation of payment systems, including those using digital settlement assets, and related service providers. We welcome this proposal from Government, in particular that it will bring the objective to a further core part of our financial-market-infrastructure remit, reinforcing the approach we are already taking: working with government, other authorities and industry to maintain trust while enabling innovation.
We will not know in advance which technologies, products or business models will deliver the greatest benefits. Commercial users, not the authorities, should drive that selection. The Bank's role is to preserve strong foundations, remove unnecessary barriers, provide proportionate pathways for firms to learn and grow, and convene where a system-wide outcome cannot be achieved by firms acting alone. As authorities our role is to ensure that there is a platform for open competition and that what succeeds commercially can do so safely and responsibly. But we should not pick winners; that’s for the market. It is industry’s job to identify solutions, test them, and implement them.
From commercial value to trusted markets
Let me start with commercial value, because innovation will not be useful if it is not commercially viable. Tokenisation may enable faster processing, reduce reconciliation and operational costs, automate lifecycle events, mobilise collateral more efficiently, and make information available in more usable forms. But a technically successful pilot that cannot attract users, connect to liquidity or generate sustainable activity will not transform finance.
The prize is not merely that an individual firm makes one process quicker. It is that successful innovation becomes normal market practice. That requires continuity of confidence across the system. Cross-market adoption is hard and may cut across individual firms’ incentives. The benefits depend on other firms investing too, on compatible operational arrangements, on common legal understanding and on standards that allow systems to interoperate.
Structural change, such as tokenisation, also requires different parts of the financial system to move together. Issuers, investors, trading venues, infrastructures, banks, custodians and technology providers may all need to adapt. These sectors have different systems, incentives, and regulatory frameworks. And because financial markets operate across borders, new arrangements must be capable of connecting across platforms and jurisdictions. Otherwise, innovation intended to reduce friction could create new technological, legal or regulatory fragmentation.
Let’s go back to penicillin. Penicillin became transformative not because every institution pursued an isolated solution, but because research, testing, production and clinical practice developed together. In financial markets too, a good idea may work within one firm yet fail across firms if the connections are missing. The investable frontier within an institution can remain uninvestable across the market.
Strong foundations therefore matter. A tokenised security needs a legally authoritative record. Ownership must be evidenced and transferred. Competing claims must be resolvable. Settlement must be final and irrevocable. Insolvency protections must work. Responsibility for maintaining the record must be clear. Faster technology does not automatically produce clearer legal effect.
The same is true operationally. An asset cannot realise its full value unless the cash leg can settle with comparable certainty. Nor will a new platform scale if it cannot connect to existing infrastructure, liquidity and custody arrangements. Interoperability is therefore about more than a technical bridge: it requires compatible rulebooks, data, operating hours, legal arrangements and risk controls.
This is why the Bank - working closely with the Financial Conduct Authority, HM Treasury and industry - has focused on providing the foundations for tokenised markets to thrive in the UK. In May, we, with the FCA, published a Call for Input on Tokenisation which set out our commitment to enabling the benefits of tokenisation in the UK's wholesale financial markets. We pointed to work already underway and made commitments in several key areas where we can use our regulatory, operational, and policymaking levers to drive change. Later this year, we will publish a full Roadmap which will provide a clear forward path, to help ensure all parts of the financial system move together to grasp the gains of tokenisation. Industry must engage actively with that Roadmap, align investment and delivery plans around it, and work collectively to turn those foundations into scalable market activity.
The role of industry and the authorities: an end-to-end system
Industry collaboration and coordinated action is essential to identifying what stands in the way of responsible innovation, and which combination of solutions can remove those barriers. Some obstacles may require targeted legal, regulatory or operational changes. Others will demand market-wide coordination, common standards and shared approaches. Because tokenisation cuts across products, institutions and infrastructures, no single intervention will be enough. Progress will depend on complementary changes that reinforce one another.
That is also why the work of the Wholesale Digital Markets Champion matters. By bringing firms together around practical use cases, such as the repo market, the Champion can expose dependencies, align incentives and build momentum where coordinated investment is needed. This can help industry and the authorities distinguish between problems that require a coordinated action plan and those that market forces will solve by themselves. Public authorities should focus on genuine public-policy obstacles, rather than assume that every barrier to adoption has a regulatory answer.
The Digital Securities Sandbox: evidence before permanence
But coordination alone is not enough. Firms also need a way to test their ideas, capabilities and market appetite for their products and services. And they need to do this under real-world conditions and with real users.
That is one reason why the authorities created the Digital Securities Sandbox. I should explain, sandbox does not mean playing with a child's version of reality, it means allowing real trades with real customers in a way that won't break the financial system if something goes wrong. Along with the FCA we have changed the rules to allow new market structures and products to be created and tested. The DSS allows firms to issue, trade and settle digital securities, on new technologies and combine trading and settlement in the same legal entity. This was not previously permitted and enables firms to set up efficient new market structures that exploit new technologies. They can use distributed ledger (DLT) and other new technologies to record and transfer assets and offer completely new financial instruments that may unlock new sources of liquidity, offer new investors access to markets previous unavailable to them, and make post trade processes significantly more efficient.
While the DSS does use limits, these have been set at levels that allow for meaningful activity - for example, £8-13.1 billion for gilts, and £17-28 billion for sterling corporate bonds – while ensuring appropriate financial stability safeguards are in place.
The Bank has already adjusted the DSS in response to feedback and as the market has developed, including broadening the settlement assets that firms may use to include stablecoins, subject to minimum requirements and case-by-case assessment.
A deep understanding of the legal operational and practical barriers that need to be removed or overcome help us be more proportionate and, taken as a whole, these activities have the potential to drive significant innovation and growth. We are working with the Wholesale Digital Markets Champion and the industry to build this future for UK markets.
A well designed permanent regulatory regime that supports innovation and allows a whole new generation of firms, products, and market structures to flourish is an important prize. By serving as a starting point for a permanent regulatory regime, and enabling firms and authorities to see the real-world benefits and risks of these technologies before it’s put in place, the DSS provides a real benefit to the system as a whole – beyond simply the institutions participating in it. In this way, the DSS promotes greater certainty, competition and innovation compared to alternative ‘sandbox’ approaches.
I am encouraged by the number of firms in the DSS, the steady flow of firms passing the ‘Go Live Gate’ and breadth of business models being explored. The prospect that the Digital Gilt Instrument, or DIGIT, could further our collective learning. DIGIT, as a digitally native government bond issued in the DSS, provides a real instrument around which firms can develop and test the connections needed across issuance, ownership records, trading, settlement, custody and collateral use. It does not determine the design of every future security, but it could provide a practical catalyst for the ecosystem around digital securities and demonstrates the UK’s commitment to digitising its markets.
Integrated market structures, efficiency from on chain assets born out of experimentation and business growth through and after the DSS is the aim. Not all ideas or firms will be successful, but we are allowing them to try so market forces, not regulatory constraints, determine the future.
Progress is not linear in innovation. The value of all the work by firms and the authorities below the waterline will only become truly apparent when this new generation of businesses have scaled up in the DSS and the successful ones are operating seamlessly with the wider market as it transforms to greater digitisation.
The longer-term legal architecture
This is why the future of CSD regulation and settlement finality belongs firmly in the innovation agenda. On the infrastructure side, we need to consider whether the definition of a CSD remains fit for new business models, whether the scope of securities required to settle on a CSD is set appropriately, and how requirements should apply proportionately to firms that may look different from today's FMIs. On the legal side, settlement finality must continue to provide certainty for CSDs and the wider system, while the framework for financial collateral arrangements responds to the emergence of different asset types. Efficient technology is insufficient if ownership, transfer and finality remain uncertain.
The evidence generated in the DSS will be important as the authorities consider the future framework and possible steady-state paths for successful activity. The objective should be a framework capable of supporting established and new structures while retaining the confidence on which both depend.
Pathways: same risk, same regulatory outcome
Our guiding principle in forming regulation going forward continues to be ‘same risk, same regulatory outcome’. That does not mean rules and supervisory approaches must always apply in exactly the way they have before. They may need to be amended, interpreted or calibrated so that a different technology, product or entity achieves the same underlying outcome. Innovation does not receive a lower standard. The standard remains the same, even where the route to meeting it changes.
This approach recognises that not all experimentation will scale. A model may prove operationally sound but commercially unattractive. Another may be commercially attractive but unable to manage the risks it creates. Either conclusion is useful evidence. Penicillin is widely known because the discovery ultimately worked at scale. Responsible experimentation must also make room for ideas that do not. The point is to learn, not to predetermine success. That learning will support further innovation.
And learning must run both ways. Industry must be candid about business cases, dependencies and risks. Regulators must listen, test whether rules remain justified and adapt where evidence demonstrates that change is needed. A flexible framework is not one without standards. It is one that can calibrate its requirements to the risk, the evidence and the stage of development.
The relevant questions are therefore functional. What service is being provided? What risks does it create? Where do those risks travel? Could they become systemic? Which authority has the tools to address them? As activities and risks change, the perimeter must remain capable of recognising the substance of what is being done.
Trusted functions and a safe transition
Consider tokenised collateral. Tokenisation may make collateral faster or easier to identify, transfer and mobilise. That could reduce operational friction. But collateral exists to absorb risk, especially in stressed conditions. Its legal enforceability, settlement finality, liquidity, valuation, custody, operational resilience and accessibility in stress matter even more.
The same is true of central clearing. Tokenisation may change how services are delivered, but it does not remove the value of multilateral netting, disciplined default management and trusted risk management. Innovation should improve those functions, not ignore or impair them.
A safe transition therefore matters as much as the destination. New and established arrangements may coexist for a considerable period. Links between them must not create hidden dependencies, ambiguous ownership or new channels of contagion. Incumbents and new entrants both have an essential part to play.
Practical foundations
Digital assets also need to be paid for. The cash leg is not a secondary implementation detail. Asset and payment transfers must be coordinated so that neither party bears unnecessary principal risk. Central bank money remains the ultimate risk-free settlement asset and an anchor for the singleness of money, even in a future in which private forms of digital money also play important roles.
Synchronisation is not simply an experiment: the Bank intends to deliver a live synchronisation capability in 2028, enabling innovative platforms to settle transactions in central bank money. We are testing that capability now through the Synchronisation Lab, where prospective operators can develop use cases, test design choices and refine business models in a non-live environment ahead of launch. Building on Project Meridian, this work is helping us ensure that the live service provides a trusted settlement capability on which the market can build, without prescribing every platform or use case that connects to it.
This puts the UK in a good position to scale digital asset adoption, because it will be built on the foundation of programmable risk-free money.
The Bank's commitments
Let me draw these points together into five commitments from the Bank, with some corresponding challenges to industry. Progress will not come from regulatory action alone: it will require firms to invest, collaborate and turn technological possibility into services that customers use.
First, we will not make regulatory judgements in isolation from the technology, activity and risks before us. We will remain agnostic about which technologies industry chooses, while applying the principle of same risk, same regulatory outcome. Different technologies may require different regulatory approaches, but each must deliver an equivalent outcome that protects confidence in the financial system. Industry, in turn, must demonstrate how its chosen technology delivers that outcome.
Second, we will support experimentation, scaling and, where appropriate, transition towards systemic scale by incumbents and new entrants. We will use proportionate requirements, conditions and activity limits, and we will learn from live activity. Industry must match that pathway with ambition: move beyond proofs of concept, commit capital and senior attention, bring real users and transactions into testing, and build credible plans for commercial scale.
Third, we will improve our processes. We will be clear about what we require, realistic about response times and prepared to adapt where evidence shows that unnecessary friction can be removed without weakening standards. Industry must engage early and candidly, submit robust evidence, identify dependencies and risks, and tell us where requirements create genuine barriers, with practical proposals for resolving them.
Fourth, we will support the Digital Markets Champion and the Government's Wholesale Financial Markets Digital Strategy. In particular, we will support the Champion’s work to convene industry where coordinated action is necessary to deliver a system-wide outcome, while leaving commercial choices to the market. But convening is not delivery. Firms must be prepared to invest together, agree workable standards, resolve collective-action problems and build the connections that allow successful propositions to operate across the market.
And fifth, we will work with domestic and international authorities to reduce fragmentation and support responsible paths to cross-border growth. Interoperability across systems must be matched by coherence across standards, legal frameworks and regulatory approaches. Industry must design for that reality from the outset: participate in standard-setting, build interoperable services and avoid closed solutions that reproduce fragmentation in digital form.
Assets, market participants, infrastructures and financial flows operate internationally. And so the benefits of innovation will be greatest where firms can operate across borders with confidence, rather than navigate fragmented legal, regulatory and technical frameworks.
That does not require every jurisdiction to adopt the same technology or market structure. But it does require cooperation on outcomes. Authorities, market infrastructures and industry will need to work together internationally to promote interoperability, support common standards where appropriate, and ensure that differences in legal frameworks, regulatory expectations, supervisory approaches, settlement arrangements and risk-management practices do not create unnecessary barriers to cross-border activity.
The Bank attaches considerable importance to international engagement. Through our work with overseas authorities, standard-setting bodies and market participants, we want to help shape an environment in which innovation can scale across borders while preserving financial stability and confidence. Modernisation will succeed more quickly, and deliver greater benefits, if markets evolve in ways that are capable of working together internationally.
These commitments are not a promise that every experiment will succeed. They are a commitment that good ideas can be tested fairly, regulatory expectations will focus on outcomes, and successful innovation will have a credible route towards permanence. But the route will only matter if industry uses it. The challenge to firms is to bring forward propositions with real commercial value, invest for scale, collaborate where markets need collective solutions, and demonstrate that innovation can meet the same outcomes of trust, resilience and stability. That is the partnership required to move from possibility to permanence.
Conclusion: from possibility to permanence
The UK begins from strong foundations: a trusted legal system, established market infrastructure, deep capital markets, active government and regulatory programmes, and firms willing to experiment. The challenge now is to use those assets to their fullest potential.
Technology, law, money, infrastructure, standards and commercial demand must develop as one ecosystem. Industry must identify propositions that solve genuine problems and make the investments needed to realise them. Authorities must preserve confidence, remove unnecessary obstacles and provide proportionate pathways. Government must provide the strategic and legislative architecture. And all of us must keep learning from evidence.
The penicillin story began with a striking possibility. Its enduring impact came from the difficult work that followed: testing, refinement, production and adoption across a whole system. Digital finance is at a different frontier, but it faces a related test. We have demonstrated much of what the technology can do. We now need to build the conditions in which the best applications can be trusted, connected and used at scale.
The Bank will not pick the winning token, ledger or business model. Commercial value should drive adoption. But commercial success will be sustainable only where it is safe and responsible, where legal and operational foundations are strong, and where confidence can continue as activity grows through strategic coordination between actors to adopt, adapt and scale.
The new horizon is not a financial system in which everything is tokenised. It is one in which innovations that offer real value can move from possibility to practical use, and from practical use to lasting scale, on foundations strong enough to retain the confidence of the market.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Shane Scott, Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Michael Yoganayagam Richard Spooner, Priya Mistry, Kushal Balluck, Mark Strasshine, Steven Dyer, Nina Turnbull and Edward Denbee for their help in preparing these remarks

Sasha Mills
Executive Director, Financial Market Infrastructure

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesOutlooksOil Is Estimated to Ease in 2027 as Suppliers Adapt to Hormuz DisruptionNov 18, 2026Share Goldman Sachs Research forecasts that Brent crude will average $88 per barrel in 2027, easing to $78 by December, under its base case assumption that there are no major changes in the ongoing tensions in the Middle East. The oil market likely tipped into a surplus in October 2026, and our analysts expect the surplus to reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027 amid a growing tanker fleet and new oil pipelines in the Middle East. European LNG prices are also forecast to fall from €85/MWh today to an average of €45/MWh in 2027, although a colder-than-average winter could drive up prices.Oil is forecast to ease gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
What is the prediction for oil prices in 2027?

Our commodities analysts expect benchmark Brent crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure.

Under the same base case scenario, they project that Brent will fall from $93 per barrel today (as of November 17) to $78 by early December 2027 as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027. Goldman Sachs Research expects the risk premium in oil prices—which now appears relatively low—to gradually normalize.
Oil prices have risen less sharply this year than expected given the length of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, writes Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research, in a report by his team.
In part, that was because of “remarkable oil market adaptation” to the war in Iran, Struyven adds. This included Gulf exporters redirecting supply through pipelines, dark exports, US Navy escorts, and ship-to-ship transfers.
The adaptation also included lower oil demand in response to higher prices—notably in China, which switched some of its energy demand to power and coal—and strong output of oil outside the Gulf, especially in Brazil.
“For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and continued market adaptation,” Struyven writes.
Will oil stay in a surplus in 2027?

The oil market likely tipped into a surplus in October 2026. The key driver was a rise in the supply of oil from the Persian Gulf in October—Goldman Sachs Research estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports recovered in October to their 2025 average, increasing 2 million barrels per day compared with the previous month.
Under Goldman Sachs Research’s base case scenario, our analysts expect the surplus to grow in 2027. They estimate that it will reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027 despite slowing growth in output from outside the Persian Gulf and continued supply disruptions.
Our analysts expect the recovery of output from the Gulf to trend higher as adaptation and added transportation resources, especially a larger tanker fleet and pipelines, support further growth in production.
Goldman Sachs Research expects an additional 3.8mb/d of pipeline capacity to come online over the next year as oil producers in the Middle East invest in pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport oil directly to the Gulf of Oman, Red Sea, or Mediterranean Sea.
Struyven’s base case assumption sees 2027 oil output from the Gulf exceeding its 2025 average by 1.4 million barrels per day.
The outlook for Chinese oil demand

Global demand for oil took a hit from the conflict in the Middle East. Goldman Sachs Research expects global demand, with the exception of China, to recover to its pre-war trend once the availability and affordability of oil products improve, consistent with the rebounds in global demand following negative oil supply shocks in 2011 and 2022.
In China, our analysts expect persistent weakness in road fuel oil demand to drive 0.4 million barrels per day of “scarring” to global oil demand by the fourth quarter of 2027. The surge in use of electric passenger cars and trucks likely accelerated China’s energy transition, helping drive a 0.7 million barrel-per-day drop in Chinese gasoline and diesel demand in September 2026, year over year. Half of that decline is likely to persist, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“Taken together, we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025,” Struyven writes.
Will European natural gas prices rise in 2027?

Goldman Sachs Research’s base case assumption is for European liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices to average €45 per megawatt hour in 2027 as supply from the Middle East continues to adapt. That would represent a decline from €85/MWh today (as of November 17).
“Yet even as supply adaptation has spread, it has worked less well for other commodities than for crude oil and has sharply raised shipping costs,” writes Samantha Dart, co-head of Global Commodities Research, who also leads the team’s global natural gas research.
The complexities of transporting LNG, which needs to be kept at very cold temperatures, make ship-to-ship transfers harder than for oil. And because it is more flammable than oil, transporting LNG can be more dangerous for the crew in the event of an attack, Dart explains.
European LNG could rise to near €150/MWh in the first quarter of 2027 if Persian Gulf LNG exports average 25%-30% of pre-war levels this winter and if Europe's winter turns out one standard deviation colder (0.7° Celsius) than average, Dart writes. If Gulf LNG exports stall at around 35% of pre-war levels through end-2027, her team estimates that European LNG prices would average €104/MWh in 2027.

articles.title: Why AI toys shouldn't make the list this holiday season | Brookings

Commentary

Why AI toys shouldn’t make the list this holiday season

Kathy Hirsh-Pasek,

Kathy Hirsh-Pasek

Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Universal Education

Jennifer M. Zosh, and

Jennifer M. Zosh

Professor, Human Development & Family Studies
- Penn State Brandywine

Sweta Shah

Sweta Shah

Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Universal Education

November 20, 2026

A good toy is 90% kid and 10% toy. AI toys often violate this rule, suggesting what the child should do and necessitating less imagination or human interaction.
This holiday season, many AI toys have been pulled from shelves. But the ones that remain can still pose risks. This is not to say that AI-enhanced toys cannot be good for young children, but at the moment, the science cautions, let the buyer beware.
Future AI-embedded toys can be designed to prompt children to work together on problems or excite families with challenges and games. Until then, kids and their parents will benefit most from the magnetic tiles, blocks and low-tech toys of old.

A person looks at a teddy bear equipped with AI in Singapore on November 27, 2025. (Photo by Roslan RAHMAN / AFP via Getty Images)

6 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

A good toy is 90% kid and 10% toy. A good toy does not direct kids, it prompts them. It does not substitute for human connection, it supplements it.
Last year, Santa packed his bag with many toys that violated this basic rule. There were plushy dolls that were advertised to become a child’s friend, robots like Miko advertised as “Safe AI for everyday learning” and even Wuffy the robot dog, designed to teach kids love and responsibility. Amazingly, the battery-powered dog did not have to eat or even go for a walk, suggesting few lessons in responsibility. These toys are better at suggesting what the child should do than becoming prompts for imaginary play. Often displayed in solo mode, a child engaging with them needs no other companions and no human interaction.
It is little wonder that the AI toys were met with an outcry from parents and policymakers. Public Interest Research Group’s (PIRG) “Trouble in Toyland” piece sparked concerns that these plushy friends would help a child find a match when asked and would even help the child light it. Similarly, Common Sense Media gives AI toys an “unacceptable risk” designation, citing an example of a child saying she “liked to jump from high places” to the toy, Miko. Miko recommended “You could try a tree, a bench, your roof, or a window. Just remember, be safe.”
These concerns fueled California to pass legislation that institutes a four-year moratorium on “the sale and manufacturing of toys with artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot capabilities for children under 16.” The New York Assembly and House recently passed similar legislation.
What happened to AI toys this year? You can still find the toys if you specifically search for them. Some toys from last year have been reshelved. PIRG retested these toys and noted that they still have unacceptable risks. Happily, however, toy companies appear to be pushing back against screen-based and AI-infused toys. In fact, even marketing for AI toys this year has emphasized that they are often screenless, even if not yet ready for prime time.
The top toy lists for the 2026 holiday season host many more old favorites that stick by the 90% child rule. The 2026 Good Housekeeping Winners, Amazon’s Top 100+ Toy List, Target’s Bullseye’s Top 50 Must-Have Toys, The Toy Foundation’s Toy of the Year Finalist Lists, and Walmart’s Top Toy List include familiar manipulatives, pretend play, block building and artistic creation toys.
The toy industry is at an inflection point. Today’s toy lists offer opportunities for children to play together and practice the human-to-human skills necessary for them to thrive in school and beyond. When children build forts and castles together with blocks, when they practice taking turns and the art of being a good winner (or loser) when playing a game, when they pretend to bake brownies in a plastic oven, or when they imagine that the plush cat they love is real and pretend to take care of it, they are building key developmental skills like spatial skills (can you put the blue block on top of the red one), and even story creation (who is the character, what is the setting and what is the character trying to do?). These skills help drive early literacy.
Parents and caregivers will still have to navigate the new technology that will undoubtedly find its way into future offerings. A 2026 Common Sense Media report finds that 49% of parents have either bought or are interested in buying an AI toy for their children, with 19% being at least somewhat interested in having that toy serve as a companion for their child. At the same time, parents also report worries about these toys collecting personal information, their own difficulty in setting limits, cybersecurity risks, toys providing inappropriate content, and a fear of these toys displacing playtime with family and friends. This is not to say that AI-enhanced toys cannot be good for young children, but at the moment, the science cautions, let the buyer beware.
Future AI-embedded toys can be designed to prompt children to work together on problems or excite families with challenges and games. These toys are just not available yet. Perhaps future toy designers can work with scientists and educators to help us use tech as a tool for building imagination and human connection rather than dampening it.
It seems that, in response to this, Santa left many of the AI toys at the North Pole this year. We look forward to seeing what developers can create in the coming years that centers play and human engagement. Until then, kids and their parents will benefit most from the magnetic tiles, blocks and low-tech toys of old—the ones that are 90% child and 10% toy.

articles.title: Outlook 2027: Investment implications - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
The global economy enters 2027 with renewed momentum, although growth remains uneven and threatened by political uncertainty, inflation, and high debt costs

In equities, we see potential opportunities in technology and in Europe’s drive towards strategic autonomy

In fixed income, we favour inflation-linked bonds as well as European investment-grade corporate bonds

The global economy enters 2027 with stability and renewed momentum but economic growth is likely to be uneven and numerous risks remain.

The International Monetary Fund recently raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from the 3.0% it projected in July but kept its 2027 forecast unchanged at 3.4%.

The US economy has been resilient, and inflation appears likely to slow. Europe’s growth outlook is more positive than it has been for some time despite a backdrop of political uncertainty.

In China, growth is likely to slow as consumption and property investment remain subdued. Elsewhere in emerging markets, we expect growth to remain resilient albeit uneven in 2027.

From a markets perspective, we expect the technology sector will remain a key driver of equity markets, though the other sectors have seen steady gains, particularly in the US.

Within fixed income, inflation and debt concerns are weighing on the outlook for government bonds. Inflation-linked bonds can potentially offer a hedge against further escalation in the Middle East. Meanwhile US and European corporate bond yields look attractive, but investors should remain selective.

Central investment themes for 2027

AI shifts from experimentation to adoption

Artificial intelligence’s economic impact could become increasingly visible in the year ahead, marking a shift from technological possibility to real-world adoption and monetisation. Advances in physical AI are beginning to translate into real-world automation, initially in factories and warehouses, alongside AI-enabled wearables such as smart glasses. This could bring notable return on investment for companies at the forefront of new AI-related products and services.

Implementation idea – Disruptive technologies

Rationale: AI infrastructure demand is expected to outpace supply through 2027, especially as innovation opens new opportunities. Companies that can translate AI investment into sustainable revenue growth and attractive returns on capital should emerge as the long-term winners.

2027 could be the year that cloud service providers demonstrate the return on investment for their unprecedented AI infrastructure spending, but the software sector will require increasingly careful navigation to distinguish AI beneficiaries from those vulnerable to disruption.

The AI safety and regulation debate will continue in 2027 meaning cybersecurity and governance will play a critical role, with stocks in this sector remaining potentially attractive despite premium valuations.

Europe’s strategic autonomy drive

As Europe aims to grow its economy while safeguarding its own interests, it is placing greater focus – and investment – in areas ranging from defence and manufacturing to energy, food and health.

Security concerns have accelerated investment in areas such as defence while digitalisation is advancing more slowly. Even so, technology remains a cornerstone of European sovereignty, which is shaping not only European policy but also presenting significant opportunities for investors. Companies capable of translating the drive for European strategic autonomy into cash flow and sustainable revenue growth could well emerge as the long-term winners.

Implementation idea – European equities

Rationale:

European strategic autonomy is driving potential opportunities for equity investors in high-growth sectors such as technology, renewable energy and energy infrastructure. Meanwhile government and corporate bond issuance is likely to increase to fund the required support, meaning potential new opportunities for fixed income investors.

At the same time, it is becoming more important for investors to be selective and distinguish between companies benefiting from policy support and increased demand, including the prospect for stable cash flows and long-term contracts, and those struggling against global competition.

Navigating inflation volatility

Geopolitical tensions, energy insecurity and rising AI investment are reshaping the inflation outlook. As the global economy moves away from the price stability of the pre-pandemic decade, investors are facing a world where inflation is likely to be more elevated and less predictable. We believe investors need to shift to a more strategic approach to inflation protection.

While inflation-linked bonds have historically been used as short-term tools, they now offer an attractive option as a long-term portfolio component. Valuations of inflation-linked bonds have become more appealing, and they can potentially provide a buffer against unexpected price shocks while preserving purchasing power.

Implementation idea – Inflation-linked bonds

Rationale:

The shift toward a more volatile inflation backdrop strengthens the case for inflation-linked bonds within fixed income or multi-asset portfolios. Unlike conventional bonds, inflation-linked bonds have cash flows that are adjusted in line with inflation, aiming to provide a structural hedge against the erosion of purchasing power.

However, because inflation dynamics vary by region, as seen in the differing impacts of US tariffs versus energy shocks in Europe, an active, global approach is essential. This can allow investors to diversify across markets and potentially manage the interest rate sensitivity of their bond portfolio while aiming to capture inflation protection.

Capitalising on Europe’s corporate resilience

The European investment-grade bond market has shown remarkable resilience against a highly uncertain backdrop. Corporate fundamentals remain healthy, with solid cash-flow generation providing a strong foundation.

Looking toward 2027, we expect volatility to persist, but we believe the European credit outlook remains constructive. Attractive bond yields and robust corporate earnings offer a potentially attractive entry point for investors, suggesting that demand for the asset class will remain supportive despite short-term market fluctuations.

Implementation idea – European investment grade bonds

Rationale: The combination of attractive yield levels and strong corporate balance sheets makes European investment-grade credit a potentially attractive addition to diversified portfolios. While higher interest rates have raised concerns, the ability of high-quality issuers to maintain profitability and manage funding costs likely limits the risk of significant rating pressure.

However, as the market becomes more differentiated, a one-size-fits-all approach is no longer sufficient. Security selection is critical, and an active approach allows investors to target potential returns in other areas such as higher-quality high-yield bonds.

Asset Class Summary Views as of 16 November

Opinions draw on investment team views and are not intended as asset allocation advice.

Rates

US Treasuries
–
The Federal Reserve kept its key interest rate between 3.75% and 4.0% in October but indicated that inflation remains too high. Markets expect the official rate to peak around 4.50%/4.75%. We expect some pressure on US 10-year government bond yields over the next few months, and anticipate they will rise to 5.10%

Euro – Core Govt.
=
The European Central Bank did not hike in October but remains open to doing so in December. However, this is already priced in by markets, with futures reflecting close to three hikes in the next 12 months. We think a December rate hike will be the last, but given oil and gas prices, pressure will remain on government bond markets

Euro – Govt Spreads
+
Government bond spreads have widened and appear attractive. We remain positive on Italy and Spain since the current high yields help compensate for the volatility

UK Gilts
+
Our highest conviction overweight position is in longer-dated gilts, as UK inflation may start to ease and growth may have peaked

JGBs
–
We expect the yield on Japanese 10-year government bonds to rise back above 3% in 2027

Inflation
+
US 10-year inflation break-evens are close to their pre-Iran war levels so look attractive. In the eurozone, break-evens have risen versus the start of the conflict but would still be attractive if there is further escalation in the Middle East

We are positive on local currency bonds but remain very selective

Credit

Euro Investment Grade​
+
Spreads widened quickly in October and stood at their widest of the year so far. Weakness has been driven mainly by other asset classes (euro government bonds, technology stocks) rather than investment-grade bond fundamentals

GBP Investment Grade​
+
Overall yields remain very attractive

USD High Yield ​
+
Selectivity is key in this asset class, even more so than at the beginning of the year

Euro High Yield ​
+
We are taking advantage of weakness in the asset class to add to our holdings, but are being very selective

Equities

US
+
Technology and AI continue to drive returns, while US business activity remains resilient amid a broader manufacturing recovery. However, higher inflation and interest rate expectations still present risks to returns. We are diversifying tech risk with exposure to the financial sector

Eurozone

Earnings momentum is slowing down which is reflected in modest positioning. Higher energy prices, tighter monetary conditions and political risks are short-term headwinds

Japan
=
Corporate fundamentals remain supportive, but valuations are now higher and the market is undergoing a reduction in exposure to equities. BoJ policy and yen uncertainty also argue against a directional view. Bank stocks look attractive

China
–
Policy support and attractive valuations provide a degree of downside protection, but consumer spending trends remain subdued and visibility on a sustained earnings recovery is still limited

Emerging Markets
+
Valuations are attractive on a forward earnings basis​

Sector
+
Preference for energy-related stocks, reflecting a positive view on commodities, and for global financials for their attractive valuation and diversification characteristics

Investment Themes*
+
Long-term positive on AI buildout, grid electrification and carbon transition strategies​

* BNP Paribas Asset Management has identified several themes, supported by megatrends, that companies are tapping into which we believe are best placed to navigate the evolving global economy: Automation & Digitalisation, Consumer Trends & Longevity, the Energy Transition as well as Biodiversity & Natural Capital; source: BNP Paribas Asset Management.

articles.title: Daily: Treasury rally highlights the opportunity in bonds
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Equities: Industrials, health care, Eurozone, and quality AI (7 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Opportunities in high-quality bonds and select EM debt (5 mins)Thought of the dayThe S&P 500 fell for a fifth consecutive trading day on Wednesday, while US Treasuries gained for the third straight session. The US 10-year yield declined by 4 basis points to 5.06% amid lower oil prices, and a USD 16bn auction of 20-year Treasuries drew steady demand.The Treasury rally came despite minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October meeting showing that almost all officials agreed that further interest rate hikes would be needed if the US economy evolved as they expected. A few policymakers said that “a shift to a more restrictive policy stance” may be required, and two participants said a move larger than 25 basis points could be warranted if inflation proves more persistent.The minutes are consistent with our view that the US central bank will continue to raise rates into 2027. But more policy tightening is not necessarily negative for fixed income. In fact, we continue to rate the asset class as Attractive in our global portfolios and believe investors should rebalance toward bonds.Additional Fed hikes are already priced in, and a prolonged cycle appears unlikely. We expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points next month and again in March 2027, and acknowledge a higher risk of consecutive hikes following stronger-than-expected inflation data. But current fed fund futures suggest that markets have already priced in more than three additional rate increases from here. In our view, the cumulative impact of rate increases and tighter financial conditions is also likely to limit the need for a prolonged hiking cycle. This means Treasury yields have room to fall as markets reassess their Fed policy expectations, leaving scope for bond prices to move higher.Inflation should moderate in 2027, pointing to more measured tightening. While recent data point to still sticky price pressures, our base case is for underlying inflation to ease gradually next year amid favorable base effects. AI-related demand remains a risk factor for higher inflation, but lower oil prices and fading tariff effects should see disinflation resume. We forecast average inflation of 2.3% in the US in 2027, compared with 3.4% this year. This backdrop should support a more measured pace of tightening, a view recently backed by San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, New York Fed President John Williams, Boston Fed President Susan Collins, and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack.Bonds offer attractive portfolio income in an otherwise uncertain environment. Elevated starting yields are a key reason behind our Attractive view on fixed income, as they provide appealing opportunities to generate portfolio income even if interest rates or yields do not fall significantly. Historically, starting yields offer a good indication of subsequent total returns, and we think current yields can more than compensate for the risks of further yield volatility. For capital losses to offset one year of income, two-, five-, and 10-year US Treasury yields would need to increase by around 255, 113, and 65 basis points, respectively, from current levels, which we consider unlikely. Conversely, in a scenario where economic and equity market risks intensify, quality bonds would likely rally, helping insulate portfolios.So, we think investors should review their bond allocations and consider adding exposure. We see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, and within fixed income, we see the best return opportunity in emerging market and high yield bonds. We favor an intermediate average duration, generally through maturities of around two to 10 years, with a preference for shorter-dated bonds in the more growth-sensitive credit segments.

Market volatility reinforces case for portfolio resilience

articles.title: Debt sustainability and the range of multiple equilibria
articles.text:
Publication Type
Working Papers

Debt sustainability and the range of multiple equilibria

Olivier Blanchard (PIIE), Gonzalo Huertas (International Monetary Fund; former PIIE) and Pedro Martínez-Bruera (International Monetary Fund)

Working Paper 26-17

November 2026

Photo Credit: IMAGO/Westlight via Reuters

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
The authors characterize the size of the range of multiple equilibria in sovereign debt markets. They show that the nature of the equilibrium depends crucially on the degree of uncertainty, which they formalize first as uncertainty about primary balances and later as uncertainty about the fiscal feedback rule. For low uncertainty, the range can be large, but it becomes smaller as uncertainty becomes larger. If uncertainty is large enough, the multiplicity disappears. The interest rate is then unique and becomes a continuous function of the debt level. Interpreting the source of an increase in the interest rate in actual situations is difficult and complicates the use of intervention by central banks.
