articles.title: New Insurer Start-up Unit
articles.text:
New Insurer Start-up Unit

The New Insurer Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new insurer in the UK.

Thinking of becoming an insurerBeing an insurer means undertaking the regulated activities of effecting or carrying out contracts of insurance. Any firm that wants to be an insurer must be authorised to undertake these activities by the PRA with consent from the FCA. Before going through the new insurer authorisation process, firms will need to consider what functions they will carry out as an insurer and submit a regulatory business plan to outline their strategy and how it meets our threshold conditions. When you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk. Upon receipt of an enquiry with the regulatory business plan, we will arrange a meeting with you to get started with the pre-application and application phases. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer, and please expand the headings below to find out more.

From a regulatory perspective, an insurer is a firm with a ‘Part 4A permission’ that includes the activities of effecting contracts of insurance or carrying out contracts of insurance. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 sets out a list of relevant regulated activities (see Chapter III Insurance) but does not attempt an exhaustive definition of a contract of insurance. Potential applicants should refer to section 6 of the FCA’s Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG 6 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window) for Guidance on the identification of contracts of insurance. The section Guidance on insurance mediation activities in section 5 may also be helpful (PERG 5 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window).
The UK insurance market covers various lines of business, to list a few:
Non-life class of business:
• Accident and sickness
• Motor vehicle liability and other motor vehicle insurance
• Fire and other damage to property
• Marine, aviation and railway rolling sock
• General Liability
• Credit and suretyship
• Other classes
Life class of business:
• Life and annuity
• Marriage and birth
• Linked long term
• Permanent health
• Capital redemption
• Pension fund management
• Collective insurance
Depending on the area of the insurance market you plan to enter, there may be alternatives which allow you to offer similar products through another insurer without becoming a direct insurer yourself. For example, if you are interested in working in a niche area of the market or perhaps prefer to test your product first, operating as an intermediary under some form of delegated authority from an existing insurer e.g. as a managing general agent (MGA) may be more appropriate. There are a range of intermediaries, and the most appropriate route will depend on a number of factors, e.g. through which sales channels the insurance will be sold. Information on how to apply for intermediary activities can be accessed via the following link to the FCA website: apply to become a consumer investments firm Opens in a new window.
A firm wanting to sell regulated products but not wishing to become directly authorised can also agree with a PRA and/or FCA authorised firm to become its appointed representative (AR). Insurance mediation activities that an appointed representative can carry out are set out in the FCA handbook Opens in a new window, however, the AR is limited to only carrying out the regulated activities the authorised firm has permission to undertake. A prospective AR will undergo fitness and propriety checks and will have to follow the rules and procedures as set by the authorised firm. Rules relating to appointed representatives are set out in SUP 12 of the FCA Handbook and applicants can also get further information about the application process via the following link to the FCA website: become an appointed representative Opens in a new window.
Will my firm be subject to the Solvency II Directive?
Within the United Kingdom, newly authorised insurers and reinsurers will be subject to the Solvency II regime if they meet all the conditions stated in PRA Rulebook. Insurance General Application | Prudential Regulation Authority Handbook & Rulebook Opens in a new window.
Firms that are not subject to the Solvency II regime are known as ‘Non-Directive Firms Opens in a new window’ and are subject to different rules around key areas such as capital requirements, governance requirements, and reporting requirements. Applicants should consider whether their firm will be subject to the Solvency II regime when preparing any application and plan accordingly.
What business will your insurer carry out?
Before contacting us, you should familiarise yourself with the PRA’s expectations around key topics such as governance and financial resources. Further information on financial planning may be found in SS4/18 Opens in a new window, while the PRA’s expectations regarding governance are detailed in SS5/16 Opens in a new window. The full range of PRA publications containing guidance on a broad range of topics may be found at Prudential regulation publications Opens in a new window.
It is important that you consider the following key areas, as these are things we will initially want to focus on in our review.
• Regulatory business plan
• Senior management, the board and governance
• Financial resources
• IT strategy
• Reinsurance
• Resolution
• Outsourcing
What if your firm is already authorised?
If your firm is already authorised by the FCA, e.g. as an intermediary, you will need to apply to the PRA and FCA to vary your permissions to add insurance activities. While this is legally a different regulatory transaction to a new authorisation, you will need to follow the same process as a new firm applying to be an insurer (because of the substantive change to your business model) and we encourage you to start pre-application with us as normal to help the process of varying your permissions run smoothly.
When can I call myself an Insurer?
A firm cannot call itself an insurer until it has been authorised. The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘Insurance’ and ‘Insurer’, ‘reassurer, ‘reinsurance’, ‘reassurance’, ’reinsurer’, ‘underwriter’ and ‘underwriting’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation in order to prevent the public from being misled. You should seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words, checking the guidance found at sensitive business names Opens in a new window.
What are the next steps?
As mentioned earlier, when you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk to discuss your application and we will arrange an initial pre-application meeting. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer.

The pre-application stage helps the firm to:

Meet the NISU team
Understand how the authorisation process works
Understand regulatory expectations of the firm, in particular, the PRA and FCA Threshold Conditions
Submit an application that is as complete as possible when the firm is ready to formally apply for authorisation
Identify any particular concerns that we might have early on and help you to decide whether you want to spend time and money on an application that may not progress further

It helps the NISU Team to:

Meet the firm and understand their business proposal
Identify any concerns, which will be communicated quickly to the firm and gives the firm the opportunity to resolve them before submitting an application
Deal with the firm’s application quickly once it has been submitted

The table below outlines what we expect from firms during the pre-application process and what you can expect from the NISU team.

Firm’s Responsibilities

NISU Team’s Responsibilities

Be open, honest and collaborate with us.

Be open, honest and give clear feedback on your proposals.

Develop your plans, complete the necessary work, prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us.

The PRA and FCA will attend all meetings unless we advise you otherwise.

Ensure key individuals at your firm who will drive the proposition forward are involved throughout the process and attend the pre-application meetings.

Ensure the pre-application meeting is productive, and the authorisation process is clearly explained.

Provide all information that you think we should be aware of. Be ready, willing and organised.

Hold the appropriate number of meetings for your application (maximum of 3) giving due consideration to the proposals in the business plan.

Address and incorporate any feedback provided by us into your Business Plan before moving to the next stage.

Ensure feedback letter is sent to the Firm within a maximum of 10 working days after each meeting.

Please note that the NISU team do not provide a consultancy service or legal advice.
We offer a maximum of three meetings for standard applications. However, additional meetings may be arranged if a firm’s proposal involves innovative or particularly complex IT systems. These meetings include the initial meeting, feedback meeting, and challenge session. Established firms, such as those seeking to open new branches or subsidiaries in the UK, may require fewer meetings.

Initial meeting
The initial meeting is held after the submission of a high-level business plan summarising your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meeting at a mutually convenient time and agree on the agenda for the meeting.

The business plan should not be a ‘sales pitch’ as the regulators will have a different focus, and you should aim to provide an explanation of why you want to be an insurer and your business strategy including:

Business plan – products, target market, customer types
Sources of funding – how will the business be funded and details of any investors and/or funding in place
Project plan – an overview and timeline of your plan to set up the new insurer. (This is particularly important if new IT systems are required)
Owner and controllers – details of proposed owners and controllers
Corporate governance – details of structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements

The initial meeting provides an opportunity for firms to discuss their plans with us and ask questions about the authorisation process. It provides the NISU team with the opportunity to raise any concerns with the proposed business at an early stage.

The NISU team will then provide written feedback to the firm within 10 working days of the meeting to enable the firm to respond to and resolve any issues. You should continue to develop your business proposition and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version

Feedback meeting
The feedback meeting will be held after the firm has submitted, and we have reviewed, a more detailed business plan, which includes the firm’s response to the feedback from the initial meeting. This meeting provides an opportunity to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the firm’s proposed business model. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. After the meeting, the NISU team will provide written feedback to the firm which we expect the firm to address in their subsequent business plan.

At the end of the feedback meeting, we will discuss the actions you will need to complete if you want to progress to the next stage. Within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. You should continue to develop your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version.

Challenge session
The challenge session are the culmination of the pre-application application process. This final meeting is held just before a firm submits an application. The aim of the meeting is to discuss your proposals in depth and provide detailed challenge on the content of the final business plan. At this stage, your business plan should be fully developed and will form the basis of the discussion at the challenge session where we will offer an honest and open assessment of your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 15 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meetings at a mutually convenient time.

Firms can expect rigorous challenge on their proposed business model. The aim is to identify any remaining issues that need to be addressed before you submit your application. The challenge session will be attended by your case officers along with senior representatives and specialists from both regulators. We expect several of your executives and, where possible, non-executives to attend. You should expect the meeting to last about two hours.

At the end of the challenge session, we will discuss next steps and actions with you and within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. If you go on to submit an application, you should finalise your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback from the challenge session.

The meetings will typically be held at the PRA’s office in London. The meetings can be held in person or virtual. We will send you an agenda before all meetings which will centre on your explanation of the materials that you have sent us and the attendees from each regulator.

Our aim is that the pre-application process will give the firm a clearer understanding of our regulatory expectations, and the opportunity to resolve any potential problems before an application is submitted. Once the application is submitted, it is expected to be of sufficiently high quality to enable the NISU team to reach a decision more quickly.

Pre-application timeframes
The pace at which a firm progresses through the pre-application stage is up to the firm. Please read through the application forms and supporting notes as you may find them helpful when preparing for the meetings.

The NISU team expect to be kept up to date on your progress and will endeavour to hold pre-application meetings in a timely manner. If, however, we do not hear from a firm for six months after a meeting we will assume that you do not want to proceed with your application and close our file.

Please contact the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk and submit a high-level regulatory business plan along with your request for a pre-application meeting. We will then organise the meeting with you. The firm’s advisors or consultants are welcome to attend the pre-application meetings, but we do not expect them to speak on the firm’s behalf.

Please note that the pre-application stage is optional. If you choose not to use it, you can send your application directly to the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk. We will then use our statutory powers as set out in FSMA to reach a decision on your application. If you have any questions about the pre-application process, please contact the NISU team, and we will be happy to assist.

Your Business Plan should cover the following points as a minimum:

business plan – details of products, delivery channels and target market
business viability – competitive advantage, market research and how your firm will make money
financial resources – financial projections (for three years), capital management strategy (as appropriate)
sources of funding – proposed funding model
owners and controllers – proposed owners and controllers
corporate governance – structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements
risk management – risk management and control framework
customer journey – products, pricing, complaint handling and on-boarding arrangements (including Anti-Money Laundering/Know Your Customer processes)
outsourcing - details of key outsourcing arrangements
IT infrastructure and systems and timescales for implementation and testing recovery and resolution plans (if appropriate)
policies and procedures – operational and regulatory policies and procedures
business continuity – business continuity plans (if appropriate)
scope of permissions – details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake reinsurance arrangements
project plan – project plan for setting up the insurer

Background to NISUThe New Insurer Start-Up Unit (NISU) is a joint initiative by the UK’s financial regulators, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), set up in 2018.NISU is a team of experts across the PRA and FCA that provides necessary information and support to prospective insurers, aiding their progression to become authorised UK insurers. Our joint assessment process ensures any firm wishing to be an insurer is authorised by both the PRA and FCA.NISU’s objective is to guide firms through the authorisation process by leading efficient pre-application engagement and formalising the application process. We frequently explore initiatives to improve our process and contribute to the PRA’s and FCA’s secondary competitiveness objectives.This NISU guidance serves as a reference tool covering key supervisory topics. While it provides valuable information, it is not exhaustive and does not encompass all applicable UK laws and regulations. Prospective firms should use this webpage to aid their business planning and ensure compliance with all relevant regulatory requirements in the UK. Before commencing the new insurer authorisation process, firms should also consider whether setting up an insurer is right for them and what functions they will carry out. The regulatory business plan (RBP) they develop must outline their strategy and how they will meet and comply with PRA and FCA threshold conditions.We also encourage prospective UK insurers to take advantage of our PRA and FCA pre-application meetings as they can be extremely beneficial for all parties.

Authorisation process and regulatory expectationsTo achieve their objective of setting up an insurer, firms should be ready, willing and organised. It is important for firms to understand the authorisation process and regulatory expectations before submitting an application to us. This will ensure that the application submitted is of high-quality and as complete as possible. Read the New insurer authorisation process and regulatory expectations.
This section clarifies why submitting a complete application is important and gives an indication of what happens during our assessment process, including decision timelines.
Please be aware that authorisation is only the start of a new insurer’s journey to being established. In our guidance below, we have outlined some of our key regulatory expectations, but firms are responsible for considering in detail and complying with all the applicable laws, rules and regulatory policies.Mobilisation regime for new insurersThe PRA created a ‘mobilisation’ regime, effective from 31 December 2024, to facilitate new insurer expansion and entry into the UK market. We welcome discussions with potential new applicants who are applying for authorisation and considering using this new mobilisation phase.

The regime offers an optional stage, beginning at the point of authorisation, during which a new firm can operate with business restrictions while it completes the final development aspects of its insurer. These newly authorised insurers-in-mobilisation are given a period up of 12 months to finish building out their business, including securing additional funding, if required, while operating with business restrictions and proportionate regulatory requirements, as well as adhering to lower minimum capital requirements. Read the mobilisation regime for insurers webpage for further information.For more details on the mobilisation framework for new insurers, refer to:
CP12/23 - Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market
PS2/24 – Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market

Other pathwaysAs well as the formal new insurer authorisations process guidance above, there are other pathways available for firms to consider.

Insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs)As part of our amendments to allow the UK non-life insurance sector to play a bigger role in the global ILS market, we have created an accelerated pathway for ISPVs that meet certain defined criteria to gain approval. In such cases, the PRA will undertake rapid assessment of applications and, where satisfied, issue approvals within 10 working days of a 'complete' application submission.We recommend early engagement with the NISU team at the PRA, to assist with ensuring completeness of your ISPV application. Email us at ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk if you are interested in this accelerated route.The specific criteria for the accelerated 10 working day ISPV process can be found here: PRA's approach to authorising and supervising UK Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles Opens in a new window.For more information, visit insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs) Opens in a new window, where you can also find applicable application forms for ISPVs, to be submitted to ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk.

Wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathwayThrough the Wholesale Insurance Accelerated Authorisation Pathway (The Pathway), developed jointly by the PRA and FCA, we aim to provide an accelerated route to authorisation for a sub-set of London Market wholesale applicants.Read our wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathway Opens in a new window webpage for more information.

Submitting an applicationThis section lists the relevant application forms and provides details about applicable fees once you are ready to submit an application.

Application feesThe PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with the PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and the FCA Handbook Opens in a new window. It is your responsibility to cross-check the fees against the PRA Rulebook and FCA guidelines before making any payment. If you are unsure what fees are applicable to your firm, please email us at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to:fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.If you cannot make payment to the FCA using BACS. Please contact NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk for instructions on how to pay by cheque.

Applications forms

Full authorisation application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window
Branch application/re-domiciliation form (DOCX) Opens in a new window

IT self-assessment questionnaire: insurers (xlsm)

SOR: Statement of responsibilities (pdf) Opens in a new window

Being an authorised insurerAuthorisation is only the start of the journey to becoming an established insurer. Insurers must continue to meet our threshold conditions at all times, as well as ongoing regulatory requirements under both PRA and FCA Supervision.

Insurers must submit regular financial, risk, and conduct reports, and ensure frameworks and policies are continually reviewed to align with risks and business growth.

As supervision evolves over time, the PRA and FCA adopt a risk-based approach, adjusting oversight based on an insurer’s size, complexity and risk profile. As staying informed is essential, the PRA and FCA provide ongoing industry guidance, thematic reviews, and policy updates that insurers must follow to ensure compliance.

Read Being an authorised insurer for further information.

FAQsVisit our Frequently asked questions page for common queries regarding the application process.

Authorised insurersVisit Which firms does the PRA regulate? for a list of authorised insurers regulated by the PRA.

Contact usIf you have any queries about becoming a new insurer, email us:NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.The NISU is part of the regulators’ ongoing work to improve the authorisation process for prospective new insurers in the UK. We want the process, information and materials to be helpful for potential applicants so that we can have an effective and efficient way of working together, and lead to an improved quality of application when the time comes. It’s really important that we hear from you, the users of the NISU, about what is working well and what we can improve.As our consideration of further developments relating to the authorisation of new insurers continues, we are also interested to hear views on challengers faced by the firm in the insurance industry and possible measures to address them. Please email NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk with your feedback and input.

When conflict between the US and Iran began in March, disruption in the Middle East put energy costs firmly back on the agenda for copper miners. As updated cost guidance has emerged, rising diesel prices have increasingly been cited as a source of pressure.
But is diesel really the biggest cost concern facing copper producers?
In this episode of Mined Over Matter, we look beyond the headlines to examine how higher diesel prices are feeding through to mine costs and why the impact can vary significantly by region and mine type.
While diesel remains an important part of the cost base, strong copper and by-product prices are helping producers absorb some of the pressure. The discussion explores why diesel exposure differs between open-pit and underground operations, and why the industry's current position looks different from previous periods of energy cost inflation.
The team also considers some of the other pressures emerging across the copper industry. Skilled labour shortages and wage pressure are becoming increasingly important issues in Chile, while acid costs, declining ore grades and more complex ore bodies could add further pressure to costs and production.
Looking ahead to 2027, these pressures could have important implications for mine economics and production. With producers investing to maintain output amid declining grades, labour pressures and changing input costs, understanding where cost and supply risks are emerging will be increasingly important.
In the full episode, we explore:

How higher diesel prices are affecting copper mine costs
Why the impact of diesel varies by region and mine type
The role of strong copper and by-product prices in supporting producer margins
Why skilled labour shortages and wage pressure are becoming increasingly important in Chile
How acid costs and contract renegotiations could feed into the cost base in 2027
The impact of declining ore grades and more complex ore bodies on costs and production
What these pressures could mean for copper mine supply in 2027

High rates, higher interest payments

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

High rates, higher interest payments

5 minutes

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Summary

While high government debt does not dictate Fed policy, it does raise the macro stakes, with higher interest rates compounding already elevated debt-servicing costs. Combined with high inflation, this means volatility in bond markets is likely to persist, underscoring the need for a diversified approach.

Bond markets are contending with elevated uncertainty, driven by factors such as a high fiscal deficit, elevated debt levels and persistent US inflation. This, together with expectations of further Fed rate hikes, has contributed to a rise in Treasury yields, with the US 10-year once again reaching the 5% level last week. Overall, we believe this reinforces the case for a flexible, diversified investment approach with a global focus.

With US bond yields rising this year, government finances have become an important topic for capital markets. High debt levels, interest payments on debt, and elevated fiscal deficits — the excess of expenditure over revenue — are some of the key yardsticks markets are tracking. US interest payments as a share of government revenues reached an all-time high of close to 20%, as shown in the chart. In fact, interest payments have been one of the main drivers of the increase in expenditure for the Federal government in the fiscal year ended 30 September. Looking ahead, this expense is likely to increase further.We think this complicated fiscal backdrop, along with high inflation, will create more uncertainty in bond markets. The latest October CPI came in above expectations at 0.4% month on month, and confirms our view that the Fed will raise rates in the near term.

This week at a glance

Global equities rose on the back of positive corporate earnings in the US and Japan. Renewed optimism in the AI sector also helped lift sentiment, despite an abrupt leadership change at a leading technology company. European markets also reached new highs. In fixed income, bond yields rose due to elevated US inflation and expectations of rate hikes by central banks. As a result, gold prices fell. Gold is a non-yielding asset, and higher interest rates reduce the appeal of the yellow metal.

articles.title: How Climate Change Is Reshaping India’s Demographic Dividend
articles.text:
Source: GettyArticleHow Climate Change Is Reshaping India’s Demographic DividendToo often, the climate solutions generated by the state are built on data that are out of date and insufficiently detailed.Link CopiedBy Apoorva JadhavPublished on Nov 16, 2026This article is part of a new Carnegie series called “India’s Unfinished Demographic Dividend.” India’s demographic transition should be a historic advantage, but structural constraints are limiting its potential. This series examines the key barriers that could cap India’s growth trajectory—and the pathways to unlocking its demographic potential. The first two articles in the series are available here and here.IntroductionIn July 2026, Mumbai’s rail, road, and airport services were disrupted across the metropolitan region, and at least thirteen people died as monsoons lashed the city. The chief minister of the state of Maharashtra said Mumbai had received nearly 90 percent of its typical July rainfall in just four days. But just one month earlier, authorities had worried about drought. The lakes supplying water to the city were at 10 percent of their total capacity, leaving ⁠Mumbai’s 13 million residents with only forty days’ worth of water.This whiplash is not an isolated event, nor is it unique to Mumbai, as El Niño complicates monsoon patterns across India. The economic and human costs of extreme weather events are substantial. Climate change has made erratic weather more regular, thus exposing weaknesses in India’s infrastructure (particularly in urban areas) as communities contend with unseasonal rains, flash floods, and droughts linked to extreme heat, leaving millions at risk of disease and displacement. The National Disaster Management Authority estimates that monsoon damage typically costs the Indian economy ₹30,000–₹50,000 crore ($3.5–5.5 billion) in infrastructure losses, agricultural damage, disrupted logistics, and health-related costs every year. Researchers find that rainfall causes more than 8 percent of Mumbai’s deaths during the monsoon season, an order of magnitude more than official statistics. By 2100, climate change could reduce the country’s GDP by 6.4 percent to over 10 percent, and an estimated 50 million people could fall back into poverty because of climate-related challenges.Behind these disruptions sits a quieter, more urgent failure. The Sixteenth Finance Commission, a constitutional body that recommends how tax revenues should be divided between the government’s center and the states, recently released its 2026–2031 report. To determine how disaster management funds are allocated to states, the commission changed its predecessor’s Disaster Risk Index to use a new, multiplicative formula: hazard x exposure x vulnerability. Hazard is the physical event itself: a heatwave, a flood, a drought, considered separately from whether anyone is standing in its path or able to withstand it. Exposure is operationalized as each state’s projected total population, not just the population that is most at risk (for instance, those in a floodplain or drought-prone district). And vulnerability is reduced to a single variable: per-capita income. The formula thus seemingly rewards sheer demographic size over disaster risk, distributing a substantial ₹2,04,401 crore ($21 billion) in disaster management grants on that basis.The problem points to a deeper data failure: Granular, hyperlocal spatial data tracking hazard zone populations are inconsistent across state lines, so the formula falls back on population sizes rather than true ecological exposures. Odisha carries the highest hazard score of any Indian state, yet Uttar Pradesh’s Disaster Risk Index is five times higher on a lower hazard score, because exposure is measured by headcount. A state can receive more funding simply because more people live in it, not because more of them live in harm’s way.India is confronting a demographic transition it can no longer accurately see. The first article in this series identified fertility and mortality as the primary forces behind India’s demographic transition, with migration emerging as a third principal pillar over the next half-century. Climate change is now reshaping all three. Importantly, it runs the causal arrow in the direction demography usually does not: The older debate asks whether population growth drives environmental damage, but this series is concerned with age structure rather than population size alone. Climate change threatens India’s demographic dividend through three growing mismatches: that between the climate risks India faces and what its instruments actually measure; between the demographic transition the state plans for and the one climate change is producing; and between the health shocks reaching Indian workers and the protection available to absorb them.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie This WeekUnderstand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.The Exposure and Measurement MismatchThe Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) treats climate risk as the product of three distinct metrics: a hazard, the people exposed to it, and how vulnerable those people are when it arrives. For any given level of global warming, the IPCC finds that the resulting level of risk depends on trends in human exposure and vulnerability. For instance, it notes that between 2010 and 2020, mortality from floods, droughts, and storms was roughly fifteen times higher in the most vulnerable regions than in the least vulnerable ones. India’s adaptation instruments are well-placed to measure the first dimension—the hazards—but they measure the second and third far less accurately. What follows is an examination of that gap across three hazards: heat, floods, and drought, each of which exposes a different part of the same measurement failure.Heat: An Invisible HazardExtreme heat can cause severe heat stress, organ failure, and even death. Beyond health challenges, the International Labour Organization (ILO) projects that India could lose the equivalent of 34 million full-time jobs by 2030 due to heat alone, mostly in agriculture and construction. Economists put the resulting drag at 2.5 to 4.5 percent of GDP annually.The district-level heat risk index created by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) is both comprehensive—drawing on climate data from 1982 to 2022—and instructive. Close to 57 percent of Indian districts, home to 76 percent of the country’s population, are currently at “high” to “very high” heat risk. Mumbai, Delhi, and much of the Gangetic plain face the highest exposure, as population density, densely built environments, and existing socioeconomic and health conditions compound one another. The unmeasured population density this series documented in the second article is not only an administrative failure, but it is also a heat trap.Mapped against this series’ three demographic groupings (see box 1), the pattern inverts what the first two articles found: Aging Frontier states carry the heaviest burden for heat, with 90 percent of their districts falling in the “high” or “very high” risk categories, compared with 66 percent in Youthful Engine states and 20 percent for the Transitioning Middle (see figure 1).In the Aging Frontier states, heat risk is driven by urban density. These states are among India’s most urbanized, and the index places significant weight on built environment and population concentration. In the drier Youthful Engine states—such as Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan—intense heat alone is the main driver, and weaker cooling infrastructure increases residents’ vulnerability. The deeper takeaway is that the states with the strongest fiscal positions and deepest administrative capacity—the Aging Frontier states—will have to adapt the most. Consequently, much of these states’ governing capacity will be devoted to managing heat in cities that are simultaneously aging and warming.
Box 1. Three Speeds of the Demographic Transition in India
India’s states and territories are at different stages of their demographic transitions. The tripartite classification utilized here is based on the number of years it took each state or territory to reach the demographic leader Kerala’s threshold of survival (life expectancy of sixty-two, reached in 1973) and fertility (based on a total fertility rate of 2.1, reached in 1988). These states and territories are then clustered into three groupings, requiring distinct policy responses:
Aging Frontier (Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Punjab, Tamil Nadu): These states converged on advanced health and low-fertility benchmarks relatively early. Their early demographic success, reflected in older, longer-living populations, has created significant fiscal pressures: high debt, persistent deficits, rising pension and welfare commitments, and modest revenue growth.
Transitioning Middle (Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, West Bengal): These states and territories achieved rapid gains in life expectancy, reaching the benchmark within roughly twenty-five years of Kerala, but their fertility rate decline lagged considerably. The mismatch between lower mortality and higher fertility means they retain sizable working-age populations while simultaneously facing rising aging-related care needs.
Youthful Engine (Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh): These states are characterized by large and growing youth populations requiring sustained investment in health, education, and skill development. They experienced significant delays in mortality decline, often twenty-five to thirty-five years behind Kerala, with fertility transitions lagging even further.

India is not starting from scratch in responding to heat risks. For example, Ahmedabad in the western state of Gujarat pioneered South Asia’s first heat action plan (HAP) in 2013, establishing the blueprint for early warning systems. Yet persistent physical hazards, chiefly extreme heat compounded by water stress, mean it remains among the world’s highest residual risk hot spots, despite adaptation plans. This paradox is symptomatic of a broader governance gap: An evaluation of thirty-seven state and city HAPs found that only two had conducted an explicit vulnerability assessment, and the plans overlooked the intersecting realities of caste, gender, class, and labor informality that shape heat risk, which is not spread evenly across the workforce.Incorporating disaggregated demographic data is essential to confront the reality of a hierarchical “division of laborers,” not merely of labor. The distinction is important. A division of labor sorts tasks, while a division of laborers sorts people into occupational groups that may be inherited rather than chosen. Researchers found, during the 2019 and 2022 heat waves, the relationship between hours worked outdoors and heat stress to be 25 to 150 percent greater for marginalized caste groups, even after controlling for age, gender, education, and economic status.Floods and Drought: Different Geographies of RiskClimate exposure does not resolve into a single variable that tracks demographic stage or governance capacity. Different hazards have different geographies, so heat, floods, and droughts must be considered separately. This also explains why the Transitioning Middle’s position on the left side of figure 1 should not be read as meaning those states are safe; it simply means that heat is not the principal hazard facing the group’s Himalayan members. There, water held in glacial ice can lead to disastrous floods, as demonstrated by the glacier collapse in August that led to tremendous loss of life and the destruction of communities and infrastructure on the Nepal–Tibet border.Consider the district-level flood and drought risk mapping released in 2024 by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) with the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC). The assessment was built to give state governments district-level risk maps to plan adaptations. Rather than matching demographic scale, the data reveal geographic concentration: Districts at “very high” or “high” risk of floods are localized across seven states, while districts with the same level of drought risk are spread across thirteen states. Comparing the top fifty flood- and drought-prone districts identifies just eleven facing simultaneous “very high” dual risks, including Patna in Bihar, Alappuzha in Kerala, and Kendrapara in Odisha—representing one in each of this series’ three demographic groupings.Sorted by demographic cluster, the fifty highest flood-risk districts demonstrate that the hazard component is relatively similar across the Transitioning Middle and Youthful Engine groupings (contributing between 30 and 32 percent of total risk). What changes is the balance of the other two terms, which move in opposite directions. For instance, exposure falls from 39 to 29 percent while vulnerability, measured using eleven development indicators, rises from 31 to 39 percent. For the Youthful Engine states, flood risk stops being a story about how many people and assets sit in harm’s way and becomes a story about how badly they withstand it. The comparison is confined to these two groupings because only one Aging Frontier district appears among the fifty. For drought, where the Transitioning Middle is represented by only three districts, the same shift is present but much weaker. One caution applies throughout: The DST index builds vulnerability from development indicators such as multidimensional poverty, female literacy, and health infrastructure, that correlate with how far a state has moved through its demographic transition. Therefore, some overlap with these groupings is expected.How India Measures Hazards, Exposure, and VulnerabilitySet against the Finance Commission’s Disaster Risk Index, the contrast is stark. But the difference is not a disagreement over the appropriate framework; both the DST and Finance Commission use the IPCC’s framework of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. However, they differ sharply in how they define and measure each term (see table 1).The Finance Commission plays the largest role in funding state disaster relief yet uses the least precise measurement to allocate funds.The three indexes apply the IPCC framework with wildly different rigor. The DST/SDC index includes eleven development indicators for vulnerability, while the Finance Commission index uses a single per-capita figure. Exposure is measured at a more granular level in two of the indexes and less so in the third. The Finance Commission, which oversees the distribution of vast financial allocations, measures the three standards most crudely—the body that plays the largest role in funding state disaster relief uses the least precise measurement to allocate funds.The Demographic MismatchHow exactly do heat, floods, and drought affect health and demographic outcomes? The answers are as varied as the climate exposures themselves, but the defining feature of this series’ demographic analysis is that we are still learning in real time. This points to a fundamental mismatch: India’s demographic instruments were built to track a transition driven from within, yet climate change is now altering it from the outside. This section examines three domains in which climate stress is easily discernible: disease exposure, pregnancy, and migration.Disease and MortalityConsider dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease. Nationally, reported dengue cases between 2016 and 2022 were three times higher than those reported between 2007 and 2015. Himachal Pradesh, a state where dengue was relatively rare, saw 168 times more cases, while Jammu and Kashmir, Mizoram, Meghalaya, and Sikkim also experienced sharp increases. Researchers cautiously attribute this surge to a combination of growing mountain tourism, better detection, and warming. Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir sit firmly in the Transitioning Middle grouping, the same cluster that appeared least at risk on the heat index. This example shows that even if warming does not directly harm health, it can bring disease vectors into territories where they are not endemic. Dengue poses a substantial risk to workers, and widespread transmission could result in significant productivity losses, particularly in labor-intensive sectors, linking the climate change and disease narrative to the demographic dividend.Even if global warming does not directly harm health, it can bring disease vectors into territories where they are not endemic.Projections suggest that by 2030, the largest proportional increases in dengue will be in Gujarat and Maharashtra, with Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu potentially seeing increases of 10 to 80 percent. Most of these are among the more urbanized Aging Frontier states. They also rank among the states with India’s highest age-standardized diabetes prevalence, according to Global Burden of Disease estimates, which increases the risk of severe dengue. Put differently, aging, urban populations with high rates of diabetes may be particularly vulnerable. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and the rest of the Gangetic Plain are projected to see fewer dengue cases, but these states also have weaker disease surveillance. A decline in reported cases could mean less dengue or less detection.However, the most important finding of the dengue projection model discussed above actually cuts across all three demographic groupings. When it comes to predicting how many dengue cases a state will report in a given year, climate variables account for only 5 to 6.5 percent of the model’s predictive power. By contrast, per capita income contributes 29 percent, hyperglycemia contributes 12.5 percent, and a simple time trend—capturing, among other things, the improvement in surveillance over time—contributes another 16 percent. This means climate variables are a factor, but their impact is dwarfed by population conditions.Climate Risk Before BirthWhile dengue is one illustration of the links between climate change, demographic outcomes, and productivity losses, the most visceral link starts before birth. The largest study yet connecting extreme heat to pregnancy outcomes in India found that exposure to extreme heat during the first trimester raised the risk of preterm birth, exposure in the second trimester lowered birth weight, and exposure in the third trimester had the strongest link to stillbirth. Risk was concentrated among people with low body mass index and those who were poorer and less educated.A separate study found that air pollution compounds the danger: Pregnant women exposed to higher ambient air pollution faced higher odds of both low birth weight and preterm birth. This can cause detrimental effects later in the child’s life. The developmental origins hypothesis, which finds that conditions in the womb shape disease risk decades later, is supported by evidence from India that low birth weight raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and coronary heart disease in adulthood. Extreme heat or air pollution increases the likelihood that a baby born today is underweight, which can result in a chronically ill worker with reduced productivity.Climate MigrationThe state can see changes in fertility and mortality through hospital records and household surveys. Migration is different. Despite being the most visible of the three demographic forces, it is the least recorded. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) counted 672,000 disaster-related displacements in India in 2025. By the end of the year, 130,000 people were still living in displacement. Floods accounted for nearly 472,000 of these displacements, with Uttar Pradesh alone accounting for more than a quarter. Smaller monsoon-related floods that occurred between June and September accounted for much of the remaining displacement. Yet even these numbers understate the typical scale. Reviewing decadal trends, IDMC found that India averages around 3.5 million flood displacements per year; the 2025 figure was roughly one-seventh as large, in part because few large cyclones made landfall.This type of displacement is one of the most visible manifestations of climate migration. But other effects—such as people being trapped and unable to leave due to fewer resources—are harder to see. India currently lacks a statistical category for climate migrants. This means that an individual fleeing a flooded village is recorded, if at all, as an economic migrant. While disaster-related displacement tends to dislodge entire households, attrition typically involves individual workers. Research shows that weather shocks push migrants toward cities in other states, and migrants from agriculture-dependent households are prone to end up at the lower end of the skill distribution. The population left behind disproportionately consists of the elderly, women, and children. Hence, climate stress drives out the household members best equipped to survive it. But, in a cruel twist, climate migrants often end up working in industries with the most heat exposure, such as construction, kilns, logistics, delivery, and street vending.Climate migrants often end up working in industries with the most heat exposure, such as construction, kilns, logistics, delivery, and street vending.India is beginning to build the statistical machinery needed to track climate migration. The National Migration Survey, which is currently in the field, marks the first government-sponsored dedicated migration survey in two decades. The survey captures respondents’ reasons for migrating, short-term and return migration data, and migrants’ employment profiles. The 2027 Census, also underway, will collect migration and fertility data (and, for the first time since 1931, caste data). However, the ability of these instruments to address existing blind spots will turn on whether they identify the environmental reasons for migration and how the results are disaggregated and published.Across all three domains, the pattern is the same: The signal exists, but the instrument cannot read it. Dengue spreads into states that record it poorly, heat and air pollution shape a worker’s health decades before that worker enters the labor force, yet no survey connects the two. The transition India is planning for and the transition it is experiencing, have begun to diverge.The Productivity MismatchPeople who survive a heat-exposed pregnancy or flood-related displacement emerge with worse health and encounter a labor market that does not allow them the space or time to recover. The mismatch here is between health shocks that are rising and increasingly chronic, and protections that reach only the small proportion of the workforce in formal employment. Air pollution is a clear example of how detrimental effects accumulate over a working life and have a material impact on productivity. Although air pollution is not a climate impact, it is closely connected with climate change: Fossil fuel combustion contributes to both, and rising temperatures can worsen pollution by increasing ground-level ozone and trapping pollutants in stagnant air.Air Pollution’s EvolutionAs India’s economy has grown, the nature of its air pollution burden has evolved. Between 1990 and 2019, the crude death rate from household air pollution fell from an estimated 122 to 44 per 100,000 people. During this period, burning solid fuels for cooking at home declined. However, deaths from ambient particulate matter (PM) pollution nearly doubled as traffic, industry, and construction increased. The two rates crossed in the mid-2010s. This is the environmental analog of the demographic transition: India is moving away from poverty-related pollution challenges as it confronts pollution inexorably linked to economic development. Youthful Engine states remain more exposed to the first, while the Aging Frontier states increasingly confront the second.India is moving away from poverty-related pollution challenges as it confronts pollution inexorably linked to economic development.This shift, rising PM2.5 pollution and declining household air pollution, is a predictable consequence of growth. Similarly, one study finds that states with a larger share of people aged thirty-five to forty-nine have higher per capita carbon dioxide emissions than states whose populations skew either younger or older. This presents something of a paradox: The cohort whose productivity is essential to delivering growth is the same cohort whose consumption, transportation, and building intensify the environmental pressures that threaten growth.When Pollution Sickens Rather Than KillsAir pollution accelerates the chronic-disease burden—the impact of conditions such as heart and lung disease, diabetes, and stroke that disable workers for years rather than killing them quickly—which the first article in this series identified as India moves past the middle phase of its demographic transition. Air pollution was responsible for an estimated 18 percent of deaths in India in 2019, and the lost output from premature deaths and pollution-related illnesses totaled $36.8 billion, roughly 1.4 percent of GDP. That study, while a few years old, separates the loss into output foregone because workers died early and output foregone because workers were sick. It spotlights interesting gradients across this series’ demographic groupings (see figure 2).In Youthful Engine states, illness accounts for 19 percent of the economic loss; the rest is output lost because people died prematurely. In the Transitioning Middle, that share rises to 23 percent, and in the Aging Frontier to 25 percent. As a state moves through its demographic transition, air pollution appears to stop killing workers and start sickening them.Illnesses from air pollution include stroke, lung cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Age-standardized death rates from lung disease have fallen roughly 26 percent globally since 1990. But South Asia’s decline has been far smaller, and its mortality rate is now more than double the global average. The contrast between prevalence and mortality is especially revealing. For instance, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom report some of the world’s highest prevalence of chronic lung conditions, but comparatively low mortality. This is because better primary care and diagnostics, such as routine spirometry, help detect disease earlier. India and Pakistan have higher mortality despite lower recorded prevalence. Lung function testing is uncommon in India, and cause-of-death certification is uneven, meaning that a low recorded prevalence alongside high mortality should not be mistaken for a healthy population. Meanwhile, ambient air pollution is the major COPD risk factor for people in South Asia. For women in poorer households, smoke from solid cooking fuels compounds that exposure. The researchers make this explicit: Lung damage accrues over time. Patients in their fifties arrive at clinics after decades of exposure to smog, construction particles, and disease infections. These are also peak working years, and the exact age when the Aging Frontier’s demographic dividend is supposed to pay out.Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) accounted for an estimated 58 percent of India’s disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2020, with their share of deaths ranging from 40 percent in Madhya Pradesh to 75 percent in Kerala. A World Economic Forum–Harvard School of Public Health study, which remains the standard reference, projected that NCDs would cost India $3.55 trillion in lost economic output between 2012 and 2030 (measured in 2010 dollars), roughly six times its projected health spending during this period.Working Through IllnessNotably, India has no official workplace program addressing chronic disease and productivity in either the public or private sector. Given the low-birth weight cycle traced above, this burden is not simply a consequence of aging. Some of it was set in motion before today’s youngest workers were even born. Protections against lost income during illness are concentrated in formal employment, leaving them unable to reach the roughly 80 percent of India’s workforce that is informal. For that majority, illness produces presenteeism: working through illness at reduced capacity. A review of ten Indian urban HAPs notes that work performance is projected to decline by up to 40 percent under high-emissions scenarios, emphasizing the urgent need to reinforce an Indian workforce against such effects.How India Can Create a Climate Resilient WorkforceThe advantages of a demographic dividend are typically lost through unemployment or through workers who lack the skills to be productive. But there is a third route: through workers who are employed and present at work but produce less because of a heat spell, a chronic condition seeded before birth, or lungs that have absorbed pollutants for decades. Fortunately, India has options to create a more resilient workforce.First, India should measure exposure rather than population. The Sixteenth Finance Commission has adopted the right framework; the task now is to fill it with high-quality data. Exposure should be weighted by the population living in hazard zones rather than the total projected population, and vulnerability should draw on multiple indicators (such as those used for measuring flood and drought risk) rather than per capita income alone. The commission’s recommendation to classify heat waves and lightning as national disasters should be implemented. Finally, HAPs and flood-risk instruments should be mandatory in vulnerability assessments, which should also incorporate occupation, informal housing, and caste.Second, India should publish the mobility data currently being collected and ensure climate data are included. The National Migration Survey already captures migration data, shifting the challenge from data collection to whether environmental factors are coded at all and, if they are, whether they are appropriately disaggregated and disseminated. The survey results should be disaggregated by environmental drivers and linked to district-level hazard data so states can track climate mobility rather than treating it as part of the black box of “economic migration.” India’s disaster architecture is built to respond to discrete events such as cyclones. Other slow-burning disasters, such as drought, do not catalyze emergency government action.Third, India should extend income protection during illness to the informal workforce. Employees’ State Insurance offers a template for wage-linked sickness benefits. Extending some form of protection beyond formal employment would support the workers most affected by climate exposure. Alongside this, maternal health surveillance should track heat and air pollution exposure during pregnancy, instead of treating them as background conditions, and routine lung function testing should be incorporated into primary care.Conclusion India’s demographic window will not wait for climate and demographic data to catch up. The first article in this series asked whether the state has the foresight and capacity to count, govern, and equitably support its population through this transition. The second article argued that the state cannot manage urbanization it refuses to accurately measure. This article identifies shortcomings in the data on who is being born, who is surviving, and who is moving. Too often, the answers generated by the state are built on data that are out of date and insufficiently detailed. Commuters in Mumbai who must wade through rainwater to get to the office, the mother whose third trimester coincides with an extreme heat wave, and the worker who left a drought-stricken district for a construction site might appear unrelated, but they are part of the same demographic story.This piece benefited greatly from the support of Milan Vaishnav, Annabel Miller, Lindsay Maizland, Alana Brase, and Amy Mellon.About the AuthorApoorva JadhavNonresident Scholar, South Asia ProgramApoorva Jadhav is a nonresident scholar in the Carnegie South Asia Program. articles.title: North American Power & Renewables Forum 2027
articles.text:
Event

North American Power & Renewables Forum 2027

Date

April 28-29 2027

Time

08:00 - 17:00 MT

Location

Omni Interlocken Hotel, Denver, CO

Register now

The early booking rate is $1395 USD per person. Register by January 8 2027 to save $700 USD off the $2095 USD standard rate.
Wood Mackenzie clients: Contact events@woodmac.com for your discount rate and promo code.

The North American power landscape is evolving
Utilities, hyperscalers, and other offtakers are seeking a broader mix of resources to balance affordability, reliability, and emissions goals – from collocated solar and storage to SMRs and gas. Solar and energy storage are gaining share, bolstered by their cost profile and development timeline. These advantages help meet the surge in demand from data centers and reshored manufacturing. At the same time, geopolitical volatility and supply-chain pressures are reshaping market conditions.
In this environment, utilities, developers, IPPs, and investors need a broad view of the power market to make sound decisions. To reflect this shift, Wood Mackenzie’s longstanding Solar & Energy Storage Summit is expanding to become the North American Power & Renewables Forum.
On the agenda for 2027, we discuss the forces reshaping the power market in North America:
• Can the U.S. achieve energy leadership over the long-term without greater policy consistency?• Tariffs, international conflicts and rising interest rates are adding cost pressures. What level of increase will stifle demand growth?• Has FERC interconnection reform successfully removed blockers to transmission development? Where is further reform needed?• Is USA-made solar and storage cheaper per watt, would it survive without credits, and who absorbs the price difference?• Every major hyperscaler has signed a nuclear PPA; what role will nuclear play in their long-term energy strategy?• To what extent can mature renewable technologies such as wind, solar, and storage contribute to clean firm generation?

Speaking and branding opportunities are now available for 2027

Be part of the agenda and get your brand in front of the audience through a panel discussion or a fireside chat with a senior Wood Mackenzie Analyst.
As a commercial partner, your organization will be mixing with the industry decision-makers and influencers who are seeking investment, partnerships, and the latest business enhancing-technologies.
To arrange an exploratory discussion:
Contact Ro Pleasant, Head of Event & Creative Sponsorships on events@woodmac.com

2027 Sponsors and Supporters include:

Event supporter: reNEWS

reNEWS, the 'digital newspaper' and real-time news website tracking the renewable energy market. Established in 2002, the reNEWS Premium newsletter is regarded as a leading source of information on the sector, providing the exclusive and unmissable stories that matter to the industry. Breaking news is available through free-to-use www.reNEWS.BIZ and across a range of digital platforms, including a customised daily email briefings service.

Find out more

Platinum sponsor: Energy Dome

Energy Dome is a leading provider of innovative capacity solutions for AI infrastructure, powered by its patented CO2 Battery technology. The company’s proprietary system delivers cost-competitive, dispatchable capacity and 24/7 clean power using readily available materials, supporting grid reliability, renewable integration, energy security, and industrial competitiveness. As global electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI workloads, hyperscale computing, and the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, Energy Dome is advancing the commercial deployment of its technology to deliver reliable, scalable, and lower-emissions power solutions for utilities, energy providers, hyperscalers, and large energy users.

Find out more

Gold sponsor: CALB

CALB is one of the top 5 LFP battery cells and energy storage systems manufacturers. Globally, CALB has already delivered more than 100GWh battery cells for projects located in North America, South America, Middle East and Europe. With strong R&D capabilities and large-scale manufacturing, CALB provides safe, reliable, and high-performance products for utility-scale and commercial applications. With a growing presence in North America, CALB delivers scalable and bankable energy storage solutions, supporting renewable integration and the global energy transition.

Find out more

Gold sponsor: Heliene

Heliene is one of North America's fastest-growing domestic module manufacturers serving the utility-scale, C&I, and residential markets. With an in-house logistics team and remarkably responsive support staff, Heliene delivers competitively priced, high performance solar modules precisely when and where customers need them to accelerate North America's clean energy transition. Founded in 2010, Heliene is recognized as a highly bankable module manufacturer and has production facilities located in Ontario and Minnesota.

Find out more

Gold sponsor: Thornova Solar

Founded in 2022, Thornova Solar is a leading FEOC compliant USA-affiliated company with integrated supply chain capabilities, covering the entire production process from silicon wafers and solar cells to modules – based on US-made polysilicon. With our state-of-the-art automated production facilities, Thornova Solar delivers the reliability and performance you expect. We deliver from the US, Kenya or Indonesia – offering the perfect mix and match of DC requirements to achieve the best cost / tax incentive ratio for your projects.

Silver sponsor: GridBeyond

GridBeyond is bridging the gap between real-time markets and energy assets, helping businesses thrive in dynamic markets while accelerating the energy transition for a net zero future. Our technology unlocks the latent power within every connected asset - whether its renewables generation, battery storage and industrial load - to ensure each piece can play a vital role in balancing the grid. From advanced demand response to Corporate Power Purchase Agreements and hedging strategies, we unlock new revenue streams and reduce energy costs for industry, while ensuring that green power producers maximise profitability and operational efficiency.

T1 Energy Inc. (NYSE: TE) is an energy solutions provider building an integrated U.S. supply chain for solar. In December 2024, T1 completed a transformative transaction, positioning the Company as one of the leading solar manufacturing companies in the U.S., with a complementary solar and storage strategy. Based in the U.S. with plans to expand its operations in America, the Company is also exploring value optimization opportunities across its portfolio of assets in Europe.

Mayfield Renewables is an engineering consultancy dedicated to empowering the commercial-scale solar, energy storage, and microgrid industries. We are electrical engineers at our core: supporting our developer and EPC clients from project conception through commissioning by providing feasibility studies, design engineering, electrical engineer of record, and consulting services. We are educators at heart: sharing lessons learned from our engineering experience and providing training resources for industry stakeholders more broadly. We solve complex problems, de-risking projects, demystifying technical topics, and setting the standard for successful mid-market complex projects.

TWAICE is the analytics platform built for real-world battery energy operations at scale. We help teams move beyond reactive troubleshooting toward proactive, data-driven operations that improve safety, reliability, and profitability across their BESS fleets.
With TWAICE, operators gain the visibility and foresight needed to run their BESS fleets proactively. Our platform provides predictive insights that help teams act before issues affect performance or revenue, supported by intuitive workflows and automation. The result: standardized operations, longer asset life, and scalable, high-performing fleets in a growing energy storage market.

Find out more

APA Solar is a leading provider of solar racking and foundation solutions for commercial and utility-scale projects. With more than 15 years of engineering expertise, APA designs, engineers, and manufactures its products in-house, delivering durable, cost-effective systems built for fast installation and long-term reliability. Its portfolio includes fixed-tilt, tracker-compatible, and proprietary alternative foundation solutions that help reduce project costs. Acquired by ARRAY in 2025, APA combines innovative products with a team-first approach, partnering closely with developers, contractors, and EPCs to optimize project execution from design through installation.

Find out more

Associate sponsor: ARRAY Technologies

ARRAY Technologies is a global leader advancing the future of clean energy. With over 30 years of innovations that have powered the solar industry, ARRAY is uniquely positioned to deliver renewable energy solutions for customers seeking clean energy adoption in markets around the globe. While our strength lies in building the world’s most reliable and efficient utility-scale solar trackers, our expertise, capabilities, and resources position us to extend into additional renewable energy solutions. As pioneers, innovators, and visionaries, we are committed to generating energy with integrity for a sustainable world.

Find out more

Bachmann offers a comprehensive range of solutions for wind energy, renewables, energy storage, grid measurement, and control. These solutions include hardware such as controllers, HMIs, software for control and supervision (SCADA) and complete condition monitoring systems (CMS).
Robustness and reliability – Bachmann solutions embody these characteristics, and we therefore perform 100% testing on every single module, including a 48h run-in test. The highly available and durable solutions are designed to withstand the toughest conditions, minimizing both capital and operational expenditure.

Find out more

Associate sponsor: Brown & Brown Risk Solutions

Brown & Brown Risk Solutions, a subsidiary of Brown & Brown, Inc., specializes in serving large, complex accounts. We are headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, and service approximately 1,150 businesses. We are built on industry specialization and utilize innovation to focus on total cost of risk and drive down cost.

Find out more

Associate sponsor: Hendrix Aerial Cable Systems

Hendrix Aerial Cable Systems, a leader in the electrical utility industry, brings decades of expertise to the renewable energy market. Hendrix spacer cable offers a cost-effective alternative for medium-voltage collector circuits in utility-scale solar and wind applications. By placing multiple circuits on a single pole, you can greatly reduce the right-of-way requirements and eliminate the heat entrapment and de-rating suffered by UG cable. With robust, weather-resistant cables, Hendrix ensures maximum durability and minimal maintenance, making our systems ideal for remote and harsh locations.

Find out more

Associate sponsor: Magnum Piering

For over 40 years, Magnum® Piering has been dedicated to designing, engineering, and manufacturing, the most trusted foundation and anchoring products for the Commercial, Electrical Power, Oil & Gas, Renewable Energy and Residential Construction Industries. Magnum® Piering has worked diligently to elevate the standards of the foundation industry with a proven customer support team and through a multi-step quality control system. We are your trusted foundation team.

Find out more

Sieyuan Electric is a leading power technology company dedicated to "Smarter Power, Better Life." It provides efficient power system solutions across transmission, distribution, energy storage, and digital transformation. With five R&D hubs and over ten manufacturing sites in China, it delivers reliable primary/secondary equipment, power electronics, and EPC services globally.

Find out more

Start-up sponsor: Veridue

Veridue is the AI-native due diligence and M&A platform purpose-built for energy infrastructure and data centres. It accelerates investment and project financing for investors, IPPs, developers, lenders and insurers: buyers screen 100x more opportunities and complete due diligence in hours rather than weeks, while owners and sellers reach bankability or a better exit faster. Veridue combines the latest AI models with a proprietary deterministic agent layer trained across thousands of energy-specific risk factors, plus in-house energy transaction experts who validate every output.

Find out more

Why attend the North American Power & Renewables Forum 2027?

The solar & energy storage journey
For 20 years, the Solar & Energy Storage Summit has grown alongside the solar and storage sectors to become a key industry gathering for developers, IPPs, and investors. The new North American Power & Renewables Forum will continue to cover solar and storage markets in depth, while placing them in the broader context of North America and global power markets. As the audience expands, the solar and energy storage community will gain greater access to their utility and C&I customers, along with crucial interconnected intelligence across technologies and markets.
What’s new at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The expanded Forum will bring together leaders from across the power sector, including renewables, conventional generation, utilities, data centers, other commercial and industrial offtakers, and government, to examine the forces reshaping North America’s power market.
What will remain the same at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The Forum will continue to showcase the deeply researched data and insight from Wood Mackenzie’s interconnected intelligence. It will dive deep into technology and market issues that drive North America’s power mix to allow attendees to understand the root of the problem and different viewpoints on solutions.
