articles.title: The effects of oil supply shocks on corporate resilience, bank asset quality and lending
articles.text: The effects of oil supply shocks on corporate resilience, bank asset quality and lendingPrepared by Stephan Fahr, Emanuele Franceschi, Dejan Krusec and Cosimo PancaroPublished as part of the Financial Stability Review, November 2026.The global supply of oil was suddenly curtailed when the latest conflict in the Middle East broke out, resulting in higher and more volatile prices for the commodity. Around 20% of global supply has been hit by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic since March 2026.[1] Before the conflict broke out, the waterway handled around 20 mb/d of crude and petroleum products, accounting for roughly one-fifth of global oil supply (Oil Market Report, International Energy Agency, March 2026). In September 2026 the conflict also spread to Saudi infrastructure and Red Sea routes. As a result, oil prices have reached levels similar to those observed after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and their volatility has increased significantly. Against this background, this box investigates the impact of oil supply shocks on corporate resilience, bank asset quality and lending activity.Oil supply shocks can have substantial macroeconomic and financial repercussions affecting the resilience of non-financial firms, bank asset quality and lending. First, higher energy costs cause input costs to increase; if these additional costs are not passed on to customers, they compress firms’ margins, leading to higher corporate defaults and eventually to higher non-performing loans (NPLs) on banks’ books. Second, as the economy weakens after the shock materialises, banks might adjust lending volumes, credit standards and conditions, especially for corporates exposed to the oil shock, leading to adverse second-round effects.[2] During the Ukraine-related surge in energy prices, credit growth to energy-intensive sectors fell by around 9% relative to low intensity firms in the first quarter after the invasion. This was accompanied by higher interest rates charged on new loans, especially for riskier borrowers. See Framroze Møller, N. and Poeschl, J., “The effects of a large energy price shock on bank credit”, Working Paper Series, No 3260, ECB, 2026. Both of these effects can heighten financial stability risks, be it through weaker resilience among firms and banks or a reduced supply of finance to the real economy.The analysis in this box shows that oil supply shocks weaken corporate creditworthiness and lead to a lagged, gradual and prolonged deterioration in bank asset quality. The analysis first considers a structural vector autoregression (SVAR) including macroeconomic variables and sector-specific one-year ahead expected default frequencies (EDFs) as a proxy for probabilities of default.[3] The SVAR includes world oil production, oil prices and euro area macro variables to estimate the dynamic effects of oil supply shocks on the macroeconomy and on corporate EDFs from Moody’s KMV (a close, market-based proxy of probabilities of default). The shock identification relies on a Cholesky decomposition in which unexpected changes to global oil production are interpreted as global supply shocks, while shocks to global economic activity represent demand-side shocks, in line with Kilian, L., “Not All Oil Price Shocks Are Alike: Disentangling Demand and Supply Shocks in the Crude Oil Market”, American Economic Review, Vol. 99, No 3, June 2009, pp. 1053-1069. A 1 standard deviation negative shock to oil supply is found to raise aggregate corporate EDFs significantly, peaking four quarters after the shock (Chart A, panel a). The impact differs substantially across sectors, with the trade and transport sectors being the most severely affected.[4] Aggregate EDF increases by 4 basis points (from a level of 0.26% at the end of 2025). The trade and transport sectors see their EDFs increase by 12 basis points after four quarters and 20 basis points after two quarters respectively. The analysis also shows that the same negative shock leads to a gradual but significant increase in the average NPL ratio across banks, using local projections and bank-level data (Chart A, panel b).[5] The identified oil supply shock in the NPL analysis follows Gazzani, A., Venditti, F. and Veronese, G., “Oil price shocks in real time”, Journal of Monetary Economics, Vol. 144, May 2024. The authors estimate a sign- and narrative-restricted SVAR at high frequency and decompose oil movements into future and current demand, and supply. The panel local projections are estimated with bank-level controls and lags of the shock. The specification also includes dummies for the pandemic period and bank-level fixed effects, with Newey-West standard errors. The total cumulative effect would add 64 basis points after three years, up from 2.81% at the beginning of 2026. Commentary

Trump, Xi, and Putin: What to expect from the APEC summit

Jonathan A. Czin,

Jonathan A. Czin

Russian artist Alexey Sergienko's new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" sits at his gallery in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026. (Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images)

21 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Question 1
The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting will take place in Shenzhen, China, on November 18-19, 2026. With another interaction likely between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on the margins of this summit, what are the major outcomes expected? What will the two leaders seek to accomplish with their third interaction of this calendar year? Can meaningful U.S.-China progress be achieved on artificial intelligence (AI), trade, and other security issues?

Back to top

Kyle Chan

Starting small on AI risks

AI is an increasingly central issue in the U.S.-China relationship. Both countries see AI as a powerful, strategic technology with the potential to reshape geopolitics and the global economy. Both countries also increasingly see AI not just as an opportunity but also as a growing source of risk that needs to be managed. Chinese and American AI models have both been misused to carry out cyberattacks or have acted far beyond the intentions of human users.
On the sidelines of APEC, the United States and China have a chance to begin the long, uncertain road to jointly mitigating these risks. The first step is to establish an incident notification mechanism, which both sides have agreed to in principle. The goal should be to develop not a rigid protocol for comprehensive disclosure but an open communication channel through which each side can share nonsensitive technical information as they feel comfortable. Such information might include which AI models or harnesses were involved, how these tools were misused or misbehaved, and what safeguards or corrective measures proved effective.
In general, expectations for U.S.-China discussions about AI should remain low, and the focus should be on selective communication. Many worry that the United States and China will move too slowly in the face of growing AI risks and rapid improvements in capabilities. But equally worrying is the risk that official U.S.-China AI talks might get derailed at the outset as mounting expectations collide with deep mutual distrust between the two countries. Starting to share limited information at a pace and level that each side feels is appropriate will be a critical early step toward potential future progress on addressing AI risks.

Back to top

Jonathan A. Czin

All thunder, no rain

“All thunder, no rain.” This Chinese aphorism has been an apt description of the last two summits between Trump and Xi—and thus far, it seems likely to apply to this next summit as well. For a long time, in the run-up to such meetings, U.S. diplomats and policymakers would “trade optics for substance”—making concessions to China on protocol in exchange for substantive concessions. Now, both sides appear content to prioritize optics over any substance. The result is pantomime diplomacy.
Theoretically, there is much for the two leaders to discuss—everything from the risks of AI to global hotspots—but it seems more likely than not that these two leaders will miss the moment, again. Instead of engaging constructively, Beijing is capitalizing on its tactical truce with Washington to fortify itself at home and intensify pressure on U.S. allies in the region. Notably, the day after Trump and Xi’s last summit, China’s Southern Theater Command announced a military exercise around Scarborough Shoal—a disputed feature in the South China Sea claimed by both China and the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally. Tellingly, the move elicited no discernible response from Washington, though the American ambassador to the Philippines did protest.
Xi is likely already looking past Trump and thinking about how the fallout from the U.S. midterm election will affect China policy in the next administration—and whether the United States will revert to a more competitive posture toward China. Xi will host Trump fresh from a major Chinese Communist Party meeting, which fortified Xi’s iron grip on the party and laid the groundwork for his next five-year term, which will begin late next year. Xi’s goal in the meantime remains to do as little as possible to mollify Trump.
The bigger question right now is what will backstop the bilateral relationship in the coming year. The two leaders are supposed to meet one more time in December on the margins of the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, but after that, no meetings are scheduled. And Xi will be increasingly preoccupied with the preparations for next year’s Party Congress as we approach the second half of the year, which will limit his time and bandwidth for another engagement with Trump. In the absence of direct engagement by the top leaders, it remains an open question which force prevails: the inertia of Trump and Xi’s gentleman’s agreement to halt the trade war, or the entropy of the two superpowers’ competitive dynamic.

Back to top

Ryan Hass

Staying the course

Typically, when the leaders of the United States and China meet, it is a major global news event. The planned meeting between Trump and Xi on the margins of APEC may be an exception. The meeting will occur in the aftermath of a resounding reckoning for Trump in the U.S. midterm elections and in the shadow of an expected trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This will be the third in-person encounter between Trump and Xi of the calendar year. Neither side is preparing ambitious deliverables for this meeting.
Even so, the two leaders will have plenty to discuss. The headline issue will be whether the two leaders agree to extend their trade truce past its current deadline in January. Since Trump and Xi plan to meet again on the margins of the G20 this December in Florida, they may not feel pressure to finalize any trade truce extension at APEC.
The two leaders will be expected to endorse progress on institutionalizing coordination on AI, including through the launch of a bilateral AI dialogue and a bilateral incident reporting channel. Efforts in this space will likely be more focused on agenda-setting and establishing processes and expectations than on any breakthroughs or major deliverables.
Trump and Xi may also use their meeting to announce progress on strengthening military crisis communication, including in the nuclear domain.
The Chinese side likely will use the meeting to amplify the shared definition both leaders have endorsed for the relationship: constructive strategic stability based on fairness, reciprocity, and mutual respect. Beijing values this shared definition as a symbol of both leaders’ investment in preserving bilateral stability and avoiding crises. Although Trump has shown less enthusiasm for the definition, he similarly appears to value keeping the U.S.-China relationship on a relatively stable track for the foreseeable future.
This will be the second consecutive year when Trump will meet Xi on the margins of the APEC economic leaders meeting. Last year, Trump never set foot in the venue where the APEC economic leaders meeting was held. It would not be surprising if Trump skips the summit proceedings this year as well. Trump’s focus will be on meeting other leaders on the summit’s margins, as opposed to the details of the summit meeting itself.

Back to top

Constanze Stelzenmüller

Europe has a stake in the Trump-Xi summit

Not being Pacific Rim nations, the countries of Europe do not have a seat at the table at the APEC meetings. (Despite its Pacific territories of French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and Clipperton Island, France is not a member.) Yet they will be watching the discussions in Shenzhen with sharp interest. Europe and China’s relationship has undergone drastic change recently, driven not least by Berlin’s volte-face on China trade; the German analyst Thorsten Benner even calls it a second Zeitenwende (historic turn) following the first one on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Despite Germany’s exploding trade deficit with China and growing concern about China’s aggressive behavior in Europe and its support for Russia against Ukraine, Berlin had long opposed tougher trade measures by the European Union (EU). But in early October, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, together with French President Emmanuel Macron, wrote a strongly worded letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to demand the commission’s decisive action against unfair trade practices, as well as a new EU instrument to counter coercion. It gave the bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčović, decisive backing for a trip to Beijing last month. The trade chief managed to avert a full-blown trade war by getting China to agree to restrictions on hybrid car exports.
But as Benner points out, this is only “the beginning of a long, arduous, and risky path to strengthen German and European industry vis-à-vis China.” To work, he argues, it must be flanked by vigorous investment and innovation at home, and a resilient network of partnerships in Asia. Hence, a recent flurry of European leaders traveling to Asia—in the second half of October, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk went to India and Vietnam, while Merz traveled to Singapore, Japan, and South Korea. The larger backdrop for these trips is a massive EU drive for diversification of its Asian partnerships since the Russian invasion—accompanied by a substantive shift from trade, market access, and development to geopolitics, security, and economic resilience. New negotiations were begun with: Singapore (concluded May 2025), Indonesia (concluded September 2025), India (concluded January 2026) and the Philippines (concluded September 2026); negotiations that had been paused for more than a decade were resumed with Thailand (September 2023) and Malaysia (January 2025).
Watching Shenzhen, Europeans will hope for a stabilization of the U.S.-China economic relationship that could benefit them as well. But they also fear a bilateral bargain that redirects Chinese overcapacity to Europe—or one that presumes to set international trade rules for the rest of the world.

Back to top

Yun Sun

The real work happens below the summit

Compared to Trump and Xi’s Beijing summit in May and Washington summit in September, the APEC summit in Shenzhen will be a multilateral occasion. Any potential side meeting between Trump and Xi will be significantly shorter in duration, which means any negotiations over concrete issues will also be limited. Before the Washington summit, it was announced that the two countries’ trade truce would be extended by two months until January 2027. This also alleviates the pressure on the two presidents to deliver major outcomes during their potential bilateral meeting in Shenzhen.
In terms of military security, the two countries have made considerable progress this year. For example, both countries participated in the Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defense Conference in Canada in late August to early September, where U.S. Pacific Command chief Admiral Samuel Paparo met with the Chinese General Yang Zhibin, the commander of China’s Eastern Theater Command. References to a memorandum of understanding on crisis prevention and communication were also made during the Washington summit. More military-to-military communications could be in the pipeline for 2027. As such, another leadership summit at APEC will be politically significant, and concrete deliverables and meaningful progress on functional issues are more likely to be generated at the working level.

Question 2
There is speculation of a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin on the margins of the APEC summit. What are the implications of this meeting if it occurs? Will it impact the future trajectory of the Russia-Ukraine war? What message will it send to America’s erstwhile allies and partners?

Back to top

Jonathan A. Czin

A three-way meeting with two winners

It is difficult to envisage a scenario in which a meeting among Trump, Xi, and Putin has a happy outcome for the United States and its interests. The visual from such a meeting alone would be an unsettling imitation of the “Big Three” meeting at Yalta in the midst of World War II. Although this meeting will be more photo op than substance, like the original Yalta, this meeting could pave the way for a carving up of Eastern Europe to accommodate Russian interests. That is a worst-case and perhaps unlikely scenario. But if these three men emerge elated from this meeting, it would likely bode ill for Ukraine—and more importantly, for European security. Last century, an America buffered by two oceans had to learn the hard way that its interests are in fact bound up with the security of Europe and East Asia—yet we seem to periodically need a remedial reeducation in the realities of geopolitics.
Alternatively, if each of these men finds himself frustrated, that is also a potentially dangerous outcome. Acrimony among heads of state is no mere spat—a personal contretemps can have enduring and dangerous consequences, inflaming rather than assuaging the many points of tension and divergence between these leaders.
While Xi and Putin are more likely to humor than to humiliate Trump, even that outcome is a poor one for the United States. It will bait Trump further down his current path of trying to conciliate rather than counter these two strongmen. And, ironically, Trump’s very willingness to participate in such a meeting with so little time to prepare will only make his nominal objective of ending the war in Ukraine even more elusive. Trump has already demonstrated that he has little appetite or wherewithal to avail himself of the leverage he might have over either leader if he were to work in tandem with American allies and partners. And both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage—and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months. That is a pittance for two leaders who can measure their tenures in decades, not years. Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.

Back to top

Ryan Hass

More downside risk than upside potential for the U.S.

The risk/reward calculation for all three leaders is different.
For Russia, this meeting offers major upside. By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognized as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah. He will have achieved his return to the top table in global diplomacy without making any significant concessions on Ukraine or elsewhere.
For China, the meeting will be mixed. On the one hand, Xi will bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other. The meeting will highlight Xi’s statesmanship and China’s centrality in the international system. On the other hand, Beijing will bear the burden of setting an agenda, ensuring a productive exchange, and holding some responsibility for follow-through on any outcomes the meeting generates. Xi typically avoids owning responsibility for high-profile diplomatic events with uncertain outcomes, so this event will stretch the Chinese side’s comfort zone.
For Trump, the meeting will pose greater downside risks than upside potential. Trump will face the risk of being outmaneuvered by more prepared and more cunning leaders. In this triangle, the closest and warmest relationship among the three leaders is between Xi and Putin, who have met over 40 times since 2013 and share a desire to diminish American leadership on the world stage. The meeting’s optics will also send a chill to America’s allies and partners, who will fear Trump is prioritizing his relations with Xi and Putin over their interests and concerns. This chill will be felt most acutely in Ukraine and Taiwan.
Ultimately, symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting. It is unlikely that there will be any breakthroughs on Ukraine or on launching trilateral arms control efforts, Trump’s putative focus for this meeting. Beijing has long been unwilling to enter arms control negotiations until it is closer to reaching parity in nuclear capabilities with the United States and Russia. Beijing is concerned that doing so could lock China into a permanently subordinate position that could expose China to risk. At best, the three leaders could find common principles to endorse, such as maintaining open sea lines of communication, reaffirming that nuclear wars can never be won and should never be fought, and affirming an interest in an end to war in Ukraine, while leaving the terms of such an end ambiguous.

Back to top

Scott M. Moore

A once-unthinkable alignment

Much has been made of Trump’s apparent rapport with the leaders of Russia and China, long regarded as America’s foremost adversaries. But a trilateral summit with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen would go well beyond bonhomie. It would dramatically signal that Washington is prepared to trade the liberal international order it built after 1945 for a concert of authoritarian-nationalist great powers.
The White House has framed the meeting around the legitimate goal of advancing nuclear arms control. But the meeting has broader implications. Holding a three-way meeting with Russia, just as Moscow says it will resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, represents Ukraine’s worst fear: the image of the war being settled among great powers, over Kyiv’s head. Beijing, too, would benefit from being portrayed as a would-be peacemaker, rather than as an enabler for sustaining Russia’s war economy.
The summit may also preview a broader convergence of interests. The Wall Street Journal reports that the Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to run for U.N. secretary-general as a joint U.S.-Russia-China candidate. Meanwhile, Beijing reportedly considered a bid to host the 2028 U.N. climate conference, the annual meeting of parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, a treaty from which the United States will formally withdraw in February 2027. Washington is not merely leaving a gap in multilateral leadership. In the Orbán case, it appears to be working with Moscow and Beijing to reshape the multilateral system.
For America’s allies, the message is stark. A trilateral meeting in Shenzhen will reinforce European concerns that their security is negotiable. In Asia, partners such as Japan and Taiwan will wonder whether their own U.S. security commitments are up for negotiation. The result could be that many will hedge, toward Beijing, toward strategic autonomy, or both.
If the summit goes ahead, it will symbolize a once-unthinkable alignment between the United States and the world’s foremost authoritarian powers. It will also speed up the fracturing of Western alliances that Moscow and Beijing have long sought and make it even more difficult to tackle shared challenges and provide global public goods.

Back to top

Constanze Stelzenmüller

No decisions about Europe without Europe

At the time of writing, a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was still just a Russian proposal, confirmed by the United States but not by China. Even so, it precisely encapsulates what appears to be an emerging political dynamic: Moscow attempting to set a worldwide great-power agenda, Washington appearing to acquiesce, and Beijing hesitating to commit either way. And the mere suggestion of such a “21st-century Yalta”—a tripartite meeting that would presumably decide the future of Ukraine and Europe over the heads of both—has a symbolic impact of its own, even if it never comes to pass.
The timing of this push is significant. Russia, bogged down at Ukraine’s eastern front, is trying to bludgeon Ukrainian resilience with its relentless and indiscriminate bombardments of energy infrastructure and civilian targets, all while losing huge numbers of soldiers. At the same time, it is waging what The Economist calls “a phoney peace … a war of sorts”—increasingly reckless acts of sabotage, assassination attempts, and other dirty tricks—in Europe, in the hopes of undermining its will to defend Ukraine.
The Trump administration, for its part, has just been dealt devastating results in the U.S. midterm elections, with affordability and the unfinished war on Iran topping the list of voter grievances. All the more important, then, to end this other war in Europe, and, based on his recent actions, the president appears to believe that it is best brought to a conclusion by siding with Russia. Trump has praised Russia (“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”), authorized Russian-origin diesel purchases, waived the Graham Act sanctions, and—according to media reports—is considering relief for a Russian state investment fund which the Biden administration had sanctioned, calling it Putin’s “slush fund.”
But—as Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute, recently pointed out—Europe in 2026 is not the Europe of 1945, when Josef Stalin, Winston Churchill, and Franklin D. Roosevelt met to hash out the shape of the postwar continent. Protests and political differences notwithstanding, today’s Europe has arms, wealth, institutions, allies, and agency. There can be no lasting and legitimate settlement without Ukraine and Europe at the table. To signal otherwise would only cause yet more damage to the transatlantic alliance.

Back to top

Yun Sun

China wants the spotlight, not arms control

Russia has been the primary driver of a potential trilateral summit during APEC, with Moscow circulating the possibility as early as this past summer. The Chinese are not necessarily actively driving such a summit. However, if the United States and Russia clearly call for it, there are few reasons why China would not embrace such an event. In recent weeks, the United States has engaged in active Track 2 diplomacy and dialogue with China and Russia. The Chinese enthusiasm is obvious, despite the struggle over the deliverables and substance of such a summit. Some Chinese officials have suggested that some in China are viewing the trilateral summit as “the most significant meeting in the history of international relations since the end of World War II.” If it happens, China will be presenting itself as the peer of the United States and Russia and playing a pivotal role in U.S.-Russia relations at a historical moment to end the Ukraine war. That is not an opportunity that Beijing would like to miss. In addition, according to Chinese and Russian interlocutors, Russia has made a genuine plea for China to host the trilateral summit. Beijing will have to develop a really strong and convincing argument about why it would refuse to do its Russian partner a solid.
Beijing is likely concerned by Trump’s and Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s references to such a summit containing a trilateral dialogue on arms control and nuclear weapons. China has consistently rejected the concept of U.S.-China-Russia trilateral arms control and nuclear dialogue, citing its significantly smaller nuclear arsenal. The Chinese do not seem to see the Ukraine war as coming to an end so soon. By the time of the APEC summit, the U.S. midterm elections will already be over, and Trump will have lost the motivation to use peace in Ukraine to boost the Republican Party’s popularity. Therefore, a trilateral summit will be unlikely to end the war in Ukraine anyway.

articles.title: Operational resilience of the financial sector
articles.text:
Operational resilience of the financial sector

We make sure banks and financial services firms in the UK can overcome disruption

Related links

Co-ordinating the response to disruption of financial services

On this pageOverviewStrategic outcomesFirm-level outputsSystem-level outputs

Overview
Operational resilience is the ability of firms and the entire financial sector to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from and learn from disruptions.
Financial firms and financial market infrastructures (FMIs) must have robust plans to deliver important services, no matter the disruption. This includes man-made threats such as physical and cyberattacks, IT system outages and third-party supplier failure. It also includes natural hazards such as fire, flood, severe weather and pandemic. These can affect firms’ safety and soundness, undermine policyholder protection and, in some cases, affect financial stability.
The Bank of England and our Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) carry out this work with the UK's two other financial authorities: the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Our approach assumes that sometimes disruptions that prevent firms from operating as usual will occur and mean they cannot provide their services for a period.

External links

Operational Resilience - Financial Conduct Authority Opens in a new window
The National Cyber Security Centre Opens in a new window

Prudential and Resolution Policy Index related links

Banking - Operational resilience
Insurance - Operational resilience

Strategic outcomes

Build firms' resilience: when severe but plausible disruption occurs, it should not affect financial stability, safety and soundness or policyholder protection. Firms must ensure high standards of IT and cyber resilience, third-party dependency risks.
Build systemic operational resilience: firms and the Bank work to ensure that when systemic operational risks crystallise, they do not impact the UK's financial stability. Third parties must be sufficiently resilient to support this outcome. It is important that firms can contribute to sector-wide incident response and can learn and evolve from failures.
Manage risks: limit the likelihood and impact of losses. Firms must set aside capital so that the crystallisation of risks is unlikely to affect firm safety and soundness.

The following outputs are designed with these outcomes in mind:

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Firm-level outputs

Operational resilience policy
Our Financial Policy Committee (FPC) looks at the entire system. Our Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) and Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) focus on the firms and FMIs we regulate.
In summary, we ask firms to:

identify important business services: boards and senior management must prioritise services that, if disrupted, would affect our objectives and the public interest;
set impact tolerances: firms must say to what extent they could continue important business services after severe but plausible disruptions; and
make sure they can stay within impact tolerances: firms must map their important business services and test their capacity to continue to the agreed extent – they should address any vulnerabilities they have identified.

The operational resilience policy SS1/21 requires firms to prepare a written operational resilience self-assessment of compliance. The aim is to document a firms’ resilience journey, identifying risks that could prevent them from delivering important business services within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. It helps the firms’ boards and senior management make informed investment decisions to address resilience gaps.
We assess the status of a firm’s implementation of our policy. This includes reviewing:

their important business services, impact tolerances and additional metrics
scenario testing details, results and assurance that the firm can remain within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios
firms’ identification of risks, threats, and vulnerabilities through mapping, testing and live incidents
response and recovery actions, remediation plans and timelines

Self-assessments allow us to identify good practices at an individual firm level while also facilitating thematic comparisons, helping us build a clearer picture of the wider systemic operational resilience picture across the industry.
Incident management and reporting
The PRA has published a policy that details requirements for reporting certain operational incidents, and notification and reporting of material third-party arrangements. It sets out expectations for regulatory reporting, which aim to enhance the PRA’s understanding of firm and sector threats and vulnerabilities.

CP17/24 – Operational resilience: Operational incident and outsourcing and third-party reporting

Third-party management
The PRA’s current policy is set out primarily in Supervisory Statement (SS) 2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management, which was published in March 2021. The Bank has a near-identical set of policies for FMIs, such as clearing houses and payment systems.
Operational risk framework
Our role is to assess whether a firm's operational risk management framework allows them to effectively identify, assess, monitor, report and manage material operational risks to which it is or might be exposed, in line with board-approved strategy and risk appetite.
We are also responsible for assessing whether firms hold sufficient capital to mitigate the impact when operational risks crystallise.
This supports the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Rules, which require us to assess whether firms’ own funds and internal capital is adequate to cover the level of the risks to which it is or might be exposed and is reflective of the firm’s operational risk profile.
Cyber resilience
Firms and FMIs should assess their cyber risk and build adequate resilience capabilities to prepare for, and respond to, potentially disruptive cyber incidents. To maintain the financial sector's cyber resilience and to support our supervisory oversight, we have developed cyber assessment tools. They include CBEST, STAR-FS and CQUEST.
CBEST
This provides a framework for regulators to work with firms using a simulated cyberattack. This allows firms to explore how to counteract an attack on the people, processes and technology of cyber security controls. We base the simulated attacks on present threats.
The aim is to test:

a firm's defences
its threat intelligence capability
its ability to detect and respond to external and internal attackers

Firms use the assessment to plan how they can strengthen their resilience.
An accredited service provider carries out the simulation, acting within legal, ethical and moral constraints. It aims to get through a firm's defences using the cyber kill chain. They also assess if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and processes that deliver a firm's important business services can be compromised.

CBEST Threat Intelligence-Led Assessments

CBEST thematic review
The annual CBEST thematic is intended to inform the sector on the findings and lessons learned from our CBEST programme, which assesses the cyber resilience of key financial institutions through security testing performed in ‘live’ corporate environments.

2023 CBEST thematic findings
2024 CBEST thematic findings
2025 CBEST thematic findings

STAR-FS
STAR-FS (simulated targeted attack and response assessments for financial services) is part of the PRA and FCA supervisory toolkit, to assess the cyber resilience of firms' important business services. This allows regulators and firms to better understand vulnerabilities and take remedial actions, thereby improving their resilience and, by extension, the wider financial system.
It promotes a threat-led penetration testing approach that mimics the actions of actors' intent on compromising an organisation's important business services as well as the technology assets and people supporting them.
An implementation guide and supporting templates are available. If your firm is interested in conducting a STAR-FS please contact your supervisor. It aims to provide:

an outcome-based assessment of financial institutions' protection, detection and response technical capabilities against cyber-attacks;
an approach, conducted through a firm-led delivery model, that can identify cyber resilience vulnerabilities within systems, people and processes;
reduced regulatory and firm effort relative to other supervisory technical assessments such as CBEST;
levels of independent technical assurance beyond those ordinarily included in firms' own penetration testing programmes; and
a testing approach accessible by a larger number of financial institutions to experience and learn from.

STAR-FS Implementation guide – Threat Intelligence Led Penetration Testing for Financial Services (PDF 2.1MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Scope Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Targeting Report Specification (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Report Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Penetration Test Report Specification (PDF 1.4MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Remediation Plan Template (PDF 0.8MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Regulator Summary (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Maturity Assessment Guide (PDF 1.3MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Detection & Response Assessment Guide (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window

CQUEST
We use the CQUEST (Cyber resilience questionnaire) to gauge the cyber risk and resilience capabilities of the sector. Firms can also use it as a self-assessment tool to consider their own cyber risk and resilience maturity. It comprises 50 questions with multiple-choice answers across six domains:

governance and leadership
identify
protect
detect
respond
recover

To achieve a reliable outcome, an organisation should identify and direct a competent party with appropriate knowledge of the business to complete the CQUEST. When it is used to inform regulatory activities, supervisors might provide additional guidance and/or they could request evidence or clarifying information in response to the answers.
The latest version of CQUEST builds upon the previous one, and encompasses lessons learned from good practice frameworks and feedback from supervisors and firms.

Download the CQUEST

System-level outputs

Collective action and incident response
The Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) leads sector-wide collective action on operational resilience. It comprises about 25 members: firms across retail, wholesale, FMIs, insurance, the financial authorities and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its co-chairs are senior executives of the PRA and UK Finance.
CMORG has three core objectives:

identify risks to the resilience of the financial sector.
develop solutions to improve the operational resilience of the sector.
share knowledge

Industry has developed CMORG-endorsed capabilities (including good practice guidance, response frameworks and contingency tools) to support the operational resilience of the UK's financial sector. The financial authorities support the development of these capabilities and efforts to improve resilience. However, their use is optional and they do not constitute regulatory rules or supervisory expectations. As such, they may not necessarily represent formal endorsement by the authorities.
Specialist subgroups support CMORG. They design, manage and deliver operational resilience improvements for the sector. Their work is voluntary. Their chairs meet regularly to discuss CMORG's activities and identify areas for more collaboration. A project management office (PMO) also supports CMORG. It is jointly resourced by us and UK Finance.

Find out more about CMORG Opens in a new window

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC) is a CMORG-led partnership. It aims to help identify, investigate and co-ordinate the response to incidents that may have consequences for the financial sector. It analyses and distributes information to produce timely outputs for the sector's benefit.

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC)

What happens if there is a disruption?
Firms should get in touch with their usual business or supervisory contacts at the Bank or the FCA. The sector's response is facilitated by the Sector Response Framework (SRF). It sets out how organisations across the sector and government are connected. It also explains how they may respond to incidents when the impact becomes broader than a single firm or FMI and requires co-ordination, information-sharing or collective action.
Its purpose is to:

allow firms, FMIs and the sector to make collective, timely and informed decisions in response to incidents
provide a reference to good practice, contingency tools and plans, which may be invoked as part of a sector response
include decision makers and subject matter experts
be organised on a modular basis, so that components of the SRF can respond
be recognised by the financial authorities as the principal structure by which the sector will respond to incidents
support collaborative engagement between the sector and the UK's financial authorities (see below)
be able to engage with frameworks in other jurisdictions, if required

The UK's three financial authorities are the Bank (including the PRA), the FCA and the Treasury. If disruptions could affect the whole sector, these authorities act together.

Find out about how we co-ordinate our response to the disruption of financial services

Sector exercising
The Bank works with the sector to co-ordinate and deliver exercises to strengthen the operational resilience of the UK's financial system.
The most prominent is SIMEX – a biennial, market-wide simulation conducted through a public-private partnership between industry participants and financial authorities. SIMEX performs a unique role in bringing the sector together to address the most challenging and complex risks that individual firms cannot manage alone.
These sector-wide exercises are based on our collective approach to resilience, working together with industry to identify emerging risks and build capabilities to enhance the system’s overall resilience.

SIMEX 24 – A major market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption
SIMEX 22 – A two-day market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption

Critical third-party oversight
The Bank, the PRA and the FCA (the regulators) are responsible for overseeing critical third parties (CTPs) to the UK's financial sector, following their designation by HMT.
Regulated firms and FMIs are increasingly dependent on a small number of third parties for the delivery of functions and services that are essential to the stability of, or confidence in, the UK's financial system. In some cases, third parties can become so critical that no single firm can adequately monitor or manage the systemic risks they pose.
The aim of oversight is to reduce systemic risks arising from the failure of, or disruption to the systemic services they provide to firms. The regulators will assess CTPs against outcomes-focused rules and expectations with the aim of ensuring the systemic services CTPs provide to the financial sector are resilient and therefore any failure of, or disruption to, those services does not threaten the stability of the UK's financial system.
The CTP regime complements, and does not replace, the existing requirements and expectations for firms on SS1/21 operational resilience and SS2/21 outsourcing and third-party risk management policy.

SS6/24 – Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
PS16/24 – Operational resilience: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
Approach to the oversight of critical third parties

Find out more about the CTP regime:

Critical Third Parties

Cyber and operational resilience stress test (CORST)
The cyber and operational resilience stress test (formerly the Cyber Stress Test or 'CST') is a key part of the Bank’s toolkit on macroprudential operational resilience. The outcomes of cyber and operational resilience stress testing inform the FPC's monitoring of sector operational resilience and its articulation of its tolerance for disruption to vital services. The objectives of testing are to:

provide insight into sector vulnerabilities and the financial stability impacts and residual risk of severe but plausible operational disruption to vital services
explore firm and sector capabilities to respond to, and recover from operational disruption, and to mitigate its impact on financial stability
share lessons to support firms in maturing their approach to operational resilience and financial stability, including firms' roles as systemic risk managers

We invite firms to participate in CORST on a voluntary basis and they identify their own lessons and remediation actions. Actions that require cross-firm co-operation are often progressed through established collective action forums or voluntary groups.
The test aims, over time to explore all systemically important firms and provide insight into not just the impacts of disruption to the services they provide, but also the impacts to their customer firms and from their third parties. Participation may be direct, indirect through co-operation with a direct participant, or through engagement at cross-firm workshops.
The CST24 thematic letter, which provides thematic findings from the 2024 test, also provides resources to support firms’ role in mitigating potential financial stability impacts of disruption to their services.

Thematic findings from the 2024 cyber stress test
Thematic findings from the 2022 cyber stress test

FPC impact tolerance for financial stability
The FPC updated its impact tolerance for payments and settlements after CST22. This was published in the March 2023 FPC Record:

it expected the financial system to be able to complete critical payments by the end of the value date in severe but plausible scenarios; timely recovery of service delivery was the first best way firms could prevent adverse material economic impacts;
in such instances where restoring services would be harmful for financial stability, or impossible, alternative mitigating actions might be appropriate; firms should, therefore plan, prepare and test for such situations and invest so that their response could effectively mitigate any impact on financial stability until service delivery was restored; and
an example of mitigation may be providing an overdraft to a retail Banking customer, so that they can still make purchases, despite a disruption to the payment systems which may have prevented the normal 'payment' being completed

Financial Policy Summary and Record – March 2023 (see paragraphs 101-108)

In Financial Stability in Focus (FSIF), the FPC noted it would regularly review the operational resilience policy toolkit and will explore ways to continue to build system-wide resilience to operational disruption.
In addition to the tools mentioned above, the FPC does this, for example, through:

assessing potential system-wide gaps in, or risks to, operational resilience which are not adequately covered by firm-level or microprudential policies
considering whether to set impact tolerances for additional vital services beyond payments.

The committee has published its macroprudential approach to operational resilience in FSIF and sets out its priorities twice a year in its Financial Stability Report.

Financial Stability in Focus: the FPC’s macroprudential approach to operational resilience

articles.title: Managing our Environmental Impact
articles.text:
Managing our Environmental Impact. Our Commitment. Our Targets. Our Progress.

Man Group is committed to reducing its absolute carbon footprint and to being consistent and transparent about the progress we are making. As a key part of our Corporate Sustainability strategy, you can read more about how we manage our environmental impact in our Corporate Sustainability Brochure.

We continue to implement changes to our operations to ensure we are on track to meet our emissions reduction target set for 2026 and are on the strategic pathway to net zero carbon in our global workplaces by 2030.

Environmental Policy

Our Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement focuses on: using natural resources responsibly; minimising the environmental impact of our activities through maximising energy efficiency; reducing greenhouse gas emissions and; recycling and / or minimising waste. We also commit to at least annual reporting of our environmental targets, data and any issues we encounter. In 2024, we achieved ISO 14001:2018 for our London office.

Board Oversight of Environmental Matters

Our Man Group Board has responsibility for Man Group's environmental impact and ensures that Man’s Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement is implemented and reviewed. The Board has a collective role in providing environmental leadership throughout Man's global operations and is committed to continual improvement in environmental performance.

Environmental Risk Management

Man Group considers operational climate risks 15+ years into the future. It does this through multi-disciplinary company-wide risk identification, assessment and management processes. The types of risks considered include current and emerging regulation, technological changes and upgrades, market risks, reputational risks, acute and chronic physical operational impacts as well as upstream and downstream risks.

Green Buildings

Minimising our environmental impact is at the centre of our real estate strategy. We occupy eight buildings certified by LEED (Leadership in Energy Efficiency and Design), one by Energy Star and one by NABERS (National Australian Built Environment Rating System), accounting for 92% of our global headcount. Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House (RBH) in London, has a Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM) ‘Excellent’ rating.

Riverbank House - London

Riverbank House is rated “Excellent” via the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM). The building has a green roof, rainwater harvesting and solar power generation.

Pfäffikon - Switzerland

Our Pfäffikon office is a short walk from Lake Zurich and is powered by renewable hydro-electric energy.

Environmental data compilation systems

We strive to deliver clear and transparent reporting that captures the measurable elements within our control. We monitor and track our global environmental impact using specialist specialist tracking software and an energy services consultancy which help us to mitigate risk, maximise opportunities and reduce our carbon footprint.

Responsible Procurement

Man Group’s offices procure goods and services that are in line with our environmental objectives. We utilise ISO standards and ratings systems (such as energy star for IT equipment and green star for paper supplies) to assist us in choosing sustainable products. We also ensure all our equipment complies with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances EU Directive.

Man Group’s Supplier Code of Conduct

As a condition of supplying services to Man Group, our suppliers are directed to adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct. This code outlines the minimum standards Man Group expects of its suppliers, regarding economic activity, impact on the environment, as well as engagement with wider communities.

Man Group intends to lead by example, and we endeavour to work closely with our suppliers to rise to the opportunity of addressing the global, social and environmental challenges that we all currently face.

Environmental Improvements

Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House, is continually assessed for energy and air-conditioning efficiency. The recommendations inform our investments.

During 2024, we achieved ISO14001:2018 for our Riverbank House office.

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)

Man Group is a supporter and signatory of the TCFD, and is committed to taking action against climate change. The Board oversees the development of our climate-related financial disclosures which cover governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, as described in our Annual Report.

Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

Man Group is a signatory to the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, the European membership body for investor collaboration on climate change.

UN Global Compact

We are also proud, active signatories of the UN Global Compact, supporting the Ten Principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption.

Environmental Training and Awareness

Environmental awareness campaigns are run in offices focusing on areas such as increasing recycling, reducing energy use, cycling to work and removing single use plastics.

We have run a number of sustainable volunteering activities across our offices including litter pick-ups, local garden and park maintenance as well as educational awareness events.

In 2025, we met all of our targets as set out in our Annual Report.

articles.title: Navigating volatility in 2027 with inflation-linked bonds
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | ARTICLE – 6 min read
Navigating volatility in 2027 with inflation-linked bonds

By
CEDRIC SCHOLTES, ELIDA RHENALS 19.11.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Inflation volatility: A structural shift?How do inflation-linked bonds work?Real yields and relative returnsTaking a global approachNavigating inflation and interest-rate risksWhat does this mean for investors?

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Cedric Scholtes, Head of Investment Team, Global Sovereign Inflation and Rates and Elida Rhenals, Senior Portfolio Manager and Co-Head of Inflation

Geopolitical and economic shocks have made inflation less predictable, strengthening the case for inflation-linked bonds

Higher real yields can provide a stronger buffer and more attractive entry points for inflation-linked bonds than in previous years

A diversified, active approach is essential to navigate changing inflation dynamics and managing interest-rate sensitivity across different markets

A series of inflationary shocks have buffeted the global economy in recent years – from pandemic-related shutdowns, followed by massive fiscal stimulus intended to protect firms and households, to wars in Ukraine and Iran, to tariffs, and most recently the artificial intelligence capex boom. Central banks have had the unenviable task of responding to these supply and demand shocks, having to judge their magnitude and persistence to calibrate policy rates.

Despite inflation having remained well above central bank targets for several years, investors have not seemed overly concerned about central banks’ willingness or ability to tackle inflation.

But geopolitical tensions, trade wars, energy insecurity, supply chain disruptions and rising investment in infrastructure and AI are reshaping the inflation outlook.

As we look to 2027, we believe that rather than assuming there will be a return to the relative price stability of the pre-pandemic decade, investors may need to prepare for a world in which inflation might be more elevated, but will also almost certainly be more volatile, less predictable, with a broader range of possible outcomes.

Inflation volatility: A structural shift?

For investors, a more volatile inflationary backdrop changes the way inflation protection should be considered. We believe it strengthens the case for inflation-linked bonds, especially now that real yields (returns adjusted for inflation) have normalised from pre-pandemic levels. Rather than a tactical response to the next inflation release, inflation-linked bonds can serve as a structural component of a fixed income or multi-asset portfolio.

Importantly, valuations of inflation-linked bonds have also become more attractive. Real yields derived from inflation-linked bonds are now significantly higher than during much of the past two decades, providing a significant buffer in case central banks need to tighten policy further than is currently priced. Exhibit 1 shows developments in generic 10-year real yields for the key US, UK, France and Italian inflation-linked bond markets.

How do inflation-linked bonds work?

Unlike conventional bonds, inflation-linked bonds have cash flows that are adjusted in line with realised inflation, in order to protect the investor’s purchasing power. Their principal and coupon payments are linked to an inflation index, providing compensation for changes in prices over the life of the bond.

However, investors should be aware that inflation-linked bonds do not always rise in value whenever inflation increases. Their mark-to-market performance depends on three main drivers:

Real coupon income: Like conventional bonds, inflation-linked bonds generate income through the periodic payout of (inflation-adjusted) coupons

Inflation accretion: An inflation-linked bond’s principal payout moves in line with the underlying Consumer Price Index, and in most cases with a floor at the bond’s original face value. As a bond ages, it accrues inflation via a formulaic uprating of the principal paid out at maturity (but which increases the bond’s market value immediately)

Duration impact: Like conventional bonds, inflation-linked bond prices are sensitive to fluctuations in yields. The magnitude of these movements depends on the bond’s duration, or sensitivity to yield changes. They tend to outperform conventional bonds when investors perceive inflation risk is rising, reflected in a widening of the spread between nominal and real yields on bonds of comparable maturity (the so-called breakeven inflation spread)

A common critique of inflation-linked bonds is that an investor who holds a 10-year bond through a period of elevated inflation may end up gaining less from inflation accretion than they lose on duration when the central bank tightens policy to combat the rise in inflation. This explains why investors looking for inflation protection have in recent years focused on short-dated inflation-linked bond funds.

Real yields and relative returns

However, the analysis is incomplete for a couple of reasons. First, starting yields matter. Today’s higher yields provide a much larger buffer against rising yields, especially if some monetary policy tightening is already priced in.

Second, most investors already own duration elsewhere in their fixed income allocations, but holding real yields could potentially be the better choice when faced with an inflation scare that initially pushes breakevens wider and then allows the investor to collect that inflation.

For some investors then, relative return, not absolute return, is the focus. By way of example, the Bloomberg one-to-30-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) index outperformed its maturity-matched comparator Treasury index by 12.6% in total return terms between 1 January 2020 and 12 December 2024, a period that covered the pandemic inflation, Ukraine war and a full Federal Reserve hiking cycle.1

This outperformance was achieved despite the rise in breakevens being temporary, and the central bank moving policy into restrictive territory, with inflation-linked bonds accreting the unanticipated rise in the CPI index.

So, for investors with a fixed duration allocation, the role of inflation-linked bonds in a portfolio is really to aim to provide diversification in the near term (when real yields diverge from nominal yields), and long-term insurance against inflation shocks (via the gradual process of inflation accretion).

Aiming for this insurance is most valuable when inflation episodes are likely to be more frequent than has been the case in the last three decades, and when the cost of the insurance (reflected in breakeven inflation rates) remains low.

With breakeven inflation rates at around 2.0 to 2.4% in the eurozone and US, the hurdle will not be hard to clear if the global economy continues to be subjected to supply shocks.

Investors looking to gain protection against inflation surprises therefore need to ask themselves two questions: which markets should they focus on and how much interest rate sensitivity should they take on.

Taking a global approach

Inflation may be a global phenomenon, but it does not evolve uniformly across countries.

The US, eurozone and UK can experience different inflation dynamics and monetary policy cycles. As a result, opportunities in inflation-linked bonds can shift between markets over time.

For example, US TIPS were attractive during 2025’s ‘Liberation Day’ tariff announcements, while 2026’s Iran-related energy shock shifted attention towards Europe and UK inflation-linked bonds. A global investment universe therefore offers access to a broader range of opportunities and allows investors to diversify their sources of inflation exposure rather than relying on a single market.

Navigating inflation and interest-rate risks

Choosing the right market is only part of the challenge. Investors must also consider maturity, duration and the inflation expectations already reflected in bond prices.

Passive inflation-linked bond indices are typically weighted according to outstanding issuance or market capitalisation. This does not necessarily provide the most attractive investment exposure and can result in significant interest-rate sensitivity. UK inflation linked bonds, for example, make an outsized contribution, both in terms of weight and duration, to global inflation-linked indices.

The soaring inflation and sharp increase in interest rates witnessed in 2022 illustrates why duration matters. Investors seeking inflation protection may not want to assume substantial exposure to the interest rate risks associated with longer-maturity bonds during periods when central banks are aggressively tightening policy.

In these circumstances, investors may favour the shorter end of the yield curve, seeking to capture inflation exposure while limiting some of the volatility associated with longer-duration bonds.

An actively managed approach allows portfolio managers to adjust exposure across countries and maturities, manage real-yield sensitivity and assess whether market inflation expectations offer attractive value.

The objective is to identify where investors are being best compensated for the risks they assume, rather than simply replicating the composition of the inflation-linked bond market.

What does this mean for investors?

The case for inflation-linked bonds rests on three considerations:

Inflation protection beyond short-term market movements: A more unpredictable inflation environment supports considering inflation-linked bonds as a structural portfolio allocation rather than a tactical trade

More attractive real yields: Investors can now combine seeking inflation protection with positive real yields, unlike during much of the previous decade

Greater scope for selective positioning: A global, actively managed approach can help investors navigate differences in inflation expectations, real yields and duration across markets

With inflation outcomes becoming less predictable, the question for investors is no longer simply when to seek inflation protection, but how best to incorporate it into their long-term allocation.

[1] Bloomberg.

For the last few months, taxes have been the talk of Hong Kong’s financial sector. Mainland residents had until October 22 to declare and pay sometimes years of back taxes on their offshore trusts, vehicles company founders have long used in part to shield holdings in offshore-listed firms—at least until the government declared them subject to tax after all.Last week, the State Taxation Administration said the crackdown had led to the declaration of more than RMB160bn in income taxes, of which at least RMB120bn was paid in October.
