articles.title: Europe’s Natural Gas Outlook for the Upcoming Winter 2026/2027
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 20, 2026
Europe’s Natural Gas Outlook for the Upcoming Winter 2026/2027
Johannes Fleck1
Europe is entering the 2026–27 winter with unusually low natural gas inventories. At the end of September 2026, gas storage in the EU was about 72 percent full, the lowest fill rate for that month since EU-wide data are available (from 2011) and about 11 percentage points below last September. Germany's inventories were especially low, at 58 percent full (Figure 1).2 The low inventories coincide with a tighter global market for liquefied natural gas (LNG) as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted LNG shipments from Qatar through the Strait of Hormuz (IEA, 2026b); European wholesale gas prices have more than doubled since February.3 These developments have raised concerns about whether Europe's gas supply will last through the upcoming winter.

Figure 1. Natural Gas Storage in the EU and in Germany

Note: Natural gas in storage as a percent of working gas capacity, for the EU (left) and Germany (right). The shaded band shows the range of the years 2011 to 2021, the gray lines, from light dotted to dark solid, the years 2022 to 2025 and the red line 2026, through October 8.

Source: Gas Infrastructure Europe, AGSI+, via Haver Analytics.

Accessible version

Against this backdrop, this note considers under what conditions Europe could face gas shortages during the 2026–27 winter. Following the analysis in Rua (2023) of Europe's energy position ahead of the 2023–24 winter, this note projects EU gas inventories through June 2027, under a Baseline and two adverse scenarios. The projections suggest that Europe can get through an average winter without running out of gas, and through a harsh winter too, albeit with stocks lower than it has tolerated in the past. However, a notable decline in LNG imports would leave storage nearly empty by the spring.

Projecting inventories requires assumptions about inflows from abroad, domestic production, and consumption, and all three now look very different from before Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The note therefore first documents how these flows have changed since 2021, using monthly data on the EU's imports by country of origin and on gas consumption, and drawing on companion work on the structural decline in gas demand.4

Inflows: Norway and LNG have replaced Russian pipeline gas

Russian gas has largely disappeared from Europe's supply. Imports from Russia fell from about 158 billion cubic meters (bcm) in 2021 to 40 bcm in 2025, or from 44 percent to 13 percent of the EU's imports from outside the EU (Figure 2).5 Since the transit contract through Ukraine expired at the end of 2024, Russian pipeline gas has reached the EU only through TurkStream (Sharples, 2025), and more than half of the remaining Russian gas arrives as LNG, which the EU has banned under short-term contracts since April 2026 and will ban under the remaining long-term contracts from January 2027.6 Norway has replaced Russia as the largest supplier of natural gas to the EU while production within the EU has fallen by 13 bcm between 2021 and 2025, mainly because the Netherlands wound down and closed the Groningen field.

Figure 2. Natural Gas Production and Imports in the EU, by Origin

Note: Imports of the 27 EU member states from outside the EU, estimated from the monthly imports that member states report, plus EU production; the United Kingdom is treated as a non-EU country in all years. Transit countries are reassigned to the country of origin. Percentages above the bars give LNG's share of imports. Other pipeline suppliers are Algeria, Azerbaijan, Libya, the United Kingdom and unreported origins; other LNG suppliers are Nigeria and smaller sources. Poland's production, confidential since October 2023, is estimated from its annual figures. The last bar covers January to July 2026. Key identifies in order from top to bottom.

Source: Eurostat (nrg_ti_gasm, nrg_ti_gas, nrg_cb_gasm, nrg_bal_c); author's calculations.

Accessible version

LNG has filled about half of the gap left by Russian gas. LNG imports nearly doubled, from 80 bcm in 2021 to 146 bcm in 2025, when they accounted for 46 percent of imports. About three quarters of that additional LNG came from the United States. Perhaps surprisingly, despite the disruptions to global energy markets that began in February 2026, imports from outside the EU were only 1 percent lower than a year earlier during the first seven months of 2026, and LNG accounted for 45 percent of the EU's total gas imports, similar to its share for all of last year.

The reason for this resilience is that, while about one-fifth of the world's LNG passes through the Strait of Hormuz, most of it is bound for Asia and Qatar supplied only about 9 percent of the EU's LNG in 2025 and about 6 percent in the first seven months of 2026. In comparison, the United States supplied about 50 percent in 2025 and in the first seven months of 2026.7

Its new reliance on LNG makes Europe's gas supply more exposed to global market conditions. For example, as Asian buyers lose Qatari supply, they compete with Europe for cargoes from the Atlantic basin. To explore the consequences of Europe's increased exposure to the global LNG market, the Import Scarcity scenario in the analysis below focuses on the risk to the European gas supply due to LNG import reductions.

Consumption: lower, especially in winter

On the demand side, EU gas consumption fell from 413 bcm in 2021 to 332 bcm in 2024, a decline of about 20 percent (Figure 3). All end users cut back: households, industry, power plants and services. Consumption edged up slightly in 2025, mainly because power plants burned more gas. In the first seven months of 2026, Europe consumed about 1 percent more than a year earlier but still 19 percent less than during the same months of 2021.

Figure 3. Natural Gas Consumption in the EU, by End User

Note: Inland consumption (Eurostat's measure of all natural gas used within a country, including in power plants and as feedstock) of the 27 EU member states. For 2015 to 2024, annual consumption is split by end user with the shares in the annual energy balances. Chemicals includes non-energy use (feedstock); other industry includes firms that generate their own electricity and heat; power and heat plants are main-activity producers; other comprises the energy sector's own use, distribution losses, transport and agriculture. 2025 and January to July 2026 (hatched) are estimates from monthly data. Key identifies in order from top to bottom.

Source: Eurostat (nrg_cb_gasm, nrg_bal_c); author's calculations.

Accessible version

Part of this decline reflects mild weather as heating degree days in the four winters since Russia's invasion of Ukraine were notably below normal. To isolate the decline not due to warmer winters, country-level models of monthly consumption with month effects, heating and cooling degree days and the pre-crisis level of consumption are estimated on data from January 2015 to August 2021.8 The resulting parameter estimates are used to project consumption using observed heating and cooling degree days from September 2021 onward under the relationship between heating degree days and gas consumption which existed before 2022. Thus, the gap between this weather-adjusted counterfactual and actual consumption measures the decline that is not explained by weather (Figure 4).

When accounting for weather effects in this manner, EU consumption remained about 15 percent below its pre-crisis level in 2023 to 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, the decline was about 13 percent. While the decline has narrowed somewhat in the heating season (to about 11 percent in the past two winters, from 15 percent in the two before), it has held up outside the heating season. For example, in June and July 2026, when an unusually hot summer would have raised gas use in power plants before the crisis, consumption was about a quarter below the pre-invasion counterfactual.

Figure 4. Natural Gas Consumption in the EU: Actual and Weather-Adjusted Counterfactual

Note: Monthly inland consumption (as in Figure 3) of the 25 EU member states with a gas market (all except Cyprus and Malta). The counterfactual sums country models estimated on January 2015 to August 2021 data and projected with actual weather; the shaded area is the 90 percent bootstrap interval. Degree days for 2026 are computed from city temperatures calibrated to Eurostat's series for the euro-area countries and estimated from neighboring countries for Czechia, Denmark, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Sweden. The vertical lines mark September 2021, when prices first surged, and February 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine.

Source: Eurostat; Open-Meteo (ERA5); author's calculations.

Accessible version

Inventories this winter: a baseline and two scenarios

These insights shape the projections of EU gas inventories from October 2026 through June 2027 (Figure 5), as they require basing expected consumption on the winters since the invasion. Stocks are rolled forward month by month, accounting for domestic production, net imports and consumption, starting from a stock of about 80 bcm at the end of September 2026. The first scenario ("Baseline") assumes that domestic production, imports from Russia and net imports from all other countries in each month equal their level in the same month a year earlier, and that consumption equals its average for that month over the four winters since the invasion (2022–23 to 2025–26). The second scenario ("Harsh Winter") keeps the Baseline's supply assumptions but sets consumption in each month to its maximum over those winters. Thus, even though the past four winters were relatively mild in historical comparison, this scenario still provides a meaningful representation of gas consumption under extreme weather conditions, such as the exceptionally cold winter of 2012–13, which had 14 percent more heating degree days than normal.

The third scenario ("Import Scarcity") assumes that Europe can only secure smaller LNG supplies from the global market: pipeline imports, exports and consumption are as in the Baseline, but LNG imports in each month are reduced by one-third from their level a year earlier. This is a pessimistic scenario as it assumes that Europe would have to proportionately share the decline in LNG supply due to a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz (one-fifth of global LNG supply) and would also receive fewer deliveries from its established LNG providers, such as the United States and Algeria.9

Figure 5. Natural Gas Inventories in the EU (End of Period)

Note: Stocks are end-of-month natural gas in storage in the 27 EU member states (national territory and abroad, Eurostat definition); August and September 2026 are estimated from GIE AGSI+ daily data. Baseline: domestic production, imports from Russia and net imports from other countries in each month equal the same month a year earlier; consumption equals its average for that month over the winters 2022–23 to 2025–26. Harsh Winter: as the Baseline, but consumption at its maximum for that month over those winters. Import Scarcity: pipeline imports, exports and consumption as in the Baseline, LNG imports at two-thirds of the same month a year earlier. Avg. 2022–2025: the average storage fill rate for each month over the winters 2022–23 to 2025–26 applied to current storage capacity. The red dotted line marks 20 percent of storage capacity.

Source: Eurostat (nrg_cb_gasm, nrg_ti_gasm) and GIE AGSI+, both via Haver Analytics; author's calculations. Eurostat data through July 2026; GIE data through September 30, 2026.

Accessible version

In the Baseline scenario, inventories enter the winter well below their recent average. Storage peaks at about 84 bcm in October 2026, compared with about 99 bcm on the path implied by the 2022–25 average fill rates. Inventories fall to about 32 bcm at the end of March 2027, or 30 percent of storage capacity, before refilling begins. That is below the troughs of the past two winters but above the 20 percent of capacity to which EU countries have historically allowed stocks to fall (Rua, 2023).10

In the Harsh Winter scenario, stocks fall to about 16 bcm at the end of March 2027, or 15 percent of capacity, and stay below the 20 percent mark from February to April. In the Import Scarcity scenario, stocks fall to about 6 percent of capacity in April 2027, far below any level seen since 2011, and they remain below the 20 percent mark through June, so that refilling would start from almost zero. In all three scenarios, refilling for the 2027–28 winter would start from a lower level than this year, requiring stronger inflows than in previous years.

How much LNG could Europe lose and still get through the winter? Variants of the Import Scarcity scenario cut LNG imports to other shares of last year's level, which was about 77 bcm over October to March. With LNG at 80 percent of that level, stocks bottom out close to the Harsh Winter path. At 70 percent, they fall to about 9 bcm. At 60 percent, storage is all but empty in April 2027. In other words, a loss of about one-fifth of last year's LNG imports leaves filling levels close to the Harsh Winter path and near the critical 20 percent filling mark; beyond that, each further tenth of lost LNG imports takes roughly another 8 bcm off the trough, so that at a one-third loss storage is nearly empty and at 40 percent it is all but exhausted.

Will El Niño help?

A very strong El Niño is under way. The Oceanic Niño Index of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reached +2.16 for July to September 2026, the highest value for that season since records began in 1950 on the traditional index, and NOAA puts the chance that the event becomes the strongest since 1950 at 83 percent for October to December.11 El Niño affects European winters mainly through the North Atlantic. According to the literature, moderate El Niño events tend to bring cold late-winter weather to northern Europe, partly because El Niño makes sudden warmings of the stratosphere, which weaken the polar vortex, more likely (Ineson and Scaife, 2009). The response reverses as events become stronger, with high pressure over the eastern Atlantic and western Europe (Toniazzo and Scaife, 2006; Ineson and others, 2026). In the five strong El Niño winters since 1980, heating degree days in the EU, weighted by gas use, were on average about 6 percent below their trend, and all five had fewer heating degree days than trend (though 1991–92 only barely).12

A winter about 6 percent milder than trend would lower non-power gas consumption by about 4 bcm in the EU. The Baseline already builds in four mild winters, however, and measured against their weather the saving shrinks to only about 2½ bcm. That cushion is also uncertain because the evidence rests on only five winters, the event expected this year would be stronger than any of them, and the stratospheric channel that brings late-winter cold spells cannot be ruled out: no sudden stratospheric warming occurred in the strong El Niño winters of 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16, but one did in 1972–73 and another in January 2024, with little effect on the surface (Ineson and others, 2026). Thus, a very strong El Niño improves the odds for Europe's gas balances to last through the upcoming winter, but it does not rule out the cold snaps that matter most when storage is low.

articles.title: No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at The Florence School of Banking & Finance Resolution Academy, European University Institute

Published on
23 September 2026

Ruth Smith discusses the Bank’s approach to managing small and medium-sized firm failure within the UK’s resolution framework. She emphasises the evolution of the resolution toolkit to ensure the regime remains robust for small and medium-sized firms, and reflects on the importance of transparency, proportionality and optionality.

Speech
Good evening, everybody. It’s a pleasure to have had the opportunity to listen to many of you over the course of today’s insightful presentations and discussions on banking resolution. Thank you to the European University Institute and Florence School of Banking and Finance for inviting me to speak today.    
Resolution is in many ways a team sport, and events like the Bank Resolution Academy are a real opportunity to learn from one another, understand the parts we each play, and look at what we can learn from a different viewpoint.    
Following on from today’s sessions on resolving medium-sized banks and the tools available to us in a resolution, I hope to provide a UK perspective on how the Bank of England prepares for resolving small to medium-sized firms.    
As you know, in the UK we have resolution regimes for banks and CCPs.  Today I am focusing on banks and will discuss what we mean in the UK when we talk about small to medium-sized firms and our approach to resolution planning for this large and varied group. I will also cover the lessons learned from the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank UK in 2023, and the new mechanisms we have added to our toolkit to improve optionality in a resolution while still seeking to lessen the burden on firms.    
Despite our recent experience of carrying out a resolution, and the improvements we have made as a result of that, there is still plenty of work to do when we consider resolution of smaller firms.   
The UK banking sector   
The UK has a diverse banking system, comprising some of the world’s large globally systemic banks right down to banks who have balance sheets in the tens of millions. This diversity requires flexibility in how our colleagues in the supervisory arm of the Bank of England, the PRA, apply their regulatory focus and equally needs us as the separate but collaborative Bank of England UK Resolution Authority, to tailor our approaches accordingly. Like any successful team, we each have distinct roles, but we are working towards the same objective of a safe and sound financial system.   
The UK remains a competitive and dynamic marketplace with multiple firms engaging in our pre-application process each year via the New Bank Start-up Unit, and the international presence remains strong, with firms of all sizes having UK subsidiaries and branches. Within the sector we see firms successfully entering, embedding their business, adapting to the demands of the marketplace, and in some cases exiting. This breadth of presence requires us, as the UK’s Resolution Authority, to be ready for those firm exits with a flexible and proportionate approach. Perhaps most importantly, we must be aligned to not only our teammates in the PRA, but where those subsidiaries and branches are part of a wider global group, to our resolution colleagues in overseas jurisdictions such as those here today.   
In practice then, what does this diversity of banking sector and tailoring our approach mean for UK resolution planning?     
We think about our banks in three broad groups,footnote [1] the first of which generally comprises our largest banks, where we plan for bail-in.    
We then have what we describe as mid-tier banks, typically with balance sheets in the £25-40 billion range, where firms can be set either a transfer or a bail-in as the preferred resolution strategy. For the firms currently in this range, we generally set a preferred resolution strategy which involves transferring these firms in resolution to a private sector purchaser, or, in the absence of a purchaser, temporarily to a Bank of England owned bridge bank – pending a further sale.    
Following an update to our policy on how much loss absorbing capacity firms must hold, or “MREL policy”, last year,footnote [2] unlike bail-in firms, transfer firms are not required to maintain MREL above minimum capital requirements. However, both bail-in and transfer firms are subject to the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF. The RAF is our framework to assess UK financial firms’ resolvability and depending on the value of deposits held, some of these banks are also required to publicly disclose their own resolution self-assessment.    
In most cases, unless a firm with assets of less than £25 billion were viewed as posing a risk to financial stability, these smaller banks are then assumed to enter liquidation as a means of resolving their business if they are unable to either recover or complete a solvent wind-down. These are the firms we would use the Bank Insolvency Procedure or BIP for and do not hold additional MREL above minimum capital requirements or maintain additional capabilities to prepare for their failure.  BIP involves a rapid pay-out of depositors by the UK deposit guarantee scheme.footnote [3]  
As always there is judgement in setting a preferred resolution strategy, it is not solely based on a firm’s size and as such a transfer strategy can nevertheless be set in circumstances where the Bank assesses that a firm below the £25 billion mark would pose an unacceptable risk if it were to enter modified insolvency.    
Since the 2007-2008 global financial crisis the focus for resolution has rightly been on the largest, most systemic banks, those described as ‘too big to fail’. For these firms, the necessary team may well be large and international, and involve each person playing their role to produce the desired outcome of a smooth resolution.  And, as we look forward at an ever more interconnected system, operationally speaking, for not only our largest firms but smaller banks too, and join this together with our experiences of a small bank failure, we find ourselves working with the same teammates, and asking the same questions about stability and confidence in the wider sector as well as the impact of that failure on the bank’s customers. With this experience still relatively fresh in our minds it is this I want to speak about in depth.   
Our approach to small firms    
For our smallest banks, those typically defined as having less than £25 billion total assets, the plan for the majority of them should they fail is theoretically straightforward. Where a firm experiences severe stress which it is unable to recover from, the simplest solution is a director led solvent wind-down, allowing the firm to exit the market in an orderly manner while remaining a going concern. This enables the firm to stay in control of its own exit, minimising disruption to customers, creditors, and the wider market.    
Not all solvent wind-downs require active involvement from the resolution authority.  The PRA leads the assessment of whether a firm can continue to meet its obligations and execute an orderly exit from the market.  Where there are concerns about the firm’s ability to complete the wind-down solvently, the Bank, as resolution authority, works closely with the PRA to understand what alternative actions may be required, such as a BIP, should the firm’s plans prove no longer credible.    
Across all our work, the close relationship we have with the PRA is one of the most important aspects of our resolution framework. They are a teammate that we cannot be successful without.   
In the situation where a firm enters solvent wind-down, both authorities must be satisfied throughout that the firm’s wind down plan is credible, that it has sufficient resources to meet its obligations to depositors and creditors, and that allowing the firm to continue with their solvent wind-down plan aligns with our respective statutory objectives.  For a smaller firm, where a solvent wind-down ceases to be credible, insolvency may be the only remaining option.    
A BIP is a modified insolvency process. While the BIP shares many of the features of a standard insolvency process, it is specifically modified for deposit takers such as banks and building societies.    
Unlike an ordinary corporate liquidation, a BIP has a key objective of protecting covered depositors, which is done in two possible ways: payout or transfer. A BIP payout involves the insolvency practitioner or bank liquidator winding up the bank, whilst the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, the FSCS, carries out a rapid payout of deposits to the eligible depositors.    
Authorities in the UK have worked to significantly improve the speed and effectiveness of this payout process, learning from our European counterparts, to help ensure that protected depositors can regain access to their funds as quickly as possible. This speed of payout is important in maintaining public confidence in the efficacy of the resolution regime, and in the stability of the wider financial system.   
The second option is a BIP transfer, which involves the transfer by an appointed insolvency practitioner of the firm’s covered deposit book to another firm, with the insolvency practitioner winding up the remainder of the firm. For many of our smaller firms, the BIP provides a credible and proportionate resolution strategy.    
 So far so good and, hopefully, relatively straightforward and with minimal disruption.    
The boundary between BIP and transfer    
However, the small bank sector in the UK is highly diverse, innovative, and faces heavy competition. These characteristics have resulted in many of these smaller firms developing specialised business models which serve key customer groups, sectors, or communities that may not be well served elsewhere in the market or not be able to quickly and easily transfer their banking services to an alternative provider.   
The BIP is ultimately a liquidation procedure, and while it ensures covered depositors benefit from FSCS protection and payout, it is not designed to maintain the continuity of banking services.    
As such, customers of the failed firm may lose access to their existing banking relationships, payments may be disrupted, and those with uncovered deposits may need to wait for distributions through the insolvency procedure. For some smaller firms’ business models this may be acceptable, but for other firms, particularly where customers rely on continued access to banking services to operate on a daily basis, the impact can be significant and potentially outside the risk appetite of the collective authorities.    
This means that the picture in the UK is nuanced, requiring our assessments of whether a BIP would meet our statutory special resolution objectivesfootnote [4] to consider not only the size of a balance sheet, but also the nature of the customers it serves and the services it provides. As the Resolution Authority we need both a clear game plan and the ability to adapt it in real time.    
Lessons learned from SVB UK    
For the Bank, our experience with Silicon Valley Bank UK in March 2023 provides a powerful illustration of why flexibility in resolution planning is so important.    
At the time, SVB UK was a relatively small institution, with a balance sheet of around £12 billion and a preferred resolution strategy of BIP. Following the failure of its US parent and intervention by the FDIC, the Bank announced on Friday 10 March that, in the absence of further information, it intended to place SVB UK into insolvency.    
Based on what was known at that point, insolvency appeared to be the option that best met the public interest and the resolution objectives.   
As the situation developed over the weekend, however, it became clear that many customers relied on SVB UK not just for deposits, but for critical banking and payment services. At the same time, we needed to be cognisant of public confidence in the system against the backdrop of several other small bank failures in the US.   
We therefore kept multiple options open over the weekend, including insolvency. HSBC emerged as the credible bidder able to complete a transaction before markets opened on Monday while ensuring continuity of critical services, and with close liaison with FDIC throughout, and consultation with the PRA, FCA and HM Treasury, we concluded that a private sector transfer would better meet the special resolution objectives than a BIP.   
Unlike a BIP, the transfer provided protection for all depositors, not just those within the covered limits, ensured continuity of banking services, and most importantly protected and enhanced public confidence in the stability of the wider UK financial system in a way that did not incur costs on public funds.     
For me, this evidences that a preferred resolution strategy provides a vital starting point in contingency planning, but authorities need the flexibility, operational readiness and judgement to adapt quickly when executing a resolution as circumstances change in real-time. In the case of SVB UK, that flexibility was critical to achieving a better outcome for customers, for financial stability, and for the public interest.   
With this in mind, I want to speak to three key takeaways from this, our most recent experience of a bank resolution - transparency, optionality and international cooperation.     
Transparency   
First, SVB UK underlined the importance of a transparent resolution regime and communicating clearly and openly with markets, and authorities. The UK’s resolution framework relies not only on the Bank’s powers as resolution authority, but also on firms, investors, and other market participants understanding how these powers are used in practice, so that they can react accordingly.    
During the resolution weekend for SVB UK, both regulatory and finance ministry authorities worked together to consider multiple strategies in parallel. While this demonstrated the flexibility of the UK's framework, it also reinforced the value of ensuring there was common understanding about how different resolution options would be executed in a live event - between authorities, potential buyers, and the firm itself. Success depended on everyone understanding their role and how the wider team would operate under pressure.   
To bolster this shared understanding, in April we published the Bank’s operational guide to transfer resolution. The guide explains how the Bank would use its transfer powers in practice, whether the transfer involves selling the failed firm to a private sector purchaser, or placing it into a temporary bridge bank owned by the Bank of England.    
It aims to provide greater transparency around the key stages of a transfer, including preparatory work for both us and the firm, buyer engagement, transaction execution, and the information needed to support an accelerated sale process.    
By setting out these operational arrangements publicly and in advance of a future stress, the guide explains that transfer is not simply a theoretical power, but a credible and operationally deliverable resolution strategy. It helps firms better understand what may be expected of them, including the importance of maintaining the information and capabilities needed to support a rapid transfer if required.  It provides transparency to all potential stakeholders within a transfer, including prospective buyers, on how the bidding process would run for a transfer, improving the quality of bids, the competitiveness of an auction, and the smoothness of running the process overall.  
We applied the same learnings on transparency and communications to the Bank’s updated operational guide to bail-in resolution.  As firms grow, they face different resolution expectations. The guide provides greater clarity on how the Bank would execute a bail-in, giving firms, investors and other stakeholders a clearer understanding of the practical steps involved. In doing so, it supports preparedness, reduces uncertainty and reinforces the credibility of the UK's resolution framework across the full spectrum of firms.   
Optionality   
Moving on then to consider the optionality that our resolution framework gives us when planning for a firm failure. While the existing regime gave us an effective and flexible set of options that we were able to use to resolve SVB UK smoothly over a weekend, since 2023 we have continued to work very closely with our colleagues in HMT, our finance ministry, to introduce a new choice in our toolkit in the form of the recapitalisation payment mechanism.    
Introduced via the Bank Resolution (Recapitalisation) Act 2025, this tool is intended to cover associated losses or recapitalisation needs in a transfer via a new industry-funded safety net.    
Simply put, assuming the failing firm meets the public interest test, the recapitalisation mechanism allows us to cover certain costs associated with transferring a firm in resolution up front, be that to a private purchaser or a bridge bank, and then recover these from the industry via the financial services compensation scheme levy ex-post. This minimises the risk to public funds while providing options to use stabilisation powers to resolve a smaller firm when in the public interest.  We were fortunate that in the case of SVB UK the write-down of the regulatory capital was sufficient to enable us to transfer the firm to an interested and credible buyer – but this will not always be the case.  
Use of the mechanism may include recapitalisation of a firm during transfer due to a capital shortfall or potentially providing funds to the purchaser upfront and possibly in the form of guarantees to address any material concerns raised during the bidding process.    
For example, we recognise that the circumstances around a failing firm are often uncertain and extremely fast moving, resulting in limited time for due diligence to be conducted by interested buyers and introducing significant barriers which must be navigated to ensure a successful transfer.    
The new mechanism also gives us the space to be more proportionate in terms of what we require from small and medium-sized firms prior to a resolution. As I have noted, transfer firms are no longer required to hold MREL, in part due to the industry-funded safety net that this new mechanism provides.   
This flexibility represents a big step forward in strengthening our resolution toolkit. However, as always, we need to balance the needs of the failing firm with those of the wider financial system – recognising that any funds used to support the transfer are ultimately repaid by the wider industry.    
Importantly, it is not a replacement for BIP – an insolvency procedure is still a viable option for many firms and dependent on the scenario, may still be the right approach to take when considering our resolution objectives. While the use of the recapitalisation payment mechanism will always be situation specific, in all cases, the Bank will seek to use any funds in the most efficient and effective way possible, and the Act will not be used inappropriately to protect creditors from losses.    
This addition to the Bank’s resolution toolkit recognises that the UK runs a non-zero failure regime, and therefore it is important for firms to be allowed to grow but also be allowed to fail and exit the market smoothly – regardless of their size. It places a portion of that accountability back onto industry, not taxpayers, and ensures the Bank as Resolution authority has more options available to it and is ready for multiple failure scenarios without excessive burden on our smaller firms.   
International cooperation and coordination   
Third and finally, SVB UK underlined the importance of close coordination between authorities, particularly where a failing firm forms part of a wider international banking group.    
Effective resolution of cross-border firms requires more than financial resources and legal powers. It also depends on strong cooperation between home and host authorities, shared understanding of the firm's operational dependencies, and a common objective of maintaining critical services for customers. Like any team, it is helpful to train together before a match, and cross-jurisdictional exercises that allow us to practice and understand how we best work together are an important part of preparing for firm failure before the moment of stress arrives.    
While SVB UK involved close coordination between the UK and US authorities, the same principles would apply to firms operating across other jurisdictions.    
As banking groups become international, maintaining these relationships and coordination channels is an essential part of ensuring that resolution strategies remain credible and operationally deliverable.    
Conclusion   
What does the evolution of our framework mean in reality then? For me, it demonstrates that within the UK resolution regime, we have a robust toolkit that gives us confidence in having options to resolve small, medium and large firms.  
But looking ahead, I can still see areas of the banking sector where we could do more, particularly when it comes to small and medium-sized firms, to better prepare ourselves as authorities and prepare firms, in “peacetime”. I have spoken about how flexible options allow us to execute a resolution in more than one way for any given firm, in order to prioritise better outcomes for depositors while still protecting the public purse and wider financial stability.  
We often envisage using these options when presented with new information that challenges our original game plan during a resolution. However, I consider that we can do more to ensure we are always ready, by working with supervisors and firms to use their existing data and regulatory reporting to identify where they may be on the boundary of a BIP or transfer strategy in advance.   
As trailed in our update to the MREL policy last year, we are reviewing the indicative threshold of 40,000 to 80,000 transactional accounts as an intervention point for when a transfer strategy may need to be set for a firm under £25 billion in total assets. In part, this review is taking into account that the recapitalisation payment mechanism gives us more optionality for firms that do not hold MREL, and that consumer banking behaviour has changed since the threshold’s original implementation, making it less in step with the judgements we have to make when setting preferred resolution strategies.   
However, by removing the burden of MREL for such firms, we still need to ensure that we can execute a transfer effectively.  As part of this review, we are working with the PRA to ensure our resolution planning and reporting policies reflect these recent developments. This includes considering the information we require BIP firms to report on regularly. Are we asking the right questions? Is there existing data that firms already have through recovery and solvent exit planning that would better support our shared readiness for resolution planning as a BIP or in preparation for a transfer strategy in the future?  
With a more established resolution regime we must ask ourselves these kinds of questions to ensure we are continually improving and evolving our approach to firm resolution across the sector. I expect that we will publish our updated approach in early 2027 and look forward to hearing industry views in due course.   
A firm’s resolvability journey is never done, and as such our job as resolution authority isn’t either. No single authority can deliver resolution alone; it remains, at its core, a team effort and we will all need to remain live to an evolving sector to ensure our capabilities and policies are in step with the firms we regulate. The world rarely stays still and advances in technology, how firms operate and where the next risk may arise from is a horizon that we must keep at the front of our mind when considering barriers to an orderly resolution. Firms are a part of our team in a resolution, and I hope by continuing to work closely with one another, we can maintain readiness through a proportionate and effective resolution regime.   
I would like to thank Mala Gopalakrishnan, Kat Hind and Amanda Tennant for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Geoff Davies, Charlotte Gerken and Dave Ramsden for their helpful comments.    

In general, for the purposes of resolution planning these three groups of firms are categorised as those with total assets of: i) £40 billion or more; ii) between £25 billion and $40 billion; and iii) less than £25 billion.

articles.title: Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
articles.text:
Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot

Given at the 2nd Annual Conference on Sustainable Finance at the Banco de México on 21 October 2026

Published on
23 October 2026

James Talbot, Executive Director for International at the Bank of England and the Bank’s Executive Sponsor for climate, explains how physical climate shocks can affect inflation and output, and how central banks can assess and respond to them. He considers two connected horizons: their near-term effects on monetary policy, and the longer-term role of economic resilience, adaptation and insurance in helping economies absorb future shocks and support price and financial stability.

Speech
Physical shocks increasingly matter for central banks
Governor, distinguished guests, I am sorry that I cannot be there with you in person at such a prestigious event. It is very much an honour and a pleasure, and my thanks to Dr. Fabrizio López-Gallo Dey for inviting me to speak today.
The physical impacts of climate change are becoming larger and more proximate, and their short-term economic impacts are also increasing. Annual global damages from weather-related events have more than doubled since the early 2000s, reaching over $200bn in 2025footnote [1].
In light of that, the economic effects of climate change are increasingly on the radar of central bankers. When extreme weather events affect production, output and inflation, that matters for our primary goal of maintaining price stability.
Let me take two examples that are close to home:
Increasingly high summer temperatures reduce water levels on key transport arteries for industrial trade, like the River Rhine in Germany. When water levels fall, ships reduce the amount of cargo they carry, disrupting the movement of goods and increasing transport costs.
Such exceptionally low water levels have become a recurring feature in recent years. The economic effects have also been material: recent research estimates that 30 days of low water on the Rhine reduces German industrial production by around 1%footnote [2].
In October 2024, extreme rainfall caused devastating flash floods in Valencia. Aside from the tragic loss of human life, economic losses amounted to over 20% of regional GDP. Spanish Q4 GDP growth was reduced by between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage pointsfootnote [3].
The economic impact would have been larger were it not for the high level of insurance protection for affected households and businesses. Around 250,000 insurance claims were filed following the floods and Spain's Insurance Compensation Consortium had paid more than €4bn in compensation by late 2025, making this the largest event the scheme has ever managedfootnote [4].
Even countries like the UK, which may be less susceptible to large physical shocks, can be affected by the impact of events abroad.
Over the past four years, as chair of the NGFS Workstream on Monetary Policy, I have worked together with more than sixty central banks to set out a framework to assess the impact of climate change on the economy, to measure its effects and to determine what monetary policymakers should do about it.
I’ll talk today about how the physical impacts of climate change can affect the economy in the near term; how we diagnose their magnitude, persistence and propagation; whether their effects belong in the central forecast or in the risks around it; and how that diagnosis informs monetary policy judgements. We set out each of these steps in an NGFS guide for monetary policymakers that we published earlier this yearfootnote [5].
I also want to look beyond the near-term policy horizon. In particular, how repeated losses, adaptation, fiscal space and insurance protection gaps shape the capacity of economies and financial systems to absorb future shocks.
I will argue that these two horizons are connected: The resilience an economy has built determines the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic impact of a shock over the monetary-policy horizon. And, in turn, repeated shocks can erode that resilience over the longer term, eventually exacerbating the effects of climate shocks when they occur.
How physical shocks transmit through the economy
Let me start with how physical shocks can affect the economy.
Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains. They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty.
Importantly for monetary policymakers, those channels can interact and may also move output and inflation in different directions, making the policy response more challenging.
But different physical hazards can transmit through the economy in different ways. To give some examplesfootnote [6]:

Heatwaves transmit as a shock to productive capacity and labour supply. They push down on GDP while increasing inflation volatility, making them relevant for monetary policy even though direct physical damage is not as visible as for a flood or storm.
Droughts reduce productive capacity in agriculture pushing down on production and up on prices. They can raise inflation both through the effect on domestic production and through more expensive imports.
Floods and cyclones damage the capital stock, reducing demand and investment, which can in turn push down on output and inflation. But floods can also be inflationary where they hit food supply, logistics or essential infrastructure.

So while there is no one-size-fits-all pattern for the effects of a physical shock, there are some common themes:

Shocks are often transmitted through a disruption to production;
That usually means that output and inflation often move in opposite directions; and
Even when shocks occur overseas, these can be transmitted through changes to exports and commodity prices, particularly for open economies. Indeed, a 2022 study for the euro area showed that for every 1% unanticipated increase in globally traded food prices, overall inflation rose by 0.1%footnote [7].

This latter channel is also particularly important for the UK since we import around 40% of our food. In recent work at the Bank of England, we have looked at the impacts of extreme weather events on commodity prices and UK inflationfootnote [8]. The estimates from the model suggest that global weather-related disruption has played a non-trivial role in UK food and headline inflation over the past two decades
This makes climate-related shocks relevant to our regular inflation forecasting. Indeed, many central banks are now assessing the impact of food, energy, supply-chain, and weather-related shocks. That is because these shocks are affecting inflation and output forecasts, or the risks around them, in an increasingly meaningful way.
The NGFS note on the economic and financial impacts of extreme weather events, produced for the 2026 French G7 Presidency, uses 31 case studies to show that these effects repeatedly appear in output, employment and prices across a geographically diverse range of countriesfootnote [9]. Supply-chain and trade linkages can also propagate these shocks beyond the country or region directly affected.
With that in mind, let me turn next to consider how central banks should diagnose the shock, assess its impact on their forecasts and the risks around them and therefore their monetary policy judgements.
A framework for assessing the impacts of climate shocks
Here I will draw on the recent NGFS guide on monetary policy strategy that I mentioned earlierfootnote [10]. The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Step one is to identify the nature of the shock itself: How large is it? How long is it likely to last? Which regions and sectors are affected? Is it localised or widespread? And is it a one-off event or one in a sequence of shocks?
Those distinctions matter.
A short-lived disruption affecting a relatively narrow part of the economy during the low season of economic activity poses a very different challenge from a shock affecting food, energy, or critical infrastructure, or services such as tourism during peak season. And a sequence of individually temporary shocks may have quite different macroeconomic consequences from an isolated event.
Having identified the shock, step two is to assess how it propagates through the economy.
Here, the familiar distinction between direct, indirect and second-round effects is particularly useful.
Direct – or first round – effects are the immediate relative-price effects from the shock: for example, a drought raising food prices, a heatwave reducing labour productivity, or a flood disrupting production and logistics.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage. If the shock is short-lived and expectations remain anchored, the standard monetary policy response is usually to look through the first-round effects, because policy operates with a lag and tightening in response to a temporary supply shock can impose unnecessary output costs.
But the initial shock can spread more widely, having indirect effects, as firms pass higher input costs across supply chains. And there can be second-round effects through wages and inflation expectations. Workers may seek compensation for higher living costs; businesses may adjust their price-setting behaviour; and households and firms may revise their inflation expectations.
Food and energy prices can be particularly important here. Households observe them frequently and a well-established literature shows that they have an outsized effect on expectations about future inflation. Research conducted at the Bank of England reinforces that result for the UK, finding that more than 60% of households report that food prices heavily influence inflation perceptions. Food prices also matter significantly more for household inflation-expectations dynamics than other components, with effects at short, medium and long horizons.
Frequency of shocks matters too. An isolated rise in prices will feel different to a series of repeated upward moves. Indeed, a sequence of individually temporary shocks which arrive before the effects of previous disturbances have dissipated can look and feel like more persistent inflationary pressure. Repeated disruption can also erode fiscal buffers and weaken private-sector resilience.
Central banks should therefore focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
From diagnosis to the monetary-policy response
Step three is next: does the identified shock create a trade-off between inflation and output?
As I noted earlier, hot and dry events provide relatively clear examples. By reducing agricultural production, a drought can weaken output while putting upward pressure on food prices. A heatwave pushing down on productivity can increase inflation volatility at the same time as hitting output. But if shocks primarily damage capital and reduce output, such as floods and storms in some circumstances, they can push down on inflation where demand effects dominate.
If you permit me a brief digression at this point, the situation becomes no easier when considering the economic impact of the policies enacted by governments to ensure that the necessary climate transition happens. These policies can also drive large and persistent relative price movements, shifts in investment and reallocation of production across sectors of the economy. Modelling the impact of these shocks is therefore no less important. Here, the NGFS and IMF published joint work earlier this year on how countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions to reducing emissions under the Paris Agreement will affect inflation and output across a range of economiesfootnote [11].
Step four is to set policy and communicate the decision.
Here, the assessment depends importantly on the wider economic environment at the point the shock arrives. If inflation is already elevated and expectations are less firmly anchored, the risk that an initial price increase develops into broader inflationary pressure may be greater, and the case for responding becomes stronger. If the economy has spare capacity and demand is weak, the case for looking through is stronger.
This is also where a central bank faces an important judgement: if the effects of a physical shock are material and sufficiently well understood, they may belong in the central forecast.
But where there is substantial uncertainty around the scale of a shock or the way it will propagate, scenarios can allow policymakers to explore and communicate risks. Scenarios can complement the central forecast by helping us explore precisely the kinds of uncertainty I have described today: whether a shock proves temporary or persistent; whether supply or demand effects dominate; and whether initial price increases generate material second-round effects.
The fifth and final step is to monitor and assess whether the economy is evolving in line with expectations and adjust policy in response to new data developments. Since there is also evidence that climate shocks can affect credit supply, collateral values or financial intermediation, central banks should also monitor the operation of the monetary transmission mechanism.
You will notice, of course, that the process I describe here is not that different to how central banks assess and respond to other economic shocks. That is because the impact of climate change is now one of the set of economic shocks that monetary policymakers consider.
From immediate shocks to the resilience threshold
Since climate shocks are likely to increase in both magnitude and frequency, another important question is whether economies and financial systems can continue to absorb rising losses from these shocks over the longer term.
The capacity of households, businesses, governments and financial systems to absorb losses is a key determinant of the recovery profile from a climate shock. Fiscal space, insurance penetration, climate adaptation, infrastructure quality, financial-market depth and institutional capacity all help to determine a country’s resilience threshold. Where those buffers are stronger, shocks are more likely to be absorbed. Where they are weaker, the effects can become more persistent and can spill into credit, financial stability and public-finance channels.
Less developed economies typically have lower resilience thresholds, meaning similar physical hazards can generate larger and more persistent macroeconomic damage. A previous study by Raddatz (2009) estimated that a climate-related disaster resulted in a cumulative per capita output loss of 0.25%, 0.5% and 1% for high, middle and low-income countries respectivelyfootnote [12].
But resilience is also not fixed. Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity. Without effective mitigation and adaptation, economies may therefore become less resilient over time, with the same physical hazard generating increasingly persistent effects on output, inflation, credit and public finances.
There is also evidence that these interactions can be non-linear. The NGFS’s 2023 work on compound risks examines precisely what can happen when shocks combine, either across time or across locations. It shows that the overall macroeconomic impact of compounding shocks can be materially greater than the sum of the partsfootnote [13].
This in turn feeds back to the short-term policy response. Resilience directly affects the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic consequences of a shock, and therefore how difficult it is for monetary policy to look through it. But if losses are absorbed quickly through insurance mechanisms or other buffers, the inflation-output trade-off may be shorter-lived.
There is therefore an important interaction between resilience and monetary policy. The more resilient an economy is, the easier it is to absorb physical shocks. As resilience erodes, the same shock can become progressively harder to look through.
Insurance protection gaps and why they matter for central banks
The provision of insurance helps economies to cushion the effect of physical shocks by pooling and transferring losses. High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.
But as physical risks increase, rising and repeated losses could place pressure on the availability and affordability of insurance in areas exposed to these shocks. If insurance coverage falls, losses will instead fall on households, businesses, banks and governments.
Two recent events provide a sobering comparison. In Spain, public-private insurance arrangements helped absorb a significant share of losses from the 2024 floods whereas in Pakistan, following the 2022 floods, only around 1% of total damages were insured, leaving households and small firms far more exposed to income and wealth losses, generating larger macroeconomic impacts.
From a microprudential perspective, withdrawal of insurance provision may enhance the safety and soundness of insurance firms, because rising insured damages can significantly dent profitability and potentially threaten firm resilience.
As the insurance supervisor, our role is not to direct underwriting decisions by individual firms. But as a macroprudential authority, we will need to take a broader view of the implications for the financial system as a whole. Indeed, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee highlighted this issue at its September 2026 meetingfootnote [14].
Where insurance coverage falls, uninsured risks will need to be redistributed:

For households, this means higher repair costs when physical risks strike, lower property values and potential difficulties obtaining a mortgage.
For businesses, it can mean bearing losses from the destruction of physical goods, capital and infrastructure.
For banks, it can mean weaker collateral values and higher credit losses.
For governments, it can mean more frequent pressure to act as insurer of last resort.

For the UK, Bank of England staff have modelled how a widening flood-insurance protection gap could spill over to the UK mortgage marketfootnote [15].
This analysis suggests that the share of UK mortgagors without insurance could rise from around 5% today to around 7-10% in 2050, or up to 16% following a severe flood event. The aggregate effects on house prices and mortgage impairments in that modelling are relatively small compared with the severe macroeconomic stresses against which the UK banking system is tested. But that does not mean the issue is trivial: the consequences for affected households, exposed lenders and local economies could still be significant.
There is an important lesson here: the answer cannot simply be more of the same insurance. Insurance capacity cannot sustainably compensate for underlying physical risks that continue to rise. Insurers will likely increasingly need to include risk prevention in product design, underwriting, and pricing practices.
Indeed, while a successful transition to net zero can limit the future increase in physical hazards, we will also need to consider the role of adaptation in a world where climate shocks are more frequent.
Investment in ensuring resilience to climate shocks can support insurability. This may require collaboration between businesses, households and governments. Updates to planning rules and building regulations could further mitigate the impact of increased physical hazards.
Actions to improve climate-related risk identification, measurement and modelling capabilities across the insurance sector, as envisaged under the recent update to the Bank of England’s supervisory expectations, should strengthen firms' ability to assess and price climate-related risksfootnote [16].
But the financial sector also has a long tradition of coming up with innovative solutions to difficult problems. In this regard, there may be scope for greater collaboration between insurers, reinsurers and banks to share data, develop products and risk-transfer mechanisms that support resilience and help narrow protection gaps.
International cooperation
Let me finish with a word on international cooperation. Climate change is an issue which transcends borders and cannot be fixed by one country acting alone. In recent years, great strides have been made in multilateral fora like the NGFS to assess and model the impacts of climate change on the financial system. The NGFS’ flagship climate scenarios are an important tool in underpinning climate risk assessment in the financial sector. The work of the International Sustainability Standards Board to ensure consistent and better climate disclosures is helping financial firms to better manage climate-related risks and to make better decisions on where to allocate capital.
The 2025 South African G20 Presidency focused on the issue of natural catastrophe protection gaps, drawing on joint work from the World Bank and the International Association of Insurance Supervisorsfootnote [17]. That work helped to raise our collective understanding of these issues as well as suggesting a range of approaches to tackle them, tailored to country circumstances.
In 2026, the French G7 Presidency took this work forward by strengthening the evidence on the macro-financial consequences of extreme weather, while examining how to tackle protection gapsfootnote [18]. This issue is also on our radar as the UK develops priorities for its own G20 Presidency in 2027. In my view, there is value in better understanding how insurance protection gaps affect the economic impact of extreme-weather events and in exploring what can help sustain insurability and resilience as physical risks increase.
That could include looking at what constrains insurability, which approaches appear capable of operating at scale, and the conditions needed for them to work sustainably.
Insurance cannot close protection gaps on its own. But better data, investment in adaptation and more resilient infrastructure can help sustain affordable cover. Timely mitigation also remains essential to limit the future increase in physical risk.
That brings me back to the two connected horizons. In the near term, central banks will need to understand how physical and transition-related shocks affect inflation, output and expectations in order to deliver on their price stability mandate.
Further ahead, the availability of insurance will determine both the economic impact of climate shocks and the capacity of economies to absorb the resulting losses. It will also shape the prevailing environment in which central banks will pursue their price and financial stability goals.
As macroprudential policymakers, we understand that the availability of insurance matters to the resilience of the financial system as a whole. So as protection gaps widen, addressing them will require concerted action across governments, regulators, international institutions and the private sector. Multilateral fora can play an important role in supporting that dialogue and sharing lessons on what works.
As climate change increasingly affects our economies and financial systems, central banks will need to understand these effects, just like any other shock. This will enable us to make sure that the financial system remains stable and that price stability is maintained. And in turn that can provide a sustainable platform for governments to deliver the climate transition.
I would like to thank Danae Kyriakopoulou for assistance in writing this speech. I would also like to thank Lukasz Krebel and Fergus Booker for their input and helpful comments, as well as India Rimmer, Hannah Copeland, Boromeus Wanengkirtyo, Dario Bonciani, Riccardo Masolo, Silvia Sarpietro, Nikoleta Anesti, Vania Esady, Matthew Naylor, Will Banks, Kemal Erçevik, Alex Curtis and Jemima Hall for their underlying research.

articles.title: How are bottlenecks in the energy development pipeline reshaping the US market?
articles.text:
Observations
How are bottlenecks in the energy development pipeline reshaping the US market?

Macquarie expert: Ed Northam, Global Head of Green Investments, Macquarie Asset Management

12 November 2026

Grid congestion, equipment shortages and stalled permits have made achieving speed to power increasingly challenging. Buyers are paying a premium for it and the advantage is shifting to developers with scale and execution capability, creating consolidation opportunities.

Electricity demand growth by sector and end use in the United States, 2015 – 2030
Total incremental electricity demand over each five-year period (TWh)

Source: IEA 2026; Electricity demand growth by sector and end-use in the United States, 2015-2030, https://www.iea.org/, License: CC BY 4.0.
Energy demand is soaring, with 420 TWh of incremental electricity demand forecast to be added in the US over the next five years, as shown above.1 This is driven by a combination of diversified demand sources including the electrification of transport and industry, heating and cooling and data centre requirements.
Developers are racing to respond, but the development pipeline is clogged by:
Interconnection queues: the waiting lists for grid connection grew 116 per cent between 2020 and 2025.2
Equipment bottlenecks: lead times for generator step-up transformers, which link new generation to the grid, have reached 144 weeks.3
Permitting delays: more than 125 wind projects across 25 states are awaiting approval.4

Speed to market is now driving what gets built. Rapid growth in power demand is outpacing available supply, a challenge compounded by stalled wind approvals in the US. Against this backdrop, developers are increasingly prioritising technologies that can connect fastest. Solar and storage lead on deployment speed and storage is emerging as a way to unlock grid capacity directly. At Aligned Data Centers’ Hillsboro campus, an on-site battery system developed by Calibrant, a Macquarie Asset Management portfolio company, supports earlier energisation than would be possible through conventional grid upgrades that would otherwise have been required to connect the site.
It is also shaping prices. As demand outpaces available grid capacity, data centres, for example, are paying more for power that can be connected sooner. In PJM North Illinois, the US’ most congested data centre market, corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are pricing $US38 per megawatt-hour (MWh) above the 2027–2041 forward curve. In ERCOT West Hub, where supply connects faster, they sit $US14 per MWh below it.5
In other words, the harder it is to connect, the higher the premium available supply commands.
Why does it matter?
The bottlenecks are changing who can compete.
Holding queue positions, reserving equipment years ahead and financing longer development timelines require balance-sheet strength and specialist teams. In our view, this complexity can push smaller platforms out, while larger developers can spread risk, absorb delays and raise capital more cheaply.
We believe the next phase of energy delivery is an execution race that sophisticated, scaled players are positioned to lead, driving further consolidation across the sector.

What we’re watching next
A pipeline is only worth what a developer can actually deliver, which puts the larger, best-equipped developers in a strong position to lead.

Grid access reform
Whether interconnection reforms shorten queue times.

Equipment supply
Whether new transformer manufacturing capacity brings lead times down.

Permitting outcomes
Whether stalled wind projects win approval, or capital shifts toward solar, storage and gas.

InsightsAnalysis and perspectives on the global economy and markets, from across Goldman SachsExplore InsightsOUR SERIESExchangesThe MarketsTalks at GSTop of MindTOPICS IN FOCUSOutlooksMarketsMacroeconomicsArtificial IntelligenceAlternative and Private MarketsIPOs and M&AEuropeFORMATSVideosPodcastsArticlesReportsNewsletter2027 OutlooksAnalysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs.
