CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchangesSteady Global Economic Growth in 2027 Outlook but Risks Tilted to DownsideNov 17, 2026ShareThe global economy is forecast to grow 2.8% in 2027, though energy and AI could test its resilience, Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research says on the Exchanges podcast. Dominic Wilson, senior advisor in Global Markets Research, predicts equity gains continuing.
Subscribe: Spotify / Apple Podcasts / YouTube
Download TranscriptKey takeaways:

Global growth is expected to remain steady: Goldman Sachs Research forecasts 2.8% growth in 2027, about even with 2.7% in 2026, supported by still-strong AI investment and lower oil prices; tighter financial conditions and a more neutral fiscal impulse could limit economic upside.
Inflation should be more benign in 2027: Hatzius expects US core PCE inflation to ease to about 2.4% by the end of the year as tariff and energy pass-throughs fade, although renewed energy-price pressure remains a risk.

Markets have upside in the baseline case: Wilson expects positive, though less dramatic, equity returns and a better environment for bonds in 2027. He says portfolios should remain diversified and protected against energy, rates, and AI-related risks.

Transcript:
Allison Nathan: The global economy has held steady this year, defying a war in the Middle East, higher tariffs, and higher interest rates. But can that resilience last? As we look forward to 2027, investors are facing a new set of questions. Will the AI boom cool down? Will higher borrowing costs hurt growth? And will energy prices remain a headwind or become a tailwind?
I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Today, we're diving into the economic and market outlook for the year ahead. I'm joined by Jan Hatzius, head of Goldman Sachs Research and the firm's chief economist, and Dominic Wilson, a senior advisor in the Global Markets Research Group.
Jan, Dom, welcome back to the program.
Jan Hatzius: Great to be here.
Dom Wilson: Thank you.
Allison Nathan: I can't believe another year has gone by. Another outlook report is out. Congratulations on getting it out, and there's a lot to talk about.
So, Jan, as I mentioned, between the war in Iran, higher tariffs, higher rates, you would've thought the global economy would've struggled in 2026. But growth has been relatively resilient. You've actually described this year as remarkably unremarkable in terms of growth. So, what's kept it going?
Jan Hatzius: 2026 has been a pretty good year, at least globally. We are on track for growth of 2.7% for the world economy. That's in line with our estimate of potential, and it's not far from what we thought at the start of the year.
Some of the headwinds you mentioned have been small. Tariffs, for example, were an issue in 2025, but not really in 2026. We did see an increase in interest rates, and that, taken by itself, is a drag on growth. But broader financial conditions have been supportive of growth for most of the year.
And then if you look at the war in Iran and the impact on energy prices, that's been smaller than what you would have perhaps expected given all the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices did go up very meaningfully, but not as much as some predicted, and I certainly would have thought, if you'd given me the entire chain of events in the Middle East.
And I think some of that is related to pipeline redirection, some of it is related to dark flows and escorted flows through the strait, and some of it is related to reduced demand for oil, in some sense, higher price elasticity in some parts of the global economy, for example, in China.
And then you had a couple of significant boosts to growth that have offset whatever drag there was. I'd mention fiscal policy, expansionary in the US on the back of the 2025 fiscal bill. In Germany on the back of the defense and infrastructure program, and in Asia in terms of fuel subsidies that insulated household cash flow. So that's been helpful.
And then lastly, of course, we've seen a big increase in AI investment throughout 2026. For the year as a whole, we think we're getting an increase that's worth about half a percent of global GDP, and that's meaningful, even though, of course, it's unequally distributed. You get a very large growth boost in East Asia, especially Taiwan and Korea. You get a moderate growth boost in the US, and then something much smaller elsewhere. But for the global numbers, it's been important.
Allison Nathan: But you expect some of those supports to fade in 2027, and you see risks to growth actually tilted to the downside. So why the more cautious tone?
Jan Hatzius: The baseline is similar. We're at 2.8% for 2027, and yes, we're seeing the financial conditions boost fade, and probably replaced by at least a moderate negative impact on growth over the next few quarters, just based on what our financial conditions indices have done.
We're also probably going to get a more neutral impulse from fiscal policy. But then there are two things that are going to be helping us.
One, still ongoing strong growth in AI investment. We do think that's probably going to be front-loaded, so the biggest impact in the early part of 2027. Then we would expect that impact to fade as we go through the year. But for the year as a whole, it looks similar to 2026 in terms of the increase.
And then we are expecting a friendlier backdrop from an energy price and energy impact on real income perspective. Our commodity strategists have oil prices gradually coming down towards the sort of $80 range in 2027. And that, combined with the fact that we're going to be lapping the biggest increases in oil prices, that should actually help household income growth increase in real terms. So, that gives us the baseline.
There are downside risks to the forecast. And I would say number one, on oil prices, we've seen much more positive near-term news flow before, but there is still a risk that ultimately we get an escalation, a renewed escalation and renewed spike in prices that would certainly upend some of the assumptions that we've been making.
We are, I think, at risk of tightening in financial conditions, for example, via spikes in bond yields. Fiscal policy is on an unsustainable path in a number of economies. I think that's true in the United States, I think it's true in the UK to a lesser degree, and then it's certainly true in the Euro area, especially in France. We've seen significant spikes in bond yields. We're working our way towards the French presidential election in April and May, and if investors don't see a clear plan for adjusting fiscal policy, then I think we're at risk of additional tensions there, and that could also spill over into broader financial conditions and slow growth.
And then lastly, on AI investment, there are a number of downside risks to this path of continued increases. Some of those are regulatory, pushback against data center investment, which is something to be focused on. I don't expect a big impact, but it's a very fluid situation and obviously very politics-dependent.
There are a lot of shortages in the semiconductor and especially memory industry, which suggests that a significant chunk of the increase in nominal spending could end up going into price rather than volume, and that would also be a downside risk for real GDP.
And then there's the question of, at what point is the buildout of the AI capital stock sufficiently advanced that you really see more of a slowdown in demand? In our baseline, that doesn't happen until 2028, 2029, but it's hard to time this, and so I think that's another risk to be focused on.
Allison Nathan: Dom, let me bring you into the conversation. We've just heard Jan's growth expectations: pretty steady, stable, but with downside risks, as he just spoke about. Are markets appropriately pricing that risk? What do you make of this?
Dom Wilson: Yeah, I think there's a similar balancing act going on on the market side. The baseline outlook that Jan laid out is pretty benign, and our baseline is for positive equity returns, for risk assets to be supported by that kind of growth picture. I don't think we're obviously underpriced to that growth view, but I do think it's a helpful tailwind if that's where we're going.
I think, like a lot of the last six months, that means a lot of the action in markets is going to be around these risks and the pricing of the distribution of risks, and that's where those opportunities are going to come from.
And I would say there are two that are still very prominent: the oil and energy risk and the AI theme, both of which Jan mentioned. I think they operate on slightly different time horizons.
If you look at the energy risk, as Jan said, the biggest near-term risk is probably that we get renewed escalation and a renewed energy price spike. I think what's happened is the market has worried a lot about that coming into the midterms. Our commodities team estimates a risk premium in oil markets, which is how far oil is trading above where we think the fundamentals would put it. That was about $30 a few weeks ago, as the worries about escalation post-midterm were particularly high. We've seen a lot of relaxation around that since that point. We're close to zero on the risk premium now. So, I would say in that sense, the market is now more vulnerable again to that near-term risk. Maybe that risk is a little underpriced.
I think the bigger story, which Jan focused on, is how the market handles the transition in the AI story and the potential peaking of the growth impulse there. And I do think relative to the economic story, that's a tougher thing for the market story, for two reasons.
The first is that the contributions that the AI investment story has made to CapEx, to earnings, to market value are quite a lot higher than to overall GDP growth in the US in particular. So, it's just been a bigger issue for markets than for the macroeconomy, and so there's more focus on those dynamics in the markets.
The second thing is that a peak in growth rates, what we think of as a second-derivative turning point, we've found historically tends to matter more for markets. It allows markets to place a limit on the upsides of distributions, so even if growth stays strong, the slowing or the peaking of that growth rate matters.
I think the market's been doing a lot of that work. The good news is we've been de-rating this AI area, particularly the infrastructure producers, for a few months, so valuations are less demanding. I think the bigger focus is now going to be on the earnings side. We've had a very sharp increase in the share of earnings, as a proportion of GDP, going to S&P 500 companies. That's been very supportive, but the big question is how much of that is really sustainable as the investment cycle peaks and fades.
There are two reasons, I think, to be more optimistic about that transition. One is that, as Jan mentioned, the absolute rates of growth. We're going to have positive CapEx growth. We’re going to have positive earnings growth, so even if you're slowing to some degree, that impulse is still positive, and that should be helpful. That keeps valuations in check as well. The other is that there may be a kind of baton-passing from the people in the infrastructure providers, who have benefited a lot, to some of the other parts of the economy, hyperscalers or the broader economy, in terms of who is benefiting from the boom.
So our base case is that this will be a more benign version of that transition. But if you think of the risks, the risk is that some of these bigger aggregate shocks, energy, financial conditions, or just the market pulling forward that AI slowdown that's sitting further out, that those have a bigger impact. We're priced well for the baseline. On those downside risks, we're still vulnerable in terms of the way the market's priced at the moment.
Allison Nathan: Right. And while I asked you to focus on the downside risks, our mainline views are generally optimistic and steady growth. So just to be perfectly clear, your mainline expectations for asset markets is more upside.
Dom Wilson: Yeah. So the mainline expectation's positive for equities, and that is supported. The returns are less dramatic than we've seen for some of the last three years, but positive, and that positive baseline growth story and some of what we think on the inflation and policy side are important underpinnings to that. But what I would say is, if we get the risk cases, the market obviously has some vulnerability to those.
Allison Nathan: We'll dig a little bit more into that in a few minutes. But Jan, let me turn back to you and ask about jobs, always in focus. The labor market looks pretty solid. We got another relatively solid upside surprise on payrolls in the US, at least recently. But AI does seem to be showing up a little bit more in the numbers. So talk to us about that and the risks to the job market from AI.
Jan Hatzius: Yeah. It's a similar story to what we've been discussing. I think the baseline is one in which the unemployment rate stays low and pretty stable. We're at 4.1%, 4.2%, and we've been there really for the US since June. Our expectation for 2027 is also in that range. That shouldn't be surprising when the economy grows at 2% to 2.5%, that’s our estimate of potential growth. You should see the unemployment rate be stable.
Underneath the surface, we are starting to see somewhat more effects from AI. Our expectation over the next several years is that those effects are going to grow, and we'll get a temporary increase in the unemployment rate, or maybe a frictional increase, in the unemployment rate of something like half a percentage point, going into the 2028, 2029, early 2030s period. And that's really based on research that we and others have done that looks at historical positive productivity shocks and what those shocks do to unemployment. And you typically get a temporary increase.
We're in the very early stages of that, we think. We have now seen over the past several months, unlike a year or two ago, we have now seen a bit more broadening out of the relationship between AI adoption at the industry level and weaker labor market outcomes. There's now a correlation across industries between higher AI adoption and slower employment growth, and also between higher AI adoption and a somewhat higher unemployment rate.
Obviously, it's not dramatic, otherwise we wouldn't be printing these strong headline numbers. And there are also offsets from other sectors, for example, data center construction. But it is something that we're focused on as an important development and probably also a downside risk to the employment outlook as we go through 2027 and into the later part of the decade.
Allison Nathan: Yeah, very interesting. I do feel like our conversation last year, we weren't seeing it, and now we are. So very interesting to note.
Let's turn to inflation. Again, very much in focus. It has surprised sharply to the upside this year in the US in particular. We just got another unfriendly report this week, maybe some slightly better data today. But in general, concerning on the inflation side. Will it remain sticky, and how are the risks to your inflation views skewed?
Jan Hatzius: So clearly, inflation has come in much higher than we thought at the start of the year. I think most of that is related to some of these temporary shocks, especially the higher energy prices, and that's obviously very visible in terms of headline inflation.
But it's also fed through into core inflation, especially in the US, to a significant degree through channels such as airline fares, which have gone up very sharply on the back of higher jet fuel prices. There's also still basically residual pass-through from the tariff increases. We're estimating that at the moment that's still contributing about 40 basis points to the year-on-year rate of core PCE inflation.
So, if we add up the pass-through from tariffs and from energy prices, we can explain most of the overshoot of core PCE relative to the 2% target. We're in the low 3s for core PCE, and obviously, that's more than 100 basis points above the target.
But as we go into 2027, we think we'll see an improvement, a very substantial improvement, in part because the tariff pass-through fully basically evaporates sometime in early 2027, and in part because of this more benign view on oil prices, and in particular, the year-on-year change in oil prices, which will really become more benign, especially starting in March and April when we lap the outbreak of the war.
I'd also note that other broader measures of pressure on the economy, especially in the labor market, still look very benign. The labor market is, in our view, in balance. The unemployment rate is low, but not too low, but consistent with a balanced labor market. And wage growth has continued to decelerate in the US. We're now in the low to mid 3s on nominal wage growth, which is very reassuring. So that gives us core PCE inflation in the 2.4% range by the end of 2027.
Maybe just briefly on other economies. In general, the news flow on core inflation outside the US has actually been pretty good. In a lot of economies, you've seen lower-than-expected numbers for most of 2026 on core. Canada has been very benign. The euro area has generally been pretty benign. Even in the UK, where inflation had been higher than in most other DM economies, in general the news flow has been better. And while we do expect somewhat more pass-through from high energy prices, for example, in airline fares in Europe, in general our expectation is that we won't be too far above the target on core inflation in 2027.
Allison Nathan: If you go back to the US for a moment and we think about our mainline forecast, which is for a decline in inflation, do you think the risks, though, are tilted to the upside on inflation?
Jan Hatzius: I think the risks are tilted to the upside, in part because the risks to energy prices are tilted to the upside. So when we look at the range of scenarios from our commodity strategists, the upside scenario is quite a bit further from the baseline than the downside scenario, and that's clearly a source of upside risk.
Other than that, I could find areas of upside risk, for example, some additional increases in AI-related pricing, and some sources of downside risk. I think having the labor market and the softness in wage and unit labor costs feed through more to the overall core inflation numbers, I think that's a potential area of benign surprises.
Allison Nathan: Interesting. So we've talked about growth, we've talked about inflation. Let's talk about the Fed and other central banks, always a tremendous focus. The conversation around the Fed has really flipped. I was looking again back at our views last year, and there were expectations for rate cuts. Obviously, now the question is how many times will the Fed and potentially other central banks hike?
So, putting everything that you expect this year, again in terms of growth and inflation together, what are you expecting for the Fed and other major central banks?
Jan Hatzius: Yeah. The monetary policy path has been a big surprise. We came into the year thinking we could still get another couple of cuts, from the adjustment that we saw downward in 2025. But the sharp increase in inflation and the war sort of upended that forecast.
The Fed ended up moving to a hike at the September meeting. There is almost certainly a hike at the December meeting. There's even been a discussion about whether that hike is going to be 25 basis points or 50 basis points. Our expectation is that it's going to be 25 basis points. And then probably the FOMC is going to signal additional tightening for 2027 through the dot plot, which is again due at the December FOMC meeting.
We think there will be one additional hike in early 2027, I think more likely at the March meeting than at the January meeting, but that's really dependent on the economic data. We think that the next couple of inflation numbers, for November and December, are likely to look more friendly than what we had the last few months. In that case, I think that supports the idea that they wait until March to deliver the hike, but it certainly could be January as well.
Ultimately, we have a benign view on underlying inflation. We do think that a lot of the inflation overshoot that we're seeing at the moment is related to these more temporary forces, and that's going to cap the amount of tightening from the Fed at a level that's less than what markets are pricing now.
But obviously, it's going to ultimately depend on the data, because right now what you're hearing from Fed officials is clearly more hawkish than what we were hearing a few months ago, because the numbers have come in higher. So time will tell.
Allison Nathan: And what about the other major central banks?
Jan Hatzius: I would say the theme is very similar that markets are pricing more aggressive rate increases than what we think is likely.
As far as the European Central Bank goes, we have a hike at the December meeting, and then there's risk of another move in 2027, but it's not our baseline. So that's clearly less than what markets are pricing.
Similar story, I would say, in the UK: one hike from here, in this case in early 2027. So it's a similar theme, that we think markets are putting too much weight on what we think are ultimately temporary upward pressures on inflation.
One outlier is the Bank of Japan, where we're looking for three hikes from here to a terminal rate of 2%, and that's actually at or a little bit above current market pricing.
Allison Nathan: Dom, bond yield volatility has been a major focus of the markets. What does everything we’ve been discussion about inflation, about the central banks, and the Fed in particular, mean for bond yields from here which again are rising in the last couple of days.
And what would be the broader asset implications if we stay at these higher bond yields?
Dom Wilson: Yeah, look, as Jan said, the most obvious implication on our baseline view is that our policy views are more benign than the market in general. The fact that we have a friendlier inflation backdrop and a friendlier policy backdrop means that the baseline story is more friendly for bonds and for broader markets through that channel.
For government bonds, as you said, 2026 has been a difficult year. They've essentially been risk-additive for most of the year, with yields going up as equities go down. We think, certainly on that baseline, that 2027 is going to be a friendlier year, and I think there are a couple of things that are going on.
First, just in terms of the starting point, you have these higher yields going into it. Your running yield is higher, and so that gives you a decent buffer in terms of the returns you can get out of a bond. But I would say also with the inflation and policy views that we have, we also have a gradual decline in those yield levels, so in principle, on that path, you're going to get a bit of capital appreciation out of your bonds too, I think probably more likely as the year progresses and some of those tailwinds become more visible. So the overall environment for bond returns is, I think, as positive as we've seen it since 2020 on the forecasts.
I think the additional thing that has been shifting, which plays into the risks and also the risks of higher yields, is that mostly this year the risks have been heavily tilted in terms of inflation and policy shifts. The market got hit with the energy shock. It got hit with a tightening cycle that it wasn't expecting. Those risks are still there. We're in the middle of the hiking cycle. As Jan said, upside risk to energy gives you an upside skew to the inflation forecast, so there's vulnerability to that. And I think particularly in the next few months, we're going to be wrestling with that issue still, again with a bigger cushion against it because of the way the market's pricing.
But definetely we're still seeing scope for some upward risk to yields, and in general that has been a brake on asset markets. It's been a headwind for equities. Those risks we've been dealing with most of this year, and I think you're starting from a better place. Those risks are still there.
But as we move through the year, if you think of the risks that Jan started with, I think what's happening is that more of those risks over time are shifting towards things that might ultimately bring yields lower. If you think of the AI-related risks, both investment slowing but also job market risks from that front. If you think of the financial stresses that could come out of just higher rates in general, which we've seen now a little bit of, the sovereign risks from France and some other places, any of the fiscal risks showing up as pressure to tighten.
And so on bonds, I think, look, when we look at the balance of risks, there's more diversification benefit in terms of things that could drive yields lower than has been the case this year. We think that's probably something that's shifting slowly. The upside risks are still there, but the more you extend that horizon, the more valuable. You're getting a better yield, but you're also getting better protection against some of these bigger risks from bonds.
So I think it's going to be choppy. It's going to be, I think, still a complicated picture, but our view is generally a better picture than 2026.
Allison Nathan: Before we wrap up, Dom, a moment on the dollar. What does all of this mean for the outlook for the dollar?
Dom Wilson: Yeah, the dollar, I think, has a little bit of the same flavor as the bond market story. Coming into this year, the energy shock and the shift to tightening from the Fed have been relatively supportive for the dollar, at least compared to where we were going into 2025, with that long depreciation in the dollar that we saw then. So we've had a range-bound dollar for most of this year, but we're up at the top endd of that with those supportive forces.
Again, on the baseline, our view is that we're going to go back to some softening in the dollar. That's because that energy force should fade, and some of those Fed risks should fade out of the picture. That's probably most clearly true against some of the undervalued Asian currencies, the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan, for slightly different reasons. Both look cheap to us. You have a big trade surplus support for China. You have the policy rate support now in Japan, and also some of the shifting in the relative policy cycles there.
The euro is a little bit more complicated. Certainly over the next few months, we're dealing with the risks from energy, and we're dealing with some of the risks coming from the French election. We've thought of the euro as a funding currency, and I think that's probably still true, at least in the more immediate future. But I think some modest softening of the dollar is more likely through the year.
I think again going back to what we've said on a number of occasions, the AI theme and how that plays out is going to be important. Part of the premium that we've built into the dollar has been this sort of tech exceptionalism and the very big inflows that have come into the US equity market on the back of that theme. The more that holds up, the more sort of we're on the very positive path there, the more support we'll continue to give to the dollar. But any of those stories where the market starts to look through that, that AI investment impulse starts to fade, that's where you could get a clearer weakening than we've got in our forecasts. I would say that just makes the dollar a bit more cyclical around that axis than we've seen.
Allison Nathan: Jan, just to wrap up, what are you watching right now to understand better whether any of these downside risks are starting to materialize?
Jan Hatzius: It's really back to the three things that are most in focus.
One, what's happening in terms of Middle East relaxation or renewed escalation, and what does that mean for the energy impulse? That's really important for both the growth side and especially the inflation side.
Number two, what are we seeing on fiscal issues, tensions in the next several months going into the French election? I think that's a big focus.
And then everything related to AI investment and labor market effects. And there's a lot of news that we'll probably learn over just the next couple of quarters. We are expecting to see ongoing increases over the next few quarters, but then a deceleration as we go into the later part of the year. And of course, every labor market release we're going to scrutinize to see whether there's more evidence for AI-related changes.
Allison Nathan: So, Dom, given what Jan just said, and our mainline views which are relatively optimistic, how should investors be thinking about the landscape in 2027?
Dom Wilson:   Yeah, look the baseline scenario we have, is a pretty comfortable one. We're expecting out of that positive returns in equities not as positive as some of the very big returns in the recent years but decent. We're expecting positive returns on bonds. A little bit of underperformance in credit, but nothing too dramatic. And commodities delivering a flattish kind of return profile. But the overall picture is pretty friendly.
But I do think, to a greater extent than is normally true, thinking about those risks and making sure that portfolios are positioned in a way that is not vulnerable to those is a bigger deal than it has been.
And I would say specifically, I think that's true tactically. We've found already over the last few months that looking at where we are in terms of the pricing of the risk around AI and energy, as the market swung pretty hard backwards and forwards, gives you quite a good sense of where some of the opportunities are coming, month by month.
Structurally, I would say there are two things that come out of that.
One is diversification. As I said, bonds are a better diversifier for equities against some of these risks than they have been. And energy, although we're forecasting pretty low commodity returns, slightly negative, in fact, in the baseline for 2027, we think still offers a lot of value in a portfolio because of that upside tail risk that we're still worried about.
And then explicitly hedging portfolios. I think just in very general terms, equity index volatility has stayed relatively low. We think it's more likely to go up than down. We think options protection for portfolios. Lots of different ways you can do that, is probably, again, more valuable in this kind of environment with this sort of uncertainty than before. And some of these positions, either for higher energy prices, lots of different ways to do that too, or for much lower rates, in case some of these broader growth risks come down, are also things that are worth considering.
So I would say it's a comfortable baseline, but much more than before, you need to be careful, you need to be focused on those risks. And I think people should make sure that portfolios are adequately set up to deal with them.
Allison Nathan: Jan, Dom, thanks so much for joining us.
Dom Wilson: Thank you.
Jan Hatzius: Thank you.
Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Friday, November 13th, 2026. If you enjoyed the show, we hope you'll subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison Nathan. Thanks for listening.

Native voters are issue-driven and underserved by both parties

Gabriel R. Sanchez,

November 19, 2026

Native American voters favored Democratic congressional candidates in the 2026 midterms, with younger Native women far more likely than younger Native men to support Democrats.
Native Americans were motivated by Tribal-specific policies as well as economic factors, naming Tribal land rights (28%), missing and murdered Indigenous people (26%), Tribal sovereignty (26%) and water rights (22%) as the most important issues.
Sustained support for Native-led civic engagement, research, and voting access efforts is essential to ensuring that Tribal Nations and Native communities can fully exercise their rights and have their perspectives represented in decisions that affect them.

MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 8: People listen as Democratic Senate candidate, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan speaks during a get out the vote event at the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Twin Cities Office on Aug. 8, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

11 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

November is Native American Heritage Month, an ideal time to reflect on the Native American electorate’s contributions to the 2026 midterm elections and the accomplishments of candidates from this important yet often overlooked community. The number of Native candidates reached an all-time high in the midterms, with a record 363 running nationwide and 92 state legislative candidates winning their primaries. Among them, Native American women made historic wins in Tribal, state, and federal elections. In New Mexico, voters elected the nation’s first Native American female governor, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland (Laguna Pueblo), and in Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan (White Earth Nation) became the first Native woman elected to the U.S. Senate. And former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), a Yup’ik woman, most recently became the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate. This is in addition to the impact of the Native American vote across several House and Senate races, including in Arizona, Alaska, New Mexico, Maine, Michigan, and Minnesota.
Despite these historic victories, it is telling that there is little to no discussion about how Native Americans voted in this critical election, which resulted in a major shift in the federal balance of power. This is unfortunately not new in American politics. In fact, Native American voters are often completely overlooked in national political discussions, or worse, have their stories told inaccurately through flawed data.
Surveying Native American communities
The 2026 Midterm Election Voter Poll, conducted by the African American Research Collaborative (AARC) and BSP Research, addresses this issue by drawing from a nationally representative sample of Native American and Alaska Native voters (n=1,387, +/- 2.6%) so that their perspectives are part of the midterm conversation. This oversample, supported by First Nations Development Institute and Advance Native Political Leadership, was designed to be representative of the Native American electorate nationally. Here, we summarize the poll’s main findings.
These data enable comparisons of voting behavior with other racial and ethnic groups, as well as variation within the Native American population by factors such as whether respondents live on or near reservations and whether Tribal languages are spoken in their home, along with standard demographics like age and gender. For example, 27% of respondents reported speaking Tribal languages at home, and 43% live on or near their Tribal lands or Alaska Native village. The survey also excluded individuals with only a distant ancestral tie to Native communities. The poll’s authors support standardizing this practice, as collecting and publishing key demographics on Native American respondents produces more dependable and representative data. Far too often, other national polls do not employ similar efforts to ensure their samples include individuals who not only self-identify as Native American but also have meaningful connections to Tribal Nations and Native communities, including through ancestry, Tribal citizenship, enrollment, affiliation, or cultural ties.
Native voters favored Democrats over Trump and the GOP
Native American voters were more likely to vote for a Democrat in congressional races across the country, with 57% indicating they voted for a Democratic candidate for Congress compared to 41% who supported Republican candidates. Another 2% cast their ballots for a candidate from a different party. This is marginally higher than in 2022, when 56% of Native Americans reported voting for a Democrat compared to 40% for Republican candidates, according to the 2022 Midterm Election Voter Poll. This relative stability is consistent with the limited literature on Native American voting behavior, which suggests that Native American voters weigh candidates’ positions on issues affecting their Tribal Nations and Native communities alongside partisan affiliation.

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

One of the major themes of the post-election analysis has been the apparent losses for Trump and Republicans among voters of color. Thirteen percent of Native American voters who backed Trump in 2024 voted Democratic in the 2026 midterm elections. Part of these losses could be due to a belief that Republicans are hostile toward Native communities. In fact, when asked directly, 24% of Native Americans said the GOP is hostile to Native Americans, compared to 9% who felt that Democrats are hostile toward their community.

Figure 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Age and gender emerged as key factors shaping party preference, with the clearest differences appearing in younger voters. Among voters ages 18 to 39, Native women were more likely to support Democratic candidates than Native men (62% vs. 46%). This difference extends to perceptions of care toward Native American communities, with men under 40 being 15 points more likely than women in the same age group to report that the GOP “cares a great deal” about Native American communities. Similarly, when asked which party is better equipped to address their most important policy issue, Native men under 40 name4d the GOP more than Native women of the same age (41% vs. 27%). These results speak to the need for a better understanding of partisan alignment in Indian Country and could have implications for the 2028 elections as younger generations become a larger share of the Native American electorate.
Tribal priorities and economic concerns drove Native voters
As noted above, the literature suggests this community is motivated by policy priorities in addition to partisanship. A strength of this survey is that it provides more policy context than the standard federal policy priorities (such as the economy and inflation) common in most exit polls. When asked what the most important issues are for Native American communities, respondents named Tribal land rights (28%), missing and murdered Indigenous people (26%), Tribal sovereignty (26%), and water rights (22%).

Figure 4

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

It was clear in the 2026 midterm election poll that a candidate’s position on Tribal sovereignty mattered to Native American voters regardless of political party, as seen in Figure 1. Nearly 9 in 10 (89%) Native American respondents said that they considered Tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, and related issues when deciding candidate to support, 11 points higher than in the 2024 American Electorate Poll. This was also evident across parties, with 92% of Native American Democrats, 85% of independents, and 90% of Republicans considering Tribal sovereignty in their candidate choice.
Respondents were also asked to identify the most important issues Congress and the president should address. The economy, including the cost of living, jobs, and health care costs, was a top concern for Native American voters, similar to the electorate overall. Cost of living and inflation ranked highest (55%), with respondents particularly concerned about food (57%), housing (41%), gas (38%), and utilities (37%). Other leading priorities included jobs and the broader economy (34%), health care costs (31%), housing affordability (30%), and gas prices (29%). When asked which party would best address their top concerns, 45% selected Democrats, compared with 31% who selected Republicans.
These priorities reflect the severe economic inequalities facing Native Americans, especially in recent years as the nation has experienced tremendous financial strain and many federal program cuts. This likely shaped policy preferences, as nearly 2 in 3 Native American voters said raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour as one of the most important or a very important issue in their candidate choice.
Outreach fell short and barriers persisted for Native voters in 2026
In closing, we draw on the survey data to show that there is significant room to improve how we engage Native American communities in federal elections, including by addressing the many barriers facing those who are already trying to vote.
Native voters were among the least contacted in 2026, a consistent trend across elections. The 2026 poll indicates that Native Americans were the least contacted racial/ethnic group in the sample, with half (49%) saying no one contacted them to vote. This is a strong reminder that despite the investment by presidential candidates in 2024 in outreach to Native American voters, there remains a tremendous need for sustained, culturally responsive civic engagement that reflects the distinct circumstances of Native communities.
Among Native American voters contacted about registering or voting in 2026, Democratic outreach slightly exceeded Republican outreach (47% vs. 44%). Respondents also reported contact from nonpartisan or civic organizations (21%), Native or community organizations (18%), and ballot initiative campaigns (15%).
Another far too common experience for Native Americans seeking to voice their opinions in federal elections is encountering obstacles when voting. More than one-third of Native American voters (37%) encountered at least one barrier when voting, including long lines, long drives, voting machines not working, and harassment outside the ballot drop-off area. Obstacles were more common among respondents who live in Tribal areas or reservations, with 26% reporting long waits in line and 11% having to drive a long way to reach their ballot box.
These obstacles are also reflected in broader concerns about voting access, as more than half (57%) of Native American voters were worried that voting rights were under attack and that the current environment was making it harder for people to vote and participate in democracy. That worry shapes policy preferences, with 77% of Native American voters backing a new voting rights act to eliminate these hurdles.
Native American organizations, along with others, are advocating for a new voting rights act that addresses the unique barriers Native Americans face when voting. Native-led organizations are already doing important work to strengthen Native civic partnership and representation. Across the country, these organizations are registering and engaging Native voters; challenging barriers to equal access through litigation that protects Native voting rights and advances fair maps; and preparing Native leaders to organize for change and serve in elected office. Together, this work is building the infrastructure Native communities need to overcome barriers to full participation in our democracy and shape the decisions that affect their lives. Sustained support for Native-led civic engagement, research, and voting access efforts is essential to ensuring that Tribal Nations and Native communities can fully exercise their rights and have their perspectives represented in the decisions that affect them.

articles.title: Japan’s forthcoming national security and defense strategies: Watch this space | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Japan’s forthcoming national security and defense strategies: Watch this space

Adam P. Liff

Adam P. Liff

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center for Asia Policy Studies

November 16, 2026

In December 2026, Japan’s government is set to announce a major update to its national security strategy, national defense strategy, and defense buildup program—years ahead of schedule.
Widespread public recognition of Japan’s worsening security environment, the Liberal Democratic Party’s lower house supermajority and new coalition partner, and significant pressure from Washington to “do more” will provide a significant tailwind for the Takaichi government’s ambitious defense reform agenda—much of which is already known.
Nevertheless, the final details will matter, and Japan’s complicated politics, severe fiscal challenges, and other factors will counsel caution as the Takaichi government puts the finishing touches on “the three security documents.”
As Tokyo and Washington chart the way forward into 2027, more proactive, positive, and constructive U.S.-Japan cooperation—including alongside other U.S. allies and partners—will be critical to strengthening deterrence in an increasingly dangerous region and world.

Members of an honour guard prepare before the arrival of Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty for a meeting with Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi at the Ministry of Defence in Tokyo on June 24, 2026. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP via Getty Images)

12 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Since Sanae Takaichi became Japan’s prime minister one year ago, her ruling coalition has carried out a strikingly ambitious national security reform agenda.
During the first 10 months of 2026, the Takaichi government raised Japan’s defense-related spending to reach a 2% of GDP target (two years ahead of schedule), significantly loosened a long-standing prohibition on lethal arms exports, oversaw Japan’s first deliveries of U.S. Tomahawk missiles, enacted stricter critical technology supply-chain protection measures, announced major investments in “strategic sectors,” and launched a new National Intelligence Bureau.
By year’s end, the government will also revise what policy analysts call the “three security documents”—Japan’s national security strategy (NSS), national defense strategy (NDS), and defense buildup program (DBP). All three documents were last updated in December 2022 under Prime Minister Fumio Kishida.
Following months of intragovernment reviews, final deliberations within the ruling coalition have just begun. Takaichi will receive an expert committee’s final report in early December. After that, it is up to her and her cabinet to decide the final content and release the documents publicly.
This is the first entry in a Brookings series examining Japan’s forthcoming “three security documents.” It provides an overview of the reasons for Japan’s significantly accelerated revision timeline, the recent domestic political realignment that will shape the outcome, and several defense priorities likely to feature prominently in the new documents.
Why now? Why so far ahead of schedule?
That the current “three documents” are set to be revised this year is itself significant. All three were updated less than four years ago. The NSS and NDS were originally intended to remain in effect for roughly a decade. Even the DBP, meanwhile, was a five-year plan.
Calls to significantly accelerate the revision timeline began circulating long before Takaichi took office and were already mainstream by mid-2025. Thus, by the time she made the official announcement after becoming prime minister, support was widespread. The reasons were hardly a state secret. The 2022 NSS had already defined Japan’s security environment as the worst since World War II; by the end of 2025, circumstances had significantly worsened.
In explaining the rationale for moving up the revision timelines, the 2026 Defense White Paper stressed the urgency of strengthening Japan’s “comprehensive national power,” encompassing its diplomatic, defense, economic, technological, intelligence, and human resource capabilities. Stated motivations include:

Challenges to the “free and open international order based on the rule of law” (hō no shihai ni motozuku jiyū de hirakareta kokusai chitsujo), such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and nuclear saber-rattling.
China’s and North Korea’s military buildups, deepening Sino-Russian and Russia-North Korea security cooperation, and China’s repeated “attempts to unilaterally change the status quo” in the East China Sea and South China Sea.
Lessons learned from the war in Ukraine, especially the proliferation of inexpensive unmanned assets and the urgent need for more robust munitions stockpiles and resilient defense production and technological bases.

Providing additional impetus for the expedited review have been growing concerns, especially since early 2025, about the United States’ mercurial foreign policy and treatment of its allies.
Against this backdrop, the new documents are all but certain to seek further “fundamental reinforcement of Japan’s defense capabilities” through significantly higher defense spending, and to accelerate progress along the three tracks at the heart of Japan’s 2013 and 2022 national security strategies: (1) strengthening Japan’s own capabilities; (2) bolstering ties with its U.S. ally; and (3) expanding security cooperation with third parties, particularly Australia, the U.K., and other U.S. allies in the Western Pacific and Europe. The new strategies also seem primed to marry the Japanese government’s long-standing emphasis on “deterring unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion” with calls for “denial defense/deterrence by denial”—thereby aligning with the recent U.S. and Australian defense strategies.
Although the three documents’ defense-related aspects will attract the greatest attention in Washington and other capitals, the overarching NSS itself addresses a much broader range of issues. As a hint of what’s likely to come, the Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) revision proposal highlighted diplomatic and economic concerns, including “the weaponization of economies” (keizai no bukika). Accordingly, economic security considerations will likely loom large and will be the focus of a separate piece in this series. The proposal additionally emphasized diplomacy, multilateral cooperation, and building up Japan’s production capacity—and not only in the defense space.
A political tailwind for an ambitious security reform agenda
There has been remarkably limited domestic backlash to Japan’s striking defense spending increases and substantial policy shifts since the Kishida government released the 2022 documents, including the Takaichi government’s own bold moves. This relative lack of widespread or sustained opposition is a testament to how much Japan’s worsening security environment and corresponding shifts in public opinion have reshaped the political environment over the past 15 years.
Although many of the headline-making defense-related developments of the past year stemmed from decisions and seeds planted before Takaichi took office, next month’s strategic updates offer her government its clearest—and likely most legacy-defining—opportunity to put its stamp on the future of Japan’s foreign and defense policy.
Two bold and consequential political decisions Takaichi made last autumn and winter are particularly salient for understanding the transformed political context in which the ruling coalition is carrying out these reforms:
First, in October 2025, after Komeito, the LDP’s longtime coalition partner, abruptly left the ruling coalition following Takaichi’s election as LDP president, the soon-to-be prime minister invited a conservative Osaka-based party, the Japan Innovation Party (Nippon Ishin no Kai, or “Ishin”), to take its place. In so doing, Takaichi replaced Komeito and its largely pacifistic support base—which had frustrated security policy reforms under LDP prime ministers for nearly a quarter-century—with a reformist party more ideologically aligned with her and the LDP’s conservative wing. In fact, on several key defense-related issues, Ishin’s positions are more forward-leaning than the LDP mainstream.
Put another way: whereas Komeito had for decades acted in the defense space as a “brake” (hadome) on ambitious LDP prime ministers like Shinzo Abe, Ishin functions more as an accelerant.
Second, in January 2026, Takaichi made the extraordinary decision to capitalize on her personal popularity and call a snap election. When voters went to the polls on February 8, they granted the LDP the largest Lower House supermajority of any political party since World War II.
Despite this apparent political wind at their back, Takaichi and her allies will continue to strike a careful balance on the most contentious issues in the months and years ahead. For starters, the LDP lacks a majority in the Upper House, and neither the party (with a 22.1% support rate at the time of writing) nor its policy agenda is nearly as popular as its Lower House supermajority suggests. Meanwhile, although Takaichi is only the latest in a long line of LDP prime ministers since the party’s 1955 founding to call for revising the 1947 Japanese Constitution’s famous Article 9 “peace clause,” doing so remains an extremely tall order politically. Political pragmatism, legal constraints, and Japan’s sobering fiscal situation all counsel caution as they chart the way forward.
Spaces to watch in the national defense strategy
Japanese elite and public recognition of Japan’s worsening security environment, the LDP’s lower house supermajority, and preelection coalition realignment, as well as significant pressure from Washington to “do more,” all provide a significant political tailwind for the Takaichi government’s ambitious reform agenda.
Space constraints prevent a full accounting of the wide array of policies, platforms, capabilities, and institutional reforms under consideration for inclusion in the new “three documents.” Specific to Japan’s defense strategy, the first of the aforementioned “three tracks”—Japan’s efforts to bolster its own capabilities—is likely to receive the greatest investment and attention. Details have yet to be finalized, and the LDP and Ishin must still iron out their differences on several key issues. Nevertheless, the LDP’s June proposal to the government is highly suggestive of what’s to come. In addition to strengthening the U.S.-Japan alliance and expanding security cooperation, industrial collaboration, and exercises and training with the United States and other like-minded partners, several key priorities will likely be:

Improving the Self-Defense Forces’ ability to respond to “new ways of warfare” (atarashii tatakaikata), including artificial intelligence and the mass deployment of inexpensive unmanned assets.
Bolstering long-range, precision-strike, air defense, and cross-domain capabilities, including in space, cyber, and the electromagnetic spectrum.
Addressing vulnerabilities in sea lanes, especially so-called “gaps” (areas) in the Western Pacific where Japan’s ability to defend its interests is limited.
Ensuring “combat sustainment capabilities” (keisen nōryoku iji), including robust munitions stockpiles, necessary for a prolonged conflict.
Investing in a robust and effective human talent base through reforms to recruitment, compensation, and organizational culture.
Strengthening domestic production and technology bases, promoting equipment transfers, and boosting surge capacity and supply chain resilience.
Enhancing cooperation and communication with local communities.

The LDP and Ishin submitted separate proposals to the government this past summer, rather than a joint one, raising questions about what will ultimately be included. In recent weeks, three as-yet-unresolved issues have attracted particular attention in Tokyo:

What, if any, concrete pledge will the government make regarding defense spending? For decades, Japan kept its core defense budget pegged to the normatively symbolic figure of 1% of GDP. The Kishida government’s 2022 commitment to surge that budget by roughly two-thirds over five years was a game-changer and laid the foundation for much of the progress achieved over the past four years. The Takaichi government is well aware of the Trump administration’s demands that allies pledge to reach 3.5% of GDP for core defense spending by the mid-2030s. But Tokyo has repeatedly indicated that it will make its own sovereign decision.
If the government does offer a specific spending or percentage-of-GDP target in the new documents, will it apply to core defense spending or to a broader category of what the government often refers to as “defense-related” or “national security-related” spending? The distinction is hardly academic. Four years ago, widespread—but erroneous—assertions that Japan had pledged to “double its defense budget” obscured the differences between the two categories. Meeting the 3.5% target for core defense spending would be extremely difficult for Japan given its fiscal, demographic, and other challenges. Nevertheless, a commitment to significant spending increases seems likely. Regardless of the precise figure, Japan increasing investments effectively and efficiently, including in coordination with the United States and other partners, matters more for deterrence than any arbitrary “percentage-of-GDP” target.

What, if anything, will the documents say about “nuclear-powered” submarines and the 1967 prohibition on introducing (presumably U.S.) nuclear weapons onto Japan’s territory? These are two issues where Ishin’s entry into the ruling coalition has immediately reshaped Japan’s defense policy debate, and in which its differences with the LDP mainstream may be significant. (Note: Contrary to widespread misunderstanding, neither of these questions relates to Japan itself developing or acquiring nuclear weapons.)
The operational desirability and feasibility of Japan acquiring nuclear-powered submarines remains heavily contested. Such a move would also raise important political and legal questions and carry significant opportunity costs; for instance, construction costs alone could be 10 times greater than those of Japan’s most advanced diesel-powered submarines. If the documents include any references to nuclear-powered submarines, precise wording will matter: a pledge to merely “consider” or “conduct research” should not be understood as a commitment to acquire them. As for whether the documents may explicitly modify the third of Japan’s “three non-nuclear principles”1 to allow, say, nuclear-armed U.S. vessels to enter Japanese ports or waters, the jury is still out.

Japan and the United States face immense challenges in a rapidly worsening East Asian and global security environment. As Tokyo and Washington chart the way forward into 2027, more proactive, positive, and constructive U.S.-Japan cooperation—including alongside other U.S. allies and partners—will be critical to strengthening deterrence in an increasingly unstable region and world.
The first 10 months of 2026 have marked a significant year for Japan’s national security and defense policy. With the Takaichi government’s revision of the “three security documents” around the corner, it is sure to be one for the history books.

articles.title: How Chain, Our AI Workspace, Helps Investigators Fight Crime - Chainalysis
articles.text:
The biggest hack in crypto history is also likely the most complex. Binance’s attackers are weaponizing automation in their race to launder billions of dollars in stolen crypto.But Chainalysis’ first responders have our newest weapon: Chain. With our AI-native workspace, we’re tracing stolen funds as they spread over tens of thousands of addresses. The launderers want Binance’s money to outpace the tracers. With Chain, we’re not letting them.Chain is the culmination of everything we’ve built over 12 years of following the money. It brings together Chainalysis attributions, the analytical expertise behind millions of investigations, and the flexibility of conversation, blending it together wherever our investigators and researchers work.So when hackers began draining billions from the world’s largest crypto exchange around 4:00pm on a Thursday, our team, armed with Chain, set off.Chain has three core capabilities useful in a crisis, as well as in everyday work: it will converse with you, it will create with you, and it will codify your labor-saving workflows. Our team used all three in responding to Binance.ConverseChain puts Chainalysis intelligence to work through conversation. Ask it a question, and it answers using the breadth of our on-chain knowledge.Our investigators held round-the-clock conversations with Chain to understand how the Binance hackers were laundering funds. Their first task was determining where to look: the attackers initially held the stolen crypto across nearly a dozen different blockchains. And they were making this map even harder to navigate by moving the funds over bridges.Rather than manually search through different blockchains, our investigators simply asked Chain: find corresponding bridge transactions.“The data was really strong,” one of our investigators said. “We didn’t need external APIs, we didn’t need explorers, we didn’t need custom scripts. We could just say, ‘Hey Chain, go find the corresponding bridge transactions,’ and it would go and do it.”CreateChain turns intelligence into the outputs investigators need. Describe what you want—a graph, a report, a brief—and Chain helps build it.Our research team utilized Chain’s creative output to chart out the impact of the Binance hack. They wanted to compare this singularly large hack to the long history of North Korean-linked thefts.Because Chain is stocked with over 12 years-worth of attribution data, it readily puts historical data points like these into context. That’s exactly what it did here. The research team came with a request—what share of annual losses to crypto hacks are North Korean hackers responsible for?— and worked collaboratively with Chain to plot out an answer.“When time is of the essence, you need to be able to collate facts quickly, correctly, and from a wide variety of sources, ” said Head of Research Eric Jardine. “Chain let us take our corpus of existing DPRK-linked hacks and flesh out other events from publicly reachable online sources. This rapid, iterative process allowed us to create a definitive dataset of DPRK-linked events, from which we could understand the trend in events and the sheer enormity of North Korea’s role in the hacking ecosystem.”CodifyTracing frenetic flows one wallet at a time can’t keep up when attackers use automation to move billions of dollars. Chain helps investigators turn their own methods into Automations that handle repeatable tracing work.Our investigators noticed the hackers’ laundering practices fit recognizable patterns. They were breaking huge sums into manageable chunks. Then they were moving those chunks through known laundering routes, like DeFi protocols that swap one token for another.Those patterns are where Chain made the difference. Once investigators understood a pattern, they could build an Automation in Chain to handle the repetitive tracing work. They applied that workflow to one deliberately convoluted laundering flow in which the attackers were swapping stablecoins back and forth.“We built an automation in Chain that said: take the address, find the swap to one stablecoin, find the recipient of that stablecoin, find the swap back to another stablecoin, and then figure out where it went,” one investigator explained. He called this automated workflow one item of Chain’s “recipe book” for tracing the flow of funds.A reactor graph of on-chain flows that Chain can codify into a workflow.Chain’s recipe book of automations give us and our customers — among them exchanges and law enforcement — the best chance to disrupt threat actors. Our private sector partners can better manage their risk exposure on their platforms, and law enforcement can develop intelligence, secure evidence and know where to seize assets.What’s next for ChainOur investigators now use Chain in their day-to-day work. That work is strengthened by partnerships like the Digital Crime Task Force, which we launched with TRON and Tether to proactively identify and disrupt financial crime.The capabilities our investigators relied on during the Binance response are what we’re now excited to bring to customers. With Chain, compliance, risk and investigations teams can get answers they can act on, build what they need, and turn their best methods into Automations that scale across the organization.As bad actors adopt new technology, the teams working to stop them need to move just as fast. Chain is now in limited preview. Register for early access to learn more.

13 November 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Tactical plays within a diversified allocation
Our calls to dial down risk since early October have helped mitigate a bear market in semiconductors and the sharpest single-day post-mid-term election downturn in US equities in over three decades.
Volatility has eased after the post-election spike, helping the IT sector partly recover. We see further upside in our opportunistic US IT and healthcare sector equity ideas.
A strong job market is likely to keep the Fed focused on lowering inflation, cementing the prospect of a December rate hike, potentially followed by another in Q1 2027. A strong economy and elevated interest rates support our overweight allocation to US financial sector equities.
In bonds, we lock in gains on US inflation-protected bonds as inflation nears a peak.

Where do you see the most favourable risk-reward within the US tech sector?

How do falling oil prices and hot US inflation data impact your Fed and bonds outlook?

Does the USD rally have further to run?

Charts of the week: Volatility drops, reviving tactical plays

US equity volatility has dropped after a spike; we stay bullish on US IT equities and lock in gains in inflation-linked bonds

US S&P500 volatility (VIX) and volatility of volatility (VVIX) indices

US IT sector equities total return index

US government inflation-linked 1-10 years total return index*

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered. *Initiated on 11 April 2025.
Editorial

Tactical plays within a diversified allocation

Strategy summary: Our calls to dial down risk since early October have helped mitigate a bear market in semiconductors and the sharpest single-day post-mid-term election downturn in US equities in over three decades. Volatility has eased after the post-election spike, helping the IT sector partly recover. We see further upside in our opportunistic US IT and healthcare sector equity ideas. In bonds, we lock in gains on US inflation-protected bonds as inflation nears a peak.
Navigating volatility. Almost five weeks ago, we cut our semiconductor segment equity exposure as market breadth narrowed ahead of the US election. Two weeks ago, we cut equities from Overweight to a core allocation, positioning for mid-cycle market dynamics. Last week, as the US equity market volatility index VIX surged above 25, we partially dialled up risk with a tactical idea on the more diversified US IT sector.
Staying tactical within a diversified allocation. Equity volatility following last week’s Democratic clean sweep in the US elections has subsided. Questions about the pace of AI data centre buildout are likely to linger until Democrats take office in in January. Nvidia’s turmoil adds uncertainty. We remain broadly diversified and balanced in our core allocation across assets, sector and regions, while seeking tactical opportunities. History suggests sharp selloffs are followed by near-term volatility, particularly during macroeconomic stress. However, the balance of historical outcomes has typically shifted strongly to the upside over a three- to six-month horizon. Besides, historically, US equity markets have delivered the strongest 12-month returns after opposition clean sweeps in the mid-terms.
Rotation driving US IT sector recovery: As volatility eases, our opportunistic US IT equities idea, launched a week ago, has performed well, despite some significantly negative company specific developments. Attractive valuations support further upside. Investors are rotating within IT from semiconductors, affected by concerns over the pace of AI data centre buildout and Nvidia’s troubles, towards software and hardware providers. The latter have strong cash flows and balance sheets and are likely to benefit from AI monetisation. Together, they account for more than 60% of the IT sector (see page 4).
.

Remain constructive on US healthcare. US healthcare earnings are projected to grow almost 23% in 2027, the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors. We see scope for further upside in the sector as innovation underpins long-term earnings growth. With the market rotating away from concentrated AI exposure, healthcare’s stable, non-cyclical demand profile offers a compelling exposure as a diversifier (see page 5).
Outside the US, Switzerland and India offer diversified returns. The Swiss equity market consists of 41% healthcare, 19% financial services and 14% consumer staples, providing a defensive alternative to investors seeking to diversify away from tech-heavy exposure. The Indian equity market has been classified as an “anti-AI” trade. Historically narrow valuation premiums vs. EMs, low foreign investor positioning and c. 15% expected 2027 earnings growth make it an attractive diversifier.
Strong jobs and inflation reports cement December Fed rate hike. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice the 70,000 consensus estimate. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Meanwhile, headline and core inflation in October, at 0.4% and 0.3% m/m, respectively, exceeded expectations as elevated fuel prices, ‘techflation’ and earlier tariffs fed into directly exposed sectors, including food, utilities and transportation services. A healthy job market keeps the Fed focused on lowering inflation, cementing the prospect of a December rate hike, potentially followed by another in Q1 2027. A strong economy and elevated interest rates support our overweight allocation to US financial sector equities.
Locking in gains from our bullish US inflation-protected bonds idea. While near-term price pressures remain elevated, we expect inflation to ease with energy costs over the coming year. Republicans’ heavy losses in the US mid-term elections increase pressure on the Trump administration to end the Iran conflict. One-year US inflation expectations have slumped alongside oil prices. A potential slowdown in the pace of AI buildout is also likely to ease techflation. Meanwhile, Fed rate hikes should further tighten financial conditions, tempering price pressures. This disinflationary outlook makes the risk-reward for US inflation-protected bonds less compelling. We close the idea, locking in a 4.4% gain (page 6).
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as neutral for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Strong US job market; improving US consumer sentiment(-)factors: Hotter-than-expected US inflation; rising odds of Fed hikes

US headline and core consumer price inflation

China’s consumer inflation eased further, while factory-gate prices accelerated in October
China consumer and producer price inflation
