Top client questions

What does history tell us about the aftermath of a single-day sell-off of 4% or more in the S&P500 index?

Our view: The S&P500 fell 4.36% on 5 November 2026, a rare daily move of 3.8 standard deviations. Since 2009, there have been only 24 occasions when the index declined by 4% or more in a single session. The immediate aftermath of such sell-offs has historically been mixed. One-month returns ranged from around -15% to +23%, with positive returns in 70% of cases. The weaker outcomes were concentrated around periods of significant macro stress, including the tail end of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 monetary policy tightening cycle.
The historical picture becomes considerably more constructive beyond the first month. All 24 episodes generated positive three-month returns, ranging from roughly +0.5% to +38%, while six-month returns were positive in 96% of cases, with gains reaching as much as +49%. Overall, history suggests sharp sell-offs can be followed by near-term volatility, particularly during periods of broader macro stress. However, the balance of historical outcomes has shifted strongly to the upside over a 3-6-month horizon.
— Maggie Au Yeung, Quantitative Analyst— Francis Lim, Senior Quantitative Strategist

S&P500 forward returns following large sell-offs
Average forward returns for S&P500 index following sharp sell-offs

Source: Bloomberg, Standard CharteredNote: 1. Since 2009 • 23 completed events • November 2026 excluded. 2. Hit rate refers to % of positive returns

Where do you see the most favourable risk-reward within the US technology sector?

Our view: We favour high-quality Big Tech companies with strong balance sheets and prefer diversified exposure through our US Information Technology (IT) opportunistic idea.
Rationale: The recent pullback in US semiconductor stocks has improved their risk-reward profile. Earnings for these companies are forecast to grow by 65% in 2027, the fastest rate among technology subsectors. Despite this outlook, recent regulatory and corporate governance concerns are weighing on sentiment. Potential state-level restrictions on data centre development following the recent US mid-term election results could weigh on semiconductor demand growth. However, we believe these risks are manageable and continued AI adoption should support demand for AI inference. We prefer diversified exposure to quality semiconductor companies with durable demand and strong volume growth.
To navigate volatility in the US technology sector, we favour Big Tech companies with strong balance sheets and resilient cash generation, as they are better positioned to sustain AI investments without relying heavily on external financing. Our US IT opportunistic idea combines these preferences through exposure to semiconductors, software and hardware, allowing investors to participate in a potential recovery across a broader range of earnings drivers.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

The semiconductor segment is expected to continue to lead US technology earnings growth in 2027
Consensus earnings growth (y/y) by US technology subsector, 2025-27 (%)

Source: FactSet, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Do fundamental drivers support a constructive view on the US healthcare sector?

Our view: We remain constructive on US healthcare, supported by its defensive characteristics and robust earnings growth.
Rationale: US healthcare earnings are projected to grow by 22.5% in 2027, the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors, driven by improving biopharma earnings. The US healthcare sector’s valuation gap against the broader market has been recovering from a steep historical discount a year ago. The sector’s forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of c. 20x now exceeds the broader US market’s c. 18.4x, but we see scope for the valuation to be supported amid investor demand for defensive growth. The sector’s broad legislative policy overhang has materially faded following the US election cycle, while targeted regulatory and oversight risks remain on the watchlist.
Healthcare innovation also underpins structural growth. Wider adoption of obesity and diabetes treatments, alongside advances in oncology treatments, medical devices and robotic surgery, should support long-term earnings growth. With the market rotating away from concentrated AI exposure, healthcare’s stable, non-cyclical demand profile presents compelling opportunities for investors seeking both defensiveness and growth in the near term.
— Jason Wong, Senior Equity Analyst

US healthcare sector earnings are projected to grow 22.5% in 2027 – the second-fastest among MSCI US sectors

Consensus 2027 earnings growth by sector in the S&P500 Index

Source: LSEG I/B/E/S, Standard Chartered

What is your outlook for China’s Big Tech sector?

Our view: We remain positive on China’s Big Tech sector, consistent with our Overweight stance on the country’s IT and communication services sector.
Rationale: Valuations across China’s technology sector remain inexpensive at 14.2x, with investor attention centred on whether AI-driven revenue can offset elevated AI-related spending, which is currently compressing margins. Elevated AI capex and negative free cash flow remain key investor concerns in the Q3 earnings season. Top-line momentum also remains uneven: soft domestic consumption continues to weigh on e-commerce, advertising and local services, whereas gaming and cloud computing are delivering resilient growth. The broader narrative is steadily transitioning towards commercialisation, with rapid enterprise penetration by AI workplace agents and upcoming AI model launches shifting the market focus towards active deployment and conversion to paid usage. Evolving regulatory frameworks covering AI governance, agent self-regulation, tax scrutiny and compliance requirements remain important variables influencing medium-term margin trajectories. Ultimately, valuation support, gradual monetisation of AI capabilities and resilient core segments support our Overweight positioning.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

China’s technology sector valuations remain inexpensive at 14.2x, nearly 1 standard deviation below the mean
Hang Seng Technology (HSTECH Index) 12-month forward P/E ratio

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Why are you closing your US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) opportunistic idea?

Our view: We are closing our opportunistic bullish US TIPS position, as the risk-reward profile has become less compelling. The trade returned 4.4% since its initiation on 11 April 2025.
Rationale: We initiated an opportunistic bullish position in US TIPS on 11 April 2025 as an oil and inflation hedge, expecting geopolitical uncertainty to keep inflation expectations elevated. The risk-reward, however, has since become less compelling, as hawkish Fed commentary, easing geopolitical risks and a potential slowdown in the pace of AI buildout are now likely to ease broader inflation and ‘techflation’ pressures. We have therefore closed the opportunistic idea, realising a gain of 4.4%.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

While real (net-of-inflation) yields remain elevated, the inflation-protection function of US TIPS has diminished as inflation expectations ease
One-year USD inflation swap, 10-year US real yield

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

How do falling oil prices and October’s US inflation data affect your Fed and bond market outlook?

Our view: Our base case envisages two further 25bps Fed hikes by mid-2027, with scope for cuts in H2 2027 if energy prices remain consistently lower and growth trajectory normalises. We favour income over chasing duration gains, focusing on higher-quality corporate bonds with 3-7-year maturities.
Rationale: Lower oil prices have a two-sided effect: they ease inflationary pressures and support growth by boosting purchasing power and lowering business costs. Cheaper energy, therefore, does not automatically justify Fed easing. Our base case envisages two further 25bps hikes by mid-2027, with scope for cuts in H2 2027 if energy prices remain consistently lower. Sustained moderation in core inflation would challenge the near-term tightening path. However, October’s US consumer inflation print reinforced our assessment that each Fed meeting now remains a ‘live’ decision.
With the US 10-year government bond yield already within our 5.0-5.25% 3-month range, we favour income over chasing duration gains. Credit performance has diverged: Developed Market high-yield bonds have outperformed both investment-grade credit and government bonds. Credit still offers attractive income, and we retain our preference for 3-7-year maturities, although heavy primary issuance remains a counterweight. We favour selective carry, with a preference for higher-quality corporate bonds. These include bonds issued by leading AI hyperscalers, where risk-reward has become more attractive. Our emphasis is on generating steady income, rather than relying on further declines in bond yields or spreads.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

Corporate bonds still offer attractive income, but fundamental quality matters
Total returns of Bloomberg US government, US investment-grade corporate, US BB-rated high-yield and US CCC-rated high-yield indices over the last 12 months

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Does the USD’s rally have further to run?

Our view: Further upside appears limited. Stronger-than-expected US core inflation in October and hawkish Fed comments have pushed the US Dollar Index (DXY) above 103. However, markets already price in more Fed tightening than we expect. We see the DXY returning to its 101.00-102.95 range in the near term, before gradually weakening towards our 12-month forecast of 98.5.
Rationale: US core consumer prices rose 0.3% m/m in October, above the 0.2% m/m expected, meeting Fed Governor Waller’s threshold for considering a 50bps December rate hike. This pushed US government bond yields higher, supporting the USD rally. However, futures now imply a Fed rate peak of 4.50-4.75% by mid-2027, compared with our expectation of 4.25-4.50% following two 25bps hikes, one in December and the second in H1 2027. We expect the Fed to begin easing in H2 2027. As market expectations gradually converge towards our view, USD support from US bond yields should weaken.
Meanwhile, falling oil and petrol prices should help ease headline inflation in the coming months, reducing pressure for further Fed tightening. This reinforces our expectation of limited USD upside, although persistent services inflation remains a key risk.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist

US dollar index’s rally above 103 looks stretched

USD index (DXY) and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Do you expect USD/JPY to sustainably break out above 160 in the near term?

Our view: We see USD/JPY rangebound with a downside bias, as growing BoJ tightening expectations and potential policy convergence will support gradual JPY appreciation.
Rationale: Renewed tech optimism has encouraged the re-establishment of carry trades, providing support to the pair lately. Meanwhile, US core inflation beat expectations for a third consecutive month in October, reinforcing expectations for a December Fed hike. Further upside inflation surprises could widen the US-Japan interest rate differential and push USD/JPY higher.
However, the risk of intervention by Japan’s Ministry of Finance is likely to rise materially around 160, limiting the scope for sustained upside. On the downside, a 25bps BoJ hike to 1.50%, accompanied by clear signals of consecutive hikes in March and June 2027, would be a significant yen-positive catalyst. A more non-linear downside scenario would be a disorderly equity sell-off, which could trigger rapid JPY appreciation through carry-trade unwinding. We see scope for the pair to test support towards 156 in the coming weeks.
— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

Global Markets and EconomyIndustry Perspectives Episode 8GROWTH: Asia-Pacific’s Investing MomentumIndustry Perspectives • Podcast • November 20, 2026View TranscriptIn Episode 7, Citi and ICI mapped the global forces reshaping capital markets. In Episode 8, the lens narrows.Hosts Amanda Hale and Andrew Newson are joined again by ICI for a market-by-market tour of the Asia-Pacific region: five of the most dynamic and consequential financial markets in the world, each at a different stage of the retail participation journey.From Hong Kong's deepening Connect Schemes with mainland China and its emergence as a digital assets hub, to Singapore's public seeding of domestic funds and its ambitions to grow its equity market; from the extraordinary untapped potential of China's household savings pool to the quiet revolution underway in Japan's NISA programme — and finally to what may be the most compelling retail participation story in the world today: India, where over 100 million SIP accounts are channeling USD 3 billion of investment every single month.Each market has its own starting point, its own policy instruments, and its own cultural relationship with saving and investing. What they share is a direction of travel — and the conviction that more people, investing more regularly, through well-governed and transparent fund structures, is good for households and economies alike.Listen now. The eastward shift in global capital markets has already begun.Amanda Hale, Director & Head of Regulatory Services, Global Trustee & Fiduciary, CitiAmanda has over 40 years of experience in the investments industry and has been with Citi since 2008. Prior to joining Citi, Amanda worked in the CIS Policy Team at the Financial Services Authority (FSA), now the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) after having been with HSBC for 26 years in various areas such as Trustee and Depositary Services, Custody, Settlements, Corporate Actions and Income. Amanda currently represents Citi on external industry committees and panel discussions as well as chairing various internal Citi regulatory committees. Joining Citi in 1999, Andrew worked as a Valuations Officer in the Citibank Private Bank before moving to Switzerland to become a Fund Management Support Manager in Zurich, where he managed a small team. On his return to London, Andrew joined Citibank Global Asset Management as Manager of the Fiduciary department, leading a team conducting post-trade compliance monitoring of private bank portfolios, institutional and sovereign wealth mandates, and Luxembourg Mutual Funds.In 2006, Andrew stepped into the funds business as a Fiduciary Relationship Manager, entrusted with managing key client relationships spanning both UK authorized and unauthorized fund structures. Since 2014, Andrew has been a driving force within Citi's Regulatory Services team, where he plays a pivotal role in preparing and delivering high-impact regulatory updates to clients, translating complex regulatory change into clear, actionable insight. Andrew has also represented Citi as its Technical representative at the UK Depositary Association.Matthew Mohlenkamp, Managing Director, Asia and Global Analytics, ICIMatthew Mohlenkamp is the Investment Company Institute’s (ICI) Managing Director for Asia and Global Analytics, where he leads ICI’s engagements on policy and regulatory matters across the Asia Pacific. articles.title: Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026
articles.text: In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, live on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. More than half the extreme poor live in nine economies, and by 2030, 87 percent will be in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile and conflict-affected situations, or both. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.Despite the reduction seen in past decades, escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching security. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, still lives on less than $8.30 a day, most of them one shock away from falling back.

articles.title: Weekly Market View
articles.text:
20 November 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Staying diversified,adding US mega caps
AI-related concerns continue to weigh on equities, especially with new US restrictions on third-country access to advanced American semiconductor chips. Renewed volatility across the AI ecosystem drove the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) back above 25.
However, two major event risks this week turned out to be less concerning – Nvidia’s Q3 revenue and earnings exceeded expectations, while Anthropic’s record initial public offering was priced above its indicative range.
Our quant models are not signalling a strong buy signal yet. However, with VIX spiking above 25 and investor positioning and sentiment indicators suggesting limited downside, we see value emerging in the US mega caps segment following its recent underperformance.
We add an opportunistic idea on US mega cap equities, which we see benefitting from scale, financial strength and potential industry consolidation.

How will US chip restrictions impact the technology sector?

What are the implications of the Fed’s latest meeting minutes on bonds?

Do you see opportunities in gold after the latest selloff?

Charts of the week: Oil’s disinflation effect

Falling oil and fuel prices likely to support disinflation in 2027; bonds are starting to offer greater diversification benefits

Projected* y/y change in crude oil and gasoline prices by quarter

21- and 126-day rolling correlation of global equities and bonds

Source: US Energy Information Administration, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *EIA projections
Editorial

Staying diversified, adding US mega caps

Strategy summary. AI-related concerns continue to weigh on equities, especially with new US restrictions on third-country access to advanced American semiconductor chips. Renewed volatility across the AI ecosystem drove the S&P500 volatility index (VIX) back above 25. However, two major event risks this week turned out to be less concerning – Nvidia’s Q3 revenue and earnings exceeded expectations, while Anthropic’s record initial public offering was priced above its indicative range.
Our quant models are not signalling strong buy signal yet. However, with VIX spiking above 25 and investor positioning and sentiment indicators suggesting limited downside, we see value emerging in the US mega caps segment following its recent underperformance. We add an opportunistic idea on the segment, which we see benefitting from scale, financial strength and potential industry consolidation.
Opportunistically adding US megacaps. Asian equities led declines this week, led by Taiwan, China and Korea, after new US export controls targeted access to advanced AI computing through overseas data centres. Licensing requirements focus on capacity supplied to restricted customers, with additional controls affecting regional hubs. These measures increase compliance burdens and financing uncertainty, potentially weighing on AI capital expenditure. We expect the market’s AI capex estimates for 2027 to be cut towards our own more-conservative projections. Established cloud operators (hyperscalers) may be better equipped to manage customer checks than smaller providers. We initiate an opportunistic idea on US mega caps as we see a catch-up opportunity, given their established franchises, strong cash generation and relatively resilient earnings prospects (see page 7 for details).
Diversifying beyond the AI trade. Although positive cross asset and sector correlations returned this week, sector rotations earlier this month reinforces the importance of maintaining exposure to different drivers of equity returns. Our preferred US sectors remain technology, healthcare, financials and materials, combining technology participation with opportunities beyond AI. Beyond the US, we like Euro area and Japanese banks, which are benefitting from elevated interest rates, actively managed global dividend strategies for income

.

opportunities, and Indian equities due to their low correlation with the AI trade.
Allure of high dividend equities. While global dividend yields remain historically low, attractive pockets persist. The Swiss equity market yields almost 4%, versus 1.6% for global equities. Euro area (3.6%), Australia (3.5%) and Singapore (3.4%) are other leading dividend paying markets. Taiwan offers almost a 2% yield, combining income with structural growth opportunities. We favour active management over simply chasing yield, avoiding value traps. Dividend equities can complement bonds within a diversified portfolio, balancing income opportunities with broader exposure across markets.
Increasing diversification offered by bonds. The one-month correlation between global stocks and bonds has turned negative after more than a year. This means bonds are offering greater diversification benefits amid the equity drawdown. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting suggest policymakers are likely to hike rates further. However, we remain dovish vs. markets on the Fed’s 12-month rates outlook (we see Fed target rate at 4.25% by end-2027 vs. market pricing above 4.5%) as lower oil prices and fading tariff effects lead to noticeable disinflation by H2 2027. Thus, we see particular value in the 3-7-year maturity bucket, with a preference for BB-to-BBB segment corporate bonds, which have resilient balance sheets and offer attractive yield pick-up. We see the US 10-year government bond offering value if the yield rises above 5.25%.
Dollar appears overbought; potential for gold upside: The USD index (DXY) has jumped over 2% in the past two weeks after stronger-than-expected US jobs and inflation reports for October revived Fed rate hike bets. Nevertheless, crude oil prices have slumped almost 20% this month as the Republican party’s heavy losses in the US mid-term elections raised the prospects of de-escalation in the Middle East conflict. Forward markets are pricing US crude oil below USD 75/bbl by Q3 next year. Lower oil prices are likely to support disinflation next year. With DXY technically overbought and Fed policy expectations excessively hawkish, we expect a pullback in USD. Conversely, gold looks oversold. We see an upside for XAU/USD, despite revising lower our 3- and 12-month targets (see page 7).
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as neutral for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Strong US retail sales; ongoing peace talks(-)factors: Broad-based China slowdown; hawkish central banks

US producer prices surged in October, though slightly below estimates, while retail control-group spending held up
US headline and core producer price inflation; US retail sales control group

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Euro area and German investor expectations both jumped to multi-month highs in November
Euro area and Germany ZEW economic expectations

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

China’s fixed asset investment slump deepened in October, while retail sales and industrial output growth moderated
China retail sales, industrial production and fixed asset investment

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions

How will the new US semiconductor restrictions impact the technology sector?

Our view: While compute is likely to remain a bottleneck for AI, greater US regulatory restrictions could weigh on AI capex.
Rationale: The US has announced broader restrictions on overseas computing capacity used by Chinese and other restricted-country companies, extending controls beyond physical chip shipments to remote access through data centres. This could delay data centre deployments and raise financing costs, as affected operators may defer expansion plans until licences or replacement customers are secured. Lower spending could weigh on chip and hardware orders, bringing consensus capex estimates closer to our forecasts. While we expect AI capex to rise 50% to USD 1.2trn in 2027, supported by projects already under construction, the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2027 and 2030 is likely to moderate to c.12%.
We therefore favour broadening technology exposure beyond semiconductors through our US Information Technology (IT) opportunistic idea, which also includes hardware and software industries. Investors should also consider diversifying into our other preferred sectors, such as US healthcare and financials.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

AI capital expenditure (capex) should continue to rise, but growth is expected to moderate from 2028
Global AI capex (USD bn)

Source: Company reports, Standard Chartered

How were Chinese technology giants’ Q3 2026 earnings?

Our view: Chinese tech giants’ Q3 earnings highlight growing demand for AI, but heavy spending is pressuring margins and cash flow, underscoring the need for stronger AI monetisation.
Rationale: Heavy AI capex continues to weigh on profitability, compressing near-term margins and deepening negative free cash flows, with share dilution a riskas tech giants may have to tap into equity markets for the AI buildout. Cloud growth points to genuine AI demand, but the AI-related revenue contribution remains small relative to the cost base. AI monetisation remains challenging, with competition set to intensify. Weak consumer spending was a common thread contributing to revenue misses. Major players reiteratedthe need for more tangible investment returns amid aggressive AI investments.
In the near term, investor sentiment remains weighed down by tightening US restrictions targeting China’s access to advanced chips, introducing downside risks to 2027 AI cloud revenue. While this could hamper the development of next-generation AI models, accelerating domestic AI chip adoption should benefit local semiconductor companies as China pushes for technological self-sufficiency.We expect rising AI adoption to benefit China’s IT sector over time, though we prefer diversifying our China equity exposure across preferred sectors, such as financials and healthcare.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

China’s technology sector valuation remains inexpensive at 12.9x, falling 1 standard deviation below the mean
Hang Seng Technology (HSTECH Index) 12-month forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What are the implications of the October Fed meeting minutes for the rate path forward and short-dated bonds? Do US 10-year government bonds now offer a good re-entry point?

Our view: October’s Fed meeting minutes maintained a hawkish-hold narrative. We continue to expect the Fed to raise rates by 25bps at its 8-9 December meeting. However, with short-dated US government bonds having largely priced in three hikes by June 2027, we see any spike above 5.25% in the US 10-year bond yield as an opportunistic bullish entry point.
Rationale: The hawkish-hold tone of the Fed’s October meeting minutes suggests the December Fed meeting is ‘live’. The market is currently pricing in three hikes by year-end 2027 (vs. our expectation of two hikes by H1 2027 followed by a potential cut in H2 2027). Short-dated government bond yields – using the US 2-year yield as a proxy – have largely priced in three hikes, and we do not expect the hawkish minutes to have a material impact on them.
Should the US 10-year government bond yield spike above 5.25%, the near-term risk-reward would become favourable, in our opinion. As we expect inflation to moderate in H2 2027, we see scope for the Fed to pivot towards easing, and we would turn more constructive on short-dated government bonds. We expect the US 2-year government bond yield to decline to 4.00-4.25% in 12 months, contributing to yield curve steepening.
— Ray Heung, Senior Investment Strategist

US short-term government bond yields have largely priced in 2-3 Fed rate hikes
US government bond yield curve, current and three months ago

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Is it time to add exposure to the EUR after its recent slide against the USD?

Our view: Yes, we are bullish on EUR/USD and favour gradually adding EUR exposure in the coming weeks. Markets are pricing in more Fed tightening than we expect. Lower oil prices support the Euro area and are likely to ease the Fed’s inflation concerns on a forward-looking basis.
Rationale: Lower oil prices are a double positive for EUR/USD, as they ease costs for Euro area households and businesses and temper US inflation, reducing the need for the Fed to tighten as much as markets expect.
Markets are pricing in a terminal Fed funds rate close to 4.63%, down from 4.72% a week ago, with the yield curve now also pricing a rate-cutting cycle after the September 2027 peak. We expect the bullish near-term USD momentum to linger until markets’ peak rate expectations converge towards our view. EUR/USD’s relative strength index (RSI) is below 30, and consolidation above 1.0950 points to oversold conditions. We expect a rebound towards 1.11 to confirm our recovery view in the next three weeks.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist

EUR/USD oversold; near-term rebound risk grows
EUR/USD and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What could support a sustained recovery in the AUD?

Our view: We believe a sustained AUD recovery requires a combination of domestic resilience and fading USD momentum.
Rationale: AUD/USD has been pressured by two key external headwinds: hawkish Fed repricing and weaker AI-related risk sentiment. A reversal in either could provide scope for recovery.
Softer US economic data or less hawkish Fed communication could ease upward pressure on US government bond yields, narrow rate differentials and weaken the USD. At the same time, a stabilisation in AI and broader equity sentiment could restore demand for the risk-sensitive AUD, particularly if Asian equities recover.
Domestic fundamentals remain a relative source of support. Still-elevated inflation should constrain the RBA’s ability to turn dovish quickly, while exporter and real-money demand for the AUD could cushion the downside. However, Australia’s rising unemployment raises the prospect of RBA rate cuts in H2 2027, potentially eroding the AUD’s carry advantage over time. With AUD/USD technically oversold, we see scope for a rebound from 0.6600, with 0.6830 as the key resistance level.
— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

Looking for a near-term AUD/USD rebound
AUD/USD and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

How will the improving oil supply-demand balance shape crude oil prices over the coming quarters?

Our view: Improving supply-demand balances should support inventory rebuilding and ease oil prices over time, despite persistent geopolitical risks, supporting disinflation in H2 2027.
Rationale: Crude oil’s recent retreat marks an important transition: expanding physical supply is finally asserting control over headline geopolitical noise. With non-OPEC production resilient, Gulf exports recovering and alternative transit routes adapting, markets are steadily pricing in an approaching supply surplus.
However, high freight costs and extended voyage times keep significant crude oil volumes tied up at sea rather than refilling local storage tanks. Crucially, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve’s crude inventories have fallen nearly 33% from pre-conflict levels, leaving a thinner buffer against renewed supply disruptions.
For investors, improving fundamentals point to gradual price normalisation as trade routes adapt, despite persistent geopolitical volatility. We expect near-term West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil to range between USD 80/bbl and USD 90/bbl. Softer energy prices should provide some relief to headline inflation, but are unlikely to materially alter the Fed’s near-term policy trajectory.
— Anthony Naab, Investment Strategist

Gulf crude flows have recovered to nearly 70% of their pre-conflict levels, easing supply constraints
Gulf crude oil exports (mb/week)

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Are there any tactical opportunities amidst the equity drawdown?

Our view: We introduce US mega cap equities as a new opportunistic idea, favouring their scale and financial strength amid heightened volatility and potential industry consolidation.
Rationale: We believe the mid-cycle backdrop favours large companies with strong cash generation, established competitive positions and the financial capacity to invest through periods of uncertainty. US mega caps’ forward P/E has fallen well below its two-year average and the -2x standard deviation level, offering a more attractive entry point into US market leaders.
A potential reset in AI capex expectations could also accelerate industry consolidation, favouring established leaders with the balance sheets, infrastructure and customer reach to sustain investment and capture market share. Key risks include a sharper-than-expected economic slowdown, weaker returns on AI investment, regulatory pressures, key man risks and concentration in a few dominant companies.
— Robin Xie, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

Equity opportunistic ideas: Adding US mega caps

Source: Standard Chartered. * Denotes new idea, with performance measured based on the S&P Top 20 Select 35/20 Capped Index

Do you see opportunities in gold after the recent sell-off?

Our view: We are lowering our gold price targets to USD 4,000/oz (three months) and USD 4,500/oz (12 months). Despite gold’s recent drop below our revised three-month price target, we continue to believe the precious metal can rebound in the medium term.
Rationale: Several factors have been driving down gold prices. A combination of stronger-than-expected US jobs, consumer inflation and producer inflation reports since early November has reinforced the case for Fed tightening. This, in turn, brought renewed hawkish Fed rhetoric, driving up the repricing of Fed rate-hike expectations. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold, while also strengthening the USD – a double headwind for bullion. In addition, recent volatility in the equity markets has raised liquidity needs for leveraged investors, causing some of them to sell gold to cover their losses.
However, at current levels, gold has undershot even our newly revised three-month price target for the precious metal. Emerging Market central banks remain structural buyers of gold as they continue to shift away from USD-denominated reserves. The US fiscal outlook remains dire, and with political gridlock now having returned to Washington, persistent fiscal deficits with no reforms will likely remain entrenched for the next two years at least. Confidence in US government finances and the USD is expected to weaken into 2027, and investors are likely to once again turn to gold as a store of value, informing our 12-month price target of USD 4,500/oz.
— Jonathan Liang, CFA, CIO, Fixed Income and FX

articles.title: Could Political Stability Spoil The Spanish Debt Miracle?
articles.text:
Could Political Stability Spoil The Spanish Debt Miracle?

Cedric Gemehl

Gavekal Research | 19 Nov 2026

Spain has achieved something unusual in Europe: a spectacular reduction in public debt despite political paralysis and little fiscal consolidation. As Spaniards head to the polls on November 29, investors will be wondering whether a change of government could derail this progress. Probably not, although greater political stability could paradoxically slow the decline in debt by allowing more fiscal slippage than continued gridlock.Spain’s public debt has fallen from a peak of 119% of GDP during the 2020 pandemic to 101% in 2025. The Spanish finance ministry expects it to decline further to 99.1% in 2026 and 92.8% by 2030. This remarkable performance has come despite two developments that have complicated the country’s fiscal position: higher interest rates and political fragmentation.

The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at Mansion House

Published on
22 October 2026

In her first Mansion House speech as Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), Katharine Braddick sets out her vision for the PRA's second decade. She outlines plans for a new five-year strategy centred on four priorities: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency, alongside a series of reforms to strengthen operational resilience, streamline regulation and improve regulatory processes for firms.

Speech
Lady Mayor, thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. It is an honour to address you and your guests and a pleasure to be speaking alongside Nikhil, who I have known for many years and who I look forward to working with in this new role.
When I joined the PRA in July I joined an organisation that in a little over a decade had succeeded decisively in its initial core mission, a mission that is vital to the success of the United Kingdom and its economy: to restore the resilience of the financial sector, so that it can properly support businesses and households across the nation.
Thanks to the work of the PRA, and significant effort by industry, that resilience has not only been restored but significantly strengthened. This hard-won stability is a source of advantage for our financial sector and this country, and it underpins our position as a leading and trusted financial centre. It is also the principal legacy of my predecessor Sam Woods: we might all wish to say we had achieved such a thing in our careers.
In that decade or so the world has also, of course, changed. Security threats increase, exacerbated by a more fractured geopolitical landscape. Interconnected financial vulnerabilities are arising from stretched sectoral valuations, rising sovereign debt levels and increased market leverage. Technology presents extraordinary opportunities and material and novel risks. And society demands accountability and transparency from its public institutions to maintain their legitimacy.
A new long-term PRA strategy
In this context, then, our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future. Next year I will publish for the first time a five-year strategy for the PRA. The strategy will set out how we intend to deliver four priorities I believe are central for the PRA’s future success:
Resilience
The first priority is resilience. Maintaining the resilience of the UK’s banking and insurance sectors is the foundation of our mission; the PRA identified early on that the need to address operational resilience as well as financial resilience is a prudential matter. Addressing non-financial resilience is an ever wider and more complex task, not least as the frequency and materiality of cyber incidents grows. Firms need to continue to invest in their capabilities, not only to prevent incidents, but to ensure they can respond to and recover from severe disruption.
The PRA similarly needs to evolve. We will significantly increase our focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The cyber challenge, in particular, is an area where we can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants. We will create a new PRA directorate, reporting directly to me, to act as a centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience. We will also consult jointly with the FCA on a new supervisory statement by the end of the year, clarifying our expectations of firms as we develop our experience and understanding.
Growth
Our second theme is growth. Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor.
In the coming period we will further develop our framework for the secondary competitiveness and growth objective. It will address not only the costs and benefits of regulation, but how our work influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide. We will set out how that framework is embedded in our day-to-day decision-making, and how we will track the effect our work is having on the growth and international competitiveness of the UK.
This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate. We will engage industry and Parliament as we shape, use and learn from it. It will enable us to be clear and confident about our role, and articulate a well-founded understanding of our contribution to the economy. This is not just a means to deliver against the secondary objective but is ultimately a foundation for good regulation.
Of course, the PRA has already taken steps to keep our regime up to date, most recently working with our FCA colleagues to devise a new captive insurance regime to enable innovation and growth in the insurance market. And to remove barriers to growth and provide predictability, we consulted earlier this month on a framework to automatically index our regulatory thresholds with nominal growth, a first among major financial regulators.
As a next step, we have today set out with the FCA a second set of significant reforms to streamline the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. These proposals reduce the number of senior management functions requiring pre-approval and remove requirements relating to the certification regime, halving its regulatory burden on firms whilst retaining clear accountability of their senior leaders.
Innovation
Our third priority is innovation. The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator. Working with industry, we will go further in refining the data we collect and how we collect it to ensure we can react to emerging issues and risks in a timely manner, while shrinking the need for ad hoc collections and removing collections whose benefits are not justified. We will take feedback from you on this as we go, refining our approach and prioritising the changes that add the most value.
We will accelerate our deployment of data analytics and new technologies, enabling supervisors to rapidly identify emerging themes and trends in risks. Working with industry, we will make it easier and more efficient to work with us by taking innovative approaches to data collection and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our rulebook and supervisory guidance, streamlining communications so that firms can quickly and easily understand what we expect.
Transparency
And our fourth priority is transparency. A sound understanding of the intentions and priorities of the regulator is crucial for firms to be able to effectively plan and manage their risks. And a stable and predictable business environment is essential to enable investors to deploy capital in the UK economy. So we will provide a clear and transparent line of sight to firms, Parliament and society about our plans and priorities, not least through the publication of and reporting on the new strategy. That will provide the means for us to be held accountable for meeting our commitments and demonstrate that we are a listening and learning organisation.
As an early example of this approach, we will take decisive steps to improve the experience of banks and building societies in relation to internal models for residential mortgages. This has been a source of particular difficulty for many firms, and we need to learn the lessons of this experience.
The PRA has already improved the approval process for firms, and we will go further by providing additional transparency about our operational performance. We will consult in Spring next year on material policy changes to improve firms’ access to a modelled approach. These proposals will be subject to challenge by an independent panel of industry and regulatory experts to ensure their feasibility, learning the lessons of the past to ensure our future policy is grounded in operational realities. Working with our colleagues in the wider Bank, we will also examine the interactions between hybrid mortgage models and stressed buffer requirements.
And we will conduct an independent review of the UK’s implementation of hybrid mortgage model requirements to identify tangible ways to assist firms as they maintain and develop their models. The work of that review will be sequenced to ensure it does not jeopardise the delivery of ongoing model approval and policy work.
Delivering the strategy
The delivery of our strategy will rely on the considerable strengths that characterise the PRA: our deeply expert and purpose-driven people; our comprehensive knowledge of the firms we regulate; and our established approach to supervision – judgement-led, forward-looking and focussed on key risks to safety and soundness. That work has underpinned the success of the PRA’s first twelve years and must never be taken for granted.
As we take the PRA into its second decade, we will build on our strengths and track record by evolving our approach to meet the challenges of today and of tomorrow. We will ensure the financial sector remains resilient to the increasingly volatile environment we now face. We will set out clearly and confidently how we contribute to growth. We will exploit technology to retain our position as a world-leading regulator and supervisor. And we will operate transparently to underpin confidence in our work and thereby in our financial sector and economy.
The PRA in 2032 will be a forward-looking regulator that is respected and trusted. A regulator that is recognised for its work supporting a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system that in turn supports a thriving UK economy. I look forward to working with my PRA colleagues, and importantly also with you all, to deliver that vision.
Now, would you please join me in raising a toast to the Lady Mayor and the Mayoral Consort.

Katharine Braddick
Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority

Revving the ETF vehicle: Roundhill’s CEO on DRAM, next-gen innovation and more
[Music]
Funmi Osiyale: The ETF industry has come a long way from traditional index investing. Today, with more than $16 trillion in assets in the U.S. ETF market, investors can access everything, from thematic exposures, derivative-based products, and increasingly sophisticated portfolio tools, all through the ETF wrapper. At the same time, the pace of innovation continues to accelerate. New investment ideas are reaching the market faster than ever, and issuers are continually entering new frontiers of what can be delivered through an ETF. Welcome to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense. I'm Funmi Osiyale from J.P. Morgan's ETF sales team. Today, I'm joined by Dave Mazza, CEO of Roundhill Investments. Launched in 2018, Roundhill has emerged as an innovator in the ETF space, helping pioneer products designed around some of the biggest trends shaping markets today – from AI and semi conductors, and the next generation of retail investing. Dave, thanks so much for being here today.
Dave Mazza: Thanks for having me. It's great to be here.
Funmi Osiyale: Many of our listeners will be familiar with Roundhill products. They'll have heard of MAGS, DRAM, and have heard of Roundhill making its mark in the ETF industry. But can you take us back to the beginning? Tell us about Roundhill's origins and how you got to the firm that you are today.
Dave Mazza: Yeah, no, happy to do so. So Roundhill was founded in 2018 by Will Hershey and Tim Maloney. They were actually in their late 20s at the time, and the impetus behind the firm was creating an asset manager that was really focused on the next generation of investors. So those are millennial investors, Gen Z investors. And most people think that, well, that means it really is only about direct retail, but actually, you know, that's an important part of Roundhill's origin story and really our focus. But when you think about the de-aging of financial advice and the team building approach that financial advisors have, and just, um, as a new generation of portfolio managers coming to the institutional side, the firm w- was well set up for that. And I joined in 2023 really with an idea of helping take that vision and mission, uh, that Will and Tim set out to see if we could, um, bring that to a larger pool of investors. And really since that time, we've been proud of our accomplishments and being able to do so as the firm has expanded markedly over the past few years.
Funmi Osiyale: Now moving on to MAGS, that's a product that really put Roundhill on the map. Can you tell us about the original thesis behind this fund?
Dave Mazza: Yeah, it's interesting. So MAGS is the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF, and this was the first ETF to provide precise exposure to the Magnificent 7 stocks. And it's funny when I think about that ETF, when we first launched it, many people were pointing the fingers and saying, "Well, this is going to be the top of the market. This is going to be the end of the Magnificent 7 story." And the term itself, and there's debate over who kind of, uh, first coined it, but at this point, I think the Magnificent 7 and the MAGS are tied at the hip. And what's been interesting to me is really how fast some of the early adoption was. But what we heard from investors is that they were really interested in that precision that, that MAGS could provide, and allowing them to be able to, to make investment in trading decisions with greater certainty of that potential outcome, at least when it comes from the exposure point of view. So, at the same time, MAGS actually, was one of the first ETFs to combine cash equities, so traditional stocks, plus derivatives, in this case, total return swaps, to provide that exposure in a portfolio. So, some of the benefits of MAGS is not just that it, it's a, a highly liquid, uh, vehicle for investors looking to access exposure to those seven names, there was also some financial innovation behind it.
Funmi Osiyale: Thanks so much for those insights. Now, what do you think was the inflection point for Roundhill? What took you from an emerging issuer becoming the firm that we see today?
Dave Mazza: I think certainly the, the growth that we saw with MAGS over the past few years really helped provide validation to the thesis that investors wanted that more precise exposure, were interested in ideas that could not just have the potential for them to outperform, should, should markets do well or the underlying exposures do well, but again, do so with greater certainty. But at the same time, Roundhill has expanded in what I call kind of a new generation of thematics or precise industries, true actively managed ETFs, and then income and other derivatives-based products. So really everything we've been laying out in the areas that we participate in, are all areas of growth and interest from investors both large and small.
Funmi Osiyale: That brings us nicely to DRAM. Take us back to the original insight. What did you see in the memory market that you felt wasn't fully appreciated, and what has surprised you most about the way investors have adopted the fund?
Dave Mazza: Yeah, it's interesting. So, DRAM's origin story has a few different components to it. So the names like Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung, uh, we had been following, transacting in, in different portfolios for some time, certainly seen, the idea that the memory semiconductor space was emerging as a true bottleneck in the AI build-out, and the underlying performance of those names have had been on a particularly strong run over the past 12 to 18 months. And then when we were looking at saying, "Hey, the ability for investors to actually access these names in a complete fashion is missing." So for example, investors have been using South Korean, equity ETFs as a proxy to gain access to Samsung and SK Hynix. Interestingly enough, the Korean equity market, those two names comprise about 50% of the exposure because their market capitalizations are so large compared to the rest of the equity market. But for an investor, that's kind of an imperfect solution, right? So you get about 50% to the names you want, and then 50% to other names. And, and they may all be good companies, but they're industrials, they're defense stocks, they're shipbuilders. So doing so with South Korea ETFs was, again, a really imperfect solution. And then you can say, "Well, hey, Dave, there's a wide range of great semiconductor ETFs that are available." Well, the challenge with those ETFs is that your exposure to memory might be limited to Micron. You may not have some of the storage names like Western Digital or Sandisk in there, and you most definitely do not have the two South Korean BMS, Samsung and SK Hynix. And until recently, those two names are really inaccessible, uh, to the majority of investors globally. Even for large institutional investors, they can be difficult and sometimes painful to transact in. And so the idea behind DRAM was combining all of those names together in a precise fashion, but also a complete fashion. So the DRAM ETF takes a full global perspective on memory. But what's interesting is that there really is only a handful of companies that are truly involved in this space, so you don't have a large tail of companies that maybe dabble in memory, but isn't really their core business. So DRAM solved a lot of those challenges for investors. And while we were certainly bullish on the outlook for adoption, by investors, I would be remiss to say that we were not surprised at how quickly that adoption came and how, how wide and far that adoption came from.
Funmi Osiyale: Now, both MAGX and DRAM focus on themes that investors were super focused on. When you think of narrowing down on a key theme to focus on, what do you think distinguishes them between being a long-term investment idea and a short-lived narrative?
Dave Mazza: Yeah, this is a really important component because the thematic ETF industry has grown markedly over recent years. A lot of 2026's growth is coming from DRAM itself. So our research team, we really take a mosaic approach to product development, and then portfolio construction so that we can ensure we have, you know, a diverse range of views and points of view on this. And that's really where there's both kind of an art and a science component to it. And so what we're really trying to identify is, is this theme structural in some way? So in the case of memory, the AI build out is going to go in fits and starts, and we're seeing some of that now, of course, with what's happening with the debate about data centers and the funding behind data centers in the U.S. But longer term, you can see the CapEx that's being spent to build what's required for the AI build out. So in that case, there's kind of a, a structural opportunity. Then there are some themes, that need a different catalyst to play out. Maybe in the case of you think of something like a cannabis or a sports betting, that needs legalization or adoption to really kind of have a wider appeal. And then there's other themes that might be a great theme and a good narrative in the market, but they are more just trades. And they may not make a great long-term ETF. So what we're really looking to do is kind of separate the wheat from the shaft to identify are there, is there a structural component, that's being tapped into to provide a longer term, tailwind, or is there something catalyst-driven that, that would provide an opportunity for investors, to access these companies prior to that catalyst happening?
Funmi Osiyale: With the success of DRAM, other issuers have actually started to launch their own derivative or leveraged products around the fund. Do you view this as a form of validation, competition, or as a natural evolution of successful idea?
Dave Mazza: Well, this may be a bit of a cop out, but I would say probably all of those combined in some different way, shape or form. So certainly, there's always a competitive aspect, uh, when someone takes, you know, an idea that you spent time working on and then applies it in a bit of a different way. But the more I've thought about it, I've come to terms with the fact that that isn't really a great sign of validation that, you know, other issuers, uh, or whether they're creating ETF products on it or there's banks creating structured notes around things like DRAM and MAGS. To me, that's real validation across the thesis. And it's saying, "Hey, there's a, essentially, an ETF here that can now be used in different ways, whether that's to provide an amplified exposure for investors, or more so traders looking for daily leverage, or are investors looking for particular outcomes on the income side that can use the options ecosystem and liquidity ecosystem that's been built around these products." I think because the ETF vehicle itself has shown the ability to be used in so many different ways to deliver so many different outcomes to investors and traders that I believe it's ultimately a sign of an evolution of a healthy market.
Funmi Osiyale: Now, Roundhill has built something that's relatively unique to the ETF industry, which is a very direct relationship with retail investors. What have you learned from engaging directly with individual investors that you may not hear through traditional institutional channels? And do you think there are any misconceptions on what the Roundhill investor looks like?
Dave Mazza: It's really interesting. So I think, we all know the book and the movie, Dumb Money and the stories about retail investors, both dating back to the TMT bubble, and then of course what we saw with meme stocks in 2020 and 2021. But if I actually look at what's occurring with direct retail investors today is they're significantly more informed than I’ve, really I think most people believe them to be. We really even view retail investors as a bit of a risk factor in the market that because they play such a greater role today in the U.S. capital markets than they did historically, prior to the COVID period, retail investors made up somewhere around 8%, 10% of daily market volume. Today, that's around, you know, and these numbers fluctuate, but today it's around 20%, 25% on average, and there's different ways to view this data, like I said, but they just play a greater influence in price setting. And they are also really interested in being part of communities. That, I think, is a really distinct component. So, you know, there's a dedicated channel on Reddit, just talking about Roundhill ETFs. So, it's a great means to be able to, to connect with these investors, understand what questions they have. Many of our most successful products have come from ideas of what we're seeing, you know, the retail community talking about.
Funmi Osiyale: So Dave, final question for you before we wrap up today's conversation. You had a front row seat to the evolution of the ETF industry. What do you hope people, five years from now, view of Roundhill and the ETF industry as a whole?
Dave Mazza: I think you hit something really interesting. I've been in and around ETFs now for a long time, and I've worked at a wide variety of firms that offer ETFs in the market. But when I think about Roundhill, the thoughtful financial innovation is something that I'd like people to look back on. Also an opportunity for them to be provided with tools to help them meet particular outcomes that they're interested in, whether that's precise exposure to memory stocks. And they know if you look at the perspectives of DRAM and then compare that to its holdings, it's pretty clear it's doing what it's intended to do. So that's kind of what I mean on the, on the thoughtful side. But also, because the market is so dynamic, I'm excited about where the future could land and where, you know, we can continue to create new, interesting ideas for investors to be able to meet any outcomes that they're looking for in their portfolios.
Funmi Osiyale: Dave, I think that's a really great place to wrap up today's conversation. Appreciate your time and look forward to the next one.
Dave Mazza: Thanks so much for having me, Funmi. This was great.
Voiceover: Thanks for listening to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense. If you've enjoyed this conversation, share your feedback by leaving a comment or review wherever you listen to podcasts. And be sure to follow our channel so you don't miss an episode!

What does the next generation of ETF innovation look like? In this episode of Making Sense, Funmi Osiyale, from J.P. Morgan’s ETF Sales team, is joined by Dave Mazza, CEO of Roundhill Investments, to discuss Roundhill’s approach to identifying investment opportunities and the thinking behind innovative ETFs, including DRAM and MAGS. They also explore the return of thematic ETFs, how investor demand is influencing product development, and what could be next for the broader ETF landscape.

articles.title: The team behind Vanguard’s equity index funds
articles.text:
Investment perspectives

The team behind Vanguard’s equity index funds

November 20, 2026

When investors choose an equity index fund, they put their trust in an investment process designed to deliver consistent results over time. At Vanguard, our equity index funds are managed with a team-based approach built on shared expertise, disciplined processes, and more than 50 years of index fund management experience.

While the individual portfolio managers named in fund documents play important roles, portfolio management responsibilities are shared across teams of portfolio managers, who collaborate on strategic decisions for their funds. This approach helps maintain continuity in each portfolio over time.

Teamwork is key in every portfolio

Managing an index fund requires thousands of decisions each year, and broad participation in investment decisions allows portfolios to benefit from the deep institutional knowledge of individual team members.
Portfolio managers, analysts, risk specialists, and technology professionals work together to evaluate cash flows, implement index changes, manage transaction costs, monitor portfolio risks, and support efficient trading execution. Each discipline brings a different perspective, helping the team operate at scale while maintaining alignment with investors’ objectives.
A distinguishing feature of our portfolio managers is that they also serve as traders. This integrated model brings investment decision-making and execution together within the same role, allowing portfolio managers to have direct oversight of how portfolio decisions are implemented. The result is a close connection between strategy and execution that helps to support efficient trading, to manage costs, and to maintain tight benchmark tracking on behalf of investors.

How teams create value for investors

While equity index funds seek to track a benchmark rather than outperform it, portfolio management decisions still matter, and these decisions are rarely made in isolation.
Our team-based structure allows us to combine specialized expertise from across the organization while maintaining clear accountability. Efficient execution, disciplined risk management, careful handling of cash flows, and thoughtful implementation of index changes can help reduce costs and support close benchmark tracking over time.
Vanguard’s equity index funds also benefit from a global trading organization. Teams in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia bring local market expertise and knowledge of regional trading conditions, helping the firm navigate different market structures, time zones, and liquidity environments. Combined with a shared investment process and coordinated oversight, this global approach supports efficient execution and close benchmark tracking across global markets.
Our approach demonstrates its value during major events like index rebalances and reconstitutions. When an index provider adds or removes securities from a benchmark, portfolio managers, traders, analysts, and risk specialists work together to determine how and when to implement those changes. By carefully managing execution, trading costs, and portfolio risk, the team seeks to minimize the costs of tracking an index and to deliver an investment experience that closely reflects the benchmark.

Built for continuity

A key advantage of Vanguard’s collaborative portfolio management model is continuity.
Knowledge and expertise are embedded across teams, processes, and governance structures rather than residing with a single individual. Because portfolio management knowledge is broadly distributed, transitions can occur without requiring changes to the underlying investment process or philosophy.
Future portfolio managers typically spend years developing expertise and assuming increasing responsibilities before taking on formal portfolio management responsibilities. As a result, portfolio manager changes effectively just formalize responsibilities that have already been shared across the broader team.
For investors, that means continuity: While the names of the portfolio managers listed in a Vanguard fund prospectus may change, the disciplined investment approach, experienced teams, and oversight of the portfolio will remain the same.

Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene

Given at London School of Economics

The extent to which the latest energy price shock feeds into more persistent inflation through second-round effects remains a key consideration for policymakers. The presence of slack in the labour market could suggest that wage pressures will remain contained, limiting the scope for second-round effects. But is this likely to be the case?
In this speech, Megan challenges this argument, drawing on a wide range of wage indicators to assess recent developments in pay growth and the likely path ahead for wages and domestically-generated inflation. She then turns to broader measures of labour market slack to examine whether current conditions are likely to restrain second-round effects via the wage-setting channel.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me to the LSE to speak. It’s nice to be back here—I often studied in your library when I was an undergraduate in the US working in London for the summer. Come to think of it, I may have snuck in so please don’t alert the authorities.
Over the past few months, a lot has happened in the world of geopolitics…and yet very little has fundamentally changed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains beset by attacks and potential new chokepoints in shipping have emerged such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although Middle Eastern oil flows have at times returned to near pre-war levels, expensive and inefficient workarounds have kept energy prices high (Figure 1). Wholesale gas prices are close to triple their level at the start of the year, with oil spot prices just under double their early-January level.footnote [1] And the prices for refined products have remained elevated despite volatile spot prices. Even if the conflict in Iran ends tomorrow, we have already been hit by a protracted energy shock.

I have previously laid out the various avenues via which such a negative supply shock can propagate through the UK economy, highlighting the important role of second-round effects in embedding inflation in the economy. As I set out in my last speech Opens in a new window in June, they can take hold through the price- or wage-setting channel, or both. For today’s purposes, I will focus specifically on the wage-setting channel.
Wages represent a material cost for firms, particularly in the services sector where labour accounts for a large share of total costs. Wages are also a significant determinant of incomes, thus underpinning consumption. As a result, measures of wage growth offer useful insight into domestically-generated inflation. Of course, not all wage growth is inflationary. If wages rise because productivity improves, the implications for inflation may well be limited. But wages can also act as the mechanism through which temporary negative supply shocks become embedded in domestic inflation, particularly when workers seek to protect real incomes and firms then raise prices to protect their margins.
The MPC has judged that there is slack in the labour market, as evidenced by the ratio of vacancies to unemployment relative to equilibrium (Figure 2). Some of my colleagues and I have argued that the wage-setting channel poses a smaller risk of generating second-round effects than the price-setting channel. If firms are facing higher costs and have experienced years of margin compression, they are likely to pass on some of their higher costs by raising prices. This is consistent with intelligence that we’re hearing from our Agents. But if there is slack in the labour market, worker power is relatively weak. Even if workers demand higher pay as their costs go up, employers may deny that request given the large pool of talent from which to choose.

Given our monetary policy strategy has relied partly on slack mitigating the impact of second-round effects, it’s worth exploring how much labour market slack there really is. The wider economy has proved surprisingly resilient, implying there is less slack than some labour market indicators suggest. If so, there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging through the wage-setting channel than we initially thought.
We may not have a clear steer on whether the shock from the Iran conflict gives rise to material second-round effects through wage- or price-setting until early next year when our Agents’ pay survey is out in February and the brunt of 2027 pay settlements are agreed in January and April. But if we wait for this evidence to lean against second-round effects with a tighter monetary policy stance, we will already be too late given the lags with which monetary policy affects the economy and inflation.
As outlined in our Forecast Evaluation Report and the Macro-technical paper Opens in a new window alongside it, predicting wage growth has been a challenge for the Bank, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. As shown in Figure 3, Bank forecasts tended to systematically predict higher wage growth than what we experienced until the Covid period, after which our forecasts systematically underestimated the strength of wage growth.footnote [2]

Our suite of wage models, like many macro forecasting models, are largely driven by historical relationships. The recent persistent undershooting of wage growth forecasts may suggest something structurally shifted in the labour market during the pandemic. As I argued in my 2024 speech (Greene, 2024), this could reflect reduced matching efficiency, lower search intensity, labour hoarding, persistent recruitment difficulties and weaker participation. It could also reflect stronger real wage resistance following the 2022 energy shock than historical relationships have implied (Pill, 2025). Wage growth has generally decelerated since 2023, suggesting these upward pressures have been unwinding, but they may not have unwound entirely.
Models inevitably simplify reality, and their performance depends critically on the quality of the signals they are trying to capture. One important development over the past decade has been an expansion in the range of wage indicators we look at, reflecting efforts to measure underlying wage pressures from multiple perspectives.
But this richer information set has brought its own challenges. At the moment, wage data are like a Rorschach Test; they can be used to confirm anyone’s preconceived view of slack in the labour market because they are giving mixed signals (Figure 4). Different indicators often tell different stories, reflecting differences in coverage, frequency, composition and methodology (Villar, Moyon, & Ahn, 2025 Opens in a new window). The task for policymakers is therefore not simply to monitor wages, but to understand the dynamics underpinning different metrics.

This brings me to my main focus today. Given the importance of understanding wage-setting behaviour and what it might mean for slack and second-round effects, I want to dig into some of our key wage indicators to parse signal from noise. I will start by examining how these indicators differ and where in the wage-setting process they are likely to be most informative. I will then consider what they can tell us about the recent developments and what signal we might glean about wage dynamics going forward. Finally, I will examine how confident we can be that a material degree of slack will restrain second-round effects and inflation via the wage-setting channel.
Getting into the weeds isn't always glamorous, but in policymaking as in gardening, sometimes you just have to get your hands dirty.
Measures of wage growth
When confronted with a range of indicators, it is often useful to take a step back and consider exactly what information each one conveys. After all, wage indicators measure different things and are collected in different ways. This is a feature, not a bug - the differences between measures allow us to build a richer picture of wage developments within the domestic economy to assess the degree of current and emerging wage pressures.
In light of this, Table 1 brings together some of the key metrics used by the Bank of England to monitor UK wage growth. While not exhaustive, the selection illustrates the breadth of information available to policymakers and the different insights a variety of measures can provide, as demonstrated by the range of questions presented in the second column: each of these metrics has something different to offer when it comes to understanding wage pressures.
