Naturally, some measures receive more attention than others. Chief among these is the average weekly earnings (AWE) series, which helps us answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. AWE is an accredited official statistic published with a two-month lag by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), derived from the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey (MWSS).footnote [3] The MWSS is issued to around 9,000 businesses and covers approximately 15 million employees across Great Britain. While adjustments are made to account for smaller firms, the survey includes only businesses with 20 or more employees. Nevertheless, AWE provides a broad measure of the change in pay levels across the economy and is thus useful for gauging domestic inflationary pressures stemming from changes in wages.
At the Bank, we tend to focus on private sector regular AWE growth as opposed to the whole economy (including the public sector) for a few reasons. Private sector pay feeds more directly into the CPI measure of inflation, particularly when it comes to services, where labour costs make up a large chunk of total costs. In addition, UK public sector pay is often determined by government policy decisions. As such, wage-setting in the private sector is generally more closely tied to labour market conditions, whereas institutional pay setting arrangements and fiscal constraints can often influence public sector pay outcomes. Monetary policy therefore has more influence over private sector pay. Furthermore, private sector regular pay excludes volatile bonuses while they’re included in total pay. For these reasons, I’m going to focus on private sector regular AWE pay growth for the rest of this speech.
Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Real Time Information (RTI) data provides an alternative read on wage growth. This is published by the ONS on a monthly basis, in conjunction with HMRC, and can be used to help answer the same question as the AWE: “what is the growth of the average wage?”. Median estimates of the data are available with less of a lag than the official AWE measure, though they are often heavily revised. In addition, its production does not rely on survey responses. Instead, the information comes directly from HMRC’s PAYE RTI system, which covers the whole population of employees payrolled by employers, allowing for more detailed breakdowns of the data. The data is presented as gross pay, which includes bonus pay and other one-off payments (but not pension contributions) unlike private sector regular AWE. Arguably, this can make it harder to gain a clear view on wage growth and makes it more difficult to compare RTI and AWE.
We can also draw on wage growth measures derived from responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey to answer the question “what assessment do firms make of their own wage growth?”. The DMP is a large, monthly panel survey of Chief Financial Officers from small-, medium- and large-sized UK businesses. Since 2022, the survey has included a number of questions focused on firms’ wages. This means that the back data available for wage analysis is limited. In 2026, the survey included wage growth data from approximately 700 firms, covering around 300,000 employees each month. Responses are used to construct measures of both realised and expected wage growth. The former tells us what has actually happened to firms’ own wage growth over the last year, while the latter gives us an idea of what firms anticipate will happen to their wage growth over the next year. Forward-looking indicators are hard to come by – an unfortunate truth for those of us in the forecasting business – but they are particularly useful given that both shocks and monetary policy take their time to work their way through the economy. As such, I am monitoring this measure closely as the current shock unfolds.
Pay settlements data can also provide us with a glimpse into the future path for wage growth. Such data allows us to shed some light on the pay decisions firms are making with regard to their current employees, helping us answer the question “what pay increases are firms agreeing for their existing employees?”. However, settlements data captures changes in basic pay and does not capture all sources of earnings growth, such as progression, merit and performance-related pay, or bonuses. We can access pay settlements data through the Bank of England’s settlements database. This database brings together information collected from businesses across the UK economy by the Bank’s Agents and external data providers, collected at various frequencies. Given that these figures can be updated retrospectively as more settlements are finalised, they are subject to some revision. We also get a sense of how pay settlements are likely to evolve over the next year in the Agents’ pay survey, released in February but with intelligence coming in from our Agents in the lead up to that.
Settlements data can only tell us so much. By its nature, its focus is on those workers already employed. But what are firms willing to pay new hires? The Indeed Wage Tracker provides insight into this, measuring the median annual change in advertised wages and salaries found on the Indeed platform across job title, region and salary-types. The sample size of each is reliant on a number of different factors, including the amount of total job vacancies, the proportion that is posted online and the share of these postings that contains wage or salary information (Adrjan & Lydon, 2023 Opens in a new window). This data is collected in the UK and a range of developed countries, allowing for cross-country comparison.
This is a whistle-stop tour of wage growth metrics. Each tells us something slightly different about wage growth pressures in the economy. I’ll now put them to use to explore present and future developments in wage growth.
Recent and current wage growth: two measures, different stories
Having gone through the various wage metrics, let’s use them to try to work out how much slack there is the labour market now and whether the wage-setting process has changed. For this, I’ll look at private sector regular AWE and its median RTI equivalent (proxied for the private sector), which both answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. The good news is that both metrics show wage growth broadly continuing to moderate since recent peaks in 2023 (Figure 5). But these two indicators tell very different stories about the extent of that progress.

After almost 3 years of gradual easing, recent AWE data broadly suggest a further and more rapid leg down in wage growth, coming in at 3.0% in August (the aqua line in Figure 5). In contrast, our primary RTI metric of private sector wage pressure – growth in median pay – remains at a considerably higher rate of 4.4% in September (the orange line in Figure 5). Historically, these measures have tracked each other reasonably closely, albeit over a relatively short sample given RTI data are only available from 2014. Since early 2026, the divergence between them has become unusually large by historical standards.
RTI and AWE measures are answering the same question and both are constructed using sectoral wage growth and weighted according to the level of employment.footnote [4] So what's behind their divergence now? To decompose the wedge between these different measures, I’ll use a measure of mean pay growth derived from the RTI data (showing annual wage growth of 5% in August), which is more comparable to mean private sector regular pay growth from AWE (showing annual wage growth of 3% in August).
The wedge between these measures is explained primarily by three factors:

Differences in wage growth within industries: for a given industry wage growth in AWE is different to that in RTI. This is possible due to the different data underlying the two (a survey in the case of AWE, administrative data for RTI).
Between-industry compositional effects: This arises because the industry shares underlying the two differ and can change over time as employment shifts between industries.
Differences in flexible pay such as bonuses: AWE regular pay doesn’t include bonuses and arrears, whereas RTI does.

Differences in wage growth between industries and within industries can both help us understand underlying wage dynamics. Wage growth driven by changes in industry shares has implications for aggregate wage pressure and can give us a sense of overall slack. Wage growth within sectors reflects firms’ pay-setting decisions and can reveal whether they have changed in the face of a shock.
Figure 6 isolates the contributions to the wedge from the three sources. In August the wedge was 2 percentage points and has grown since late 2025 due to steadily rising compositional differences (pink area), fluctuating contributions from within industry differences in pay growth (purple area) and bonuses (blue area).

Of the three main components explaining the wedge between AWE and RTI, let’s first address the easiest to interpret: flexible pay. AWE private regular pay data exclude bonuses and arrears, while private sector RTI data include them. We want to compare apples-to-apples when we are gleaning signals from the two series. To do this, we assume that the bonuses (and arrears) captured in the AWE measure of total pay are also present in the RTI data and subtract their contribution from the RTI measure. This is necessarily a simplifying approximation and so the results should be interpreted with some caution. Bonuses and cost of living payments played a significant role in explaining the wedge between the two series in 2022-23 and earlier this year before waning more recently. During 2022-23 bonuses and one-off payments were common across sectors, whereas more recently these have been concentrated primarily in finance and professional services.
Now let’s turn to the role of compositional effects in creating a wedge between AWE and RTI. We can do this by comparing the changes in sectoral employment weights in private sector AWE and private sector RTI over the past year (Figure 7). This chart shows the year-on-year changes in the latest data, but it reflects trends that have persisted throughout 2026. AWE shows employment shifting towards lower-paid sectors, with rising weights for industries such as accommodation and food services and falling weights for higher-paying sectors such as financial and professional services. RTI, however, paints the opposite picture, with employment shifting slightly away from lower-paying sectors towards higher-paying ones.

What signal can we draw from this? There is really no silver bullet here, and this is exactly why we look at multiple indicators to get a complete picture of the labour market. But on balance, I’d put slightly more weight on the compositional story from the RTI. The RTI series is drawn from administrative data rather than a survey. RTI doesn’t require imputing employees who work in small firms (under 20 employees) as the AWE series does. Finally, the narrative from the RTI data chimes with the Labour Force Survey (LFS), which also indicates that employment has shifted to higher paid industries over the past year. There are reasons to treat the LFS with caution; it suffers from low response rates and the industry classifications are self-reported and may not always be accurate. On balance, I place slightly more weight on the RTI’s narrative that workers are shifting towards higher paying industries. This means that the AWE may be giving us an artificially low reading of wage growth because of the specific compositional effects it incorporates.
Let’s now take a look at differences in pay growth within industries in the AWE and RTI series. Figure 8 shows wage growth within various sectors in the latest AWE and RTI releases. This chart shows year-on-year changes in the latest data, but this is consistent with the trends we have seen over the past year. The AWE data suggests that, on balance, wage growth in lower paying sectors was running hotter than for higher paid sectors. The RTI data, however, suggest wage growth was faster in higher paying sectors.footnote [5] For the reasons I’ve just explained, I have a bit more faith in the RTI data. But again, these discrepancies point to the importance of making use of a range of metrics.

To isolate wage growth within industries, we can adjust AWE and RTI for compositional effects and strip out bonuses from RTI (Figure 9). These adjusted measures are shown in the solid lines, whereas the original series are represented in the dotted lines. Comparing the solid and dotted aqua lines shows that compositional effects are currently pushing down on the AWE by 0.4pp. Doing the same for the purple lines shows that compositional effects and bonuses are pushing up on RTI by 0.6pp (0.2pp due to compositional effects and 0.4pp due to bonuses). These adjusted measures indicate wage growth of 3.4% according to the AWE and 4.5% for the RTI measure.footnote [6] In my view, both remain above levels consistent with an inflation target of 2% and suggest there may be less labour market slack than we thought.footnote [7]

Where does this leave us? Our adjusted measures of wage growth remain above levels consistent with our inflation target of 2%. The most frequently cited indicator that we use, private sector regular AWE, seems to have been consistently undercooking actual private sector wage growth since late-2025.
Looking ahead: what can guide us?
Over the past year, different metrics of wage growth have told different stories. However, there is strong evidence to suggest that underlying wage growth is higher than that reported by private sector regular AWE. What we ultimately want to know, however, is how wage setting will evolve going forward, particularly in light of yet another negative supply shock. For this, I’ll look at some forward-looking indicators—specifically the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker.
The DMP has been an invaluable source of information on wages since wage questions were introduced in 2022. The survey directly asks firms about wage changes for their employees, and so arguably provides the clearest window into firms’ wage-setting processes. Realised wage growth has broadly tracked the trends in AWE and RTI, though there have been some periods of divergence. The DMP recorded a lower peak in 2023 and indicated more gradual moderation in wage growth thereafter. We can see this in Figure 10, which plots DMP realised wage growth and one-year ahead expected wage growth, at the time of the survey, alongside the RTI and AWE measures.

Expected wage growth and realised wage growth have also diverged, most notably when the wage questions were introduced in 2022. When asked in the middle of 2022, DMP respondents reported year-ahead expected wage growth of around 5%. The DMP errors appear smaller than the MPR forecast’s; firms have seemingly been better at anticipating wage growth than we have. In the three months to September, the DMP's one-year-ahead wage growth expectations point to a levelling-off in wage growth at 3.4% rather than a material further easing.

The noticeable gap between private regular AWE and pay settlements over the past five years can be explained by the state of the labour market. Faced with recruitment difficulties and elevated staff turnover, firms had stronger incentives to raise pay to attract and retain workers. As a result, there was ‘pay drift’; actual wage growth often exceeded that implied by pay settlements, reflecting pay for new workers, retention-related pay increases and other adjustments outside formal settlement rounds. This is consistent with academic literature that finds that workers achieve faster pay growth when outside job opportunities improve, and that the threat of higher turnover can prompt firms to raise pay more broadly across their workforce (Jäger, Roth, Roussille, & Schoefer, 2024 Opens in a new window) (Sokolova & Sorensen, 2021 Opens in a new window).

As I outlined in a recent speech (Greene, 2026), the labour market is considerably weaker now than it was in 2022. As aggregate demand has softened, demand for labour has also eased, reducing recruitment difficulties and, in turn, the pressure on firms to grant large pay increases. Expected pay settlements may therefore provide a more reliable guide to future wage growth than they did during the post-pandemic period.
At present, our Agents report that expected settlements for 2027 will be similar or only slightly lower than in 2026, suggesting the wage disinflation process may be stalling. For the past two years, actual settlements have come in above what was projected in the Agents’ pay survey (4% in 2025 vs 3.7% in the pay survey; current estimate of 3.6% in 2026 vs 3.4% in the pay survey), so I expect the risk to the latest guidance is to the upside. Moreover, the vast majority of pay settlements will be agreed between January and April (Figure 15), when we expect inflation to be above 4%. This is well above the threshold in which households are more sensitive to inflation outturns in forming their expectations.

Finally, the Indeed Wage Tracker offers a highly forward-looking and high frequency insight into wage pressures. The Indeed Wage Tracker captures the pay firms are willing to offer new recruits and therefore captures those workers that the pay settlements data omits. Their main limitation is that they – typically – represent a small proportion of the work force who have in recent years made a relatively small contribution to overall wage growth. However, as retention pressures have eased and firms are less reliant on large pay increases to retain staff, wages offered to new recruits may play a somewhat larger role in explaining overall wage developments as they did in the years before the pandemic.
Since late 2023, the Indeed Wage Tracker has tended to imply slightly higher wage growth than private sector regular AWE (on average about 0.8pp) (Figure 4). In August, the UK Indeed UK Wage Tracker stood at 4% (Figure 15) and while UK wage growth remains high relative to many of its peers, it has become less of an outlier in recent months. However disinflationary wage momentum here also seems to be levelling off, with the wage tracker remaining stuck at around 4% since the turn of the year.

Taken together, I place considerable weight on the DMP and pay settlements, while monitoring the Indeed Wage Tracker as a higher frequency indicator of broader labour demand conditions. Collectively, these measures suggest that the wage disinflation process is stalling out with pay growth likely to stabilise over the coming year closer to 3.5% than 3%. I believe this remains above levels consistent with our inflation target and suggests there is less labour market slack than we thought.
What will I be monitoring for the emergence of second-round effects?
There is a plethora of wage growth indicators that can help inform our view of slack in the labour market. Our investigation of these different measures leads me to believe that underlying wage growth is running above rates consistent with our 2% inflation target and this looks set to continue. This suggests there is not as much slack as we had expected, and so there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging from the wage-setting channel.
But we need not only focus explicitly on wage measures in making our assessment of slack. Other labour market and activity measures can provide insights on the degree of slack in the economy, and as I have demonstrated previously Opens in a new window, wider economic conditions play a role in determining the extent to which second-round effects are likely to take hold. Taking stock of these conditions suggests that it may be unwise to assume that labour market slack and weak demand will mitigate the risks. Other labour market indicators also suggest there is less labour market slack than we thought and that it may have peaked. As with wages, there is no one perfect metric of employment growth – particularly in recent years given issues with the Labour Force Survey. Bank staff produce an estimate of underlying employment growth drawing on a range of surveys and hard data. Figure 17 shows that employment growth was essentially flat in 2025 and below the rate of population growth—consistent with a degree of slack opening up. However, underlying employment growth has been steadily rising this year. This has recently been corroborated by the KPMG/REC jobs report, according to which measures of employment and labour demand have risen above pre-conflict levels.

Figure 17: Underlying employment growth has started to pick up in the past few months
Indicators of employment growth (a)

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England Agents, DMP survey, HMRC, KPMG/REC UK Report on Jobs, Lloyds Business Barometer, ONS, S&P Global and Bank calculations.(a) Bank staff’s indicator-based measure of underlying employment growth is constructed using a dynamic factor model, following the approach of (Doz, Giannone, & Reichli, 2011 Opens in a new window). The model extracts a common component from monthly survey indicators, capturing comovements across series. The common component is scaled to align with LFS employment growth between 2000–19.

Meanwhile, there are other signs that labour market slack may have peaked: the unemployment rate has fallen from 5.2% in the three months to January 2026 to 4.7% in August; redundancies have come down from their peak of 150,000 in the three months to October 2025 and are currently running at just above 100,000, in line with the average observed since 2012; and vacancies show signs of stabilising.
A stable or slightly improving labour market is consistent with more resilience in activity than we and other forecasters had been expecting. In April, HM Treasury’s summary of independent forecasts for the UK economy showed a median GDP forecast of 0.7% in 2026, roughly in line with our middle projection (Scenario B) in April of 0.8% growth this year. By September, HM Treasury’s summary of forecasts showed median growth of 1.3% this year and our central projection in July predicted 1.1% growth in 2026 . There has been a trend towards revising UK GDP forecasts for this year up, particularly as stronger-than-expected data has come in.
Surveys of firms and consumers tell a similar story. September's flash PMI ticked down modestly but remained in positive territory, reflecting an expansion of output. Purchasing managers are reasonably positive about the future as well, with the future output index at 67.4, just a little below the long-run average of 68.2.
The economy has proven surprisingly resilient even in the face of tighter financial conditions. Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict, financial conditions have tightened largely as short-term interest rates and mortgage rates have increased. But while the price of credit has risen, the impact on credit volumes has been muted. Although mortgages for home purchases have fallen since the conflict began, overall gross mortgage lending was £23.6bn in August—slightly below pre-conflict levels (an average of £24bn in the second half of 2025), but above the average level since 2024 (£21.9bn). Monthly consumer credit (credit cards, car finance and other non-mortgage credit) hit a high of £2.5bn in August, and over the past 6 months monthly net finance raised by corporates has remained above the average level since 2024. It is not obvious to me from this data that our monetary policy stance is meaningfully restrictive.
Meanwhile, household and firm inflation expectations remain elevated. As I have previously argued Opens in a new window, attentiveness to inflation has risen after over five years of inflation remaining above target. Inflation is also currently already within the threshold at which outturns impact expectations. Greater inflation attentiveness is reflected in an increase in the frequency of UK Google searches for a variety of inflation-related terms in recent years (Figure 18).

Figure 18: UK google searches for inflation-related terms
Frequency(a)

Footnotes

Sources: Google and Bank calculations.(a) The series are three-month rolling averages. The frequency is a relative measure for each individual search term, over 2005 – September 2026, where 100 indicates the highest frequency over that time period. Latest data points are for September 2026 and data are not seasonally adjusted.

According to the DMP, firms’ expected year-ahead own-price growth remains elevated at 3.7%, compared with 3.4% in February before the outbreak of the Iran conflict. Similarly, households’ inflation expectations jumped following the Iran conflict, abated but remained elevated subsequently and picked up sharply in September to 4.5% for short-term expectations and 4.3% for longer-term expectations (Figure 19). The risk of elevated inflation expectations translating into second-round effects is greater if there is less slack in the economy.

Figure 19: Inflation expectations have risen since the conflict began
Household inflation expectations(a)

Footnotes

Source: Citigroup, YouGov and Bank calculations.(a) The data are from the Citi/YouGov survey and are based on responses to the questions: ‘How do you expect consumer prices of goods and services will develop in the next 12 months?’, and ‘And what do you think will happen to the prices of goods and services, on average, over the longer term – say five to ten years?’. The dashed lines represent the series averages over 2010–19. The latest data points are for September 2026.

Conclusion
Our monetary policy strategy since the outbreak of the Iran conflict has relied to some degree on labour market slack mitigating the risks of second-round effects taking hold. But not all of our wage metrics support this argument. A closer look at the two main metrics we use to understand the recent evolution of wage growth—private sector regular AWE and private sector RTI—suggests wage disinflation has stalled at levels above those consistent with inflation at 2%.
If getting a better handle on the evolution of wage growth to date is tricky, devising a clear view of the future is trickier. The forward-looking indicators we consider—the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker–all point to wage growth that is likely to plateau closer to 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. The risks to this are skewed to the upside, in my view. Not only have we tended to underpredict wage growth since the pandemic, but realised pay settlements have been above those predicted in the Agents’ pay survey the past two years. Furthermore, the majority of 2027 pay settlements will be agreed at a time when inflation is above 4%.
Our broad range of wage indicators suggests there is less slack in the labour market than we thought and it may have peaked. This is reflected in broader indicators for the labour market and activity. All together, this suggests the risk of second-round effects taking hold is higher. This is even more so the case as energy prices have remained high and volatile for longer. In my view, this makes a risk management approach to our monetary policy strategy even more appropriate.
When it comes to managing risks around second-round effects, we face two main scenarios. In the first one, we proactively lean against second-round effects by hiking interest rates and later discover this was unnecessary and adjust our policy stance. In the second one, we are too sanguine about second-round effects and set policy accordingly before course correcting. I believe the evidence laid out in this speech shows the risk of second-round effects is greater than we thought. Furthermore, staff simulations suggest setting policy as if you were in a stronger second-round effects scenario and then adjusting policy upon learning you are in a minimal second-round effects scenario leads to better outcomes than doing the opposite. I therefore continue to believe we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round effects.

The AWE measure is also used to calculate earnings growth under the current Triple Lock framework.

Another reason weekly (as measured by AWE) or monthly pay (as measured by RTI) could be changing is due to changes in hours worked. If pay is rising because people are working more hours that has different implications for wage pressure than if their hourly pay is rising. The LFS is the only timely source of data on hours worked but comes with an additional health warning. The ONS recently explained Opens in a new window that declining response rates on the LFS, coupled with the non-response imputation method and reliance on respondent recall, had led the LFS to overstate hours worked on average. Nevertheless, across the whole economy, the LFS suggests average hours worked for employees increased from 31.8 to 32 per week in the year to the second quarter of 2026. In some sectors where pay growth has been weak according to the AWE data – such as accommodation and food services – average hours worked have fallen. Similarly, in some sectors where the RTI data suggests monthly pay growth has been strong – such as finance and insurance – there has been a rise in average hours worked. Overall, we can tentatively conclude that shifts in hours may account for a marginal part of changes in wage dynamics over the past year.

The ONS provides its own decomposition of private sector regular average weekly earnings. In August it estimated that the wages contribution was 3.4%.

The wage growth consistent with an inflation target of 2% depends on labour productivity growth, the share of imports in consumption and import price inflation, and margins. I think that labour productivity growth is likely to be lower and import price growth higher than 1% and so my estimate of target-consistent wage growth is closer to 3%.

articles.title: The split screen war | RBCCM
articles.text:
The nine-month Iran conflict has increasingly become a split screen war, with market observers and security experts reaching starkly different conclusions about the trajectory and duration of the conflict. One set of market participants focuses singularly on exports moving through Hormuz, assuming most disruption is in the rear-view mirror. Meanwhile, an increasing number of security experts in Washington and the region are alarmed by Iran's willingness to pursue an escalation strategy designed to break the economic siege and reduce the American footprint in the Middle East.
The 2027 glut thesis rests partly on the assumption that current Hormuz transit patterns will persist despite ever-more-deadly maritime attacks, or that Washington and Tehran are approaching a diplomatic deal enabling a return to pre-February conditions. Since the war began, deal headlines have helped contain prices against a backdrop of drone, missile, and mine attacks. White House messaging about resolution coming "soon" has also reinforced short-duration expectations among market participants.

"The history of armed conflicts in the post-WWII period shows that short wars are actually something of an anomaly, not the norm."
Helima Croft, Head of Global Commodity Strategy and MENA Research, RBC Capital Markets

Yet the history of armed conflicts in the post-WWII period shows that short wars are actually something of an anomaly, not the norm, with the average interstate conflict lasting 2.1 years and the average intrastate conflict lasting 3.5 years. The June 2025 12-day war between U.S./Israel and Iran is therefore a notable outlier, even as it has served as a key reference point driving recency bias in the market.
The ability of the U.S. to deploy enormous military resources to assist with cargo evacuation through Hormuz has been cited as evidence of the market's invisible hand finding a workaround. A recurrent theme in Washington conversations is that rising transits have come at enormous cost not only to the U.S. Treasury but also to U.S. force readiness. A clear consensus from these discussions is that Iran shows no signs of dropping its maximalist demands for full enforcement of the June MoU despite the blockade's mounting economic cost. Iran has been one of the most sanctioned countries on earth since the 1979 revolution, and its leadership has developed a resistance-economy playbook, even at the cost of enormous civilian suffering.
Even the leading proponents of the "let-the-blockade-do-the-work" strategy in Washington and the region concede that it will require a significant amount of time to achieve its stated objectives, with estimates ranging from 8-9 additional months to as far out as two years. All the while, Tehran is expected to continue its steady escalation of strikes on Hormuz tankers and U.S. military assets, with Kuwait and Bahrain bearing the brunt of recent Iranian fire. If Iran continues to move the conflict up the escalation ladder, regional energy facilities could also come under increasing fire to raise the stakes for blockade supporters.

View detailed data

A horizontal bar chart titled "Figure 1 - Duration of US/Iran War Versus Reference Conflicts/Campaigns (Years)" displays the duration in years of nine conflicts, measured along an x-axis ranging from 0 to 25 years in intervals of five. Reading from top to bottom, the conflicts and their approximate durations are: Gulf War (1991) at 0.6 years; US-Iran (2026-) at 0.75 years, rendered in a bright royal blue bar to distinguish it as the focal data point; Average Inter-state at 2.1 years (denoted with an asterisk as post-World War II); Korean War (1950-53) at 3.1 years; Average Intra-state at 3.5 years (also asterisked); Russia-Ukraine (2022-) at 4.7 years; Iraq War (2003-11) at 8.8 years; Vietnam War (1965-75) at 10.2 years; and Afghanistan War (2001-21) at 20.0 years. All reference bars appear in dark navy, while the highlighted US-Iran (2026-) bar appears in bright royal blue. The chart features a medium-blue title, thin dark grey horizontal dividing lines framing the chart area top and bottom, and a white background. A footnote at the bottom-left reads: "Sources: The Correlates of War Project, RBC Capital Markets; *In post-World War II era."

The Houthi entry into the conflict has provided Tehran with an invaluable assist. Not only has Houthi action inflicted damage on Saudi infrastructure, but it has also signaled the limits of U.S. security guarantees to Gulf allies, with Washington resisting direct participation in operations against the Yemen-based fighters.
A key question is how long Iran can continue this pattern of escalation without a more forceful response from Washington. Exit-strategy scenarios being discussed in Washington contain a final salvo dynamic, including a potential U.S. strike on Iran's fortified Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility. The U.S. would likely need to use a MOAB ordnance or weapon not previously deployed on the battlefield to disable the mountain-embedded site. This carries the risk of a correspondingly extreme retaliatory response and/or more determined Iranian resolve to impose its terms on the region following an American exit. Whether elevated exports could be maintained in a hasty American withdrawal scenario is highly questionable, especially if concurrent with removal of U.S. military assets aiding transits and absent a maritime management agreement among key regional players.
Neither the current unstable stalemate nor an escalation-to-exit scenario appears to provide a beneficial backdrop for elevated exports or production over the next 6-9 months. A peace deal would indeed be a game changer, but all signs indicate that such an offramp will likely continue to prove elusive during this period.

Helima Croft authored "Postcard from DC: Split Screen War," published on November 18, 2026. For more information on the full report, please contact your RBC representative.

articles.title: Financing Infrastructure After LGFVs
articles.text:
Financing Infrastructure After LGFVs

Xiaoxi Zhang

Gavekal Dragonomics | 20 Nov 2026

The math for financing infrastructure projects doesn’t work anymore. For years, China’s local governments have relied on a combination of public, on-balance-sheet financing and hidden, off-balance-sheet funding to deliver high volumes of investment without blowing up their official debt numbers. But the repeated bailouts of local government financing vehicles’ (LGFVs) hidden debts have made the central government wary of this model, and it has been gradually curtailing off-balance-sheet financing.Those curbs have built up over time, and are now materially constraining infrastructure spending. Fixed-asset investment in infrastructure sectors is down 7.3% in the year through October, with the decline deepening in recent months despite government pledges to stabilize investment. The reality is that the financial returns on infrastructure projects remain too low to attract private-sector investors. That leaves the government with an unpleasant trade-off: either pay for infrastructure projects entirely with government bonds, and accept rising debt, or allow infrastructure investment to keep declining, and accept weaker growth. It is choosing the latter.

articles.title: A Regressive subsidy, an unequal reform: The Rich benefited, but the poor paid in missed healthcare: Guest post by Xufeng Liu
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

A Regressive subsidy, an unequal reform: The Rich benefited, but the poor paid in missed healthcare: Guest post by Xufeng Liu

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 18, 2026

This page in:

English

English

This is the 10th in this year’s series of posts by PhD students on the job market.
Economists have long argued that fuel subsidies are expensive and regressive: richer households buy more fuel, so they capture far more of the benefit than poorer ones. When Nigeria's new president declared on May 29, 2023 that "the fuel subsidy is gone," pump prices nearly tripled within days. But a subsidy that is regressive in who receives it need not be progressive in who bears its removal.
In my job market paper, my co-author and I find that the short-run disruptions to healthcare access and utilization following Nigeria's reform fell hardest on poorer and rural households who benefited least from the subsidy while it was in place.
Transportation is part of the price of healthcare, and fuel subsidies help keep healthcare accessible
Early-life healthcare requires numerous, separate visits to health providers. WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts, and Nigeria's immunization schedule asks parents to bring a child back six times in the first 15 months. Additionally, an average African child under 5 experiences a new acute infectious illness every 3 to 5 weeks; more trips are potentially needed if the child is sick and needs curative medical care. While vaccines are free and other maternal care is subsidized at some government health facilities, the journey to the clinic still costs time and often money, with one-third of rural women citing distances as a main barrier to accessing care.
Fuel subsidies help keep the cost of these trips low by holding petrol prices below market levels. They are also a major form of government intervention with a total of $1 trillion spent worldwide in 2022, twice the annual subsidies on agriculture and ten times the subsidies on industry and technology. In Nigeria, the consequences of removing this support were immediate: between May and June 2023, average within-city bus fares rose by 98 percent. Yet despite the scale of these interventions, we know surprisingly little about what happens when subsidies are removed. Of 77 studies on fossil fuel subsidy we reviewed, 56 rely on simulation; only seven analyze actual removals, and none study health or broader behavioral changes.
Identification based on the pre-reform fuel supply network
Because the reform was nationwide with no Nigerian community untreated, we leverage the differences in communities' exposure to the reform based on their proximity to the fuel-supply network. Before the reform, the subsidy functioned as a binding national price ceiling that absorbed inland transport costs and kept petrol prices similar nationwide. Therefore, although subsidy removal raised fuel prices nationwide, there were larger increases in communities further from key points in the supply network.
To exploit this spatial gradient, we digitized 375 daily government petroleum-distribution reports to reconstruct the pre-reform network and identify “mother depots,” which receive fuel without relying on roads. We measured road distance from communities in the 2018 and 2023–24 Demographic and Health Surveys to their nearest mother depot. Household-reported and official petrol-price data show that one standard deviation (197 km) of additional distance was associated with approximately 6 percent larger post-reform price increases within states. We then interact depot distance with the post-reform period to estimate a continuous difference-in-differences model. One key identifying assumption is strong parallel trends: absent the reform, changes in healthcare utilization would not have varied systematically with depot distance, conditional on our controls.
We make several checks to support our identification strategy. Before the reform, household characteristics were broadly similar across depot distances, and event studies show no systematic differential healthcare trends. We also assess the sensitivity of our estimates to potential violations of parallel trends using the HonestDiD approach of Rambachan and Roth. Placebos permuting reform dates and depot distances suggest the results are unlikely to reflect chance. We also find no evidence of anticipation by households or fuel suppliers. We include state fixed effects to absorb persistent differences and geopolitical-zone-by-post fixed effects to absorb concurrent macroeconomic shocks, including the foreign-exchange reform.
Figure 1 presents the DiD estimates. We also use the same interaction between depot distance and the post-reform period as an instrument for local petrol prices, yielding broadly similar conclusions.

Preventative care was skipped; time-sensitive care was downgraded
For preventative care, every standard deviation further from a mother depot, the probability that a child received a vaccine dose that had come due fell by 4.7 percentage points after the reform, about 9 percent of the pre-reform rate of 55 percent. Antenatal care followed the same pattern. Any antenatal visit declined by 3.2 percentage points, antenatal care at public primary facilities by 3.6 points, and receipt of three or more doses of preventive malaria medication during pregnancy by 3.4 points.
For acute healthcare needs, households changed the type rather than simply forgoing care. Attendance of a skilled practitioner at birth declined by 2.4 percentage points. Among sick children, parents were more likely to rely on informal providers and symptomatic-only treatment, such as antimotility drugs for diarrhea which clinical guidelines advise against due to serious side effects.
Healthcare disruptions were concentrated among poorer and rural households
We next examine who bore the greatest burden of the reform by comparing healthcare responses across wealth, rural residence, and local health-facility availability. Vaccine-dose receipt fell by 6.9 percentage points among poorer children, while the corresponding estimates for richer and urban children were smaller and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Declines in antenatal care and shifts toward informal treatment were similarly concentrated among poorer, rural households and communities with fewer health facilities. Richer women, by contrast, shifted from private toward public primary facilities for antenatal care, without substantially reducing their overall use. Skilled birth attendance was an exception. It declined by 8.2 percentage points among richer women but little change among poorer women. This likely reflects that richer women had more formal care to lose: before the reform, 75.7 percent of richer women had skilled attendants, versus only 17.5 percent of poorer women.
Health Impacts: cleaner air but mostly in cities
Beyond healthcare utilization, we find no overall effect on neonatal mortality or self-reported health status, but some evidence of health improvements in cities: greater gestational exposure to the post-reform period was associated with lower neonatal mortality among urban births. One possible explanation is cleaner air due to less fuel consumption: relative to comparison countries, PM2.5 declined by about 10 percent in urban Nigeria, compared with 3 percent in rural areas.
Compensation should not solely be based on forgone subsidy benefits
Our findings do not argue for maintaining an expensive and regressive subsidy. Rather, they highlight an asymmetry in the distribution of the reform’s health consequences. In the short run, healthcare utilization fell most among poorer, rural households, while potential air-quality benefits concentrated in cities. This contrasts with the conventional incidence analysis which finds richer and more urban households typically capture the largest benefits. Compensation based solely on foregone subsidy benefits may therefore miss the households most affected by removal.
Finally, our analysis captures short-run effects; longer-term consequences of reduced vaccination and antenatal care require further follow-up. Evaluating fuel-subsidy reform therefore requires looking beyond fiscal savings and the distribution of subsidy benefits to consider who loses access to healthcare, who benefits from improved environmental conditions, and how these changes shape health over time.

Xufeng Liu is a PhD candidate in Agricultural, Environmental, and Development Economics at The Ohio State University.

articles.title: KPMG 2026 Global CEO Outlook
articles.text:
Economic outlook

Technology and AI

Talent

Sustainability

KPMG leaders' perspectives

Sector insights

CEOs back growth as cyber, AI and skills gaps reshape investment decisions

The 12th KPMG Global CEO Outlook reveals a widening gap between CEOs’ outlook for their own businesses and for the global economy. Confidence in their organizations’ three-year growth prospects has increased from 79 percent in 2025 to 84 percent, while confidence in the global economy has fallen from 68 percent to 65 percent, the lowest it has been since 2021. Earnings expectations have also strengthened: 68 percent anticipate annual growth of at least 2.5 percent, compared with 61 percent in 2025. The findings suggest CEOs believe they can continue to deliver growth within their businesses despite a less certain external environment, but 79 percent feel under more pressure to ensure the long-term prosperity of their organizations.Confidence in growth is being tested by a shifting risk environment, with cybersecurity and data security now the leading threats to growth. In response, 45 percent of CEOs say they plan to increase investment in cyber and digital risk resilience over the next three years, making it the top area for investment. AI presents a similar tension between ambition and delivery. It remains a top investment priority for 79 percent of CEOs, up from 71 percent in 2025, and 66 percent believe their organization is moving at the right pace or ahead of the curve. Yet the implementation challenges they rate most highly – ethical challenges, cybersecurity, cost and data sovereignty – show how much turning that investment into value depends on governance and operational readiness.As they pursue growth, CEOs are focused on addressing skills gaps across their workforce and training employees to work with AI, their two leading workforce concerns. Continued investment in upskilling and reskilling, providing tailored role-specific training on how AI can support people in role, alongside open communication about AI’s impact, will be critical to preparing the workforce for the future.Sustainability is moving deeper into strategy: 63 percent of CEOs describe their primary response over the past year as embedding it more deeply, and 70 percent weigh its costs and returns in at least some investment decisions. AI sits on both sides of that agenda. Around eight in ten CEOs believe it can support climate priorities, yet 95 percent agree that there is concern across their organization about its environmental impact more broadly.Across the findings, the decisions shaping growth increasingly overlap.

CEOs are facing challenges ranging from cybersecurity risks and regulatory pressures to the impact of AI on the way we work. They are also facing broader global issues such as economic uncertainty and geopolitical instability. It’s clear that leaders are tackling this situation head-on, investing in technology, strengthening workforce capabilities and positioning their organizations for long-term growth.

The pace of change remains significant, but this year’s CEO Outlook shows business leaders are approaching that challenge with confidence and a clear focus on the opportunities ahead.

Gary Wingrove

Global Chair & CEO

KPMG International

Economic outlook Cyber leads a crowded risk agenda

CEOs’ confidence in their own businesses sits alongside a demanding external outlook. Cybersecurity and data security is cited as the most common threat to growth, cited by 31 percent. Global economic uncertainty follows at 28 percent, with geopolitical instability and regulatory pressure both at 26 percent.Only five percentage points separate those four risks, with supply-chain resilience close behind at 24 percent. CEOs are preparing for several sources of disruption rather than organizing their response around one overriding concern.

Investment priorities mirror that range of pressures. Cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience is the most commonly selected area in which CEOs have increased investment to mitigate business risks, cited by 45 percent. Regulatory compliance and reporting follows at 36 percent, with AI integration into operations and workflows at 32 percent.Most CEOs are maintaining their existing appetite for risk, at 61 percent. Sixteen percent are taking more risk to capture opportunities, 17 percent are becoming more cautious, and six percent are prioritizing risk mitigation over new opportunities.Cyber provides the clearest connection between risk and response. It is the leading threat to growth, the leading area of increased risk-mitigation spending and one of the AI implementation challenges CEOs rank most highly. This highlights the role of resilience in supporting both growth and technology adoption.

Technology and AI CEOs back AI, but ethics, security and cost shape delivery

AI is firmly embedded in CEOs’ investment plans. Seventy-nine percent say it remains a top priority over the next three years, up from 71 percent in 2025. Confidence is also high: 66 percent believe their organization is moving at the right pace or ahead of the curve. A further 29 percent are cautiously optimistic, while approximately 5 percent are struggling or uncertain. Nearly three-quarters of CEOs (72 percent) expect to spend more than 10 percent of their budget on AI over the next year.With investment commitment and confidence both high, the more immediate question is how to implement AI and optimize value. Ethical challenges1 are most frequently rated very or mostly challenging, at 57 percent. Cybersecurity follows at 52 percent, with cost at 51 percent and data-sovereignty requirements at 50 percent. Taken together, these findings suggest that trust, security and embedded controls are becoming important considerations alongside technical capability in the AI agenda.Governance and regulation are central to that work. Fifty-nine percent say AI and data sovereignty are prompting greater attention to internal data governance and controls. Sixty-six percent expect the pace of AI regulation to present a barrier to organizational success. For businesses operating across borders, the challenge is to scale AI while varying requirements continue to develop and differ between markets.The wider technology environment is also becoming more consequential. More than eight in ten expect AI integration, cybercrime and technology-infrastructure costs to effect organizational prosperity over the next three years, all notably higher than in 2025.

Returns are expected over the medium term: Seventy-one percent anticipate seeing a return within one to three years, while 17 percent expect it within 12 months.

The challenge for CEOs is to turn AI investment into value. That means addressing ethics, cybersecurity, cost and data governance from the outset, while giving people the skills and tools they need to leverage the technology effectively. Organizations that embed and address these considerations into their governance foundations may be better positioned to scale AI effectively and responsibly.

Lisa Heneghan

Global Chief Digital Officer

KPMG International

Talent Headcount growth continues, but capability is the workforce challenge

Eighty-nine percent of CEOs expect their organization’s overall headcount to increase over the next three years, although 62 percent believe that increase will be under 5 percent. To support that growth, CEOs are focused on building the skills and capabilities their organizations will need for the future. Skills gaps are considered a significant workforce challenge, identified by 56 percent. Upskilling and training employees in AI systems follows at 52 percent, with attracting and retaining talent at 47 percent.

Workforce resistance sits near the bottom of AI implementation challenges, with 26 percent rating it very or mostly challenging. CEOs are responding through communication and development. Over the next 12 months, 51 percent plan to communicate openly about AI’s effect on roles; 46 percent plan reskilling and upskilling programs; and the same proportion plan tailored training on how AI can support people in their jobs.

As AI continues to reshape jobs and ways of working, the priority for CEOs is developing a workforce with the skills and adaptability to succeed alongside new technologies. That means investing in continuous learning, building confidence through clear communication, and helping people combine AI with human expertise, judgement and experience to create value in new ways.

Colm Gorman

Global Head of People

KPMG International

Sustainability CEOs embed sustainability more deeply into strategy

Most CEOs say recent geopolitical developments and internal pressures have brought sustainability closer to core business strategy. Sixty-three percent describe their primary response over the past year as embedding sustainability more deeply. A further 21 percent are refocusing on the issues most critical to the business, while 14 percent are expanding their efforts.Sustainability also features in capital allocation. Seventy percent consider the costs and potential returns of sustainability initiatives in at least some investment decisions, including 29 percent who do so in every major capital decision.Delivery remains difficult. Ninety-one percent say differences in sustainability regulation and expectations across markets create significant or moderate challenges. The leading barriers to achieving Net Zero or similar climate ambitions are decarbonizing supply chains, cited by 22 percent; inconsistent regulation across jurisdictions, at 20 percent; cost, at 16 percent; and a lack of skills and expertise, at 15 percent.AI adds a further tension. CEOs see significant potential for the technology to support climate and sustainability priorities, yet 95 percent agree that there is concern across their organization about the broad environmental impact of increased AI use.

Energy sourcing forms a related, but separate, part of CEOs’ plans. Over the next three to five years, 49 percent expect their primary approach to focus on diversifying external supply through renewable or lower-carbon energy. Thirty-seven percent expect to focus primarily on reducing demand through efficiency, while 13 percent plan to add dedicated generation, storage or backup capacity.

As CEOs navigate growing pressures across supply chains, energy and regulation, sustainability is becoming increasingly embedded in strategy and investment decisions. At the same time, organizations are adapting to an AI-driven world. While AI has the potential to accelerate sustainability progress, responsible adoption requires a clear understanding of its environmental footprint to ensure its benefits ultimately support climate goals.

Gauthier Acket

Global Head of Sustainability

KPMG International

The 2026 test: turning confidence and investment into lasting value

The findings describe CEOs as willing to back their businesses, but growth increasingly depends on more than the allocation of capital. Cyber resilience shapes both risk and AI deployment. Workforce plans depend on closing skills gaps. Sustainability is moving closer to strategy and capital allocation, while energy choices form part of CEOs’ operational planning.These priorities interact. Responsible AI scaling may require appropriate security, governance and workforce capability. Scaling technology brings infrastructure costs and energy use into business decisions. Sustainability ambitions depend on practical decisions about supply chains, regulation and capital. A more integrated approach may help organizations identify potential gaps between ambition and delivery.The defining task for CEOs in 2026 is to make these decisions reinforce one another. That requires a shared view of value and clear accountability across strategy, technology, risk, people and sustainability.Organizations may be better placed to pursue growth when they connect these decisions and build the capabilities to deliver them.

articles.title: Aviation Benefits Beyond Borders 2026
articles.text:
Webinar

In Partnership with

Aviation Benefits Beyond Borders 2026

Register Now

1 December 2026 – 2.00pm GMT (London / 9am New York)

online

Aviation plays a vital role in connecting people, businesses and communities around the world, supporting economic growth, employment, international trade and tourism.

Aviation Benefits Beyond Borders 2026, produced by ATAG with analysis from Oxford Economics, provides an updated assessment of the economic and social benefits of air transport at the global and regional levels. The report highlights the industry’s contribution to jobs and economic activity, as well as the wider benefits of aviation in enabling global connectivity and supporting development.

This webinar will introduce the new report and present its key findings, offering participants an opportunity to better understand and communicate the value of aviation to economies and societies worldwide.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Sami Hamroush

Sami leads a team of economists who undertake economic impact studies for multinational corporations, industry groups, and governments in Europe and the Middle East. Since joining Oxford Economics in June 2023, Sami has led a number of large consulting projects for clients in the energy, aviation, and beverages sectors.

Before joining Oxford Economics, Sami spent nearly ten years in the UK Government Economic Service at both the Department for International Trade and Office for National Statistics, where he developed expertise in global supply chains analysis, assessing the impact of foreign direct investment, and compiling Balance of Payments statistics.

Sami holds a BSc (Hons) in Economics from Manchester Metropolitan University and a MSc in Economic Policy from School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London.

Associate Director, Economic Footprint & Sustainability

Chloe Parkins

Chloe is a Lead Economist with Tourism Economics, specialising in European tourism forecast services. On top of forecasting, she takes a key role in European consultancy work including regular outputs for the ETC and STR. She previously worked on both the industry and macro services within Oxford Economics for seven years where she developed her skills in forecasting, modelling, data visualisation and bespoke consulting work.

Lead Economist, Tourism Economics

Stephen Rooney

Stephen manages the Air Passenger Forecast service which offers short- and long-term forecasts of air passenger flow for almost 4,000 routes and total flows for 183 countries, as well as alternative forecast scenarios for strategic decision-making. He has developed and maintained various bespoke forecast models for a range of clients from across the travel and tourism space as well as regularly contributing to the team’s consultancy output.

Stephen holds a First Class Economics with Politics degree from the University of Ulster.

Lead Economist, Tourism Economics

Haldane Dodd

Haldane Dodd is Executive Director at the Geneva-based Air Transport Action Group (ATAG). This organisation, the only global grouping of players from across the aviation industry, brings together airports, airlines, air navigation service providers, aircraft and engine manufacturers and SAF producers to agree common goals. ATAG’s current mission is to provide a platform through which the aviation sector is working to reduce its climate change impact. ATAG works with Principal Partner members ACI, IATA, CANSO, Airbus, ATR, Boeing, GE Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce and Safran to ensure aviation is able to respond to global decarbonisation and sustainability objectives. Previously, Haldane was Head of Communications and Advocacy at ATAG and Communications Manager with Airports Council International World where he worked on issues such as the environment, security and airport economics. A British native, Haldane also holds New Zealand citizenship and started his aviation career at the listed company Auckland International Airport Limited, which runs New Zealand’s busiest airport. He has a background in broadcast media and holds a Bachelor of Communications Studies.

Executive Director, Air Transport Action Group (ATAG).

articles.title: Pulitzer Prize Winner Dan Yergin on How the Iran War Is Reshaping the Energy Map, and the Race to Power AI
articles.text:
Research & Insights

Pulitzer Prize Winner Dan Yergin on How the Iran War Is Reshaping the Energy Map, and the Race to Power AI

By Daniel Yergin, Atul Lele, CFA, Ian Singer, Jake Davidson

When we look at the major dynamics reshaping the world today—from modern mercantilism, to the rise of artificial intelligence, to the war in Iran—it’s striking how often the energy market sits at the center of them. In today’s podcast, we’re sharing the highlights from a recent discussion diving into each of these topics, featuring Daniel Yergin, one of the world’s leading energy experts, in conversation with Bridgewater’s Atul Lele, Head of Portfolio Strategists, and Ian Singer, Head of Commodities.Across the conversation, Dan, Atul, and Ian explore how energy producers are likely to respond to what Dan calls “the mother of all supply shocks,” the implications of a global push for energy security on markets and economies, how the race to power the AI build-out is playing out, the political debate around AI energy use, and more.Dan is Vice Chairman at S&P Global and the author of several books, including The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money, and Power, which won a Pulitzer Prize, and The New Map: Energy, Climate, and the Clash of Nations.Editor’s note: The views of external guests do not necessarily reflect the views of Bridgewater. articles.title: Markets Edition: Writing on the Wall(er): Fed Hawks Are Back in Town
articles.text:
Skip to main content

Global Markets and EconomyIndustry Perspectives Episode 7GROWTH: Raising Global Investor ConfidenceIndustry Perspectives • Podcast • November 18, 2026View TranscriptFor decades, capital market regulation meant one thing: protection. But a quieter, more consequential shift is now underway. Policymakers from Washington to Brussels, Tokyo to London are no longer asking only how to guard investors — they're asking how to grow them.In the latest episode of Citi's Industry Perspectives Podcast Series, hosts Amanda Hale and Andrew Newson are joined by four senior experts from the Investment Company Institute (ICI) to explore what this shift really means — and what it will take to get right.From the democratization of private markets, and the global rise of ETFs, to the pension pressures of ageing populations and the promise of childhood investment accounts, this episode maps the forces reshaping capital markets on every continent.One message is consistent throughout: growth, investor protection and empowerment are not competing goals. They are mutually reinforcing ones.Amanda Hale, Director & Head of Regulatory Services, Global Trustee & Fiduciary, CitiAmanda has over 40 years of experience in the investments industry and has been with Citi since 2008. Prior to joining Citi, Amanda worked in the CIS Policy Team at the Financial Services Authority (FSA), now the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) after having been with HSBC for 26 years in various areas such as Trustee and Depositary Services, Custody, Settlements, Corporate Actions and Income. Amanda currently represents Citi on external industry committees and panel discussions as well as chairing various internal Citi regulatory committees. articles.title: Solana’s Institutional Breakpoint
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Solana’s Institutional Breakpoint

Written by:

Lucas Tcheyan
Vice President, Research

research • November 20, 2026

Solana’s Institutional Breakpoint

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDSolana's annual Breakpoint conference took place Nov. 15–17 in London under the theme "Token Supercycle," showcasing the network's growing ambitions in payments, tokenization, and institutional finance. The event also marked Solana's graduation from "mainnet beta" to Mainnet 1.0, following a series of infrastructure upgrades that halved target block times to 200 milliseconds (ms) and reduced target finality to approximately 150 ms through the Alpenglow consensus protocol.Institutional adoption dominated the announcements. Zelle, the bank-owned payments network that processed more than $1.2 trillion in 2025, demonstrated a $1.25 million confidential stablecoin transfer and outlined plans to launch ZelleUSD on Solana for international payments. Global remittance giant MoneyGram and wallet provider Solflare announced USDC-to-cash conversions across 170 countries and territories, while fintech lender SoFi highlighted Solana as a preferred network for stablecoins and tokenized assets.Tokenization was another major theme. The DTCC outlined plans to connect its Tokenization Service to Solana in the second half of 2027, while wealth management platform Allfunds, banking giant BNY, and investment manager Baillie Gifford highlighted initiatives bringing traditional investment products onchain. Other announcements spanned tokenized equities, regulated derivatives, decentralized compute, and agentic payments, reflecting Solana's efforts to expand beyond its established strengths in retail trading and decentralized finance.OUR TAKE Solana's evolution since 2023 has created a growing disconnect between how the network is perceived and what its ecosystem is attempting to become. For less engaged observers, Solana remains synonymous with memecoin speculation and the sometimes unsavory activity that accompanies it. For those following the ecosystem more closely, however, the network is increasingly positioning itself as infrastructure for payments, tokenized assets, and other forms of financial activity that could bring considerably larger pools of users and capital onchain.These two identities are not mutually exclusive. Solana's success as an onchain casino has been a powerful engine for attracting users, developers, liquidity, and investment. Its ability to support high-frequency, low-value financial transactions at scale helped establish a competitive advantage in a market where speed, cost, and usability were often sufficient to win. However, the conditions that allowed Solana to dominate that segment are materially different from those governing the next phase of adoption. Payments, tokenization, and agentic commerce are increasingly attracting the attention of the world's largest financial institutions, payment providers, and technology companies. These players have considerably greater resources and distribution than crypto-native startups, and Solana is one of several networks they are exploring, alongside proprietary infrastructure they can develop and control themselves.For institutions, performance is increasingly a prerequisite rather than a differentiator. Privacy, compliance, operational accountability, distribution, and access to pools of liquidity are equally consequential. Solana's realistic opportunity, at least in the near term, is therefore less about becoming the universal settlement layer for global finance and more about establishing itself as a leading neutral venue for the subset of financial activity that benefits from shared, composable, high-performance public infrastructure.A recent paper from J.P. Morgan's Kinexys and MIT's Digital Currency Initiative illustrates the challenge. Financial institutions recognize the appeal of public blockchains as shared infrastructure that no single participant controls, the paper notes. But their requirements for confidentiality, compliance, governance, and other operational necessities can conflict with the characteristics that make these networks valuable in the first place. Accommodating those requirements often means reintroducing intermediaries, permissioning, or centralized controls, potentially undermining the neutrality and interoperability that distinguish public blockchains from traditional systems. Yet building proprietary networks creates its own challenges, particularly when competing institutions must coordinate across fragmented systems. The likely outcome is not a wholesale migration from private to public infrastructure, but a gradual and selective adoption of public networks where their advantages are sufficiently compelling.Breakpoint offered evidence of the opportunity and its limitations. Zelle's confidential-transfer demonstration, DTCC's planned integration, and initiatives from major asset managers suggest that Solana is increasingly being considered for financial activity well beyond its crypto-native base. Its presence in tokenized-equity trading also demonstrates that the network can attract meaningful activity in emerging asset classes. Solana accounted for approximately 42% of onchain tokenized-equity trading volume between January and September 2026. But there is an important distinction between being selected as a supported network and becoming the primary venue where liquidity, users, and economic activity ultimately concentrate. DTCC's integration, for example, forms part of a broader multichain strategy rather than an exclusive commitment to Solana. Nor is Solana entering these markets without crypto-native competition. Hyperliquid remains a formidable competitor in onchain perpetual derivatives, while the emerging agentic economy has yet to produce a clear winner or a compelling reason why payment and coordination infrastructure must concentrate on Solana. Privacy tooling is improving, but its maturity, regulatory compatibility, and institutional adoption remain important questions. These dynamics make the ecosystem's ability to attract and retain builders particularly consequential. Solana's dense developer culture and willingness to experiment have been central to its recovery and growth, and preserving those characteristics will matter as the network courts institutional capital.Solana has made substantial progress in addressing the technical limitations that once threatened its credibility. The more difficult task ahead is translating that progress into durable distribution, liquidity, and institutional dependence in markets where performance alone is unlikely to determine the winner. Breakpoint demonstrated that Solana has earned a place in those conversations. Whether it can turn that position into an enduring advantage, rather than remain one capable option in an increasingly competitive and multichain financial system, is the more consequential question.

articles.title: The Nvidia Blast Zone
articles.text:
The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal now looks certain to topple CEO Jensen Huang, who had affairs with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, and with one of his subordinates. The questions now are what the longer-term impacts will be both on Nvidia and the US and Chinese AI ecosystems. Understandably, much coverage has focused on the spying and sex angles, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere.The biggest risk to Nvidia is if it or Huang is found to have knowingly colluded in the diversion of export-controlled chips from a Singapore datacenter to unauthorized end-users in China. The biggest risk to China’s AI industry is that the scandal leads to a tightening of US export controls on advanced chips and chip-making equipment, possibly by the end of this year. And while the US AI industry can probably weather the tumult inside Nvidia—especially if the board swiftly ousts Huang and installs credible new leadership—the scandal raises the chance that the incoming Democratic Congress will push for much tougher regulation of the sector.

articles.title: Chart of the Week: How Polymarket Repriced Jensen Huang’s Exit
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Chart of the Week: How Polymarket Priced Odds of Huang’s Exit

Written by:

Will Owens
Research Analyst

Topics

Prediction Markets

research • November 13, 2026

Chart of the Week: How Polymarket Priced Odds of Huang’s Exit

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia was a slow-building story before it became a fast one. As they say: gradually, then suddenly. The New York Times first reported his close relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, on Oct. 29. On Nov. 8, Huang admitted infidelity in a letter to employees and the company said the board had opened an investigation. At the time, Nvidia said he remained committed to continuing as CEO.

Nevertheless, observers began speculating (in the armchair sense) whether he was on his way out, and financial speculation followed as prediction markets spun up. Initially, they gave low odds for a Huang departure. Then, on Nov. 11, the Times reported Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Within about two hours, Polymarket contracts on whether Huang would leave had repriced from ~17-30% to ~90%. About 12 hours later, Nvidia announced his ouster.Data note: Prices are Polymarket CLOB price history (1-minute fidelity) for each contract’s YES token, with token IDs pulled from the Gamma API. Price history is a sampled series, not individual trades.
