articles.title: Anthropic Prices Record IPO in a Market – and World – on Edge
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Anthropic Prices Record IPO in a Market – and World – on Edge

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Topics

AI

Markets & Macro

research • November 20, 2026

Anthropic Prices Record IPO in a Market – and World – on Edge

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDAnthropic completed the largest IPO in history on Wednesday evening, pricing at $83 per share, after updating its prospectus last week with an expected price range of $70 to $78. Strong demand led the AI company, best known for its Claude chatbot, to upsize its offering, selling about 980 million shares and raising $81.3 billion, up from the 825 million originally planned. That figure surpasses Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June, and Anthropic's IPO price implied a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion for a company founded barely six years ago. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal, as they did for SpaceX. Ahead of the open, Cboe’s JJ Kinahan said demand was running almost seven times the offering, and CNBC sources reported that retail demand was the largest in history.Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT at 11:48 a.m. ET on Thursday. The first print was $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, which briefly gave the company a market capitalization of $2 trillion. The stock hit its intraday high of $114.99 in the minute after the first trade and then spent the rest of the session fading. By the afternoon it was trading in the mid-$90s, at $94.67, up about 14% from the offering price, as of 2:18 p.m. ET. The decline from the open was unusually steep. Of 20 big US IPOs since 2008, only Coupang was doing worse at the same point in its first day, according to Yahoo Finance; the group’s average was up about 3.5%. The broader market also sold off as soon as the stock opened. Stocks fell to their session lows the moment Anthropic began trading, and chip stocks including Nvidia and Broadcom erased their gains. Listed ANT options are set to start trading on Monday.Onchain, Hyperliquid showed the success of its pre-IPO perp market yet again. Its markets correctly called the deal pricing, with the perp trading well above the $70-78 range for weeks, signaling that demand was stronger than the underwriters’ original target. The perp ultimately undershot the open by about 7%, with the contract trading around $103.67 at 8:40 AM ET, roughly 25% above the $83/share offer price. Thursday morning’s perp price was roughly in line with market consensus (Cboe’s Kinahan said the first trade should land around $103 or $104), but ultimately both the perps and the pros were off with the first trade ultimately printing at $111.50. But the perp nailed where the stock ended up trading. For most of the week before listing, the perp sat in the mid-to-high $90s. It was about $96.93 as of Nov. 17 and $98.83 on the hourly chart the night before pricing, having briefly fallen below $94 during the earlier tech selloff. After the opening pop faded, the stock traded right back into that band, around $94–$97 by the afternoon. One could argue the perp’s week-long equilibrium was a better estimate of “fair” first-day value than the opening print, which looked like a short-lived demand spike.OUR TAKEThere was something strange about watching Anthropic’s staff clap on the Nasdaq floor as they IPO’d a company whose primary media narrative is that AI might kill us all. Although we are not equity analysts, we agree with the S-1 risk factors section that the end of humanity could materially affect Anthropic’s results.This week has been the most doomer week in recent memory, coming off the back of Microsoft’s O365 outage Thursday, the nationwide FAA ground stop Friday, bank outages on Monday, even the NSA’s internal comms system reportedly disrupted (twice?). Costco reported a wave of panic buying, people pulled cash out of banks, and prepping content went viral on social media. Chatter among traders included tips on which types of solar-powered batteries to buy, how to store substantial amounts of dry food in a New York City apartment, and which are the best routes to escape the city in the event of a grid collapse. So maybe it’s only fitting that this week’s blockbuster IPO was one in which the S-1’s risk factors included “the end of humanity.” (Although we are not equity analysts, we agree that the end of humanity could materially affect Anthropic’s earnings.)Since Oct. 1, the S&P 500 is down 7%, gold is off 12.2%, and BTC is in the red 25%. Treasuries have depreciated, inflation is hot, rates are expected to rise, commodities are falling, and the Democrats swept to power largely on calls to solve the “affordability crisis.” Our own Bitcoin fear & greed index is printing near all-time lows (meaning “extreme fear”), the VIX is trading at levels comparable to those from the breakout of the Iran War in March, though not quite the level from the “Tariff Tantrum” in April 2025. Stanley Druckenmiller said he is “more uncertain than ever after 50 years of investing” and that his firm’s equity positions are “basically flat.” Another Wall Street luminary, Howard Marks, argued in a Nov. 11 memo entitled “A Layman Thinks About AI” that the breakneck speed of AI development is a big risk, even for Anthropic. Paul Tudor Jones said in mid-October that “2027 is going to be a really difficult year for the stock market.” So it’s fair to say the stock market intelligentsia is uneasy.

Some have theorized that recent risk asset headwinds were enhanced by the liquidity drain caused by allocators pulling assets to buy the Anthropic IPO. This does feel intuitively right, though there’s not much evidence to directly support it. Bitcoin’s price did behave similarly when it traded poorly into the SpaceX IPO in June and made its current bear-market low on July 1 ($57,717 on Coinbase). Whether BTC and other risk assets will receive some respite now that ANT is a public stock remains to be seen. The reality is that Americans are fearful and psychologically traumatized. Polarization has long been a characteristic of the American political landscape, but the Democratic sweep was so dramatic that big swings are expected on things like tax policy, AI policy, legislative priorities, and more. Layer on the never-ending drumbeat of cyber vulnerabilities and a spectrum of AI outcomes that is so wide it contains both the possibilities of permanent utopia and impending obliteration of the species, and it’s easy to see why markets are unsteady. There’s a sense that one more piece of big bad news could tip markets over the edge – a major cyber-attack, an escalation of the Iran or Ukraine wars, an outbreak or substantial natural disaster. Alternatively, a major peace deal or initiative emanating from Trump’s visit with Xi and Putin, cessation of major regional conflicts, or a legislative breakthrough in Congress could assuage the fears. As they say, if you’re going through hell, keep going. The only way out is through. Everything is different, yes, but everything is fine. Bitcoin keeps producing blocks uninterrupted, and I just coded a slick new dashboard to monitor the situation.

articles.title: Daily: Market volatility reinforces case for portfolio resilience
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo:Year Ahead 2027 | CIO’s Mark Andersen on building portfolio resilience(5 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Equities: Industrials, health care, Eurozone, and quality AI (7 mins)
Video: Year Ahead 2027 | Opportunities in high-quality bonds and select EM debt (5 mins)Thought of the dayWhat happened?
US equities fell again on Thursday as concerns about the AI trade combined with a more hawkish interest rate backdrop. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed down 2% and 2.3%, respectively, and the sell-off continued in Asia on Friday. The Nikkei 225 slid over 5%, while Taiwan's benchmark index was 6.2% lower.The market weakness was relatively broad. All major S&P 500 sectors traded lower, while declining stocks substantially outnumbered advancing stocks on both the NYSE and Nasdaq. Recent selling has followed persistent pressure on chipmakers and cloud companies as investors question the scale of investment required to build AI infrastructure.Monetary policy uncertainty has added to fragile market sentiment. Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting indicated that nearly all policymakers expected further tightening to be necessary if the US economy evolves as anticipated. Markets were pricing a near certainty of a 25-basis-point increase in December, with persistent inflation pressures also supporting the US dollar. US two-year and 10-year Treasury yields fell 4bps and 2bps, respectively, while the US dollar held recent gains. Higher rate expectations and dollar strength weighed on gold, which fell to a 14-month low of around USD 3,575 an ounce at the time of writing.Without taking single-security views, sentiment was also dented by reports from the Financial Times and newswires that investigative research house Hunterbrook had published a short-sell report on AMD (-7.7%) over fears that its business with China may be affected by stricter US chip restrictions; NVIDIA (-3.3%) also extended its recent losses despite having issued an upbeat revenue forecast earlier in the week.What do we think?
As outlined in our recently published Year Ahead publication, we do not think that the economic expansion, corporate earnings cycle, or structural AI investment story has broken. Our base case for 2027 remains for economic growth close to trend, rising corporate profits, further growth in AI investment, and moderating inflation later in the year. We still expect this combination to support additional equity gains and positive fixed income returns.But the risk-reward in equities has become more balanced. We recently downgraded global equities from Attractive to Neutral, reflecting elevated expectations, high index concentration, and a wider range of potential outcomes around AI. In particular, the AI debate is shifting from whether investment will continue to whether it can generate sufficient revenues and shareholder returns. Today's price action supports this shift in focus.Cumulative US technology investment in AI infrastructure could approach USD 5tr by the end of 2028. But we estimate that AI model and application revenues will probably have to reach at least USD 1.5tr by 2030 for the industry to earn an adequate return. While this is possible, it is unlikely that every company will reap the rewards from this: Competition, price cuts, costly monetization, and open-weight models may threaten returns. Financing, regulatory, and company-specific risks also add to uncertainty.Tighter monetary policy expectations add another source of volatility. While we foresee further near-term rate increases (namely 25bps hikes in the US in December 2026 and March 2027), we do not anticipate a prolonged tightening cycle. The cumulative effects of higher rates look set to weigh on consumer demand, while we believe base effects will contribute to a moderation in underlying inflation.How do we invest?
In our base case, we expect upside for equity markets in 2027. But the range of potential outcomes is broader. The challenge for investors in 2027 is constructing portfolios that can prove resilient across a variety of scenarios.Refocus equity exposure. In our base case, we expect corporate earnings growth to support equities, with around 15% S&P 500 earnings growth in 2027. But with the top 10 companies accounting for 39% of the index, relatively small changes in expectations about a handful of AI-linked businesses can have an outsized effect on returns.The Eurozone is our preferred equity region, with 15% earnings growth forecast for 2027, a lower valuation than the US, and earnings drivers spanning manufacturing, defense, infrastructure, and electrification. At a sector level, we favor industrials and health care, while equal-weight strategies in the US can be a convenient way to help reduce technology concentration.Within US technology, we favor financially strong hyperscalers with visible AI monetization, alongside select leaders in compute, foundry, semiconductor equipment, and infrastructure software. We remain cautious on leveraged capacity providers, lower-quality suppliers, and companies whose valuations depend on persistent bottlenecks or distant cash flows.Rebalance into fixed income. Elevated yields offer an attractive combination of income and potential portfolio resilience, while providing a return cushion even if rates do not decline materially. We favor intermediate duration, broadly two to 10 years. We see attractive return opportunities in quality bonds, and within fixed income, we see the best return opportunity in emerging market and high yield bonds. EM sovereign and corporate bonds currently yield roughly 7.1% and 7.0%, respectively, while US high yield offers around 8.3%.Use volatility, rather than fear it. Investors should prepare for volatility instead of trying to predict every setback. Structured strategies can help investors build exposure in more tailored ways, potentially limiting losses, generating additional income, or allowing more measured market participation. Higher implied volatility, all else equal, may raise the appeal of such approaches. However, investors must understand the potential trade-offs, including capital loss, issuer, liquidity, and opportunity-cost risks, so we favor diversification and careful sizing of structures.To read our views in more detail, please see Year Ahead: Sustaining resilience and Monthly Letter: Sustaining resilience.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
articles.text:
Finance and Economics Discussion Series (FEDS)

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 2026

Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols

Abstract: We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.
Keywords: AI, Artificial Intelligence, Data Centers, Investment, Labor supply and demand, Prices, business fluctuations, and cycles

articles.title: The economic impact of the UK's beer and pub industry
articles.text:
Consulting Report

13 Nov 2026

The economic impact of the UK’s beer and pub industry

The beer and pub industry plays an important role within the UK economy both culturally and economically.

We completed an economic impact assessment of the beer and pub industry across the UK, capturing the separate impact of the breweries, pubs, off-trade and the rest of the on-trade sectors. The approach isolated the industry’s total impacts across the UK at both local authority and parliamentary constituency levels. We also completed Scottish and Welsh reports as part of this, with the latter translated into Welsh.

The beer and pub industry plays an important role within the UK economy both culturally and economically. Pubs are at the heart of many local communities, spread across the length and breadth of the country. Yet the total footprint of the industry is greater than just pubs, as it also considers the brewing of beer, as well as the sales of beer throughout hotels, restaurants, sports clubs, and in the retail trade. The beer and pub industry, therefore, has a footprint in every local community across the country.

To understand the current scale of its economic footprint in the UK economy, the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) commissioned Oxford Economics to update our economic impact analysis of the industry. These estimates consider the impacts from four subsectors of beer and pub activity. These are the brewing of beer, the activity of pubs, the proportion of activity in the rest of the on-trade (excluding pubs) that is attributable to the sale of beer, and the share of the off-trade that is dependent on beer sales.

Key findings from the report:

We estimate the beer and pub industry generated a total of £37.8 billion in gross value added (GVA) contributions to UK GDP in 2025.

The beer and pub industry supported almost 1 million jobs across the UK in 2025, and £21.2 billion in employee compensation.

In 2025, Oxford Economics estimate that the UK’s beer and pub sector directly employed 711,300 people, supporting £11.7 billion in employee compensation, and generating £18.6 billion in GVA contributions to GDP.

The beer and pub sector provides a vital source of employment for the young and those seeking to work part-time. Across the UK, 341,900 workers between the ages of 16 and 24 year were employed in the beer and pub industry in 2025. This represents almost half (48%) of total direct employment in the sector, compared to just 11% across the UK economy more broadly.

articles.title: Adapting to a changing crisis landscape
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

Adapting to a changing crisis landscape

Gallina Andronova Vincelette

Carolina Sánchez-Páramo

Rucheta Singh

November 19, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

English

Français

Photo credit: Allison Kwesell / World Bank

Hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes arrive with a visible point of impact. But many of today’s crises don’t. A conflict thousands of miles away can raise energy prices, disrupt food supplies, and strain budgets in countries on the other side of the world. As economic and climate shocks intensify and geopolitical tensions ripple across borders, governments need to be ready.
To help countries prepare for these risks, the World Bank Group developed the Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit. Originally designed to strengthen preparedness for disasters and other emergencies, the Crisis Toolkit is now helping countries respond to a broader range of interconnected shocks, including those that spread through global energy, food, and economic systems. By combining pre-arranged financing, rapid-response mechanisms, and scalable support, it enables governments to access resources quickly, protect development gains, and strengthen resilience. Since its launch in 2024, 80 countries have adopted at least one of its instruments.
Initially, countries mostly used the Crisis Toolkit’s instruments to prepare for and respond to disasters. When Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica in 2025, the country was prepared and drew on multiple financing tools from the Crisis Toolkit put in place before the disaster. These included a pre-arranged credit line that can be drawn on quickly after a disaster or emergency, known as a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (Cat DDO), as well as financial protection through a catastrophe bond that pays out when pre-agreed conditions are met. The catastrophe bond provided a $150 million payout, while Jamaica also drew down the $42 million programmed under the Cat DDO as well as an additional $42 million in scalable financing that was available under the same facility. Together, these layers of financing gave Jamaica rapid access to resources, allowing the country to focus on response and recovery rather than scrambling to secure funds after the disaster struck.
In Colombia, following the recent earthquake, the government drew $200 million from a pre-arranged credit line through its Cat DDO. As needs became clearer, Colombia also accessed additional financing through the scalable option. These efforts reflect a broader shift toward embedding crisis preparedness and resilience into development planning, ensuring that countries are better positioned to withstand shocks when they occur.
While natural disasters were the Crisis Toolkit’s first test, the ongoing Middle East conflict demonstrated something equally important: its ability to respond to crises without a clear geographic boundary. Unlike a localized natural disaster, its impacts have extended across borders, with countries far beyond the immediate conflict zone experiencing significant spillover effects. The crisis became the first large-scale demonstration of the Crisis Toolkit’s adaptability and scalability in responding to a complex, multi-country, and manmade shock. To date, 24 countries have received support for the Middle East conflict: 10 countries have reoriented financing toward crisis-related needs using the Crisis Toolkit, while 18 countries have accessed new financing, with some countries using both.
In Bangladesh, the government rapidly redirected funds from existing World Bank projects toward urgent needs through a Contingent Emergency Response Project (CERP). This type of project allows a country to repurpose and use part of the financing already available in its World Bank portfolio when a crisis creates new and immediate priorities. Faced with disruptions in global energy markets, Bangladesh redirected existing financing toward energy imports, helping mitigate nationwide power shortages and load-shedding.
In Djibouti, the government used a similar approach to address food insecurity, shortages of essential medicines, and wider economic spillovers associated with the crisis. By tapping into pre-approved financing, the government quickly channeled resources toward urgent priorities while helping protect vulnerable people from rising prices and constrained supplies.
In the Marshall Islands — a small island state far from the source of the conflict—the government used pre-arranged financing in existing World Bank projects to provide emergency top-up transfers for more than 41,000 people. It then complemented this with additional budget support through supplemental financing operation as needs evolved. Through the existing social protection system, the government reached households with support quickly, helping people cope with the rising costs and economic impacts associated with the fuel crisis. 
Preparedness is no longer just about responding to hurricanes, floods, or earthquakes. It is about helping countries navigate a world where risks are increasingly interconnected and where crises can emerge in unexpected ways. The Crisis Toolkit’s experience of the past two years shows that countries that invest in preparedness before a shock occurs are better positioned to protect people, safeguard development gains, and recover faster when crises hit. As risks continue to evolve, the ability to adapt, respond at speed, and scale support when needed will be essential. The Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit is helping countries do exactly that.

articles.title: Increasing International Interdependence: Global Supply Chains and Cross-Border Macroeconomic Spillovers
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

November 20, 2026
Increasing International Interdependence: Global Supply Chains and Cross-Border Macroeconomic Spillovers
Francois de Soyres1
International production is increasingly organized through networks of firms that source inputs, assemble products, and supply customers across borders. As these networks deepen, conditions in one country matter more for output and prices in another, so domestic outcomes depend less on domestic conditions alone and more on the economies and sectors on which domestic production relies. This note analyzes whether this interdependence has increased in recent years, looking at two dimensions: first the association of supply-chain pressures at home and abroad with domestic inflation, and second the relationship between intermediate-input trade and business-cycle comovement.

Both dimensions build on a large literature on global inflation and its link to input trade (Ciccarelli and Mojon 2010; Auer et al. 2019; de Soyres and Franco 2019) and on trade and output comovement (Frankel and Rose 1998; di Giovanni and Levchenko 2010; Johnson 2014; de Soyres and Gaillard 2022, 2026). This note updates this evidence and asks whether these relationships have strengthened in recent years.

Conceptually, when a firm's foreign suppliers face disruptions or strong demand, its inputs become costlier or slower to obtain, and it raises prices or cuts output over and beyond the state of domestic slack. Such price pressure should show up in producer prices, which are directly exposed to input costs, and in consumer prices to the extent it is passed on. The same linkages carry demand and supply shocks across borders and can pull output cycles together. Consistent with this, I find that longer supplier delivery times, at home and among a country's foreign suppliers, are associated with higher inflation beyond what domestic slack explains, especially for producer prices. The association with foreign suppliers is much stronger in the most recent period, and the link between intermediate-input trade and GDP comovement is also larger in the latest sample, although imprecisely estimated.

These links matter because they suggest that domestic developments, in both prices and quantities, are increasingly influenced by developments abroad. This makes monitoring international conditions, and not only domestic ones, increasingly important.

1. Supply-Chain Pressures and Inflation

Since the pandemic, a growing literature has asked whether supply-chain pressures help explain inflation. Much of this work uses a single world measure of supply-chain pressure, most prominently the New York Fed's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI), which combines shipping costs with delivery-time and backlog information from manufacturing surveys (Benigno et al. 2022), and generally finds that supply-chain pressures contributed to the rise in inflation after 2020 (di Giovanni et al. 2022; Blanchard and Bernanke 2023; Comín, Johnson, and Jones 2023; Bai et al. 2024). A world index has a limitation. It is the same for every country, so it cannot show which economies are more exposed, and its estimated effect comes from movements over time that are common to all countries and hard to separate from other global shocks. This note uses country-specific measures instead. Each economy's own supplier delivery times capture conditions at home, and a foreign index built from the delivery times of its actual trading partners, weighted by their share in its intermediate-input imports, captures exposure to suppliers abroad. The estimates thus draw on differences across countries and not only over time, and I ask whether the relationship has changed since the pandemic.

A Phillips curve relates inflation to the amount of slack in the economy, usually measured by the output gap, together with lagged inflation, which captures persistence (on its evolution, see De Michelis et al. 2024), and cost shocks such as changes in energy prices. The output gap speaks to demand relative to capacity. It says little about whether firms can obtain the inputs they need: a firm facing long delivery times may raise prices or cut output even when demand has not changed. Delivery times could therefore carry information about inflation that the output gap does not. To see whether they do, I add supplier delivery times (SDT) to a standard Phillips curve.2 SDT comes from the manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI), a monthly survey in which purchasing managers report whether their suppliers' delivery times have become longer or shorter than in the previous month. The responses are summarized in a diffusion index, whose distance from 50 reflects the balance of firms reporting longer versus shorter delivery times. Monthly values are averaged within each quarter. For economy i in quarter t,

πi,t=αi+β1gapi,t+β2SDTi,t+∑k=03δkOilt−k+γπi,t−1+εi,t,πi,t=αi+β1gapi,t+β2SDTi,t+∑k=03δkOilt−k+γπi,t−1+εi,t,

where πi,tπi,t is year-on-year inflation, gapi,tgapi,t is the output gap,3 OiltOilt is year-on-year oil price inflation (entering in the current quarter and three lags), and αiαi is a country fixed effect. SDT is signed so that higher values indicate longer own delivery times. The equation is estimated separately for consumer prices (CPI) and producer prices (PPI), on a quarterly panel of 15 economies4, with standard errors clustered by country. Delivery times lengthen both when supply is disrupted and when demand is strong, so SDT captures supply-chain pressure without distinguishing between these sources.

I estimate the equation on the full sample and on two sub-periods, before 2020 and since 2023. The years 2020 to 2022 are deliberately left out of the sub-periods. The pandemic was an unusual episode, with very large shocks that hit all countries at once and pushed inflation and activity together, so including it would make it hard to tell lasting changes from pandemic effects. Comparing the periods before and after the pandemic instead asks whether the relationship has changed durably.

Figure 1 shows a positive and statistically significant coefficient on a country's own delivery times, for both consumer and producer prices, in the full sample and in the periods before 2020 and since 2023. The relationship is much larger for producer prices than for consumer prices. Point estimates are higher since 2023 than before 2020. Delivery times therefore carry information about inflation beyond the output gap, consistent with constraints in input availability, logistics, or production capacity that standard measures of slack miss.

Figure 1. Own Supply-Chain Stress and Inflation

Note: Coefficient on a country's own supplier delivery times (SDT) in a regression of year-on-year inflation on the output gap, own SDT, current and three lags of oil price inflation, and lagged inflation, with country fixed effects. Sample: CPI 1992q2 to 2026q2, PPI 1996q2 to 2026q2. 'Full sample' uses all available quarters; 'Before 2020' quarters before 2020; 'Since 2023' quarters from 2023 onward. Fifteen economies (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States), quarterly data. Error bars are 90 percent confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered by country. * p<0.1, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.

Source: Haver Analytics; author's calculations.

Accessible version

To gauge magnitudes, consider a one-standard-deviation change in each variable, measured within countries. A rise of that size in delivery times (about 6.7 index points) is associated with consumer price inflation 0.19 percentage point higher and producer price inflation 0.82 percentage point higher. The same-sized rise in the output gap (about 2.7 percentage points) is associated with inflation 0.11 percentage point higher for consumer prices and 0.13 for producer prices. The delivery time effect is therefore about 1.8 times as large as the output gap effect for consumer prices and about 6.4 times as large for producer prices. Because inflation is persistent, effects accumulate over time: a permanent one-point rise in delivery times is associated with annual inflation that is 0.3 percentage point higher for consumer prices and 0.7 percentage point higher for producer prices once the adjustment is complete.

Domestic prices may also reflect pressures in the economies from which firms source intermediate inputs. For each economy I construct a foreign SDT index,

SDTFi,t=∑j≠iwij,tSDTj,t,SDTi,tF=∑j≠iwij,tSDTj,t,

where wij,twij,t is the share of partner jj in economy ii's intermediate-input imports.5 For partners without a manufacturing PMI, I use the New York Fed's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index in place of their delivery times. I then replace own SDT with this index in the equation above, so that own and foreign delivery times enter separate regressions.6

Figure 2 shows a positive relationship between foreign delivery times and both consumer and producer price inflation. The relationship is much stronger since 2023 than before 2020, and the increase is statistically significant at the 1 percent level for both price measures. As with a country's own delivery times, the effect is much larger for producer prices, which is what one would expect if stress at foreign suppliers shows up first in input costs and is only partly passed on to consumer prices. The stronger relationship since 2023 suggests that conditions at a country's suppliers have become more important for its domestic prices, in line with increasing interdependence across economies.

Figure 2. Foreign Supply-Chain Stress and Inflation

Note: Coefficient on the foreign SDT index in a regression of year-on-year inflation on the output gap, the foreign SDT index, current and three lags of oil price inflation, and lagged inflation, with country fixed effects. The foreign SDT index is the average SDT of an economy's trading partners, weighted by their share in the economy's intermediate-input imports. Sample: CPI 1998q1 to 2026q2, PPI 1998q1 to 2026q2. 'Full sample' uses all available quarters; 'Before 2020' quarters before 2020; 'Since 2023' quarters from 2023 onward. Fifteen economies (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States), quarterly data. Error bars are 90 percent confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered by country. * p<0.1, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.

Source: OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables; New York Fed Global Supply Chain Pressure Index; Haver Analytics; author's calculations.

Accessible version

These results point to a possible cross-border channel for domestic price pressures, although delivery times abroad may reflect supply disruptions, strong demand, or both, and I do not separate them. Appendix Figures 1A to 4A report estimates by economy.

One may ask whether country-specific delivery times add anything to a single global index. Replacing the foreign index with the New York Fed's GSCPI, on the same sample and specification, gives a similar fit and the same message in most cases. That said, a country-specific foreign index fits better price movements for producer prices since 2023. This suggests that country-specific measures built from a country's own suppliers could be a fruitful way forward relative to a single world index, which is the same for every economy.

These results should not necessarily be read as saying that firms have not diversified their sourcing. After repeated shocks, firms may well have diversified suppliers or sourced less from abroad, which would weaken the link between foreign conditions and domestic prices. The regressions do not measure sourcing. What the larger coefficient since 2023 says is that domestic prices moved more closely with conditions at the suppliers that countries used in 2022. This is consistent with greater exposure, but also with a given exposure mattering more when stress is high, or with the foreign index partly reflecting common global conditions. One possible explanation, which I do not test, is that supply disturbances have made up a larger share of recent shocks, and that these may pass through to other economies' prices more than demand shocks do, especially in economies with slack. The period since 2023 is also short, and it will be important to update the analysis once more time has passed, to evaluate its robustness. Section 3 will also turn to how the sources of imports have changed.

2. Production Linkages and Business-Cycle Comovement

A long-standing finding in international economics is that countries with stronger trade ties tend to have more synchronized business cycles (Frankel and Rose 1998; Kose and Yi 2006). Trade in intermediate inputs is especially relevant because it links production processes across borders: changes in demand or production in one economy can affect activity in its trading partners (Burstein et al. 2008; di Giovanni and Levchenko 2010; Johnson 2014; de Soyres and Gaillard 2022, 2026). I revisit this relationship with updated data and ask whether it has changed over time.

For each pair of countries i and j and each ten-year window w, I estimate

corr(GDPi,GDPj)w=αij+βln(TIij,w)+δln(PIij,w)+εij,w,corr(GDPi,GDPj)w=αij+βln(TIij,w)+δln(PIij,w)+εij,w,

where the dependent variable is the correlation between the two countries' GDP cycles in window ww, TIij,wTIij,w,ww is the pair's trade intensity in intermediate inputs, PIij,wPIij,w is their bilateral portfolio investment, and αijαij is a country-pair fixed effect. In line with the literature, in a given year, trade intensity is the sum of the intermediate inputs that country ii sells to country jj and that country jj sells to country ii, divided by the sum of the two countries' GDPs (all in U.S. dollars). Portfolio investment is scaled in the same way, using the sum of the two countries' holdings of each other's portfolio securities (gross asset positions from the IMF Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey, counted in both directions). For each pair, the logs of these ratios are computed each year and then averaged over the years of window ww. Because of the fixed effects, ββ reflects how the relationship varies within a pair over time, and standard errors are clustered by country-pair.

The pandemic cannot be set aside as cleanly here as in the previous section, because each correlation is computed over ten years. I compare windows ending before 2020 with the two latest windows, ending in 2023 and 2024, and leave out the windows ending in 2020 to 2022. The two latest windows still contain the pandemic years. The Hodrick-Prescott filter used to extract GDP cycles draws on observations on both sides of each year, so the fall in 2020 and the rebound in 2021 would distort the estimated cycle in neighboring years. I therefore replace GDP in 2020 and 2021 with a straight line in logs between 2019 and 2022 before filtering. As a check, Appendix Table 1 drops 2020 to 2022 from every window: the since-2023 estimate is then smaller and no longer statistically significant.

Figure 3 shows a positive relationship in the full sample and over windows ending before 2020. For the two latest windows, ending in 2023 and 2024, the estimate is much larger, but the confidence interval is wide. The relationship is not accounted for by financial integration: the estimates are broadly similar when the portfolio investment control is dropped (Appendix Table 1).

Figure 3. Intermediate-Input Trade Intensity and GDP Comovement

Note: Coefficient on the log of bilateral intermediate-input trade intensity (intermediate inputs sold between the two countries, in both directions, divided by the sum of their GDPs) in a regression of the correlation of two countries' GDP cycles over a 10-year window on trade intensity and the log of bilateral portfolio investment, with country-pair fixed effects. Twenty-six economies, 325 pairs. 'Full sample' covers windows ending 1999 to 2024; 'Before 2020' windows ending before 2020; 'Since 2023' the two windows ending in 2023 and 2024. Error bars are 90 percent confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered by pair. * p<0.1, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.

Source: OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables; IMF Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey; Haver Analytics; author's calculations.

Accessible version

Overall, global supply chains look like a useful lens for understanding output fluctuations: when production is shared across borders, a shock to demand or production in one economy reaches the economies that supply it and buy from it, and their cycles tend to move together more where production linkages are denser.

3. Interdependence as Trade Patterns Shift

The geography of international production is changing alongside geopolitical fragmentation. Gopinath et al. (2025) document weaker trade and investment links between geopolitically distant economies since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and Airaudo et al. (2025a) find that, after the invasion, trade between countries in opposing blocs is 9 to 24 percent lower than trade within blocs, depending on how geopolitical distance is measured. Trade patterns have also shifted unevenly, with China at the center. China's imports from advanced economies have fallen sharply as a share of its GDP, while advanced economies' imports from China have risen in many advanced economies, the U.S. being a notable exception (Airaudo et al. 2025b). Across the fifteen economies in the inflation panel, China's average share of intermediate-input imports rose from 2.2 percent in 2000 to 10.4 percent in 2022, and in 2022 China was the largest single source for Australia, Brazil, Japan, and South Korea.

The regressions do not measure how firms source their inputs, so I look directly at where imports come from. For each economy, I compute the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of its import sources, the sum of the squared shares of each source country in its imports, so that a higher value means that imports come from fewer countries, together with China's share of its imports. The data are UN Comtrade records of total goods imports, so they cover all goods and not only intermediate inputs, and they run through 2025. Figure 4 compares 2019 with 2025 for the thirteen economies of the inflation panel with 2025 data. Import sourcing has neither broadly concentrated nor broadly diversified: the index changes by less than 0.005 in nine of the thirteen economies, on a scale from 0 to 1, and the median change is close to zero. Imports became noticeably less concentrated in Canada, Ireland, and the United States, and more concentrated in Brazil.

Figure 4. Concentration of Import Sources and China's Share of Imports, 2019 and 2025

Note: Panel A shows the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of import sources, the sum of the squared shares of each source country in an economy's total goods imports; panel B shows China's share of those imports. All goods are included, not only intermediate inputs. Both axes use a log scale, and an economy on the dashed line is unchanged.

Source: UN Comtrade; author's calculations.

Accessible version

China's share of imports rose in ten of the thirteen economies, by just over one percentage point at the median and by much more in Brazil. The United States is the main exception: China's share roughly halved and Mexico became its largest source, consistent with the shift in U.S. supply chains after the 2018 to 2019 tariffs on China documented by Aristizabal-Ramirez et al. (2026). Source countries do not necessarily show who produces the goods, however, as that work and Avalos, Hoang, and Van Leemput (2026) find that part of the gains of Mexico and Vietnam in U.S. imports is linked to Chinese firms. These patterns do not support a broad diversification of sourcing since 2019: for most economies the concentration of import sources is little changed, and China accounts for a larger share of imports.

This matters for how interdependence should be read. When many economies rely on the same supplier, a disruption in China reaches all of them at once, and the foreign delivery-time index of these economies partly reflects the same conditions in China. Keeping China's role in mind is useful when thinking about how price pressures and output fluctuations spread across countries.

Data and methods. The New York Fed's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index is a static download. All series except the Comtrade data were retrieved in October 2026 (the Comtrade data in November 2026), and the scripts that produce every number and figure in this note are available on request.

GDP comovement. The 26 economies are Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States. GDP cycles are obtained by applying a Hodrick-Prescott filter (smoothing parameter 100) to annual log real GDP. Because a two-sided filter would spread the 2020 collapse and the 2021 rebound into neighboring years, I first replace 2020 and 2021 log GDP with a log-linear interpolation between 2019 and 2022. Trade flows and GDP are in U.S. dollars, and the OECD tables end in 2022, so the two windows ending in 2023 and 2024 use trade data through 2022 only. Bilateral portfolio investment is the sum of the two countries' positions in each other, and non-positive values, which arise from reporting asymmetries, are set to half the smallest positive value before taking logs.

Inflation. The panel covers Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Consumer price inflation is the year-on-year change in the OECD price index for private consumption, a consumption-deflator proxy and not headline CPI. Producer price inflation is the year-on-year change in the producer price index. The output gap is a quarterly production-function estimate for Australia, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States; an annual IMF estimate, held constant within the year, for Austria, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, South Korea, and Spain; and, for Brazil, a Hodrick-Prescott filter of log real GDP (smoothing parameter 1,600). Oil price inflation is the year-on-year change in the quarterly average of the spot oil price. The sign of each country's SDT series is set so that the global supply-chain disruption of 2021 shows up as higher stress. The since-2023 sample has 204 country-quarters. Figure 4 uses the value of goods imports by source country from UN Comtrade, for all goods (not only intermediate inputs), as reported by the importing economy, across all customs procedures and modes of transport. World totals, residual groups of countries not elsewhere specified, bunkers, free zones, special categories, and the importing economy itself are dropped, and the shares are computed over the remaining source countries. Taiwan is Comtrade partner code 490. Values for 2019 and 2024 are from annual files. Annual files for 2025 are not yet available for most economies, so the 2025 values are the sum of the monthly files, except for Brazil and Japan, which have annual files; Greece has eleven months. Where both exist (2019 and 2024), the HHI from monthly sums differs from the one from the annual file by less than 0.001, and China's share by at most 0.1 percentage point. Austria has no 2025 data and France only January and February, so neither is shown. Using 2024, the latest year with annual data for all fifteen economies, the HHI is lower than in 2019 in thirteen economies, mostly by small amounts, and higher only in Brazil and Germany, while China's share rises in ten. For 2019 and 2022, the Comtrade HHI is highly correlated with the one computed from the OECD intermediate-input shares (correlation of 0.98 or higher in levels), and its change has the same sign in thirteen of the fifteen economies.

articles.title: Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks

Related Content

Financial Stability Report

Monetary Policy Report

Financial Stability Monitoring (PDF)

Mapping heat in the U.S. financial system

Federal Reserve staff regularly and systematically assess a standard set of vulnerabilities as part of their periodic review of financial stability. These assessments generally are provided to the Board and Federal Open Market Committee four times per year. Using a range of data sources as well as insights gained from discussions and engagement with domestic and foreign counterparts, staff regularly monitor vulnerabilities in four areas:

1. Elevated valuation pressures are signaled by asset prices that are high relative to economic fundamentals or historical norms and are often driven by an increased willingness of investors to take on risk. As such, elevated valuation pressures imply a greater possibility of outsized drops in asset prices.

2. Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable to distress if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

3. Excessive leverage within the financial sector increases the risk that financial institutions will not have the sufficient capacity to absorb losses when hit by adverse shocks. In those situations, institutions will be forced to cut back lending, sell their assets, or, in extreme cases, shut down. Such responses can substantially impair credit access for households and businesses.

4. Elevated funding risks can occur when financial institutions raise funds from the public with a commitment to return investor money on short notice, but those institutions then invest much of the funds in illiquid assets that are hard to sell quickly or in assets that have a long maturity. This liquidity and maturity transformation can create an incentive for investors to withdraw funds quickly in adverse situations, commonly referred to as a “run.” Facing a run, financial institutions may need to sell assets quickly at “fire sale” prices, thereby incurring substantial losses and potentially even becoming insolvent.

These vulnerability assessments inform internal Federal Reserve discussions concerning both supervision and regulatory policies and monetary policy. Two times a year, the Federal Reserve publishes its Financial Stability Report summarizing its current assessment of these vulnerabilities, the salient risks to the financial system originating in the United States and abroad, and how they might interact. A shorter summary of current vulnerabilities is included in the twice-yearly Monetary Policy Report to Congress. They also inform Federal Reserve interactions with broader monitoring efforts, such as those by the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board.

Asset Valuations and Risk Appetite

Asset valuations are the prices of assets after accounting for economic fundamentals, such as future expected cash flows and interest rates. Valuations that are high relative to history or to economic fundamentals constitute a vulnerability because the unwinding of high prices can be destabilizing in the financial system and economy. Moreover, stretched asset valuations may be an indicator of a broader buildup in risk appetite leading to investors taking on higher levels of risk, or new risks that are not fully understood.

This dynamic can be more concerning when (1) the assets are widely held and the values are supported by excessive borrowing, (2) the maturity of the asset is significantly longer than the maturity of the liability financing that asset, or (3) there is a lack of publicly available information about the asset.

However, it is very difficult to judge whether an asset price is overvalued relative to fundamentals. As a result, analysis typically considers a range of possible valuation metrics, as well as developments in areas where asset prices are rising especially rapidly, the size and pace of inflows to an asset class, or the implications of unusually low or high levels of volatility in certain markets.

Borrowing by Businesses and Households

Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. A default can significantly limit their ability to obtain credit in the future. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

Leverage in the Financial System

Highly leveraged financial system intermediaries—those with significantly more debt than equity—can amplify the effect of negative shocks in the financial system and broad economy. For example, if highly leveraged institutions collectively respond to a negative shock in the economy (e.g., a sharp decline in house prices) by tightening lending standards and shrinking their balance sheets more than called for by the shock itself, perhaps because outsized credit losses threaten their solvency, the resulting contraction in credit will aggravate the decline in economic activity resulting from the shock.

Sufficiently large losses for highly leveraged institutions, especially if those institutions have a significant share of short-term funding, can lead to “fire sales,” where assets are unloaded quickly at extremely low prices. These fire sales then reduce the value of similar assets held by other financial institutions, potentially leading to a negative feedback loop.

The Federal Reserve monitors leverage in the banking sector with the help of an extensive data collection program. This includes the data collected in support of the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests for large banking institutions, the quarterly Reports of Condition and Income for all banks, and the Consumer Credit report. Additionally, periodic surveys of nonbank providers of leverage, such as the Senior Credit Officer Opinion Survey, as well as collaboration and data sharing among all the financial regulatory agencies offer valuable insights on nonbank financial leverage.

Funding Risks and Maturity Transformation by the Financial System

One key benefit provided by the financial system is to aggregate short-maturity liabilities so that they can be used to fund long-maturity assets. This function has historically occurred primarily in the traditional banking system or other depository institutions, which use deposits from consumers as part of the financing to provide multiyear auto or mortgage loans. In recent decades, nonbank financial institutions have grown substantially. For example, mutual funds offer their investors the convenience of daily withdrawals even though they invest in longer-term debt instruments.

However, as seen during the 2007–09 financial crisis and the outbreak of COVID-19 in March 2020, the mismatch between long-term assets and short-term funding creates systemic vulnerabilities that can threaten the functioning of financial markets and the broader economy. This manifests when a large fraction of those investors withdraw their funding suddenly in response to an increase in risk aversion after a negative shock.

Deposit insurance provides some protection against this vulnerability within the traditional banking system. However, firms that use short-term liabilities such as repurchase agreements (or “repos”) or commercial paper, and the financial institutions that invest in them, like money market mutual funds, are also prone to run risk. Indeed, money market mutual funds came under considerable pressure during both the 2007–09 financial crisis and the pandemic in 2020. For this reason, the Federal Reserve actively monitors—as best it can, given available data and measurement—both liquidity risk and the degree of maturity transformation in the financial system.

articles.title: America's lost advantage in the strategic triangle | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

America’s lost advantage in the strategic triangle

Patricia M. Kim

Patricia M. Kim

Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center, Center for Asia Policy Studies

November 17, 2026

Rather than restoring America’s centrality in great power diplomacy, the Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral in Shenzhen may underscore how far Washington’s position has eroded since the triangular diplomacy of the 1970s.
During the Cold War, America’s central position in the international system gave both Beijing and Moscow strong reasons to improve relations with Washington, providing American leaders with leverage to advance U.S. interests.
Today, China and Russia have forged a close strategic partnership, limiting Washington’s ability to exploit differences between them. Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s transactional approach to allies has undermined its ability to draw on the collective strength of its alliances and partnerships.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping shake hands during a signing ceremony at the Great Hall of the People on May 20, 2026 in Beijing, China. (Maxim Shemetov - China Pool/Getty Images)

7 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Half a century ago, Washington occupied the pivotal position between Beijing and Moscow. Both China and the Soviet Union had strong reasons to seek better relations with the United States, giving American leaders leverage over them. Today, that triangle has been turned upside down. China and Russia have forged a close strategic partnership, limiting Washington’s ability to exploit differences between them, while the decline in American leadership in the international system has further weakened its ability to influence them.
An unprecedented meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen is unlikely to produce major breakthroughs on arms control or the war in Ukraine. Instead, the meeting may reveal just how much America’s standing in the strategic triangle has changed.
The logic of triangular diplomacy
To understand this shift, consider what made triangular diplomacy effective in the first place. In the late 1960s, China’s leaders had an interest in welcoming U.S. President Richard Nixon’s overtures. The Sino-Soviet split had escalated into armed border clashes in 1969, and rapprochement with Washington offered Beijing an important counterweight to Soviet military pressure.
But the appeal of improved relations with the United States extended beyond just the Sino-Soviet rivalry. Beijing sought U.S. recognition of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and progress toward acceptance of its sovereignty claims over Taiwan. For a China emerging from decades of relative international isolation, Washington offered a path toward broader diplomatic and economic engagement with the world’s most advanced economies, many of them American allies in Europe and Asia. In other words, Beijing found Washington appealing not only because of what the United States could offer bilaterally, but also because of Washington’s central position in the international system and the influence it exercised through its extensive network of alliances and partnerships.
The Nixon administration also presciently understood that rapprochement with China would provide Washington leverage in its dealings with Moscow. Presented with the likelihood of warming U.S.-China ties, Soviet leaders made their own moves toward détente with Washington. In 1972, the United States and the Soviet Union reached agreements through the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks that imposed important constraints on the nuclear arms race. Washington and Moscow continued arms control negotiations to build on these foundations, even as their bilateral competition persisted. Détente did not eliminate the Cold War’s dangers or prevent renewed confrontation in later years, but it demonstrated how high-level diplomacy, backed by strategic leverage and sustained negotiations, could produce tangible gains.
A strategic triangle turned upside down
Today, the strategic triangle has fundamentally changed.
China and Russia no longer regard each other as their principal security threat. Instead, they have forged a close strategic partnership rooted in shared grievances and a common desire to challenge what they perceive as a Western-dominated international order. This convergence has been building since the end of the Cold War and is unlikely to be attenuated by American overtures. Nor is the PRC the isolated country it once was during the first half of the Cold War. Today, it has an extensive network of strategic partners, as I write about in my forthcoming book: “No Constraints: China’s Global Quest for Partners and Influence.” Russia has also cultivated alternative markets and partnerships to mitigate Western sanctions and isolation.
Yet the United States is hardly without leverage. China’s economy continues to be reliant on American markets, technology, and financial networks, and Beijing has compelling reasons to avoid a destabilizing confrontation with Washington. Moscow has shown little interest in winding down its war against Ukraine, but U.S. and European military assistance and diplomatic support for Kyiv are still critical to the war’s progression. Moreover, Western sanctions continue to squeeze Russia’s long-term economic prospects.
Although Washington’s expansive network of allies and partners should give it considerable leverage over Beijing and Moscow, the Trump administration is working against itself. Its transactional approach to allies, statements casting doubt on U.S. commitments to their defense, and willingness to impose tariffs on friends and rivals alike have resulted in Washington being less capable of marshalling collective strength toward common objectives. This has not only diminished the United States’ ability to respond to Chinese and Russian challenges but also positioned it as a less attractive negotiating partner.
Meanwhile, Trump’s eagerness to secure diplomatic breakthroughs with Xi and Putin has further eroded Washington’s leverage. He has turned the screws on Ukraine and eased sanctions on Moscow without securing any corresponding concessions from Putin. While touting his personal relationship with Xi and focusing on sector-specific wins, such as China’s promises to purchase U.S. agricultural products and Boeing jets, Beijing has been given a pass on addressing long-standing structural economic disputes. Questioning U.S. commitments to Taiwan and suggesting that U.S. arms sales could be on the table during negotiations with Beijing have further weakened American credibility and bargaining power.
A summit with unequal benefits
Against this backdrop, a trilateral summit in Shenzhen would offer strikingly unequal benefits.
For Xi, hosting Putin and Trump for a trilateral meeting would represent a diplomatic victory, reinforcing Beijing’s image as a peacemaker and indispensable center of global diplomacy. For Putin, simply having the opportunity to appear alongside Trump and Xi would elevate his international standing and ease Moscow’s diplomatic isolation—all without having made a single meaningful concession on the war in Ukraine. For Trump, the gathering would offer a historic encounter. But what would the United States gain?
Trump and the White House have suggested that a trilateral summit could make necessary progress on nuclear arms control. As with some of Trump’s foreign policy instincts, the underlying idea of trilateral diplomacy is not inherently misguided. Considering that the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, the last remaining U.S.-Russia strategic arms-control agreement, expired earlier this year, and China is in the middle of an unprecedented nuclear buildup, reviving arms control discussions would support U.S. interests. But successful negotiations require a strong strategic position and thorough working-level preparations. It’s difficult to see how a last-minute summit stage-managed by Beijing will set a solid foundation for the kind of breakthrough that Trump is seeking.
During the era of détente, American leaders understood that U.S. diplomacy was most effective when the United States could leverage the collective strength of its alliance networks and draw on its strategic advantages to shape its rivals’ calculations. While the trilateral in Shenzhen will surely be historic, instead of restoring the image of American power and preeminence that was evident during the Cold War, the meeting may only reveal how far Washington’s position has eroded since the triangular diplomacy of the 1970s.

articles.title: What's missing from the map of global internet infrastructure?
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

What's missing from the map of global internet infrastructure?

Stephen Song

Tim Kelly

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The Open Fiber Data Standard provides a common framework for mapping terrestrial fiber networks and improving visibility into global internet infrastructure. Pictured, a close up of empty conduits for fiber optic cables in a construction site in Brake, Germany. / Image: Heide Pinkall / Shutterstock.com

Optic fiber cables form the backbone of global communications. An often-cited statistic is that submarine cables carry approximately 99% of the world's Internet traffic. Unfortunately, the typical framing of that statistic contains a subtle error. It is true that approximately 99% of internet traffic is carried by undersea cables, but this refers to 99% of intercontinental traffic. In a well-functioning internet, the majority of traffic for a typical user is not likely to travel via undersea fibre optic cables but remain on national terrestrial networks.
To know where these are, the World Bank Group has supported the development of the Open Fiber Data Standard (OFDS), a common language for describing and mapping terrestrial fibre optic networks. Since 2022, the work has been guided by a consortium of organizations, including the World Bank Group, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the Internet Society, Mozilla, Liquid Intelligent Technologies, CSquared, and Digital Council Africa. Since that time, the importance of global internet resiliency has risen dramatically in the wake of multiple disruptions to fibre optic cables, most recently affecting air traffic control in the US. OFDS is more important than ever as a result.
When we connect to the internet, our interactions are often localized because we are communicating with people or services in our own countries or region. When we access international services and content, we are often served by local Content Distribution Networks (CDNs). The globally distributed nature of a CDN means reduced distance between users and website resources. Instead of connecting to a website’s origin server, a CDN lets users connect to a geographically closer data center. Less travel time means faster service. It is true that CDNs must be refreshed from their global sources, but their very existence suggests that local traffic predominates.
Our growing social and economic dependence on internet infrastructure, combined with some serious cable breaks in the Red Sea, off the coast of Côte d’Ivoire, and elsewhere in recent years, has focused more attention on the need for a more resilient global internet infrastructure. Much-needed effort is now being placed on critical submarine cable issues such as route diversity and the availability of repair ships. However, if we accept that terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure plays an equally important role in internet infrastructure resilience as submarine cable infrastructure, we should ask why terrestrial fibre has not received the same level of attention. The answer may lie in the image below.
Telegeography, a telecommunications data and research firm, maintains an excellent resource in its submarine cable map, tracking the development and lifespan of more than 600 undersea cables. Resources like this provide wonderful visibility for submarine cable infrastructure. However, the absence of similar data on terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure perpetuates the idea that terrestrial fibre is of lesser importance. The very lack of visibility of terrestrial infrastructure in these maps diminishes its significance.

What’s missing from this picture? / Credit: Telegeography

Yet terrestrial fibre infrastructure plays a critical role not only in regional connectivity but also in undersea cable resilience. When undersea cables were disrupted in the Baltic Sea, restoration of internet services was enabled in part by routing traffic through terrestrial links. Terrestrial and undersea cable infrastructure are two sides of the coin of global internet resilience. One must wonder whether the lack of visibility of terrestrial fibre optic infrastructure has led to it largely being left out of global discussions on internet infrastructure resilience.
But it is not just for resilience that terrestrial fibre networks matter. Terrestrial fibre networks are critical to the mission of connecting the unconnected because of their sheer capacity. Terrestrial fibre networks can carry orders of magnitude more data than any other access technology. This means they can support multiple operators and purposes. They also represent a long-term investment in infrastructure. Terrestrial fibre networks can last more than 20 years and often may be upgraded in place. As such, terrestrial fibre networks are the solid foundation on which long-term, affordable, resilient internet infrastructure is built.
This is what makes OFDS such an important initiative now. The common descriptive framework enabled by OFDS makes it possible to assemble the jigsaw puzzle of connectivity infrastructure in a collaborative and distributed manner. It also enables different levels of sharing, ranging from essential public information to more sensitive data restricted to regulators or operators themselves.
The multi-stakeholder nature of OFDS means that regulators, operators, researchers, infrastructure investors, and civil society can all have a voice in what should be captured by the data standard. Since 2025, the Internet Society has hosted the secretariat and provided support to the independent governance board convened for the first time in August of this year.
Anyone interested in the overall resilience of global Internet infrastructure should be interested in developing a clearer picture of the deployment and interconnection of national, regional, and international terrestrial fibre optic networks. OFDS is the beginning of that conversation. To find out more, visit OFDS’ website or get in touch at outreach@ofds.info.
