articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Gambit to Enhance its Regional Role
articles.text: Source: GettyArticleMalcolm H. Kerr Carnegie Middle East CenterSaudi Arabia’s Gambit to Enhance its Regional RoleThrough the Beijing and Mecca agreements, Riyadh seeks to shape a Middle Eastern order over which it has greater influence, particularly in times of crisis and conflict.Link CopiedBy Hesham AlghannamPublished on Nov 16, 2026IntroductionThe U.S. order in the Middle East is changing in a way that worries Saudi Arabia. Although the United States still serves as the essential security guarantor for Saudi Arabia (and the other countries that make up the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council), its influence is waning noticeably. This reality is highlighted by several regional crises that have left the Gulf states questioning the consistency and predictability of American involvement. These crises gave rise to the China-mediated Beijing agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023, and the subsequent Mecca agreement in 2026, a defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. Taken together, the two accords show how Saudi diplomacy is becoming more flexible. Riyadh is no longer treating diplomacy and deterrence as opposite choices. It is choosing both. The underlying objective is to ensure that Saudi Arabia’s security relationships, whether with adversaries or allies, serve its own interests.The Changing Saudi Security OutlookDespite the current U.S. war on Iran drawing in Saudi Arabia on the side of the United States, the diplomatic framework established by the Beijing agreement has survived. Mediated by China, it restored diplomatic relations and reopened embassies between the two countries, and as recently as this year, Saudi and Iranian officials met again to reaffirm their commitment to implementing it in its entirety. The agreement’s endurance stems in no small part from the fact that Saudi Arabia remains keen on keeping tensions and conflicts in the region from escalating. This is part of the country’s strategy to ensure that the Gulf does not slide into instability. Though Riyadh will continue to rely in part on the United States as a security guarantor, it wants to cultivate ties with China, an emerging superpower (and major importer of both Saudi and Iranian oil) that can influence decisionmaking in Tehran.Nevertheless, Saudi Arabia is also looking to enhance its position in the region vis-à-vis Iran itself, preferably via the development of a new regional bloc. The most obvious manifestation of this desire is the recently concluded Mecca agreement. The accord signals the emergence of a mutual defense architecture anchored in Riyadh, where its permanent secretariat will be based, rather than Washington. It brings together top oil exporter Saudi Arabia, military heavyweight Türkiye, and nuclear-armed Pakistan.For decades, Saudi Arabia managed its rivalry with Iran by avoiding a direct fight. Containment, indirect pressure, and the American security umbrella formed the core of Riyadh’s approach. The underlying calculation was that Saudi Arabia should stay out of a war with Iran, rely on the United States to check major shifts in the regional balance, and use Gulf coordination, economic weight, and diplomacy to limit Iranian influence.This formula became harder to sustain as Iran extended its reach through allied governments and networks or armed nonstate actors in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen. Riyadh nevertheless held to the position that the costs of confronting Iran directly outweighed any likely gains, and that the U.S. military presence in the Gulf would deter attacks on the kingdom’s vital interests. Policy therefore mixed competition with restraint. Iran was to be contained, not engaged in open war, inside a security order still underwritten only by Washington.The attacks against the Abqaiq and Khurais Aramco oil facilities on September 14, 2019 exposed the limits of the longstanding Saudi model. In the incident, explosive drones were used to strike these oil facilities. Ansarollah (also known as the Houthis), an armed Yemeni group against which Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognized government were engaged in a military campaign since 2015, claimed responsibility. The attacks cut Saudi oil production by about 5.7 million barrels a day; this was more than half of the national output and roughly 5 percent of global supply. A Yemen-only operation was difficult to accept at face value. Indeed, a UN assessment found no evidence that Ansarollah was in possession of the type of weapons used in the attacks, though it did not attribute the strikes to Iran. A later investigation by the United States indicated that the sites were bombed from Iran, something the Iranians denied.What followed was noteworthy. Saudi Arabia did not retaliate against Iran. And the United States did not respond militarily on the kingdom’s behalf. This was the moment a structural weakness became hard to deny. It had become apparent that a close Saudi partnership with Washington could not prevent a high-impact, asymmetric attack. Nor did it produce an automatic U.S. military response once one had occurred.The Beijing agreement should be read against this record. Restoring diplomatic ties with Tehran was neither capitulation nor a break with Washington. It was a recalibration—handle part of the rivalry directly, reduce Iran’s incentive to apply pressure through regional partners, and try to insulate Saudi territory, energy infrastructure, and Vision 2030 development projects from regional turmoil. The change was not the abandonment of deterrence, but its widening, from a model centered on external protection and containment toward one that combined military capability, strategic diversification, and direct political management of the Iranian relationship. When the U.S.-Iran war broke out, several analysts assumed that the Beijing agreement would be the first thing to crack. This did not happen, despite Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz and launching missiles at Gulf capitals and oil facilities. Instead, Saudi Arabia and Iran demonstrated diplomatic resilience by sustaining foreign minister–level contact throughout the most intense phases of the conflict. By doing so, the two countries preserved crucial channels for deescalation and potential conflict resolution.A related example of Saudi Arabia’s new orientation was its conviction that there was no military solution to the U.S.-Iranian conflict. To that end, Riyadh denied the United States use of its military facilities and airspace for offensive operations against Iran, and also supported Pakistan’s efforts to negotiate an end to the war. Islamabad’s diplomacy bore fruit in May with a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for a U.S.-Iranian ceasefire that was accepted by both sides. Although the MoU subsequently fell through, Saudi Arabia and Iran kept talking. This was in large part due to the Beijing accord, which provided for continued dialogue.The Mecca agreement takes the logic of the Beijing agreement a step further, but in a different direction. Both reflect the same basic Saudi concern, which is that Riyadh no longer wants its security to depend heavily on a single outside power. The Beijing agreement addressed that problem by attempting to reduce the danger itself. Instead of relying mainly on Washington to contain Iran, the kingdom opened a direct channel with Tehran and used Chinese mediation to lower tensions. Beijing was about making conflict less likely.The Mecca pact, on the other hand, is about making Saudi Arabia less vulnerable if conflict still breaks out. By drawing Türkiye and Pakistan more closely into its security calculations, Riyadh is widening the range of partners on which it can rely and forging military relationships that do not depend entirely on the United States. This is important due to continued ambiguity from Washington following Iranian missile strikes on energy infrastructure and Gulf cities as part of Iran’s confrontation with the United States. For example, in July 2026, President Donald Trump stated that the United States was “locked and loaded”—but then held off on striking Iran. From the Saudi perspective, this level of uncertainty further threw into question the reliability of the partnership with Washington. In contrast, following heavy Ansarollah drone and missile strikes targeting Saudi cities and infrastructure in October 2026, Pakistan, Türkiye, and Saudi Arabia agreed to coordinate deterrence measures.Essentially, Saudi Arabia wants to be able to talk to Iran even as it strengthens defense ties with Türkiye and Pakistan. Indeed, October 2026 witnessed the first high-level meeting between representatives of the Mecca agreement countries and those of Iran; significantly, the event took place in Tehran. Similarly, Riyadh wishes to remain closely aligned with the United States while making sure that Washington is not the only pillar of its security. Seen this way, the move from Beijing to Mecca is not a break with Saudi Arabia’s traditional partnerships. Rather, it is an attempt to gain more control over how the kingdom manages risk, both by reducing threats where possible and by preparing more seriously for them where necessary. This approach further demonstrates Saudi Arabia’s efforts to uphold diplomacy and strategic independence in an uncertain regional environment.How the Beijing and Mecca Agreements Figure in the New Saudi Calculus Once Saudi Arabia concluded that organizing the Gulf entirely around dependence on the United States was no longer sustainable, the country’s leadership began to formulate a new approach. Maintaining security ties with the United States would be part of this new approach—dispensing with such ties was out of the question—but so would reaching out to China. Both the Beijing and Mecca agreements should be viewed as part of this reorientation.The Beijing accord showed that Riyadh was prepared to manage its most difficult regional relationship without waiting for Washington to decide when and how engagement with Tehran should take place. Yet this Saudi autonomous streak had limits. Saudi Arabia and Iran had already spent nearly two years in talks hosted by Iraq and Oman, but the final breakthrough came only through Chinese mediation. This suggests that Riyadh wanted the backing of a major power with enough influence in Tehran to help transform dialogue into an actual agreement. The Mecca agreement carries the same search for more room to maneuver into the field of deterrence. Rather than depending almost entirely on the existing U.S.-led security framework, Riyadh joined Türkiye and Pakistan in building an additional collective defense arrangement. Both agreements show Riyadh trying to widen its options, rather than leave its security dependent on a single external relationship.The Beijing agreement’s foundations may have been diplomatic, but the leverage that made China useful to Saudi Arabia was largely economic. By 2025, China was buying roughly 90 percent of Iran’s oil exports. Riyadh came to realize that Beijing’s ties to Tehran created an effective two-way communication channel through which Chinese economic power could be exerted in a manner that might benefit Saudi Arabia, something that Western capitals could not easily replicate. Aside from depending on China as its main oil customer, Iran is reliant on the country as one of its most important sources of hard currency. This gives Beijing influence over Tehran without requiring it to present itself as a security guarantor, or as another outside power trying to reshape the region. For Saudi Arabia, that was the attraction. China could raise Saudi concerns with Tehran while remaining a partner to which Iran had strong reasons to listen. Beijing occupied a position that few other powers could match. What made the agreement durable was, in part, how little pressure it placed on the issues most likely to break it. There were no Chinese security guarantees and no formal enforcement mechanism. The agreement restored diplomatic relations, reaffirmed sovereignty and noninterference, and revived earlier Saudi-Iranian agreements on security and economic cooperation. It did not try to settle the deeper rivalry between the two states.Similarly, neither side had to give up a core strategic position. Iran was not required to dismantle its regional network of armed partners, and Saudi Arabia did not have to weaken its security relationship with the United States. What emerged was narrower, and easier to maintain, which is a channel both sides could use when their interests aligned, without forcing agreement when they did not. That helps explain why the agreement survived the war. Had it required Iran to rein in every allied armed group, or Saudi Arabia to distance itself from the United States, it would have been far more vulnerable once those commitments became difficult to sustain.Yet just as Saudi Arabia is not willing to give up on its historical security ties to the United States in favor of turning wholly to China, neither is it going to rely entirely on the latter to keep Iran in check. This is why the Mecca agreement sits comfortably alongside the diplomatic track opened through Beijing. Riyadh is not trying to choose between engagement and deterrence. It is trying to use both. An explicitly anti-Iranian bloc would work against much of what Saudi diplomacy has tried to achieve since 2023. It would harden regional divisions and make continued communication with Tehran more difficult. The Mecca framework gives Riyadh more room than that. Saudi Arabia can keep talking to Iran while also building relationships that make military pressure against the kingdom more complicated and potentially more costly.The difference between the two agreements is just as important as the connection between them. Beijing was an agreement with an adversary, mediated by an outside power, and aimed at managing competition. It did not create a military alliance or a collective-defense obligation. Mecca is different in both purpose and structure. It brings together security partners and is meant to strengthen deterrence, defense coordination, and military cooperation.The Beijing accord tried to improve Saudi security by lowering the risk of conflict. The Mecca agreement tries to improve it by raising the costs an adversary would face if conflict occurred. Riyadh can talk directly to Tehran while strengthening defense ties with Ankara and Islamabad. It can remain closely aligned with the United States while making sure that Washington is not the only pillar of its security. Seen this way, the move from Beijing to Mecca is not a break with Saudi Arabia’s traditional partnerships. It is an attempt to gain more control over how the kingdom manages risk, both by reducing threats where possible and by preparing more seriously for them where necessary.The larger pattern, then, is a multi-track strategy. The United States provides military depth. China, through the Beijing agreement, provides access to Iran and a degree of economic leverage. The Mecca accord gives Riyadh the beginnings of a regional framework in which Saudi Arabia has more say over how deterrence is organized. Ultimately, Riyadh’s objective is to shape a regional order in which it has more influence over the rules, relationships, and available responses when crises emerge.ConclusionIt is likely that Saudi Arabia will continue to maintain its newly strengthened relations with China in order to keep open an indirect channel with Iran. This is the fruit of the Beijing agreement. The relationship with China also grants Saudi Arabia some maneuverability when negotiating with the United States. Specifically, it demonstrates that Riyadh has alternative options for trade, technology, and defense cooperation.The Mecca agreement also looks likely to hold. However, it has its limits. And should the accord take the form of an anti-Iranian political alliance, it would almost certainly lead to increased tensions with Tehran. This would defeat its purpose. After all, Saudi Arabia wishes to deter Iran—not provoke it.About the AuthorHesham AlghannamNonresident Scholar, Malcolm H. CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesTalks at GSAdam Goldston and Ryan Goldston on Defining Luxury Performance FootwearNov 17, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyYouTubeAppleDownload TranscriptWhen APL (Athletic Propulsion Labs) set out to create basketball shoes that helped athletes instantly jump higher, the technology worked so well that the NBA banned the shoes for providing the wearer with an undue competitive advantage. That sparked viral global demand for the shoes and propelled APL to success. Adam Goldston and Ryan Goldston, co-founders of APL, explain the “luxury performance” philosophy of their footwear, their strategies for growing their business, and how they drew design inspiration from ziplines and Japanese soufflé pancakes. In a conversation with Meena Flynn, chair of global Private Wealth Management and co-head of One Goldman Sachs, the Goldstons also articulate how the experience of running an independent, founder-owned firm, a focus on product, and flexible decision-making guide APL’s long-term growth and dynastic strategy.
Transcript:
Adam Goldston: There's not that many moments in your life when you realize, okay, this can be a defining moment, and everything can change based on what you do right now.
Ryan Goldston: We still feel like we're at the very beginning and there's all of this runway in front of us because of this dynastic lens that we've looked at the business and the brand through and also just the sheer opportunity that's in front of us.
[MUSIC INTRO]
Meena Flynn: I am Meena Flynn. I chair our global private wealth management business and I'm co-head of One Goldman Sachs. I am thrilled today to be joined by Adam and Ryan Goldston, co-founders and co-CEOs of APL, Athletic Propulsion Labs.
They actually began the company when they were both two sport college athletes at Division I USC playing football and basketball. And APL was born from a business plan that one professor told them was doomed to fail.
That being said, in 2010, the NBA banned their shoes, saying that their shoes created an unfair technology advantage. Since then, they built APL into a category defining brand at the center of sports, performance, and luxury. So, please join me in welcoming both Adam and Ryan today.
So, let's start with the problem that you were trying to solve with APL. It came out of your needs living every day as college athletes and really wanting to jump higher, perform better, and push beyond whatever existing footwear could do.
You began with technology and then really built the product around it. And so, when did you first set out to build and what gap were you trying to address?
Ryan Goldston: Adam and I are not six foot ten, as you guys can probably tell. And we both played basketball and football at USC. So, we were always focused on doing anything we could to increase our performance. But there was never anything that could make it so we could do it instantly.
So, when I was an entrepreneurship program, I used APL as my business plan. And I said there are three things that were going to make it unique. One, we're going to create a shoe that instantly makes you jump higher. Two, we're going to price it at $300, which at the time was twice the price of anything else within the market. And three, we're going to start by selling direct to consumer.
So, this is back in 2008/2009. DTC wasn't the same that it is now. Price points weren't where they are now. And there was never a shoe that instantly made you jump higher.
So, what we did is we identified a category we wanted to create, which was luxury performance. We started in a micro niche where we had authenticity and credibility because we were college athletes. And we tried to create something that was for ourselves that we felt was not just a want, but a need from a performance standpoint and something that hadn't previously existed within the market.
The fact that my professor at the time told me it'd be a massive failure. I didn't get top 10 in the business plan competition. And we actually started the company that I wrote in that business plan, was to us proof that we had something unique and different and that we were going to be able to create a category that was defining and that we could own.
And so, I would say that it came out of a want and a need from us from a performance standpoint. We felt like we had a unique point of view that we were bringing to the market. And ultimately, we had groundbreaking technology that set the trajectory for us to create this category of luxury performance.
Meena Flynn: So, the NBA banned your shoes in 2010.
Why did they ban your shoes? I mean, it became viral overnight. And how did you approach that situation?
Adam Goldston: So, that was probably the singular moment that changed our lives more than anything. When the NBA banned our concept one, because they said it provided the way with an undue competitive advantage over their opponents, that was the best thing that ever happened to us. So, we had created a singular product. And for us, like we believed in it because we made it for ourselves.
But we were 22 at the time when it happened. So, we had finished college. We're in this small office. Created this revolutionary product. And when it happened, Ryan and I essentially looked at each other and said, we can either try and fight this, or we can lean into this. Keep in mind, we had zero marketing budget back then.
So, we're in a way different situation today than we were then. Zero marketing budget and the difference back in 2010 versus today is news cycles were much longer. So, when these big moments happened, there was a much longer tail to them than it is today.
So, now with the attention economy, if something goes viral or it's huge, it may last a couple of days if you're really lucky, but then it deteriorates very quickly. Back then, it was just continuing to go and compound for us. So, when it happened, Ryan and I were sitting in the office and we were essentially like, we need to change the website right away. And like, you know now, like, aesthetics are so important to us and all these things. At that moment, being clear in the messaging was the most important thing to us.
We realized, I think there's not that many moments in your life when you realize, okay, this can be a defining moment, and everything can change based on what you do right now. There's not a lot of moments in people's lives like that. That was a clear moment in our life when we were like, if we make this decision and we lean into this, we don't know what the outcome will be, but we know that this is a once in a lifetime opportunity.
So, we leaned all the way into it, and we put these big "banned by the NBA" in red letters across the website. And it went out. And seven minutes after it went out, our life changed. And so, when that happened, it was the number one news story in the world. Number two, three, and 17 most searched terms on Google. There were over a million articles written or posted about it within 10 days. We sold nine months of inventory in three days. And we just were like, I can't believe this is happening.
And so, we leaned into it and we kept pushing. And it took us roughly four to five years to get to a strong inventory position where we had the ability to really start growing, expand into different categories. But just we could not keep up with the demand. And it was the best thing that ever happened to us.
We had no money for marketing. And because of that, we're now able to sit here on stage with you today.
Meena Flynn: Let's fast forward today. Can you talk us through your business now and what the composition looks like and really a little bit about luxury performance and why you guys decided that's the category that I'm going to define?
Ryan Goldston: Yeah. So, we really wanted to create this category of luxury performance. And we knew that we had to start in a micro niche where we had authenticity and credibility.
So, basketball shoes that instantly make you jump higher was the foundation for what we created. And we felt like would really open up the opportunity to create this category.
So, like Adam said, for four years, we just sold men's basketball shoes exclusively through our website. Then June 17th, 2014, we launched our men's and women's running shoes. Our first retailer for men was Saks Fifth Avenue. Right away, we had the two top selling SKUs there. Our first retailer for women was Net-A-Porter, which we launched with on January 1st, 2015. Within six days, we became the fastest selling new designer of all time, hit our season's target sell through.
And what we did is we grew our wholesale distribution from there. And while we started direct to consumer to begin with, the reason why we went to wholesale and really looked to build it out is we wanted to create this category and we wanted to do it in an authentic way that we felt like could scale and do it in meaningful way where there was authenticity with these retailers.
So, luxury had always been defined by these retailers and there had never been performance in their stores. So, we knew that we could enter in, we could own this category, we could be a first mover, and we could bring something very differentiated within the market.
That's why also in 2016, we became the first members from an athletic brand inducted to the CFDA. So, it was the first time they're saying not only is this sport and performance, but it's also luxury and fashion. And that kind of ties into what the thesis of the brand was when we were creating and is that there's these two pillars. One is sport and performance, the other is luxury and fashion. And we want to be the bridge that connects the two. Or it's like a Venn diagram. You have one circle that's sport and performance, the other that's luxury and fashion. And we wanted to sit at the center.
So, we really focused on creating this category, entering in an authentic way, and then having the product that really you could change your clothes throughout the day and keep your footwear the same.
Meena Flynn: Can you talk to us about how your travels and your real-life experiences really helped you create Zipline? And why do you think this personal story also resonates with your consumers?
Adam Goldston: So, I think brands are living, breathing things. And so, as you become larger, there's definitely an opportunity where you lose some of those personal aspects. I think the fact that we are a founder-led brand gives us a unique advantage, specifically in the spaces which we exist.
So, the Zipline, perfect example, was inspired by a trip that Ryan and I took to Tokyo, where we walked 14.3 miles in one day to get these Japanese souffle pancakes. So, they're these soft, fluffy, just like wobbly type of pancakes. And when we sat down, it was honestly Ryan that really, really wanted these. We looked at them, and Ryan was like, we need to create a compound that feels the way that these look.
And so, we didn't walk there for inspiration. We walked there because we wanted pancakes. It turned into inspiring our number one selling shoe. But you never know when that inspiration is going to strike.
And then the upper of the shoe was inspired by a trip that Ryan and I took to Dubai. So, we're speaking at this really large conference. And then we ended up going ziplining the next day. So, we went over the marina. And it feels like this incredibly freeing experience, but you can still move your limbs. So, you feel like you have this freedom, but that you're locked in.
And so, when we were at home, it was during the pandemic, Ryan had put together a design brief for like how should we dream up of ideas. And we were reflecting on the things that were important to us, and like the trips that we had the most fun on and what we missed. And one of the experiences we had brought up was ziplining across the marina in Dubai.
And Ryan said, what if we create an upper that feels the way that that experience felt and gives your foot the structural support that you need, but it also feels free. So, end up creating the Zipline off of that. And launched it in April of 2022. And it just continued to be incredible for us. It's a juggernaut for the business today.
And for us, we've just tried to find inspiration in all aspects of our lives. Like, I think from where we started to where we're at today, we've been very lucky that we've got to do incredible things from our Formula One partnerships, travel across the world, create products that exist all across the world, build physical flagships. But all of those moments of inspiration have not been planned. It's simply from experiencing things.
And I think, again, being a founder-led business, and we see it across plenty of businesses, it's a unique advantage because you're able to draw things from your mind and then bring them into the world at a faster rate than larger conglomerates could. And for us, we are always excited when we get struck with inspiration. And that was a combination of the two. And led to our best-selling product today.
Meena Flynn: I love that story. So, you talked about being founder led. You're also 100% founder owned.
So, can you tell us why you have stayed fully independent? And also, this has been 17 years. You've had to scale and really be disciplined and also decide when to lean in. So, what has led that to be the right structure to date?
Ryan Goldston: I mean, it's a great question, because obviously, it's uncommon both from where we were and where the landscape has been. And a big part of that was we wanted to build the dynastic brand. And to do that, it takes making non-consensus right decisions where you're focused on the long-term.
That being said, when we were initially starting, not only the professors, but most people that we talked to didn't believe in the idea and the concept. So, the fact was, we had this idea that was very unique, that was very different. We were entering into a very competitive landscape with a lot of apparent risk. But in our mind, the apparent risk actually lowered the competitive risk, because you're able to really stand for something different and be unique.
And we've done it for 17 years. We believed in building a super, super strong foundation during that process because we felt like the most enduring brands spend the time on the front end, investing and showing who they are to the customer, to the market, and doing different things.
I mean, when you just asked the question about the Zipline and how our personal story connected to the design of the product. And I think that's a big part of being founder led and founder owned is that we're able to invest in these different moments that we believe in, that we feel strongly about, that traditionally wouldn't be something that would connect with an investor if you're describing it.
But once it's built, there's a real connection to it. Whether it's talking about Japanese souffle pancakes with a performance sneaker, or even the flagships that we've designed. When creating the luxury performance category, we've looked at it from a very different lens. And it's been our belief that investing in areas that are unique to us, that create this competitive moat, that are able to own this category, so we're able to be very different from what else exists in the market, has been something that we're passionate about, that has taken time to build, but has allowed us to do something very different.
And so, I would say that being 17 years in, having never raised any outside capital, and being able to build APL and a brand that is super unique, has allowed us to create this category where even though we're 17 years in, we still feel like we're at the very beginning, and there's all this runway in front of us, because of this dynastic lens that we've looked at the business and the brand through. And also, just the sheer opportunity that's in front of us.
And I think that realizing that there's people that now really believe in it. And knowing that there's a belief in the category, in the brand, the enduring aspect of APL, and the fact that we have something very, very special within the market.
Adam Goldston: So, I think one of the other things about Ryan and I too, as leaders and CEOs, but also as founders, is that you have to be flexible in terms of the path that you want to take. So, like, you want to be very strict in terms of, like, how you make specific decisions and whatnot, but you need to be flexible in the path because none of us have a crystal ball.
And so, we've made a lot of, to Ryan's point, non-consensus right decisions to get to where we're at today. And the luxury of being 100% independent allowed us to do that. But as we think of becoming the definitive world leader of luxury performance, we always have to have our mind open.
And so, I think that that tight stubbornness in the beginning has also got us to the point that we're at today. But like, as we continue to grow, so did our aperture of the world. So, I think that now we have a more open idea in terms of how do we grow the business.
Meena Flynn: Let's go to a quote that I think you shared with me, which is a Larry Ellison quote that stuck with you, which is the bigger the apparent risk, the fewer people will try to go there. How do you compete in a category that has so much scale already embedded in it? And what does it take really to stay differentiated and really not lose your unique brand, your identity, your values?
Ryan Goldston: So, that's a quote that Adam has referenced from the beginning of the company. And it's something that's guided us in a lot of ways. I mean, I said it earlier, but it is true. The greater the apparent risk, potentially the lower the competitive risk, because there are less people that are going to go into the market. Even though there's a lot of big competition, there are less people.
The way that we always defined it was it's this massive ocean, and we can be a paradise or utopia within it, which allows us to be true to ourselves, different from whatever exists within the market. And you're able to have this North Star that guides you through.
The other part of that is by going and creating something different and unique, and like I said, this bridge that connects sport and performance and luxury and fashion, you have a very large TAM. And that's just a real thing where you're getting to play in both markets, be different in both.
So, in sport and performance, we sit at the top when it comes to price, design, material. Our design philosophy, when you think about it compared to what else exists within the market is we don't use big and blazing logos. We let the material, the color, the technology, and design tell the story. And that's very luxury coded in the process of what we create.
And then within the luxury space, the fact that we have these underpinnings in our foundation is in performance and shoes that instantly make you jump higher, instantly make you run faster, allows us to really stand out within the market and offer something completely different.
And so, for us, we're able to look at it from that perspective. And it allows us to really be differentiated in two very large markets, be true to ourselves. And I think a lot of times when you're creating a business, choosing the correct market and the correct positioning for your brand defines what your opportunity is not only now, but into the future. And we picked two large markets with a unique positioning in both. And while there weren't very many competitors, it allowed us to be something that is really, really special. And as the years go on, we get more confidence in that decision and the uniqueness of the spot that we sit at.
Meena Flynn: Well, I would say it's just so inspiring to hear the background of, you know, back at USC to where you are now, the relationship that you have with each other, and really where you're going to be able to take this business. And like you said, you're still in the early innings and we got a lot of runway. But we're just really grateful for the two of you guys joining us today. So, thank you.

articles.title: Health Care And A Blast From The Past
articles.text:
Health Care And A Blast From The Past

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 20 Nov 2026

Back in 2005, we published a book entitled Our Brave New World (the e-copy is available for free on the website). The very first chapter of the book started as such: “Up until recently, a typical company did the following: it designed a product, manufactured the product, and then sold the product. Take Ford for example. Ford designs an Expedition SUV. Ford manufactures the truck at a plant in Detroit. Ford then sends the truck on to a Ford dealership somewhere in the US to be sold. This vertical design/produce/sell business model has been the model de rigueur for the past 50 years. Really successful companies followed this model at home, then abroad… This was yesterday’s business model. The new business model is to produce nowhere, but sell everywhere. In recent years, we have witnessed the birth of a new breed of company that we shall call the ‘platform company’.Platform companies know where the clients are and what they want and where the producers are. Platform companies then simply organize the ordering by the clients and the delivery by the producers (and the placing of their logo on the product just before delivery). Platform companies keep the high added-value parts of research, development, treasury and marketing in-house, and farm out all the rest to external producers… An increasing number of Western companies are looking at their business models and saying: ‘out of the three things I do—designing, producing and selling—producing is a mug’s game. Producing ties up a lot of capital. It is often labor-intensive. It forces one to keep expensive inventories. It is highly volatile. And I do not get rewarded for it in the market place… I would be better off leaving the producing to some other mug, and focus on the non-cyclical, high value-added part of my business, namely designing and selling.’”

The complexity of capital allocation for oil and gas companies

Opinion
3 October 2024
Ten key considerations for oil & gas 2025 planning

View Neivan Boroujerdi's full profile

As the war in Iran has sent shock waves through energy markets and the global economy, national oil companies (NOCs) in the Middle East have been in the eye of the storm. Neivan Bouroujerdi, Director, Corporate Strategy and Analytics Service, analyses Saudi Aramco, ADNOC and QatarEnergy, three of the giant NOCs in the region.
I asked him how they have fared through the turmoil, how the war is changing their strategies and the future appeal of Gulf resources to international oil companies (IOCs).
How has the war affected Middle East NOCs’ performance?
All Gulf-based NOCs took a production hit from export constraints over the past nine months, caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to infrastructure. Alternative oil export routes that circumvent the Strait, however, have proved invaluable for some, effectively acting as an insurance policy. By getting their oil to market and capturing high prevailing prices, Saudi Aramco and ADNOC have generated US$35 billion more operating cash flow (OCF) in 2026 than we forecast at the start of the year.
That option was not available to producers further north, including Kuwait and Iraq. Nor is there any alternative shipping route for LNG. QatarEnergy (QE), the world’s biggest LNG producer, lost 17% of its liquefaction capacity to war damage and, with the Strait effectively closed since February, has exported only minimal cargoes to its customers. Its OCF is US$10 billion lower than we forecast at the start of the year, despite the start-up of its new 18-mmtpa liquefaction facility on the US Gulf Coast, Golden Pass.
What lessons have we learned from the crisis?
Building resilience into the system has leapt to the top of the agenda, with access to alternative export routes now a must for these export-dependent economies. The UAE is adding 1.5 million b/d to the capacity of its 1.8-million b/d pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Saudi Arabia’s alternative export pipeline capacity could rise from 7 million b/d to up to 10 million b/d by 2030 – technically sufficient for all of its exports.
Geography, though, is (almost) everything. Qatar, Kuwait and Iraq face stiffer challenges to develop alternative liquids export capacity at scale. Gas presents additional complexity. Alternative routes for Qatar LNG exports would realistically involve cross border arrangements for gas pipelines and liquefaction infrastructure. Ceding sovereign control of critical parts of the value chain will come with significant risks and costs.
Will Middle East NOCs look to diversify overseas?
A strategy for some time, the rationale has been strengthened by the war, with gas and LNG at the forefront of their efforts. Government-to-government relationships are providing an increasingly important route to overseas opportunities. Leveraging existing partnerships with IOCs that operate with an NOC domestically, notably in the UAE and Qatar, has also proved to be another useful option.
• ADNOC: the strategy for XRG, ADNOC’s vehicle for international growth, is bold. Launched in December 2024, XRG has already built positions in the Americas, Africa and the Caspian. It is reportedly targeting a US$15 billion-plus US shale gas position and exploring a stake in LNG Canada. The announcement of XRG’s acquisition of Shell’s North West Shelf LNG stake earlier this month bulks up the overall portfolio to 22 mmtpa. If the ambitious goal of 47 mmtpa by 2035 is achieved, ADNOC would become the fifth-largest LNG supplier globally. And we could see further deals both upstream and downstream of these positions to support integration.
• Saudi Aramco: Aramco has been pursuing multiple international LNG opportunities, both independently and through its (now reduced) stake in MidOcean Energy, targeting 10 to 20 mmtpa of supply by 2030. To date, it’s secured two LNG sales and purchase agreements with US LNG projects, Rio Grande and Commonwealth LNG, and has ambitions to build further.
However, the biggest opportunity in LNG might be domestic. We estimate Aramco could have 6 bcfd of surplus domestic gas production early next decade, sufficient to support up to 40 mmtpa of LNG exports. At present, foreign participation in Saudi oil and gas production is not permitted, though domestic funding requirements and ambitions in gas may open up parts of the country’s upstream sector to strategic partners.
• QatarEnergy: QE recently signed up for 7 mmtpa of US LNG via deals with Cheniere and Woodside Energy – undoubtedly a response to events in the Gulf – and more deals are likely. Combining these deals with its 70% stake in Golden Pass makes QE the largest offtaker of US LNG, shoring up its LNG marketing position and playing to an existing strategy to diversify the LNG portfolio and build LNG trading capabilities.
QE has also leveraged its relationships with its domestic partners to build an exploration-led international upstream portfolio, one that could produce over 200,000 boed next decade. We expect organic investment and perhaps even M&A deals.
• KUFPEC: Kuwait Petroleum’s international business, KUFPEC, has been investing overseas for decades and produces around 80,000 boed. Even after recent deals to enter offshore Brazil and progress on the Lang Lebah gas project in Malaysia, more business development is needed to reach its target of 200,000 boed.
Do IOCs still want to invest in the Middle East?
Undoubtedly. Recent deals struck by ExxonMobil, BP and ConocoPhillips in Iraq, and BP and TotalEnergies' Bab Gas Cap deal in the UAE show the appetite is still there. Kuwait’s extension of enhanced technical service agreements to BP and Shell may be a precursor to offshore investment opportunities for IOCs.
Big Oil faces a longevity challenge, with declining production over the next decade. Discovered resource opportunities in the Middle East can help address at least part of the problem, offering access to significant long-life and low-cost reserves. And while returns are typically modest, we expect Middle East governments will be increasingly keen to attract investment in a competitive environment for capital.
