articles.title: New Bank Start-Up Unit
articles.text:
New Bank Start-up Unit

The New Bank Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new bank in the UK.

On this pageIntroductionThinking of becoming a bank in the UK?Engaging with the NBSUNew Bank Pre-application engagementSubmitting the applicationThe application feeThe authorisation (including decision making) processRegulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

Introduction
Firms that want to operate as banks in the UK (see ‘thinking of becoming a bank’ section) must be authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), with the consent of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
International banks seeking to establish a banking subsidiary and/or branch in the UK should, in parallel with referring to the NBSU website, consult SS5/21 (International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision), as well as the FCA’s Approach to international firms publication Opens in a new window.
The New Bank Start-up Unit (NBSU) is a joint initiative set up by the UK financial regulators, the PRA and the FCA, to provide information and support for firms interested in, or currently applying for, authorisation as a bank in the UK.
To advance the PRA and FCA’s primary and secondary objectives (information on the PRA’s objectives, goals and latest business plan. Information on the FCA objectives Opens in a new window, both regulators will assess whether a firm meets the Threshold Conditions, which are the minimum standards that all firms must meet at their point of authorisation, and on an ongoing basis while operating as a bank.
The Threshold Conditions for the PRA and FCA (below) are set out in Schedule 6 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 Opens in a new window.

Legal status: Deposit-takers must be corporates or partnerships;
Location of offices: A UK incorporated corporate body must maintain their head offices and, if one exists, their registered office in the UK;
Prudent conduct of business: The firm must conduct their business in a prudent manner, which includes having appropriate financial and non-financial resources;
Suitability: The firm must satisfy the PRA that they are a ‘fit and proper’ person with regard to all circumstances to conduct a regulated activity; and
Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the PRA.

Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the FCA;
Appropriate non-financial resources: The firm’s non-financial resources must be appropriate in relation to the regulated activities they seek to carry on, having regard to the FCA’s operational objectives;
Suitability: The firm must be a fit and proper person. The firm’s management must have adequate skills and experience and act with integrity (fitness and propriety). The firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in place, and it must appropriately manage conflicts of interest; and
Business model: The firm’s strategy for doing business must be suitable for a person carrying on the regulated activities it undertakes or seeks to carry on and must not pose a risk to the FCA’s objectives.

Thinking of becoming a bank in the UK?A ‘bank’ is an entity that carries out deposit-taking business. The PRA and the FCA glossaries define a ‘bank’ as a firm with a Part 4A permission, which includes accepting deposits and is a credit institution, but is not a credit union, friendly society, or building society.The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 Opens in a new window defines the regulated activity of accepting deposits (see Chapter II Accepting Deposits) and stipulates that, to accept deposits, one of the following statements must be true:a) Money received by way of deposit is lent to others or;
b) A firm uses deposits to materially fund a business line.Firms must consider if their proposed business satisfies the definition of accepting deposits and be able to justify this assessment to regulators. You should also consider the following:

Firms should consider their options for accessing payment systems as early as possible and adequately reflect this in their plans. Payment systems are critical to allow the transfer of funds between people, businesses and financial institutions – new banks are unlikely to be able to operate without access to a payment system. The NBSU encourages firms to consider the guidance on payment systems access.
New banks can access a payment system in the following ways:
Full direct access – where the new bank will have a direct technical and settlement relationship with the payment system provider (PSP);
Direct technical access – where the new bank will have a direct technical relationship with the PSP but use a sponsor for settlement; or,
Indirect access – where an Indirect Access Provider (IAP) acts as the new bank’s sponsor for both technical and settlement sponsorship.
There are a variety of software vendors with products and services that may reduce the cost and complexity of the direct access option, as well as several IAPs providing indirect access offerings. Further information about direct and indirect access can be found on the Payments Systems Regulator Opens in a new window and Payment System Operators’ websites, and in the Code of Conduct for Indirect Access Providers Opens in a new window.

If the firm is already FCA solo-authorised (for example an investment firm seeking to broaden their funding base to take on retail deposits), they will need to apply to vary their permissions to add deposit-taking. Whilst this is a different regulatory transaction, the firm should follow the same authorisation process as fully unauthorised firms. In this instance, the NBSU recommends that, like unauthorised firms, the solo-regulated firm should follow the pre-application stages before applying to become authorised. In addition, the NBSU encourages FCA solo-authorised firms seeking dual authorisation to consider their capital and ownership structures and ensure that those are as simple as possible.

The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘bank’ and ‘banking’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation to prevent the public from being misled. Firms cannot call themselves a ‘bank’ until they have been authorised by the PRA. Prospective firms must take care when liaising with press, prospective investors, and posting on social media, prior to obtaining authorisation.
Firms may begin the application process as ‘Example Ltd’ but only once they are authorised as a bank can they call themselves ‘Example Bank Ltd’.
Firms must seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words including ‘bank’ and ‘banking’. Further information can be found on the FCA’s sensitive business name Opens in a new window page.

Please refer to ‘Should I become a bank Opens in a new window’ guide to help firms understand whether being a bank is the appropriate model for them.
Are there alternatives to being a bank?
Yes, please refer to the ‘alternatives to being a bank Opens in a new window’ guide for further information on some of the alternatives.

The NBSU is open to listening to proposals and answering any questions you may have - before any significant work has been undertaken towards becoming a bank in the UK. If you have a proposal that you would like to raise or discuss, please email NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk with your proposal/enquiry – someone from the team will get back to you within five working days.

Engaging with the NBSUTo navigate the authorisation process as efficiently as possible and achieve their objective of setting up a bank, firms should be ready, willing and organised. We have provided below some examples of how firms can demonstrate this. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list:
Ready and thinking ahead – Firms should ensure that they have a well thought through proposition which has undergone robust challenge and consideration of the inherent risks (this should also be appropriately reflected into their key documents). Firms should ensure that they will have in place appropriately skilled staff and operational infrastructure to commence trading at the point of being authorised. This includes a robust IT framework, a robust governance framework, risk management framework, premises, and finances;
Willing – Firms should demonstrate that they have done their research, understanding not only the activities that they will be undertaking but the rules and regulations which their business will be governed by; and
Organised – Firms should ensure that they are operationally ready to carry out the regulated activities at the time of their authorisation (if successful).
We aim to have positive regulatory relationships with firms along their journey, from pre-authorisation to becoming authorised and later becoming established banks. We do this by keeping an open and constructive dialogue:

Be open and honest;
Have considered the guidance provided on this website
Provide all the necessary information to undertake our assessments
Notify us of any changes, challenges or concerns as soon as possible
Develop plans, complete the necessary work, and prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us;
Fully consider and address the feedback we provide on key documents such as the Regulatory Business Plan (RBP)/the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)/the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP) documents
Understand, consider and demonstrate how they will meet the required standards at authorisation and on an ongoing basis.

To clearly set out the process and requirements for setting up a bank;
To host pre-application meetings to discuss the firm’s proposals and highlight any concerns;
To provide firms with clear feedback on their proposals including formal written feedback;
We will end our pre-application engagement with firms if our feedback is not adequately addressed in the development of their proposition and key documents
To help firms understand the standards required of being an authorised bank.

New Bank Pre-application engagement
(Optional but recommended)
The NBSU offers firms a ‘complimentary service’, which includes enhanced engagement and support as firms build out their proposals before applying for a banking licence.
Although pre-application engagement is optional and not part of the statutory authorisation process, it is something that the NBSU encourages firms to take advantage of at an early stage (feedback from previous applicant banks has shown how valuable they have found it).
Early engagement allows the NBSU to provide input into the development of regulatory business plans, by guiding potential applicants towards what the PRA and FCA are most interested in, as well as helping them understand regulatory requirements. It also allows the NBSU to identify any significant issues or showstoppers at an early stage.
Pre-application engagement with the NBSU is usually focussed around three stages (although this is flexible and all three stages might not be necessary):
i. business proposition;
ii. draft regulatory business plan; and
iii. technical sessions.
If you would like to take advantage of this complimentary pre-application engagement service, then please contact NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.

Although still early in a firm’s preparations, you will have reached the stage where you can present (usually as a PowerPoint presentation) high level information on your business model, financial forecasts, governance, source of funding, ownership, controllers and risks. You should also provide an indication of the timeframes that you are working towards and indicate whether you will be applying for full authorisation or authorisation with restrictions (also known as mobilisation), as this will impact your planning, as well as the information requirements for your application.
Upon receipt of your business proposition, the NBSU will review and schedule a meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt (this meeting may be over MS Teams so progress can be made as efficiently as possible). You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

The RBP forms a critical component of the assessment of a potential application, and therefore the NBSU expects your RBP to already be at a detailed stage prior to submission and should include the following:

Business model and financials covering business strategy, route to profitability, financial projections;
Market analysis and research that underpins the business model assumptions;
Corporate governance setting out board and committee structure as well as proposed approach for recruiting senior managers;
Risk register and stress testing;
Risk management and control framework;
Funding plans, which includes details around the owners and controllers. Where funding is still being sought, you should provide details of your plan to bring in investors;
Conduct risk of harm and consumer duty (if applicable);
Financial Crime Risk Management Framework;
Operational resilience covering outsourcing, IT infrastructure timescales to implement/test and business continuity;
Details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake (please refer to the application form for further information on the regulated activities that can be applied for);
Mobilisation plan (if applicable);

Please refer to the Regulatory Business Plan guide for further information on why an RBP is important, what should be included and the common challenges.
Once you have submitted your RBP (it is useful to be notified of the planned RBP submission date two weeks in advance), the NBSU will review and schedule a face-to-face or hybrid MS Teams meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt. You will also receive written feedback within the three weeks following the meeting.

At this stage, the expectation is that you have addressed all the feedback provided and can submit a fully developed RBP. For UK start-ups and subsidiaries of international banks, you will also have drafted and submitted your ICAAP and ILAAP documents by this stage.
The firm’s management team should own ICAAP and ILAAP and be able to discuss these in detail at the technical session. The ICAAP and ILAAP should have gone through a full review and challenge by someone other than the author (the Board or the key guiding minds of the firm), before they are submitted to the NBSU.
At this stage, the PRA will assess the ICAAP and ILAAP, which includes engagement with the relevant technical specialists. The assessment will focus on whether the ICAAP and ILAAP meet the relevant regulatory expectations and consider whether the documents would be sufficient to set capital and liquidity requirements during an application.
The NBSU will also consider the latest RBP to assess if there is any further feedback prior to the firm submitting the application. Further, depending on the nature of the proposed business model and operational design, the FCA may also look to hold focused technical sessions on the financial crime control framework.
Following the submission of the near final RBP, ICAAP and ILAAP, the NBSU will schedule a face to face or hybrid MS Teams meeting. Typically, this will be within six weeks from date of receipt. As this review involves technical specialists, it is important to give both the PRA and FCA as much notice as possible prior to submitting, and to provide at least two weeks' notice, so that both regulators can line up the necessary resource and avoid delays. You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

Submitting the application
The application process commences with the submission of the New Firm Authorisation application (and supporting documentation), and the payment of the PRA and FCA’s non-refundable application fee. It is entirely up to the firm to decide when it should submit its application, but this should be at a point where the firm can demonstrate that their business is ready, willing and organised to be authorised as a bank.
There are two routes available for applying to be a bank in the UK:

Full authorisation; or
Authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation) – this route is primarily targeted at UK start-ups. Although the Threshold Conditions still need to be met, the NBSU’s approach to the information requirements will be proportionate to the restrictions that will be put in place, and therefore will likely result in a quicker authorisation (the information instead will be required during the mobilisation period and will be assessed as part of the application to remove the restrictions). Please refer to the further information on mobilisation.

The application forms
Please note, firms will need to send an email with an electronic copy of their application (and supporting documentation) to the PRA at the following mailbox: NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
If the file size exceeds 25 MB, please use multiple emails to accommodate your submission.

Full authorisation application form (doc)

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (doc)

Branch application form (doc)

Corporate controller form (doc)

Individual controller form (doc)

Partnership controller form (doc)
Trust controller form (doc)

Please refer to Senior Managers Regime where the Long Form A, Short Form A and Form M can be downloaded.

Please refer to Holding company approvals.

Please refer to Banking capital instruments - pre/post-issuance notification (PIN).

This form can be downloaded from the FCA website: FCA IT Controls Form Opens in a new window.

The application fee
The PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and FCA Handbook Opens in a new window.
The total fee payable (covers both PRA and FCA fees) to seek permission to accept deposits (other than a credit union) is £56,300.
The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA, who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.
Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:
Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.
When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).
Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to: fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
Information on how to pay the fee is also contained within the application form.
Please note that in the case of a firm withdrawing its application, and later re-submitting another application, they would likely need to pay the full fee again.

The authorisation (including decision making) process
The NBSU will acknowledge receipt of your application within two working days.
Usually, the NBSU will communicate whether your application is complete or incomplete within three weeks of receiving it (if incomplete, the regulators will inform you of any missing information).

For complete applications (i.e., the NBSU has received the application fee and all the necessary applications and supporting documents, which should be of sufficient quality and detail for completion of the assessment) – the PRA targets four months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within six months).
For incomplete applications – the PRA targets 10 months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within twelve months).

During the assessment period the NBSU welcomes regular dialogue and encourages you to reach out as and when you need. The NBSU will keep you informed on the progress of any reviews and proactively highlight any significant risks or issues identified. In addition, the NBSU will typically meet monthly with the firm’s senior management.
The PRA aim to issue a decision as quickly as possible, but this depends on how complete your application is and how promptly you respond to our requests for information. We may have questions or need more details from you during our assessment. Responding quickly and thoroughly will help speed up the process.
The decision-making process:

Both the PRA and FCA will independently decide whether to authorise your bank.
Without FCA consent, the PRA cannot authorise your bank

If authorised, you'll receive:

An authorisation letter
A Scope of Permission Notice detailing your permissions and any requirements
A welcome pack

Your bank’s details will be added to the Financial Services Register on the date shown in the authorisation letter.

Initial notification
If during our assessment of the application we think there are grounds for refusing your application, we'll inform you both verbally and in writing where you'll have time to address our concerns.

Minded to refuse letter
If you can't address the concerns, we'll send you a letter explaining why and which rules or threshold conditions haven't been met.

At this point you can either withdraw your application (and reapply later when issues have been addressed) or, if you want to proceed, the PRA and FCA will follow its decision-making process
Issuing statutory notices (Warning Notices and Decision Notices)
Please refer to SoP1/24 - The Prudential Regulation Authority’s allocation of decision making and approach to supervisory decisions, which sets out

the PRA’s allocation of decision-making regarding statutory notices (Warning Notices, Decision Notices, and Supervisory Notices);
the PRA’s approach to decision-making on statutory notices in relation to supervisory decisions under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000; and
the PRA’s approach to publication of decisions in supervisory cases.

Regulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – full authorisationThe areas that the NBSU assess as part of a new bank application are set out below but should not be considered an exhaustive list. Firms are responsible for considering in detail all relevant laws, rules and regulatory policies, and ensuring that they understand and can fully comply with them.

Read information on ‘regulatory expectations’ (including where expectations are different for branches)
The assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)
It is up to firms to propose to the NBSU which activities they complete in mobilisation (please refer to the application form for details of the activities that can be applies for). Therefore, the key for the NBSU’s assessment is that all the design work is complete with a clear plan to deliver everything with a plausible timeframe.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)
Once a new bank is authorised with restrictions, it enters a mobilisation period, which typically lasts no longer than 12 months. During this time, the bank's deposit-taking permission is restricted to a total of £50,000, while it completes the remaining build-out of its operations. This period allows new banks to secure further investment, recruit staff, invest in IT systems, and commit to third-party suppliers, as they are now an authorised bank.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

The PRA and FCA anticipate that new banks will want to progress quickly through the mobilisation phase. This could take as little as a few months but cannot continue indefinitely and should take no longer than 12 months. For a new bank to exit mobilisation, they should submit a Variation of Permission (VoP) application via Connect.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)
At this stage, the firm should be fully operational and in a position to fulfil its business proposition as agreed with the PRA and FCA.

Authorisation is only the start of the journey towards becoming an established bank.
New banks must always meet their capital and liquidity regulatory requirements and the Threshold Conditions.
New banks must ensure that they submit their regulatory returns on time and keep up to date with the latest regulatory information.
New banks must ensure that risk management frameworks and controls evolve commensurately with the scale of business growth.
The PRA and FCA will assess how new banks are managing the key prudential and conduct risks, respectively, to their businesses through supervisory engagement.
Read: Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions).

Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

SS3/21 Non-systemic UK banks: The Prudential Regulation Authority’s approach to new and growing banks – This outlines the PRA’s expectations of firms and new banks and how those evolve throughout the authorisation journey.
Climbing mountains safely – a speech by Sarah Breeden – This speech, published alongside the CP on the PRA’s approach to new and growing banks, sets out key aspects from the consultation (i.e. what firms need to consider becoming an established bank).
PRA’s approach to banking supervision – This sets out the PRA’s approach to supervising regulated firms.
SS5/21 International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision – This sets out the PRA’s proposals regarding its approach to supervising the UK activities of PRA-authorised banks and designated investment firms that are headquartered outside of the UK or are part of a group based outside of the UK.
Financial Services Register Opens in a new window – Where a new bank’s details will appear and includes the mobilisation restriction applied.
Read: New banks authorised since 2013.
If you have any queries about becoming a new bank, please contact NewBankStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.

articles.title: Food prices climb as conflicts and El Niño tighten grain supplies
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Food prices climb as conflicts and El Niño tighten grain supplies

John Baffes

Dawit Mekonnen

Kaltrina Temaj

November 12, 2026

This page in:

English

Español

English

Español

According to our latest Commodity Markets Outlook, global grain supplies are projected to decline in 2026-27 while inventories tighten, increasing the risk of higher food prices and food insecurity. / Image: Shutterstock

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here.

The World Bank Group's food price index eased in October after reaching a three-year high in September but remained 15 percent above its year-earlier level. Grain prices surged 9 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), driven by attacks on Black Sea shipping and ports, dry weather in major grain-exporting countries, and the early effects of a very strong El Niño. Maize and wheat prices rose 8 and 13 percent, respectively. Oils and meals edged down in the third quarter but remained 17 percent higher than a year earlier, supported by biofuel demand. The World Bank Group’s food price index is projected to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and 7 percent in 2027, with risks tilted to the upside.

Global grain supplies are set to shrink for the first time in four years. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s November update, global grain supply, including production and beginning stocks, is projected to fall by about 20 million metric tons (mmt) in 2026–27. Even so, supplies would remain the second highest on record, limiting upward pressure on prices. Wheat faces the strongest headwinds, with global output projected to decline by 2 percent. U.S. output is projected to drop by 23 percent to its lowest since 1970–71, and Ukraine’s exports are expected to fall by 18 percent. Global maize and rice production are also expected to decline, by 3 and 2 percent, respectively, with rice posting its first drop in a decade as El Niño weighs on Asian harvests.

Edible oil supply growth is slowing just as biofuel demand surges. Global edible oil supply is projected to grow by 2.7 mmt in 2026–27, well below the long-term average annual increase of 5.7 mmt, partly because of the ongoing very strong El Niño. Meanwhile, demand for soybean and palm oil as biofuel feedstocks continues to rise, supported by elevated energy prices, record U.S. biofuel volume requirements, and Indonesia's increase in the palm oil share of biodiesel blends from 40 to 50 percent. The World Bank Group’s oils and meals index changed little in 2026Q3 (q/q) but was still 17 percent higher than a year earlier.

Declining global inventories leave markets more exposed to shocks. The global stocks-to-use ratio for maize (a measure of inventories relative to consumption) is projected to fall to 21.5 percent in 2026–27, its lowest level since 2012–13, though still well above its 2010–11 low of 13.2 percent. Ratios for wheat and rice are expected to edge down to 34 and 37.2 percent, respectively, while the ratio for edible oils is set to fall to 12.5 percent, its lowest since 2009–10. These tight buffers could amplify the price effect of weather or trade shocks.

Food price inflation is picking up, threatening recent gains against hunger. Median food price inflation in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) rose to 3.9 percent (y/y) in 2026Q3 from 3.5 percent in 2026Q2. It reached 7.4 percent in the World Bank’s Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region, and reached 122 percent in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Meanwhile, severe food insecurity fell from 837 million people in 2021 to 779 million people in 2025, aided by a 21 percent drop in global food commodity prices during this period. With prices projected to rise a cumulative 18 percent in 2026–27, that tailwind is set to become a headwind.

Food prices are set to keep rising, with risks tilted to the upside. The World Bank Group’s food price index is projected to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and 7 percent in 2027, before easing by 5 percent in 2028. Grains are forecast to rise by 14 and 9 percent and oils and meals by 17 and 8 percent in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Prices for other food items are expected to remain broadly stable in 2026 and edge up in 2027. Risks remain tilted to the upside: stronger-than-expected effects of El Niño, prolonged Black Sea hostilities, export restrictions, higher energy prices, and stronger biofuel demand. Under a scenario of prolonged conflicts and stronger El Niño effects, the food price index would exceed the 2027 baseline by 12 percent and would also surpass its 2022 level.

articles.title: US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

17 Nov 2026

US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook

Household spending power has become more concentrated over time

Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.

Spending has become more reliant on high-income, asset-rich households, buoyed by equity and housing wealth, while lower-income households have struggled. This bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran and will continue to influence spending going forward.

Another trend that will shape spending is the aging of the population. As seniors gradually take up a greater share of the population, where they live and what they buy will matter more for spending growth.

Although high-income metros (e.g., San Jose) and retiree hotspots (e.g., The Villages) feature toward the top of our medium-term spending growth rankings, many of the top performers are still those with the strongest job growth prospects (e.g., Austin), most of which are located in the Sun Belt. By contrast, several Northeast and Midwest metros are forecast to lag, hindered by sluggish employment and population prospects, and in some cases, exposure to the spike in the price of essentials.

Slower-growing but large metros should not be dismissed as offering limited opportunities. The sheer size of cities like Chicago means that lower growth rates can still translate into huge spending level gains.

We expect discretionary categories (e.g., recreation and culture) and health to record the fastest growth over the medium term, supported by high-income households and seniors, respectively.

articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 19 November 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

CJEU rejects Source State loss recalculation for dividend WHT refunds

At a glance: The CJEU ruled that a source State may not require loss-making non-resident companies to systematically recalculate their result under its own tax rules to obtain a dividend withholding tax refund.Taxpayer impact: The judgment may create new refund opportunities for loss-making corporate investors that have suffered dividend WHT, particularly in jurisdictions where refund procedures similarly require losses to be recalculated under domestic tax rules.

CJEU – Free movement of capital – Dividend withholding tax – Loss-making non-resident companies – Refunds – Deferral of taxation – Burden of proof – Tax consolidation – Proportionality

Key findings of the CJEU

The CJEU Grand Chamber in its judgement in case C‑241/25opens in a new tab held that requiring non-resident companies to systematically recalculate their taxable result under the source State’s rules in order to obtain a refund of dividend withholding tax is an additional administrative burden borne only by non-residents and constitutes a restriction on the free movement of capital.In the Court’s view, the restriction could not be justified by the need to preserve the balanced allocation of taxing powers or the coherence of the tax system. The fight against tax fraud and evasion is a legitimate objective, according to the Court, but a systematic recalculation requirement is disproportionate, as it rests on a generalized suspicion of fraud and makes it excessively difficult for a non-resident loss-making company to obtain a refund or deferral.

Background

The plaintiff in case C‑241/25opens in a new tab is a company resident for tax purposes in France and part of a French tax consolidated group. In 2012, it received dividends from Swedish companies (shareholdings below 10 percent) on which Swedish dividend withholding tax was levied.The plaintiff applied for a refund of the withholding tax with respect to a tax year during which it was loss-making, arguing that a comparable Swedish company would not have been taxed on those dividends. According to the plaintiff, the withholding tax therefore constituted an unjustified restriction on the free movement of capital under Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).The Swedish Tax Agency rejected the request on the ground that the claimed loss had not been calculated under Swedish tax rules. On appeal, the Administrative Court in Falun found that the French tax returns filed for the plaintiff and its tax group showed significant tax losses in France for the year concerned. However, in its view, the returns did not demonstrate that the loss was equivalent to the loss a Swedish company would have incurred in the same situation, as the plaintiff had not recalculated the result of the tax group as a whole under Swedish tax rules.At the time of the facts, Swedish law did not provide for a specific deferral or refund mechanism for loss-making non-resident companies (a refund was only available for tax withheld in excess of the applicable treaty rate). Following the CJEU’s judgment in case C-575/17, Sweden introduced rules, effective from January 1, 2020, under which a non-resident legal person established in the EU may apply for a deferral of the dividend tax payment. The deferral is granted for as long as the company records a loss calculated under Swedish tax rules. Where the applicant belongs to a group subject to consolidated taxation in its State of residence, the deferral is calculated by reference to all group members. Although these rules did not apply to the case at hand (which preceded their application), the Swedish Tax Agency required the plaintiff to provide the evidence they prescribe. Sweden has no tax consolidation regime but allows profits and losses to be balanced within a group through intra-group transfers, subject to certain conditions.Against this background, the Swedish Supreme Administrative Court referred the following questions to the CJEU:Is it compatible with Article 63 TFEU for a source State to require a non-resident company claiming to be in a situation objectively comparable to that of a loss-making resident company to prove this by recalculating its taxable result under the source State’s rules for resident companies?If the non-resident company is subject to consolidated taxation, is it compatible with Article 63 TFEU for the source State to require the result of the tax group as a whole to be taken into account in determining comparability?Is the answer to the second question affected if the source State has no tax consolidation regime but does have rules on intra-group transfers that, in certain circumstances, allow profits and losses to be offset within the group?On June 18, 2026, Advocate General Richard de la Tour recommended in his opinionopens in a new tab that the Court find that Article 63 TFEU precludes the rules under dispute – please refer to E-News Issue 232 for details of the AG’s opinion.

CJEU decision

On November 17, 2026, the Grand Chamber of the CJEU delivered its judgment, largely following the AG’s Opinion. The Court examined the three questions together.Existence of a restriction on the free movement of capitalThe CJEU recalled its settled case law, according to which disadvantageous treatment of dividends paid to non-resident companies, compared with the treatment accorded to dividends paid to resident companies, is liable to deter non-resident companies from investing in that Member State and therefore constitutes a restriction on the free movement of capital. Such a difference in treatment is prohibited by Article 63.The Court recalled that a restriction on the free movement of capital may result not only from the substantive conditions for a tax advantage, but also from the evidence non-resident companies must provide to obtain it. The CJEU noted that, under the Swedish practice, loss-making non-resident companies could, in principle, avoid immediate taxation of dividends in the same way as resident companies. However, unlike resident companies, they had to systematically recalculate their taxable result under Swedish tax rules. The Court held that this additional administrative burden, borne only by non-residents, impedes cross-border transactions and constitutes a tax disadvantage.In the Court’s view, the practice was liable to deter non-resident companies from investing in Sweden and therefore represented a restriction on the free movement of capital.ComparabilityThe CJEU recalled its settled case-law under which, once a Member State taxes dividends paid to both resident and non-resident taxpayers, those taxpayers are, in principle, in objectively comparable situations for the purposes of that taxation. Since Sweden taxes dividends from shareholdings below 10 percent regardless of whether they are paid to resident or non-resident companies, the Court found the two categories of taxpayers to be objectively comparable.The CJEU therefore rejected the arguments put forward by Germany and Sweden that resident and non-resident loss-making companies were not in objectively comparable situations.In particular, the Court rejected the Swedish Government’s argument that comparability would require the same rules to apply to the income and expenses of resident and non-resident companies, which could require non-resident companies to adjust their accounts. The CJEU emphasized that the possibility to defer taxation or obtain a refund is generally intended to reflect a taxpayer’s reduced ability to pay where it records an overall loss. A company’s ability to pay is not affected by the fact that it might have recorded a profit under another Member State’s tax rules, and any recalculation concerns a hypothetical situation. In the absence of harmonization, differences between national rules may work in either direction and cannot call comparability into question.The Court also dismissed the objections raised by the German and Spanish Governments against the CJEU’s decisions in cases C-575/17 and C-601/231. The Court clarified that the comparability analysis under its settled case-law is not limited to the taxation of dividends as such, for example their inclusion in the tax base, the applicable tax rate or mechanisms for avoiding economic double taxation.The Court further held that arguments based on the principle of territoriality do not affect the assessment of comparability. Rather, they must be considered when examining whether a difference in treatment can be justified and whether it is proportionate. The case law relied on by Germany concerning the deduction of expenses directly linked to dividend income (C-10/14, C-14/14 and C-17/14) was not considered relevant, as it concerned the tax base rather than the timing of tax payment.Justification and proportionalityHaving found that the rules under dispute represent a restriction on the free movement of capital with respect to objectively comparable situations, the CJEU analyzed and rejected the justifications brought forward by several Member States.The Court first rejected Sweden’s argument that the restriction could be justified by the need to preserve the balanced allocation of taxing powers between Member States. Drawing on its previous case law2, the CJEU reiterated that a system under which loss-making non-resident companies are subject to immediate and final taxation on dividends, while comparable resident companies are effectively taxed only once they become profitable, cannot be justified on this basis. For the same reasons, this justification cannot support a national administrative practice that imposes an additional administrative burden on non-resident companies seeking the tax advantage concerned, where resident companies are not subject to that burden.The Court also rejected Sweden’s argument based on the need to preserve the coherence of the national tax system, noting that such a justification requires a direct link between the tax advantage concerned and a specific tax levy offsetting that advantage. In the Court’s view, Sweden failed to demonstrate the existence of such a link.With respect to Sweden’s plea that the rules under dispute were justified by the need to fight against tax avoidance (risk of shifting shares and dividend rights to a loss-making non-resident), the CJEU recalled that, whilst combating abuse is a legitimate objective, the measures nevertheless need to be proportionate. Based on settled case law, tax authorities are entitled to require taxpayers to provide the evidence necessary to verify that the conditions for a tax advantage are met, including evidence that a non-resident company is genuinely loss-making and that the conditions for a tax deferral or withholding tax refund have not been artificially created. However, the Court stressed that non-resident taxpayers cannot be required to provide documentation complying in every respect with the form and level of detail prescribed by the Member State granting the tax benefit, where the documentation actually provided enables the tax authorities to verify clearly and precisely that the conditions for the benefit are met. Moreover, even assuming that the rules under dispute were capable of achieving the objective of preventing tax fraud and evasion, the CJEU found that the requirement to compute losses under Swedish law is disproportionate to the objective pursued because it is based on a general presumption of fraud and not on evidence suggesting that fraud or an artificial arrangement intended to avoid payment of dividend tax is at issue.Finally, the Court held that its conclusion was not called into question by its decision in case C-446/03 (commonly referred to the “final losses doctrine”), under which foreign losses may, in principle, be taken into account only in exceptional circumstances, namely where they are definitive. The Court distinguished that case law on the basis that the present case did not concern the deduction of foreign losses. Rather, it concerned the point in time at which Sweden, as the Member State in which the dividends originated, may exercise its right to tax income generated within its territory.The Court therefore ruled that the free movement of capital precludes a practice of a Member State’s tax authority requiring a non-resident company that belongs to a tax consolidated group in its State of residence, and that relies on its loss-making position to obtain a refund of withholding tax levied on dividends from a resident company, to prove that position by systematically recalculating its taxable result under the rules applied to resident companies.

ETC Comment:

It is interesting to note that the case was heard by the Grand Chamber at the request of the German Government. The Grand Chamber, composed of 15 judges rather than the three or five judges typically sitting in Chambers, hears cases of particular importance, or when a Member State or an EU institution requests it. According to the text of the decision, the German Government, supported by the Spanish Government, raised objections in principle to the Court’s findings in its judgments in cases C-575/17 and C-601/23 (please refer to Euro Tax Flash 386 and Euro Tax Flash 554, respectively for further details on the two cases). In particular, the Court held in those judgements that loss-making resident and non-resident companies receiving dividends are in objectively comparable situations. The Court ultimately maintained its settled case-law and largely followed the AG’s opinion in finding that the two situations are objectively comparable. The Court further clarified in its decision in the present case that its cited case law cannot be interpreted as relating solely to the taxation of dividends as such (i.e., the inclusion of dividends in the taxable base and the applicable tax rate, or to mechanisms for avoiding chain taxation). Importantly, the judgment clarifies a practical question left open by the earlier rulings: how a non-resident company may demonstrate that it is loss-making. The Court held that the source State cannot systematically require a non-resident company seeking a withholding tax refund to prove its loss-making position by recalculating its taxable result under the tax rules applicable to resident companies.Following C-525/24, which concerned Portuguese evidentiary requirements imposed on non-resident pension funds seeking a dividend withholding tax exemption or refund, the judgment provides another example of administrative practices and evidentiary requirements giving rise to restrictions on the free movement of capital. As Member States align their substantive rules with CJEU case law, such procedural requirements may therefore become increasingly relevant in assessing compliance with EU law.Loss-making EU corporate investors that have suffered dividend withholding tax should review pending and potential refund claims, bearing in mind applicable limitation periods.

Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate to contact KPMG’s EU Tax Centre or, as appropriate, your local KPMG tax advisor.

articles.title: 2027-2029 SSM Supervisory Priorities
articles.text:
On 19 November, the European Central Bank (ECB) published its new SSM Supervisory Priorities for 2027-2029opens in a new tab. This follows established ECB practice of issuing updated priorities each year for the coming three years. The new priorities are based on the ECB’s assessment of the principal risks facing euro area banks and take account of the results of the 2026 Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP)opens in a new tab, published in parallel. (See our analysis of the 2026 SREP results here.)

Banks are resilient, but risks remain

As in previous years, the priorities begin with an overall assessment of the European banking sector. The ECB finds banks to be resilient: capital and liquidity buffers are robust, asset quality is stable and profitability solid. This is despite significant economic headwinds from a challenging geopolitical environment.Nonetheless, the ECB warns of growing challenges facing the European economy and banking system. The geopolitical environment remains highly uncertain. Geopolitical shocks can impact on banks only after some time, depending on exactly how they filter through the various transmission channels to affect the economy, financial markets and individual banks. Similarly, the effects of increasing climate- and nature-related risks may take time to materialize. Meanwhile, high public debt levels could restrict governments’ capacity to cushion the impact of future shock on businesses and households. The ECB therefore emphasized the need for banks to maintain sufficient capital and liquidity buffers to ensure they can absorb future shocks, along with robust internal governance and prudent risk management.The ECB also highlighted the more challenging operational risk environment in which banks must now function. The development of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled hacking tools has intensified the risk of cyber attack. Meanwhile European banks’ growing use of cloud and AI services increases their dependencies on a small number of critical third-party IT providers, many based outside the EU. In this environment, the ECB calls on banks to remain agile in tackling these challenges, while ensuring the continuity of critical services and compliance with regulatory requirements including the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

Supervisory priorities

Against this background, the ECB set out two strategic priorities for 2027-2029. In line with previous years, each addresses a set of prioritised vulnerabilities identified by supervisors. These are summarized in the diagram below:

The latest priorities are broadly similar to those from last year. Geopolitical risk and operational resilience remain key themes. The conflict in the Middle East, and rapid advances in AI over the past twelve months, have only intensified the ECB’s focus on these issues.Within financial resilience, credit risk will remain a priority issue. The ECB will launch a campaign of on-site inspections of banks’ credit underwriting and loan pricing, following up on its 2026 thematic review of underwriting. Supervisors will also probe banks’ exposures to non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), after last year’s surge in redemption requests from various private market funds. In parallel, the ECB will continue its scrutiny of banks’ implementation of CRR III, with targeted reviews of risk-weighted asset calculations, operational risk capital calculations, and synthetic risk transfer securitisations. The ECB will also continue work on banks’ management of climate- and nature-related risks, with a thematic review and targeted OSIs on prudential transition plans and a deep dive into banks’ physical risk capabilities.Under operational resilience, cyber security and ICT risk remain central themes. The ECB will launch two OSI campaigns on cyber security and third-party risk management, alongside targeted reviews of banks’ cloud service provider dependencies and ICT change management, and will conduct threat-led penetration tests, in line with DORA requirements. This will be supported by a system-wide strategy on remediation of outstanding ICT risk findings, to ensure persistent deficiencies are addressed. Building on the ECB’s 2026 work to understand banks’ use of AI, supervisors will conduct pilot off- and on-site reviews of banks’ AI use-cases, governance and risk management. And as a new theme, the ECB will examine banks’ readiness for quantum computing, with a survey of preparations for post-quantum cryptography. Finally, the ECB will continue with its RDARR remediation strategy, backed up with targeted RDARR OSIs, to ensure long-standing shortcomings are effectively addressed.

Implications for banks

ECB supervisory activities will thus affect virtually all areas of banks’ operations in the year ahead. KPMG set out our main recommendations for banks on each area of priority and vulnerability that the ECB has identified.

Priority 1: Banks should strengthen their financial resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial shocksContinue to ensure that geopolitical risks are fully embedded in risk-identification processes, risk-appetite frameworks and internal (ad hoc) scenario analyses and stress testingReview credit underwriting and loan pricing frameworks, taking account of feedback from the ECB’s 2026 thematic review were appropriatePrepare for OSIs on exposures and links to NBFIs, including funding, brokerage and asset-based lendingEvaluate RWA calculations and their compliance with CRR III requirementsPrepare for ECB targeted review operational risk capital requirement calculation under CRR IIIContinue integrating climate- and nature-related risks into their risk management frameworksPrepare for ECB scrutiny of prudential transition plans developed in line with CRD VI requirements, including targeted OSIs on transition plansEnhance integration of physical risk into wider risk frameworks, and prepare for deep dives into physical risk and potential OSIs on water-related risk integration

Priority 2: Banks should strengthen their operational resilience and foster robust ICT capabilitiesContinue to ensure full DORA compliance, with particular focus on third-party risk management and dependencies on cloud providersPrepare for third-party risk management OSIs, targeted review of cloud dependencies and threat-led penetration tests in line with DORA requirementsEnhance cyber security frameworks to ensure effective controls, detection capabilities and incident management systems, and to address previous supervisory findingsReview AI governance and risk management frameworks and ensure these are fully documented in anticipation of potential ECB scrutinyPrepare for ECB survey of quantum computing readiness and scrutiny of plans for migration to post-quantum cryptographyRefresh and continue executing RDARR remediation plans and prepare for targeted OSIs assessing progress against ECB RDARR expectations

As in previous years, the ECB emphasizes its readiness to use its full supervisory toolkit – including administrative penalties – to ensure that supervisory findings are addressed effectively and in a timely manner.KPMG advises banks to analyse the priorities closely, identify areas of greatest challenge (and where forthcoming supervisory activities have already been communicated in supervisory examination plans) and develop action plans in advance. KPMG professionals stand ready to advise and support banks responding to supervisory requirements and in the wider evolution of their business.

articles.title: Equity investment outlook: The great divides - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
We expect the current divergence between technology and non-tech stocks, as well as between hardware and software companies, to continue into 2027

While there is uncertainty over the long-term winners of AI development, earnings growth expectations are positive, offering potential opportunities for investors who can tolerate volatility

We believe equity markets can generate a positive return in 2027, driven by a supportive economic environment and the impact of AI, despite likely short-term fluctuations

The great divides that characterised equity markets in 2026 – first, between tech and non-tech stocks, and second within the technology sector between semiconductor/hardware and software stocks (including hyperscalers) – is likely to persist into 2027.

Returns for technology stocks fell into two phases in 2026: in the first half of the year, we saw a big rally in global semiconductor and hardware stocks, when they rose by 58% (local currency terms).1

This gain was partly mirrored by declines in software companies’ stocks including the hyperscalers, who were the principal customers of the semiconductor/hardware companies, or in those whose business models were themselves at risk from artificial intelligence technologies.

In the second half of the year, waning confidence in the capital expenditure outlook led to a reversal of performance, with semiconductor and hardware stocks declining 23%, while software stocks recovered their losses, rising 9%.2

Through all of this, non-tech stocks marched steadily higher (see Exhibit 1).

Growth despite earnings uncertainty

We expect these divides to persist, but the key question is, which pattern we will see?

Part of the high levels of volatility witnessed recently in tech stocks stems from the extreme uncertainty around how AI will develop, its impact on society, the economy and corporate profits. Views on who the winners and losers will be change almost daily with periodic ‘out of the blue’ surprises (like the launch of Chinese start-up DeepSeek’s AI model in January 2025) to shake things up even more.

This uncertainty can be seen in the big increase in the standard deviation of earnings estimates for tech stocks – showing how much analysts’ forecasts differ from one another. It has increased more than five times over the last two years, while for non-tech stocks it has been steady (see Exhibit 2).

Given the wide range of forecasted profits, any marginal news can have a big impact on stock prices. This dynamic is likely to remain part of the AI investment universe.

As for the pattern we may see next year, we anticipate semiconductor and hardware stocks posting good returns given the still very high levels of planned capital expenditures.

The performance of software stocks, including the hyperscalers, is harder to predict. There is intense competition between them, and it is unlikely all the investments being made today will generate a sufficient and timely return on investment.

Revenue generation, however, is increasing as companies learn how to incorporate AI into their operations and see meaningful productivity gains. Consumers, too, may be willing to pay more in the future for the benefits AI tools can provide.

Looking beyond volatility

Investors should not lose sight of the medium-term opportunity. It is essentially a question of how fast technology sector earnings will grow. Consensus estimates are for nearly 90% earnings growth over the next two years.

Even if it turns out to be ‘only’ 70%, that would still imply strong stock appreciation, particularly as valuations are currently below average. The z-score of the forward price-to-earnings ratio – which indicates how far valuations sit below their historical average – is around -0.2 for the Nasdaq 100 index and -1.4 for emerging market technology stocks. For all the volatility over the last few months, the earnings trajectory remains positive.

This dynamic, though, of high potential returns alongside high volatility, presents a challenge to investors who want to participate in the gains but are concerned by the wide swings in stock prices.

The slices of the AI ‘pie’ will continue to expand and shrink (and in some cases disappear). Some of the challenges ahead include higher financing costs, increasing competition (notably from China), and energy supply constraints. Nonetheless, we believe the pie will continue to grow over time. An investor who can accept the volatility may find there is potential for returns above those of the broad market over the medium term.

At the same time, the high volatility offers significant potential opportunities to portfolio managers who are able to identify the winners and avoid the losers.

The wider market

Of course, few investors would dedicate their entire portfolio to AI; the technology sector still only represents about 40% of the MSCI All Country World Index by market capitalisation.

Returns for the other sectors have been steadily positive, as Exhibit 1 illustrates. This has been driven by strong growth in the US and lower, but still steady, growth in Europe. The most recent earnings season saw double digit gains across many of the major equity indices and forecasts for next year are also good (18% for MSCI ACWI). We foresee this supportive economic environment continuing, even with interest rates likely to be higher on average in 2027 than in 2026, in our view.

The opportunity, however, may be in identifying those companies which are able to incorporate AI into their operations and accelerate profit growth. This is where the US may have an advantage.

To the degree that AI allows companies to reduce labour costs, US companies are among the quickest to adjust the size of their workforce, in contrast to those in Europe and Japan. This dynamic has its own implications for consumer demand depending on how quickly displaced workers move into new roles, but currently the US adult unemployment rate remains low and steady.

From a market perspective, the superior returns of the Russell Value index compared to other indices with a similar sector composition is perhaps evidence already of this phenomenon.

The potential for European companies may be best among those who are able to monetise the significant amount of funds behind the European strategic autonomy initiative in sectors such as defence and infrastructure.

The positive global macroeconomic outlook bodes well for equity returns in 2027. AI is likely to continue to play an outsized role in equity returns, with different dynamics between software companies and hyperscalers relative to semiconductor and hardware manufacturers. The medium-term outlook is positive, but it is unlikely to be a smooth path. Meanwhile, we expect non-tech sectors to see steady growth, with upside potential in those companies who are best able to leverage the AI revolution.

[1] Source: FactSet, BNP Asset Management.

[2] As of 5 November 2026.

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing

The Shape Of Export Controls To Come

AJ Cortese, Laila Khawaja
16 Nov 2026

For the past four years, Washington policymakers and the US AI industry have been split over a big question. Should the US tightly restrict China’s access to advanced computing capacity, in order to solidify its lead in the AI race? Or should it sell more chips and equipment to China, in order to lock China into dependence on US hardware, and support open-weight AI models? The sudden fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, the biggest commercial champion of diffusion, has shifted power in Washington to the restrictionists. A bipartisan majority now supports more export controls, both to contain China and to rein in what many see as the corruption that has tainted Trump’s tech policies. Today’s China Tech Brief examines what is on the menu.

Gavekal Technologies: Chips

The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber
12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal looks sure to topple CEO Jensen Huang and put the company on a very rocky course for a few months. The headlines have focused on the romantic and spy stories, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere. The big risk for Huang and Nvidia is that they might be found guilty of breaking US export control rules by colluding in the illegal transshipment of AI chips from Singapore to China. The Chinese AI industry, which already has a tough time getting enough advanced chips, could soon find it even tougher, as there is a good chance that the US Congress will soon act to tighten up export controls.

More research

Permitting Reform’s Big Chance

10 Nov 2026

Efforts to clean up the US’s sclerotic system for approving energy infrastructure have failed twice before. The third time may be the charm, as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or BAAJA cleared its first procedural hurdle in the Senate on Monday. If it passes despite last-ditch opposition by environmental groups, it will massively boost America’s ability to scale up its electricity grid, on a three to-five year horizon. This will remove an important constraint on both AI data centers and manufacturing.

How Wuxi AppTec Stayed Sanction-Proof

2 Nov 2026

China’s two “Wuxi” biotech firms—AppTec and Biologics—are key partners for the US pharmaceutical industry, as contract developers and manufacturers of hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds. Washington lawmakers are increasingly uneasy about rising American reliance on the Wuxi firms. But their efforts to curb Wuxi’s access to the US market have been blocked, thanks to strong lobbying by the US pharma and biotech industries.

Power Lessons From China

26 Oct 2026

The US data center boom is facing a power crunch. So far, delays and cancellations due to electricity shortages have been sporadic but by some point in 2028, they could force a significant slowdown in data center construction. It will be important for the US to figure out how to better use batteries and distributed renewables generation to make power demand and supply more flexible. China is already ahead in this effort.

The State Of Chinese AI

19 Oct 2026

The AI world suffered tremors last week, as doubts began to surface about the frontier labs’ revenue growth and the rising amount of high-priced debt used to finance the US’s data center building binge. The risks raise a question: when and if the American AI bubble pops, can China race ahead? Probably not.

Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. While Chinese nuclear firms have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter.

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.
